Every step of the warm-up you built. Click one to jump to it.

title: Vocal Warm-up
text:
How it works

Body first, then breath, then voice. Stretches loosen the neck, shoulders, jaw and ribs, which all pull on the larynx. Breathing steps wake up the low, wide breath. The singing starts on hums and lip trills (semi-occluded sounds that are easy on the folds) and only then opens onto vowels, wider leaps and the top of the range.
The piano plays the starting chord, then the pattern with you, then moves up a half step. It climbs from the low middle of your voice to a comfortable top (not your highest note) and comes back down. Set Range if it sits too high or low.
The band plays two short grooves: one to sing a scale over as the key climbs, and a slow one to hum over as a cool-down.
Gentle routines stay lower, shorter and softer; Performing soon adds agility and a wider top, and ends ready rather than cooled down.
Fun swaps in sound-effect sirens, a countdown shake, tongue twisters (spoken, then sung) and bouncy “pizza” staccatos. The English twister avoids r/l, f/p, v/b, z/j and th, which are hard for speakers of Korean and some other languages, and there is one in Japanese and one in Korean, so other students get to lead.







Warning



Stop if anything hurts, tickles or feels tight. Warm-ups should feel easy: if a note strains, let the pattern go by and come back on the way down. Sip water between steps.

title: Scale Patterns
text:
On your instrument

The instrument notes are general teaching advice, not yet checked against a source; more on each band instrument is coming.

title: Scale Patterns
text:
How it works

Key and spelling. Every note takes its letter from the scale’s own degrees, so G♯ harmonic minor has its F𝄪 and the blues scale has both the ♭5 and the 5. The key signature is the scale’s mode on the tonic (Dorian on D: no sharps or flats); harmonic and melodic minor use the natural minor’s, as printed scale books do. Enharmonic keys (F♯ / G♭) are spelled with the fewer accidentals, and for a transposing instrument with the fewer in the key you read.
Transposing instruments read written pitch (B♭ instruments a step up, E♭ alto a sixth up, horn in F a fifth up, guitar and bass an octave up); playback sounds at concert pitch.
Patterns move up the scale one step at a time, then down. “Mirror” turns the figure upside down on the way down (Hanon’s way); off, the same shape moves down (the jazz way, so an enclosure still lands on its target from both sides).
Swing is written as straight eighths; the playback swings them, and with the band the band’s own swing feel plays.
Hanon. Nos. 1–20 (The Virtuoso Pianist, Part I) are played note for note, with Hanon’s fingering, from the Mutopia Project’s edition (after Schirmer, 1900), read by a script. They keep Hanon’s two octaves; on another scale the same degrees are used, and on a scale that isn’t seven notes the figure changes shape.

title: Notation Rules
text:
What the entry pages do with the keys you play: which notes are chords and which melody, where each one lands on the bars, how long it is written, how it is spelled. Part 1 runs the engine on a take (a preset, or the log the Chord Entry page keeps) and shows what every rule decided; change a setting and see what it would have written. Part 2 is the rules themselves, with the numbers the engine really uses.

  
    1. Try it
    
      Start from
      Load the last take from Chord Entry
    
    A take log is what the Chord Entry page copies with Copy the take log: every key and pedal event with its time, and the settings. Paste one here and Load it. The settings below then work on the same playing, so you can see what a different rule setting would have written.
    
    Load this logDownload the log
    

    
      EntryChordsMelodyChords and melody (split)
      Key
      Meter4/43/46/812/82/45/4
      Bars
      Tempo
      SwingSwung (by the tempo)StraightAs in the log
      Shortest noteEighthSixteenth
    
    
       Notes struck together are written as a chord
      Together within (ms)
      A chord closes after (ms)
      Snap chords toBarHalf barBeatEighth note
      Melody from
       Slash chords
    
    
      BeamsWithin a beatWithin half a barNone
      SyncopationAs playedTied across the middle of the barTied across every beat
      Short detached notesNote and restStaccato note
      Long notes before a restThe simplest nearby lengthAs released
      TripletsNeverWhere the playing fits
      Notes before bar 1Leave them outWrite them (a pickup bar)
      Grace notes within (ms)
    

    What did I mean?
    
    What was written
    
    
    The take against the bars
    
    a chord's notes as playeda melody note as playedthe melody as writtena chord as placedthe pedal held

    Bars
    Melody notes, one by one
    Chords, one by one
    Pedal
    Copy a report of this run
    The report holds the log, the settings as set here, what was written and every table above. It is everything needed to run the same take again, so it is the thing to send when a take comes out wrong.
  

  
    2. The rules
    In the order the engine applies them. Each rule says what it does, the number it uses (the numbers are read from the engine, not typed here) and where to see it in the tables above. Chords and melody are the same take: the keys you play are sorted into one or the other first (rule 1), and then each follows its own rules.

    Time
    T1The clock: beats from the first downbeat
      Every key and pedal event carries a time in milliseconds from the first downbeat after the count-in (negative in the count-in). A beat is 60 / tempo seconds; in 6/8, 9/8 and 12/8 a beat is a dotted quarter, as the band counts it. On a click the page subtracts the sound card's output latency, and the Timing offset or Nudge field moves everything by the milliseconds you give it (a positive number is earlier).
      Seen in: the log's events, and the played column of the note and chord tables.
    T2The bars, and how the pedal changes them
      The take starts with the meter chosen and that many bars. The beat never moves; only where bars begin does. Hold the pedal (MIDI controller ) across two downbeats and the bars from the first of them on are as long as the gap between them, in whole beats. Notes within  beats count as one strike (a chord is one downbeat); only the first and last strike while the pedal is down are used. The gap and the first downbeat are rounded to whole beats.
      A change that falls inside a bar cuts that bar short (a 2/4 bar in a 4/4 tune). A change less than one beat after a bar line moves back to the bar line. In compound meters the new length is counted in dotted quarters, so three beats make 9/8. A second change must come after the first. Over chords already entered the bars are fixed and the pedal is ignored.
      Seen in: the Bars table and the Pedal table (its strikes are the beats it used).
    T3Swing: a swung off-beat is put back on the even grid
      When the playing is read as swung, the second eighth of each beat is taken to sit late: at a fraction s of the beat (0.5 would be straight). s comes from the tempo: 0.68 − 0.08 × clamp((bpm − 100)/120) − 0.05 × clamp((bpm − 220)/80), so it is about 0.68 at a ballad tempo and 0.60 near 220. A time that far into the beat is moved back to the half beat (unswing) before it is rounded to the grid. This is why swung eighths come out as plain eighth notes, and the band swings them again when it plays them. Bars in compound meters are always read straight. Chords are unswung the same way before they snap to the grid.
      Seen in: unswung in the note table (units from the first bar, before rounding) and the Swing setting above.
    T5Pickups: notes before the first bar
      A note (or chord) struck up to  of a beat before the first downbeat is taken as on it. Struck earlier than that, in the count-in, it is dropped, unless Notes before bar 1: Write them is on: then the earliest such note sets the length of a short bar in front of bar 1, rounded up to whole beats (never longer than the count-in), and everything is written in it, with no meter mark. The chart then reads it as a pickup (anacrusis). A chart that already has a pickup bar uses its length.
      On the Backing Track page, when the take starts at a later bar (a section, or "Start at bar"), the count-in is the bar before the one recorded from, so notes played in it are written at the end of that bar: a pickup into a verse goes at the end of the interlude before it. Only at the very start of the tune does a pickup get a short bar of its own.
      Seen in: the Bars table (a short first bar), the note table (bar 1 is the pickup) and the roll (the count-in is to the left of the first line).
    T4The grid: rounded to the nearest eighth or sixteenth
      A melody note's start is rounded to the nearest eighth note (or sixteenth, if chosen); the unit is an eighth, so a beat is 2 units in x/4 and 3 in compound meters. A note struck up to  of a beat before the first downbeat is moved onto it; one struck earlier than that is dropped. A note that rounds to the same spot as the next one is dropped and the later one stays. A note after the last bar is dropped. Chords snap by the Snap setting instead (a bar, half bar, beat or eighth).
      Seen in: on grid and result in the note table.

    Notes
    N1Which keys are chords and which are melody
      In a chords take every key goes to the chord reader; in a melody take every key goes to the melody line. In a split take the keys below the split key are chords and the split key and those above it are melody. The pedal strikes count notes from either side.
      Seen in: the Entry and Melody-from settings; the roll shows chord notes in orange and melody notes in teal.
    N2Notes struck together
      Melody notes struck within  ms of the first of them are one strike. By default only the highest is written and the others are left out; with Notes struck together are written as a chord all of them are written as an ABC chord, [CEG], with one length. A note struck later than that window is a new note.
      Seen in: left out in the note table, and the notes column (several pitches are one strike).
    N3One note at a time
      The line is one voice: a new note ends the one before it, even if you are still holding it.
    N4How long a note is written
      A note lasts until the next note starts (it is written legato), unless the gap between its release and the next start is  of an eighth or more: then it is written as released (rounded to the grid) and a rest follows. The last note is written to its release. A note is never shorter than one grid step. A note cannot run past the next note or the last bar line.
      So a line played short and detached, as swing is, is written with full note values and no rests unless a gap is clear.
      Where a rest does follow a note longer than an eighth (the end of a phrase), the moment you let go is not much of a guide: with Long notes before a rest: The simplest nearby length (the default) the note ends wherever, near the release, the note and the rest after it are simplest to write. The end may move up to  of the note's length (at least one grid step, at most a beat). The candidates are scored by the written symbols of the note and the rest (a dotted one counts one and a half), an end that is off the beat, and the distance moved; holding the note right on to the next one, losing a rest that was played, costs  more. So a quarter let go a sixteenth early is a quarter, not a dotted eighth and a sixteenth rest, while a dotted quarter and a clear eighth rest stay as played. As released writes the release rounded to the grid.
      Seen in: length in the note table says which case applied and the gap it measured.
    N5Bar lines, chord changes and ties
      A note that runs over a bar line is split and tied. A note that runs over a chord change is split at the change and tied, so each chord symbol sits above the note under it. Only lengths that are written as one note are used:  grid steps (a dotted note is 3 or 6); any other length is split into those and tied.
    N6Spelling: which letter and which accidental
      Notes of the key are spelled as the key spells them. A note outside the key takes whichever of its sharp and flat spellings is nearer the middle of the key on the line of fifths (centre + ); when they are equally near, the flat. So in C: E♭, A♭, B♭, F♯ and D♭; in F: G♭ (not F♯) and A♭.
      An accidental is written only where it differs from the key signature or from what the same letter in the same octave had earlier in that bar. Octaves: middle C is C, the C above it c, then c'; below, C,.

    N7Detached notes: staccato
      By default a short note followed by a rest is written as the note and the rest (an eighth and an eighth rest). With Short detached notes: Staccato note, a note followed by a rest exactly as long as itself, where the two together make a length that can be written, is written as one staccato note of both: eighths with eighth rests become staccato quarters. A staccato note is played by the band at half its length. (Triplet notes are not changed.)
      Seen in: length in the note table ("a note and an equal rest are written as a staccato note of both").
    N8Triplets
      Off by default. When on, each beat of a simple meter whose beat is two units (2/4, 3/4, 4/4, …; not 6/8 and the like, where the beat is already three) is read as three even parts if its notes fit thirds of the beat better than the eighth-note grid by more than  of a beat (summed over the beat's onsets). The check is made on the raw time (a swung off-beat is compared after the swing is taken out, so a swung pair is not mistaken for a triplet; the same pair read as straight is). A beat read as triplets is written under a bracket: three notes (3CDE, or a quarter and an eighth (3:2:2C2D. Only whole beats are triplets (no quarter-note triplets over two beats, no sixteenth sextuplets yet).
      Seen in: triplet in the note table gives the two numbers compared.
    N9Grace notes
      Off by default. When on, a note whose next note starts within the chosen milliseconds (never more than  of a beat, a thirty-second note) is not a note of its own but a slashed grace note of the next one: {/D}E. A run of such notes is all grace notes of the first note after them. This is for the quick note into a blue note; it is why a note that was struck first but let go before the next began is not folded into a chord (rule N2 only joins notes that are still held together). The band does not play grace notes back.
      Seen in: graces in the note table.
    N10Parallel thirds and other double stops
      Above the split key (or in a melody take) two notes struck together are one melody note. With Notes struck together are written as a chord on, both are written in one bracket ([CE], [DF], …) with one length, tied as a pair; with it off only the top one is written. They never reach the chord reader, so they are not named as a chord. Notes of the pair that are struck slightly apart still count as together if they are inside the Together-within window and the first is still held when the second arrives.

    Chords
    C1When a chord is finished
      A chord is closed  ms after its first note. Keys still held from the chord before count as part of the next one, unless three or more new keys arrived. It is timed at its first note.
      Seen in: the Chords table, notes played.
    C2Naming a chord
      Every note played must be accounted for by the chord (the Director page, by contrast, accepts extra notes). Every pitch class played is tried as the root against the table below. A reading in which every note is a chord tone wins; a perfect fifth may be left out of any chord of four or more notes. If two readings fit equally (C6 and Am7), the lowest note played decides; then the reading whose root is nearer the key; then the order in the table. If nothing fits exactly, the closest match is written and the chord is marked as a guess. Two or more different notes are needed. Inversions are written as plain chords unless Slash chords is on (C with E at the bottom is then C/E).
      Seen in: candidates in the Chords table: the five best readings, best first.
      
    C3Where a chord goes
      A chord is timed at its first note. Its position in the bar is unswung (T3), then moved to the nearest point of the Snap setting. A chord struck up to  of a beat before the first downbeat goes on it. The chord sits there until the next one.

    Writing it down
    W2Beams
      In ABC a space between notes breaks a beam, so the notation joins eighth notes (and shorter) by writing them without a space: within a beat by default, or within half a bar (four eighths in 4/4; three in 6/8 and the other compound meters are a beat already) with Beams: Within half a bar, or not at all. A rest, a note longer than an eighth, a chord change that starts a new group, or a triplet bracket ends a beam; a triplet is beamed under its own bracket.
    W3Syncopation: ties across the beat
      Jazz writes a quarter note on the “and” of 2 as one quarter. Classical notation writes it as two tied eighths. Syncopation: Tied across the middle of the bar splits a note that starts after the first beat and runs over the middle of the bar (beat 3 in 4/4; a half note on beat 2 too). Tied across every beat also splits a note that starts off the beat and runs over any beat. A note that starts on a beat, or on the bar's first beat, keeps its length. Only the written ABC changes (the band hears the same notes).
    W1The ABC
      Bars of four to a line (the melody bars are written with the beams and ties above); M: is the opening meter and a bar of another meter gets [M:n/d] in front of it. The unit is a quarter note when nothing in an x/4 take sits between the beats, else an eighth, else a sixteenth when sixteenths were used. Chord symbols are quoted above the note or rest at their position. Rests fill what is left.

title: IPA Chart for Singers
text: The International Phonetic Alphabet gives one symbol to each sound, so a singer can read the same sounds in any language. Click a symbol for a description and reference words in English (General American and RP), Hindi, Marathi, German, French, Korean and Japanese. A language is left blank where it does not have the sound.

title: IPA Chart for Singers
text:
Find and filter



Tick languages to dim every symbol that none of them uses, and to list only those languages in the detail panel. Search matches symbols, descriptive names, words, romanisations and glosses.

title: IPA Chart for Singers
text:
Vowels
Tongue height runs down the page (close to open) and tongue position across it (front, central, back). Drag anywhere on the chart, away from the symbols, to hear a synthesised vowel glide through the space: up and down moves the first formant, across moves the second. Rounding, voice and pitch sit below the chart; Hold keeps the sound going so you can click symbols to glide between them. The chart also takes arrow keys and Space. What the synthesiser is doing, and what F1 and F2 mean: Formants: what makes a vowel.

title: IPA Chart for Singers
text:
Notes for singers


How classical diction uses IPA
A transcription records sounds, not spelling. Coaches and diction books write a song’s text in IPA so everyone sings the same vowels and consonants, then add stress, linking and the places where a sung line differs from speech. Learn the sounds once and you can read the transcription for any language you meet.


Pure vowels
Most sung languages here are built on steady vowels (Italian, German, French, Japanese, Hindi, Marathi, Korean). In English, [eɪ], [oʊ] and [aɪ] are diphthongs: sing the first element for nearly the whole note and add the second at the very end. Italianate five-vowel thinking ([a e i o u], with open and closed e and o) is a good basis for all of them.


English
General American and RP differ most in r (after vowels), in the vowels of bath, lot and thought, and in the flap [ɾ] of water. Unstressed syllables have schwa in speech, but singers often give them a clearer vowel on long notes. Aspiration of initial p, t, k is a strong cue for audibility.


German
Final voiced stops are voiceless (Tag [taːk]). Two ch sounds: [ç] after front vowels and l, n, r; [x] after a, o, u, au. Vowel length is meaningful, and the stage r is the tongue-tip trill [r] while everyday speech uses [ʁ]. Vowel-initial stressed syllables begin with a light glottal onset [ʔ].


French
No diphthongs and no aspiration. Four nasal vowels, front rounded vowels [y ø œ], and the mute e, which is pronounced when sung. Liaison and enchaînement link words, and French syllables are even in stress.


Hindi and Marathi
Keep dental (त द) and retroflex (ट ड) apart, and learn the four-way contrast (p, pʰ, b, bʱ). Hindi drops the inherent a at the end of words, and sometimes inside them; sung text may restore it. Marathi has the extra affricates [t͡s d͡z] and the retroflex lateral [ɭ].


Korean
Three kinds of stop: lax, tense and aspirated. Lax stops are voiced between vowels. Tense and aspirated stops raise the pitch of the following vowel in speech. Final stops are unreleased.


Japanese
Five vowels, with [ɯ̟ᵝ] spread-lip rather than rounded. Long vowels, double consonants and moraic ん count as extra time. Vowels i and u are often devoiced between voiceless consonants in speech. Japanese [ɾ] is a single tap.

title: IPA Chart for Singers
text:
Language notes


About the examples
Examples use broad transcription of standard forms: General American and RP, Standard Hindi, Standard Marathi, Standard German, Metropolitan French, Seoul Korean and Tokyo Japanese. Individual speakers, regions and poetic or sung styles differ. For Devanagari, Hangul and kana the highlighted piece is the written syllable containing the sound (Devanagari and Hangul write a syllable as a unit); romanisation is a transliteration, not IPA. Check anything you will perform with a native speaker or diction coach.


Hindi and Marathi
Both use the Devanagari script. Hindi has the Persian-Arabic sounds [f z x ɣ q] in loanwords, shown with a dot (nuqta) under the letter; many speakers replace them with native sounds. Marathi usually does not write the nuqta; its loan sounds are often assimilated. Marathi च and ज are [t͡s d͡z] before a, ā, u, o, and [t͡ʃ d͡ʒ] before i, e.


Korean
Hangul writes sounds in syllable blocks. The Korean vowel ㅡ is [ɯ], and ㅓ [ʌ]. Final consonants are pronounced differently from initial ones.


Japanese
Written in kana and kanji; the examples give kana. The し and ち sounds are alveolo-palatal ([ɕ], [t͡ɕ]) and ふ is [ɸɯ̟ᵝ].


Symbols without examples
Some symbols (for example ɨ, ʉ, ɘ, ɵ, ɤ, ɞ, ɶ) are on the chart but are not separate sounds in any of the seven languages here. They are shown dashed and have no reference words.

title: Tune Your Guitar by Ear
text:
Pick a way to tune, then follow the steps one string at a time. The fretboard shows where to put your fingers; click any
spot on it to hear that note. No guitar knowledge needed: strings are numbered 6 (the thickest, nearest your chin) to 1 (the thinnest),
and frets are counted from the end where the tuning pegs are.

Your ear is the tuner. Every method here asks you to listen: to two notes agreeing, to a wobble slowing
down, to a chord sounding sweet. The microphone reading is there to check your ear, not to replace it. With Ear first ticked it stays
blurred until you've said what you hear. Start that habit today: musicians who only tune by looking at a screen can't hear when they've drifted
out of tune halfway through a song.

  Tips that apply to every method
  
    Tune up to the note. If a string is sharp, go below the note and come back up. The string then holds its pitch better.
    Turn while the string rings. Small turns. You hear the change happen.
    Hum or sing the note. If you can sing the reference and then sing the string, your ear is doing the work.
    Finish with a chord. Every method ends at your ear: strum something and adjust any string that sounds sour.
    New strings stretch and go flat for a day or two. Tune, play, tune again.
  
  Why there are several methods, and what each gets wrong: Tuning 1: your ear and beats,
  Tuning 2: fifth-fret, harmonics, octaves,
  Tuning 3: tuners and their limits. Something always out however you tune?
  The Setup Check finds out whether the guitar needs an adjustment.

title: Guitar Input Check
text:
How it listens
When the sound gets suddenly louder (a pick or strum), the page waits 80 ms for the attack to pass, takes the next 16,384 samples, and looks for the notes whose harmonics carry the most energy, one at a time. A single note is graded on the exact note, octave included. A chord is graded the way a MIDI chord is: every pitch class asked for, the right bass, and nothing else.
This is the basic version of the plan in scripts/guitar-di/GUITAR-IN.md. Its accuracy numbers come from synthetic plucked strings (about 8 chords in 10 read exactly), not yet from a real guitar. If it gets one wrong, re-strum and let it ring.

text:
Fast passages get learned in small pieces. Cut the passage into chunks, play each one at a tempo you can
  play clean, then link them together and bring the tempo up.

      Keys, pedals and what "clean" means
      Space play / stop, M listen, Y clean, N not yet, ← → steps.
      "Clean" means right notes, right rhythm, no tension.
      Pedals: Clean is the top key of an 88-key keyboard (C8) and Not yet the bottom key (A0). Change them, or bind a
      footswitch, with MIDI buttons in the top bar.
      In Quick, saying nothing counts as clean, so one pedal (Not yet) is all you need.
      With the click going round, answer any time during the pass or in the clicks after it. A missed stretch try costs
      nothing; a missed working try drops the tempo a step.
    
  

  
    Best clean tempo for each step
    
    Clear
    Kept in this browser for this passage. Click a step to go to it.
  

  
    For teachers: how it works
    
      Quick. Chunks link forwards; the click never stops; each clean pass is about a fifth of the way from 70% of the target to the
      target, a slip a step back. Saying nothing is a clean pass, so a student needs only to own up to the misses.
      Chunks. Small enough to play clean on the first or second try. Ending on the next chunk's first note practises the joins.
      Linking. Forwards: each new chunk alone, then with the one before, then everything so far. Backwards does the same from the end,
      so the end of the passage gets the most practice.
      Changing tempos (Full control). Each step cycles a working try, a slow try (two steps under), a working try, and a stretch (a step over).
      Clean working tries in a row raise the tempo a step; a clean stretch becomes the new working tempo. A linked step starts a little under the
      slowest of its chunks' best.
      Keyboard grading. With a MIDI keyboard each pass is checked note by note: the right key, within about a third of the shortest
      note's length (60–140 ms) of the click; a missed, wrong or extra note is not clean. A Clean / Not yet press overrides it.
      Rhythm variants. Long–short and short–long reshape pairs of equal notes, so each note gets a turn to be the long one.

When one of them is chosen above, its amp is listed under the EQ, stage by stage in the order the sound passes through: Input gain is how hard the amp is hit, Drive how much it distorts, Output level makes up the loudness afterwards. The EQ comes after the amp.
      Five bands for each sound, remembered on this computer. Every band can be a bell (boost or cut around a frequency), a shelf (everything below or above it), or a cut (low cut removes what is below the frequency, high cut what is above; the amount does not apply). Width is how narrow the band is: low is broad, high is narrow. The settings belong to the sound, so the jazz guitar keeps its tone whatever tune or style is loaded.
      
    
    
      Drum kit mix

      Info
    Each fader is on top of the Drums volume. The ride and crash start low because the sampled cymbals ring loudly; Reset faders returns to those settings.
    
    
    
      Outputs (mixing desk)
      
      Info
      With a mixing desk that is also a USB audio interface (a Behringer X32 with its USB card shows the computer 32 channels), each instrument can arrive on a channel strip of its own, and the desk does the EQ, compression, reverb and panning, or places the instruments around the room through its buses and matrices. Connect the desk by USB, choose it as the Device here (Chrome and Edge) or as the computer's sound output, pick "One channel per instrument" and press Check channels. On the desk, set the channel inputs to the USB card. The parts leave dry and mono; channels 1–2 can still carry the usual stereo mix, for headphones or a recording. A home receiver needs HDMI for this (optical carries only stereo), and Bluetooth is always stereo.

    The loop controls are in the Play panel at the top. Click a bar on the chart to start there, then press L and click the bar the loop should end on; L again turns the loop off and on. An end bar before the start loops over the end of the form (10 to 2 plays 10, 11, 12, 1, 2). With the loop on, a click moves its end and Shift-click moves its start. The second tempo box alternates with the first: 8 then -3 goes up 8, back 3, up 8, back 3. Stopping returns to the tempo you set.
    
  

  
    Recording
    Open the song file from Timestamp Notes (or a bar map) and the recording that goes with it. Clicking a bar on the chart then moves the recording there, and the band can follow the recording’s own tempo, bar by bar.

    A setup is the changes (in their key and meter) with the tempo, style and every band, mixer and loop setting. Setups are kept in this browser on this device, and they also appear at the bottom of the Changes menu. Download all saves them as a file you can import on another device. To make one a built-in for everybody, press Show JSON for the defaults and send that text to whoever maintains the site: it is pasted into apps/shared/band/presets.js.

    Info
    While the band plays, this shows the chorus you are about to hear: it is drawn before the chorus starts (during the count-in for the first one, and during the last bar of each chorus for the next) and stays while that chorus plays. Change a band setting and the bars not yet played are written again. With "Each repeat" tempo steps on, it shows the last chorus played instead. The piano is on a grand staff, with the bass clef holding what the left hand plays. Swung eighths are written as plain eighths; in 6/8 and 12/8 each beat is three written eighths. The bass is written an octave above where it sounds, and note lengths are rounded to eighths.

    Info
    Press Record melody and play one note at a time along with the band. It plays the changes from the start bar with the count-in, and writes the first chorus. Bars that repeat in the changes (repeat signs, a section that comes round again) take the first time through. Only the bars you played are replaced, so you can record a section at a time by setting the start bar. A swung line is written as plain eighth notes; the band swings them when it plays the melody back. The melody follows the bar numbers: it is dropped if the number of bars changes, and moves with the Key menu. The ABC you edit above does not change; Copy the ABC with the melody, or Download it, to keep the notes.

    Edit the changes (ABC)
    Enter chords or voicings from a keyboard
    Paste ChordPro
      
      Use these chords
      Each line of words is a bar per chord, as on the Notation page; a line of bars ([G] | [C] [D] |) is played as written. {start_of_verse}, {start_of_chorus} or {c: Bridge} start sections; {time:}, {key:}, {tempo:} and {title:} are read. Chords over words copied from Ultimate Guitar work too. The result replaces the ABC below.
      
    
    
    Info
    The chord symbols in quotes are what the band reads. Where a symbol sits in the bar sets the beat it lands on, so "Cm7"z2 "F7"z2 gives each chord two beats. The rests only fill out the bar. A line such as P:Verse or P:Chorus names the section that starts at the next bar: the drummer fills into each one, a section called Chorus is played up, and the Sections menu by the Play button can hold each section until you press Next. "^fill" (or "^small fill", "^big fill") in a bar makes the drummer fill at the end of it, and "^stop" makes it a stop-time bar; a line %%style bossa nova under a P: line plays that section in another style from the Style menu, and single parts can follow it, as in %%style Swing; voicing drop2; rhythm charleston; bass two (in a bar, "^style bossa nova" does the same from there to the next section); the Fill on bar and Stop on bar boxes write these for you. The M: line sets the meter: the band plays 3/4 as a jazz waltz and counts 6/8 and 12/8 in dotted quarters.

title: Accompaniment Styles
text:
These patterns are built into the accompaniment engine and can be selected on any tune page.
    Each style adapts automatically to the tune's meter and chord chart.
    Styles marked any meter work in 2/4, 3/4, 4/4, and 6/8; fixed-meter styles
    fall back to block chords when the meter doesn't match. Examples shown in C major at 110 bpm.
  

  
    By genre
    By instrument
    Backing Track band
  

  

  
  

    
      Jazz
      

        
          
            Jazz Charleston
            charleston
            4/4
            ▶
          
          
          Chord on beat 1 and the and-of-2, leaving beats 3 and 4 open. Named for the 1920s dance; the defining syncopation of early jazz and Swing Era big-band writing.
          
            Jazz
            Swing
            Piano
            Full band
          
        

        
          
            Jazz waltz
            jazzwaltz
            3/4
            ▶
          
          
          Swung bass on beat 1, ride-cymbal implied chord on beat 3. The feel of bebop and post-bop piano trios — Evans, Peterson, Monk in 3/4.
          
            Jazz
            Bebop
            Piano trio
          
        

        
          
            Walking bass
            walk
            4/4
            ▶
          
          
          Bass moves in step-wise quarter notes through chord tones and approach notes; right-hand comping on beats 2 and 4 (Charleston rhythm). The defining texture of jazz trio and big-band rhythm-section playing from bebop onward.
          
            Jazz
            Bebop
            Piano
            Bass
          
        

      
    

    
      Latin
      

        
          
            Bossa nova
            bossa
            4/4
            ▶
          
          
          Tresillo-derived bass pattern with chords on the off-beats; ride cymbal and side-stick percussion. Rooted in the guitar style of João Gilberto and the samba-jazz fusion of late-1950s Rio.
          
            Latin
            Jazz
            Brazilian
            Guitar
            Piano
          
        

        
          
            Tango
            tango
            4/4
            ▶
          
          
          Habanera rhythmic cell in the bass (long–short–short–long) with syncopated chords. Descended from Cuban contradanza via the Argentine arrabal — the tresillo pattern that underlies both the habanera and early tango.
          
            Latin
            Argentine
            Cuban
            Bandoneón
            Piano
          
        

        
          
            Son montuno
            montuno
            4/4
            ▶
          
          
          Cuban piano tumbao: bass-chord-chord repeating against the clave. The foundational piano pattern of son cubano and salsa; the rhythmic motor behind virtually all Afro-Cuban popular music.
          
            Latin
            Cuban
            Salsa
            Piano
          
        

        
          
            Cha-cha
            chacha
            4/4
            ▶
          
          
          Bass on beat 1, chord on 2, then three quick chords on "3–and–4" — the "1·2·cha-cha-chá" count. Evolved from the mambo in 1950s Cuba; named for the shuffling footwork of dancers.
          
            Latin
            Cuban
            Piano
            Full band
          
        

        
          
            Calypso / mento
            calypso
            4/4
            ▶
          
          
          Bass on beats 1 and 3, light chords on every upbeat — the Trinidadian and Jamaican "afterbeat." Mento is the Jamaican root form; calypso developed in Trinidad. Both patterns flowed into ska and reggae.
          
            Latin
            Caribbean
            Roots
            Guitar
            Piano
          
        

        
          
            Samba
            samba
            4/4
            ▶
          
          
          Surdo-style kick on beats 2 and 4 (absent on beat 1), snare on beat 3, hi-hat fills every eighth. The rhythmic foundation of Brazilian carnival parade music; transferred to the drum kit from the samba bateria.
          
            Latin
            Brazilian
            Drum set
            Bateria
          
        

        
          
            Mambo
            mambo
            4/4
            ▶
          
          
          Kick on beat 1 and the "and-of-3" (a clave-derived anticipation), snare on beat 3, hi-hats throughout. Developed in 1940s Havana by Dámaso Pérez Prado; bridged Cuban son and American big-band.
          
            Latin
            Cuban
            Drum set
            Full band
          
        

      
    

    
      Funk & R&B
      

        
          
            Funk
            funk
            4/4
            ▶
          
          
          Kick on beats 1 and 3; syncopated snare on the "and-of-2" and "and-of-4"; hi-hat anchors the eighth-note pulse. James Brown's drummers — Clyde Stubblefield and John "Jabo" Starks — defined this feel.
          
            Funk
            R&B
            Drum set
          
        

        
          
            Half-time feel
            halftime
            4/4
            ▶
          
          
          Snare moves to beat 3 (rather than 2 and 4), making 2 bars feel like 1. Common in hip-hop, stadium rock, and ballad bridges where the tempo needs to feel broader without actually slowing down.
          
            Pop
            Hip-hop
            Rock
            Drum set
          
        

        
          
            New Orleans second line
            secondline
            4/4
            ▶
          
          
          Kick on every beat; snare on the "and-of-1" and "and-of-3." The marching parade groove of New Orleans brass bands; adopted by jazz funk, R&B, and rock drummers (the Meters, Allen Toussaint, Dr. John).
          
            Funk
            New Orleans
            Jazz
            Drum set
            Marching
          
        

      
    

    
      Waltz & Dance
      

        
          
            Waltz
            waltz
            3/4
            ▶
          
          
          Bass on beat 1, chord on beats 2 and 3. The universal dance-band formula for 3/4 time. The slight delay before the chord creates the characteristic lilt that distinguishes waltz from a march.
          
            Dance
            Classical
            Piano
            Orchestra
          
        

        
          
            Viennese waltz
            viennese
            3/4
            ▶
          
          
          A short downbeat chord followed by slightly-early beats 2 and 3 (the "anticipated" Viennese lilt). The elastic timing distinguishes the Strauss concert hall waltz from the plainer ballroom waltz.
          
            Dance
            Classical
            Romantic
            Orchestra
            Piano
          
        

        
          
            Boom-chick
            oompah
            any
            ▶
          
          
          Root on the downbeat, chord on every other beat. The engine of polka, march, and German dance-band styles; derived from tuba–horn interplay in brass ensembles.
          
            Folk
            Polka
            March
            Brass
            Accordion
          
        

      
    

    
      Folk & Country
      

        
          
            Folk — alternating bass
            folk
            any
            ▶
          
          
          Alternating root–fifth bass note with a chord on the off-beat. The defining guitar and banjo accompaniment pattern in American folk, bluegrass, and country; also called the "Carter scratch."
          
            Folk
            Country
            Bluegrass
            Guitar
            Banjo
          
        

      
    

    
      Pop & Rock
      

        
          
            Pop / ballad
            pop
            any
            ▶
          
          
          Bass on beats 1 and 3, steady quarter-note chords on all beats. The most common piano and keyboard pattern in popular music since the 1950s.
          
            Pop
            Rock
            Piano
            Keyboard
          
        

        
          
            Driving 8ths
            driving8
            any
            ▶
          
          
          Steady eighth-note chords with no gaps. Propulsive and energetic; fills every subdivision. Found across rock, country, and pop guitar — sometimes called a "strum pattern."
          
            Rock
            Country
            Pop
            Guitar
            Piano
          
        

        
          
            Offbeat chords
            offbeat
            any
            ▶
          
          
          Chord only on the off-beats, silence on the downbeats. The defining rhythmic gesture of ska and reggae; known as the "skank" or "chop." In reggae, the kick lands on beat 3 (the "one-drop").
          
            Ska
            Reggae
            Guitar
            Keyboard
          
        

      
    

    
      Classical & Piano
      

        
          
            Block chords
            block
            any
            ▶
          
          
          All voices together on every beat, sustained until the next chord. The simplest possible accompaniment; used for chorale writing, teaching chord shapes, and very slow tempos.
          
            Classical
            Chorale
            Piano
            Keyboard
          
        

        
          
            Piano arpeggio ↑
            arpflow
            4/4
            ▶
          
          
          Rising arpeggios through the full bar (root–third–fifth–octave). Characteristic of Romantic-era piano writing and nocturne accompaniment; adds forward motion when chord changes are sparse.
          
            Classical
            Romantic
            Piano
          
        

        
          
            Arpeggio (root–5th)
            arpcell
            any
            ▶
          
          
          Root and fifth as individual tones in a repeating per-beat cell. Creates a light, open texture that suggests harmonic motion without dense block chords; useful for harp or guitar figuration.
          
            Classical
            Pop
            Harp
            Guitar
            Piano
          
        

        
          
            Bass line (roots)
            bassroot
            any
            ▶
          
          
          Root note only in the bass, no chord voices above. Use as a harmonic foundation when the melody instrument carries the full harmonic content, or when learning to hear bass motion in isolation.
          
            Teaching
            Minimal
            Bass
          
        

      
    

  

  
  

    
      Piano & Keyboard
      
        
          Block chordsblockany
          Sustained block voicing on every beat. The starting point for learning chord shapes and for chorale-style writing.
          ClassicalChorale
        
        
          Waltzwaltz3/4
          Left-hand bass on 1, right-hand chord on 2–3. The standard piano waltz texture from Chopin through the ballroom repertoire.
          DanceClassical
        
        
          Pop / balladpopany
          Bass on 1 and 3, chords on every beat. Ubiquitous in pop piano; easy to adapt to either hands-together or stride-style playing.
          PopRock
        
        
          Piano arpeggio ↑arpflow4/4
          Rising broken chord through the full bar. Nocturne and ballad texture; standard left-hand figure in Romantic piano writing.
          ClassicalRomantic
        
        
          Viennese waltzviennese3/4
          Elastic 3/4 with the characteristic early-beat anticipation. Strauss orchestra and salon piano repertoire.
          DanceClassical
        
        
          Jazz Charlestoncharleston4/4
          Syncopated 4/4 comping with a chord on beat 1 and the and-of-2. Common in Stride, Swing, and mainstream jazz piano.
          JazzSwing
        
        
          Jazz waltzjazzwaltz3/4
          Swung bass on 1, light chord on 3. The texture of jazz piano trios playing in 3 — Evans, Peterson, Monk.
          JazzBebop
        
      
    

    
      Guitar & Plucked Strings
      
        
          Folk — alternating bassfolkany
          Thumb alternates root–fifth in the bass; fingers strum the chord on the off-beat. The foundational fingerpicking and flatpicking pattern in folk, bluegrass, and country guitar.
          FolkCountryBluegrass
        
        
          Driving 8thsdriving8any
          Steady downstroke eighth notes, no rests. The strum pattern behind countless rock, country, and pop songs.
          RockCountryPop
        
        
          Offbeat chordsoffbeatany
          The ska/reggae "skank": chord only between the beats. In reggae the downstroke is muted, leaving only the upstroke chop.
          SkaReggae
        
        
          Bossa novabossa4/4
          Tresillo bass with off-beat chords. João Gilberto's original bossa guitar part is the blueprint; the pattern is also widely adapted to keyboard.
          LatinBrazilianJazz
        
        
          Arpeggio (root–5th)arpcellany
          Open-voiced ascending tones per beat. Evokes harp, classical guitar, and lute figuration; widely used in Renaissance and Baroque lute tablature.
          ClassicalPop
        
      
    

    
      Brass & Ensemble
      
        
          Boom-chickoompahany
          Tuba carries the root on 1; horns answer with the chord on 2 (and 4). The pattern maps directly to the brass section interplay in polka bands, march bands, and German Blasmusik.
          PolkaMarchFolk
        
        
          Tangotango4/4
          Habanera cell in the bass with syncopated upper chords. In Argentine tango this interplay moves between bandoneón and piano; in orchestral tango (Piazzolla) it drives the entire ensemble.
          LatinArgentine
        
      
    

    
      Bass & Foundation
      
        
          Bass line (roots)bassrootany
          Root note only, no chords. Use this when practicing bass lines in isolation, or when the melody is dense enough to imply the harmony on its own.
          TeachingMinimal
        
      
    

    
      Drum Set
      
        
          Backbeatbackbeat4/4
          Kick on beats 1 and 3, snare on 2 and 4. The universal pop and rock groove; the first drum pattern most students encounter.
          PopRock
        
        
          Driving 8thsdriving84/4
          Continuous eighth notes on the hi-hat with backbeat snare. Energetic pop and rock feel; common in anthemic and uptempo styles.
          PopRock
        
        
          Ska / reggae (one-drop)ska4/4
          Kick displaced to beat 3; snare and hi-hat emphasise the off-beats. The rhythmic foundation of ska, rocksteady, and roots reggae.
          ReggaeSka
        
        
          Swing — ride cymbalswing_ride4/4
          Swung ride pattern with kick and snare on beats 2 and 4. The standard jazz ride pattern from Swing through bebop.
          JazzSwing
        
        
          Swing — hi-hatswing_hats4/4
          Swung quarter-note hi-hat pulse; lighter texture than ride-cymbal swing. Used in small-group jazz and ballad settings.
          JazzBallad
        
        
          Swing — open hi-hatswing_hats_open4/4
          Swung hi-hat opening on beats 2 and 4; airy, washy texture. Common in contemporary jazz and fusion where the drummer wants more cymbal wash than the closed-hat version.
          JazzFusion
        
        
          Swing — brushesswing_brushes4/4
          Wire-brush swirl with soft backbeat. Quiet jazz trio and intimate club setting; the standard brush technique for standards and ballads.
          JazzBallad
        
        
          Jazz waltz — ridejazzwaltz_ride3/4
          Swung ride in 3; kick on beat 1, light snare elsewhere. The jazz-waltz drum feel behind Bill Evans, Miles Davis, and the post-bop trio repertoire.
          JazzWaltz
        
        
          Jazz waltz — hi-hatjazzwaltz_hats3/4
          Closed hi-hat pulse in 3 with a light swing feel; more understated than the ride-cymbal version. Used in intimate trio settings where the drummer wants less projection.
          JazzWaltz
        
        
          Bossa novabossa4/4
          Ride cymbal tresillo with side-stick; the drum kit adaptation of Brazilian percussion. Foundational in bossa nova and samba-jazz.
          LatinBossa
        
        
          Tango (habanera)tango4/4
          Habanera kick cell with closed hi-hat. The rhythmic engine of Argentine tango and early-20th-century Latin dance music.
          LatinTango
        
        
          Son montuno (clave)montuno4/4
          Cuban clave rhythm on the kick; snare and hi-hat fill the groove. The drum kit version of the son montuno pattern.
          LatinCuban
        
        
          Waltzwaltz3/4
          Kick on beat 1, hi-hat on 2 and 3. Straightforward triple-meter groove for waltzes, country, and folksong accompaniment.
          DanceFolk
        
        
          Compound (6/8)compound66/8
          Kick on the two main beats, hi-hat subdivisions filling the compound pulse. Used in jigs, compound-feel pop, and gospel 6/8.
          FolkGospel
        
        
          Half-time feelhalftime4/4
          Snare on beat 3 only; kick and hi-hat fill the rest. Makes the bar feel twice as wide without changing tempo. Widely used in hip-hop, stadium rock, and ballad bridges.
          PopHip-hopRock
        
        
          Funkfunk4/4
          Kick on beats 1 and 3; syncopated snare on the "and-of-2" and "and-of-4"; hi-hat on all eighths. The foundational James Brown / Clyde Stubblefield groove.
          FunkR&B
        
        
          New Orleans second linesecondline4/4
          Kick on every beat, snare on the upbeats of 1 and 3. The marching street-parade groove; adopted by the Meters, Dr. John, and rock drummers worldwide.
          FunkNew Orleans
        
        
          Sambasamba4/4
          Surdo kick on beats 2 and 4; snare on beat 3; hi-hat throughout. The drum kit adaptation of the samba bateria; common in Brazilian jazz and fusion.
          LatinBrazilian
        
        
          Mambomambo4/4
          Kick on beat 1 and the "and-of-3" (a clave-derived anticipation); snare on beat 3. The driving groove of 1940s Havana; ancestor of modern salsa.
          LatinCuban
        
        
          Calypso / mentocalypso4/4
          Floating kick (no downbeat on 1); side-stick on beat 3; hi-hat emphasises the upbeats. The Trinidadian and Jamaican afterbeat; ancestral to ska and reggae.
          CaribbeanReggae
        
      
    

    
      Hand Percussion
      
        
          Bongo — martillobongo_martillo4/4
          Steady eighth-note alternation between hi and lo bongo; the "hammer" pattern. The default timekeeping groove in Cuban son and salsa.
          LatinCuban
        
        
          Bongo — quarterbongo_slow4/4
          Quarter-note hi/lo alternation; a relaxed, open texture. Works well as a simplified bongo part for classroom or beginner settings.
          LatinTeaching
        
        
          Conga — tumbaoconga_tumbao4/4
          Open tone on the and-of-4, muted tones elsewhere. The foundational Cuban conga pattern; ubiquitous in salsa and son.
          LatinCuban
        
        
          Conga — tumbao (dense)conga_tumbao_dense4/4
          Eight-note tumbao with slap and open tone variations; a fuller, more active feel than the standard four-note version.
          LatinCuban
        
        
          Conga — sonconga_son4/4
          Alternating lo-conga open tones across the bar; simpler and more open than the tumbao. Common in son cubano and early salsa.
          LatinCuban
        
        
          Conga — waltzconga_waltz3/4
          Conga tones on the three main beats in 3/4; pairs with Latin waltz and compound-feel songs.
          LatinWaltz
        
        
          Conga — 6/8conga_6_86/8
          Open and muted conga tones across the compound-triple pulse. Works with 6/8 Afro-Cuban styles and compound jigs.
          LatinAfro-Cuban

title: Secondary Dominants: Practice for Chapter 17
text:
This page goes with Chapter 17, Secondary Dominant Chords of Robert Hutchinson’s open textbook Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom. Read each section there first; the book is the reference for the terms used here. It builds on Chapter 7, Roman Numerals, Chapter 8, Seventh Chords and Chapter 9, Harmonic Progression.
Every drill has Settings, and is also on the Theory Drills page. ▶ Hear it plays the chord and then the chord it resolves to.
Typing a secondary dominant: V/V, V7/ii, V7/IV. After the slash comes the chord being tonicized, and its case is its quality, as before: ii is minor, IV is major. Inversions use the figured-bass numbers the book uses: V6/vi and V64/V for triads, V65/V, V43/IV and V42/ii for seventh chords. V6/5/V and V7 of ii work too.
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Secondary Dominants: Practice for Chapter 17
text:
17.1 Examples
Secondary dominants are everywhere, in popular and classical music. Here are the book’s examples. Listen for the chord that sounds “borrowed” from another key. Its chromatic note pulls toward the next chord. The rest of the chapter explains what it is. Read 17.1

title: Secondary Dominants: Practice for Chapter 17
text:
17.2 Tonicization
Tonicization treats a chord other than I as if it were a tonic for a moment, by putting its own dominant in front of it. That dominant is a secondary dominant: a major triad or a dominant seventh chord whose root is a perfect 5th above the root of the chord it resolves to. It is written V/x, said “V of x”. In C major, D–F♯–A goes to G, the V chord, so it is V/V. D7 is V7/V. Read 17.2
Why not call D major “II” in C? Because ii in a major key is minor. A major chord on 2 is chromatic, and calling it V/V says what it does: it leads to V. Diminished chords are never tonicized (vii° in major, ii° and vii° in minor), because a diminished chord cannot sound like a tonic.
Start with triads in C, G and F major. Which chord is it?
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Secondary Dominants: Practice for Chapter 17
section: 17.3 Secondary dominants in major and minor
text:
17.3 Secondary dominants in major and minor
Both kinds work as secondary dominants: the major triad and the dominant (major–minor) seventh chord. Usually the chromatic note is raised. It is the leading tone of the chord being tonicized. The exception in major is V7/IV: its seventh is lowered (B♭ in C major), the way the last flat added to a key signature is 4̂ of the new key. Read 17.3

title: Secondary Dominants: Practice for Chapter 17
text:
17.4 Analysing secondary dominants
The book’s two steps for a chord with a chromatic note:

Stack it in thirds to find the root and the quality. If it isn’t a major triad or a dominant seventh, it isn’t a secondary dominant.
Go down a perfect 5th from the root. If that note is the root of a major or minor chord in the key, the chord is V (or V7) of that chord.

The chord on the staff is followed by the chord it tonicizes. Name the first one:
Read 17.4



With inversions. The book’s example is an F♯ major triad in first inversion. B, a perfect 5th below F♯, is 5̂ of the key, so the chord is V6/V. Read the bass note to choose the figure:

title: Secondary Dominants: Practice for Chapter 17
text:
17.5 Writing secondary dominants
The book’s procedure, worked here for V43/V in B♭ major (the book’s own example is a different chord):

Find the root of the chord after the slash: V in B♭ is F.
Go up a perfect 5th: C.
Build a major triad or a dominant seventh there: C–E–G–B♭.
Put it in the inversion asked for. 43 means the 5th is in the bass: G–B♭–C–E.

Read 17.5



With inversions, major and minor:

title: Secondary Dominants: Practice for Chapter 17
text:
17.6 Irregular resolutions
A secondary dominant does not always go to the chord it names. The book’s examples, with its analysis:

V/V → IV: “Yesterday”, and V7/V → IV in “Forget You”. IV can stand in for V in popular music.
V/V → ♭VII: “I Want You to Want Me” (in A major). ♭VII also stands in for V.
V42/IV → V7/ii → ii: “Baby Love” (in C major in the book’s example: C7 over B♭, then A7, then Dm). The B♭ falls by half step to A as expected, but A is the root of a new secondary dominant instead of the third of F.
V7/vi → IV: “(Sittin’ On) The Dock of the Bay”, “Imagine”, and Beethoven’s “Waldstein” Sonata. You can think of it as iii–IV with a chromatic note, or as a deceptive resolution inside the key of vi.

Read 17.6

Chords drilled: V and V7 of every major and minor triad of the key: major ii iii IV V vi, minor III iv V VI VII. A chord made only of the key’s notes is left out (V/IV in major, which is I; V/III and V/VI in minor, which are VII and III; V7/III in minor, which is VII7). This is because without a resolution they can’t be told from diatonic chords. So IV is drilled only as V7/IV, and III in minor not at all.

title: Roman Numerals: Practice for Chapter 7
text:
This page goes with Chapter 7, Roman Numerals of Robert Hutchinson’s open textbook Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom. Read each section there first; the book is the reference for the symbols used here. It assumes Chapter 6, Triads.
Every drill grades each answer and has Settings (your teacher’s link may set them; you can change them, and Back to the link’s settings undoes it). They are also on the Theory Drills page. Typing is case-sensitive, because the case is the quality: V is a major chord, v a minor one.
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Roman Numerals: Practice for Chapter 7
text:
7.1 Roman numeral symbols
A Roman numeral names a chord by the scale degree of its root, so the same pattern looks the same in every key. Capitals are major (I), small numerals minor (ii), a small numeral with ° diminished (vii°), a capital with + augmented (III+). The key is written before a colon: a capital letter for major (G:), a small one for minor (f:). Until figured bass (Chapter 16), the book shows an inversion by naming the chord member in the bass: V/3rd is V with its third in the bass, iv/5th is iv with its fifth in the bass. Read 7.1 · musictheory.net: Roman Numeral Analysis · Open Music Theory: Roman Numerals
The drills accept 6 for /3rd and 64 for /5th as well, if you already know figured bass.
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Roman Numerals: Practice for Chapter 7
text:
7.2 Diatonic chords in major
Build a triad on every note of a major scale, using only the notes of the key, and the qualities always come out the same: I ii iii IV V vi vii° (major, minor, minor, major, major, minor, diminished). Read 7.2 · musictheory.net: Diatonic Triads



The other way round: given the key and the numeral, write the chord’s notes (the book’s exercise 2).









Tipmusictheory.net: Key Signature Identification (a warm-up)





Every Roman numeral question starts with the key. musictheory.net has no Roman numeral exercise of its own, so this is the one to embed here.
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Roman Numerals: Practice for Chapter 7
text:
7.3 Diatonic chords in minor
Minor has three scales (natural, harmonic, melodic), so its 6th and 7th degrees can be raised or not, and there are 13 possible diatonic triads. The ones used most are i ii° III iv V VI VII vii°. V and vii° take the raised 7th (the leading tone) from harmonic minor, so they need an accidental. VII, the subtonic, is built on the lowered 7th and needs none. The rarer ones (v, III+, ii, IV, ♯vi°) are in the drill’s Chords in minor setting. Read 7.3 · musictheory.net: The Minor Scales · Open Music Theory: Minor Scales
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Roman Numerals: Practice for Chapter 7
text:
7.4 Cadences
A cadence is the harmonic arrival at the end of a phrase. The book names four:

Authentic (AC): V to I.
Plagal (PC): IV to I.
Deceptive (DC): V to something other than I, most often vi.
Half (HC): the phrase stops on V.

Read 7.4 · musictheory.net: Phrases and Cadences · the site’s own Cadences lesson, where the band plays each one
Name the cadence: look, listen, or both (Show in Settings; Sound only is ear training).

title: Harmonic Progression: Practice for Chapter 9
text:
This page goes with Chapter 9, Harmonic Progression and Harmonic Function of Robert Hutchinson’s open textbook Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom. Read each section there first; the book is the reference for the terms used here. It builds on Chapter 7, Roman Numerals and Chapter 8, Seventh Chords.
This chapter is about chords in order, so most of the practice here is listening. The drills play each progression on the piano (or show it, or both); the clips are the book’s own, cut where the book cuts them. Every drill has Settings, and is also on the Theory Drills page.
Typing a progression: the chords in order with spaces between them: I vi IV V. Case is the quality, as before. Type b or ♭ before a numeral for ♭VII. With Answer with: lead-sheet symbols, type C Am F G (a small letter is minor here too).
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Harmonic Progression: Practice for Chapter 9
text:
9.1 The circle of fifths progression
Each chord’s root is a fifth above the next one’s (or a fourth below): I IV vii° iii vi ii V I in major, i iv VII III VI ii° V i in minor, with only the notes of the key, so one fifth (IV to vii°) is diminished. The bass makes a sequence: a short idea repeated at a lower pitch, which is why the progression sounds so inevitable. Read 9.1 · Open Music Theory: Diatonic Sequences



The book’s exercise 1 writes the circle on paper, in F major and B minor. This drill asks for the same chords as lead-sheet symbols:

title: Harmonic Progression: Practice for Chapter 9
text:
9.2 Harmonic rhythm
Harmonic rhythm is how long each chord lasts: a chord a bar in “Fly Me to the Moon” and “I Will Survive”, two chords a bar in the Mozart and Wagner. It can change inside a song: in “Pompeii” it doubles, from four beats a chord to two. Read 9.2



Bastille, “Pompeii”: listen for the chords changing twice as often

title: Harmonic Progression: Practice for Chapter 9
text:
9.3 Shorter progressions from the circle
Pieces of the circle are everywhere, especially in jazz standards and pop: ii–V–I; vi–ii–V–I and its rotations I–vi–ii–V and ii–V–I–vi; iii–vi–ii–V, often looped, and its rotation ii–V–iii–vi. Read 9.3

9.4 Harmonic function
A chord’s function is what it tends to do next. The book uses four:

In minor, VII (the subtonic) has one job: it leads to III. Two exceptions: IV has tonic prolongation function when it goes straight to I (the plagal cadence), and I/5th has dominant function when it goes to V. The deceptive cadence (V–vi) is the other exception to the flowchart. Read 9.4 · Open Music Theory: Introduction to Harmony

9.5 Exceptions created by sequences
When a progression breaks the flowchart, look for a sequence: a pattern of chords repeated a step or more lower or higher, which takes the chords wherever the pattern goes. The book’s examples are “Flashdance… What a Feeling” (the book’s clip of it is no longer on YouTube) and the verse of “Hotel California”: Read 9.5

title: Harmonic Progression: Practice for Chapter 9
text:
9.6 ♭VII in popular music
In rock and pop, ♭VII (a major chord on the lowered 7th, B♭ in C major) is everywhere. It can come before tonic, pre-dominant or dominant chords, so it can stand in for any function except tonic, and ♭VII–IV–I is a common way to end a phrase. Read 9.6 · Open Music Theory: Modal Schemas

9.7 The best-seller progression
I–V–vi–IV is in so many hit songs that it has its own name, and its rotations vi–IV–I–V and IV–I–V–vi are just as common. vi–IV–I–V can also be heard in the relative minor as i–VI–III–VII: which one you hear depends on which chord feels like home. Read 9.7 · Open Music Theory: Four-Chord Schemas

title: Pitch Notation from Do: Letter Names, Clefs and Accidentals
text:
This page goes with Chapter 1, Basic Concepts of Robert Hutchinson’s open textbook Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom.
You already know this. You read and write tonal patterns on the staff: you find do from the do signature and read the rest from there. This chapter gives every line and space a fixed letter name. Gordon calls letter names “the alphabet of music”: knowing them is not the same as audiating, but once you can already read, they explain the notation you understand (Gordon 36–37). That is the order you have learned in: sound first, then syllables, now letters.
Press ▶ to hear an example, or ▶ Sing to hear it sung on syllables. Click any heading to fold its section.

title: Pitch Notation from Do: Letter Names, Clefs and Accidentals
text:
1.1–1.2 Pitch and the staff
The book’s first sections cover what you already use: higher and lower sounds, the five-line staff, and the clefs that fix which line is which letter. Read 1.1 · Read 1.2
Syllables move, letters stay. Your syllables are tied to do: move the do signature and every syllable moves with it. Letters are tied to the clef: in treble clef the second line is always G, whatever the signature. So the question changes from “where is do?” to “what letter is do on?”

A note’s name and a note’s job
A letter name is a note’s name: G is G in every key, in every piece. A syllable is the note’s job in the music you’re hearing: home (do), the dominant (so), the leading tone that pulls home (ti). Change the key and the same note gets a new job.
The circle of fifths shows both at once. The outer ring is the letters, and they never move. The inner ring is the syllables. Pick a new key with the menu, or click a letter on the wheel, and watch the syllables turn while the letters stay put. Follow one note, say G: it’s so in C, do in G, re in F, ti in A♭. The note keeps its name and changes its job.



The same works for the book’s other names. Choose scale degrees as the note names (in the Drone or Circle settings), and the inner ring shows 1̂ to 7̂ instead: degree numbers are jobs too.
Here is a tonic pattern, do–mi–so–mi–do, in the treble clef and in the bass clef. Same syllables, same letters, an octave apart:






A way in from what you know. The letters run A B C D E F G and start again. Sing do re mi fa so la ti do in C and say the letters instead: C D E F G A B C. In the key of C, do re mi and C D E line up, which makes C a good place to learn the letters.


Practise: name the note
Treble and bass clef, no accidentals. Open Settings to add ledger lines and accidentals.

1.3 Octave registers
The same letter comes back every eight notes. The book tells them apart with a number: middle C is C4, the C an octave above is C5, and each number runs from C up to the B above it. Read 1.3
You already know this as “the same pattern, higher”. In the two examples above, the treble pattern starts on C4 and the bass pattern on C3.






NoteThe same registers in ABC and LilyPond





Text notations write the register with letter case and marks instead of a number.

ABC: a capital letter is the octave from middle C (C4–B4) and a lower-case letter the octave above (C5–B5). Each , takes a note down an octave and each ' takes it up one. The C major scale from middle C is C D E F G A B c.
LilyPond: a plain letter is the octave below middle C (C3–B3), and each ' or , moves it an octave, so middle C is c'. The same scale is c' d' e' f' g' a' b' c''.
The trap: LilyPond’s plain c is C3 but ABC’s plain C is C4, so the same-looking letter is an octave apart.
LilyPond’s \relative mode (common in published files) works differently: each note is placed nearest the note before it, and ' or , only marks a jump of more than a fourth.

title: Pitch Notation from Do: Letter Names, Clefs and Accidentals
text:
1.4–1.5 Accidentals and enharmonic notes
A sharp (♯) raises a note a half step, a flat (♭) lowers it, and a natural (♮) cancels either. In a key signature they apply to the whole piece; written in the music, to the rest of the bar. Read 1.4 · Read 1.5
From what you know. A key signature’s sharps and flats are what put the half steps on mi–fa and ti–do (see Chapter 2). An accidental in the music marks a note outside that pattern, a chromatic. You hear it as a new syllable: in harmonic minor, so is raised to si (Gordon 70), and the music shows it with a sharp or natural.
Enharmonic notes sound the same but are spelled differently: F♯ and G♭, or B and C♭. Which spelling is right depends on the key, just as which syllable is right depends on the tonality. In D major, the note between F and G is F♯, because D major is spelled with one of each letter: D E F♯ G A B C♯.
Where the book and MLT see this differently. Gordon warns against learning letters, accidentals and key signatures before audiating (Gordon 36–37, 65). You haven’t: you’re learning them now, as names for music you can already read.
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Pitch Notation from Do: Letter Names, Clefs and Accidentals
text:
Bridging: from syllables to letters

Find do and name it. “Do signature of two sharps: do is on D.”
Sing the pattern on syllables, then again on letters: do mi so → D F♯ A.
Every letter in the signature is altered everywhere. In two sharps, every F and every C is sharp, in any octave.
Write in both clefs. Write the pattern in treble, then an octave lower in bass. The letters stay the same; the lines and spaces change.

title: The Neapolitan Chord: Practice for Chapter 20
text:
This page goes with Chapter 20, The Neapolitan Chord of Robert Hutchinson’s open textbook Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom. Read each section there first; the book is the reference for the terms used here. It uses the Roman numerals of Chapter 7 and the harmonic functions of Chapter 9.
Every drill has Settings, and is also on the Theory Drills page. ▶ Hear it plays the chord and then V.
Typing it: N in root position, N6 in first inversion. The book writes N, not ♭II, but ♭II, bII and ♭II6 are accepted too. Other chords: iv, iv6, IV6, ii6, ii°6 (type o for °).

title: The Neapolitan Chord: Practice for Chapter 20
text:
20.1 The Neapolitan chord
The Neapolitan is the ♭II chord: a major triad built on the 2nd degree of the scale lowered a half step. In C that is D♭–F–A♭, in major and in minor alike. Classical analysis labels it N instead of ♭II. It is most often in first inversion, with its 3rd (scale degree 4) in the bass, written N6. Since it is an altered ii chord, it has pre-dominant function: it goes to V. The book points out how composers sometimes mark the moment with a change of texture, register or loudness. Read 20.1



Beethoven, Symphony No. 7, Op. 92, I (the book’s Figure 20.1.1)





To find it: go up a minor 2nd from the tonic, and build a major triad there. The root takes the next letter name up (D♭ in C, not C♯). In a minor key only the root is outside the key signature; in a major key the 5th is too (A♭ in C major).

title: Modes: Three Meanings of One Word
text:
You will hear the word mode used by three groups of musicians, and they don’t mean the same thing. A choir teacher trained in Music Learning Theory, a classical theory textbook and a jazz teacher can all look at the same notes and give three different answers to “what mode is this?” None of them is wrong. They are answering three different questions:
Click any heading to fold its section.

title: Modes: Three Meanings of One Word
text:
1. Music Learning Theory: mode = tonality
In Edwin Gordon’s Music Learning Theory (MLT) the word tonality is used for what most people call a mode. Gordon says tonality “best refers to what is usually called a mode,” and adds that people forget “major and minor are also modes.” He lists at least eight tonalities: major, harmonic minor, Dorian, Phrygian, Lydian, Mixolydian, Aeolian and Locrian (Gordon 149). Notice that harmonic minor gets its own place, separate from Aeolian.
A tonality is something you hear. It is defined by its resting tone, the note the music feels “at home” on. Gordon keeps three ideas apart (Gordon xiii, 150):

Tonality: the kind of home (major, Dorian, Mixolydian…), named by its resting tone in solfège.
Keyality: which pitch that home is on (C, G, E♭…), called the tonic. Gordon made up the word to keep it separate from:
Key signature: the sharps and flats you see. One sharp could be G major, E minor, A Dorian or D Mixolydian. “A key signature is seen”; keyality is heard.

“A tonality may be in any keyality and a keyality may be in any tonality” (Gordon 150): Dorian on C, Dorian on F, major on C, all different combinations.
How you name it. MLT teaches movable do with a la-based minor, so a syllable always names the same relation to the other notes. The resting tone of each tonality then gets its own syllable:

The MLT question: Sing the resting tone. If you can, you have heard the tonality. You don’t need to know a scale, a key signature or a chord to answer. Music can stay in one tonality (unitonal) or move between them (multitonal), for example from harmonic minor to Mixolydian while staying in E♭ keyality (Gordon 152, 157).
The order matters in MLT: you learn to hear and sing major and minor tonalities first, then other tonalities, and only later learn their names and notation. See Audiation and the Tonal Patterns page, which has pattern sets in every tonality.

title: Modes: Three Meanings of One Word
section: 2. Classical theory: church modes, then major and minor
text:
2. Classical theory: church modes, then major and minor
In classical theory, “mode” has a history with two layers.
The church modes. Medieval chant was sorted into eight modes, in four pairs. Each pair shares a final (the note a chant ends on). An authentic mode runs up an octave from the final; its plagal partner (with the prefix hypo-, as in Hypodorian) uses the same final but sits lower, with the range moved down. Today the eight are often numbered 1–8. In 1547 the Swiss theorist Heinrich Glarean, in his book Dodecachordon, added four more: Aeolian and Ionian with their plagal partners (“Mode (music)”).
Major mode and minor mode. Ionian is our major scale and Aeolian our natural minor. As the major/minor system took over, “mode” came to mean simply major mode or minor mode, and the older modes became a special colour composers reached for: the sound of the church, or of folk music (“Mode (music)”). That is why a classical textbook can say a piece in C minor is “in the minor mode,” and why mode mixture means borrowing chords from the parallel minor mode.
How a classical student finds the mode. Look at the notes used and the final (or the tonic chord), then match the pattern of whole and half steps. Two ways of learning modes are both common:

Relative (white-key) way: D Dorian is “C major from D to D.” Quick for spelling, but it makes Dorian sound like a part of C major.
Parallel way: C Dorian is “C major with ♭3 and ♭7.” This keeps the home note fixed and asks what changes, which is closer to how the mode sounds (the right-hand column of the table above).

The classical question: What scale, final and step pattern does this music use? The answer can come from the page, without playing a note, though a good analyst checks it by ear.
crumbs: Modes: Three Meanings of One Word

title: Modes: Three Meanings of One Word
section: 3. Jazz: a scale for each chord
text:
3. Jazz: a scale for each chord
In jazz, “mode” usually means a scale you play over one chord while it lasts. This is called chord-scale theory. When the chord changes, the scale changes.
Robert Hutchinson’s open textbook gives the method: write all the notes of the chord, including any extensions and alterations, then fill the gaps between them “with the most logical choices, avoiding augmented seconds and consecutive half steps.” His table of the usual pairs (Hutchinson, “How to Determine Chord-Scale Relationships”):

Cm7
C Dorian or C natural minor (Aeolian)


C7

C Locrian or C Locrian ♯2


CmΔ7
C melodic minor (ascending)

C Lydian dominant

C octatonic, whole–half



The jazz question: What notes sound good over this chord? Every new chord gets a new answer, named from its own root.

title: Modes: Three Meanings of One Word
text:
Same notes, three answers
Take the most common jazz progression in C major: Dm7 – G7 – CΔ7 (ii–V–I). Every chord uses only the white keys.










Dm7
G7
CΔ7




Jazz says
D Dorian
G Mixolydian
C Ionian


Classical says
ii
V7
I, all in C major


MLT says
one tonality, major, with do (C) as the resting tone, throughout





The jazz musician names three modes, because each is a scale built on a different chord root. Yet the notes never change. The classical and MLT answers agree here: one key, one home. For a piece to be in Dorian in the classical or MLT sense, D itself has to feel like home for the whole passage, not just for one chord.
Now the other way round: a folk tune uses only the white keys and ends on D, and the tune clearly rests on D.

MLT: Dorian tonality, D keyality. Resting tone re.
Classical: D Dorian (mode 1, authentic, if it ranges an octave up from D).
Jazz: a jazz player would likely hear it as a long Dm chord and play D Dorian over it. Here, for once, all three agree.
