title: Minor Scales and Key Signatures: From La
text:
This page goes with Chapter 3, Minor Scales and Key Signatures of Robert Hutchinson’s open textbook Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom.
You already know this. You sing in minor with la as the resting tone (movable do, la-based minor; Gordon 105), you sing harmonic minor with the raised si (Gordon 70), and you read both from the do signature. This chapter names what you already do. La-based minor gives you a head start: the book’s “relative minor” is the minor you’ve always sung.
Press ▶ to hear an example, or ▶ Sing to hear it sung on syllables. Click any heading to fold its section.
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Minor Scales and Key Signatures: From La
section: What you know → what the book calls it
text:
What you know → what the book calls it







You say (MLT)
The book says (Hutchinson ch. 3)




la, the resting tone in minor
tonic of the minor key, 1̂


la ti do re mi fa so la
natural minor scale (Gordon: Aeolian tonality)


the same notes with si for so
harmonic minor scale (Gordon: harmonic minor tonality)


the do signature, resting on la
the minor key signature: “A minor”


major and minor with the same do signature
relative keys


the same tonic letter, major and minor
parallel keys

title: Minor Scales and Key Signatures: From La
text:
3.1 Three kinds of minor
Read 3.1
Natural minor is la to la with no changes, the notes of the do signature from la. You’ve sung it as the minor of folk tunes and of Gordon’s Aeolian tonality.



Harmonic minor raises so to si, so the scale has a half step into la like the half step ti–do in major. That’s the dominant sound you sing in harmonic minor patterns such as mi si ti re (Gordon 100). The book shows it as an accidental: in A minor, G becomes G♯.



Melodic minor raises both fa and so on the way up, and goes back to natural minor on the way down. This one may be new: you have the sound of si, but probably not of the raised fa. In movable do, raised fa is usually sung fi (the syllable is common practice, not yet checked against an MLT source).



Where the book and MLT differ. The book treats natural, harmonic and melodic minor as three forms of one minor key. Gordon treats harmonic minor and Aeolian as two different tonalities, each with its own characteristic patterns (Gordon 149). Both see the same notes; Gordon names what you hear, the book names what is written.
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Minor Scales and Key Signatures: From La
section: 3.2 Minor key signatures: the same do signature
text:
3.2 Minor key signatures: the same do signature
Read 3.2
You already read a do signature and rest on la. The book calls that key “the relative minor”:

Find do, then go down to la (two letters down, or up six). One sharp: do is G, la is E → E minor. Three flats: do is E♭, la is C → C minor.
Relative keys share a signature: C major and A minor, G major and E minor. In MLT terms they share a do signature, with different resting tones (Gordon 155–156).
Parallel keys share a tonic letter: A major and A minor. In MLT terms, do moves: A major has do on A; A minor has la on A, so do is on C.

The same tune, on the same do signature, ends on do (major) or la (minor):






The harmonic minor accidental isn’t in the signature. Si is always written in the music. That’s why C minor’s signature is three flats, but its scale needs a B♮.

Practise: name the minor key
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Minor Scales and Key Signatures: From La

The book numbers minor from its own tonic, so la is 1̂. The names are the ones from major, with one change: so (a whole step below la) is the subtonic, and si (a half step below) is the leading tone, as ti is in major.

title: Minor Scales and Key Signatures: From La
section: Bridging: from la to the book’s names
text:
Bridging: from la to the book’s names

Find do, then la. Say both letters: “do is B♭, la is G: G minor.”
Sing la to la, then again on letters. That’s natural minor.
Swap in si: raise the letter under so with a sharp or natural. That’s harmonic minor.
Parallel key? Keep the tonic letter, move do: G major has do on G (one sharp); G minor has la on G (do on B♭, two flats).
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Minor Scales and Key Signatures: From La
text:
Check yourself

Two sharps. What is the relative minor?
In D minor, what letter is si?
In E minor harmonic, which note gets an accidental?
What is the parallel minor of E♭ major, and its signature?
In minor, which syllable is the dominant, 5̂?







TipAnswers






B minor (do is D, la is B).
C♯.
D becomes D♯ (so → si).
E♭ minor, six flats (la on E♭, so do is on G♭).
Mi.

title: Melodic Analysis: Practice for Chapter 11
text:
This page goes with Chapter 11, Melodic Analysis of Robert Hutchinson’s open textbook Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom. Read each section there first. The book is the reference for the terms used here. It builds on Chapter 10, Non-Chord Tones, which you need for ornamentation.
The book takes a melody apart at four sizes, smallest first: the motive, which can be split into fragments; and the phrase, which can be split into subphrases. The drills here are about motives and how they change. Phrases and subphrases are practised by listening, with the book’s clips, and by looking at themes in the site’s Classical Themes collection.
For writing your own motives and developing them, see the lesson Composing 2: Developing a Motif.
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Melodic Analysis: Practice for Chapter 11
text:
11.1 Motive
A motive (or motif) is the smallest melodic idea you can recognize as itself. It is usually two to seven notes, and it is recognized by its rhythm and shape more than by its exact pitches. A composer develops a motive: repeats it, moves it to other notes, changes it.
The book’s example is the first theme of Beethoven’s Symphony No. 1, where it finds four motives in four bars. Here is the theme with the book’s labels (the book’s Figure 11.1.1, engraved for this page; the Classical Themes collection has the same theme from its first downbeat, without the opening run):




Motive 1: a quick run down four steps to a long C.
Motive 2: a dotted pickup, G up to B, into C. It comes twice.
Motive 3: four short notes, C C G B, also twice.
Motive 4: a scale of quarter notes rising through the C major chord and up to C.

Later in the movement Beethoven takes each motive out of the theme and builds whole passages from it, usually as a sequence: the same motive repeated higher or lower. The book’s clips follow each one:






NoteListen: the theme, and what Beethoven does with each motive








The first theme






Development of motive 1






Development of motive 2






Development of motives 2 and 3 together






Development of motive 4 (it follows straight on from the clip before)








Try it: the opening of Beethoven’s Fifth (Classical Themes, two themes) is one of the most famous motives there is. How many notes is it? Where does it come back, and what changes when it does?









TipOne answer





Four notes: three short repeated notes and a long note a 3rd below. It comes straight back a step lower, as a sequence. In the next three bars only the three short notes are kept, each time after a rest, and they climb: G, then A♭, then up to E♭. Then the line falls to a long C. That keeps a fragment of the motive (11.3). This analysis is the site’s, not the book’s.
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Melodic Analysis: Practice for Chapter 11
text:
11.2 Melodic alteration
The book names seven ways to change a motive. Move it to other notes and keep its shape, and it is a sequence. The book does not count that as an alteration, because it is so common. So the drill offers Sequence as an answer too, and you have to tell it apart from the real changes.








Alteration
What changes
What stays




Inversion
every interval turned upside down (up becomes down)
the rhythm


Intervallic change
some intervals (not all), so the shape changes a little
the rhythm


Augmentation
every note twice as long
the intervals


Diminution
every note half as long
the intervals


Rhythmic change
some of the note lengths
the notes


Ornamentation
notes added between the motive’s notes (passing tones, neighbor tones)
the motive’s notes, the length


Extension
notes added at the end
the whole motive, at the start


Retrograde
the order: the notes from last to first
the notes



The book’s inversions in tonal music are tonal: mirrored by steps of the scale, so a major 3rd may become a minor 3rd. The drill’s inversions are tonal too. Read 11.2
In the drill: bar 1 is the motive, bar 2 the changed copy. Press ▶ Hear it to hear both. Start with the changes you can see at a glance:



Changes of rhythm:



Changes that add or alter notes:



The book’s own example of rhythmic change is the Pathétique Sonata. In the slow introduction, motive 1 is a dotted figure. It is heard here as the top line, as in the Classical Themes collection. The book marks motive 1 from the second note of each bar:



In the development section the motive comes back with its rhythm changed. In the next bar it is shortened and moved up a step.






NoteListen: the book’s examples of each alteration








Bach, Invention No. 1 in C, BWV 772: the motive in bar 1 is inverted in bar 3






Ray Noble, “The Very Thought of You” (Ella Fitzgerald): intervallic change






10cc, “I’m Not in Love”: intervallic change, one with a change of direction






Bach, Invention No. 1: augmentation of the motive’s first fragment






Holst, The Planets, “Uranus”: diminution of the first four notes






Salt-N-Pepa, “Push It”: rhythmic change






Beethoven, Pathétique Sonata, I: motive 1 in the introduction






Beethoven, Pathétique Sonata, I: motive 1 with its rhythm changed, in the development






Stevie Wonder, “Sir Duke”: ornamentation, and extension






Britney Spears, “Toxic”: retrograde
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Melodic Analysis: Practice for Chapter 11
text:
11.3 Fragment
Some motives are compound: long enough to break into smaller pieces, called fragments (some writers say “germs”). Each fragment can then be developed on its own. The book’s example is the seven-note motive that opens Bach’s Invention No. 1. It splits into two four-note fragments that overlap (they share the middle note). Bach later augments the first and inverts the second. Read 11.3
Listen back to the Beethoven Fifth example above: after the first two statements, only the three repeated notes are kept. That is a fragment of the motive.






NoteListen: Bach, Invention No. 1, the two fragments developed








Fragment “a” in augmentation






Fragment “b” inverted, leading to a cadence in G major
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Melodic Analysis: Practice for Chapter 11
text:
11.4 Phrase
A phrase is the smallest section that sounds complete. In classical music a phrase ends with a cadence (Chapter 7). In popular music a phrase may end without one: the melody reaches four bars, or a line of the lyric ends. Most phrases are four bars long, some eight. Five, six and seven bars also happen, and three is rare. Read 11.4
Listen and count: play each clip and count the bars until the music sounds finished. The book’s answers are in the captions, under Answer.



The Temptations, “My Girl”


Answer

Four bars, complete without a cadence.







Chaka Khan, “I’m Every Woman”


Answer

Four bars.







Beyoncé, “Irreplaceable”


Answer

Five bars. It ends on a minor iv chord, yet sounds complete.







Mozart, Symphony No. 40, K. 550, III


Answer

Six bars, ending with V7–i in G minor.







Mozart, Piano Sonata in C, K. 545, II


Answer

Eight bars.
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Melodic Analysis: Practice for Chapter 11
text:
11.5 Subphrase
A subphrase is bigger than a motive and smaller than a phrase. It is usually two bars, half of a four-bar phrase. Other books call it a phrase segment or phrase member. The book labels subphrases with letters. A repeat with small changes gets a prime: a′ (“a prime”), then a″. A subphrase that is only transposed keeps its letter (a, not a′). Read 11.5
Try it: label the subphrases of this Schubert theme (Classical Themes; two bars each):









TipOne answer





a (bars 1–2). a′ (bars 3–4): the same rhythm, but it starts on A, a step lower, and the leap up to F is bigger (a 4th instead of a 3rd). a″ (bars 5–6): bar 5 is bar 1 moved up a 4th, but the held note at the end is replaced by running eighth notes down from A. You could also argue that bars 5–6 are new (b) because of the eighth notes. This analysis is the site’s, not the book’s.









NoteListen: the book’s subphrase examples








Fleetwood Mac, “Don’t Stop”: a and a′ share their first six notes






LMFAO, “Party Rock Anthem”: a four-bar phrase, subphrases a and b






Journey, “Don’t Stop Believin’”: ideas at three levels (motive, subphrase, phrase)






“The Very Thought of You”: two-bar motives or subphrases? The book discusses the ambiguity
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Melodic Analysis: Practice for Chapter 11
text:
11.6 Everything together
All nine answers, major and minor keys. Set Questions to 20 for a score. Practice exercises with answers (11.6)



By ear only (the staff appears after you answer). Intervallic change and ornamentation are left out here, as they are hard to hear at speed:



The book’s exercise 4 analyses Schumann’s “First Loss” (Album for the Young, Op. 68 No. 16): motives with their alterations, and subphrases. Listen, then try it on the book’s score:



Schumann, “Erster Verlust” (First Loss)





More to analyse: the Classical Themes collection has over two thousand themes with recordings. Pick one, find its motive, and look for the motive’s next appearance in the theme: is it a sequence, or one of the alterations?






NoteFor teachers






Links with your settings: open a drill’s Settings, then Copy a link with these settings. Add &lock=1 for a test, &count=20 for a score.
The drill: a motive of two to six notes filling half a bar of 4/4, in a major or minor key (natural minor), then one change of it. The answers are the book’s seven alterations, with augmentation and diminution counted separately, plus Sequence. Inversion, augmentation and diminution may also be transposed. The other changes start on the motive’s own first note (retrograde on its last), so only the change itself differs. A question is asked only when exactly one answer fits, which the drill checks before asking. Ornamentation adds one passing tone or neighbor tone and keeps the motive’s length. Retrograde reverses the pitches and the rhythm.
Checked: node tests/lessons/motive-drill.test.js reads thousands of questions back from their notation and classifies each change with its own code. Exactly one alteration must fit, and it must be the answer. It also checks the bar lengths and that the notes played are the notes drawn.
Not drilled: fragments, phrases and subphrases. Recognizing them needs real melodies, and the analysis is often open to argument (the book says so for subphrases). They are taught with the book’s clips and short examples from the Classical Themes collection.
Analyses: the Beethoven Symphony No. 1 motives and the Pathétique motive are the book’s (Figures 11.1.1 and 11.2.8). The answers for the Beethoven Fifth and Schubert examples are the site’s own. The themes come from the Musical Theme Dataset (Barlow and Morgenstern’s themes, newly engraved; CC BY 4.0), as credited on the Classical Themes page.
Videos: the clips use the book’s YouTube links and start and end times. Each title was checked against YouTube.
The text on this page is written for the site, not copied from the book (the book is under the GNU Free Documentation License).

title: Jazz Theory: Practice for Chapter 31
text:
This page goes with Chapter 31, Introduction to Jazz Theory of Robert Hutchinson’s open textbook Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom. Read each section there first; the book is the reference for the terms and symbol rules used here. It builds on the seventh chords of Chapter 8 and the ii–V–I of Chapter 9.
Every drill has Settings, and is also on the Theory Drills page. The band demos play with ▶ Play; the strip at the bottom of the page shows the bar.
Typing chord symbols: as the book writes them, with b and # for ♭ and ♯. Δ can be typed maj, M or ^; minor as m, min or -; half-diminished as ø, h or m7b5; diminished as °, o or dim. Parentheses are optional: C7(#9b5), C7#9b5 and C7(♯9♭5) are the same.
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Jazz Theory: Practice for Chapter 31
text:
31.1 Jazz chord basics
The book’s ground rules for jazz chord symbols:

Every number up to the highest is there. C9 has the 7th as well; C13 is C E G B♭ D F A, everything up to the 13th. So for C E G B♭ D A (no 11th) the book writes C9(13). Players write C13 for that chord and leave out the clashing 11th, but the book is exact.
9, 11 and 13 are major or perfect (from the major scale) unless marked: 9 is the 2nd an octave up, 11 the 4th, 13 the 6th.
Δ or maj applies to the 7th: CΔ9 is a major 7th chord with a 9th, not a “major 9th”. m or – applies to the 3rd.
+ and – before 5, 9, 11 or 13 mean ♯ and ♭. C+7 is an augmented triad with a minor 7th.
“add 9” when there is a 9th but no 7th; 6/9 when there are a 6th and a 9th (C6/9 = C E G A D).
The minor-major 7th (mΔ7) is common in jazz too.
Double sharps and flats get respelled (and sometimes B♯, C♭, E♯, F♭), the way a pianist would think of them.
The bass is the root here; slash chords come later. Read 31.1
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Jazz Theory: Practice for Chapter 31
text:
31.2 Chord symbol specifics
Three rules for choosing between names:

6 or 13: call it 6 only without a 7th. With a 7th, it is 13.
11 or sus: sus (the 4th) replaces the 3rd. With a 3rd present, the 4th is an 11. C7sus is C F G B♭.
♭5 or ♯11: with an ordinary 5th in the chord, F♯ over C is ♯11. Without one, either name is fine. Read 31.2

The drills follow these rules when they check a name. A name is right when it means the same notes over the same root. A 5th the chord leaves out is fine: C9 counts for C E B♭ D.
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Jazz Theory: Practice for Chapter 31
text:
31.3 Altered dominant 7ths
A dominant 7th is altered when its 5th or 9th is raised or lowered (or both). The root, 3rd and 7th never change. - ♯5 may be written as ♭6 on the staff (G♯ or A♭ over C), to agree with the ♭7. - ♯9 is usually written as a ♭10 (E♭ over C), so the chord seems to have both a major and minor 3rd. It is still not a minor chord: ♭11 isn’t used, because that note is the major 3rd. - The book prefers ♯5 to ♭13. ♭13 means the 5th is there too; ♯5 means it isn’t. - 7alt says the 5th and 9th are altered without saying how, so it doesn’t name exact notes. - Dominants are usually altered when they work as dominants, resolving down a 5th, and usually left plain when they are the tonic, as in the first chord of a blues. Read 31.3
Write the altered dominants. Either spelling of ♯5 and ♯9 counts, as the book allows:

title: Jazz Theory: Practice for Chapter 31
text:
31.5 Writing jazz chords
Start from all the major and perfect notes up to the 13th (1 3 5 7 9 11 13: on D, D F♯ A C♯ E G B). Keep what the symbol’s highest number includes, then change what the symbol changes. DmΔ11: minor 3rd, major 7th, then 9 and 11, so D F A C♯ E G. E7(♯11♯9♯5): E G♯ B D, then ♯5 (B♯, written C to agree with the D), ♯9 (F𝄪, written G) and ♯11 (A♯, or B♭). Read 31.5

All the chords, on every root:

title: Jazz Theory: Practice for Chapter 31
text:
31.6 Analysing jazz chords
The same scratch-paper method in reverse. Write all the major and perfect notes up to the 13th on the bass note. Compare, and work out, in order: 1. the quality of the 7th chord; 2. the upper notes (9, 11, 13); 3. what is altered; 4. what may be respelled.
Two checks from the book’s examples: - Spot the sus. With no 3rd but a 4th, the chord is sus, and the 4th isn’t also an 11. - 5ths are often left out. Read 31.6



With sus, added-note, altered and other chords:
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Jazz Theory: Practice for Chapter 31
text:
31.7 Guide tones and voicings
The guide tones are a chord’s 3rd and 7th: they decide its quality. In a progression by fifths (ii–V–I, iii–vi–ii–V), each guide tone moves by a half or whole step, or stays put. Below, dominant 7ths go round the circle of fifths: the bass plays the roots and the right hand plays only the 3rd and 7th. Each chord’s 3rd becomes the next one’s 7th, and each 7th falls a half step to the next 3rd. The engraving is this site’s, of the exercise the book describes:



Two chords a tritone apart (C7 and F♯7) share the same guide tones, swapped: that is what makes the tritone substitution in 31.8 work. Read 31.7
Name the guide tones of each chord:



The book’s voicings have five notes. In close voicings, the root is in the left hand and the other four sit close together in the right, with the 3rd or the 7th lowest. In spread voicings, the root, 3rd and 7th are lowest, with the other notes above them, often a 4th or 5th apart. (A sus chord’s 4th takes the 3rd’s place; a 6th takes the 7th’s.) This drill plays close voicings. Name the quality by ear: listen to the guide tones first.
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Jazz Theory: Practice for Chapter 31
text:
31.8 Standard progressions

ii–V–I
The most common progression in jazz. The book’s examples are “Autumn Leaves”, “What Is This Thing Called Love”, “Tune-Up”, “Pent Up House”, “Lady Bird” and “Firm Roots”. In major the book voices it Dm9 – G9(13) – CΔ9, in minor Dm7(♭5) – G7alt – Cm6/9. The band plays both. (The band’s chord symbols are written its own way; it plays a 13 chord without the 11th, as players do.)



Type the ii–V–I in each key. Any usual version counts: Dm7, Dm9 or Dm11; any dominant on V; CΔ7, CΔ9, C6 or C6/9.








Turnarounds and tritone substitution
A turnaround fills the last two bars of a tune with movement back to I: iii–vi–ii–V (or I–vi–ii–V). Make every chord a dominant 7th (E7–A7–D7–G7 in C). Then any of them can be swapped for the dominant 7th a tritone away, which has the same guide tones: E7–E♭7–D7–D♭7. The bass then slides down by half steps. Read 31.8



The same trick works on V–I alone: ♭II7 for V7. In C, the book’s example puts D♭9(13) in place of G7(♯9♯5). These two chords have the same upper notes; only the bass differs.



Listen: V7 or its tritone substitute? (Listen to the bass on the third bar.)





The blues
The book closes 31.8 with two choruses of a jazz blues, one in each kind of voicing, and points out that the voices move by step or by a 3rd. The site’s blues lessons cover the jazz blues and its substitutions with the band.
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Jazz Theory: Practice for Chapter 31
text:
31.9 Scales
The book’s scales are for improvising: they tell a soloist which notes go with a chord. - The blues scale is the minor pentatonic with ♭5 added: 1 ♭3 4 ♭5 5 ♭7. ♭3 and ♭5 are the blue notes. The book’s example is “Sunshine of Your Love”. - The bebop dominant scale is Mixolydian with the major 7th added as a passing note going down (8 – 7 – ♭7). A first step in improvising: run it down in eighth notes from a chord tone on the downbeat. - The rest of the book’s table: the classical scales, the modes, the modes of melodic minor, and the synthetic scales (whole tone, octatonic, hexatonic). Read 31.9






NoteListen: the book’s example








The blues scale: Jack Bruce and Eric Clapton, “Sunshine of Your Love” (Cream)








Name each scale from the book’s table. Start with the modes and the jazz scales:



The whole table, every root:



Write them:
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Jazz Theory: Practice for Chapter 31
text:
31.10 Chord-scale relationships
To find a scale for a chord, write the chord’s notes (with every extension and alteration) as a scale inside an octave. Then fill the gaps, avoiding augmented 2nds and two half steps in a row. CΔ7(♯11) gives C D E F♯ G A B: Lydian. Where a chord has a minor 3rd, the gap can be filled two ways, so the book lists two scales. The key matters too. Over the opening Fm7 of “All the Things You Are” (vi7 in A♭), play F natural minor, not F Dorian: Dorian’s D♮ would clash with the key’s D♭. Read 31.10
Which scale does the book’s table give for each chord? Where it lists two, either is right:
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Jazz Theory: Practice for Chapter 31
text:
31.11 Harmonizing the bebop scale
The book shows Mark Levine’s way (from The Jazz Theory Book) of harmonizing the bebop major scale in four parts. The tonic chord alternates with vii°7 chords in different inversions, so every passing note gets a diminished 7th. The book suggests singing each part, and points to Count Basie’s “London Bridge Is Falling Down” for a similar harmonized scale. Read 31.11






NoteListen: the book’s example








Count Basie and His Orchestra, “London Bridge Is Falling Down”
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Jazz Theory: Practice for Chapter 31
text:
31.12 Everything together
The book’s practice exercises: 31.12. Its voice-leading exercise (five-voice close and spread voicings through a progression) needs four- and five-part writing, which this site can’t check yet.















NoteFor teachers






Links with your settings: open a drill’s Settings, then Copy a link with these settings. Add &lock=1 for a test, &count=20 for a score.
Chords: exactly the book’s Figures 31.4.1–8, on twelve roots (C D♭ D E♭ E F F♯ G A♭ A B♭ B) or the naturals. The drawn chords are stacked in thirds on a grand staff, ♯5 written as ♭6 and ♯9 as ♭10 next to a ♭7, as in the book’s figures.
Checking a name: the typed symbol is read by the book’s rules (31.1–31.2) and must mean the same notes over the same root, spelled as drawn (D♭9 is wrong for C♯9). A 5th the chord leaves out is fine, so C7(♯11) counts for C E G♭ B♭ (31.2). With a 5th or ♯5 present the match is exact, so C7(♭13) is wrong for C7(♯5) (31.3). C13 is wrong for C E G B♭ D A, which the book calls C9(13); “7alt” isn’t accepted as a name, since it doesn’t say which alterations.
Checking written notes: the root must be spelled as in the symbol; the other notes are checked by sound over the root, in any order, since the book allows respelling altered notes.
ii–V–I: a typed answer counts if the roots are right and the chords are of the right kind (m7-type ii, half-diminished ii in minor, any dominant V, a major- or minor-type tonic). The book’s own versions are shown as the answer.
The ear drill plays the book’s close voicing (root in the bass, the other notes within an octave, the 3rd or 7th lowest) on a random bass note.
Band demos: the band’s symbols are its own (G13 for the book’s G9(13)); its voicings are its own, not the book’s. The charts are this site’s examples of the progressions the book describes. Nobody has yet listened to check them.
The guide-tone example is this site’s engraving of the exercise the book describes in 31.7.1.
Not here: the book’s five-voice voice-leading exercise (31.12 ex. 3) and its blues choruses (31.8.3).

title: Exercise Builder
text:
Make a set of exercises from the chapters of Robert Hutchinson’s Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom you choose. Answer them here and press Check my answers, or Print worksheet for class (tick with the answer key for a copy with answers on a page of its own).
Sharing a set: the questions come from the number in the link (seed). Copy Link to this set and everyone who opens it gets the same questions. New set makes different ones.
The chorales are made by the site, not taken from real music: four voices, four-bar phrases, using the chords of the chapters you chose and the ones before them. Every one is checked for voice-leading errors before it’s shown. Writing notes: type each note with its octave (middle C is C4), e.g. E4 D4 C#4. Your notes appear in the score as you type.









NoteFor teachers






Chapters set the chords in the chorales (up to the highest chapter ticked, favouring the ones ticked: 7 triads and cadences, 8 seventh chords, 16 inversions and the cadential 6/4, 17 secondary dominants, 18 secondary diminished chords, 19 mixture, 20 the Neapolitan), and which drill questions appear. Periods need chapter 13. Augmented sixths (21) and jazz (31) appear as drill questions, not in chorales.
Roman numerals are checked against the generator’s analysis, in the book’s figures (V65, I6, iiø7, V7/V, vii°7/V, N6, ♭VI). The cadential 6/4 is labelled I64 (i64); Cad64 and V64 are also accepted.
Cadences are read from the voiced chorale (7.4): PAC needs V or V7 to I, both in root position, with the tonic in the soprano; otherwise V or vii° to I is an IAC.
Periods (13.3): the first cadence weaker (HC or IAC) than the second (PAC). Parallel when the two phrases begin with the same bars, contrasting otherwise. Two phrases ending PAC count as “not a period”. The book’s other combinations (double periods, phrase groups, elisions) aren’t generated.
Writing a voice: any answer without voice-leading errors in its bars (ranges, crossing, spacing, parallel 5ths and octaves, doubling the leading tone or a 7th, a chord with no root or 3rd) counts. Unresolved leading tones and 7ths, and direct 5ths and octaves, are pointed out but not marked wrong. One good answer is in the key.
Notation answers: typed into the exercise for now. The choice of input is a setting (input= in the link), so the Notation page can be added as another way in.
Checked: node tests/lessons/exercises.test.js (thousands of chorales through the voice-leading checker, which is itself tested on planted errors) and node tests/lessons/exercise-builder.cdp.js (the page).

title: Augmented Sixth Chords: Practice for Chapter 21
text:
This page goes with Chapter 21, Augmented Sixth Chords of Robert Hutchinson’s open textbook Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom. Read each section there first; the book is the reference for the terms used here. It follows the other chromatic chords: secondary dominants (Chapter 17) and secondary diminished chords (Chapter 18).
Every drill has Settings, and is also on the Theory Drills page. ▶ Hear it plays the chord and then where it goes: to V, or (German sixths) to I64 and then V.
Typing: notes with spaces, bass first (Ab C Eb F#). Chord symbols as Ab7, Ab7(b5), Ab7(no5). The chords’ names as It, Fr, Ger, EnGer (with or without +6).
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Augmented Sixth Chords: Practice for Chapter 21
text:
21.1 Augmented sixth chords
An augmented sixth chord leads to the dominant from both sides at once. ♭6 in the bass falls a half step to 5, and ♯4 above it rises a half step to 5. The two notes are an augmented sixth apart, so they move outward to an octave. In C, that’s A♭ and F♯ moving to the two Gs. In a minor key, ♭6 is already in the key signature, so only ♯4 needs an accidental. These chords do a pre-dominant’s job: they come before V. Read 21.1
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Augmented Sixth Chords: Practice for Chapter 21
text:
21.2 The three types
All three start from the same three notes: ♭6, 1 and ♯4. What’s added decides the name:

In C

(major only)



The EnGer+6 sounds the same as the German sixth, but ♭3 is spelled ♯2, because it rises to 3 of a major I64. It only occurs in major keys. The book notes that the national names have no known reason behind them. Read 21.2
Write each chord, bass first. Start with C and keys near it:



Then add the enharmonic German and more keys:

title: Augmented Sixth Chords: Practice for Chapter 21
text:
21.3 Analysing augmented sixth chords
Stack any of these chords in thirds and you find a diminished third (A♭ C E♭ F♯ in C becomes F♯ A♭ C E♭, where F♯ to A♭ is a diminished 3rd). No chord met before this chapter has one, so the book’s rule is: a diminished third means an augmented sixth chord. Then find ♭6 and ♯4, and the remaining note tells you the type. Read 21.3
Name each chord on the staff (keys i, f, g, e):
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Augmented Sixth Chords: Practice for Chapter 21
text:
21.4 Lead-sheet symbols
A chord symbol shows root, quality and inversion, not where notes go, and there is no chord symbol with a diminished third. So for lead-sheet symbols, the book treats each augmented sixth chord as a dominant seventh on ♭6 whose seventh is misspelled (F♯ for G♭):

It+6 → A♭7 (no 5th)
Fr+6 → A♭7(♭5)
Ger+6 and EnGer+6 → A♭7

That’s how the chords are written in jazz and pop, and it matches how they sound. Read 21.4
From the name to the symbol:



And back. A plain 7th chord on ♭6 going to a major I64 can be spelled either way, so both German answers count there:
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Augmented Sixth Chords: Practice for Chapter 21
text:
21.5 Examples
The book’s examples, cut where the book cuts them. The popular-music ones (Ellington, Coltrane, Mancini, Fiona Apple, Menken) spell the chord as a 7th chord on ♭6, as in 21.4. “Friend Like Me” repeats Am – F7 – E: i – Ger+6 – V. Read 21.5






NoteListen: the book’s examples








It+6. Beethoven, Symphony No. 5, I (C minor, written as an augmented sixth)






It+6 spelled as a 7th chord without its 5th. Duke Ellington, “It Don’t Mean a Thing (If It Ain’t Got That Swing)” (Tony Bennett and Lady Gaga)






Fr+6. Schubert, Winterreise, “Der Wegweiser”






Ger+6 to I64. Rossini, William Tell Overture






Ger+6 (as VI7) to V. John Coltrane, “Mr. P.C.”

21.6 Telling chromatic chords apart
What to look for first, after the book’s Table 21.6.1:

The German sixth and a dominant 7th on ♭6 sound the same. Only the spelling tells them apart: - A♭ C E♭ F♯ in C is a Ger+6, going to V. - A♭ C E♭ G♭ is a dominant 7th, V7 of D♭. D♭ is the Neapolitan in C, so the chord is V7/N. (Naming it V7/N is this site’s addition; the book’s chapter on the Neapolitan is Chapter 20.)

21.7 Descending chromatic bass lines
A bass line that falls by half steps from 1 to 5 (1 – 7 – ♭7 – 6 – ♭6 – 5) turns up in music of every century since the 1600s, under many different chords. The book’s table lists how each of its examples harmonizes it. Read 21.7
Here is the harmonization the book lists for Beethoven’s 32 Variations in C minor (i – V6 – V42/iv – IV6 – Ger+6 – i64), here with a V – i added to finish. The voicing is this site’s, not Beethoven’s:

title: Augmented Sixth Chords: Practice for Chapter 21
text:
21.8 Chromatic pre-dominant chords
The chapters on chromatic chords add new members to the pre-dominant group. Besides IV and ii there are now V/V and vii°/V, the borrowed iv and iiø7, the Neapolitan N6, and the three augmented sixths. Read 21.8
Five of them have ♭6 or 4 in the bass, so they are easy to confuse by ear. This drill plays I – ? – I64 – V – I and asks for the second chord. Things to listen for: - iv6 and N6 are plain triads. - It+6 is thin: only three different notes. - Ger+6 sounds like a dominant 7th. - Fr+6 has its own colour: all four of its notes belong to one whole-tone scale.
Keys: v, n, i, f, g.



In major and minor, with the Neapolitan too:

title: Reger: On the Theory of Modulation
text:
In 1903 Max Reger published a short book of modulations: one hundred examples, each a few chords long, that get from one key to another, often a distant one, as quickly as possible. Most go by a pivot chord: a chord that belongs to both keys, very often the Neapolitan (N⁶) or a dominant of the dominant (V/V). Each new key is then confirmed with a cadence: Cad⁶₄ (I⁶₄), V, I.
The examples are grouped by the key they start from, in the book’s order. Where an example has an A and a B version, B goes to the minor key with the same tonic. How to read the labels and use the scores: Analysed Scores.
crumbs: Reger: On the Theory of Modulation

title: Reger: On the Theory of Modulation
text:
Things to find

The pivot: in each example, find the first chord after the new key is named. Which chord is it in the old key?
The Neapolitan: N⁶ appears in 45 of the examples, mostly the far ones (from C major to the sharp keys, 6–12 and 24–31, and all of 86–99 except 98). V/V appears in 25. In each, is it the pivot, or does it come after the new key is reached?
Enharmonic spellings: the far keys are written as they are named, so C♭ major and A♯ minor appear with all their flats and sharps. The keys B𝄫 major (21) and E♯ minor (30) are spelled out too.

title: Analysed Scores
text: Real music, analysed by experts, with the Roman numerals under the notes where each chord begins. Each piece has its own page. The analyses come from When in Rome, a collection of harmonic analyses gathered by Mark Gotham and others.

title: Analysed Scores
text:
The pieces

Bach: “O Haupt voll Blut und Wunden” (“O Sacred Head, Now Wounded”), a four-part chorale from the St Matthew Passion, analysed by Dmitri Tymoczko. Short, with a key change at nearly every phrase.
Beethoven: “Moonlight” Sonata, I, the whole first movement, analysed by Tsung-Ping Chen and Li Su. Slow harmony, the Neapolitan, a tour of keys, and the form part by part.
The library: 360 of Bach’s four-part chorales, 22 preludes from The Well-Tempered Clavier Book I, 41 movements of Beethoven’s piano sonatas and 39 of Mozart’s, and 137 nineteenth-century songs (Schubert, the Schumanns, Hensel, Brahms, Wolf, Reichardt, Lang, Chaminade, Coleridge-Taylor and others), each with its analysis under the notes, on one page with a searchable list.
Harmony by the Numbers: every analysis in the corpus counted: the chords each repertoire uses, what follows what, how often the chromatic chords appear, where the music modulates, and pieces to find each chord in.
Bach: Brandenburg Concerto No. 2, a listening guide to all three movements: the four soloists, ritornello form, and each movement bar by bar with annotated excerpts (no full score yet).
Kodály: Dances of Galánta, a listening guide: verbunkos, the ten old Viennese tunes Kodály borrowed, and the piece section by section with each tune set against his version (no full score yet).
Reger: On the Theory of Modulation, all 100 short examples from Max Reger’s 1903 book of modulations, from one key to any other in a few chords, analysed by Néstor Nápoles López and others.
Modulation Finder: about 800 modulations in one list, sorted by the starting and ending key’s mode and the distance between them in half steps: the 200 textbook examples below, and short passages around the key changes in Bach’s chorales and 19th-century songs.
More modulation examples from harmony textbooks, also analysed by Nápoles López and others:

Rimsky-Korsakov: Practical Manual of Harmony, 37 short four-voice modulations from C major or A minor.
Tchaikovsky: Guide to the Practical Study of Harmony, 25 modulations from C major.
Aldwell and Schachter: Harmony and Voice Leading, seven examples: Bach chorales, Mozart and a progression.
Kostka and Payne: Tonal Harmony, 15 examples from Bach, Mozart, Beethoven, Schubert, Dvořák and Tchaikovsky.

title: Analysed Scores
text:
Reading the labels
A key followed by a colon (d:) means the music has moved to that key (capital letter major, small letter minor); the numerals after it are in the new key. The figures are those of Chapter 16 (6, 64, 7, 65, 43, 42). ° is diminished and ø half-diminished, as in the book. V/iv and vii°7/V are the secondary chords of Chapters 17 and 18; N6 is the Neapolitan. A numeral sits under the bass where its chord starts; where the bass holds a note through a chord change, the note is written as tied notes so the label has a place (it sounds the same).

title: Analysed Scores
text:
Using the scores

Play: Space plays and pauses. Click a note to move there.
Resizing: drag the line at the right edge of a score to make it wider or narrower (double-click it to reset); the bars re-flow to fit, and the size is kept for every score.
Keys: above a score, the key strip shows every key the analyst names, in order, as wide as the time spent there. Click a key to light its bars and hear them.

title: Bach: Brandenburg Concerto No. 2
text:
Bach signed the dedication of six concertos to Christian Ludwig, Margrave of Brandenburg, on 24 March 1721, while he was music director at the court of Cöthen. He had probably played for the Margrave two years earlier, on a trip to Berlin to collect a new harpsichord, and been asked to “send some of his compositions”. No. 2 is the loudest and most brilliant of the six: four soloists, one of them a high trumpet, against strings and continuo.
Bar numbers like 8⁴ mean bar 8, beat 4: many sections start on an upbeat.
Freiburger Barockorchester on period instruments, with the score scrolling, so you can follow the bar numbers below.

title: Bach: Brandenburg Concerto No. 2
text:
The soloists
A concerto grosso sets a small group of soloists (the concertino) against the full string band (the ripieno), with the continuo (harpsichord and a bass instrument) underneath everything. Here the concertino is unusual: four instruments that sound nothing alike.


Trumpet A natural trumpet, with no valves, playing in its highest register. Bach writes “tromba”; some argue for a horn, but a high trumpet is the usual reading.


Recorder Bach writes “fiauto”: a treble recorder in F, not the transverse flute he asks for in No. 5. Modern performances sometimes use a flute.


Oboe Close to the modern oboe, with fewer keys.


Violin Gut strings and a lighter, shorter bow than a modern violin.


The continuo is cembalo (harpsichord) and violone, a large bowed bass that sounds an octave below the written note, usually doubling the cello. Notice that the trumpet drops out completely in the slow movement.

title: Bach: Brandenburg Concerto No. 2
text:
Ritornello form
The fast movements of a Baroque concerto are usually in ritornello form: the full band plays a theme (the ritornello, “little return”), and it comes back, often shortened and in new keys, between episodes for the soloists.
Tutti (“all”) and solo describe who is playing. Ritornello and episode describe what material is played. They usually line up, but not always: in Bach a soloist can play ritornello material, and the full band can join a solo passage.
A ritornello often has three parts (Wilhelm Fischer’s names, 1915):

Initial statement (Vordersatz): the opening idea that makes the theme recognisable.
Spinning out (Fortspinnung): a sequence that develops it.
Ending (Epilog): a short closing cadence figure.

Later ritornellos may use any one of the three parts. The keys usually follow a plan like this:

I → V


Ritornello 2

Ritornello 3

Ritornello 4

See it in Vivaldi: Violin Concerto Op. 3 No. 6, I, the first ritornello marked up

  


Vivaldi’s ritornellos are easy to hear. Bach’s are much harder to find in this concerto, which is the point of the next section.

title: Bach: Brandenburg Concerto No. 2
text:
I. [Allegro], F major
The boundaries between ritornello and solo are blurred: the soloists play the ritornello theme, and long stretches are counterpoint between them. Some passages could be called either. Take the outline as one reasonable reading.
The ritornello has two ideas played at once: Motive A in the soloists and violins (flute, oboe, solo violin and violin I in unison, violin II in thirds) and Motive B, running semiquavers in the lower strings. The trumpet can’t play Motive A in this key, so it enters in bar 2⁴ with an ascending figure of its own, which returns later.

Is it a fugue or a ritornello movement? It opens like a fugue: the trumpet plays a subject alone over continuo, and the other soloists answer it in turn. title: Bach: “O Haupt voll Blut und Wunden”
text:
Things to find

The key changes: the phrases end in F, then D minor, then B♭ and G minor, then C and back to F. Each new key is reached through its own dominant, as in Chapter 22.
Bar 6: IV⁶₄ over a held F in the bass, then I.
Bar 7: IM⁷. The analyst’s notes give other readings: a deceptive cadence to vi⁶, or IM⁷ followed by a lower neighbor.

title: Accompanimental Textures: Practice for Chapter 14
text:
This page goes with Chapter 14, Accompanimental Textures of Robert Hutchinson’s open textbook Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom. Read each section there first. The book shows each texture in notation and in recordings. Here you can play each one: the site’s backing band plays the same chords in each texture, and you switch between textures while it plays.
How the demos work: press ▶ Play, then try the buttons under it. The band keeps going and changes texture at the next bar. Who plays turns each part on and off. Under the buttons the band’s whole pass is written out when Play starts, before it sounds, so you can see what is coming. (The quiz shows the notes only once you have answered.) Tempo and Stop are in the strip at the bottom of the page. The quiz at the end plays a texture without naming it, and you say which one it is.

title: Accompanimental Textures: Practice for Chapter 14
text:
14.1 Texture
The book looks at texture two ways. Vertically: how many notes sound at once (how full the chords are, how many voices there are). Horizontally: how busy the rhythm is (are the most common note values long or short?). Read 14.1
Below are the same four chords played three ways. Held chords are full but slow. Repeated eighth notes keep the same notes and make the rhythm busy. An arpeggio is busy too, but it plays one note at a time, so it is thinner at any one moment.









NoteListen: the book’s two examples








Samuel Barber, Adagio for Strings: many voices, long notes






Mozart, String Quartet K. 428, IV: four voices, mostly sixteenth notes

title: Accompanimental Textures: Practice for Chapter 14
text:
14.2 Chorale texture
In a chorale texture there is a new chord for (nearly) every melody note, so all the parts move in the same rhythm. This is also called homorhythmic. A hymn played on the piano is the plainest case. The band’s hymn style below holds each chord until the next one, with three voices over the bass. With a melody on top, it would be a chorale texture. Read 14.2 · Pattern lesson: Hymn, four parts



The second button is the book’s quarter-note texture: a chord on every beat. The book’s practice exercises ask for it (17.7, exercise 3).

title: Accompanimental Textures: Practice for Chapter 14
text:
14.3 Arpeggiated accompaniments
An arpeggio plays a chord’s notes one after another instead of all together. The bass usually holds the root underneath, as in the book’s first example, Beethoven’s Moonlight Sonata. The band can arpeggiate up and back down, or rock between the lowest and highest notes. Alberti bass goes low, high, middle, high, again and again. Read 14.3 · Pattern lessons: Arpeggio, up and down · Arpeggio, low and high · Alberti bass



The book points out the Alberti pattern in a Mozart sonata, and the same pattern lower down and in E minor in “Pipeline”. Here is Alberti bass on its own, in major (bass off: the pattern supplies its own low note):

title: Accompanimental Textures: Practice for Chapter 14
text:
14.4 Block chord accompaniments
Block chords strike all the notes of the chord together. What makes one block-chord accompaniment different from another is its rhythm. The book names four:

“1 (2) &”: two chords a bar, on beat 1 and on the and of 2. Count it aloud and stay silent on the number in brackets.
The “Barbara Ann” rhythm, over two bars: 1 2 3 (4) & | (1) & (2) & 3.
Repeated eighth-note chords: a chord on every eighth note, in classical music and in rock.
Repeated quarter-note chords: a chord on every beat.

Read 14.4 · Pattern lessons: Charleston (the 1 (2) & rhythm) · Barbara Ann · Driving eighths · Quarter-note chords



The band calls the “1 (2) &” rhythm the Charleston: jazz musicians use that name for the same two hits. The book points out that the bass in “Let’s Get It On” and “Thinking Out Loud” has a similar rhythm. The bass here plays the dotted 1, and of 2, 3 line with it. Turn the drums and bass off to hear the chords alone.

title: Accompanimental Textures: Practice for Chapter 14
text:
14.5 Afterbeats and off-beats
Afterbeats is Arnold Schoenberg’s word for repeated chords that come after the downbeat. Off-beats are chords that keep to the upbeats and stay off the downbeats. The book looks at two styles built on off-beats: polka and reggae. Read 14.5 · Pattern lessons: Boom-chick · Every off-beat
Polka: the bass on the beat and the chord in between. The band counts the bar in four, so the chords fall on 2 and 4. Counted in a fast two, those are the off-beats.



Reggae: short chords on the and of every beat, often on electric guitar, over a drum part (the one-drop) that leaves beat 1 empty.









NoteListen: the book’s afterbeat, polka and reggae examples

title: Accompanimental Textures: Practice for Chapter 14
text:
14.6 The 3–2 son clave and 3+3+2
The 3–2 son clave is a two-bar rhythm at the root of Afro-Cuban music: three strokes in the first bar and two in the second. Its first bar divides eight eighth notes into 3+3+2. In popular music it is also called the Bo Diddley beat. The 3+3+2 bar on its own is everywhere in pop. In sixteenth notes it is called tresillo, and the book follows it into the habanera and the reggaeton beat. Read 14.6 · Pattern lessons: 3–2 clave in the chords · 3+3+2 · The Bo Diddley beat on drums · Dembow (reggaeton)



The habanera bass (Bizet, Carmen) and the reggaeton beat: long chords, the bass on 3+3+2, the dembow on the drums.

Some songs are known by their riff: a short bass (or guitar) figure repeated under the chords. The band’s bass lines are not those riffs. They are general patterns that fit any chords. title: Country train beat
text: Open the Country train beat style in the Backing Track

title: Country train beat
text:
What it is
The country rhythm that sounds like a steam train: a snare (often with brushes) on every eighth note, accented on 2 and 4, a bass on root and fifth, and a boom-chicka guitar.

title: Country train beat
text:
A little history
The sound is most associated with Johnny Cash’s Tennessee Two at Sun Records in Memphis: Luther Perkins’ muted boom-chicka electric guitar and Marshall Grant’s slapped bass on Folsom Prison Blues (1955) and I Walk the Line (1956). Drummer W. S. Holland joined in 1960 and the train beat became a drum pattern. Train songs had been part of country and blues since the 1920s (Jimmie Rodgers), and the beat has stayed in rockabilly, bluegrass-flavoured country and country rock.

title: Country train beat
text:
The band’s version

Bass: Root and fifth. Comping: a boom-chicka strum. Drums: train beat.

title: Swing
text: Open the Swing style in the Backing Track

title: Swing
text:
What it is
The rhythm section of small-group jazz from the late 1930s onward: a bass that plays a note on every beat, a drummer whose main voice is the ride cymbal (ding, ding-a, ding, ding-a) with the hi-hat closing on 2 and 4, and a piano or guitar that “comps” (accompanies, complements): short chords placed off the beat, answering the soloist instead of marking time.

title: Swing
text:
A little history
In the 1920s the bass part of a jazz band was usually a tuba or a slapped string bass playing on beats 1 and 3 (the two-beat feel; see Jazz ballad). In the Count Basie band of the mid-1930s, bassist Walter Page walked four even beats a bar, guitarist Freddie Green strummed a quiet chord on every beat, and drummer Jo Jones moved the time-keeping from the bass drum to the hi-hat. Basie himself played sparse fills instead of a full stride left hand. That “All-American Rhythm Section” is where the modern swing feel comes from.
In the 1940s bebop drummers (Kenny Clarke, then Max Roach) moved the pulse to the ride cymbal and used the snare and bass drum for accents (“dropping bombs”). Pianists such as Bud Powell stopped playing on every beat and comped in short syncopated stabs. By the late 1950s, rootless left-hand voicings (Bill Evans, Wynton Kelly, Red Garland) became the standard piano sound: the bassist has the root, so the pianist plays the 3rd, 7th and colour tones. That is the sound the band’s piano uses here.

title: Swing
text:
The band’s version

Bass: Walking: root on beat 1, chord tones and scale steps, an approach note on beat 4.
Comping: syncopated rhythms chosen from a set of figures (the Charleston, anticipations, and so on).
Drums: ride-cymbal pattern, hi-hat on 2 and 4, light comping on the snare.
Voicings: rootless piano voicings, shell voicings on guitar. Players add unmarked 9ths and 13ths.

Real walking lines move far more freely than any rule set; the band’s bassist is a beginner’s model.

title: Stride Piano
text: Open the Stride piano style in the Backing Track

title: Stride Piano
text:
What it is
Solo piano music from Harlem in the late 1910s to the 1930s. The left hand does the work of a whole rhythm section: a low bass note on beats 1 and 3 and a chord in the middle of the keyboard on 2 and 4, the hand leaping (“striding”) between them on every beat. The right hand plays the melody, decorated, over it.
Stride and boogie-woogie grew up side by side: both are piano music for dancing at parties, both put a whole band into the left hand, and both feed into swing. They differ in what the left hand does. The lesson Two Left Hands plays them side by side.

title: Stride Piano
text:
A little history
Stride comes out of ragtime. A Scott Joplin rag already has the oom-pah left hand, written as a march. In New York around the First World War, pianists such as James P. Johnson, Luckey Roberts and Willie “The Lion” Smith played it faster and swung it, took it from rags to popular songs and the blues, and added runs, tenths and cross-rhythms. They played at rent parties, where tenants paid the rent by charging for food, drink and music, and in cutting contests against each other. Johnson’s Carolina Shout was the test piece: Duke Ellington learned it from a piano roll, slowed down.
Johnson’s pupil Fats Waller made stride popular on records and radio, from 1934 with a small band, Fats Waller and His Rhythm: bass, drums and guitar playing in two under the piano’s left hand. That is the sound this style copies. Art Tatum took stride to its technical limit; Count Basie began as a stride pianist and pared it down to almost nothing; Thelonious Monk kept stride passages in his playing all his life.
Johnson also wrote Charleston (1923). Its rhythm, a long note on 1 and a short one on the and of 2, is the Charleston comping figure jazz pianists still use.

title: Stride Piano
text:
The band’s version

Comping: Stride: on the piano, a low bass note on 1 and 3 (the root as an octave where a chord starts, its fifth on beat 3) and the chord in the middle of the keyboard on 2 and 4. On the guitar it is plain boom-chick.
Bass: Two-feel: half notes on 1 and 3, with the piano’s left hand.
Drums: Jazz time, lightly.
Voicings: plain triads and seventh chords, all their notes.

Real stride left hands reach for tenths, walk them up and down between chords, and break the pattern for a run; the right hand carries the tune. The band’s pianist keeps the pattern and plays no melody. That is your part.

title: Reggaeton
text: Open the Reggaeton style in the Backing Track

title: Reggaeton
text:
What it is
Spanish-language dance music from Puerto Rico and Panama, built on the dembow: the kick on every beat, and the snare on the last sixteenth of beat 1 and the and of 2 (and again in beats 3 and 4), a 3+3+2 in sixteenths over each half bar, under long synth chords and a rapped or sung vocal.

title: Reggaeton
text:
A little history
The rhythm is named after Shabba Ranks’ Jamaican dancehall record Dem Bow (1990), whose riddim (the backing track, by Steely & Clevie, built on their Poco Man Jam) was copied everywhere. In Panama, artists such as El General sang Spanish lyrics over dancehall riddims (reggae en español). In Puerto Rico in the 1990s DJ Playero and others made underground mixtapes on the same beats; the name reggaeton took hold around the turn of the century. Daddy Yankee’s Gasolina (2004) was the international breakthrough, Luis Fonsi and Daddy Yankee’s Despacito (2017) one of the most-streamed songs ever, and Bad Bunny the genre’s biggest star of the 2020s.

title: Reggaeton
text:
The band’s version

Bass: 3+3+2 (tresillo). Comping: long held chords. Drums: dembow.

title: Ragtime
text: Open the Ragtime style in the Backing Track

title: Ragtime
text:
What it is
Composed piano music from about 1895 to 1920, built like a march: several 16-bar strains, a left hand that plays a bass note on the beat and a chord off it, and a right hand whose melody is syncopated (“ragged”) against that steady left hand. Its eighth notes are straight, not swung.
Ragtime is where stride came from: the stride left hand is the ragtime left hand, played faster and swung, with songs and the blues in place of written rags. The lesson Two Left Hands plays the two one after the other.

title: Ragtime
text:
A little history
Ragtime grew among Black pianists in the saloons and dance halls of the Mississippi valley in the 1890s, and became the first African American music to sell across the country, mostly as sheet music for parlour pianos. Scott Joplin’s Maple Leaf Rag (1899), published in Sedalia, Missouri, sold hundreds of thousands of copies. Joplin, James Scott and Joseph Lamb wrote the “classic rags”; Tin Pan Alley turned out ragtime songs by the thousand. Bands played rags too, and ragtime fed straight into early jazz in New Orleans and into Harlem stride.
It was largely forgotten until the 1970s, when Joshua Rifkin’s recordings of Joplin and the film The Sting (1973), with Marvin Hamlisch’s arrangement of The Entertainer, brought it back.

title: Ragtime
text:
The band’s version

Comping: Stride: on the piano, a low bass note on 1 and 3 and the chord on 2 and 4, in straight time.
Bass: Root and fifth on 1 and 3, like the tuba in a march band.
Drums: Boom-chick: kick on 1 and 3, snare on 2 and 4.
Voicings: plain triads and seventh chords, all their notes.

A rag is written down, and its right-hand melody is the point. The band plays only the left hand’s pattern; the ragged melody is yours.

title: Piano ballad

title: Piano ballad
text:
What it is
The slow pop or rock song led from the piano: octaves in the left hand, the chord broken or rocked in the right (often in first inversion, so the top moves smoothly), and a band that comes in half-time, with the backbeat on beat 3.

title: Piano ballad
text:
A little history
The piano was the home instrument of popular song long before rock: Tin Pan Alley sold sheet music for it. In the 1970s singer-songwriters at the piano (Carole King’s Tapestry, 1971; Elton John; Billy Joel) made the piano ballad a staple of rock. The 1980s power ballad put it under big drums, and from the 2000s Coldplay, Alicia Keys and Adele (Someone Like You, 2011, over nothing but broken piano chords) kept it at the top of the charts.

title: Piano ballad
text:
The band’s version

Comping: three right-hand patterns (rocking, half-broken, syncopated) in four-bar spans.
Bass and drums: half time; a quiet kick and a cross-stick on 3. The hi-hat sits low.

title: Son montuno
text: Open the Son montuno style in the Backing Track

title: Son montuno
text:
What it is
The groove of Cuban son and of salsa: a two-bar repeating piano figure (the montuno or guajeo), a bass that plays ahead of the beat (the tumbao), and a clave pattern every part is fitted to.

title: Son montuno
text:
A little history
Son grew up in eastern Cuba and reached Havana around 1910-20, played by small groups on tres (a guitar with three doubled strings), guitar, bongó, maracas, claves and a marímbula or bass. The second half of a son, the montuno, is a vamp where a lead singer improvises against a chorus. In the late 1930s and 1940s Arsenio Rodríguez enlarged the group into the conjunto: piano, trumpets, and a conga. He is credited with the anticipated bass: the bass skips beat 1 and lands on the and of 2 and on 4, so that each chord is heard a little before the bar it belongs to. Mambo bands (Pérez Prado, Machito) and the New York salsa of the 1960s and ’70s (Eddie Palmieri, Fania Records) built on the same parts.
Clave is the two-bar rhythm (3-2: three hits then two; or 2-3) that the parts are written around. The band plays 2-3.

title: Son montuno
text:
The band’s version

Bass: tumbao, anticipating each bar. Comping: the two-bar montuno.
Drums: clave. Congas: a tumbao moving to the second drum every other bar.

title: Freylekhs / polka
text: Open the Freylekhs / polka style in the Backing Track

title: Freylekhs / polka
text:
What it is
The fast 2/4 of Eastern European dance music: the bass on every beat, alternating root and fifth, and the full chord on every off-beat (oom-pa oom-pa). A freylekhs (“joyful”) is the most common klezmer dance tune; the polka is its Central European cousin.

title: Freylekhs / polka
text:
A little history
The polka started in Bohemia in the 1830s and was danced across Europe and America within a decade. Its bands (brass, then accordion) gave it the bass-and-off-beat accompaniment. Klezmer is the instrumental music of Ashkenazi Jewish weddings in Eastern Europe. Immigrant clarinettists Naftule Brandwein and Dave Tarras recorded it in New York in the 1920s, with bands that played the same driving off-beats on piano, brass and drums. It faded after the war and came back in the 1970s revival (the Klezmorim, Andy Statman, Kapelye, later the Klezmatics). Songs like Hava Nagila and Hanukkah songs are still played this way.

title: Freylekhs / polka
text:
The band’s version

Bass: Root and fifth on every beat, with a run up into the next bar now and then.
Comping: chords on the off-beats. In half-time bars the piano switches to ballad patterns.

title: Emo / pop-punk

title: Emo / pop-punk
text:
What it is
Guitar-band rock at punk tempos with melodic, often confessional singing: a distorted guitar chugging palm-muted power chords in the verse, ringing open in the chorus, over root eighths and a rock beat, with half-time choruses and breakdowns.

title: Emo / pop-punk
text:
A little history
Emo (“emotional hardcore”) began in Washington, D.C., in 1985 with Rites of Spring and Embrace, who took hardcore punk’s speed into more personal songs. The 1990s brought a quieter, intricate “Midwest emo” (Cap’n Jazz, American Football). Pop-punk runs from the Buzzcocks and the Ramones to Green Day’s Dookie (1994), which sold millions, then Blink-182. Around 2000-2007 the two merged into a mainstream sound: Jimmy Eat World, My Chemical Romance, Fall Out Boy, Paramore. It came back in the 2020s, from Olivia Rodrigo to a revival of the bands themselves.

title: Emo / pop-punk
text:
The band’s version

Bass: Root eighths. Comping: palm-muted chugging in verses, open strumming in Chorus bars.
Drums: rock backbeat; mark bars Half-time for a half-time chorus or breakdown.

title: Dance pop
text: Open the Dance pop style in the Backing Track

title: Dance pop
text:
What it is
The disco beat and its descendants: a kick drum on every beat (four on the floor), the open hi-hat on every off-beat, a bass jumping between the root and its octave, and chords on a 3+3+2.

title: Dance pop
text:
A little history
Disco grew out of New York and Philadelphia clubs in the early 1970s. Earl Young, the drummer of Philadelphia International’s house band MFSB, is often credited with the steady kick and open hi-hat (The Love I Lost, Harold Melvin & the Blue Notes, 1973). The octave bass became disco’s other mark (Chic’s Bernard Edwards). Giorgio Moroder and Donna Summer’s I Feel Love (1977) put the beat on synthesizers and pointed toward house and techno (Chicago and Detroit, mid-1980s). Since then the four-on-the-floor beat has stayed at the centre of dance pop: Madonna, Kylie Minogue, Daft Punk, Dua Lipa.

title: Dance pop
text:
The band’s version

Bass: Octaves. Comping: a 3+3+2, on the electric piano. Drums: four on the floor.

title: Folk carol

What it is
Traditional carols played by a folk-rock band: a strummed steel-string guitar, upright bass on 1 and 3, light brushes. Between the four-part hymn and acoustic strum.

title: Folk carol
text:
A little history
Many English carols are older than the hymns sung beside them: dance songs and wassails collected by Cecil Sharp and Ralph Vaughan Williams in the early 1900s and published in The Oxford Book of Carols (1928). The British folk revival of the 1960s and the folk-rock bands that followed (Steeleye Span, Fairport Convention) played them with guitars, fiddles and drums, and many carol albums since have done the same.

title: Bossa nova
text: Open the Bossa nova style in the Backing Track

title: Bossa nova
text:
What it is
Brazilian song style from Rio de Janeiro in the late 1950s: samba slowed and quietened for a voice and a nylon-string guitar. The guitarist’s thumb plays the bass on beats 1 and 3 (in 2/4 counting, the two beats of the bar) while the fingers play syncopated chords that repeat over two bars.

title: Bossa nova
text:
A little history
Samba’s percussion section (the surdo bass drum, tamborim, agogô) was too loud for the small apartments and clubs of Copacabana. João Gilberto moved the parts onto the guitar: the thumb took the surdo, the fingers took the tamborim’s syncopations. His single Chega de Saudade (1958, song by Antônio Carlos Jobim and Vinícius de Moraes) is usually called the first bossa nova record. Jobim’s harmony (major sevenths, ninths, chromatic inner lines) came from jazz and from Debussy and Ravel.
American jazz musicians took it up after Charlie Byrd and Stan Getz’s Jazz Samba (1962). Getz/Gilberto (recorded 1963, released 1964), with Astrud Gilberto singing The Girl from Ipanema, made it a world style. Jazz drummers turned the guitar’s rhythm into the brush or cross-stick pattern the band plays: a two-bar figure close to the son clave, over a steady bass drum on 1 and 3.

title: Bossa nova
text:
The band’s version

Bass: root and fifth with pickups. Comping: the two-bar pattern.
Drums: bossa clave on the cross-stick. Voicings: jazz voicings with added 9ths.
Feel: straight eighths. Bossa never swings.

title: Boogaloo
text: Open the Boogaloo style in the Backing Track

title: Boogaloo
text:
What it is
A jazz band playing straight (not swung) eighth notes over a repeated bass figure, with piano or organ chords locked to the riff and a backbeat on the drums. It sits between hard bop, R&B and Latin music.

title: Boogaloo
text:
A little history
The word covers two related things from the mid-1960s. Latin boogaloo was a New York dance music that mixed Cuban son and mambo with R&B; Joe Cuba’s Bang! Bang! (1966) and Pete Rodríguez’s I Like It Like That (1967) were hits. In jazz, soul jazz players on labels like Blue Note took up the same straight eighths. Herbie Hancock’s Watermelon Man (1962) and Lee Morgan’s The Sidewinder (recorded 1963) came first, and Lou Donaldson’s Alligator Bogaloo (1967) put the name on the jazz version. Drummers such as Idris Muhammad and Bernard Purdie played a backbeat with busy sixteenth-note hi-hats; the tunes were often blues forms over one riff. Mongo Santamaría’s cover of Watermelon Man (1963) carried the Latin side, with congas, back into the charts, which is why the band adds a conga tumbao.

title: Boogaloo
text:
The band’s version

Bass: Boogaloo riff: root on 1, root pushed on the and of 2, fifth and flat seventh on 4.
Comping: stabs on the same rhythm as the riff.
Drums: straight-eighth backbeat. Congas: a tumbao.
Voicings: rootless jazz voicings.

Your teacher tells you which lesson you’re on. Practise a little every day: go through the steps below in order, and tick each one when you’ve done it. The microphone lets the page hear your saxophone and tell you which notes it heard.

title: My Saxophone Practice
text: Today’s practice

title: My Saxophone Practice
text:
All my notes
Every note you’ve learned so far, with its fingering, written for your saxophone.

title: My Saxophone Practice
text:
Practice tips

Sing first. If you can sing it, you can play it: the song and the patterns go in your ear (audiation) before your fingers.
Breathe before you play every pattern, the way you do in class.
Short and often. Fifteen minutes every day beats an hour once a week.
Don’t look at the music at first. Play by ear; the music is there for checking.
Ask: if a fingering doesn’t sound right, show your teacher next lesson.

title: My Saxophone Practice
text:
For the teacher
This follows the class sequence on JRI Recorder, on Saxophone (Book One, Units 1–12), in concert B♭, E♭, C minor and G minor. “Where we are in class” picks the section; the notes he knows are the ones introduced up to it. The echo patterns use only those notes in the key practised now, starting on the resting tone and moving by step; rhythm patterns are the class’s sets chanted by the site’s conversational chant (RhythmChant), in the song’s meter or the other (divisions from Unit 5B). Each lesson’s songs are the new song and two reviews, plus songs from the JRI Recorder, Mullen and elementary collections so that major and minor, duple and triple all come up; songs are moved into the class keys. Before the echo patterns, the rhythm patterns and every song with the band, the page establishes tonality, meter or both in one of the ways the MLT books describe (apps/shared/mlt/establish.js, picked at random by the teacher’s weights). The saxophone notes (holding it, embouchure, tone, tuning, care) are from Saxophone. Progress is kept in the student’s browser only.

Choose the band or a melody line, a tonality, a level, and press Start. You hear three versions, A, B and C. title: Odd Progression Out
text:
Borrowed chords and reharmonising
Borrowed chords is off unless you turn it on. Off, every chord stays in the key (the tonality), and the “slightly different” progression at levels 5 and 7 is a reharmonisation: another chord of the key that still holds the melody’s notes there. A melody resting on so that usually gets V could instead get I or iii (both hold so) and still fit. It could get IV, with so as IV’s 9th: the chord is played as IV(add9) for a gospel sound. On, those levels bring in borrowed, applied and chromatic chords instead.
With A tune on top, the band plays the same tune in all three clips. The difference is then only under the tune: listen for the chord changing while the melody stays the same. Without it, the reharmonised chord still shares the 3rd or 5th of the chord it replaces: the note a melody would hold there.

title: Odd Progression Out
text:
Tonalities
Every level works in each of the eight tonalities in Learning Sequences in Music (Gordon, p. 149): major, harmonic minor, Dorian, Phrygian, Lydian, Mixolydian, Aeolian and Locrian, or Any tonality for a mix. Each has its own progressions, built on the chords that make it sound like itself:








Tonality
Typical progressions
“Cousin” change at levels 5+ (borrowed chords on)




Major
I–vi–IV–V, I–IV–V–I, ii–V–I
IV→iv, ii→II7, V→bVII


Harmonic minor
i–iv–V–i, i–bVI–bIII–bVII, i–ii°–V–i
iv→IV, V→v, ii°→ii; bII (Neapolitan) as a chromatic change


Dorian
i–IV–i–IV, i–bVII–IV–i
IV→iv (now Aeolian), v→V


Phrygian
i–bII–i–bII, i–bvii–bVI–bII
bII→ii°, bvii→bVII


Lydian
I–II–I–II, I–II–vii–I
II→IV or ii (now major)


Mixolydian
I–bVII–IV–I, I–v–IV–I
bVII→V, v→V (now major)


Aeolian
i–bVI–bIII–bVII, i–iv–v–i
v→V (now harmonic minor), iv→IV


Locrian
i°–bII–i°–bII, i°–bV–bII–i°
i°→i, bV→v



Harmonic minor progressions also use the natural 7th’s chords (bIII, bVII), as minor-key music does. In a tonality other than major, a level whose own kind of change has no chord to work on falls back to a chord a third away or one with another function. The progressions are this site’s inventions in each tonality’s idiom; the “typical” column is not taken from a source.

title: Odd Progression Out
text:
The levels: a melody line
One line with no accompaniment, each version on its own instrument. The two same versions are different melodies over the same chords.







Level
The line




1 · Chord tones only
one chord tone a beat, the root or third on each downbeat


2 · Passing tones
a passing tone may fill a third on a weak beat


3 · Neighbour tones
eighth notes, passing and neighbour tones, sevenths in the line


4 · Appoggiaturas and suspensions
non-chord tones on strong beats that resolve by step; two chords a bar


5 · Anything
anticipations, escape tones, chromatic neighbours, chromatic chords



After you answer, the melody notation labels each non-chord tone (P, N, CN, A, S, Ant, E).

title: Odd Progression Out
text:
For teachers

The progressions are common patterns in each tonality, written as Roman numerals and played in a random key; the voicings, styles and melodies are made fresh each time. They are this site’s inventions, not transcriptions.
At levels 1–3 the band’s styles are pop, rock and folk; jazz styles voice chords with extensions of their own, so they come in at level 4 (The band → Styles overrides this).
Your last ten answers at each level stay in this browser; eight of ten suggests moving on.

The sets. The same sets as Tonal Patterns: the stepwise and I–V sets, the 322–324 sets, and any set you make there. The first patterns of a set use the same chords as the rest, so learning them gives you the sound of each chord before you’re tested.
Fingering. The page works out the fingers itself. It keeps the hand in one position (no thumb-under, as these patterns are short), goes with the letter steps (C E G is 1 3 5), and keeps the thumb off black keys where it can. This is a rule of thumb, not taken from a method book: a teacher may prefer other fingers.
