title: Hearing Harmony
text:
The paths
Each path puts the same chords in a different order. Start with the one closest to the music you play or listen to.








Path
Starts with
Comes late




MLT (Gordon / Mullen)
I and V7 in major, then minor, then IV; the modes (Dorian IV, Mixolydian ♭VII)
vi7, viiø7 and the diminished chords; ii last of all


Rock and pop
I–IV, I–V, three chords, ♭VII
ii and iii, borrowed chords (iv, ♭VI), the 12-bar blues


Jazz
ii7–V7–Imaj7 from the first level
turnarounds, secondary dominants, tritone substitutes, backdoor


Classical (Hutchinson)
cadences, predominants (ii and IV together), deceptive cadence
circle of fifths, secondary dominants, mixture, the Neapolitan


Make your own
the tonality and chords you tick




The MLT path follows Gordon: I V7 I first, then I IV I, then the two joined, then the same in harmonic minor before any more major (Learning Sequences in Music, pp. 318–319). The subdominant in Dorian and vi (relative keys) are taught with them. Next come the seventh chords on vi, vii and ♭VII, the diminished chords and the other modes, which he calls moderately difficult. Patterns with the supertonic are held back until after all of these (p. 320). The rock, jazz and classical orders are this site’s own. The classical path follows the chapters of the theory text (see Harmonic Progression).

title: Hearing Harmony
text:
The questions
They follow Gordon’s four stages of readiness for hearing harmony. At stage 1 you don’t notice that a chord changed. At stage 2 you notice the change but not what kind it is. At stage 3 you know what kind it is. At stage 4 you can also guess what comes next (Learning Sequences in Music, p. 305).

Did the chord change? Two chords. Stage 2.
Name each function (tonic, dominant, subdominant, subtonic…), each bass note in solfège (or the scale degrees or sargam chosen site-wide), or each chord as a Roman numeral. Stage 3. By default the first chord is given, as a starting point.
Same or different? Two progressions, at most one chord apart.
What comes next? You hear all but the last chord. Stage 4.
Which tonality? On levels that mix major, minor or modes.
Inversions: the bass, then root or not. Two steps a chord. First name the lowest note in solfège, then say whether it is the chord’s root. With Inversion step 2 set to Root, 3rd, 5th or 7th, say which chord member it is instead. The answer shows the book’s figures (I6, I64, V65, V43, V42).
Follow a voice. Name the note the soprano (or alto, tenor, bass: Voice to follow under Sound and options) sings in each chord, in solfège. Turn on Bring out for the same voice at first.

▶ My answer plays what you have entered so far, at any time, before or after checking. Empty boxes stay silent. Named functions play the level’s chord with that function. In Inversions, “Root” plays the chord with that root and “Not the root” puts your bass under the real chord.
Notation. ♫ Show notation (in the button bar, or Notation under Sound and options: hidden, after answering, always) draws the exercise on a grand staff, exactly as voiced, with the notes lit as they sound. The Roman numerals, with inversion figures, appear under it once you have answered. Each chord is spelled from its numeral (V7 in A minor has G♯), and the key signature is that of DO.
Entering answers. Tap the buttons: each fills the outlined box and moves to the next. Tap a filled box to empty it. On a computer you can also type into the outlined box: numerals as written (V7, ii, bVII, viio for vii°, viih7 for viiø7; capitals matter), syllables (do, so), functions (tonic, dom…), r or n for root or not. An answer fills in as soon as only one button fits. Otherwise press Enter (V waits, because V7 also starts with V). Backspace undoes and Space plays it again. There is no text box, so a phone never opens its keyboard.
Under the answer boxes, ▶ 1, ▶ 2… play one chord at a time. Turn on Bass alone and they play only its bass note, which helps with inversions. Before you answer What comes next?, the last chord has no button.
After each answer you see the progression, its key, its bass line in solfège and each chord’s function. ↻ Again plays it once more. Ten answers with eight right marks a level as done; nothing is locked.

title: Hearing Harmony
text:
Settings
Under Sound and options:

Voices. Three: the bass and two notes above it (3rd and 7th of a seventh chord). Four: the bass and three above, voice-led like a chorale (the site’s satb.js).
Key. A random key each time, or one key.
Tempo and beats per chord.
Silence between chords: from none to 5 seconds after each chord, time to think or sing the bass. The chord’s own length is still beats per chord.
Bring out: one voice louder and the rest softer (soprano, alto, tenor or bass; with three voices: top, middle or bass), or a chord member wherever it lies (the root, 3rd, 5th or 7th). The 3rd is good for hearing major against minor.
Leave out: drop one voice, to hear what the others do without it.
Arpeggiate: play the notes of each chord together, rolled, up from the bass, or down from the top.
Pan the voices: four voices S +50, A +20, T −20, B −50 (right is +); three voices top +50, middle 0, bass −50. With headphones, each voice has its own place.
Spacing: voice-led (the smoothest motion, the default), close (upper voices within an octave) or open (wider than an octave). The Close, Open and Voice-led buttons under the answer replay the current exercise in that spacing without changing the setting.
Drone: the resting tone (or the resting tone and its 5th) held low under the progression, to hear each chord against home.
Repeats: with Play each: twice, the second time can be in a new key (with its own cadence first). You track the function, not the pitch.
First hearing: at tempo, or the first play of each new question at half speed (replays at tempo).
Top voice sound: give the soprano its own sound (the electric pianos or the organs) so its line stands out by colour as well as loudness.
Voice to follow: for the Follow a voice question.
Notes: held, or short and detached.
Chord register: the upper voices an octave lower or higher (the bass stays).
Chords: the length of progressions on levels that make their own (Make your own, and levels such as F2).
Establish the key: a cadence, the tonic chord, or nothing (harder).
Inversions: off (every chord in root position), some, or many. This works with every question: Name each bass note then asks for the real lowest note. The last chord always stays in root position.
Inversion step 2: root or not, or which member.
First chord: given, or you name it too.
Play each: once or twice.
After answering: wait, or go on by itself (hands-free on a bus).
Chords on and Bass on: the band’s piano sounds and bass sounds, or off. There are no drums.

The sounds load from the internet the first time, so start a session while you still have a signal.

title: Hearing Harmony
text:
For teachers

Bass in the band’s bass, chords on the band’s piano. Chords are in root position unless Inversions is on. Voicing is chosen for the smoothest motion; in four voices it follows satb.js’s rules. In three voices the rules are only nearest motion and the root in the bass, with no check for parallel fifths.
Minor is harmonic minor in the MLT and classical paths (V7 has si). Aeolian uses ♭VII instead.
Gordon has the class sing I IV V7 I in three parts: top so la so so, middle mi fa fa mi, bottom do do ti do. In minor: mi fa mi mi, do re re do, la la si la (Learning Sequences in Music, pp. 318–319). Three voices here is close to that, with the bass added under it.
Saving to a class account (Supabase), singing answers into a microphone and more instruments are planned. The plan is in research_notes/ear-training-plan.md.

title: Bass Lines by Ear
text:
The levels








Level
Where the bass plays
What may differ




1 · Chord roots
chord changes, always (the style and Bass on are ignored)
one chord on another root of the key


2 · Roots: a different chord
chord changes
one chord’s root, a third away (I for vi, IV for ii, V for iii)


3 · Roots: inversions
chord changes
the 3rd or 5th of a chord in the bass instead of the root, or a different root


4 · Macrobeats: chord tones
each macrobeat
one note goes to another note of the same chord


5 · An embellishment in or out
each macrobeat
one embellishment added or taken away


6 · Which embellishment?
every beat
one embellishment swapped for another


7 · Walking: a step apart
every beat
one note a scale step away


8 · Walking: a semitone apart
every beat
one note a semitone away (a chromatic approach from above instead of below)


9 · Anything
left to chance
any of these, any tune



Half the questions are “same”. ♫ Show notation (any time; it stays on until you turn it off) shows the first line with the melody and chord symbols on a grand staff. The second line appears after you answer, with the changed notes marked ▼; before you answer, a button shows it early. The bass is written an octave above where it sounds, as bass parts are. After you answer you see what changed and where, the tune and its chords, and you can hear each bass line alone. Levels 1–3 use the easiest tunes, 7–8 the harder ones; Tune can pick any tune or one tune.

title: Bass Lines by Ear
text:
Where the bass plays
Bass on overrides the level:

Only on chord changes: one note a chord, held. Best for hearing reharmonisations and inversions.
Each downbeat and change: a note at the start of every bar as well.
Each macrobeat: in 2/4 every quarter, in 4/4 and 2/2 every half, in 3/4 every bar (dotted half), in 6/8 every dotted quarter. This is Gordon’s macrobeat in usual duple and triple meter (Learning Sequences in Music, pp. 175–176).
Every beat: every quarter (every dotted quarter in 6/8). In the jazz style this walks.
Leave it to chance: the changes, and about half of the other beats.

With fewer notes the embellishment levels have less to work with, so a question may fall back to an inversion or a different root.

title: Bass Lines by Ear
text:
The styles
Each style has its own embellishments. The lines are made fresh each time from the tune’s chord symbols, in the style’s idiom: they are this site’s inventions, not transcriptions. Unverified: the descriptions of each idiom below are from memory and not yet checked against a source.







Style
Embellishments it uses




MLT (Gordon)
roots and fifths on the macrobeats, an octave, a passing tone now and then


Rock and pop
roots, eighth-note pumping, octaves, a fifth, a scale step into the next chord


Jazz
two-feel roots and fifths, chord tones, walking steps, a chromatic approach on the last beat before a change


Classical
passing and neighbour tones, the bass by step, first inversions to smooth the line

title: Bass Lines by Ear
text:
The tunes
135 tunes from the Tune Library, the first eight bars of each, chosen by scripts/bass-ear-corpus.mjs from the 786 with chord symbols that it can read. A tune is left out when it has only one chord, unreadable chord symbols, chords that begin late, or a meter other than 2/4, 3/4, 4/4, 2/2 or 6/8. Each is put in a tier:

Tier 1: two or three chords, all in the key, at most one change a bar (Lightly Row, Bell Horses, Lucy Locket).
Tier 2: more chords or faster changes, at most one outside the key (many standards).
Tier 3: chords outside the key, slash chords, extended jazz harmony.

Within a tier, tunes with a change every bar or so, a melody that is not too busy and a melody well above the bass come first.

title: Bass Lines by Ear
text:
For teachers

Same is easier to hear than different (Learning Sequences in Music, p. 219). Start at level 1 (chord roots only), then move to macrobeats before the walking levels.
Melody on the band’s piano (or a guitar), bass on the band’s bass. No chords, no drums. Second time can play the melody again with the second line, which is harder: the melody has to be heard past.
Not yet: the tune’s own written bass lines (none of the tunes in the library has a bass part), and saving results to a class account.

title: Rote Song by Ear
text:
Choose a song, then go through the steps in order with Next →, or jump to any step in the list. The notation is never shown: the song is learned by listening, moving and audiating. title: Lesson: Write an Ending
text: Every song here stops two bars short. The chords for those bars are already written in: V, then I (or i in a minor key). That’s an authentic cadence, the strongest way to end. Your job is to write the melody that goes over it.

title: Lesson: Write an Ending
text:
Pick a song
Loading the tune library...


  ▶ Hear it as written
  The last two bars are silent. Only the chords play there.

title: Lesson: Write an Ending
section: What makes an ending sound finished
text:
What makes an ending sound finished

Land on the tonic. End on the home note (D in these songs) on a strong beat. Make it long.
Over V, sit on the leading tone or the 2nd. In D, that’s C♯ or E. Over A, both pull you home to D.
Step down into the last note. 3–2–1 (F♯–E–D) or 2–1 sounds settled. A leap up to the tonic sounds bolder.
Echo the opening. Bar 5 already repeats bar 1. Let your bars 7–8 answer bar 6 the way bars 3–4 answered bar 2.
Slow down. Use longer notes in the last bar than in the rest of the song.

title: Lesson: Write an Ending
text:
Write it
The chords are already in place. Choose rhythm patterns: they fill the empty bars in order, and once the last bar is full the song is complete (no bar is added). Then choose how to enter the notes (letters, the computer keys, or a MIDI keyboard) and enter them; they fill the rhythm from the first empty note. The score above the tools shows your ending as you go. Your work is saved for each song.

  ▶ Hear my ending
  Start this song over

title: Lesson: Write an Ending
text:
Compare
Write two different endings for the same song. Write one that steps down 3–2–1 and one that leaps up to the tonic. Then play them back to back. Which sounds more final? Which sounds more like this song?

title: Watermelon Man for Congas
text:
Watermelon Man is a 16-bar blues that a conga player can learn in an afternoon, once the tumbao is under the hands. If you have not played the tumbao yet, start with How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao. This page assumes the heel, toe, slap and open tones, and the part Heel Toe Slap Toe Heel Toe Open Open.
How to use the page. Every step has two bars of the part written large, a chord chart, and the whole chorus written on a conga staff. The note that is sounding lights up in the notation as the band plays. Press ▶ and the band plays it; the bar that is sounding lights up on the chart. Tick Congas alone to hear the congas without the bass and piano, and Leave out the congas to take over. Each step starts in its own style and tempo; the strip at the bottom changes both. The sounds are General MIDI stand-ins, so the heel, toe, slap and bass tones are approximations: listen to a real player for the sound.

title: Watermelon Man for Congas
text:
The tune and its history
Herbie Hancock wrote Watermelon Man for his first album, Takin’ Off (Blue Note, 1962), with Freddie Hubbard, Dexter Gordon, Butch Warren and Billy Higgins on drums. No conga player is listed on that record. It is in F, in even eighths: Hancock said Higgins played “somewhere between straight eighth notes and the swinging triplets of jazz”. It goes at roughly 120 to 130 beats a minute.
Late in 1962 Hancock filled in on piano in the band of the conga player Mongo Santamaría for a weekend at a club in the Bronx, and Donald Byrd urged him to play the tune for Mongo. Mongo’s band recorded it on 17 December 1962 “in a cha-cha beat”, with Kako Baster on timbales, Victor Venegas on bass and Ray Lucas adding a backbeat on drums. The single came out on Battle in 1963 and reached the top ten or eleven of the Billboard Hot 100 (sources differ). It is slower than Hancock’s, and is often named as a starting point of boogaloo and Latin soul. A much later remake, on Head Hunters in 1973, has Bill Summers blowing into beer bottles after the Central African hindewhu.
What this lesson teaches, and what it does not. No published transcription of the conga part on Mongo’s record was found. What you learn here is the standard tumbao, the part a conga player plays in a cha-cha beat. Listen to the record and copy what you hear.

title: Watermelon Man for Congas
text:
Reading the part
Click a note head to hear that stroke. The conga is written on the top space; a low drum, when there is one, sits on a lower space. A plain head is the open tone (or the bass tone), an ✕ is the slap, a triangle is heel or toe, and a diamond is the muted tone. Two lines of words sit under the notes: the stroke (H heel, T toe, S slap, O open, M muted, B bass) and the hand (L or R).

title: Watermelon Man for Congas
text:
The form
It is a 16-bar blues: a 12-bar blues whose bars 9 and 10 (C7 and B♭7) are played three times. In F, with one chord to a bar:

Bars 1 to 4: F7, F7, F7, F7
Bars 5 to 8: B♭7, B♭7, F7, F7
Bars 9 to 12: C7, B♭7, C7, B♭7
Bars 13 to 16: C7, B♭7, F7, F7

The Backing Track has the same form as its “Watermelon Man (16 bars)” preset, with the band stopping on bar 14 (the break). The steps below use it.

title: Watermelon Man for Congas
section: 1. The form, with the open tones only
text:
1. The form, with the open tones only
Start with the two open tones, on 4 and the and of 4, and nothing else. Count the sixteen bars out loud. Listen for the three C7 to B♭7 pairs in bars 9 to 14: that is the part of the form a 12-bar blues does not have.

title: Watermelon Man for Congas
text:
2. The right hand
Add the slap on 2. The right hand plays the slap, then the two open tones. The slap on 2 lands with the backbeat.

title: Watermelon Man for Congas
text:
3. The tumbao, slowly
Now the whole part: Heel Toe Slap Toe Heel Toe Open Open, hands L L R L L L R R, one bar at a time, in a cha-cha beat at about 100 beats a minute. Do not speed up to catch the band; keep the left hand quiet and the slap and open tones clear.

title: Watermelon Man for Congas
text:
4. The break
On bar 14 the band stops. The congas play one open tone on beat 1 with the band, then nothing, and come back in on bar 15 with the band. Count the silent beats. The two bars shown large are bars 13 and 14.



The bar after the stop is the hard part: nothing in the band tells you the time but your own counting. Say “1 and 2 and 3 and 4 and” out loud through bar 14.

title: Watermelon Man for Congas
text:
5. With the melody
The tune, written in F, above the chart. The band plays it on the piano with the congas. Tick Leave out the tune to hear the congas and the band alone. In this step the band plays straight through the break, so the melody is not cut off.



Read the melody as you play. The riff in bars 1 and 2 is the line everyone knows.

title: Watermelon Man for Congas
text:
6. Mongo’s way and Herbie’s way
The same part in two styles. The first plays the congas in the Cha-cha at a moderate tempo, as Mongo’s band recorded it, with the break on bar 14. The second is the Boogaloo at about 126, with straight eighths and the break, nearer Hancock’s own tempo. Change between them with the Feel menu at the bottom. The part is the same tumbao in both.
Mongo’s way: Cha-cha, a moderate tempo.



Herbie’s way: Boogaloo, about 126.

title: Watermelon Man for Congas
text:
7. Two drums
As an extension, the same form with two drums in the Son montuno: every second bar the right hand plays two open tones on the low drum, on the and of 2 and on 3, in place of the toe and the heel. Which bar of the pair takes the low drum depends on the clave, and this lesson does not say which way the clave runs on the record. A one-bar tumbao avoids the question: stay with step 6 until you can play it through without thinking.

title: Watermelon Man for Congas
text:
Where to go next

Play step 6 with the congas left out and the tumbao in your hands for ten choruses.
Learn the five strokes properly in How to Play Congas.
Blues for Drums has the same kind of steps for a drum kit.
Tools → Backing Track has the “Watermelon Man (16 bars)” preset and a Congas menu that works in any style.
Listen to Mongo Santamaría’s record and copy what you hear.

title: Pop Singing: Speech, Mix, Runs and the Mic
text:
Pop singing sounds like talking on pitch. The words come first, the tone stays close to your speaking voice, and the style lives in small things: how a note starts, a little cry or breath, a run at the end of a line. This lesson builds those things one at a time, from breathing to riffs and harmony.
How to use the page. Each exercise has a staff and a ▶ button. The exercises are written for a middle voice. Choose Your voice once and every exercise moves into your range; men read treble-clef notes an octave lower, as usual. Exercises marked Step up climb a half step each time you press it, the way a warm-up works through the range. Click a heading to fold a section away.
crumbs: Pop Singing: Speech, Mix, Runs and the Mic

title: Pop Singing: Speech, Mix, Runs and the Mic
text:
Breath and posture
Stand as if you were about to talk to a friend across the room: feet under the hips, knees soft, head level, shoulders loose. Breathe in low and quietly, so the belly and lower ribs widen and the shoulders don’t rise. Then let the air out slowly and steadily, without squeezing.
Exercise: hiss out on “sss” for a count of 8, then 12, then 16, keeping the sound even. Then do the same on a hum.
The aim isn’t a huge breath. It’s a steady one you don’t have to fight.
crumbs: Pop Singing: Speech, Mix, Runs and the Mic

title: Pop Singing: Speech, Mix, Runs and the Mic
text:
Starting the note: the onset
A note can start three ways:

Breathy: air first, then sound, as in a sigh, “hhhey”.
Hard: a little click of the vocal folds first, as in “uh-oh!”.
Balanced: air and sound together.

Pop uses all three for effect, but a balanced onset is home base. Sing the five notes below on “mum”, starting each note gently with the M.



Now sing the first note three times, once with each onset: “hhhum”, “’um” and “um”. Hear the difference, then go back to the balanced one.
crumbs: Pop Singing: Speech, Mix, Runs and the Mic

title: Pop Singing: Speech, Mix, Runs and the Mic
text:
Speech level and the mix
Your speaking voice and your high, light voice (head voice) join somewhere around the middle of your range. Pop singers keep the sound speech-like through that join. That blend is the mix. The safest way to find it is with exercises that keep the throat easy: lip trills (a horse’s “brrr”) and a bratty “nay”.
Sing this on a lip trill first, then on “nay” (bright and a bit nasal, like a teasing kid). Let the sound stay small at the top. Don’t shout up there.



As you step up, the top note will want to “flip” into a lighter sound. Let it flip at first. Over weeks, the “nay” helps the flip smooth out into a mix.

If your jaw juts or your neck tightens at the top, go back down two steps and make the sound smaller. Pop high notes come from a lighter, more speech-like voice, not from more push.
crumbs: Pop Singing: Speech, Mix, Runs and the Mic

title: Pop Singing: Speech, Mix, Runs and the Mic
text:
Vowels and words
Sing the words the way you’d say them: “love” is “luv”, not an operatic “lahv”. Two habits help.

Sing on the vowel and get to the consonant late. In “night”, hold “ah” and save the “-eet” ending for the very end of the note.
Narrow the vowel a little on high notes. “Ah” leans toward “uh”, and “ee” toward “ih”. The word still reads, and the throat stays easier.

Sing this line on “I can’t stop thinking ’bout you”, holding the vowels and putting the consonants late.
crumbs: Pop Singing: Speech, Mix, Runs and the Mic

title: Pop Singing: Speech, Mix, Runs and the Mic
text:
Belt, carefully
Belting is the strong, speech-like sound of pop and musical theatre on high notes, like a call across a playground: “Hey!”. Done well it is bright and forward, not shouted. Keep it short at first, and keep it well inside your comfort zone.




Belt for a few minutes at a time, not a whole session. If you feel any squeeze in your throat, go back to “nay” (the previous section). A teacher in person is the best guide for belting.
crumbs: Pop Singing: Speech, Mix, Runs and the Mic

title: Pop Singing: Speech, Mix, Runs and the Mic
text:
Riffs and runs
A run is a quick string of notes on one syllable, usually at the end of a phrase. Most pop runs come from the pentatonic scale. Learn each run slowly, on “ah”, until every note is clean. Then speed it up.
This run starts on A minor pentatonic: A, C, D, E, G.



And a common descending one from C major pentatonic: C, D, E, G, A.



Practice: sing each run at half speed with a metronome, then at full speed. A clean slow run is worth more than a fast blur.
crumbs: Pop Singing: Speech, Mix, Runs and the Mic

title: Pop Singing: Speech, Mix, Runs and the Mic
text:
Style: cry, breath and flips
These colours are what make a singer sound like pop:

Cry: a slight whimper or sob in the tone, like the edge of tears. It lightens the sound and helps it climb.
Breathy tone: let a little air into the start of a quiet phrase for intimacy. Don’t use it all the time, or the voice tires.
Flip (a yodel break): let the voice jump into a lighter sound for a moment on the way up, as in many folk and R&B lines.
Fry: the creaky sound at the bottom of the voice, used to start a phrase. Keep it light and brief.

Sing the line below twice: plainly, then adding a flip on the high note and a little breath at the start.
crumbs: Pop Singing: Speech, Mix, Runs and the Mic

title: Pop Singing: Speech, Mix, Runs and the Mic
text:
Phrasing and the mic

Sit a little behind the beat. Pop singers often land a word just after the beat, like a relaxed conversation. Try a line both ways with the Backing Track playing.
Shape each phrase. Most lines rise toward an important word and fall away after it.
Use the mic (more in Recording 5: Miking a Voice). Sing close (a finger or two away) for quiet, intimate lines. Pull back a few inches for loud notes, so they don’t blast. Point the mic at your mouth, not your chin.
crumbs: Pop Singing: Speech, Mix, Runs and the Mic

title: Pop Singing: Speech, Mix, Runs and the Mic
text:
Harmony: singing a third above
Backing vocals often sing a third above the melody: two scale steps higher, moving in parallel with it. Sing the melody below, then sing the harmony line written above it.



Practice: play it and sing the melody (the lower line), then the harmony. Then sing the harmony while the recording plays the melody.
crumbs: Pop Singing: Speech, Mix, Runs and the Mic

title: Pop Singing: Speech, Mix, Runs and the Mic
text:
Where to go next

Jazz singing: swing, scat and singing the changes.
Classical singing: breath, pure vowels and legato.
Four-chord loops: sing melodies and harmonies over the loops of most pop songs.

title: Classical Singing: Breath, Pure Vowels and Legato
text:
Classical singing fills a room without a microphone. It does that through resonance, not force: a steady breath, tall and pure vowels, and a seamless legato line that carries from the bottom of the voice to the top. Most of its training comes from the Italian bel canto (“beautiful singing”) tradition. This lesson follows that tradition’s order: breath, onset, vowels, registers, agility and the long note.
How to use the page. Each exercise has a staff and a ▶ button. Choose Your voice once and every exercise moves into your range; tenors and basses read treble-clef notes an octave lower. Step up exercises climb a half step at a time, as in a teacher’s warm-up. Click a heading to fold a section away.
crumbs: Classical Singing: Breath, Pure Vowels and Legato

title: Classical Singing: Breath, Pure Vowels and Legato
text:
Posture and the appoggio breath
Stand tall but not stiff: feet hip-width apart, weight forward slightly, sternum comfortably high, shoulders down, head balanced. Breathe in low and wide, so the lower ribs, belly and back expand.
As you sing, keep the ribs open and let the belly come in slowly. Singers call this balance appoggio (“leaning”): the breath is supported rather than pushed out, so the tone stays steady.
Exercise: breathe in for 4 counts, then hiss out on “sss” for 12 counts, keeping the ribs wide. Next time, go for 16 counts, then 20.
crumbs: Classical Singing: Breath, Pure Vowels and Legato

title: Classical Singing: Breath, Pure Vowels and Legato
text:
Onset and legato
Begin each phrase with a clean, balanced onset: air and tone together, with no click and no rush of air first. Then join the notes so the sound never breaks between them. That’s legato, the basis of classical singing.
Sing this five-note scale on a single “ah”, sliding nothing and dropping nothing between notes.
crumbs: Classical Singing: Breath, Pure Vowels and Legato

title: Classical Singing: Breath, Pure Vowels and Legato
section: Pure vowels: i e a o u
text:
Pure vowels: i e a o u
Italian has five pure vowels: [i] as in si, [e] as in che, [a] as in la, [o] as in no, [u] as in tu. Unlike English vowels, they don’t glide into a second sound: Italian no is [nɔ], never “no-oo”. Classical singers learn to sing every language on these clean vowel shapes.
Sing them on one pitch, keeping the same space at the back of the mouth as the lips change shape.



Then sing them on a scale.



The IPA chart shows these and the other sounds singers meet in Italian, German, French and English.
crumbs: Classical Singing: Breath, Pure Vowels and Legato

title: Classical Singing: Breath, Pure Vowels and Legato
text:
Resonance and the tall vowel
A classical tone rings because the throat stays open and the soft palate is lifted. That’s the feeling at the start of a yawn, or of a pleasant surprise. Singers call the ring squillo, and the warmth that comes with it chiaroscuro (light and dark).
Exercise: sing an easy “ng” (as in sing) on a middle note, then open slowly to “ah” without moving the pitch. Keep the buzz you felt in the “ng”.
crumbs: Classical Singing: Breath, Pure Vowels and Legato

title: Classical Singing: Breath, Pure Vowels and Legato
text:
Registers and the passaggio
Every voice has a lower register (chest) and a higher one (head), with a transition zone called the passaggio. Classical training aims for one even sound across it. To do that, singers modify vowels slightly as they go up: “ah” darkens a little toward “aw”, and “ee” toward “ih”. That keeps the throat open and the tone even.
The arpeggio below climbs through the voice. Step it up a half step at a time, and as you near the top of your comfortable range, round the vowel and lighten the sound rather than push.




If the voice cracks around the passaggio, that’s normal at first. Sing the same arpeggio more quietly, on “oo”, where the voice blends most easily, then return to “ah”.
crumbs: Classical Singing: Breath, Pure Vowels and Legato

title: Classical Singing: Breath, Pure Vowels and Legato
text:
Agility: the nine-note scale
Quick runs (coloratura) need a light, flexible voice with the breath still steady. This scale of nine notes up and down is a classic warm-up. Sing it slowly and clean at first, keeping each note distinct, never “ha-ha-ha”.
crumbs: Classical Singing: Breath, Pure Vowels and Legato

title: Classical Singing: Breath, Pure Vowels and Legato
section: The long note: messa di voce
text:
The long note: messa di voce
Messa di voce means “placing the voice”: one long note that grows from soft to loud and back to soft, with the pitch and the vowel unchanged. It’s the most demanding exercise in breath control, and a lifelong one.



Practice: start on a comfortable middle note, and make the swell only as big as you can keep steady.
crumbs: Classical Singing: Breath, Pure Vowels and Legato

title: Classical Singing: Breath, Pure Vowels and Legato
text:
Vibrato
A trained classical voice has a natural vibrato: a regular, even pulse in pitch, about five to seven times a second. It isn’t made deliberately. It appears when the breath is steady and the throat is free. If yours wobbles slowly or flutters fast, the cause is usually in breath or tension, and is best fixed with a teacher, not by trying to control the vibrato itself.
crumbs: Classical Singing: Breath, Pure Vowels and Legato

title: Classical Singing: Breath, Pure Vowels and Legato
section: Words: diction in Italian, German and French
text:
Words: diction in Italian, German and French
Classical singers sing in many languages, and each has its rules:

Italian: pure vowels; double consonants held longer (nòtte, “night”); a flipped or rolled R.
German: long and short vowels clearly different; final consonants crisp; the “ich” sound [ç] and the “ach” sound [x]; ü [y] and ö [ø] with rounded lips.
French: nasal vowels ([ɑ̃] in chant, [ɔ̃] in mon); the rounded [y] of tu; a smooth line with every syllable even.

The IPA chart gives each of these sounds with examples. Singers write IPA under the words of a song to learn its pronunciation before they sing it.
crumbs: Classical Singing: Breath, Pure Vowels and Legato

title: Classical Singing: Breath, Pure Vowels and Legato
text:
Reading and solfège
Classical singers read music. Tonal Sequences practises solfège, which names the notes by their place in the key, so a singer can hear a line before singing it. Sing this phrase on solfège.
crumbs: Classical Singing: Breath, Pure Vowels and Legato

text:

Jazz singing: swing, scat and the changes.

title: Tuning Systems: Just Intonation and Equal Temperament
text:
A piano is slightly out of tune on purpose. Every chord on it, apart from the octave, is a little wrong, and the wrongness is spread so evenly that all twelve keys sound alike. The alternative is just intonation (JI), where intervals are tuned to the simple ratios that the harmonic series gives you, and they sound smooth and still. This lesson shows what each costs, with ears first and numbers second.
How to use the page. Every widget has a ▶ button. The bar at the bottom of the window sets the volume (start low). The Drone button in the top navigation bar is the same drone as the one on this page. Click a heading to fold a section away, or use On this page on the right to jump (shift-click folds the others). The lesson on the harmonic series goes further into where the ratios come from.
crumbs: Tuning Systems: Just Intonation and Equal Temperament

title: Tuning Systems: Just Intonation and Equal Temperament
section: The harmonic series gives the ratios
text:
The harmonic series gives the ratios
A note on a real instrument is a stack of frequencies at whole-number multiples of the lowest, the fundamental: 1×, 2×, 3×, 4×, and so on. Those are the harmonics. Each interval between neighbouring harmonics is a simple ratio of whole numbers:



Between harmonics
Ratio
Interval

2 and 3

Harmonics 4, 5 and 6 together are a major triad, 4:5:6. That is the reason a major chord sounds stable: it is already inside every note you hear. Below, the first sixteen harmonics are written out over any root, with how many cents each is from the nearest piano note. A cent is 1/100 of a piano half step, so an octave is 1200 cents. Press Harmonic, then tempered and listen to the harmonics that are most out of tune with the piano (7, 11, 13 and 14).



Frequencies multiply, but we hear pitch by ratio: going up a fifth always multiplies the frequency by 3/2, whether you start on a low note or a high one. To compare ratios, take 1200 × log₂(ratio) to get cents. A pure fifth, 3:2, is 1200 × log₂(1.5) = 701.96 cents. A pure major third, 5:4, is 386.31 cents.
crumbs: Tuning Systems: Just Intonation and Equal Temperament

title: Tuning Systems: Just Intonation and Equal Temperament
section: Why pure intervals do not beat
text:
Why pure intervals do not beat
When two notes are close in frequency, their waves line up and then fall out of step, over and over. The sound swells and fades at a rate equal to the difference in their frequencies. That is a beat: 440 Hz with 443 Hz beats three times a second.
Beating also happens between the harmonics of two different notes. In a pure major third (4:5), the 5th harmonic of the lower note and the 4th harmonic of the upper note are exactly the same frequency, so they simply reinforce each other. When the interval is slightly off, those two harmonics are a few hertz apart and beat. A pure fifth (2:3) has the same matching harmonics, the 3rd of the lower note and the 2nd of the upper.
The widget shows it. With Only the two harmonics that should match the sound is just two sine waves, and the picture is their sum: it swells and fades as they drift in and out of step. Switch the tuning between Just and Equal temperament and hear the beating start and stop. The wavy line is drawn slowed down; the real rate is in the text under the controls.



Now the same with all the harmonics of two notes, which is what a real chord does. Choose another interval with the Interval menu. Notice that the fifth beats slowly (it is only 2 cents off) and the thirds and sixths beat fast (14 to 16 cents off). That is why equal temperament is so much kinder to fifths than to thirds.
crumbs: Tuning Systems: Just Intonation and Equal Temperament

title: Tuning Systems: Just Intonation and Equal Temperament
section: Two commas: why tuning cannot be perfect
text:
Two commas: why tuning cannot be perfect
Pure tuning runs into arithmetic. Two facts about ratios cannot both be true:

Stack twelve pure fifths (3:2) and you arrive at the note seven octaves up, almost. Twelve fifths are (3/2)¹² = 129.746; seven octaves are 2⁷ = 128. The gap is the Pythagorean comma, 531441:524288, or 23.46 cents, nearly a quarter of a half step.
Stack four pure fifths and reduce by two octaves and you get a major third, but a wide one: 81:64 (407.8 cents), compared with the pure 5:4 (386.3 cents). The difference, 81:80 or 21.51 cents, is the syntonic comma.

So the pure thirds of the harmonic series (5:4) and the pure fifths (3:2) are made of different building blocks, and they do not fit together. A tuning system is a decision about which of those to keep and which to spoil.
crumbs: Tuning Systems: Just Intonation and Equal Temperament

title: Tuning Systems: Just Intonation and Equal Temperament
section: Just intonation, and why it cannot modulate
text:
Just intonation, and why it cannot modulate
In a just scale, every note is a whole-number ratio of the tonic (Do). The common major scale version is:



Do
Re
Mi
Fa
Sol
La
Ti
Do




1
9/8
5/4
4/3
3/2
5/3
15/8
2



The I, IV and V chords (Do–Mi–Sol, Fa–La–Do, Sol–Ti–Re) are pure 4:5:6 triads, and they sound beautifully still. The trouble starts with the other chords. The ii chord is Re–Fa–La: from Re (9/8) to La (5/3) the ratio is (5/3) ÷ (9/8) = 40/27, which is 680.4 cents. That is a fifth 21.5 cents flat, a syntonic comma off, and it sounds sour. To get a good ii chord you would need a different Re (10/9), but then the notes of V would be wrong. In the key of C, the note D has two jobs and a different pure frequency for each.
That is the main limit of just intonation on a fixed-pitch instrument (a keyboard, a fretted guitar, a marimba). Tune the keyboard for C major and the same keys give poor chords in D major or E♭ major. You would want more than 12 notes per octave, or a retune for each key. Voices, violins, trombones and other instruments that can adjust each note do this naturally: a choir singing Do–Mi–Sol will tune the triad pure, and a progression like C – Am – Dm – G – C will drift upward in pitch by a syntonic comma over each lap if every chord is tuned pure.
Here is the drone, held on Do with Mi and Sol above it (a major triad). Pure tunes Mi to 5/4 and Sol to 3/2 of Do; Equal uses the piano’s notes. Switch back and forth while it sounds. Listen for the third: in the pure setting the chord sits still, and in equal temperament it has a faint shimmer, the beating from the last section.



Try this: with the drone sounding, sing or play (on any instrument that can bend its pitch) the note Mi above the drone, first sliding toward the piano’s version, then toward the pure one. The pure one locks into the drone. It is the pitch that stops beating.
crumbs: Tuning Systems: Just Intonation and Equal Temperament

title: Tuning Systems: Just Intonation and Equal Temperament
text:
Equal temperament: twelve equal steps
Equal temperament (12-TET) solves the key problem by making every half step the same size. An octave is a 2:1 ratio and has twelve steps, so each step multiplies the frequency by 2^(1/12) = 1.059463. A semitone is exactly 100 cents, and every interval of the same size is the same in every key. Twelve fifths then come out to exactly seven octaves, and the Pythagorean comma is spread evenly: each fifth is narrowed by 23.46 ÷ 12 = 1.96 cents.
The price is that no interval except the octave is pure. The fifth is only 2 cents flat, which is close enough to ignore. But the thirds and sixths are 14 to 16 cents off, enough to hear:

In words: the tempered major third is about 14 cents sharp of the pure 5:4, the tempered fifth about 2 cents flat of 3:2, and the tempered minor third about 16 cents flat of 6:5. Thirds are the most exposed because the ear uses them to decide whether a chord is major or minor, and because the beating of two harmonics (the 5th and the 4th) falls in a region where the ear is most sensitive. The minor sixth and the major sixth are the thirds turned upside down, so they are wrong by the same amount.
Equal temperament is the standard for the piano, the guitar, MIDI and nearly every synthesizer. Its strength is that it lets you play in any key, modulate anywhere, and use chromatic and jazz harmony that no pure system supports. Many singers, string players and brass players move toward just intonation while they play, without thinking about it.

title: Tuning Systems: Just Intonation and Equal Temperament
section: Hear and play it: chords and solfège
text:
Hear and play it: chords and solfège
The keyboard below names what you play in solfège and gives the chord. Its Tuning menu switches between the sampled piano, an organ tone in equal temperament and the same organ tone in just intonation (every note a ratio of the key note, here C). Play a C major chord (C, E, G) in each of the two organ settings, then try the A minor chord or the C major seventh. Turn on Hold notes to build a chord one key at a time. Pure chords from the key note are smooth; notice what happens in the pure setting with D minor (D, F, A): that is the ii chord from above, and the pure fifth D–A is not available.

title: Tuning Systems: Just Intonation and Equal Temperament
text:
Other systems, briefly
Equal temperament is one answer to the comma problem, and not the only one used.

Pythagorean tuning. All fifths are pure 3:2, and the thirds come out wide (81:64, 407.8 cents, 21.5 cents sharp of 5:4). It suits melody, with its sharp leading tones and bright, tense thirds, and it was the system of medieval Europe, whose music was built on fifths and fourths. One fifth, the wolf, is out by the Pythagorean comma (678.5 cents).
Quarter-comma meantone. Renaissance and early Baroque keyboards narrowed each fifth by a quarter of a syntonic comma (696.6 cents) so that the major thirds came out pure (386.3 cents). Chords in the home keys are lovely. The cost is an even worse wolf fifth (about 737.6 cents), and keys with many sharps or flats are unusable.
Well temperaments (Werckmeister, Vallotti, Kirnberger and others). Eighteenth-century tunings that spread the comma unevenly so that every key works but each has its own colour: keys near C have nearly pure thirds, and distant keys are tenser. In Werckmeister III four fifths (C–G, G–D, D–A, B–F♯) are narrowed by a quarter of the Pythagorean comma and the rest are pure. In Vallotti six fifths (F–C–G–D–A–E–B) are narrowed by a sixth of the comma and the rest are pure. Bach’s Well-Tempered Clavier (1722) has a prelude and fugue in all 24 keys, so it needs a tuning where every key is playable. Its exact temperament is still debated; “well tempered” did not mean equal. Many listeners find these keys have individual character, which equal temperament flattens.
Equal temperament gradually took over in the nineteenth century, as chromatic harmony and modulation made key colour impossible to keep.

title: Tuning Systems: Just Intonation and Equal Temperament
text:
Beyond twelve notes
Not all music divides the octave into twelve.

Arabic maqam. Many maqamat use the “neutral” second and third, about halfway between a minor and a major one (roughly 150 and 350 cents), notated with a half-flat sign. This is often described as quarter tones (24 notes to the octave), but the actual pitches vary by maqam, region and performer, and are set by ear.
Equal divisions other than 12. 19-TET has an almost pure minor third (315.8 cents against the 6:5 of 315.6) but a weak fifth (694.7). 31-TET has near-pure major thirds (387.1 cents) and a good fifth (696.8), and was proposed in the 16th century to improve on meantone. 53-TET has a fifth within 0.07 cent of 3:2 and a major third within 1.4 cents, which is why it is a favourite for theorists approximating just intonation. All need special keyboards or a computer.
Gamelan. Indonesian ensembles use two scales, five-note slendro (roughly equal steps of about 240 cents) and seven-note pelog (unequal steps, normally five of the seven in a piece). Every ensemble is tuned to itself, and no two are the same, so the instruments belong together. Paired instruments are often tuned slightly apart on purpose to give a shimmering beat, the ombak (“wave”), the same beating you heard above, used as a colour rather than avoided.

title: Tuning Systems: Just Intonation and Equal Temperament
section: Seeing it: a strobe tuner, pure intervals, and why pianos are stretched
text:
Seeing it: a strobe tuner, pure intervals, and why pianos are stretched
A needle tuner gives one number. A strobe tuner gives one row of moving stripes for every partial of the note you play. Row k listens at k times the pitch you are aiming at (the microphone signal is multiplied by a sine and cosine at that frequency and averaged; the phase of the result moves the stripes). If that partial is exactly where it should be, its stripes stand still. If it is sharp they drift to the right, and if flat to the left, at a speed equal to the error in Hz. Rows fade where the partial is weak, and the first tenth of a second of each note is ignored, because the attack is not a steady pitch.
Choose the target below: the equal-tempered note, a just interval over a tonic you pick, a step of 31-ET, or any number of cents above the note (350 is a neutral third). The conventional readout (nearest note and cents) is underneath. The microphone is asked for only when you press Start, and Stop lets it go. No microphone? The made-up string is a stack of oscillators you can detune.



Hear just intervals. With the tonic on A, the note E is aimed at 3:2 over A. Play (or sing) an E against an A drone (the Drone button in the top bar): when the beats stop, your E is the pure fifth, and every row stands still. It is about 2 cents wider than the piano’s E. Change the tonic to C: the target E is now the pure major third, 5:4, which is about 14 cents narrower than the piano’s. That is the number behind the beating in the widgets above, and the reason a choir with no keyboard drifts toward pure intervals.
Why a piano is stretched. The harmonic series of an ideal string is exactly 1, 2, 3, 4… times the fundamental. A real string has stiffness, so it resists bending near its ends, and the effect grows quickly with the partial number: partial k sounds at about k f √(1 + B k²), where B is the string’s inharmonicity (a mid-range piano string has B of the order of 0.0001 to 0.001, and the short thick bass strings and the shortest treble strings have more). Every upper partial is therefore sharp of the exact multiple. When two notes an octave apart are tuned, the beats a tuner listens to are between the upper note’s fundamental and the lower note’s second partial, which is already slightly sharp: so the upper note is tuned a little sharp of 2:1, and so on up the keyboard. The bass ends up flat and the treble sharp of the equal-tempered scale. This is called stretch tuning. Try it: set the source to the made-up string, press Start, and raise the stiffness. Row 1 stays still and the higher rows drift to the right, row 6 more than row 2. Notice that the readout above the bands, which reduces the whole sound to one pitch, is pulled sharp by the upper partials, while row 1 shows that the fundamental has not moved.

title: Tuning Systems: Just Intonation and Equal Temperament
text:
Things to try

In the major-third widget, set the lower note to 110 Hz, then 440 Hz. At which pitch is the tempered third’s beating faster? (The beat rate is in Hz, so it doubles per octave.)
In the second widget, step through the intervals in Equal temperament mode and rank them from most to least beating. The fifth and fourth should be at one end and the thirds and sixths at the other.
Start the drone on Do with Mi and Sol, set to Pure, and hum along. Switch to Equal and hum again. Can you feel your pitch pulled toward the pure Mi?
Play a D minor chord in the chord keyboard in just intonation and in equal temperament. Which sounds worse, and why? (The fifth D–A is 21.5 cents flat in the pure scale.)
In the stiff-string tuner, set the stiffness to 0 and then to 0.0020. At which row does the drift first pass 10 cents? (Row k is sharp by 600 × log₂(1 + B k²) cents, from the formula above.)
Calculate for yourself: the cents between two frequencies is 1200 × log₂(f₂ ÷ f₁). Check that A at 440 Hz and E at 660 Hz (a pure fifth) is 701.96 cents, and that the piano’s E is 659.26 Hz.

title: How a Strobe Tuner Works
text:
A needle tuner gives you one number. A strobe tuner gives you a picture that stands still when the note is in tune, and drifts one way if you are sharp and the other way if you are flat. It is the most precise tuner there is, and the way it works is a lovely piece of physics that you can play with. This lesson builds one from the spinning disc of the 1930s to the few lines of arithmetic in the tuner on this site, with a widget at every step. Click a section’s heading to fold it; the “On this page” bar at the right jumps to any section and opens it.
How to use the page. The pictures with a Pause button move on their own; the sliders change what they show. The sound widgets have a ▶ button, and the bar at the foot of the window sets the volume (start low). Nothing here needs a microphone: the last two widgets listen to the page’s own sound. The Strobe tuner button in the top bar is the same tuner on every page of the site, and works with the microphone, with the page’s sound, with a video on the page, or with another browser tab. For where the numbers 3:2 and 5:4 come from see the harmonic series; for what the tuner is used to compare, see tuning systems.

title: How a Strobe Tuner Works
text:
1. The mechanical strobe tuner
The first strobe tuners (the Conn Strobotuner, 1936, is the famous one) had no electronics to speak of. A small motor spun a disc at a fixed, very steady speed. Printed on the disc were rings of black and white segments, a different number in each ring, one ring for each note (or octave of a note) to be tuned. A microphone and an amplifier fed the note you were playing to a neon lamp behind the disc, and the lamp flashed once for every cycle of the note’s sound. You looked at the disc through the flashes.
Take a simple disc with rings of 8, 16, 24 and 32 segment pairs, turning 13.75 times a second (825 rpm). The 8-pair ring sweeps 8 × 13.75 = 110 pairs past any fixed spot every second, the 16-pair ring 220, and so on. So ring 1 is a ruler for 110 Hz (the A two octaves below the A at 440), ring 2 for 220 Hz, ring 3 for 330 and ring 4 for 440. Set the lamp to flash at 110 times a second and look at ring 1: each flash lights the disc at the moment it has turned exactly 8 pairs further round, which looks exactly like the last picture. The ring appears to stand still.
Now play 112 Hz, a little sharp. The flashes come slightly faster than the ring’s pairs pass, so each flash catches the ring a little further round than the last, and it creeps round at 2 pairs a second, the difference between the note and the ring’s frequency. Flat, and it creeps the other way. That is the whole idea: the speed of the creep is the number of hertz you are away, and its direction is sharp or flat. The disc really turns 825 rpm; the lamp’s light is what makes the difference visible.



Try this. Set the lamp to Steady and the disc is a grey blur: without the flashes there is nothing to see, since the disc turns too fast to follow. Switch to Flashing and slide the note: ring 1 stops at 110 Hz, ring 2 at 220 Hz, and so on. Between those, every ring crawls or blurs. Press Match the nearest ring to see the one that stops.

title: How a Strobe Tuner Works
section: 2. Why a pattern stands still: aliasing
text:
2. Why a pattern stands still: aliasing
The trick of “looking at something in flashes” has a name, stroboscopic aliasing, and you have seen it in films, where a car’s wheels appear to stand still or turn backwards. A film camera takes (say) 24 pictures a second. If a spoked wheel turns a little less than one spoke-gap between pictures, the spokes look as if they have moved forward a little. If it turns a little more, they look as if they have moved back. And if it moves exactly one spoke-gap each picture, the wheel stands still although it is turning fast.
What you see is the difference between the wheel’s rate (spokes passing a point per second) and the flash rate, wrapped round so it is never more than half a flash away from zero:

apparent rate = (spokes × turns per second) − (flashes per second) × (the whole number that makes this as small as it can be)

The widget below has a wheel with eight identical spokes on the left (the truth, drawn continuously) and the same wheel as the strobe light shows it on the right. Give the wheel a speed, give the strobe a rate, and watch.



Things to find: the wheel at 2 turns a second has 16 spokes passing a point each second; at 16 flashes a second it stands still. Raise the flash rate to 20 and the spokes appear to go backwards. Drop it to 8 flashes a second and it stands still again: the wheel moves two spoke-gaps between flashes, and the spokes all look the same. Tick Mark one spoke and both stillnesses go, because the marked spoke is now different from the others: only 2 flashes a second (one whole turn between flashes) stands still.
In the disc tuner the wheel was the disc ring and the flash rate the note. A tuner lights up with a pattern that stands still only when the note is an exact multiple of the ring’s rate. That is the mechanical strobe tuner, and the rest of the lesson is the same idea done with arithmetic.

title: How a Strobe Tuner Works
text:
3. One band, one partial
A real note is not one frequency. A guitar string vibrates in halves, thirds, and so on all at once, so the sound has a stack of partials at (nearly) 1, 2, 3, 4… times the fundamental. See the harmonic series for why. A lamp that flashes with the wave flashes at the fundamental but also with the partials, so on a disc tuner the rings for 1×, 2×, 3× each get their own pattern, and they all stand still together when the string is in tune. That is a mixed blessing: you can read several rings at once, and each ring is a different ruler.
The tuner on this site makes that explicit. It has one band (a row of stripes) for each partial. Band k is a ruler tuned to k times the reference pitch. The sound has a partial at k times the string’s own fundamental. If the string is exactly at the reference, partial k matches band k and the stripes stand still. If the string is c cents sharp, partial k is at k × f × 2^(c/1200), so band k drifts at

drift (Hz) = k × fref × (2^(c/1200) − 1)

which is k times faster for the kth band. The upper bands are k times more sensitive: a small error shows on band 6 six times sooner than on band 1.
Here are the bands with no microphone: a computed string, so you can see what a tuner should show for a given error. The small picture above shows the string’s partials (bars) against the bands’ rulers (the vertical lines).



Set the String is off by slider to +8 cents: all six bands drift to the right, band 6 six times faster than band 1. Now add stiffness. A real string is a little stiff, like a thin rod, and a stiff string’s partials are pushed up: partial k is at k f √(1 + B k²), so the high partials are sharp even when the fundamental is on the note. You will see the lower bands stand still and the higher ones drift right: the string is in tune where it matters, and the strobe shows exactly how much its upper partials are stretched.

title: How a Strobe Tuner Works
section: 4. The software version: multiply and average
text:
4. The software version: multiply and average
A computer cannot spin a disc, but it can do what the disc and the lamp do together, with two multiplications. This is called demodulation, and radios do it too. For band k, keep two reference waves going, a cosine and a sine at k × fref. Multiply the incoming sound, sample by sample, by each of them, then average (a low-pass filter) the results.
Why it works: multiplying two sine waves gives two new ones, at the difference and at the sum of their frequencies. The sum is fast and the average wipes it out. The difference is slow: it is zero if the sound is exactly at the reference, and then the average is a steady number; if the sound is 0.5 Hz sharp, the average is a number that swings slowly at 0.5 Hz. The cosine’s average and the sine’s average are two numbers I and Q, and together they are the corner of a right-angled triangle, a point on a circle. The angle of that point is the phase: where the stripes are. If the note is in tune, the point stays put; otherwise it goes round the circle once for every Hz of difference, counter-clockwise if sharp and clockwise if flat. The stripes you see are drawn at that angle.
The widget runs the arithmetic on a slowed-down signal, so you can watch each step. The reference is 4 Hz (instead of 110 Hz or more) and the “note” is a slider. Step through it.



Check that the averaged traces (step 4) are a cosine and a sine of the difference frequency: at a note 4.5 Hz against the 4 Hz reference they swing at 0.5 Hz, and the dot on the circle goes round once in two seconds. At exactly 4.0 Hz nothing moves. The sum frequency, 8.5 Hz, which you see in the products at step 3, is gone from step 4. (The first second or so is the average filling up, and the tuner ignores it. The real tuner also ignores the first 100 ms of every note, the pluck, since the attack is a noisy burst.)
The bank of bands in apps/shared/pitch-detect.js does exactly this, at the sound card’s sample rate, for each of up to ten bands at once. It reads the angle every 128 samples and works out the drift in hertz from how fast the angle turns; the cents are then 1200 × log₂((kf + drift) / kf).

title: How a Strobe Tuner Works
section: 5. Drift is the beat rate; hertz to cents
text:
5. Drift is the beat rate; hertz to cents
The drift in hertz is exactly the beat rate you would hear if you played the reference and your note together. A note 3 Hz sharp of the reference beats 3 times a second against it, and the stripes go round 3 times a second. That is how a piano tuner sets a string by ear against a fork, and the strobe is the same measurement made visible and made at every partial.
To turn hertz into cents, remember that a cent is a ratio, not a number of hertz. One cent is a factor of 2^(1/1200), about 1.000578. So the same pitch error is a small drift at a low note and a bigger one at a high note:

It also explains why strobe tuners are so exact for low notes. To see 1 cent on the open low E string of a guitar (82 Hz), band 1 needs 20 seconds to cross one stripe; band 6, being tuned to 494 Hz, crosses six times quicker. Using the higher bands is how you resolve small errors on a low string quickly. The calculator below does the sum.

title: How a Strobe Tuner Works
text:
6. Why several bands help
If the fundamental were always the loudest partial, one band would do. Two things make that untrue for a guitar.
A weak fundamental. On the low strings of a guitar and on a bass, the speaker or pickup and the string itself give a fundamental that is often weaker than the second or third partial. A tuner that listens for the lowest frequency, or that computes one pitch from the whole waveform, can then jump to the octave above or flicker between two answers. A strobe tuner has no such trouble: the rows are independent, and the bands that have a strong partial are bright and the others fade. In the tuner below, turn the fundamental down to 5% and the first row fades while the others stay bright; the readout above the bands (which is a single pitch worked out by a different method) may get unsettled, and the rows are still telling the truth.
Stiff strings. Real strings are stiff, so the upper partials are pushed sharp by k f (√(1 + B k²) − 1) as in section 3. A piano’s bass strings and a guitar’s thickest strings are the stretched ones. Tuning by the fundamental (row 1) leaves the upper partials a few cents sharp, which is why a piano tuner stretches the octaves: they tune the octave so that the partials beat as little as possible, not the fundamentals. Look at the rows with the stiffness at 0.0008 and decide which row you would trust.



Press Start (nothing here opens the microphone: the source is the made-up string), then drag Fundamental’s strength up and down, and String is off by to a few cents. Row 1 is the one a single-pitch tuner would trust. Notice that when you detune the string every row moves together, row k by k times as much.

title: How a Strobe Tuner Works
section: 7. Just and equal temperament, on the bands
text:
7. Just and equal temperament, on the bands
Tuning systems shows that the pure major third, 5:4 (386.3 cents), is 13.7 cents narrower than the piano’s 400. A strobe tuner makes this visible, because it needs a target: it can be set to 12-tone equal temperament or to a just interval over a tonic, and then it shows how far the note you are playing is from that.
The widget gives the tuner a target (the note and its tuning system) and tunes a computed string to either system. When both agree, every band stands still. When the string is just and the target equal (or the other way round), the whole stack drifts, and the higher bands drift faster.



Pick Major third with the target 12-ET and the string Just over C: the string (327.0 Hz) is 13.7 cents flat of the piano’s E (329.6 Hz), so band 1 drifts left at about 2.6 Hz, and band 6 six times faster, which is a blur on the screen (as the fast wheel was in section 2) but is still read in cents in the number beside the band. Set the target to Just over C and the string stands still. For the fifth the difference is only 2 cents, a slow creep of 0.4 Hz. That is the size of the compromise a piano makes in every chord.

title: How a Strobe Tuner Works
section: 8. Watch it follow this page’s own sound
text:
8. Watch it follow this page’s own sound
The tuner does not need a microphone to listen. Each sound the site makes (the lesson widgets, the drone and metronome in the top bar, the chord keyboard, the Backing Track) hands its output to a small registry, AudioTap, and the tuner can listen to that instead: choose This page’s sound. It works with headphones on, there is nothing to pick up from a room, and it hears nothing but the page.
Below, the oscillator plays a sine wave at 221 Hz. The tuner’s target is A3 = 220 Hz, which is 7.8 cents flat of it. Press ▶ on the oscillator, then Start on the tuner (the source is already This page’s sound) and watch the bands drift to the right. Slide the oscillator’s frequency down through 220 Hz and the stripes slow down, stop, and reverse. The sine has only one partial, so only row 1 is bright.






Switch the oscillator’s wave to sawtooth or square and the other rows light up: those waves are sums of partials at whole-number multiples (see the harmonic series), so they stand still on the bands together.
The same choice is in the Strobe tuner in the top bar, which also has two sources that never touch the microphone: a video or audio file on the page (the Timestamp Notes player, say), and another browser tab (a YouTube video, in Chrome: it asks which tab to share, and you must tick “Share tab audio”). Try the top-bar tuner while the drone is playing: it listens to the drone through exactly the same tap.

title: How a Strobe Tuner Works
text:
Things to try

In the wheel, set 3 turns a second. At what flash rate does the eight-spoke wheel stand still? (24, since 24 spokes pass a point each second.) Which lower rates do it too, without a marked spoke? (12, 8, 6 and so on: 24 divided by a whole number.) With a marked spoke? (3, or 1.5, 1: only a whole number of turns between flashes.)
In the disc, play 165 Hz. Does any ring stop? (No: it is halfway between ring 1 at 110 and ring 2 at 220, so both are 55 pairs a second out and blur.) Then play 220, and then 224, and find which way the ring creeps.
In the bands widget, find the stiffness at which band 6 is 10 cents sharp with the string in tune. (600 × log₂(1 + B × 36) = 10 gives B of about 0.00032.)
In the demodulation widget, set the note to 3.5 Hz, then 4.5 Hz. The dot goes round in opposite directions. Which direction means sharp?
At 220 Hz, how many cents is a drift of 0.5 Hz on band 1? On band 3? (Convert with 1200 × log₂(1 + drift / (k f)): 3.9 cents and 1.3 cents.)
In the last widget, tune the oscillator to 220 Hz, then play a sawtooth. Which rows light up, and do they all stand still?

title: Sources 1: Where Did You Find That? (Grades 6–8)
text: When you write about music, a source is where you found out something you didn’t know before. It might be a book, a website, a video, a recording, a score, or a person you asked. Every time you write a fact you found somewhere, the reader should be able to ask “where did you find that?” and get an answer.
crumbs: Sources 1: Where Did You Find That? (Grades 6–8)

title: Sources 1: Where Did You Find That? (Grades 6–8)
text:
Kinds of sources








Kind
What it is
Example




The music itself
A recording or a printed score
The album, the sheet music


The people who made it
The musicians, in their own words
An interview with the drummer, the album notes


People who studied it
Writers who know a lot about the music
A book about the blues, a music encyclopedia


Places that teach
Schools, museums, libraries
A music museum’s website, a university page



The best research uses more than one kind. Listen to the music and read what people who know about it say.
crumbs: Sources 1: Where Did You Find That? (Grades 6–8)

title: Sources 1: Where Did You Find That? (Grades 6–8)
section: Four questions to ask about any source
text:
Four questions to ask about any source

Who made it? Is there a person’s name or an organisation’s name? Do they know about music?
How do they know? Were they there? Did they study it? Do they say where they found it?
When was it made? Old is fine for history. For gear and apps, you want something recent.
Can someone else find it again? If your teacher can’t find it, they can’t check it.

If a source can’t answer the first question, be careful with it.
crumbs: Sources 1: Where Did You Find That? (Grades 6–8)

title: Sources 1: Where Did You Find That? (Grades 6–8)
section: Google’s AI summary is not a source
text:
Google’s AI summary is not a source






WarningThe box at the top of Google is not a source



When you search, Google (and Bing, and other search sites) often shows a summary written by a computer at the top of the page. It might be called an AI Overview. Other apps, like chatbots, write answers the same way.
You can’t cite it, and you shouldn’t trust it. Here’s why:

Nobody wrote it. A computer made it by guessing which words come next. No person checked it.
It makes mistakes. In 2024 Google’s AI Overviews told people to put glue on pizza and to eat a small rock every day. It got the glue idea from a joke someone posted online.
It changes. Ask again tomorrow and you may get a different answer. Your teacher can’t look up what you saw.



What to do instead:

Scroll past the AI summary.
Click on a real web page in the results, from a person or a group you can name.
Ask the four questions about that page.
Find a second good source that says the same thing.
Write down the page you used, not the summary.
crumbs: Sources 1: Where Did You Find That? (Grades 6–8)

title: Sources 1: Where Did You Find That? (Grades 6–8)
text:
What about Wikipedia?
Wikipedia is a good place to start, but not to finish. Anyone can edit it, so it can be wrong for a while. At the bottom of each article is a list of references: the books and websites the article used. Click those. They are often better sources, and you can use them.
crumbs: Sources 1: Where Did You Find That? (Grades 6–8)

title: Sources 1: Where Did You Find That? (Grades 6–8)
section: What about MuseScore, YouTube and other uploads?
text:
What about MuseScore, YouTube and other uploads?
Anyone can upload sheet music to MuseScore or a video to YouTube. Some of it is excellent and some is full of mistakes. For sheet music, check whether it matches the recording, or ask your teacher for a published copy. For a video, ask who made it. A video from the band itself, a museum, or a music school is better than one from a stranger.
crumbs: Sources 1: Where Did You Find That? (Grades 6–8)

title: Sources 1: Where Did You Find That? (Grades 6–8)
section: Writing down where you found it
text:
Writing down where you found it
Every time you use a source, write down:

Who made it (the author or the organisation)
What it’s called (the title)
Where it is (the website’s name and the web address, or the book’s publisher)
When it was made, if it says

For music, also write down where in the music: a time in the recording (“at 1:24”) or a bar number in the score (“bar 12”).
For example:

Hanna, Abby. “Who Was Robert Johnson?” Example Music Museum, 2023, www.example.org/robert-johnson.

(That page is made up, to show you the pattern. Your real one will have a real address.)
crumbs: Sources 1: Where Did You Find That? (Grades 6–8)

title: Sources 1: Where Did You Find That? (Grades 6–8)
text:
Try it
Pick one question, such as “Who invented the electric guitar?” or “Where does the steel drum come from?”

Search for it. Look at the AI summary, if there is one, and then scroll past it.
Find two real web pages that answer the question. Ask the four questions about each one.
Do they agree? If they don’t, find a third.
Write down both sources in the pattern above.
Now look at the AI summary again. Did it match what your good sources said? Did it tell you where it got its answer?

Next: Sources 2: Checking and Citing (grades 9–10).

title: Sources 2: Checking and Citing (Grades 9–10)
text: In Sources 1 the question was “where did you find that?” Now there are two more: is it true? and how do you show the reader exactly where it came from?

title: Sources 2: Checking and Citing (Grades 9–10)
text:
Primary and secondary sources
In music research, a primary source is the music itself, or the people directly involved in making it:

recordings and live performances
scores, lead sheets and the composer’s manuscripts
interviews with the composer or the performers, their letters, the album’s liner notes

A secondary source is written about the music by someone who wasn’t part of it:

books and journal articles by music researchers
music encyclopedias (such as Grove Music Online)
documentaries, reviews and critical editions of scores

Good research uses both. The primary sources show what the music does. The secondary sources tell you what’s normal for that style, its history, and what the experts have found. One song isn’t enough to tell you what’s typical of a whole style. If you listen to one blues and it has a 16-bar form, that doesn’t mean the blues uses 16 bars.

title: Sources 2: Checking and Citing (Grades 9–10)
section: Check a source by reading around it
text:
Check a source by reading around it
Fact-checkers don’t decide whether a web page is good by staring at it. They open new tabs and find out what other people say about the page and its author. Mike Caulfield’s SIFT method puts this into four moves:

Stop. Before you use something, ask whether you know who made it.
Investigate the source. Open a new tab and search for the author or the site. Who are they? What do others say about them?
Find better coverage. Look for other trusted sources on the same claim. If good sources agree, you’re on firm ground.
Trace claims back to the original. If a page says “the band said in an interview…”, find that interview.

title: Sources 2: Checking and Citing (Grades 9–10)
section: AI search answers can’t be cited
text:
AI search answers can’t be cited






WarningAI summaries are not sources, and they aren’t reliable



The AI answers at the top of Google, Bing and other search engines, and the answers chatbots give, are not citeable sources:

There’s no author who is responsible for the claim, and no editor checked it.
There’s nothing fixed to cite. The text is generated fresh each time. Your reader can’t go and look at what you saw.
They get things wrong, confidently. Google’s AI Overviews told people to add glue to pizza (from a joke on Reddit). They said a US president who died in 1875 had earned degrees between 1947 and 2012.
Their own “sources” are often wrong. In a 2025 test by Columbia University’s Tow Center, eight AI search tools were asked to find the source of real news quotes. They got it wrong more than 60% of the time. Google’s Gemini gave a completely correct answer only once out of 200, and two of the tools gave more made-up links than real ones.

Style guides like MLA do show how to cite a chatbot. That’s for when you quote what the chatbot said, for example in an essay about AI. It doesn’t turn the chatbot into evidence for a fact about music.


What to do instead:

Treat an AI answer, at most, as a hint about what to look for. Then go and find a real source that says it.
Click through to the page it claims to be summarising, and read that page. Often it doesn’t say what the summary said.
Cite the page, book, recording or score you actually read.
If your teacher allows AI for brainstorming, say that you used it, following your school’s rules. Still check and cite every fact against a real source.

title: Sources 2: Checking and Citing (Grades 9–10)
text:
Where to look

Your school library’s databases: Grove Music Online (the standard music encyclopedia), JSTOR (journal articles), and the library catalogue for books. Ask your librarian for the login.
Scores: IMSLP (the Petrucci Music Library) has scans of published scores whose copyright has run out. The publisher’s edition is better than a fan’s upload.
Interviews and liner notes: the musicians’ own words, from a magazine, a radio show, a museum archive, or the album itself.
Museums and archives: the Library of Congress, the Smithsonian, and national music museums.

title: Sources 2: Checking and Citing (Grades 9–10)
text:
Citing in MLA
A citation has two parts.
1. In the text, where you use the source, put the author’s name (and the page, if it’s a book) in brackets:

The twelve-bar form was already common in the earliest blues recordings (Smith 45).

(Smith is a made-up author, to show the pattern.)
For music, point to the exact place: “the bass drops out at 2:13” or “the modulation in bar 33”.
2. At the end, in a list called Works Cited, the full entry, in alphabetical order. The pattern is:

Author. “Title of the Part.” Title of the Whole, Publisher, Date, Location.

Some patterns for music:







Source
Pattern




A song on an album
Davis, Miles. “So What.” Kind of Blue, Columbia, 1959.


A score
Composer. Title. Edited by Editor, Publisher, Year.


A web page
Author. “Page Title.” Website Name, Date, URL.


An interview
Person interviewed. Interview by Interviewer. Where It Appeared, Date, URL.


A video
“Video Title.” YouTube, uploaded by Channel, Date, URL.



Quoting is using the exact words, in quotation marks. Paraphrasing is putting the idea in your own words. Both need a citation. The idea came from someone else, even when the words are yours.

title: Sources 2: Checking and Citing (Grades 9–10)
text:
Try it
Pick a style you’re studying, for example reggae, bossa nova, or Baroque dance music.

Ask a search engine one question about it, and copy down the AI summary.
Using SIFT, find two primary and two secondary sources on the same question.
Mark each sentence of the AI summary: confirmed (and by which source), wrong, or couldn’t confirm.
Write four sentences about the style, each with an in-text citation. Then write the Works Cited list.
