title: Sound 2: Oscillators and Pulse-Width Modulation
text:
An oscillator is the part of a synthesizer that makes a repeating wave. Its two settings are the shape of the wave and how fast it repeats (the frequency, heard as pitch). This lesson plays the classic shapes from the harmonic series lesson on a real oscillator, then makes the pulse wave move.
How to use the page. Press ▶, or play the computer keys (a w s e d…), the on-screen keyboard or a MIDI keyboard; the widget sounds while a key is held. Keep the volume in the bottom bar low to start with. The bright waves are loud.

title: Sound 2: Oscillators and Pulse-Width Modulation
text:
Four shapes



Play the same note with each Wave and watch both pictures:

Sine: one spike in the spectrum.
Triangle: a few odd harmonics that die away fast. Softer than you’d guess from the pointed shape.
Sawtooth: a comb of every harmonic. The brightest and the most useful, because a filter can carve almost anything out of it.
Square: only every other spike. Listen for the hollow, woody tone.

Move Pitch up and down. On the spectrum the whole comb slides along together, keeping its pattern. That pattern (the timbre) is independent of the pitch.

Frequency and pitch. Each octave doubles the frequency: A2 is 110 Hz, A3 220 Hz, A4 440 Hz. That’s why the spectrum’s frequency axis is drawn with every octave the same width.

title: Sound 2: Oscillators and Pulse-Width Modulation
text:
Pulse width
A pulse wave is up for part of each cycle and down for the rest. The fraction of the cycle it spends up is the pulse width (or duty cycle). At 50% it is a square wave.



Drag Pulse width slowly from 50% down to 5%. The sound goes from hollow to nasal to thin and reedy. On the spectrum, gaps appear and move: at width 1/k, every kth harmonic is missing. Widths of 30% and 70% sound the same: one is the other upside down.
Inside the browser there is no pulse oscillator, so the widget makes one the way some analogue synths did: it takes a sawtooth and subtracts a delayed copy of the same sawtooth. The delay, as a fraction of the cycle, is the pulse width.

title: Sound 2: Oscillators and Pulse-Width Modulation
text:
PWM: pulse-width modulation
Now let something move the width for you. PWM rate is how many times a second the width swings, and PWM depth is how far.



A slowly swinging pulse width gives the rich, chorus-like shimmer of 1980s string machines and synth pads: the gaps in the spectrum sweep up and down, a little like a phaser. Turn the rate up to 5 Hz or so for a wobble. The thing doing the moving is an LFO, a low-frequency oscillator, which gets its own lesson.

title: Sound 20: Tremolo and the Rotary Speaker
text: Tremolo is the volume going up and down, over and over. It’s one of the oldest effects: guitar amps had it built in from the 1950s, long before pedals. An LFO does the work. Move the position instead of the volume and it’s auto-pan. Spin a real speaker and you get both at once, plus a pitch wobble: the rotary speaker.
crumbs: Sound 20: Tremolo and the Rotary Speaker

title: Sound 20: Tremolo and the Rotary Speaker
text:
Tremolo and auto-pan




Rate: how many times a second. Slow is a throb; fast is a shimmer.
Depth: how far the volume falls. At 100% it goes all the way to silence.
Shape: a sine wave swells smoothly; a square chops the sound on and off (Chopper).

Try Surf tremolo on the Synth riff, then switch to Auto-pan with headphones on: the chords float from ear to ear. Push the rate up past about 15 Hz on the LFO page and tremolo stops sounding like a wobble and starts sounding like a new tone: that’s amplitude modulation, a cousin of FM.
Guitarists say “tremolo” for two different things, confusingly: the tremolo arm on a Stratocaster actually bends the pitch (that’s vibrato), while a tremolo effect changes the volume. Fender named them backwards in the 1950s and the names stuck.
crumbs: Sound 20: Tremolo and the Rotary Speaker

title: Sound 20: Tremolo and the Rotary Speaker
text:
The rotary speaker
Don Leslie built a speaker cabinet for the Hammond organ in the 1940s with two spinning parts: a horn for the high frequencies and a drum for the low ones. As each turns toward you it gets louder, higher in pitch (the Doppler effect, as when a siren passes) and moves across the stereo field.




Slow (chorale) and Fast (tremolo): the two speeds. Organists switch between them in the middle of a song. Press Slow ⇄ Fast while it plays and listen to the change: the light horn gets up to speed in about a second, while the heavy drum takes several. That lurch, the two parts going at different speeds for a moment, is the sound people love.
Crossover: where the highs (horn) and lows (drum) are split.
Amp drive: the Leslie’s own valve amp, pushed until it growls.

Try it on the Synth riff and your Microphone as well. The Beatles put voices and guitars through a Leslie (“Tomorrow Never Knows”), and Stevie Ray Vaughan’s “Cold Shot” guitar is one.

title: Sound 23: Stereo
text:
You have two ears, and you can tell where a sound is coming from with them: from which ear hears it louder, and which ear hears it first. A stereo recording has two channels, left and right, and mixing engineers use both of those clues to place each sound somewhere between the speakers. Headphones on for this page.
How to use the page. The square is a vectorscope. A sound that’s the same in both ears (mono) is a vertical line. One that’s only on the left leans left; only on the right, leans right. A wide stereo sound is a fuzzy blob. Press Mono to fold left and right together, as a phone speaker or a club sound system does.

title: Sound 23: Stereo
text:
Pan, Haas and width



Pan (the first tool) uses loudness: more in one ear than the other. Move it and watch the line lean. It’s how most sounds are placed in a mix: bass, kick and lead vocal in the middle, the rest spread around them.
Haas delay uses time. Choose it: the right channel is the same sound, a few milliseconds late.

Under about 1 ms the sound just moves toward the left, the side that arrives first.
From about 5 to 35 ms you don’t hear an echo. The sound seems to come from the earlier side, but much wider. Helmut Haas measured this in 1951 (the precedence effect); it’s how your ears ignore the reflections in a room.
Above about 40 ms it breaks apart into a slapback echo.

Width (mid / side) makes a stereo sound narrower or wider. Any stereo sound can be split into the mid (left + right: what’s the same in both) and the side (left − right: what’s different). Width turns the side up or down. At 0% the sound is mono; at 200% it’s wider than the speakers. Watch the blob.

title: Sound 23: Stereo
text:
The mono check
Set Haas delay to about 1 ms and press Mono. Then try 3, 5 and 10 ms. When the two channels are added back together, the delay cancels some frequencies and reinforces others: a comb filter, the hollow, phasey sound of a flanger standing still. A trick that sounds wide on headphones can sound thin and odd on a phone, a Bluetooth speaker, or a club PA, all of which are often mono. That’s why engineers press their mono button all the time. Now try Width at 200% in mono: the side cancels out completely and the extra width simply disappears.

title: Sound 16: Reverb
text:
Clap in a cathedral and the sound goes on for seconds after your hands stop. It bounces off the walls, the floor and the ceiling, thousands of times, each echo a little quieter and a little duller, until they blur into a smooth wash. That wash is reverberation, and every room has its own. A reverb effect puts a dry recording into a room that isn’t there.
How to use the page. The source starts as single hits, so you can hear each hit’s tail die away. The strip under the controls is the room’s impulse response: what one instant click would sound like in this room.

title: Sound 16: Reverb
text:
The room




Decay time (RT60): how long the tail takes to fall by 60 dB, which is about until you can’t hear it. A living room is about 0.5 s, a concert hall about 2 s, a cathedral 5 s or more.
Pre-delay: the gap before the reverb starts. In a big room the first reflection takes a while to come back. A little pre-delay keeps a voice clear in front of its reverb.
Damping: in real rooms the high frequencies die first, absorbed by air, carpet and people. Lower damping makes a darker, warmer tail.
Early reflections: the first few distinct echoes from the nearest walls. They tell your ear how big the room is before the tail arrives.
Mix: how far away the sound seems. More wet signal pushes it to the back of the room.

Try the presets: a small room, a hall, a cathedral, a plate (a big steel sheet with a pickup, used in studios since the 1950s: bright and dense, no early reflections) and reverse, the impulse response played backwards so each sound swells into itself.

title: Sound 16: Reverb
text:
How it is made: convolution
This reverb is a convolution reverb. It needs one thing: the impulse response of the room. To capture a real room, engineers play a click (or a sweep) in it and record what comes back. The computer then replays that recording once for every sample of the input, scaled by that sample’s level, and adds them all up. That’s a lot of arithmetic, which the browser does for us.
The impulse responses here aren’t recordings. They are made from decaying noise that gets duller as it fades, plus a few early reflections. That’s close to what a real room does, and it means every control can change the room instantly.

title: Sound 16: Reverb
text:
Spring reverb
Before digital reverb, a guitar amp couldn’t carry a room around with it, so it carried a spring: a coil of wire with a small speaker-like driver at one end and a pickup at the other. The sound runs down the spring, bounces off the far end, runs back, and keeps bouncing.



Listen to a single snare hit. Instead of a smooth wash you hear a “drip” or “boing”: a quick falling whistle that repeats. A spring carries low frequencies faster than high ones, so each bounce arrives as a sweep from high to low (a chirp), and the bounces come back at a steady rate, which you can see as the evenly spaced bursts in the strip. Room size here sets how long the spring is, so how far apart the bounces are.

Surf guitar (Dick Dale, the Ventures) is a spring turned all the way up, with a clean, bright guitar hitting it hard.
Dub reggae engineers kicked their spring units to get a crash of thunder.
Most Fender amps since 1963 have one; pick a guitar amp up and shake it and you’ll hear it.

Compare it with Plate and Hall on the drum loop: the spring is the one that never quite sounds like a real place, and that’s why people like it.

title: Sound 16: Reverb
text:
Shimmer and freeze
Two modern reverb tricks, both loved by ambient musicians and post-rock guitarists.




Shimmer: part of the reverb tail is pitch-shifted up an octave and fed back into the reverb. Every trip round, the tail climbs another octave, so a chord grows a halo of high notes that rises and glows above it. Brian Eno and Daniel Lanois made it in the 1980s with two machines; now pedals like the Strymon BigSky do it alone. Try the Fifths interval too.
❄ Freeze: press it while the chords play. The last second of sound is held forever (by reading it as overlapping grains) and the live input is shut off. Change the chord on your keys and the frozen one stays underneath. Press again to let go.

title: Sound 16: Reverb
text:
On music
Switch the source to the chords, the drum loop or your microphone (headphones on). Long reverb makes chords smooth and huge but turns drums to mush; fast music wants short reverb or a lot of pre-delay. Singing into the cathedral preset and listening to your own voice come back is the best way to learn what reverb does.

title: Sound 19: Phaser
text:
A phaser sweeps a few notches up and down the spectrum, and the result is a soft, swirling “whoosh”. It’s the sound of the electric piano in a thousand 1970s records, and Eddie Van Halen’s guitar on the first Van Halen album.
How to use the page. The source starts as chords. The red line on the spectrum shows the notches moving. Turn Mix to 100% and the effect disappears (to the ear), which says something about how it works.

title: Sound 19: Phaser
text: The effect

title: Sound 19: Phaser
text:
How it works
A phaser passes the sound through a chain of all-pass filters. An all-pass filter is a strange kind of filter: it doesn’t change how loud any frequency is. It only delays some frequencies more than others, so it shifts their phase. On its own you can’t hear it.
But mix that phase-shifted copy back with the original, and wherever the copy has been shifted exactly half a cycle the two cancel. Those cancellations are the notches. The stages here are the browser’s all-pass filters, each of which makes one notch, so Stages = 4 gives four notches. (A guitar pedal uses simpler stages, and needs two of them per notch.) An LFO sweeps the all-pass filters up and down, and the notches sweep with them.
That’s why the wet sound alone (Mix at 100%) sounds plain. The notches only exist when the shifted copy meets the original. 50% gives the deepest notches.

title: Sound 19: Phaser
text:
The controls

Stages: more stages, more notches, a stronger effect. The MXR Phase 90 has two notches; 12 here is very dramatic.
Centre and Sweep: where the notches sit and how far up and down they move.
Rate: slow for a swirl, fast for a warble.
Width (Q): how sharp the phase change in each stage is, and so how narrow the notches are.
Feedback: feeds the output back to the input; the areas between the notches turn into resonant peaks and the effect becomes more vocal and whistling. (The red line doesn’t show the feedback.)

title: Sound 19: Phaser
text:
Phaser or flanger?
Both sweep notches. A flanger uses a short delay, which makes many evenly spaced notches, like the teeth of a comb, so it sounds metallic and jet-like. A phaser uses all-pass filters, which make a few notches that aren’t evenly spaced, so it sounds softer and more liquid. Switch the source to noise on both pages and compare the spectrum.

title: Sound 6: LFOs
text:
An LFO, or low-frequency oscillator, is an oscillator too slow to hear as a pitch, typically between a tenth of a beat and twenty times a second. Instead of being listened to, it moves a control: the pitch, the volume, a filter, the stereo position. Almost every effect that “moves” (vibrato, tremolo, wah, chorus, phaser, PWM) is an LFO turning a knob for you.
How to use the page. Press ▶ or play the keys. The strip above the scope draws the LFO itself over the last two seconds; the red dot is where it is now.

title: Sound 6: LFOs
text:
What an LFO can move



Leave the shape on Sine and try each target with Rate about 5 Hz:

Pitch gives vibrato: the note bends slightly sharp and flat. Singers and string players use 5 to 7 cycles a second. Too deep and it sounds seasick; too fast and it sounds nervous.
Volume gives tremolo: the note gets louder and softer. The “tremolo” on a guitar amp is this, and so is a vibraphone with its motor on.
Filter cutoff gives an automatic wah. Slow it right down (0.2 Hz) for a slowly opening and closing sound; speed it up for a “wobble” bass.
Pan moves the sound between your left and right ear (auto-pan). Use headphones.

Depth is how far the LFO moves the control, and Rate is how fast. Those two plus the shape are all an LFO has.

title: Sound 6: LFOs
text:
Shapes

Sine and triangle: smooth back-and-forth.
Square: jumps between two values. On pitch it’s a trill; on volume, a chopped “gate”.
Sawtooth (ramp): rises slowly, then drops. On pitch it sounds like a siren.
Random (sample & hold): jumps to a new random value every cycle. On the filter it’s the bubbling “computer” sound of 1970s science fiction.

title: Sound 6: LFOs
section: When an LFO gets fast enough to hear
text:
When an LFO gets fast enough to hear
Set the target to Volume, the shape to Sine and slowly push the rate past 20 Hz. The tremolo stops sounding like a pulse and becomes a rough, buzzy tone, and new pitches appear on the spectrum on both sides of the note. That is amplitude modulation. Do the same with Pitch and past about 30 Hz the vibrato becomes a metallic, bell-like timbre: that is frequency modulation, the subject of Sound 8. An LFO and an audible oscillator are the same thing at different speeds.

title: Sound 6: LFOs
text:
LFOs elsewhere on these pages

The PWM in Sound 2 is an LFO on the pulse width.
Chorus (Sound 18) is an LFO on a very short delay.
A phaser (Sound 19) is an LFO sweeping a chain of filters.
The Leslie speaker in the organ lesson is a mechanical LFO: a spinning horn moves pitch, volume and direction all at once.

title: Sound 10: Granular Synthesis
text:
Take a few seconds of recorded sound and cut it into hundreds of tiny pieces, each a few hundredths of a second long, each faded in and out so it doesn’t click. These are grains. Play them back overlapping, dozens a second, and you can do things a tape never could: hold one moment of a sound forever, stretch a sound to ten times its length without making it lower, or scatter it into a glittering cloud. That’s granular synthesis. The idea goes back to the composer Iannis Xenakis in the 1950s, who cut tape into tiny pieces with scissors.
How to use the page. Pick a sound to cut up (or record three seconds of your own voice), press ▶, and move the Position. The strip shows the sound; each flash is one grain being read.

title: Sound 10: Granular Synthesis
text:
The grain cloud




Position: where in the sound the grains are read from.
Scan speed: how fast the position moves on its own. At ×1 it plays the sound at normal speed; at ×0.2 it plays it five times slower, but at the same pitch, because each grain still plays at the normal speed. At 0 the sound is frozen.
Grain size: under about 20 ms each grain is a click, and you hear the rate of the clicks as a buzz. From 50 to 200 ms you hear the sound itself, smeared.
Grains per second: few grains give a crackle; many give a smooth cloud.
Spray: each grain is read from a slightly random place near the position. More spray, more blur.
Pitch and Random pitch: each grain can be played faster or slower. With random pitch the grains turn into a shimmering chord.
Backwards grains and Stereo spread make the cloud stranger and wider.

title: Sound 10: Granular Synthesis
text:
Try this

Freeze on Vowels. Move the position slowly through the sound: you can stop on any vowel and hold it.
Stretch (slow motion) on the Synth riff: the riff, five times slower, at its normal pitch. Video editors and DJs use this to fit a sound to a length without changing the key.
Shimmer: the grains an octave up and spread wide. Ambient music lives here.
Record your own voice and choose Scatter.
Play the keys: the whole cloud moves to the note you play, a melody made from your voice.

title: Sound 10: Granular Synthesis
text:
Where you’ve heard it
Time-stretching in every DAW (Ableton’s warp modes, Melodyne) is granular underneath. So are the “frozen” pads of ambient music, the shimmering textures of film scores, and many synths: Ableton’s Granulator, Mutable Instruments’ Clouds, the Tasty Chips GR-1. The glitch effects and the freeze button on the reverb page use grains too.

title: Sound 8: FM Synthesis
text:
FM (frequency modulation) synthesis makes harmonics by a different route from subtractive synthesis. Instead of starting rich and filtering, it starts with two plain sine waves and uses one to wobble the pitch of the other so fast that the wobble becomes new frequencies. John Chowning found this at Stanford in 1967; Yamaha built it into the DX7 in 1983, and its electric piano, bells and slap bass are all over the music of the 1980s.
How to use the page. Press ▶ Demo or play the keys or MIDI. Choose a preset, then change one control at a time. The dashed lines on the spectrum mark where FM puts its new frequencies.

title: Sound 8: FM Synthesis
text:
Carrier and modulator




The carrier is the sine wave you hear. Its frequency is the note you play.
The modulator is a second sine wave that you don’t hear directly. It moves the carrier’s pitch up and down.
The ratio is the modulator’s frequency divided by the carrier’s.
The index is how far the modulator pushes the pitch. At 0 there’s no modulation: a plain sine.

This is the vibrato from the LFO lesson, sped up into the audio range. Below about 20 Hz you hear a wobble; above it you hear a new timbre.

title: Sound 8: FM Synthesis
text:
Sidebands
With the preset Steady (to study) loaded, hold a note and slowly raise the index from 0. New spikes appear on the spectrum on both sides of the carrier, spaced by the modulator’s frequency: carrier ± 1 × modulator, ± 2 ×, ± 3 × and so on. These are sidebands. The higher the index, the more sidebands, and the brighter the sound.
Now change the ratio:

Whole-number ratios (1, 2, 3…) put every sideband on a harmonic of the note. The sound is pitched and “musical”. Ratio 1 gives every harmonic, like a sawtooth; ratio 2 gives only odd harmonics, like a square or a clarinet.
Other ratios (1.41, 3.5…) put the sidebands between harmonics. The sound is inharmonic: metallic, bell-like, clangorous. That’s how FM makes bells and gongs so easily, which subtractive synths find hard.
Modulator fine tune detunes the modulator a few cents: the sidebands beat against each other and the sound shimmers.

title: Sound 8: FM Synthesis
text:
Envelopes make FM come alive
In FM the index does the job of the filter in a subtractive synth: it sets the brightness. Give the index its own envelope and the brightness changes during each note, the way real instruments do.

Bell: index starts high and dies away, the volume dies away more slowly. The clang at the start fades into a pure hum.
Electric piano: ratio 1, a quick index decay: a bright “tine” attack and a mellow body.
Brass: the index rises with the attack, so the note gets brighter as it swells.
Bass: a short burst of index gives the slap at the start of each note.

Try the Bell preset and change only the ratio: 3.5, 1.4, 2.76, 5.19. Each is a different metal.

title: Sound 8: FM Synthesis
section: FM and the spectrum, in one sentence
text:
FM and the spectrum, in one sentence
Subtractive starts with all the harmonics and removes some; additive (Sound 1) sets each harmonic by hand; FM makes a whole family of frequencies from two sine waves, controlled by just two numbers: the ratio decides where they go and the index decides how many.

title: Sound 11: The Equaliser
text:
An equaliser (EQ) turns some frequencies up and others down. You met the parts on the filter page: high-pass, low-pass, shelves and bells. An EQ is several of them in a row, and it’s the most used tool in any recording studio. Every track in a mix gets some, to make room for the others.
How to use the page. The pink curve on the spectrum is the EQ: above the middle line is a boost, below is a cut. Use Bypass often. Your ears get used to a change within seconds, and only comparing tells you whether it’s better.

title: Sound 11: The Equaliser
text:
The bands




High-pass (low cut): removes everything below a frequency. The most useful control on the desk: almost nothing except bass and kick needs anything below 80–100 Hz, and rumble there muddies everything.
Shelves lift or lower everything above (high shelf) or below (low shelf) a frequency, like the bass and treble knobs on a stereo.
Bells (peaking filters) boost or cut around one frequency. Q is how narrow: a high Q touches only a few notes’ worth of frequencies, a low Q a wide region.
Low-pass (high cut) removes the top: hiss, harshness, or everything at once for a muffled effect.

A rough map of what lives where:








Range
Called
Sounds like




20–60 Hz
sub
felt more than heard: kick drum thump, synth sub bass


60–250 Hz
bass
warmth and weight; too much is boomy


250–500 Hz
low mids
“mud” and “boxiness”: most mixes are cut a little here


500 Hz–2 kHz
mids
the body of most instruments; too much honks


2–5 kHz
upper mids
presence, the bite of a voice or guitar; too much is harsh


5–10 kHz
highs
clarity, the “s” sounds


10–20 kHz
air
sparkle and openness

title: Sound 11: The Equaliser
text:
Cut before you boost
Try Cut the mud and Presence on the chords and on your microphone. Engineers usually cut what’s wrong rather than boost what’s missing: a cut makes room, a boost makes everything louder and soon everything is fighting. Two sounds that both have a lot at 300 Hz will mask each other; cut one of them there, and both become clear.
Telephone keeps only 400 Hz to 3.2 kHz, the band a phone line carries. Scooped is the classic metal guitar curve: big lows and highs, a hole in the middle.

title: Sound 11: The Equaliser
text:
Find the problem
Recordings often have one frequency that rings: a drum’s overtone, a boomy room, a harsh voice. The trick for finding it is boost and sweep:

Set Hidden problem to A ringing frequency. Something is now wrong with the sound.
Press Search (narrow boost): Bell 2 becomes a tall, narrow boost.
Sweep Bell 2 frequency slowly. At most places it just sounds odd; at the problem frequency the ring suddenly leaps out.
Now turn that boost into a cut (Bell 2 gain to about −12 dB) and listen: the ring is gone.
Press Reveal to see how close you were. Then try Boomy and Harsh.

title: Sound 12: Distortion
text:
Distortion changes the shape of a wave by squashing its loudest parts. A changed shape means a changed recipe of harmonics (Sound 1), so distortion adds harmonics that weren’t there. A little gives warmth; a lot gives the roar of a rock guitar.
How to use the page. Every effect on these pages has a Source menu (what goes in), a Mix (how much of the effect you hear), and Bypass to switch it out and back in. The square graph is the distortion curve: the input level runs across, the output level up. The dashed diagonal is “no change”.

title: Sound 12: Distortion
section: A sine wave in, harmonics out
text:
A sine wave in, harmonics out



The source starts as a pure sine tone: one spike on the spectrum. Raise Drive slowly.

The curve bends over at the ends: loud parts of the wave can’t get any louder.
The scope shows the sine’s peaks being flattened toward a square.
New spikes appear on the spectrum at 3, 5, 7… times the frequency: odd harmonics, because the top and bottom of the wave are squashed the same way. That’s the square-wave recipe.

Now try the other curves:








Curve
What it does
Sound




Soft clip
bends over gradually
overdrive: a warm, singing tone, like a valve amp turned up


Hard clip
flat-tops the wave at a fixed level
fuzz: buzzy and aggressive


Uneven (tube-like)
squashes the top and bottom differently
adds even harmonics (2, 4, 6) too, which sound sweeter and fuller


Wavefolder
folds the peaks back down instead of flattening them
the West-coast synth sound: glassy, metallic, changes wildly with drive


Bit crusher
rounds the wave to a few steps
the gritty sound of old computers and samplers



Tone is a low-pass after the distortion: almost every guitar amp has one, to tame the fizz that heavy distortion adds at the top.

title: Sound 12: Distortion
text:
Overdrive, distortion or fuzz?
Guitarists use three words, and the pedals really are different. All three clip the wave; they differ in how hard they clip, what shape the clipping is, and what they do to the sound before and after.



Play the synth riff and step through the presets, with Bypass to compare with the clean sound. Watch the curve and the scope.










Overdrive
Distortion
Fuzz




Curve
soft clip: bends over gently
hard clip: flat tops
lopsided: one side clips much sooner, and a dead zone in the middle


Drive
low: clean when you play softly, gritty when you dig in
high: distorted however softly you play
extreme: nearly a square wave


Before
cuts the bass so the low notes don’t turn to mud (the “mid hump” of a Tube Screamer)
some bass cut
nothing: the full, fat low end goes in


After
a tone control
a darker tone control to tame the fizz
dark and woolly


Sound
a turned-up valve amp: warm, still sounds like the instrument
tight and aggressive: metal and hard rock
buzzy, spitting, raw: “Satisfaction”, Hendrix, the White Stripes


Inside
diodes in the op-amp’s feedback loop
diodes after the op-amp
two transistors pushed far past their limits



Two things to try:

On Overdrive, choose the Uneven riff source (loud and soft notes). The soft notes stay almost clean and the loud ones break up: overdrive responds to how hard you play. On Distortion every note is equally squashed.
On Fuzz, play a Sine tone and lower the Drive. The tone starts to sputter: quiet parts of the wave fall into the dead zone and vanish. Fuzz pedals with an old, dying battery do this on purpose, and the note cuts out raggedly as it fades.

title: Sound 12: Distortion
text:
On music
Switch the Source to Chords or the Synth riff. Distorting a chord sounds much messier than distorting one note: every note’s harmonics clash with the others’, and the curve also creates new frequencies at the differences between the notes (intermodulation). That’s why heavy rock guitar plays power chords (root and fifth only). The difference frequencies of a fifth are another octave of the root, so it stays clean.
Try your own voice or instrument through it with Microphone (and headphones).

title: Sound 13: The Compressor
text:
A compressor is an automatic hand on the volume knob. When the sound gets louder than a set level, it turns it down; when it gets quieter, it lets it back up. The loud parts and the quiet parts end up closer together. Almost every vocal, bass line and drum track on a record goes through one.
How to use the page. The source starts as an uneven riff (some notes loud, some barely there). The graph shows input level across and output level up. The red dot is the sound right now, and the red bar on the right is the gain reduction: how many decibels the compressor is turning the sound down at this moment.

title: Sound 13: The Compressor
text:
The controls




Threshold: the level where the compressor starts working. Anything quieter passes through unchanged; on the graph the line follows the dashed diagonal until the threshold.
Ratio: how hard it turns down what goes over. At 4 : 1, a sound 8 dB over the threshold comes out only 2 dB over. At 20 : 1 almost nothing gets over: that’s a limiter.
Knee: how gently it starts. A soft knee bends into compression gradually.
Attack: how fast it reacts when the sound goes over. Slow attack lets the very start of each note through before clamping down, which keeps drums punchy.
Release: how fast it lets go when the sound drops back.
Make-up gain: compression makes everything quieter, so you turn the whole thing back up. Now the quiet notes are louder than before.

Press Bypass on and off with the uneven riff: compressed, the quiet notes come forward and the loud ones stop jumping out.

title: Sound 13: The Compressor
text:
Hearing attack and release
Switch the source to the drum loop, set the ratio to 8 : 1 and the threshold to about −30 dB.

Attack 1 ms: the snare’s crack is flattened; the drums sound small and thick.
Attack 30 ms: the crack gets through before the compressor reacts; the drums punch.
Release 30 ms with a fast attack: the sound “pumps”, rising between hits. Dance music uses this on purpose.

title: Sound 13: The Compressor
text:
Parallel compression
Turn Mix down to 50%. Now you hear the untouched drums and a heavily squashed copy together. The natural hits stay sharp and the squashed copy fills in between them. Engineers call it “New York” compression.

title: Sound 13: The Compressor
text:
Your own playing
Choose Microphone (headphones on) and play or sing from very soft to loud. With a threshold of −40 dB and a ratio of 6 : 1, watch the gain reduction bar follow you. The site’s backing band runs through a compressor too (threshold −12 dB, ratio 4 : 1, attack 3 ms), and these sound pages end in a limiter so that nothing comes out too loud.

title: Sound 25: Chiptune
text:
The music of 1980s home computers and game consoles wasn’t recorded. A small sound chip played it live, note by note, as the game ran. The Nintendo Entertainment System (NES, 1983 in Japan as the Famicom) had two pulse waves, one triangle wave and one noise channel, plus a channel for short, low-quality samples that most games barely used. The Game Boy had nearly the same four: two pulses, a small wave channel of your own design, and noise. The Commodore 64’s SID chip had three voices.
Each channel could play one note at a time. That’s four notes in all, and one of them is noise, so it can’t hold a pitch. Composers such as Koji Kondo (Super Mario Bros., 1985), Hirokazu Tanaka, Tim Follin, and on the Commodore 64 Rob Hubbard and Martin Galway still wrote full arrangements: melody, harmony, bass and drums. The music people now call chiptune grew out of the tricks they used to do it.
How to use the page. Press ▶ to hear a four-bar tune written for the four channels. The buttons mute and unmute each channel. Hold two or three keys (computer keys, the keyboard below, or MIDI) and the chord channel arpeggiates your chord in place of the song’s. Start with the volume low.

title: Sound 25: Chiptune
text:
Four channels



Every channel has a job, and the jobs follow from what each channel can do:








Channel
What it can do
What composers gave it




Pulse 1
a pulse wave at 12.5%, 25% or 50% width, 16 volume levels
the melody


Pulse 2
the same
harmony, a counter-melody, or an echo of the melody


Triangle
a triangle wave, an octave lower than the pulses, no volume control: on or off
the bass


Noise
noise, high or low, 16 volume levels
the drums



The pulse width is the instrument choice. 50% is the hollow square wave (odd harmonics only; Sound 2). 25% is fuller and more nasal, and 12.5% is thin and buzzy. Try both pulse widths while the tune plays. Composers often changed the width partway through a note to give it more movement.
Because the triangle has no volume control, chip bass lines never fade. A note sounds at full level until it’s cut off, so bass lines are written as bouncing octaves or with short gaps to make the rhythm. Drums are short bursts of noise: a low, quick one for the kick, a brighter one for the snare, a tiny high one for the hi-hat (built the same way as in Sound 3). Mute the other three channels to hear how little each drum is.

title: Sound 25: Chiptune
text:
Rows and frames
The music was played by a small program that ran once every screen refresh: 60 times a second on American and Japanese machines (50 in Europe). Each run is a frame. Nothing in the music could happen between frames, so every note change, volume step and vibrato wobble fell on a 1/60-second grid.
Composers wrote in trackers: a spreadsheet of notes, one column per channel, read from top to bottom. Each line is a row, and the “speed” is how many frames a row lasts. Six frames a row, with four rows to a beat, gives 150 beats per minute. Tempo only comes in steps: move Frames per row and the tempo jumps between fixed values. Some composers alternated two speeds from row to row to get a tempo in between.
The program also made the expressive details by hand. The melody’s volume steps down frame by frame after each attack (you can see the steps in the oscilloscope), and after a long note has sounded for a while its pitch starts to wobble. That’s vibrato, written in software. Turn it off to hear how flat the long notes sound without it.

title: Sound 25: Chiptune
text:
Chords from one channel
With one channel for the melody, one for the bass and one for drums, only one channel is left for harmony. One channel can play one note. A chord needs at least three.
The answer was the arpeggio: play the chord’s notes one after another, so fast that the ear can’t hear them as separate notes. Played every frame or every other frame, that’s 30 to 60 notes a second. Below about 50 ms per note, the ear stops following a tune and hears a texture instead: a buzzing, shimmering chord. It’s the most recognisable chiptune sound.
Compare the three settings of Chords on pulse 2:

Arpeggio (one channel): what the composers actually did.
Root only: what you’d get from that channel without the trick. The harmony is gone, and the F and C bars sound like they’re missing something.
Real chord (three channels): what the chip couldn’t do. It’s smoother, but now three channels are busy with one chord and there’s nothing left for the tune or drums.

Then go back to Arpeggio and slow it down with Frames per arpeggio note. At 12 or 15 frames a note you hear a tune of single notes going up and down. Speed it back up and somewhere around 4 to 6 frames the separate notes merge into a chord. The pattern matters less at full speed: Up, Up and down and Up, then the octave all sound like the same chord, each with a slightly different buzz.
In trackers this became a one-line effect: 047 on a note means “add 4 and then 7 semitones above it, each for one frame, over and over”: a major chord on one channel. 037 is minor.

title: Sound 25: Chiptune
text:
Write your own: a tracker
This is the same tune in a tracker, laid out the way chip composers wrote it. Each column is a channel, each line is a row, and time runs down the page. The shaded lines are beats, and the darker ones start a bar. Press ▶ and edit while it plays: a change is heard the next time that row comes round.



What to type in a cell:








Column
Type
Example




Pulse 1, Triangle
a note: letter, - or #, octave
A-4, C#5


Pulse 2
a note, then an arpeggio effect 0xy
A-4 037 (minor), C-5 047 (major)


Noise
K kick, S snare, H hi-hat
S


any
--- stops the note; an empty cell lets it ring on




In the effect 0xy, x and y are how many semitones above the note to add. They’re written in hexadecimal, so C means 12, an octave. 037 is a minor triad, 047 a major one, 038 a minor triad in first inversion (the C chord in bar 3), 05C a fourth plus an octave, and 07C the open fifth heard in a lot of game music. Arrow keys and Enter move around the grid. Click a cell and play a note on MIDI or the on-screen keyboard to write that note in (Pulse 2 keeps its effect). Frames per arpeggio note starts at 1 here, which is how trackers play 0xy.
Some things to try:

Change the chords: make bar 2 F-4 037 (F minor) and hear the whole tune go darker.
Give the triangle a walking bass line, a note every beat, instead of octaves.
Write a drum fill in the last bar: an S on every row.
Speed up to 3 frames per row and write a run of sixteenths that no one could play.

Your grid is kept in this browser. Example tune brings back the original, and Clear empties everything.

title: Sound 25: Chiptune
text:
Music no one can play
Write that arpeggio out as sheet music and it isn’t playable. At 150 bpm, a new note every two frames is 12 notes per beat: steady 48th-note triplets. A note every frame is 24 to a beat. The fastest human trills and tremolos reach roughly 15 to 20 notes a second, and only on two notes, not a chord broken note by note. A pianist playing a chip tune “as written” would need to play the melody plus a chord broken into 30 notes a second in the other hand, perfectly even, for the whole song.
Composers knew no one would ever play it. The parts were written for a machine, so the usual limits of hands, breath and bows didn’t apply. Some of them made a style of that:

Rob Hubbard (Monty on the Run, 1985) and Martin Galway on the Commodore 64 wrote long, fast arpeggio passages and pitch slides that are part of the melody, not hidden behind it.
Tim Follin’s NES music (Silver Surfer, 1990) has arpeggios, echoes and runs at speeds that sound like a much bigger chip.
Fast single-note runs, octave leaps every frame, and drum fills on the noise channel quicker than any drummer are common.

Other tricks came from the same limits:

Echo: pulse 2 plays the melody a few rows late and quieter, to sound like a delay (Sound 17) the chip didn’t have.
Channel stealing: a sound effect (a jump, a coin) takes over a pulse channel for a moment, and that part of the music drops out. Composers planned the music so that it still made sense with a part missing.
Pitch sweeps: a note sliding down fast is a laser, or, on the triangle, a kick drum with more punch than noise alone gives.
Shared drums: a quick noise hit and a triangle blip together, so a snare has a pitched body (Sound 3 builds a snare the same way).

title: Sound 25: Chiptune
text:
Chiptune today
Many musicians still write for these chips, on the original machines or in trackers such as FamiTracker and LSDj (which runs on a Game Boy). They follow the old limits on purpose: four channels, frame timing, arpeggiated chords. A lot of the sound is the struggle with the limits. Pop and electronic producers also use pulse waves and fast arpeggios, without the limits, when they want that sound.

title: Lesson: Sing it, then Notate it
text: Sing an ending for a song three times. The computer works out which of the site’s familiar rhythm patterns and familiar tonal patterns you sang. Then you write it into the song on the Notation page, and it tells you when the rhythm is right and when the pitches are right.

title: Lesson: Sing it, then Notate it

You sing an ending for Unfinished Song #1 from the tune library: its last two bars are empty, over V then I. The key, the tonality and the meter come from the song.

text:
Sing it three times
Press Play and sing once. The song plays three times in a row without stopping. Each time, sing your ending in its last two bars, where only the chords play. Only those two bars are recorded. Sing every note on a syllable (“da”, “la”), and separate repeated notes.

  
    Turn on the microphone

What I heard
Nothing yet.

  ▶ Hear what I understood
  Show the answer

title: Lesson: Sing it, then Notate it
text:
Notate it
Write what you sang in the song’s two empty bars: choose the rhythm patterns, then enter the notes with letters, the computer keys or a MIDI keyboard. The rhythm and the pitches are checked separately, each confirmed once. Octave does not matter for the pitches.

Sing three takes first.

title: Lesson: Sing it, then Notate it
text:
How it works

Candidates. Rhythms come from the Rhythm Sequences bank (apps/rhythms/rhythm-pattern-object.js), bars of the chosen meter only; any two bars together make a candidate. Tonal patterns come from the Tonal Patterns bank (apps/patterns/pattern-object.js), the chosen tonality only, as semitones above the tonic, so the key does not change the match.
Your three takes (the song’s last two bars, each time round) are put on a sixteenth-note grid. A note counts when two takes agree on it. Your tuning drift (up to about a third of a semitone, sharp or flat all the way through) is removed.
The match. Every rhythm is scored by how well its onsets fit yours; the pitches are covered with as few tonal patterns as possible, in whichever octave you used. It is lenient: onsets count up to about a third of a beat early or late, a repeated note counts as one pitch of a pattern, a pattern’s notes count in any octave (5 down to 1 is the pattern 5 1), and held notes over whole beats (half notes) are familiar rhythms. A fit needs rhythm 66%, pitches 66% and the takes mostly in agreement. A note a half step out of the key never counts. Otherwise you get a warning and a chance to sing again, never a guess.

title: Score Reading 3: Transposing Instruments
text: A clarinettist and a pianist both read a C, and they play different notes. That is not a mistake. The clarinet is a transposing instrument: its part is written at a different pitch from the one that sounds. This lesson explains how to work out what sounds, and how scores show it.

title: Score Reading 3: Transposing Instruments
text:
1. What “in B♭” means
The key in an instrument’s name is the note that sounds when the player reads a written C.

Clarinet in B♭: written C sounds B♭, a major 2nd lower. Every note sounds a major 2nd lower.
Horn in F: written C sounds F, a perfect 5th lower.
Alto saxophone in E♭: written C sounds the E♭ a major 6th lower.
Clarinet in E♭: written C sounds the E♭ a minor 3rd higher. The name gives the note, not the direction: small instruments usually sound up, large ones down.

An instrument “in C” (flute, oboe, violin, piano, trombone, voice) is non-transposing: it sounds what it reads.
Here is concert middle C, the same sound, as it is written for five instruments:

title: Score Reading 3: Transposing Instruments
text:
3. Moving the key signature
The part’s key moves the opposite way from the sound. If the instrument sounds a major 2nd lower, its part is written a major 2nd higher.

Concert C major → B♭ clarinet part in D major (2 sharps).
Concert F major → horn in F part in C major.
Concert E♭ major → alto sax part in C major.

A quick rule for keys: a B♭ instrument’s part has two more sharps (or two fewer flats) than the concert key; an E♭ instrument’s has three more sharps; an F instrument’s has one more sharp; an A instrument’s has three more flats.

title: Score Reading 3: Transposing Instruments
text:
4. Notes, one at a time
To find the sounding note, move the written note by the instrument’s interval. Keep the octave in mind, but for naming notes the letter and accidental are what count.

title: Score Reading 3: Transposing Instruments
text:
5. Octave transpositions and octave discrepancies
Some instruments transpose only by octaves. Their parts keep the concert key signature; only the register is moved, so the notes sit on the staff instead of on a ladder of ledger lines.

Sound higher: piccolo (8va), xylophone and celesta (8va), glockenspiel (two octaves).
Sound lower: double bass, guitar, bass guitar, contrabassoon, tenor voice (8vb).

Octave discrepancies to watch:

Same key, different octave. Soprano sax and tenor sax are both “in B♭”, and the B♭ clarinet and bass clarinet too. The bigger one sounds an octave lower than its smaller sibling. The name says the key, not the octave.
Doublings that are not unisons. A cello and double bass reading the same written line play in octaves, not in unison. A flute and piccolo on the same written line do too.
Guitar and tenor. A guitar’s written middle C sounds the C below. A score that shows the guitar at sounding pitch in plain treble clef would have its notes an octave lower than the player reads, deep in ledger lines.
Bass clarinet and horn bass clef: the old conventions in lesson 2.

title: Score Reading 3: Transposing Instruments
text:
6. Transposed scores and concert-pitch scores
A conductor’s score comes in one of two forms.
Transposed score. Every staff is written as the player reads it. The clarinet staff has a different key signature from the violins; the horn’s notes look a fifth higher than they sound. This is the traditional form, and it lets the conductor see exactly what each player sees, which helps in rehearsal (“clarinets, your written F♯ in bar 12”).
Concert-pitch score (C score). Every staff is at sounding pitch, all with the same key signature. Harmony is far easier to see. Some composers have written whole orchestral scores this way, Prokofiev among them. Most film, jazz-band and study scores, and the “concert pitch” view in notation software, work like this too.
What a concert score still transposes. Even a C score usually keeps the octave transpositions: piccolo, glockenspiel, xylophone, celesta, double bass, guitar and contrabassoon are still written in their own octave, because writing them at sounding pitch would bury them in ledger lines. Always check the score’s preface; it usually says “Score in C” and lists the exceptions.
How to tell which one you have. Look at the key signatures at the start. If the clarinets, horns and trumpets have a different key from the strings, it is transposed. If every staff matches, it is in C (or the music has no key signature, in which case look for a note at the top of the first page).

Writing parts from a concert score. Notation software will do it, but check every part: look for awkward keys (a concert B major gives a B♭ clarinet C♯ major, seven sharps, and you may prefer D♭ major with five flats), and look for notes outside the instrument’s written range.

Next: Score Reading 4: Why Transpositions Exist.

The doubled letter comes from an old English way of naming octaves, where the octave below the bass staff was written with double capitals: CC, DD … BB. “BB♭” means the low B♭, telling the contrabass apart from a smaller instrument “in B♭” such as the euphonium.
What that means for reading. In orchestras, wind bands and most of the world, every tuba reads bass clef at concert pitch. The F, E♭, CC or BB♭ is only which instrument you hold; the player learns each one’s fingerings. In British-style brass bands the E♭ and BB♭ basses read treble clef as transposing instruments: the E♭ bass sounds an octave and a major 6th below written, the BB♭ two octaves and a major 2nd below.

title: Score Reading 4: Why Transpositions Exist, and Horns in Every Key
text: Transposing parts look like a puzzle invented to annoy conductors. They are actually a solution, and each one solved a real problem for players. Knowing the history also explains why an 1800 symphony asks for “horns in E♭” in one movement and “horns in C” in the next.
crumbs: Score Reading 4: Why Transpositions Exist, and Horns in Every Key

title: Score Reading 4: Why Transpositions Exist, and Horns in Every Key
text:
1. Natural horns and trumpets
Before valves, a horn or trumpet was a single long tube. It could play only the notes of one harmonic series: the fundamental and its overtones. On a tube built for C that means C, G, C, E, G, B♭, C, D, E… and nothing in between, except what horn players could bend with a hand in the bell (hand-stopping, which also changes the tone).
To play in another key, the player changed the length of the tube by fitting a crook, an extra coil of tubing. A longer crook gave a lower series. Crooks were in common use by about 1740, and a horn player carried a set: B♭ alto, A, G, F, E, E♭, D, C, B♭ basso and more.
crumbs: Score Reading 4: Why Transpositions Exist, and Horns in Every Key

title: Score Reading 4: Why Transpositions Exist, and Horns in Every Key
section: 2. Why the part stayed in C
text:
2. Why the part stayed in C
Whatever crook was fitted, the player’s lips worked the same way: the third harmonic felt like the third harmonic. So composers wrote the part as if the horn were in C, and named the crook: “Corno in E♭”. The player fitted the E♭ crook and read the same written notes with the same feel; the instrument did the transposing. Many such parts have no key signature: the few notes needed outside the harmonic series were written in with accidentals.
That is why the horn and trumpet parts of Haydn, Mozart, Beethoven and Brahms are “in” so many keys, sometimes changing between movements while the player swapped crooks.
crumbs: Score Reading 4: Why Transpositions Exist, and Horns in Every Key

title: Score Reading 4: Why Transpositions Exist, and Horns in Every Key
section: 3. Valves, and the horn in F
text:
3. Valves, and the horn in F
Valves (Heinrich Stölzel applied them to the horn in 1814) let one instrument switch tube length instantly, so one horn could play every note. Players settled on the horn in F, and later the double horn in F and B♭, but composers kept writing for horn in E, D, E♭ well into the century. Today’s players still meet all of them, and read them on the F horn by transposing at sight.

title: Score Reading 4: Why Transpositions Exist, and Horns in Every Key
text:
5. Trumpets in every key
Trumpet parts went through the same history: natural trumpets in D, E♭, F and others, with parts written in C. Modern players read them on a B♭ or C trumpet, or pick a smaller trumpet (D, E♭, piccolo) for high Baroque parts. On a B♭ trumpet: a part in C reads up a major 2nd, in D up a major 3rd, in E♭ up a perfect 4th. Careful with old trumpet parts “in F”: they sound a 4th above written, unlike the horn in F.
crumbs: Score Reading 4: Why Transpositions Exist, and Horns in Every Key

title: Score Reading 4: Why Transpositions Exist, and Horns in Every Key
text:
6. Clarinets in B♭ and A
Early clarinets had few keys and could not play chromatically, so they were limited to keys close to their own. Builders made clarinets in several keys, and the composer chose the one that made the part easy: a concert-sharp key went to the A clarinet, a flat key to the B♭. Keywork improved, the C clarinet faded, but remote keys stayed awkward, so orchestral clarinettists still keep a B♭ and an A clarinet side by side and parts still switch between them (“muta in A”, change to A).
crumbs: Score Reading 4: Why Transpositions Exist, and Horns in Every Key

title: Score Reading 4: Why Transpositions Exist, and Horns in Every Key
section: 7. One fingering for a whole family
text:
7. One fingering for a whole family
Adolphe Sax patented the saxophone in 1846, as families in E♭/B♭ and C/F. Every size uses the same fingering, so a written note means the same finger pattern on soprano, alto, tenor or baritone. Writing them as transposing instruments lets a player switch sizes without relearning anything. The E♭/B♭ family won.
British brass bands took the idea furthest: every instrument except the bass trombone reads treble clef as a transposing instrument, so a player can move from cornet to tenor horn to euphonium to bass with the same fingerings for the same written notes.
crumbs: Score Reading 4: Why Transpositions Exist, and Horns in Every Key

title: Score Reading 4: Why Transpositions Exist, and Horns in Every Key
text:
8. Octave transpositions: just ledger lines
The last reason is the simplest. Piccolo, glockenspiel, double bass and guitar would spend their lives on ledger lines at sounding pitch, so their parts are moved by whole octaves to sit on the staff.

title: The Saxophone
text:
The saxophone is a woodwind made of brass. It counts as a woodwind because its sound starts at a reed vibrating against a mouthpiece, like a clarinet, not at your lips buzzing, like a trumpet. This page follows the alto sax, the one most beginners start on, but the fingerings work on the tenor and baritone too.
Want to practise patterns by ear with these fingerings? Try Sax Patterns by Ear.

title: The Saxophone
text:
Where it came from

Adolphe Sax, a Belgian instrument maker who played flute and clarinet, invented it in the 1840s and patented it in 1846, after moving to Paris in 1842.
He wanted an instrument between the woodwinds and the brass: the mellow tone of a clarinet with some of the power and brilliance of a trumpet. Woodwinds got more volume; brass got more agility.
His patent covered two families of seven saxophones each. The ones in B♭ and E♭ were for military bands and caught on; today’s saxophones come from them. The ones in C and F, for orchestras, never did.
When the patent ran out in 1866, other makers changed the design: a longer bell and extra keys for lower notes, then more keys and alternate fingerings for the high notes.
It is the youngest woodwind, and the only one that has never been made of wood.

title: The Saxophone
text:
The saxophone family








Saxophone
Key
Notes




Sopranino
E♭
The smallest: under 20 inches long. Rare.


Soprano
B♭
Usually straight. Not a good first sax.


Alto
E♭
The usual first saxophone.


Tenor
B♭
Has a curve in the neck. Big in jazz.


Baritone (“bari”)
E♭
The low voice of the band; has a spit valve.


Bass
B♭
Used in 1920s jazz records (it recorded better than a tuba or double bass); rarely written for now.


Contrabass
E♭
The largest: about six and a half feet.



At first the sax was mostly a military band instrument. In the 1900s it became central to concert bands, big bands and jazz, which use alto, tenor and baritone.
Why start on alto? Alto parts are often harder than tenor and bari parts, so alto builds your technique and reading. Many bands let players take turns on the bigger saxes. Starting on soprano is not recommended.
Same fingers, different sound. The saxophones are transposing instruments: a written note is fingered the same way on all of them, but each one sounds a different pitch. Written C sounds as concert E♭ on alto (a major 6th lower), concert B♭ on tenor (a major 9th lower) and concert E♭ on bari (an octave and a 6th lower). The fingering chart below shows both.

title: The Saxophone
text:
The parts
From the end you blow into, down to the bell:

Reed: a thin strip of cane. The thin tip vibrates against the mouthpiece and makes the sound.
Mouthpiece: holds the reed. Its cap protects the reed when you aren’t playing.
Ligature: the metal or fabric band with screws that clamps the reed to the mouthpiece.
Cork: on the end of the neck. The mouthpiece pushes onto it; how far it goes on tunes the sax.
Neck: the curved tube between the mouthpiece and the body. Holds the octave key pad.
Neck screw: tightens the neck into the body.
Body: the big conical tube with all the keys, and the bell at the bottom. The neck strap hooks onto a ring on the back, and there are two thumb rests: left thumb on top, right thumb underneath.

title: The Saxophone
text:
Putting it together


Wet the reed: put its thin end in your mouth. If the cork is dry, put a little cork grease on it.
Mouthpiece on the neck: twist it on gently, with the flat side of the mouthpiece lined up with the bottom of the neck.
Ligature: loosen its screws, slide it up a little, slip the reed in behind it, then slide it back down.
Line up the reed: centered on the flat part, with just a hairline of mouthpiece showing above the tip of the reed. Tighten the screws until snug, no tighter.
Neck strap: put it around your neck and hook it to the sax.
Neck into body: slide the neck into the top of the body and tighten the neck screw.

title: The Saxophone
text:
Holding it

Sit up straight near the front edge of the chair, on its right side, feet flat on the floor.
Right thumb under the lower thumb rest, kept straight. Left thumb on the upper rest at about a 45° angle (so it can roll onto the octave key).
The sax sits on your right side.
Adjust the neck strap, neck and mouthpiece so your head stays straight: bring the sax to you, not you to the sax.
Curve your fingers into a relaxed “C”, as if holding a tennis ball. Wrists straight.
Relax. Chin level with the floor, elbows away from your body.

Left hand on top (first three fingers on the B, A and G keys, pinky on the table of four small keys), right hand below (F, E, D keys, pinky on the two low keys, the side of the hand on the side keys).

title: The Saxophone
text:
Embouchure and your first note
Your embouchure (OM-boo-shur) is the shape of your mouth on the mouthpiece.

Take the neck and mouthpiece off the body.
Slide a piece of paper between the reed and mouthpiece, down from the tip until it stops.
Put your thumb tip on the reed just below the line the paper makes. That’s where your lower lip goes.
Hold your thumb there and take the paper out. Shape your mouth as if you’re saying “whee” and then “too”.
Roll a little of your lower lip over your bottom teeth.
Put the mouthpiece in until your lower lip touches your thumb. Top teeth rest right on top of the mouthpiece. Close your lips around it like a drawstring bag. Chin flat and pointed. Check in a mirror.
Take a full breath through your mouth and play a long, steady note. With the whole sax together, the first note is G♯ on alto, E on tenor and bari (find them in the chart below).

Checklist (have a friend or teacher watch): sitting straight · sax on your right · neck strap right · thumbs in place · fingers curved · wrists straight · elbows out · head up · right amount of mouthpiece · top teeth on the mouthpiece · chin flat and pointed · even pressure all round the mouthpiece · breathing low and full · a good, steady tone.

title: The Saxophone
text:
Fingering chart
Pick a note. Dark keys are pressed down, white keys are open. Hover over a key (or long-press on a phone) for its name. Where there’s more than one fingering, the first is the usual one; the others (alternate fingerings) make some fast passages easier.

How to read the diagram: the teardrop on the left is the octave key (left thumb). The big circles are the left hand (top three) and right hand (bottom three) first, second and third fingers; the small circle between 1 and 2 is the bis key. The ovals at the top right are the palm keys (high D, E♭, F), the circle above them all is the front F key. On the right: the left pinky table (G♯, low C♯, low B, low B♭). On the left: the right hand side keys (high E, C, B♭) and the alternate F♯ key; at the bottom, the right pinky keys (low E♭ above the line, low C below).

title: The Saxophone
text:
Build a fingering
Press keys on the diagram yourself. In What note is this? the page names the note your fingering makes. In the Quiz it gives you a note and you build its fingering.

title: The Saxophone
text:
Trill chart
A trill is a fast wobble between two notes. Some trills are awkward with the normal fingerings, so there are special ones: hold the dark keys down and move only the gray key(s).

title: The Saxophone
text:
Voicing and the altissimo
Above high F there is a whole extra register called the altissimo (Italian for “highest”). There are no keys for it. You reach it by choosing an overtone: every note the saxophone plays is really a stack of pitches, and with the right shape inside your mouth you can make the horn jump to one of the higher ones.
Donald Sinta calls that skill voicing. In his book with Denise Dabney, voicing means being aware of, and controlling, the muscles and soft tissue inside your mouth and throat: mostly where your tongue sits. It is not biting harder or pinching the reed. Sinta’s idea is that if you can hear the pitch in your head before you play it, your mouth learns to find it.

Overtone ladder
Finger low B♭ and don’t change it. Then try to make the notes below come out, one at a time, using only your tongue and throat. Listen first, sing the note, then play it.

Tips (from Jack Thorpe’s altissimo articles):

Airy, dull, low note? Your tongue is probably too low or the air too fast. Raise the middle and back of your tongue a little.
Squeak above the note? Your tongue is too high or the air too slow.
Altissimo needs a slightly slower, warmer air stream than you’d guess. Keep your jaw relaxed: don’t bite.
Check your tuning against a drone. Practise slurring up from palm-key F♯ before trying altissimo G.



Altissimo fingerings (alto)
These are for alto (and soprano). Tenor and bari often need different ones. The ★ fingering is Crunch G, named for the way you “crunch” up your right hand: right first finger on F while the side of your hand presses the side B♭ and alternate F♯ keys. Many players learn it as their first altissimo note.

Altissimo fingerings change from horn to horn, so if one won’t speak, try another. The Woodwind Fingering Guide lists dozens.

title: The Saxophone
text:
When the tone goes wrong








What it sounds like
Probably because…
Try this




Choked, pinched
Biting: too much lower-lip pressure
Relax, make your mouth more of an “O”



Too little mouthpiece in your mouth
Take in a bit more



Mouthpiece too closed for you
Ask about a mouthpiece that blows more easily



Ligature too high on the reed
Move it down


Rough, squawky
Too much mouthpiece in your mouth
Take in a bit less



Embouchure too loose
Firm up into more of an “oo” shape



Reed too hard
Use a softer reed


Nasal, thin
Air too slow
More support, faster air



Reed too soft
Use a stronger reed


Wobbly
Top lip on the mouthpiece instead of top teeth
Put your top teeth on the mouthpiece


Hard to blow
Reed too hard
Use a softer reed



Reed too high on the mouthpiece
Line it up with a sliver of mouthpiece showing



Ligature too high
Move it down



Leaking pads
Take it to a repair shop



Loud and soft. Like most woodwinds, the sax tends to go flat when you play loud and sharp when you play soft. Firm the embouchure as you get louder and relax it as you get softer. Practise long tones: hold one note for four bars, growing from pp to ff and back to pp, watching a tuner to keep the pitch still.

title: The Saxophone
text:
Playing in tune
You can’t tune a bad tone: good tone first. Saxophones are built to play in tune at A = 440.

Push the mouthpiece about halfway onto the cork.
Play written G, then F♯ (both on the top of the staff, then both an octave lower), holding each.
Check the F♯ on a tuner (the navbar has one). Sharp? Pull the mouthpiece out a little. Flat? Push it further on.

Some notes are out of tune on most saxophones, so listen for them and adjust:

tends to be flat: written C♯5 (middle C♯, no keys pressed);
tend to be sharp: written D5 (with the octave key) and A5.

title: The Saxophone
text:
Vibrato
Vibrato is a small, quick, even wobble in pitch that makes a note warmer. It never replaces a solid tone, and you should always be in control of how fast and how wide it is. Saxophonists make it with the jaw, as if saying “ya-ya-ya”.

Metronome at 76. Hold a comfortable note, such as B on the middle line.
Move your jaw slightly as if saying “ya” once on each click.
Then twice per click (“ya-ya”), evenly.
Then three times, then four. Four per beat at 76 suits most music.
Use it on slow scales in whole notes, then in simple melodies.

title: The Saxophone
text:
Looking after it
After every practice:

Bari only: press the spit valve and shake out the water.
Take off the ligature and reed. Put the reed in a reed holder to dry, never left on the mouthpiece.
Wipe the inside of the mouthpiece with a soft clean cloth. Ligature and cap back on.
Take off the neck, shake it, and dry it with the wool end of the neck cleaner.
Alto and tenor: drop the weighted swab into the bell end, turn the sax over, and pull the swab through the body.
Put each part back in its own place in the case as you finish with it. Latch the case.

title: The Saxophone
text:
Players to listen to
Ask your teacher before you look these up: not every recording is suitable for school.

title: Sampling 3: Pitch and Time-Stretch
text: A sample almost never arrives at the tempo and key of your track. There are two ways to change it.

title: Sampling 3: Pitch and Time-Stretch
text:
Repitch: speed and pitch together
Play a record faster and it gets higher; slower and it gets lower. That is repitching. A turntable’s pitch fader does it, and so do the classic samplers (the E-mu SP-1200, the Akai MPC60, the SP-404’s pitch knob).

Twice as fast = one octave up (12 semitones). Half speed = an octave down.
One semitone is a speed change of about 5.95 % (the twelfth root of two is 1.0595).
So a turntable’s ±8 % pitch range is about ±1.3 semitones; ±16 % about ±2.6.

Repitching keeps transients sharp and sounds natural, because nothing is invented: it is the same sound, faster or slower. Pitching soul vocals up gave the “chipmunk soul” sound of early-2000s hip-hop; slowing whole songs down is the Houston “chopped and screwed” style.

title: Sampling 3: Pitch and Time-Stretch
text:
Time-stretch: apart
Time-stretching changes the length without changing the pitch (and pitch-shifting the pitch without the length). The computer cuts the sound into tiny overlapping grains and spaces them further apart or closer together. Done simply, you hear it: drums smear, a “phasey” or metallic sound appears. Modern algorithms (Ableton Live’s Warp modes, élastique in many DAWs, DJ software’s key lock) hide it much better, but stretch anything far enough and it shows.

title: Sampling 3: Pitch and Time-Stretch
text:
Hear the difference




Pick pad 1 (a chord). Set Pitch to +5 in Repitch mode. Shorter and higher, like a sped-up record.
Change Mode to Stretch. The same +5 semitones, but the chord keeps its length.
Leave pitch at 0 and set Length to ×2 in each mode. Repitch: an octave down and twice as long. Stretch: same pitch, twice as long, and listen to the attack: blurred. This sampler uses plain overlap-add on purpose, so the smear is easy to hear.
Load the Funky Break, slice At the hits, and stretch a snare to ×1.5 in each mode. Which would you put in a track?

title: Sampling 3: Pitch and Time-Stretch
section: Matching a sample to your track
text:
Matching a sample to your track
The arithmetic: the speed you need is your tempo ÷ the sample’s tempo. A 90 BPM break in a 100 BPM track: 100 ÷ 90 = 1.111, so 11.1 % faster, which repitched is about +1.8 semitones. If the key matters, choose:

Repitch to the nearest key and adjust the track’s tempo to fit (producers often build the track at the sample’s speed), or
Stretch to the exact tempo and pitch-shift separately, accepting some artefacts.

title: Sampling 3: Pitch and Time-Stretch
section: The DJ’s version: pitch fader and key lock
text:
The DJ’s version: pitch fader and key lock
On a turntable the pitch fader is repitch. Below, push deck A’s fader to +8 %: BPM and key both move; the readout shows the shift in semitones. DJ software and CDJs add key lock (Master Tempo on Pioneer gear): tempo changes, pitch stays, by time-stretching.

title: Sampling 3: Pitch and Time-Stretch
text:
In other gear





Akai MPC
Roland SP-404
Ableton Live




Repitch
Tune (semitones, cents)
Pitch knob / Speed
Clip Transpose with Warp off, or Re-Pitch warp mode (Tempo and Warping)


Time-stretch
Warp / Time Stretch
Time Stretch (MKII: BPM sync)
Warp modes: Beats, Tones, Texture, Complex

title: Sampling 3: Pitch and Time-Stretch
text:
Many samples, one instrument
Pitch a single note far and it stops sounding like the instrument. A real instrument’s body resonates at the same frequencies whatever note is played, but a repitched sample moves those resonances with the note: a piano sample shifted up an octave sounds small and “chipmunked”, shifted down it sounds slow and woolly. So sampled instruments are built from many recordings (a multi-sample):

Key zones. A note recorded every few semitones (often every minor third), each covering the keys around it, so no note is pitched far.
Velocity layers. The same note recorded soft and hard. A hard hit isn’t just louder: it’s brighter, with more attack. Turning a soft recording up doesn’t make it sound hard.
Round robin. Several takes of each note and layer, played in turn. Repeat one recording and you hear the machine-gun effect, the same hit every time.

Choose Multi-sample in the sampler’s menu. The demo is a plucked string recorded at C2, C3, C4 and C5, soft and hard, three takes each (24 recordings). The map has keys across and velocity up; each coloured block is a zone.




Click across the bottom of the map, then across the top. The top uses the hard layer: brighter, with a knock.
Click the same spot again and again, then untick Round robin. Now every hit is the same take.
Tick One sample only and play from C2 up to C6. Every key now comes from the C4 recording. Low notes go dull and slow, high ones thin. That’s why instruments are sampled every few notes.
With your own recordings: name each file with its note (and, if you have them, a layer and a take), e.g. Guitar_E2_soft_rr1.wav, then Load recordings…. Spread zones fills the keyboard between them.

In other gear this is a sampler instrument: Ableton’s Sampler (Zone editor), Logic’s Sampler (Mapping pane), Kontakt, and the SFZ and SoundFont file formats. On an MPC it’s a keygroup program.

title: Sampling 5: Flipping a Sample
text: To flip a sample is to make something new from it, so the listener hears your song, not the record you took it from. A loop of someone’s chorus with drums under it is not a flip. A chord chopped, re-pitched and played in a new order, under a new melody, is.

title: Sampling 5: Flipping a Sample
text:
The flipper’s moves

Reorder: play the chops in a sequence the original never had. Four chords become a new progression.
Re-pitch: move chops up or down until they make a new harmony (a minor chord pitched up 3 semitones sits on a new root).
Reverse: backwards attacks swell instead of hitting; reversed cymbals and vocals are a classic transition.
Filter: a low-pass filter removes the old record’s drums and top end and keeps the warm middle, so new drums fit on top.
Change the time: half-time (half the speed) or a different tempo turns a ballad into a club track, and the reverse.
Layer: add your own bass, drums and parts so the sample becomes one voice among several.

title: Sampling 5: Flipping a Sample
text:
Flip it



The soul loop has one chord a beat in the first slices. A plan, one step at a time:

Play pads 1, 5, 9, 13 (the first beat of each bar): the original progression.
Re-pitch pad 9 by −2 and pad 13 by +3 (select a pad, then Pitch). Play 1, 5, 9, 13 again: a new progression from the same sound.
Reverse pad 16 (Reverse) and use it as a swell into bar 1.
Record a two-bar pattern with these pads (● Rec), with Quantize 1/8.
Then load the Funky Break on the next sampler and record drums at the same tempo (84) over a click. Two machines, one song.

title: Sampling 5: Flipping a Sample
section: The DJ’s flips: edits, acapellas, mashups
text:
The DJ’s flips: edits, acapellas, mashups
DJs flip whole songs, live or before the gig:

An edit (or re-edit) rearranges a song for the dance floor: a longer intro with just drums for mixing in, the best section repeated, the slow bridge cut. Disco DJs made them on tape with a razor blade; now they are made in a DAW.
An acapella is a vocal on its own; an instrumental is the song without it. Play one over another track and you have a mashup or a live remix. Matching key matters more here than anywhere: see DJ 6.
Stems: DJ software can now split a song into vocals, drums, bass and the rest as it plays, so any song becomes an acapella.

Try a live mashup: deck A has a house groove, deck B a vocal phrase in the same key and tempo. Start A, then start B on a downbeat; bring B’s channel up and cut A’s Mid EQ a little so the voice sits on top.

title: Sampling 4: A Beat from Chops
text: The Akai MPC (1988 onwards) put a sampler and a sequencer in one box with 16 rubber pads. You chop a record onto the pads, tap out a pattern while the sequencer loops, and the box remembers it. The pads respond to how hard you hit them; the swing and quantize settings shape the timing. Much of 1990s and 2000s hip-hop was made this way; the Roland SP-404 carried it into lo-fi and beat scenes.

title: Sampling 4: A Beat from Chops
text:
Pads and keys
The pads below follow the MPC layout: pad 1 is bottom left. With the sampler focused (click it), the keys play the pads:



1 = 13
2 = 14
3 = 15
4 = 16


Q = 9
W = 10
E = 11
R = 12


A = 5
S = 6
D = 7
F = 8


Z = 1
X = 2
C = 3
V = 4



A MIDI pad controller or keyboard works too (Connect MIDI): notes 36–51 (C1 up), the first bank on most controllers.

title: Sampling 4: A Beat from Chops
text:
Make a beat




Find a kick, a snare and a hat among the pads (sliced at the hits). Note which keys they are on.
Press ● Rec. The click counts the beats; each pass round the pattern is two bars. Tap kicks only, on 1 and the and of 2.
Next pass, add snares on 2 and 4. Recording keeps going round and adds what you play (overdub). Made a mistake? Undo removes the last pass.
Stop recording, press ▶, and listen. Turn Quantize off and record a hat pass: the hits land exactly where you played them, human and uneven. With 1/16 they snap to the nearest sixteenth.
Change the Tempo from 100 to 88. The pattern slows down, but each chop still plays at its own speed: the beat now has gaps. Try Length ×1.15 on the snare pad (Repitch) to fill them, and hear it drop in pitch.

title: Sampling 4: A Beat from Chops
text:
Chords over drums
A beat from one break is a start. Producers layer: drums from one record, a chord stab from another, a bass note from a third. Load Old Soul Record into a second sampler, slice it One a beat, and play chords over the pattern you recorded above.

title: Sampling 4: A Beat from Chops
text:
Timing feel

Quantized to 1/16 sounds tight, machine-like: the house and trap way.
Unquantized keeps your timing. J Dilla famously turned quantize off on his MPC3000, so kicks fall slightly late and hats drag: the “drunk” feel.
Swing delays every second sixteenth. An MPC’s swing setting (50 % straight, 66 % triplet) is how many classic beats got their bounce.

title: Sampling 4: A Beat from Chops
section: The DJ’s version: finger drumming and the sampler
text:
The DJ’s version: finger drumming and the sampler
DJ software has a sampler too (slots you fire from pads on a controller), and the controllers’ performance pads fire hot cues, loops and samples. Setting hot cues on a break’s kick and snare and drumming a new pattern live is the DJ’s beat from chops.
