title: Recording 5: Miking a Voice
text: A voice is the one instrument everyone knows the sound of: a vocal that’s boomy, popping, hissing or boxy is heard at once. Most of the fixes are in where the mic goes, before any plug-in.

title: Recording 5: Miking a Voice
section: Which mic, for the room you have
text:
Which mic, for the room you have

Large-diaphragm condenser, 15–25 cm away: the studio sound, open and detailed. It also hears the room, so it needs a quiet, treated room (or a well-made vocal booth).
Dynamic (SM7B, SM58 type), close (2–8 cm): hears much less of the room. The better choice in an ordinary bedroom, for loud singers, and on stage. Many famous vocals were recorded on one.
Whichever you use, it’s a cardioid: point its dead back at the noisy things (the computer, a window, the headphones’ spill) (Recording 2: Polar patterns).

title: Recording 5: Miking a Voice
text:
Distance
Close is intimate and bass-heavy (the proximity effect), and every lip noise is there; further back is more natural and has more room in it. A singer who moves changes the level and the tone: keep a fixed distance (a hand’s width is a handy measure with a condenser), or move on purpose, back for loud notes, in for quiet ones (Recording 3: Distance).

title: Recording 5: Miking a Voice
text:
Pops and esses




Plosives (p, b, and some t, d, k) push a jet of air straight out of the mouth, a little downward. A mic in that jet gets a thump of wind that no EQ removes cleanly. A pop filter (mesh or metal, 5–10 cm from the mouth) stops it. So does moving the mic out of the jet: a little above the mouth, pointing down at it, or slightly to the side.
Sibilance (s, sh) is high and beams forward. A mic slightly above or to the side hears less of it. A bright condenser makes it worse; a de-esser in the mix is the last resort.

Drag the mic around the singer. Listen to the “p” at the start of each phrase and the “s” in the middle, then try the pop filter, the dynamic, and the three rooms:

title: Recording 5: Miking a Voice
text:
Height and angle
Start at mouth height or a little above, 15–20 cm away for a condenser, pointing at the mouth. Pointing at the nose gives more nasal sound; at the chest, more chest. Have the singer stand as they’ll sing: a lyric sheet on a stand below the mic makes them look down and sing into the floor. Put it at eye height.

title: Recording 5: Miking a Voice
text:
The room
A condenser in a bare room records the room: a boxy, hollow sound from reflections close behind and beside the singer. The walls behind the singer matter most (that’s where the mic’s front points). A duvet or thick blanket hung behind the singer, a wardrobe full of clothes, rugs on the floor: all help. Foam squares on the wall only take the top off. A dynamic close up hears much less of it.

title: Recording 5: Miking a Voice
text:
Headphones, level and takes

Closed-back headphones, not too loud: their spill gets into a sensitive mic (Recording 6: Monitoring).
Set the level on the loudest part of the song, with headroom (Recording 1: Gain Staging).
Record several takes; singers warm up as they go (the Vocal Warm-up first).

title: Recording 5: Miking a Voice
text:
On stage
A handheld dynamic, close: lips a finger or two from the grille. Hold it by the handle, never the grille (cupping it turns it omni and it feeds back: Recording 2). Keep its back toward the wedge monitor, and back off on loud notes (Pop Singing: the mic).

title: Recording 3: Distance, Bleed and Phase
text: Where the microphone goes changes the sound more than which microphone it is. Move it a few centimetres and the tone changes; move it a metre and the room becomes part of the recording.

title: Recording 3: Distance, Bleed and Phase
text:
Distance

Close (2–15 cm): big, intimate, dry. Lots of the source, little of the room. Every mouth noise, breath and pick scrape is there. Plosives (p, b) hit the diaphragm.
Medium (20–60 cm): the usual distance for a voice with a condenser or an acoustic guitar. More natural, the instrument has room to “bloom”.
Far (1 m and more): the room is part of the sound. Great in a good-sounding room, terrible in a small boxy one.

The level drops about 6 dB every time the distance doubles (the inverse-square law). So a singer moving from 5 cm to 10 cm changes the level as much as moving from 50 cm to a metre. Close up, small movements make big level changes; a little further back, the performer can move without the level jumping.

title: Recording 3: Distance, Bleed and Phase
text:
Proximity effect
Directional mics (cardioid, figure-8) boost the bass as the source gets close: below about 10 cm it can be +10 dB or more at 100 Hz. Radio voices use it on purpose. On an acoustic guitar it makes boom. Back off, or use a high-pass filter (a low cut around 80–100 Hz, often a switch on the mic or the interface). Omni mics have no proximity effect.



Bring the mic in and listen to the bass grow; then try omni:



Hear what a low cut and a bass boost do:

title: Recording 3: Distance, Bleed and Phase
text:
Where on the instrument

Acoustic guitar: not at the soundhole (boomy). Start pointing at where the neck meets the body, about 20 cm away; move towards the soundhole for warmth, towards the neck for brightness.
Guitar amp: close on the speaker. At the centre of the cone, bright and aggressive; towards the edge, darker and rounder. Turn the amp down: it doesn’t need to be loud to sound good on a mic.
Voice: at mouth height or slightly above, pointing a little down; a pop filter 5–10 cm in front. Slightly off to the side cuts plosives and sibilance (s, sh).
Snare: 3–5 cm above the rim, angled at the centre of the head, the back of the mic towards the hi-hat.

Listen in headphones while someone else moves the mic, and choose by ear.

title: Recording 3: Distance, Bleed and Phase
text:
Bleed
Bleed (spill) is one instrument getting into another’s microphone: the drums in the vocal mic, the guitar amp in the piano mics. It happens whenever more than one thing is recorded in one room.
Bleed isn’t always bad: a band playing together with some bleed sounds alive and glued together. But it takes away choices: you can’t re-record the vocal if the drums are in it, you can’t EQ one without the other, and Auto-Tune on a vocal with drums in it makes the drums warble.
To reduce it:

Get closer to the source you want. Each halving of the distance gains 6 dB over the bleed.
Aim the dead side of the mic (the back of a cardioid, the side of a figure-8) at the loud thing.
Separate players: across the room, behind gobos (movable baffles), amps in another room or a cupboard, bass and keys through DI.
Dynamic mics on loud close sources pick up less of the room.
Headphones for everyone, not speakers (see monitoring).
Try it: bring the singer close, then turn the mic so the drums sit at its quiet side.





After recording, a gate or careful editing can remove bleed between hits (tom mics, mostly):

title: Recording 3: Distance, Bleed and Phase
text:
Phase
Two microphones on one source at different distances get the same sound at slightly different times. Added together, some frequencies cancel (a comb filter, as in Sound 18), and the sound goes thin and hollow. Bleed causes it too: the snare in the snare mic and in the overheads.

The 3:1 rule: the second mic at least three times as far from the first source as the first mic is. A singer 20 cm from one mic and a guitarist 20 cm from another: keep the two mics 60 cm or more apart.
Two mics on the same speaker or drum: put them at the same distance.
A mic above and a mic below a snare (or front and back of an open-back amp) face opposite ways: flip the polarity (Ø) of one.
Check by listening to both mics together and flipping polarity on one: choose whichever has more bass and body. Check the mix in mono.

Drag mic 2 away from mic 1 and watch the comb filter in the spectrum. Flip the polarity and compare the mono sum. Then switch to the 3:1 demo, where each mic has its own player:

title: Recording 7: Mixing
text: Mixing is making the recorded tracks into one piece of music: each part heard, each in its own place, the song coming across. Most of a good mix is done with the plainest tools: level, pan, EQ, compression, and space, in about that order.

title: Recording 7: Mixing
text:
Prepare

Name and colour the tracks, group them (drums, bass, guitars, keys, vocals, effects).
Clean up: cut silence and noise between phrases, fade every edit, check for clicks.
Gain-stage: trim each track to an average around −18 dBFS (see gain staging), so faders start near 0.
Listen to a reference: a finished song you love in the same style, at the same level as your mix.

title: Recording 7: Mixing
text:
Balance
Faders first, with nothing else. Start with the most important element (usually the vocal, or the kick and bass), bring everything else in around it. A good balance with no plug-ins already sounds like a song; no plug-in will rescue a bad one. Mix quietly: if the balance works quietly it works loud.

title: Recording 7: Mixing
text:
Practise a balance
Press ▶, start from “A bad mix” and fix it with faders only, then pan, high-pass and a little reverb. Check it with Mono on, and press B to compare with a reference.

title: Recording 7: Mixing
text:
Pan
Spread things across the stereo picture so they don’t sit on top of each other.

Centre: kick, snare, bass, lead vocal: the foundation.
Off centre: guitars, keys, backing vocals, percussion. Two similar guitars hard left and hard right.
Drums panned as the audience sees them (or the drummer does; pick one).
Check in mono: everything should still be heard. Why, and what goes wrong: Recording 9: Mono and Stereo.

title: Recording 7: Mixing
text:
EQ
EQ gives every part its own range of frequencies.

High-pass everything that doesn’t need deep bass (vocals, guitars, keys, overheads), around 80–150 Hz. It clears room for kick and bass and removes rumble.
Cut before boost. Find what’s ugly (boxiness 300–600 Hz, honk around 1 kHz, harshness 2–5 kHz) with a narrow boost swept around, then cut it.
When two parts fight (kick and bass, guitar and vocal), cut a little of one where the other lives.
Judge EQ in the mix, not soloed.

title: Recording 7: Mixing
text:
Compression
A compressor evens out the level so a part stays in place.

Vocals: almost always, 3–6 dB of reduction on the loud phrases. Often two compressors gently, rather than one hard.
Bass: steadies the notes. Drums: punch (slow attack lets the hit through) or sustain.
Too much makes it lifeless and pumps. Match the level with it on and off before deciding it helps.

title: Recording 7: Mixing
text:
Space
Reverb and delay put the parts in a room and in front or behind.

Put them on sends (aux buses): one or two reverbs and a delay that many tracks share, so they all sound like one place.
Drier and brighter sounds close; more reverb, darker and quieter sounds far.
Pre-delay (20–80 ms) keeps a vocal up front while still giving it a room.
High-pass and low-pass the reverb return so it doesn’t muddy the bass or hiss.

title: Recording 7: Mixing
text:
Automation and finishing

Automate fader moves: the vocal up a little in the busy chorus, a guitar up for its fill, the reverb up on the last word.
Take breaks. Listen on other speakers, earbuds, a phone, a car (monitoring).
Leave the master peaking around −6 dBFS, no limiter on it, ready for mastering.
Export a 24-bit WAV at the session’s sample rate.

title: Recording 8: Mastering
text: Mastering is the last step: the finished stereo mix is made to sound its best on every system and alongside other records, and turned into the files that get released. It works on the whole song at once, with small moves. If something in the mix is wrong (the vocal too quiet, the bass boomy on one note), go back and fix the mix; mastering can’t reach inside.

title: Recording 8: Mastering
text:
Fresh ears
Mastering was traditionally a different engineer in a different room, for a reason: you’ve heard the mix a hundred times. Leave it a day. Listen to references. Listen on the speakers you know best.

title: Recording 8: Mastering
text:
Tonal balance
A gentle EQ on the whole mix, compared with a reference:

Moves of 0.5 to 2 dB, wide curves. More than 3 dB means the mix needs work.
Too much low end (muddy, boomy on small speakers), too little (thin), harsh 2–5 kHz, dull top.
A high-pass below 20–30 Hz removes rumble nobody hears but that eats headroom.

title: Recording 8: Mastering
text:
Glue compression
A slow, gentle compressor on the whole mix (ratio 1.5:1–2:1, 1–2 dB of gain reduction, slow attack, release timed to the beat) makes the parts move together. Often done in the mix already (“mix-bus compression”).

title: Recording 8: Mastering
text:
Loudness and limiting
The limiter is the last plug-in: a very fast compressor with an infinite ratio that stops any peak crossing a ceiling, so the whole song can be turned up.

Set the ceiling at −1 dBTP (true peak: the level between the samples, which is what a converter or an MP3 encoder actually reaches). This keeps lossy streaming versions from clipping.
Raise the input until it’s loud enough, then back off: past a few dB of limiting the drums lose their punch and the sound gets flat and tiring.
Loudness is measured in LUFS (loudness units relative to full scale), averaged over the song, which follows how loud it sounds rather than its peaks.
Streaming services turn loud songs down to a target (Spotify, YouTube, Tidal about −14 LUFS; Apple Music −16). A master squashed to −8 LUFS is just turned down to −14, and now sounds smaller than a dynamic master at −14. For streaming, around −14 to −10 LUFS integrated is plenty; dynamic genres (jazz, classical, acoustic) often sit at −16 to −20.


Hear what over-limiting costs
A looping song through a limiter, measured the way streaming services measure it (LUFS, with a true-peak reading). Play it, then compare Dynamic with Crushed: the crushed one is louder, and has lost its punch. Now switch streaming normalisation on: both are turned to the same level, and the crushed one is simply smaller. Watch the peak-to-loudness figure shrink as the drive goes up.

title: Recording 8: Mastering
text:
Stereo and mono
Check in mono (Sound 23: Stereo): the vocal and bass must stay solid. Keep the bass (below ~120 Hz) in the centre; wide bass cancels on mono systems and cuts badly on vinyl. More on mono playback, one earbud, live sound and subwoofers in Recording 9: Mono and Stereo.

title: Recording 8: Mastering
text:
Finishing

Sequence an album: the order, the gaps, matching levels so no song jumps out.
Fades at the start and end; trim silence.
Dither when reducing to 16-bit (CD, some distributors): a tiny noise that replaces the distortion of rounding. Only once, at the very end.
Files: a 24-bit WAV at the mix’s sample rate for streaming distributors, a 16-bit/44.1 kHz WAV for CD, and an MP3 for the band’s phones.
Metadata: title, artist, ISRC codes if you have them.

title: Recording 1: Gain Staging
text: Before any microphone choice or plug-in, one thing decides whether a recording is usable: how loud the signal is at each step on the way in. Too quiet and the noise of the gear comes up with it; too loud and the top of the wave is cut off, for ever. Getting this right at every stage is gain staging.

title: Recording 1: Gain Staging
section: The chain on the way in
text:
The chain on the way in
A sound reaches the computer through a few stages, each with its own ceiling:

Source: the voice or instrument, and the room.
Microphone (or a DI box for a guitar or keyboard).
Preamp: the gain knob on the interface. A microphone puts out a tiny voltage (mic level, around −60 to −40 dBu); the preamp raises it by 30–60 dB to line level.
Converter (A/D): turns the voltage into numbers. Its ceiling is 0 dBFS (decibels relative to full scale): the largest number it can write. Nothing goes above it.
The DAW: tracks, plug-ins, buses, the master.

The gain knob is the one that matters most, and it is the one to set first, with the fader in the DAW left at 0. A fader turns down what was recorded; it cannot un-clip it.

Clipping at the converter is permanent. A clipped take sounds harsh and crackly on every peak, and nothing later removes it. When in doubt, record quieter.

title: Recording 1: Gain Staging
text:
How loud to record
In 24-bit recording (the default in every DAW now) there is about 144 dB between the noise floor of the numbers and 0 dBFS, far more than any preamp or room can use. So there is no reason to record hot.

Aim for peaks around −12 to −6 dBFS and an average around −18 dBFS. That is where most analogue gear and plug-ins are designed to sit (−18 dBFS is about 0 VU, “line level”).
Set the gain while the player performs the loudest part of the song, not while they warm up. People play louder in the take than in the sound check; singers louder in the chorus than the verse.
If the meter touches red even once, turn the gain down a few dB and do it again.
16-bit recording (old gear, some phones) has 96 dB of range; there it is worth recording a bit hotter, but still never into the red.

title: Recording 1: Gain Staging
text:
Hear it go wrong
The signal chain from Sound 24, with every stage clipping above 0 dB like real gear. Press Too hot, watch a stage go red, then lower the Input gain until nothing does.



Notice that turning down the output after a clipped stage only makes the damage quieter.

title: Recording 1: Gain Staging
section: Try it: gain, clipping and hiss
text:
Try it: gain, clipping and hiss
A quiet microphone-level voice (or drum loop) goes through a preamp, a converter that cuts hard at 0 dBFS, and then the fader in the DAW. Press play, then the three Try buttons in turn.

Too hot, fader down: the track meter looks safe, the red light has latched, and it still sounds crunchy. The fader came after the damage.
Too quiet, fader up: nothing clips, but the signal-to-noise figure is poor and the hiss comes up with the voice.
Just right: peaks around −12 to −6 dBFS, hiss far below.

title: Recording 1: Gain Staging
section: Pads, DI and the gain knob
text:
Pads, DI and the gain knob

Pad (−10 or −20 dB switch on the interface or the mic): for very loud sources (kick drum, guitar amp, a belted high note close to a condenser) where even the lowest gain clips. It cuts before the preamp, so the preamp isn’t overloaded.
Instrument / Hi-Z input: an electric guitar or bass plugged straight in needs a high-impedance input (the “Inst” switch) or a DI box. On a mic input it sounds thin and dull.
Line input: keyboards, drum machines, the outputs of other gear. Already loud; little or no gain.
Too little gain then turning up in the DAW raises the preamp hiss with the signal. Too much is clipping. Somewhere between, the gain is right.

title: Recording 1: Gain Staging
text:
Inside the DAW
Floating-point DAWs (all modern ones) won’t clip inside a track; only the converter and the final file have a hard ceiling. But plug-ins that model analogue gear react to level: hit a vintage compressor or saturation plug-in at +6 dBFS and it distorts. Keep each track and bus around the same −18 dBFS average, use the clip gain or a trim plug-in at the start of a track rather than pushing faders far up, and leave the master peaking well below 0 before mastering.

title: Recording 1: Gain Staging
text:
Checklist

Faders at 0, gain at minimum, then bring gain up while they play the loudest part.
Peaks −12 to −6 dBFS. Never red.
Pad for loud sources, Inst/DI for guitar and bass.
Record 24-bit (48 kHz or 44.1 kHz).

title: Process 1: Keeping a Process Journal
text:
A process journal is the record of how a piece of music was made: the ideas you had, what you tried, what you heard, what you changed, and why. The finished piece shows what you made. The journal shows how you got there, and in MYP and DP Music that is assessed as well as the piece.
It is not a diary. “Today I worked on my song. It went well” tells a reader nothing. A useful entry lets someone else see and hear what you tried and follow your reasons.

title: Process 1: Keeping a Process Journal
text:
1. What to capture



Capture
Looks like
Why it matters




Ideas
a voice memo of a hummed tune, a chord loop, a lyric line, a rhythm on the desk, a photo of a sketch
shows where the piece came from


Versions
chorus v1, v2, v3, each saved, not overwritten, with a line on what changed
shows that you explored, not just the result


Tests
a recording of you or a player trying it, dated
shows how you found out what works


Feedback
who said what (“Sam: the bridge is too long”), and what you did about it
shows you used it, or chose not to, and why


Decisions
“I kept v2 because …”
the most important line in any entry


Research
a piece you listened to and what you took from it, with its source
links your choices to music you studied (see Sources 1)


Reflection
what you’d do differently, what you learned about yourself as a musician
the evaluating part of the work




Keep every version. The most common mistake is saving over the old file. Once v1 is gone, you can’t show how far you came. Save a copy each time you make a real change.

title: Process 1: Keeping a Process Journal
section: 2. A weak entry and a strong one
text:
2. A weak entry and a strong one


Weak

12 Oct. Worked on the chorus. Tried some different things and it sounds better now. Next time I’ll do the verse.



Strong

12 Oct. Chorus melody. Tried three versions over C–G–Am–F (2026-10-12_chorus_v1.m4a, _v2, _v3). v1 starts on the tonic and sounded flat; v2 jumps up to the high E on “hold” and sounded more like arrival; v3 had the same jump but too many words. Kept v2 because the chorus needs to be higher than the verse and the jump puts the stress on “hold”. Played it to Mia: she said the last line was rushed (0:21 in v2). Next: slow the last line to half notes.



The strong entry has: more than one version, named so they can be found; what each sounded like; a decision with because; feedback with a timestamp; a next step. It took about five minutes to write.

title: Process 1: Keeping a Process Journal
text:
3. Evidence other people can check

Recordings. Name files with the date, the section and the version: 2026-10-12_chorus_v2.m4a. Then a reader can find “v2 at 0:21”. The Timestamp Notes tool can stamp the moments you want to talk about.
Scores and screenshots. Crop to what matters, and annotate: arrows, labels, and a sentence on why (“moved the melody up an octave so the violin is heard over the piano”). A before and an after, side by side, shows a decision better than a paragraph does. More on this in Writing Music Down.
Your own words. Use the terms the subject uses (motif, sequence, period, countermelody, texture). They make your reasons precise.

title: Process 1: Keeping a Process Journal
text:
4. How often, and where
A short entry every working session is better than a long one at the end, which you’d be writing from memory. Five minutes at the end of the lesson is enough.
Paper notebook, a document, a slide deck, a folder of recordings with a text file: any of these work if your teacher agrees, as long as recordings and pages stay together and in date order. Many schools ask MYP arts students for a process journal in every unit. Check what yours expects.

title: Process 1: Keeping a Process Journal
text:
5. Write an entry
Fill in the boxes for today’s work. Preview checks for the parts a strong entry has; Keep this entry stores it in this browser, and Download all gives you every kept entry as one file to put in your journal.

title: Process 1: Keeping a Process Journal
text:
6. For MYP and DP

MYP: the journal is where Criterion B (Developing) is shown: your practical exploration of ideas and your artistic intention. Process 2 goes through it. It also feeds Criterion D (Evaluating): you can’t reflect on your development without a record of it.
DP: the same habit supplies the evidence for the Experimenting with music report and the HL project: annotated scores, screenshots and timestamped recordings, with reasons. See the assessment guidance in the DP Music course book.

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in C, Am, F, G
text:
Four chords, C, Am, F and G, are under more pop songs than any other progression: I, vi, IV, V. It can sound plain, and it can sound rich, depending on what the players do to it. Almost every move is one of four: add a note to each chord, walk the bass between chords, approach a chord with its own dominant, or split a bar into a two-five. This lesson adds those moves one at a time, on the same four bars. The site’s backing band plays every chart on this page, so you can hear each change as it arrives.
How to use the page. Press ▶ on any chart and the band plays four choruses after a one-bar count-in. The bar that is sounding lights up. The strip at the bottom of the window sets the key, the feel, the tempo and the chord instrument for the whole page, and you can change them while the band plays. Under every chord is its Roman numeral, which stays the same in every key. (The numerals only name the chord’s root, so a III7 in bar 1 is the dominant of Am, and a vii7 before it is its two.)
crumbs: Lesson: Changing the Changes in C, Am, F, G

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in C, Am, F, G
text:
1. The basic changes
One bar each of I, vi, IV and V. Plain major and minor triads. The bass moves down a minor third, then down a third, then up a step, and the G at the end pulls back to the C.



Learn this version first. Every other version on the page is this one with something added, so you should be able to hear the plain one underneath.
crumbs: Lesson: Changing the Changes in C, Am, F, G

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in C, Am, F, G
text:
2. Add extensions
Extensions are notes added on top of the triad without changing what the chord is. Cadd9 adds a D. Am7 adds a G, and Fadd9 adds a G. Gsus2 takes out the B and puts in an A, so the chord has no third: it is neither major nor minor. It sounds suspended, and the ordinary G that follows it, or the C it leads to, feels like the answer.



Use Hear it without the changes to compare with the chart before. The shaded bars are the ones that differ. Listen to bar 4: the leading tone B, which is what pulls G to C, is not there.
crumbs: Lesson: Changing the Changes in C, Am, F, G

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in C, Am, F, G
text:
3. Add passing chords
Two bars are split in half, so that the bass can walk instead of jump.

Bar 1: C, G/B. The bass steps down C, B and arrives on A in bar 2. The G/B is a G chord with its third in the bass.
Bar 2: Am, C/G. The bass keeps stepping down, A then G, to land on F in bar 3.
Bar 3: F, F♯dim. Now the bass goes up, F, F♯, and arrives on G in bar 4. The F♯dim is built from F♯, A and C, three of the four notes of D7, so it pulls up to G.




Listen to the bass. There is no jump anywhere in the line: every note is one step from the last. A slash chord such as C/G is the C chord with G as its lowest note.
crumbs: Lesson: Changing the Changes in C, Am, F, G

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in C, Am, F, G
text:
4. Secondary dominants
A dominant seventh chord pulls to the chord a fifth below it. The home key has one, G7, which pulls to C. A secondary dominant is the dominant of some other chord of the key, played just before that chord, so that chord gets to sound like home for a moment.

E7 goes to Am. It has a G♯, which is not in the key of C.
C7 goes to F. It has a B♭, which is not in the key of C either.
D7 goes to G. It has an F♯.
G7 goes to C: the usual dominant, now with its seventh.




Each bar now has a note from outside the key, and each of them leads by half step into the next bar’s chord (G♯ to A, B♭ to A, F♯ to G). That is why the progression sounds like it is travelling.
crumbs: Lesson: Changing the Changes in C, Am, F, G

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in C, Am, F, G
text:
5. ii-V-Is
A dominant can have a chord in front of it, the ii chord, a fifth above, so that the approach itself is a progression: ii, V, then I. Here each secondary dominant gets its own two.

Bar 1 keeps C for two beats, then Bm7 E7, a two-five into Am.
Bar 2 keeps Am for two beats, then Gm7 C7, a two-five into F.
Bar 3 is Fmaj7 for two beats, then Am7 D7, a two-five into G.
Bar 4 stays on G7.




Strictly, the two-five into a minor chord uses a half-diminished ii (Bm7♭5), but plain Bm7 is the common way to write it in pop and the band plays it as written. Compare the last chord of each of the first three bars with section 4: it is the same dominant, with a two in front.
crumbs: Lesson: Changing the Changes in C, Am, F, G

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in C, Am, F, G
text:
Build your own chorus
Choose one option for each bar and the chart rewrites itself. Change a menu while the band is playing and the new chords come in at the next bar. All of the options fit together, so there is no wrong combination: try a plain first bar with a busy last bar, or the reverse.

title: Pop Changes for Guitar: From Open Chords to Passing Chords
text:
This lesson is for a guitarist who knows the open chords. It puts the shapes of the lesson on C, Am, F, G on the neck. Each step has fretboard diagrams for its chords, the chart and the staff, and the band plays the chords on piano, guitar or organ (the Chords menu in the strip).
How to use the page. Press ▶ on a chart and the band plays it four times after a one-bar count-in. The bar that is sounding lights up, on the chart and on the staff. Under every chord is its Roman numeral, which stays the same in every key. The strip at the bottom of the window sets the key, the feel, the tempo and the chord instrument, and you can change them while the band plays. Shaded bars are the ones that differ from the version named under the chart.
crumbs: Pop Changes for Guitar: From Open Chords to Passing Chords

title: Pop Changes for Guitar: From Open Chords to Passing Chords
text:
1. The basic chords
C, Am, F, G. The four chords as open shapes. The diagrams show the neck standing upright: string 6 is on the left and the nut is at the top. A dot labelled R is the root. In a key that has no open shape the diagram shows the barre shape instead.
crumbs: Pop Changes for Guitar: From Open Chords to Passing Chords

title: Pop Changes for Guitar: From Open Chords to Passing Chords
text:
2. Extensions
Cadd9, Am7, Fadd9, Gsus2. Each of these is the basic shape with one finger moved or lifted. Check the diagrams for what changed: the new note carries a 9, 7 or 2.
crumbs: Pop Changes for Guitar: From Open Chords to Passing Chords

title: Pop Changes for Guitar: From Open Chords to Passing Chords
text:
3. Passing chords
C, G/B | Am, C/G | F, F♯dim | G. The bass note moves by step. A slash chord such as G/B is the G chord with the note after the slash as its lowest note: the diagram shows the G shape, and you play B (string 5, second fret) beneath it.
crumbs: Pop Changes for Guitar: From Open Chords to Passing Chords

title: Pop Changes for Guitar: From Open Chords to Passing Chords
text:
4. Secondary dominants
C, E7 | Am, C7 | F, D7 | G7. Four dominant sevenths. Each has one note from outside the key, and it is the one that leads into the next chord.
crumbs: Pop Changes for Guitar: From Open Chords to Passing Chords

title: Pop Changes for Guitar: From Open Chords to Passing Chords
text:
5. The two-five-one
Dm7, G7, Cmaj7. The chord before the G7 is Dm7, and the G7 goes home to C. Each root is a fifth below the last. All three are open shapes: Dm7 (x x 0 2 1 1), G7 (3 2 0 0 0 1) and Cmaj7 (x 3 2 0 0 0). Hold each for its bar and listen to the G7 pull toward the C.
crumbs: Pop Changes for Guitar: From Open Chords to Passing Chords

title: Pop Changes for Guitar: From Open Chords to Passing Chords
text:
6. The two-five-one in minor
Dm7♭5, G7, Cm7. The same fall in C minor. The first chord is half-diminished (D, F, A♭, C) and the home chord is minor. The library gives Dm7♭5 as a small four-string shape up the neck (fifth fret on the A string); Cm7 is a barre at the third fret. Change the key and watch which shapes move.
crumbs: Pop Changes for Guitar: From Open Chords to Passing Chords

text:

Pick a chord for each bar from the ones in this lesson. Fretboard diagrams and the staff follow your choices. Try a two-five in bars 3 and 4.

title: West African Bell Patterns and Cross-Rhythm
text: In much music of West and Central Africa, a drum ensemble is built from several short parts that repeat, each fitting the same cycle in its own way. No part is “the” rhythm: the music is the way they lock together. The Ewe people of Ghana and Togo are the example most often studied, and this page uses an Ewe-style texture. It is a simplified model for practice, not a transcription of a particular piece.
crumbs: West African Bell Patterns and Cross-Rhythm

title: West African Bell Patterns and Cross-Rhythm
text:
The cycle: twelve pulses
Many of these pieces run on a cycle of twelve fast pulses. Twelve divides by 2, 3, 4 and 6, so it holds four beats of three and three beats of four at once. That is why the music can feel like 12/8 and 3/4 at the same time.



Dancers often step the four beats. Listen to the four, then let the three pull against it.
crumbs: West African Bell Patterns and Cross-Rhythm

title: West African Bell Patterns and Cross-Rhythm
text:
The bell pattern
The part that holds the ensemble together is usually an iron bell (in Ewe music the double bell gankogui). Its most widespread pattern is seven strokes in twelve pulses, often called the standard pattern:
x . x . x x . x . x . x



The pattern is uneven on purpose: long and short gaps (2 2 1 2 2 2 1). Players and listeners use it as the reference for where every other part goes, the way a jazz drummer’s ride cymbal works.
Try it. Mute the bell and clap it against the four beats. Then mute the beats and step them while the bell plays.
crumbs: West African Bell Patterns and Cross-Rhythm

title: West African Bell Patterns and Cross-Rhythm
text:
Layering the ensemble
Add parts one at a time: the bell, a shaker on every pulse with an accent each beat, a low drum on the four, and a high drum playing three.



Mute layers in turn. With only the bell and the three, the music seems to be in three; with the bell and the four, in four. With all of them it is both.
crumbs: West African Bell Patterns and Cross-Rhythm

title: West African Bell Patterns and Cross-Rhythm
text:
Hearing it from the inside
A useful exercise from many teachers: keep the four beats with your feet, clap the bell, and say the three. Start very slowly. When it feels stable, change which part you clap. The goal is to hear each part as a line in its own right, not as an off-beat of something else.
crumbs: West African Bell Patterns and Cross-Rhythm

title: West African Bell Patterns and Cross-Rhythm
text:
Unverified, to check
The facts on this page are from memory and have not yet been checked against a source: the name gankogui, the term “standard pattern” (usually credited to A. M. Jones), and the dancers’ four-beat step. They are listed in the sources file as unverified.

title: Polyrhythm in Jazz
text: Jazz rhythm sits on a steady four, but a great deal of it plays against that four. The tension is part of its West African inheritance through the blues and New Orleans music.

title: Polyrhythm in Jazz
text:
Swing: three inside two
A swung eighth note is close to a triplet: the beat is felt in three while the bass walks in four and the music is counted in two-beat halves. The ride cymbal pattern “ding, ding-a ding” sits on triplets:



Swing ratios vary with tempo and player; the even triplet here is a starting point only.

title: Polyrhythm in Jazz
text:
Three-beat figures across the bar
A common jazz device is a phrase that repeats every three eighth notes (or every dotted quarter) over 4/4. It goes round the bar, landing on a different beat each time, and meets the downbeat again after three bars. This is polymeter: same pulse, different lengths.



Pianists use it in comping and solos; horn sections in big band riffs.

title: Polyrhythm in Jazz
text:
3 against 4 and 4 against 3
Drummers and pianists also play true even polyrhythms over the beat, such as three half-note triplets across a 4/4 bar or quarter-note triplets (three against two beats).

title: Polyrhythm in Jazz
text:
Players to hear
Drummers known for playing across the time include Elvin Jones (with John Coltrane’s quartet), Max Roach, Tony Williams and Jack DeJohnette; pianists include McCoy Tyner and Brad Mehldau. This list is from memory and is a starting point for listening, not a checked claim about particular recordings.

title: Polyrhythm in Jazz
text:
Practice

Keep the four with your foot. Clap the dotted-quarter figure until you can stop on any downbeat without losing it.
Mute the figure in the player and play it on your instrument over the four.
Play quarter-note triplets for one bar, then back to quarter notes, without the beat moving.

The skill is to keep the time steady while the figure crosses it: if the four moves to follow the figure, the effect is gone.

title: Clave and 6/8 in Afro-Cuban Music
text: Afro-Cuban music grew from West African and Spanish traditions, and much of its rhythm keeps the West African tension between three and two. The key pattern is the clave, played on two sticks (claves), which all the other parts line up with.

title: Clave and 6/8 in Afro-Cuban Music
text:
Tresillo: three over two
The tresillo divides eight pulses 3 + 3 + 2:



It is not an even polyrhythm (the three notes are not equal), but it is heard as three against the two beats, and it is everywhere from Cuban son to New Orleans and pop.

title: Clave and 6/8 in Afro-Cuban Music
text:
Son clave
Son clave is two bars: a tresillo-like “three side” and a “two side”.
x . . x . . x . | . . x . x . . . (3-2)



Played starting from the second half it is 2-3 clave. Which side comes first is fixed by the song, and the other parts are written to fit it.

title: Clave and 6/8 in Afro-Cuban Music
text:
Rumba clave
Rumba clave moves the last note of the three side one pulse later, which pulls harder against the beat:



Mute one clave at a time to hear the one note that differs.

title: Clave and 6/8 in Afro-Cuban Music
text:
6/8: the bell against four
In Afro-Cuban 6/8 styles (often called bembé), the bell plays the same 12-pulse pattern as in the West African lesson, and the band moves between feeling four beats and six.



Mute the four, then the six. The bell sits comfortably over both, which is 3 against 2 at the level of beats: a hemiola.

title: Clave and 6/8 in Afro-Cuban Music
text:
Practice

Step four beats and clap son clave. Then rumba clave.
Step four beats and clap the 6/8 bell.
In the Polyrhythm tool, type your own variation of clave and hear it against four.

text:

title: Drum groove: Waltz in one
text:
This is a lesson on one drum groove the Backing Track band plays: Waltz in one. It is built up from a simpler pattern, one step at a time, and every step is played by the band and written out as it plays. How the examples work: press ▶ Play, switch players in and out with the buttons beside it, and read what the band will play on the staff underneath: the whole pass is written out when Play starts, before it sounds. The tempo slider at the bottom of the page slows everything down.

title: Drum groove: Waltz in one
text:
The pattern
For a quick 3/4: kick on 1, a brushed snare on 2 and 3. Four bars make one phrase: the kick leans on the first and third, the snare answers in the second and fourth, and the fourth leads back in. In 4/4 it is the two-beat.
It belongs in Waltz (in one), Boom-chick and Folk carol. Here it is in the waltz (in one) style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Drum groove: Waltz in one
text:
Step 1: Two-beat
Start with something simpler. Kick with the bass on 1 and 3, a soft snare with the chords on 2 and 4. In 3/4: kick on 1, snare on 2 and 3.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums play alone first; switch the bass and chords on when it is steady.

title: Drum groove: Waltz in one
text:
Step 2: Waltz in one, slowly
Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.

text:
The pattern

It belongs in Country train beat. Here it is in the country train beat style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

text:

text:

Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.

text:
The pattern
The backbeat at half speed: kick on 1 and the and of 2, one snare on beat 3.
It belongs in Piano ballad, Straight-eighth rock and Emo / pop-punk. Here it is in the straight-eighth rock style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

text:

Start with something simpler. Closed hi-hat on every eighth note, all of one weight, kick on 1 and 3, snare on 2 and 4. The basic rock beat. In 3/4: six eighths, kick on 1, snare on 3.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums play alone first; switch the bass and chords on when it is steady.

title: Drum groove: Half-time
text:
Step 2: Rock backbeat
Eighths on the cymbal and a full snare on 2 and 4. The kick changes over four bars: 1, 3 and the and of 3; then 1, the and of 2 and 3; the last bar adds a pickup on the and of 4. Sixteenth-note fills.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums play alone first; switch the bass and chords on when it is steady.

The pattern
Brushes on the snare: a swish on every beat, leaning on 2 and 4, and taps on the ride pattern (1, 2, the skip after 2, 3, 4, the skip after 4). Hi-hat foot on 2 and 4, a kick you feel more than hear. No fills.
It belongs in Swing, Jazz ballad, Folk carol and Boom-chick. Here it is in the swing style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

The pattern

title: Comping rhythm: Every off-beat
text:
The pattern
A short chord on the and of every beat and never on the beat: the ska and calypso afterbeat.
It belongs in Calypso, Ska / reggae, Freylekhs / polka and Boogie-woogie. Here it is in the ska / reggae style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Comping rhythm: Every off-beat
text:
Step 1: Quarter-note chords
Start with something simpler. The chord on every beat, held. On the piano the left hand adds the root underneath as each chord arrives: Let It Be, Imagine, Someone Like You.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Comping rhythm: Every off-beat
text:
Step 2: Boom-chick / oom-pah-pah
Short chords on the beats the bass leaves free: 2 and 4 in 4/4, 2 and 3 in a waltz. Goes with the Root and fifth bass line.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Comping rhythm: Every off-beat
text:
Step 3: Every off-beat, slowly
Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.
How to play it. Never on the beat: a short chord on every and. Count 1-AND-2-AND aloud, tap the beat with your foot and play only with the and. On guitar it is a chop, the chord choked right after it sounds.
The band plays it on piano here; the step after next has it on guitar.

title: Comping rhythm: Every off-beat
section: Step 4: Up to tempo, with the band

The whole band, at 80 beats a minute. Play along, then switch the band’s chord player off and take the part yourself.

title: Comping rhythm: Every off-beat
text:
Step 5: On the guitar
The same rhythm on the guitar. On guitar each chord is a strum or a pluck of a chord shape; a short chord is choked by easing the fretting hand off the strings.

title: Comping rhythm: Strum: D, D-U, U-D-U
text:
The pattern
The strum most songbooks start with: down on 1, down-up on 2, then up, down-up through 3 and 4 (the hand misses the strings on beat 3).
It belongs in Acoustic strum, Straight-eighth rock, Boom-chick and Folk carol. Here it is in the acoustic strum style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

Start with something simpler. One ringing downstroke on every beat. The first strum to learn, and the usual one for a slow song.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Comping rhythm: Stride in tenths
text:
The pattern
Stride with a wider left hand: on beat 1 a tenth (the root with the chord’s 3rd an octave above it, together); on beat 3 the fifth, or, when the chord is about to change, a tenth walking to a step from the next root. Chords in the middle of the keyboard on 2 and 4. A tenth that would crowd the chords is played as its low note alone. On the guitar it is plain boom-chick.
It belongs in Stride piano and Ragtime. Here it is in the stride piano style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Comping rhythm: Stride in tenths
text:
Step 1: Boom-chick / oom-pah-pah
Start with something simpler. Short chords on the beats the bass leaves free: 2 and 4 in 4/4, 2 and 3 in a waltz. Goes with the Root and fifth bass line.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Comping rhythm: Stride in tenths
text:
Step 2: Stride
The stride pianist’s left hand: a low bass note on beats 1 and 3 (the root in octaves where a chord starts, its fifth on beat 3) and the chord in the middle of the keyboard on beats 2 and 4. In 3/4 the bass on 1 and the chord on 2 and 3. On the guitar it is plain boom-chick.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Comping rhythm: Stride in tenths
text:
Step 3: Stride in tenths, slowly
Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.
How to play it. The stride left hand, stretched: on beat 1 the root with the 3rd an octave above it, both at once (roll them if your hand will not reach). On beat 3 the fifth, or, before a chord change, a tenth a step away from the next root, so the bass walks into it. Learn the leaps first with single notes, then add the top of each tenth.

title: Comping rhythm: So What: the answer
text:
The pattern
A two-bar pattern. Nothing in the first bar, under the bass call. In the second, two chords: the voicing a whole step above the chord, held from beat 3, then the chord itself, short, on the and of 4. Use the Fourths voicing for the sound of the record.
It belongs in Swing. Here it is in the swing style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

text:
Step 1: Hymn: four parts
Start with something simpler. Every chord played once and held until the next one. On the piano or organ it is four parts: the root in the left hand and three voices above it that move as little as possible from chord to chord. It follows the chart’s chords, so a carol written with a chord on every beat sounds like the hymnal.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

text:

text:

title: Bass line: Root and fifth
text:
This is a lesson on one bass line the Backing Track band plays: Root and fifth. It is built up from a simpler pattern, one step at a time, and every step is played by the band and written out as it plays. How the examples work: press ▶ Play, switch players in and out with the buttons beside it, and read what the band will play on the staff underneath: the whole pass is written out when Play starts, before it sounds. The tempo slider at the bottom of the page slows everything down.
All the accompaniment patterns · Bass lines

title: Bass line: Root and fifth
text:
The pattern
The boom of boom-chick: the root on beat 1 and the fifth on beat 3, short, the same every bar. In 3/4 it is one note a bar, root one bar and fifth the next.
It belongs in Boom-chick, Calypso, Ska / reggae, Country train beat, Acoustic strum, Folk carol, Waltz (in one), John Prine Fingerpicking, Stride piano and Ragtime. Here it is in the boom-chick style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Bass line: Root and fifth
text:
Step 1: Roots on 1 and 3
Start with something simpler. The root on beats 1 and 3, held; one note a bar in 3/4. A chord that changes in between gets its root when it arrives.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Bass line: Root and fifth
text:
Step 2: Root and fifth, slowly
Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.
How to play it. Root on 1, fifth on 3, both short so the chords can be heard on 2 and 4. The fifth is one string up and two frets up from the root, or on the string below at the same fret: use whichever is closer to the next root.

title: Bass line: Root and fifth
section: Step 3: Up to tempo, with the band
text:
Step 3: Up to tempo, with the band
The whole band, at 104 beats a minute. Play along, then switch the band’s bass off and take the part yourself.

title: Bass line: Root and fifth
section: Step 4: Two chords in a bar
text:
Step 4: Two chords in a bar
Harder: now some bars have two chords, two beats each. Each chord gets its root when it arrives; the pattern squeezes into the beats it has.

title: Bass line: Root and fifth
text:
Step 5: In 3/4
The same pattern in a waltz: three beats to the bar. Listen for what it keeps and what it drops when the bar is a beat shorter.

The same bass line in other styles it fits. The other players change; yours does not. Notice how the same part sounds different in a different band.

title: Ornaments by Period
text:
An ornament sign is shorthand, and what it stands for has changed over 300 years. A small note before a main note, or a tr over it, can mean four or five different things depending on when and where the piece was written. Reading the sign isn’t enough. You have to know whose shorthand it is.
This page:
Press ▶ on any example to hear it. The notes shown are what is played, not just what is written.

title: Ornaments by Period
text:
One sign, five meanings

A small note before the main note
Every reading in the table below starts from the same written notes:










Idiom
How it's played
Played




Baroque
to c. 1750
An appoggiatura: on the beat, leaning on the dissonance, long. Half of the main note is the default, more before a long note.





Classical
c. 1750–1820
The same: on the beat and long, usually half (Leopold Mozart; Türk). Short graces before quick or repeated notes. Mozart often writes the long ones out in full-size notes.





Romantic
c. 1820–1900
Mostly short. Chopin wants it on the beat, struck with the bass (Eigeldinger). Later in the century short graces often go before the beat (Brown).





20th and 21st century
Before the beat, as quickly as possible, so the main note lands on the beat. Scores that want something else say so in a performance note (Gould).





Jazz and blues
A smear: one note sliding into the next, before or across the beat. ▶ plays it as a slide on guitar.







The key line runs between Classical and Romantic. Before about 1820 the small note is a real note that takes the beat and much of the main note’s time. After that it’s usually a quick flick, and from the 20th century it goes before the beat.


A trill
Every reading starts from the same written trill:










Idiom
How it's played
Played




Baroque
From the note above, on the beat, leaning on the first note. The trill is a decorated appoggiatura (J. S. Bach; C. P. E. Bach).





Classical
Still from the note above, now even, often with a closing turn into the next note (Türk; Clementi).





Romantic
From the main note: Hummel (1828) says the start from above "was made for the voice". Chopin too, unless he writes a small note before the trill (Hummel; Ekier).





20th and 21st century
From the main note, unmeasured: as many notes as fit, as fast as possible. The speed, the note it trills with, even a slowing or speeding trill, may be written into the score (Gould).





Jazz
A shake: a wide, loose lip trill (on trumpet, often a third or more), with no fixed number of notes (Pejrolo and DeRosa; Barnhart). ▶ plays it on guitar.

title: Ornaments by Period
section: Baroque: the player finishes the music
text:
Baroque: the player finishes the music
A Baroque score is incomplete on purpose. Composers expected the player to add graces, and in France each composer printed a table of his own signs (d’Anglebert 1689, Couperin 1713). The defaults are clear: ornaments start on the beat, and from the note above (J. S. Bach; C. P. E. Bach). How many to add, and where, is taste. Some scholars argue that Bach’s trills could start on the main note too (Neumann, Ornamentation in Baroque). Most players today still start them from above.
Here is the opening of the Sarabande from Bach’s English Suite No. 3, as plain as Bach wrote it the first time. He then wrote out an ornamented version of his own (Les agréments de la même Sarabande).


Valid

French style: graces on the strong notes. An appoggiatura leans on beat 2, where a sarabande puts its weight. A trill from above goes on the leading tone, and a mordent on the last note. The tune stays the same.





Valid

Italian style: fill in the long notes. The long notes become running notes (passaggi, or divisions) that circle the written pitch. The notes on the beat are still Bach’s, so the harmony doesn’t change.


Not appropriate

Ornaments everywhere, and a trill on the resolution. A mordent on every note flattens the dance: beat 2 no longer stands out. The trill on the final G is the worst of it. A trill adds tension, so it belongs on the note before the resolution, never on the resolution itself.


Not appropriate

A 19th-century reading. The trill starts on the main note, and the grace on beat 2 is crushed into a flick before the beat. Both are right in Chopin. Here they lose the two dissonances, the leaning A against B♭ and the trill’s upper note, that the Baroque ornaments exist to make.

title: Ornaments by Period
section: Classical: written down more, still on the beat
text:
Classical: written down more, still on the beat
The rules hardly change from the late Baroque. Appoggiaturas fall on the beat and take half the main note, or two-thirds of a dotted one (Leopold Mozart; Türk; Clementi), and trills start from the note above. What changes is how much the composer writes. Mozart often writes his appoggiaturas as full-size notes and writes out the decorations of a slow movement, so there is less for the player to add (Neumann, Ornamentation and Improvisation in Mozart). There are still two places to improvise: the cadenza at the fermata in a concerto, and the short Eingang (lead-in) at a pause before a theme comes back.
The phrase below is written for this page in the Classical style.


Valid

The textbook reading. Each appoggiatura takes half its note, on the beat. The short grace before the quick F is short, and the trill starts from above and ends on a quick anticipation of the last note.


Valid

On the repeat, a little more. A turn fills the first bar and a rising figure leads into the third. Every decoration starts and ends on the written notes. This is what Mozart writes out himself when a melody comes back.


Not appropriate

Crushed graces and a main-note trill. Every appoggiatura is flicked away, so the sighs (D against C, A against G) disappear. Leopold Mozart and Türk both treat the long appoggiatura as the expressive heart of the phrase. The trill from the main note is the 19th-century habit.

title: Ornaments by Period
section: Romantic: short, and the composer decides
text:
Romantic: short, and the composer decides
Through the 19th century grace notes get shorter and move towards (or before) the beat, and trills start on the main note (Brown; Hummel). Composers write ever more precisely what they want, and the player’s job shifts from adding ornaments to shaping the ones written. Chopin is the famous exception: grace notes and trills start with the bass note, on the beat (Eigeldinger; Ekier).


Valid (Chopin)

With the bass. The grace note sounds together with the low E♭, as a quick lean, and the trill starts on its main note F.


Valid (later 19th century)

Before the beat. In much later Romantic music (and in Chopin’s early Contredanse, by his editors’ reading) the grace goes before the beat, so the bass and the main note sound together (Brown; Ekier).


Not appropriate

A Baroque appoggiatura. A long lean on C takes half the beat and smothers the melody’s first note. The trill starts from above, and an extra turn is added. None of it was asked for: by now the composer writes what he wants.

title: Ornaments by Period
text:
20th and 21st century: read the legend
Concert music after about 1900 mostly writes out exactly what it wants. Where signs survive, the general conventions are: grace notes before the beat, trills from the main note and as fast as possible, and nothing added (Gould). Many scores invent their own signs, for microtones, trills that speed up or slow down, or extended techniques, and explain them in a performance note at the front. That note overrules any period rule. Improvisation returns in a new form: some scores give a box of notes to repeat freely, or a graphic to interpret, and say so.


Valid

The default. The grace goes before the beat, and the trill is unmeasured from the main note.


Valid, if the legend says so

On the beat. Some composers ask for graces on the beat. If the performance note says so, that’s the right reading, and only then.


Not appropriate

A Baroque reading. A long appoggiatura on the beat and a trill from above would be right in Bach. Here they change the composer’s rhythm and harmony.

title: Ornaments by Period
section: Jazz: the player owns the sound
text:
Jazz: the player owns the sound
In jazz the written notes are an outline. Grace notes, falls and scoops are part of a player’s sound: they come before or across the beat, in swing time, and are mostly not written at all (Caniato). A big-band chart writes them as signs (fall, doit, scoop, plop, shake), and the section plays them the way its lead player does. Singers and soloists add them freely. ▶ plays the slides on a clean electric guitar, so a fall really falls.


Valid

A fall off the long note. The line is swung, and the last note falls away at its release, never before the beat.


Valid

Scoop in, shake out. The first note slides up from below, and the long note gets a shake after it has sounded straight for a moment. That’s Armstrong’s “terminal vibrato” made wider (Schuller).


Not appropriate

A Classical trill, played straight. Even eighths and a measured trill from above, closed with a neat turn. Every note is “right”, but the line no longer swings, and a jazz shake is looser and wider than this.

title: Ornaments by Period
text:
Improvisation, then and now
Ornaments are what remains in the notation of a much larger habit of making music up on the spot. How much of that habit a score expects changes from period to period:








Period
What the player was expected to invent
Today




Baroque
Graces on almost any note; divisions on slow movements, above all on the repeat; the chords over a figured bass; cadenzas at fermatas (C. P. E. Bach; Quantz)
Early-music players add their own again. Bach’s written-out agréments and ornamented editions of Corelli’s slow movements are the models.


Classical
Cadenzas in concertos, Eingänge at pauses, decoration of repeats in slow movements and arias (Neumann, Ornamentation and Improvisation in Mozart)
Players play written cadenzas (Mozart’s own, Beethoven’s) or write their own; singers decorate the repeats in Mozart’s arias.


Romantic
Less and less: composers write the ornaments and the cadenzas themselves
Play what’s written. Shape the written ornaments with rubato and tone instead of adding to them.


20th and 21st century
Nothing, unless the score asks. Then sometimes a great deal: free repetition, graphic scores, open form.
Follow the performance note.


Jazz
Almost everything: the melody’s shape, the ornaments, the solo
The heart of the style. The written melody is a starting point.



Two things hold across all of them:

Ornaments serve the structure. Baroque, Classical and jazz improvisers all decorate weak notes and long notes, and leave the arrivals (cadences, downbeats, chord tones) clear.
More isn’t better. C. P. E. Bach compared too many ornaments to too much seasoning (C. P. E. Bach, ch. 2). A Basie section player would say much the same about a fall on every note.

Which way do I play it?

title: Writing Music Down: Choosing the Right Notation
text:
There is no single right way to write music down. A notation is a tool. Each one shows some things clearly and leaves others out, and each belongs to a tradition whose players read it fluently. This lesson writes one melody six ways so you can compare them side by side, then says when to reach for each.
The melody is the opening of Mò Lì Huā (茉莉花, Jasmine Flower), a Chinese folk song known across the world. It uses only five notes (a pentatonic scale), which also exists in Indian music: Hindustani musicians call that scale rāg Bhūpālī and Carnatic musicians rāga Mōhanam. So it can be written naturally in every system on this page.
▶ Hear the melody

Every example below is this same phrase.
crumbs: Writing Music Down: Choosing the Right Notation

title: Writing Music Down: Choosing the Right Notation
section: The six notations at a glance
text:
The six notations at a glance









Notation
Shows well
Leaves out or blurs
Typical home




Staff (Western) notation
exact pitch and rhythm, harmony, several parts at once
tuning between the 12 notes, ornaments of other traditions, timbre
Western classical, jazz, film, band, most published music


Jianpu (numbered notation)
scale degrees, rhythm, lyrics; quick to write and to transpose
harmony and multiple parts are clumsy
Chinese folk, pop and instrumental music; also Indonesia, Japan


Sargam (Hindustani and Carnatic)
scale degrees in a rāga, rhythm against the tāla cycle
the ornaments (gamaka, mīnd) that matter most; it’s a memory aid, not a full score
Indian classical teaching and composition


DAW screenshot (piano roll, arrangement)
exact timing, velocity, structure, layers, effects and automation
key, harmony and musical meaning; it is a picture of data, not something to read
electronic, pop production, any music made in a computer


Waveform
loudness over time, where sounds start, silence, clipping
pitch, harmony, almost everything else
editing audio, checking timing and dynamics


Spectrogram
which frequencies sound when: timbre, harmonics, vibrato
it’s hard to read notes, rhythm or harmony from it, especially with several instruments
acoustics, voice, sound design, analysis of non-pitched music
crumbs: Writing Music Down: Choosing the Right Notation

title: Writing Music Down: Choosing the Right Notation
text:
Staff notation



Five lines, notes placed on lines and spaces for pitch, note shapes for length. Its strengths: exact pitch (every one of the 12 notes in every octave), exact rhythm, and many parts at once lined up vertically, so harmony and counterpoint can be seen. That’s why orchestral, choral and band music, and almost all analysis of Western harmony, uses it.
Its weaknesses: it assumes the 12 equal notes of a piano, so pitches between them (blue notes, Arabic maqām, Indian shruti, the slides of Chinese erhu playing) need extra signs or prose. It also needs training to read quickly.
Use it when: writing for Western instruments or ensembles; analysing harmony, voice leading or form in Western music; when exact rhythm and pitch must be communicated to a reader who will play it.






NoteMYP and DP notes: staff notation






MYP: you don’t have to use staff notation in MYP Music, but when you analyse Western music, short notated examples (a motif, a chord progression) are the clearest evidence. Label what you’re showing: circle the motif and name it, write the chord symbols above. In your process journal, a scan of a hand-written sketch is fine.
DP: when you discuss a Western work in the Exploring music in context portfolio or an analysis, quote short, annotated excerpts with bar numbers instead of long unmarked pages, and say where they come from. For your own compositions, staff notation is expected where the music is written for performers to read; use notation software and check that what is written matches what you intend to be played.
crumbs: Writing Music Down: Choosing the Right Notation

title: Writing Music Down: Choosing the Right Notation
text:
Jianpu (numbered notation)



Jianpu (简谱, “simplified notation”) numbers the notes of the scale: 1 to 7 are do, re, mi, fa, sol, la, ti. The key is given at the start (1 = F means do is F). A dot above a number puts it an octave up, a dot below an octave down. A plain number lasts one beat; each line under a number halves it; a dash after it adds a beat. Bar lines are as in staff notation.
It was spread in China in the early 20th century from a French numbered system, and is still how most Chinese musicians write and read folk songs, pop songs and parts for traditional instruments like the erhu, pipa and dizi. Because it writes scale degrees, not fixed pitches, the same page can be played in any key just by changing “1 =”.
Use it when: writing or studying Chinese music, or when the players read jianpu; writing a single melody with lyrics quickly; teaching melodies by scale degree (it pairs naturally with tonal solfège).






NoteMYP and DP notes: jianpu






MYP: if you investigate a Chinese musical tradition (Criterion A, Investigating), showing the music in jianpu, with a short key that explains the dots, lines and dashes, demonstrates that you understand how the tradition itself writes music. Put staff notation next to it if your reader won’t know jianpu.
DP: in the portfolio or an analysis, quoting music from a Chinese tradition in its own notation is a sign of working in context. Provide a legend the first time, and if you compare it with a Western piece, a parallel staff version helps the examiner follow. Don’t just transcribe it into staff notation and leave the original out.
crumbs: Writing Music Down: Choosing the Right Notation

title: Writing Music Down: Choosing the Right Notation
text:
Sargam: Hindustani and Carnatic notation
Indian classical music names the notes of the scale Sa Re Ga Ma Pa Dha Ni (sargam), shortened to their first letters. Sa is the home note, chosen by the singer; like jianpu, it writes scale degrees, not fixed pitches. The two classical traditions write it a little differently.

Hindustani (North Indian): Bhatkhande notation



Developed by Vishnu Narayan Bhatkhande in the early 20th century. Each box is one mātrā (beat). Notes sharing a beat are joined by a curve beneath. A dot above a note is the upper octave (Ṡ), a dot below is the lower. A dash holds the previous note (some books use the Devanagari sign ऽ instead). Underneath, the tāla (the rhythmic cycle) is marked: X is sam, the first and strongest beat, and 0 is khālī, the “empty” beat. This melody fits exactly one cycle of the eight-beat Keherwā tāla. A flat (komal) note is shown by a line under it, and the raised Ma (tīvra) by a line above.


Carnatic (South Indian): swara notation



Carnatic notation writes the swaras in lower-case letters (s r g m p d n), with dots for octaves, a comma to extend a note by one time unit and a semicolon for two. The tāla is marked with bar lines at the end of each section: one line after the laghu (four beats here) and after each drutam (two beats), and a double line at the end of the cycle. Eight beats is Ādi tāla, the most common Carnatic tāla, so this melody fills exactly one cycle of it too.


What sargam leaves out
The most important part of a rāga is how notes are approached: slides (mīnd), oscillations (gamaka), which notes are lingered on. The written swaras give the skeleton only, and students learn the rest by ear from a teacher. Many pieces are never written at all. So sargam notation is a reliable memory aid and teaching tool, not a complete score.
Use it when: studying, teaching or composing in an Indian tradition; showing the shape of a rāga; showing how a melody sits against a tāla cycle.






NoteMYP and DP notes: sargam






MYP: in an investigation of Indian music, use the tradition’s own terms (rāga, tāla, sam, khālī, swara) and its notation for short examples. Explain in your own words what the notation cannot show, such as gamaka, and support it with a timestamped recording (“listen at 1:42 for the slide from Ga to Re”).
DP: for the portfolio or an analysis of Indian music, sargam with a legend, plus precise timestamps in a named recording, is stronger evidence than a staff transcription alone. Staff notation can’t show the shruti and gamaka you’d be discussing. If you do transcribe to staff for comparison, say what it loses. Name the tradition (Hindustani or Carnatic), and the rāga and tāla.
crumbs: Writing Music Down: Choosing the Right Notation

title: Writing Music Down: Choosing the Right Notation
text:
DAW screenshots






A digital audio workstation (DAW) shows music the way the computer stores it. The piano roll (top) is a grid: time runs left to right, pitch bottom to top, each bar is a note, and its shade is how hard it is played (velocity). The arrangement view (bottom) shows every track as a lane of blocks (regions or clips), with lines for automation: a volume fade, a filter opening.
What it’s good at: exact timing and velocity, how a track is layered and structured, which sounds, effects and automation were used. For electronic music, hip hop and most pop production, this is the score: the music was never written any other way.
What it’s bad at: it doesn’t tell the reader the key, the chords or the beat they should feel. It’s a picture to be explained, not something a performer can read. A wall of tiny clips means nothing without labels.
Use it when: the music was made in a DAW; showing production decisions (layers, effects, automation, edits); showing a process (before and after).






NoteMYP and DP notes: DAW screenshots






MYP: screenshots are excellent process-journal evidence for Criterion B (Developing) and C (Creating): show a “before” and “after” with a sentence on why you changed it. Crop to what matters, zoom so it’s readable, and add arrows and labels. A full-screen screenshot of the whole project with no annotation shows very little.
DP: in the Experimenting with music report and in production-based Presenting music or HL project work, annotated DAW screenshots are often the most appropriate evidence for music created in a DAW. Annotate them: name the track, the plug-in and the setting, and say what musical effect it had. Pair a screenshot with a timestamp in the audio (“the filter opens at 0:48”). For anything that will be performed by players, include a readable score or lead sheet as well.
crumbs: Writing Music Down: Choosing the Right Notation

title: Writing Music Down: Choosing the Right Notation
text:
Waveforms



A waveform draws the sound itself: how far the speaker cone moves, over time. Zoomed out (top), it shows loudness over time: where notes start, how they fade, where the silences are, and whether the recording is clipping (flat-topped at the edges). Zoomed right in (bottom), you can see individual cycles of the wave (see Sound 1).
That’s about all it shows. You cannot read the pitches, the harmony or the instruments from it.
Use it when: showing where an edit, an entry or a hit happens; comparing the dynamics of two performances or two masters; showing that a recording is too quiet or distorted.
crumbs: Writing Music Down: Choosing the Right Notation

title: Writing Music Down: Choosing the Right Notation
text:
Spectrograms



A spectrogram shows time left to right, frequency bottom to top, and loudness as brightness. Each note appears as a stack of lines (its harmonics), so it shows timbre, vibrato and which frequencies are present when. Here you can see the melody’s notes, each with its harmonics above, and the slight vibrato on the long notes.
With one clean instrument, it can be surprisingly readable. With a full band it becomes a dense cloud from which notes, chords and rhythm are very hard to pick out. Specialists use it for voice (formants), acoustics, birdsong, and for music where pitch isn’t the point: electronic textures, noise music, extended techniques.
Use it when: your point is about timbre, a sound’s frequency content, vibrato or a texture with no clear notes, and only with labels that point at what to look at.






NoteMYP and DP notes: waveforms and spectrograms






MYP and DP alike: use them only when they show the point you’re making (dynamics, timing, timbre), and say what to look at. A waveform or spectrogram dropped in as decoration isn’t evidence of anything, and it won’t stand in for notation. One cropped, labelled image with a timestamp beats a full-track screenshot.
DP: in an analysis of electronic or non-notated music, a spectrogram with a labelled feature (“the sweep from 200 Hz to 5 kHz is the filter opening”) can support a point about timbre or production that no score could show. Keep it as support for your writing, not a substitute.
crumbs: Writing Music Down: Choosing the Right Notation

title: Writing Music Down: Choosing the Right Notation
text:
Choosing: a short checklist

Whose music is it? Use the notation the tradition itself uses (staff for a Bach chorale, jianpu for a Chinese folk song, sargam for a bandish, a DAW view for a track made in Ableton), and add a translation only if your reader needs it.
What’s the point you’re making? Harmony → staff. Scale degrees and melody → jianpu or sargam. Production → DAW. Dynamics or timing of a recording → waveform. Timbre → spectrogram.
Who has to read it? A performer needs something playable. An examiner needs something labelled.
What does it leave out? Say so, and fill the gap with a recording and a timestamp.
Crop, label, cite. Short excerpts, bar numbers or timestamps, the source of every example.







NoteMYP and DP notes: presenting evidence in general






Legends. The first time you use any notation your reader might not know (jianpu, sargam, a graphic score), give a two-line key.
Accuracy. Wrong notes or rhythms in a notated example undermine the point it makes. Check every example against the recording.
Citations. Every quoted score, recording and screenshot of someone else’s work needs a source.
Recordings and timestamps. For music that isn’t primarily written down, the recording is the primary source, and a timestamp is your “bar number”.
Your own work. In both programmes, evidence of process (sketches, screenshots of versions, short recordings of tries) counts. Date it and say what changed.

title: Live Sound 1: The X32 Channel Strip
text: The Behringer X32 is our main mixing desk. It has 32 input channels, and every one of them is the same strip of tools, in the same order. Learn one channel and you know all 32.
crumbs: Live Sound 1: The X32 Channel Strip

title: Live Sound 1: The X32 Channel Strip
text:
The strip, in order
Press a channel’s Select button and the knobs in the middle of the desk (the channel strip) all work on that channel. The X32 manual lists its sections in signal order:

Config / Preamp: Gain (how much the mic signal is amplified, −12 to +60 dB), 48 V phantom power for condenser mics, Ø polarity flip, and the Low Cut filter (20–400 Hz).
Gate and Dynamics: the noise gate turns the channel down when it’s quiet; the compressor turns the loud parts down.
Equalizer: four bands (Low, Lo Mid, Hi Mid, High), each with Type, Freq, Gain and Q.
Bus Sends and Main Bus: monitor mixes, effects, and the send to the main speakers (pan, and the fader at the bottom of the strip).

Each section has a button that switches it on (lit) or off (dark), and a View button that opens all its settings on the screen. The compressor can sit before or after the EQ (the Pos setting on the Dyn page).

On the fader strip itself you also get Mute, Solo, a small input meter, and two little lights that show when the gate and compressor are working on that channel.
crumbs: Live Sound 1: The X32 Channel Strip

title: Live Sound 1: The X32 Channel Strip
text:
Try it: one X32 channel
This is one channel of the X32, laid out left to right instead of top to bottom. The knobs have the X32’s ranges. Drag a knob up or down (Shift for fine), use the mouse wheel or the arrow keys; double-click to reset.




Speakers is your volume, not part of the desk.
The input meter next to Gain shows the level after the preamp, with the X32’s marks (−54 to clip).
The graph under the EQ shows the EQ curve (amber) over what is coming out (blue).
The strip at the bottom shows the last 4 seconds: grey is the level the gate sees, amber what comes out, and dashed lines for the gate and compressor thresholds when they’re on.
⤓ WAV saves the source sound so you can play it through the real desk (see Live Sound 7).

Every source here has something wrong with it on purpose. The next lessons fix them one at a time.

title: Live Sound 1: The X32 Channel Strip
text:
Gain is not volume
The single most common mistake on a live desk: using the Gain knob as a volume control, or the fader as a fix for bad gain. They do different jobs. Live Sound 2 is all about it.
