title: Live Sound 4: Gates
text: A drum mic hears the whole kit. Between kick hits, the kick mic is picking up the snare, the hats and the cymbals: bleed. A gate closes the channel when the level falls below a threshold, and opens it again when the drum is hit.

title: Live Sound 4: Gates
text:
The X32 gate
Press Gate on the channel strip to switch it on and turn its threshold knob. On the screen (View) there is more:

Mode: GATE closes all the way down to the Range. EXP2, EXP3, EXP4 are expanders: below the threshold they turn down gradually (by 2, 3 or 4 times as much as the signal drops), which sounds more natural. (DUCK does the opposite, turning down when something else is loud; not used here.)
Threshold (−80 to 0 dB): the level that opens it. Above the bleed, below the quietest hit you want.
Range (3–60 dB): how far it closes. 60 dB is nearly silent; 10–20 dB just tucks the bleed down.
Attack (0–120 ms): how fast it opens. On drums, as fast as possible, or the start of each hit is lost.
Hold (up to 2 s): how long it stays open after the level drops.
Release (5 ms – 4 s): how fast it closes. Too short chops the drum’s ring; too long lets the bleed back in.

The fader strip’s gate light shows when it’s working.

title: Live Sound 4: Gates
text:
Try it: the kick



Watch the strip at the bottom: the grey line is the level the gate sees, the dashed green line its threshold. The kicks are the tall spikes; the snare bleed the smaller ones in between. Put the threshold between them. Careful: one kick near the end is played softly (a ghost note), and it must still get through.

title: Live Sound 4: Gates
text:
Try it: the toms
Toms ring for a long time, and a tom mic sits right next to the snare and under the cymbals.



Here the Release matters: set it short and every tom hit is cut to a click. A longer Hold and Release keep the ring. Try EXP3 with a Range of about 20 dB too: it’s less “on/off”.

Gating every drum isn’t always right. In a small room the kit is loud on its own, and the bleed is part of the sound. Gate the toms and maybe the kick; leave the overheads alone.

title: Live Sound 6: Monitors and Feedback
text: The players on stage hear themselves through monitors (wedges on the floor, or in-ear monitors). On the X32 every monitor is a mix bus: each channel has a send to each bus, and the bus goes to a wedge.

title: Live Sound 6: Monitors and Feedback
text:
Monitor sends on the X32

In the Bus Sends section of the channel strip, choose a bank and turn the send for that wedge. The screen (View) shows every send.
Monitor sends are usually pre-fader: when you move a channel’s fader for the audience, the singer’s wedge doesn’t change. The X32 lets each bus take its signal pre-EQ, pre-fader or post-fader.
Ask each player what they need more of. Their own voice or instrument usually comes first.

title: Live Sound 6: Monitors and Feedback
text:
Feedback
A mic hears the wedge, the wedge plays the mic, the mic hears that louder… and one frequency starts to ring and grow into a howl. That is feedback. The fixes, best first:

Aim it. A cardioid mic is deaf at the back: point that side at the wedge.
Closer. The closer the singer is to the mic, the less gain the channel needs.
Less. Turn down the send. Everyone wants more; the room has a limit.
Cut the ringing frequency with a narrow EQ cut (on the bus, so the main mix isn’t affected). The X32’s effects include 31-band graphic EQs (GEQ) you can insert on a bus.

title: Live Sound 6: Monitors and Feedback
section: Try it: a mixer channel with a wedge
text:
Try it: a mixer channel with a wedge
This is the simpler mixer channel from Gear 3, with a monitor send into a wedge that the mic can hear. Keep your speakers low. Feedback shows it happening; the two Fixed presets show two cures.

title: Live Sound 6: Monitors and Feedback
text:
Ringing out a monitor
Before the band arrives, with the mic in its place:

Turn the wedge send up slowly until it just starts to ring.
Find the frequency (sweep a narrow EQ on the bus, or a graphic EQ: the slider that makes it stop).
Cut it 3–6 dB, narrow. Turn up a little more until the next one rings. Two or three cuts is plenty; more and the wedge sounds hollow.

title: Live Sound 5: Compression
text: A singer sings the verse softly and belts the chorus. A bass player pops some notes. In the mix, the quiet parts vanish and the loud parts jump out. A compressor turns the loud parts down automatically so the level stays more even; then you turn the whole channel back up.

title: Live Sound 5: Compression
text:
The X32 compressor
Press Comp (the Dynamics button) and turn its threshold. On the Dyn page:

Threshold (−60 to 0 dB): above this level it starts turning down.
Ratio: the X32 offers 1.1, 1.3, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 4, 5, 7, 10, 20 and 100 to 1. At 4:1, a signal 8 dB over the threshold comes out only 2 dB over. 2–4:1 for vocals; 10:1 and up is limiting.
Knee (0–5): 0 starts compressing suddenly at the threshold; higher numbers ease in.
Attack (0–120 ms) and Release (5 ms – 4 s): how fast it turns down, and how fast it lets go. A very fast attack flattens every consonant and pluck; 5–20 ms keeps the start of each note.
Gain (0–24 dB): makeup gain, to bring the level back up.
Det: PEAK reacts to every peak; RMS to the average loudness (smoother, more like the ear).
Pos: before (PRE) or after (POST) the EQ.

The channel’s gain reduction meter shows how hard it is working; on the fader strip a light shows it.

title: Live Sound 5: Compression
text:
Try it: the vocal
The verse is about 18 dB quieter than the chorus.



Bring the Threshold down until the gain-reduction meter moves on the chorus but hardly on the verse, try a ratio of 3:1 or 4:1, then add makeup Gain until it’s as loud as before. Press Check my channel. Squashed shows going too far: flat, lifeless, and the breaths and room come up with it.

title: Live Sound 5: Compression
text:
Try it: the bass
Some notes are popped, about 12 dB louder than the rest.

title: Live Sound 5: Compression
text:
Compressor or fader?
A compressor reacts in milliseconds; you can’t. But it doesn’t know the song. Use the compressor to keep the level in a sensible window, and still ride the fader for the big changes (a solo, a quiet verse).

title: Out-of-Tune Overtones: Strings, Winds, Voice, Bars, Bells and Drums
text:
The harmonic series says a note is a stack of partials at 1, 2, 3, 4… times the fundamental. That is exactly true for an ideal vibrating string or an ideal pipe, and only roughly true for the real ones. Some instruments (a bowed violin, a clarinet, a singer) are harmonic almost to the cent. Others (a piano bass string, a marimba bar, a church bell, a timpani) have partials that are not whole-number multiples at all, and yet we hear a clear pitch. This lesson asks why, shows the numbers instrument by instrument, and asks who gets to change them: the player, or the maker. Click a section’s heading to fold it; the “On this page” bar at the right jumps to any section and opens it.
How to use the page. The tuner widgets are the strobe tuner of this site, listening to a made-up instrument instead of the microphone: press Start, pick a Practice instrument in the menu, and read the bands. Band k stands still when a partial is exactly k times the reference pitch; if it drifts right that partial is sharp of k, if left, flat, and the readout shows how many cents. The other widgets compute things (a ladder of partials, a string calculator, a pluck-position chart) and most have a ▶ button; the bar at the foot of the window sets the volume (start low). Nothing here needs a microphone. Numbers in square brackets, like [1], are the references at the end; where I could not find a source I say so.
crumbs: Out-of-Tune Overtones: Strings, Winds, Voice, Bars, Bells and Drums

title: Out-of-Tune Overtones: Strings, Winds, Voice, Bars, Bells and Drums
section: 1. Harmonic, stretched, and not even close
text:
1. Harmonic, stretched, and not even close
Three different things get called “inharmonic”, and the rest of the lesson keeps them apart.

Slightly stretched. A stiff string. Partial k is a little sharp of k times the fundamental, more so for larger k. The ear still hears one note.
Clean but wrong for the key. A brass instrument’s partials are exact multiples, but the multiples themselves (the 7th, 11th and 13th harmonics) fall between the notes of 12-tone equal temperament. UNSW’s page on string harmonics says the same of the 7th and 11th: they lie about halfway between equal-tempered notes [6].
Designed or accidental, far from harmonic. A free bar’s modes are at 1 : 2.76 : 5.40 : 8.93 times the first, a church bell’s at 0.5 : 1 : 1.18 : 1.51 : 2 and so on, a timpani’s at 1 : 1.59 : 2.14 : 2.30 : 2.65 before the air gets to it. We hear a pitch from these anyway, and makers go to great trouble to arrange it.

The widget below lays the partials of each practice instrument over the ideal harmonics, in cents off the nearest harmonic, and against the nearest note of 12-ET. It is the same table the tuner uses, so what you see here is what the strobe bands show below. (The ratios are in the source of synth-kit.js, each with its reference.)



For every instrument, “band 1” is the reference the tuner is set to. For the church bell it is the hum, the lowest partial, so the strike note you hear (the prime) is band 2. For the chime and the timpani it is the virtual pitch you hear, with nothing sounding there at all: the ear finds it from the spacing of the partials above (the “missing fundamental”, see [16] and [21]).
crumbs: Out-of-Tune Overtones: Strings, Winds, Voice, Bars, Bells and Drums

title: Out-of-Tune Overtones: Strings, Winds, Voice, Bars, Bells and Drums
text:
2. Strings: stiffness stretches the partials
An ideal string is pulled back only by its tension. A real one is also a springy rod, and bending it costs extra energy that rises with the shape’s curvature, so the more loops the string makes, the more extra restoring force there is, and the sharper the partial. For a plain round wire, with the partial numbers counted from 1:

fk = k f1 √(1 + B k²), where B = π³ E d⁴ / (64 T L²)

E is Young’s modulus of the wire, d its diameter, T the tension and L the vibrating length [2]. The sharpness of partial k, in cents, is 600 × log₂(1 + B k²), about 866 B k² for small B [3] (the strobe lesson uses the same formula for its test). For steel, E is about 2 × 10¹¹ Pa; the only source I retrieved for the range, 200 to 207 GPa, is a forum post, so treat it as the handbook figure it is [3].
What the formula says, which sources agree on [4] [2]: thicker (the fourth power of d), shorter, and lower tension all make B larger. At a fixed pitch the three are tied together, because a fatter string needs less tension to make the same note, so a thick string is stretched on both counts. Making the string thinner, longer, more flexible or higher in tension reduces it. Wound strings do it from the other side: the winding adds mass without adding bending stiffness, so only the core resists bending [4] [6]. That is why the lowest strings on both guitar and piano are wound.
Fletcher, Blackham and Stratton built piano tones from measured partials and asked listeners to compare them with real ones. They found that the partials of notes below middle C had to be inharmonic to sound piano-like, and that some inharmonicity contributes to the “warmth” [1] [5].
Try the calculator. The six-string presets use typical electric-guitar gauges and a 648 mm scale; the gauges and the wound strings’ mass factors are my own typical values and estimates, not from one source. The tension is worked out from the string’s mass per length (steel, 7850 kg/m³) and the pitch, so changing the gauge or the length moves the tension too. Raise fret to see B at a shorter vibrating length: with the tension unchanged, shortening L by 2fret/12 multiplies B by 2fret/6 (four times at the 12th fret). That is straight from the formula, and it is why the same string is more stretched up the neck. UNSW adds that the high harmonics of thick strings drift out of tune after about the twelfth, and that the “touch at 1/n of the length” rule for harmonics fails above about the eighth [7] [6].



Piano stretch. A piano tuner hears an octave as in tune when the upper note’s fundamental matches the lower note’s second partial. If that partial is sharp because of B, the upper note has to be tuned sharp too, and the effect accumulates: bass notes are tuned flat, treble notes sharp, the Railsback curve [4] [10]. The curve is empirical, not an equation, and the sources I found for its size in cents were forum posts that disagree, so I give no figure. Giordano’s JASA paper explains the stretch as the tuning that minimises sensory dissonance among the stretched partials, in agreement with Railsback [10]. Small pianos suffer most in the bass: a short case forces thicker bass strings, which have a larger B [4] [7]; a longer string is the cure but needs room.
The guitar’s plain G. UNSW notes that the solid G string of a classical guitar tunes poorly at higher frets [6]. That the steel-string plain G is the notorious one (a thick plain string whose tension and stiffness make the 12th-fret harmonic, the open note and the fretted note disagree by a few cents) is widely repeated by guitarists; I found only an anecdotal forum post for it and no measurement, so call it practitioner lore. The calculator will tell you what B the physics predicts for it.



Press Start. With the string in tune on band 1, the upper bands drift right by 600 log₂(1 + B k²) cents: you can tune a stiff string so that its fundamental is right and its upper partials sharp, or the reverse. A tuner that listens to one partial has to choose, which is the next sections’ point about who chooses.
crumbs: Out-of-Tune Overtones: Strings, Winds, Voice, Bars, Bells and Drums

title: Out-of-Tune Overtones: Strings, Winds, Voice, Bars, Bells and Drums
text:
3. Old strings versus new
Players say old strings are “dead” and hard to tune. What is established, and what is not:

Established. Strings that become inhomogeneous, for example from grease build-up, “tune successively worse”; dirty or worn strings are inharmonic and washing helps [6] [7]. Wikipedia adds that rust or dirt in the windings can raise the frequency of the higher modes [5]. UNSW’s demonstration is a small mass added at the middle of a string: it lowers the odd modes and leaves the even ones, so the tone becomes less pitched and more like a “bad quality bell” [7].
Not what I expected. Jont Allen measured B for new and old guitar strings, expecting B to change with age, and reported that what changed was the damping of the high partials, “the real source of the aging effect” (as he described it in a 1976 Catgut Acoustical Society Newsletter article, quoted second-hand on the AUDITORY list, which I could not retrieve itself) [8].
Practitioner lore, no source found. That the uneven mass of grime in the windings causes false beats (a note that wobbles) and split partials (two close frequencies where there should be one) is what players and luthiers say, and it is plausible from the mass-loading model above, but I found no measurement of it. The “old string” preset below is an illustration: every partial is stiff-sharp, scattered by a few cents and split into two components 4 to 14 cents apart, and the high ones die away faster. The sizes are made up.




Press Start and watch the rows that wobble rather than drift: a split partial is two stripes patterns slipping across each other, and that is a beat.
crumbs: Out-of-Tune Overtones: Strings, Winds, Voice, Bars, Bells and Drums

title: Out-of-Tune Overtones: Strings, Winds, Voice, Bars, Bells and Drums
section: 4. Mode locking: why bowed and blown notes stay harmonic
text:
4. Mode locking: why bowed and blown notes stay harmonic
A plucked string is a free vibration: each mode rings at its own frequency, whatever that is, so the stretch of section 2 shows up in the sound. A bowed string, a reed, the lips of a trumpeter and the vocal folds are different. They are self-sustained oscillators: the string (or air column, or vocal tract) gets pushed by something nonlinear that is itself switched by the motion. Fletcher showed in 1978 that such an oscillator can lock its modes to exact whole-number multiples of one frequency even when the resonator’s own modes are not, provided they are not too far off, their amplitudes are large and the drive is strongly nonlinear [9]. Exactly periodic motion has an exactly harmonic spectrum, and UNSW says the near-harmonic spectra of bowed strings, winds and voice are because their sound production is nonlinear [7].
So the same stiff string gives a stretched spectrum when plucked and a (nearly) harmonic one when bowed: “bowing largely removes the inharmonicity through mode locking, which comes from the stick-slip action of the bow; plucked or struck strings keep it” [7]. The limit is that locking needs the resonator to be nearly harmonic to begin with (Fletcher’s condition); a bar or a bell cannot be locked by a mallet, because a mallet only starts it.
This is the single most important fact for the question in section 9: what a player can change on a locked tone is the level of each partial, never its pitch.
crumbs: Out-of-Tune Overtones: Strings, Winds, Voice, Bars, Bells and Drums

title: Out-of-Tune Overtones: Strings, Winds, Voice, Bars, Bells and Drums
text:
5. Winds: bells, mouthpieces, tone holes
Brass. A trumpet’s air column is a long tube with a mouthpiece at one end and a flaring bell at the other, and neither is harmonic. HyperPhysics describes how the mouthpiece and bell shift the resonances toward a harmonic series: “the mouthpiece forces the upper resonances down (the mouthpiece effect) and the bell forces the lower resonances up (the bell effect)” [11]. The lowest note, the pedal note, is the fundamental of the series but “is not a resonant frequency of the air column”: players sound it by buzzing at that frequency so the harmonics above, which are resonances, produce it between them [11]. The same page says the upper harmonics are not exactly in tune with equal temperament and singles out the seventh [11].
How far off? The kth harmonic is 1200 log₂(k) cents above the first. The 7th is 3368.8¢ up, 31¢ below the equal-tempered minor seventh two octaves up; the 11th is 4151.3¢, 51¢ above one equal-tempered note and 49¢ below the next; the 13th is 4440.5¢, 41¢ sharp of A♭ and 59 flat of A. These are my arithmetic; the principle that the 7th and 11th fall “about halfway between” equal-tempered notes is in [6]. A trumpeter or horn player who needs these notes lips them into tune (see section 9) and a natural-horn player also puts a hand in the bell to change the resonances; I found no source for the hand-stopping on the pages I retrieved, so that part is general knowledge.
Clarinet. A cylinder closed at one end (the reed) and open at the other has resonances at the odd multiples only, so the clarinet’s tone has mostly odd harmonics; the register key kills the fundamental and the instrument jumps up a twelfth, the third harmonic [12]. Tone holes and the bell then bend the real resonances, and mode locking (section 4) puts the played partials back on exact multiples. I did not find a source for multiphonics, so I leave them out.



Start the Clarinet preset: bands 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9 stand still and the even rows are empty. Switch to Brass and every band stands still, with a weak first: the weak pedal note. The tuner measures against exact multiples, so it cannot show you that the 7th is 31 cents from the piano; for that, set Target tuning to something else, or look at the ladder in section 1.

title: Out-of-Tune Overtones: Strings, Winds, Voice, Bars, Bells and Drums
section: 6. Voice: harmonics are fixed, formants move
text:
6. Voice: harmonics are fixed, formants move
The vocal folds are a self-sustained oscillator, so a sung vowel on one pitch is exactly harmonic [9]. What the throat and mouth add is filtering: “A band of enhanced frequencies is called a formant”, and moving the tongue and lips moves the bands independently of the harmonic lines, which are a fixed comb [14]. The vowel is the formants; the pitch is the comb. The voice preset has exact harmonics whose levels follow two illustrative formants (F1 700 Hz and F2 1100 Hz, round numbers for an “ah”, not data) so every band stands still but their strengths ride a bump.



Change the Note to another octave while it plays: the rows that are strong change, because the same formants now sit over different harmonics. That is why a vowel changes colour as a singer goes up, and why sopranos do something about it (section 9). I did not find retrievable sources for vocal fry (subharmonics) or jitter in the pages I used, so they are not covered here.
crumbs: Out-of-Tune Overtones: Strings, Winds, Voice, Bars, Bells and Drums

title: Out-of-Tune Overtones: Strings, Winds, Voice, Bars, Bells and Drums
text:
7. Bars: marimba, xylophone, vibraphone, glockenspiel
A free uniform bar is a beam, and the beam equation gives mode frequencies that grow roughly as the square of an odd-ish integer. With the standard free-free roots 4.7300, 7.8532, 10.9956, 14.1372 (the solutions of cos x cosh x = 1), the modes are in the ratio 1 : 2.756 : 5.404 : 8.933 (my arithmetic from the roots). Stanford’s CCRMA notes give the glockenspiel’s bars as 1 : 2.76 : 5.40 : 8.90 [16], and the overtones stay unrelated to the fundamental: you hear a bright, bell-like “ting” with a pitch that is clear only because the fundamental is loud.
Larger bars are given an arch, an undercut at the middle, which lowers the fundamental far more than the overtones. Yoo and Rossing: “the middle part of each bar is undercut and as a result the 1st mode frequency is lowered as the 2nd mode frequency becomes 4 times higher than the 1st” [18]. A plain bar’s first overtone is about 17.5 semitones above the fundamental (the 2.76 ratio is 1753 cents; MMDigest says about 18 semitones) and the undercut widens it toward two octaves [17].

Marimba: modes tuned 1 : 4 : 10 [18] (patent text; makers call tuning the third mode “triple tuning” [19]). CCRMA’s notes give the marimba’s second partial at 4 but the third near 9.2 [16]: so 10 is the target, and real bars can land near it. Vibraphone bars: CCRMA gives the first overtone at about 4 [16]; one European patent for vibraphone bars regulates to 1 : 4 : 8 [18], so vibraphones are not simply 1 : 4 : 10.
Xylophone: the first overtone tuned to a twelfth, 1 : 3 [16]. The sound is dry and short, and the third partial helps the ear hear one note.
Glockenspiel, raw bar: not tuned beyond the fundamental.

I did not retrieve Rossing’s own text; where I cite Rossing (The Science of Percussion Instruments, 2000) it is through the sources that cite him [20]. The finite-element and modal work on marimba bars (Bork and colleagues, 1999, with 25 modes found below 8 kHz on one bar) is the reference for why a bar is tuned by trial and measurement rather than by one equation [19].



Compare the presets Marimba bar, Xylophone bar and Raw bar: in the first two the bands for the overtones stand still; the raw bar’s overtones slide over every band, a bar’s version of “no harmonic relation”.

title: Out-of-Tune Overtones: Strings, Winds, Voice, Bars, Bells and Drums
section: 8. Tubular chimes and church bells: pitch from partials that are not there
text:
8. Tubular chimes and church bells: pitch from partials that are not there
Chimes. For a tubular bell, modes 4, 5 and 6 “appear to determine the strike tone”, with frequencies in the ratios 9² : 11² : 13² (or 81 : 121 : 169), “close enough to the ratios 2 : 3 : 4 for the ear to consider them nearly harmonic”; the pitch you hear is an octave below mode 4, the missing “1” [21] (via Rossing 2000, pp. 67 to 69). That pitch is a virtual pitch: nothing sounds at that frequency. Mode 6 is 81 : 169 over mode 4, 4.17 against 4, so it is 72 cents sharp of the series, which the ear forgives.
Church bells. Each mode of a bell contributes one partial, with traditional names. For a well-tuned bell the table of ratios to the prime is [22] (as tabulated from Rossing 2000):

The strike note is the pitch heard when the bell is struck, “determined by three partials (the octave, upper fifth and upper octave)” and “generally close to the prime in a well-tuned bell”; it is a virtual pitch, a perceptual effect, not a radiated tone [22]. Hibbert’s study of the quantity measures it as a missing-fundamental effect and shows it can shift by fractions of a semitone, so the “an octave below the nominal” rule of Lord Rayleigh (1890) is not always exact [22].
Do bells sound minor? The research confirms the claim in the narrow sense: the tierce is a minor third above the prime, with a perfect fifth (quint) above it, so a struck bell contains a minor triad’s third; Starmer in 1902 already wrote “there are also present a minor third and perfect fifth in the first octave” [22]. A carillon page calls the tierce “somewhat melancholic” [24]. It is not that the tune is minor but that every note carries a minor third in its tone, which is why a carillon plays runs and arpeggios rather than thick chords [22]. A major-third bell has been made: after earlier failures, a Technical University of Eindhoven project and the Eijsbouts foundry produced one in 1985 (a secondary page; a 1987 paper by Lehr reports it) with an unusual shape with a bulge at the waist; carillonneurs were critical, other listeners generally positive [24].



Pick Church bell: band 1 is the hum, band 2 the prime and band 4 the nominal, all standing still. The tierce is at 2.366 times the hum, between bands, so it slides through rows 2 and 3, and the quint and upper octave sit a few cents off bands 3 and 8. Switch to Tubular chime: band 1 is the strike pitch with nothing sounding, band 2 stands still (mode 4), band 3 is 7 cents flat, and band 4 is 72 cents sharp.

title: Out-of-Tune Overtones: Strings, Winds, Voice, Bars, Bells and Drums
section: 9. Timpani: a drum that has a pitch
text:
9. Timpani: a drum that has a pitch
An ideal circular membrane has modes at the zeros of Bessel functions: relative to the lowest mode (0,1), the (1,1), (2,1), (0,2), (3,1) modes are at 1.593, 2.136, 2.295, 2.653 times it (my arithmetic from the Bessel zeros 2.405, 3.832, 5.136, 5.520, 6.380), nowhere near a harmonic series. A timpani is different. The surrounding air loads the membrane, and Packer’s 1993 Durham thesis concluded that air loading moves the modes that have only radial nodes toward a harmonic series, “creating a distinct sensation of musical pitch”, while the fundamental (0,1) is damped out [25]. Mills’s 1980 NIU thesis found that the effective mass of the air is the dominant cause of the shift [25]. In Rossing’s description the (1,1) mode carries the note and the next three radiate a fifth, an octave and a tenth above it [25], which makes the frequency ratios 2 : 3 : 4 : 5 of the modes (1,1), (2,1), (3,1), (4,1), and the pitch you hear a virtual pitch an octave below the loudest mode. (I found the 2 : 3 : 4 : 5 target stated in a Purdue dissertation abstract and via Rossing’s ratios, though not in Rossing’s text itself [25].)
Where the drum is struck changes which modes start. A strike a quarter of the way in from the rim excites the preferred modes well; that is what drummers say and what a 2022 Emory thesis found when it modelled strike positions (0.75 of the radius from the centre fitted best) [25]. Rossing’s own statement of the quarter figure was not among the pages I retrieved.



Timpani preset: band 1 is silent (the virtual pitch), bands 2 to 5 stand still. The ratios 2 : 3 : 4 : 5 are the point: they are a harmonic series with the fundamental missing, which is how a drum, and a bell, can have a pitch at all.

title: Out-of-Tune Overtones: Strings, Winds, Voice, Bars, Bells and Drums
text:
10. Gamelan and timbre-matched scales
If the instrument’s partials are not harmonic, which intervals sound smooth? William Sethares’s answer in Tuning, Timbre, Spectrum, Scale is that consonance depends on the spectrum, not only on the interval: a scale and a spectrum “are related” if the dissonance curve for the spectrum has its minima at the scale steps. The book’s gamelan chapter argues that the inharmonic spectra of gamelan instruments are related to the gamelan scales, and the preface says the same of the Thai renat [26]. The corollary for a maker: give an instrument a different set of partials and you get a different best scale. I read the book’s own pages and a secondary summary of the chapter, not the chapter itself, and I did not find the stretched-octave claim in them.

title: Out-of-Tune Overtones: Strings, Winds, Voice, Bars, Bells and Drums
section: 11. Can a player tune one overtone while performing?
text:
11. Can a player tune one overtone while performing?
Short answer: not its pitch. On a sustained, self-driven tone (a bowed string, a wind, a voice) mode locking (section 4) ties every partial to an exact multiple of the fundamental [9]. A player can change each partial’s level, not its pitch. On a plucked or struck instrument the partials can be out of tune with each other, but they were set before the performance. So a player chooses which partials are heard and lines the note up with other players’; tuning an individual partial is done at the workbench (section 12).

How players change the levels

Singers: formant tuning. The vocal-tract resonances R1, R2 are not harmonics, and a soprano whose pitch rises above her speaking R1 can tune R1 to the fundamental (and at the very top R2): louder, more even, easier, at some cost to the vowel (Joliveau, Smith & Wolfe 2004; Smith & Wolfe 2009; Henrich, Smith & Wolfe, who measured R1 and R2 of 22 singers across four vowels and found sopranos tuning R1 near f0 over part of their range) [13]. Vowels blur up high because the formants have been told to follow the pitch, not the vowel.
Overtone singers. A narrowed formant picks out one harmonic from a fixed drone. Bergevin and colleagues’ study of Tuvan throat singing reports singers shaping the tract to narrowly focus overtones near 1 to 3 kHz, by merging two formants, and argue that it is linear filtering, not a nonlinear source [15]. That the chosen harmonic is typically the 8th to 12th and the melody therefore in just intonation is the standard description of khoomei, but I did not find that figure in the paper’s pages; the melody is just because harmonics are exact multiples (section 4).
Winds and didgeridoo. Embouchure, air speed and the player’s vocal tract change which harmonics are strong. Wolfe’s didgeridoo page: the lips drive the tract “working backwards”, so the mouth shapes the output; a sung note adds more frequencies, and a fifth above the played note gives a Tartini tone an octave below [14]. I found nothing on the jaw harp in my sources.
Strings: where, how fast, how hard. Pluck or bow a string where a harmonic has a node and that harmonic is missing: touch at 1/4 of the length and you get 4f [7]; pluck at the 12th fret, the middle, and the even harmonics vanish. Bow position mostly changes the “node frequencies” in the spectrum, and bow force relative to the limits of the Schelleng diagram changes how much high partials are emphasised, with bow speed alone able to shift timbre [28]. Touched harmonics (flageolets) also work by killing the modes that have no node there. Sul ponticello and sul tasto are the same idea (bow near the bridge or over the fingerboard); I did not retrieve a source for them on their own.






What players tune instead
They tune the note, so that their partials line up with other players’.

Barbershop. The 7th of a dominant seventh is lowered to 7 : 4 (about 969¢, 31¢ under the piano’s), a harmonic seventh, so it continues the overtone series 4 : 5 : 6 : 7 of the chord. Barbershop quartets are generally expected to tune to it [27]. Hagerman and Sundberg (1980) measured singers’ accuracy in barbershop chords in STL-QPSR and found the choice of fundamental frequency extremely accurate and not dependent on vowel, but sources note their data challenge the accuracy of the 7 : 4 claim [27]; I could not confirm the “ring” or “expanded sound” explanation (partials coinciding) from a source and give it as the usual explanation, not a measurement.
Brass and string sections. In just intonation a 5 : 4 third is 13.7¢ below the piano’s, and a 3 : 2 fifth is 2.0¢ above, see tuning systems. Section players adjust until the beats between neighbouring parts’ partials stop: that is a listening procedure, not a measured result I can cite.
Natural horn and trumpet. Lipping the 7th, 11th and 13th harmonics and, on the horn, hand-stopping (section 5; no source retrieved for the hand).



Plucked and struck instruments

Guitar. Players pick which partial to tune by: the 12th-fret harmonic against the fretted 12th-fret note, the harmonic at the 5th fret against the 7th on the next string, or beats between partials. Stiffness (section 2) makes these disagree by a few cents, and UNSW notes that tuning the 4th harmonic of the E string to the 3rd of the A string gives a fourth wider than a true harmonic one, which partly offsets the equal-temperament error [6].
Piano and harp. The strings’ partials cannot be changed during a performance at all.
Timpani is the nearest to “yes”: the pedal and the strike point change the overall tuning and the balance of modes during the piece, but the modes move together [25] (a reading of the above, not a measurement).

Summary. A player chooses which partials are heard and lines them up with the other players. Tuning an individual partial is done at the workbench.

title: Out-of-Tune Overtones: Strings, Winds, Voice, Bars, Bells and Drums
text:
12. Tuning overtones in the workshop
The player’s choices end where the instrument’s partials are fixed. Makers set them. The practice instruments above are the target of each trade.
Piano tuners choose which partials to match. For an octave they match the upper note’s fundamental to the lower note’s second partial, and because that partial is sharp, the tuned scale stretches from flat bass to sharp treble: the Railsback curve [4] [10]. Which pair of partials to match (the 4th of the lower note against the 2nd of the upper, the 6th against the 3rd, and so on) is the tuner’s choice, and different choices give different stretches; I found no source that lays the choices out, so I do not rank them. Stretching is “a comparative term”, so the first note tuned, usually in the middle, is not stretched [4]. Electronic tuning devices reproduce stretched octaves rather than a simple harmonic series [5]: aural tuners listen to beat rates, electronic ones measure the piano’s B and compute a stretch. I did not retrieve sources on the commercial products’ stretch profiles, so I name none. Designers reduce B with longer bass strings and winding (section 2); the limit is the case size [4].
Marimba, xylophone and vibraphone bars are tuned by removing wood: the undercut at the centre lowers mode 1 most, and cuts elsewhere move modes 2 and 3 [18] [19]. A Curtin University thesis describes a search algorithm that finds the undercut shape needed to tune the second and third bending modes to the fundamental, using Timoshenko beam receptances [19]. Marimba makers describe tuning each mode in turn and check with a strobe tuner or spectrum analyser [19]; I found no source on the best order of cuts, so I do not claim one. The result is the 1 : 4 : 10 or 1 : 3 of section 7: try the marimba and xylophone presets in the tuner.
Church bells are tuned in a lathe by shaving metal from the inside at chosen heights, so that hum, prime, tierce, quint and nominal move separately. Hibbert’s history of Taylors: Canon Simpson wrote to the foundry in 1894 and published on true-harmonic tuning in 1895 and 1896; Taylors bought tuning forks in 1894 and installed a tuning machine in 1895, and by 1896 were making bells with hum, prime and nominal in octaves [23]. Cutting inside the shoulder can flatten a prime but cannot sharpen it much; hums could only be brought to the true octave by changing the shape, and tierces depend mainly on the soundbow shape [23]. That is why the major-third bell needed a new profile, not a new cut (section 8). Whitechapel’s practice I did not retrieve.
Tubular chimes. The pitch comes from modes 4 to 6 (section 8). I found no source for the roles of length, end plugs and caps, so I do not describe them.
Steel pans. Hansen and Rossing report the lowest three partials of a pan note usually tuned as an octave and a twelfth or double octave, with the (1,0) mode usually tuned to the octave and (0,1) to the twelfth; the fundamental is tuned by hammering from above and below, inside and outside the edge of the note area; hammering for the others is concentrated in the central and outer region; and since one note’s deformation changes the others, the tuner cycles through the notes repeatedly [29].
Gongs, gamelan and Thai instruments. Tuned by hammering or filing; gamelan sets are tuned as an ensemble (embat). I found no source for the filing or embat details here. For why a scale suits an instrument see Sethares [26].
Wind-instrument makers adjust the bore, tone-hole size, undercutting and bell flare to bring the resonances into alignment, so that the notes are in tune and mode locking is stable. HyperPhysics’ mouthpiece and bell effects (section 5) are the principle [11]; the maker-level detail (Benade, Fletcher & Rossing) was beyond what I could retrieve.
Guitar and string builders. Saddles are compensated: the string is made a little longer than the scale length, since fretting stretches it and raises the pitch; the sources I found disagree on how much is stiffness and how much stretch (one luthier’s tests showed bending stiffness had negligible effect on intonation; another source pointed to string stretch as the main factor) [30]. Gauge choice sets B and tension (calculator, section 2). Fanned frets: no source found.
What a tuner cannot fix. The strobe tuner shows you what each partial is doing, band by band. It cannot make a bell’s tierce major or a stiff string’s twelfth true: players set levels, makers set partials.

text:
Things to try

In the calculator, load the plain G (196 Hz), then raise the fret from 0 to 12. By what factor does B grow? (4.) Then switch to the wound D and compare B with the plain G.
In the ladder, pick Marimba bar then Raw bar: which partial of the raw bar is closest to a harmonic? (The fourth, 8.933, is only 13 cents flat of the 9th harmonic, by coincidence; the second is 146 cents flat of the 3rd and the third 130 sharp of the 5th.)
In the tuner, Church bell: which bands stand still? Switch to Timpani: which row has nothing in it, and which pitch do you hear?
In the pluck chart, where must you pluck so that the 3rd harmonic vanishes? (A third of the way along; check the 6th, 9th too.) Which harmonics vanish at the 12th fret?
In the tuner, Brass: band 7 stands still. What does the piano say about that note? (31¢ off the minor seventh: see section 5.)
Run the Old, dirty string next to the stiff string and say which rows wobble.

title: Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths
text:
This lesson is for a drummer who can already play a basic beat: the bass drum on 1 and 3, the snare on 2 and 4, and something steady on top. It is about the “something on top”, and about everything the hi-hat can do besides keeping time. You need a hi-hat with a pedal, a snare and a bass drum. Each step is a little harder than the one before; stay on a step until you can play it through the whole chorus without watching your hands.
How to use the page. Every step has two bars of the groove written large and the whole chorus on a drum staff. Press ▶ and the band plays it; the note that is sounding lights up in the notation. Tick Drums alone to hear the drummer without the bass and piano, and Leave out the drums to take over. The straight steps are played over four bars of F7 by the Straight-eighth rock or Acoustic strum band, and the swing steps over the 12-bar blues by the Swing band. Each step starts at its own tempo; the strip at the bottom changes the tempo, and the Feel menu changes the band. If you cannot yet play a step at its tempo, slow it down until you can.
crumbs: Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths

title: Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths
section: 0. The three sounds of the hi-hat
text:
0. The three sounds of the hi-hat
The hi-hat is two cymbals on a stand, one above the other, with a pedal that opens and closes them. That gives it three sounds you will use all through this lesson.

Closed, with the stick. The pedal is down, the cymbals are together, and you hit the top one. A short, tight “tick”. This is the hi-hat sound you hear in most rock.
Open, with the stick. You let the pedal up a little, so the cymbals are apart, and hit. The sound rings and hisses until something stops it.
Closed, with the foot. You press the pedal and the cymbals come together on their own, with no stick. A soft “chick”.

Click a button to hear each one, and the last button to hear an open note being closed.


Closed, stick


Open, stick


Closed, foot


Open, then the foot


Here is how each is written. All three are an ✕, because they are cymbals. A closed note sits above the staff. An open note is the same ✕ with a small circle over it. A note played with the foot is an ✕ below the staff, and its stem points down like the bass drum’s. Click a head to hear it.



The foot closes the cymbals, and that stops an open note. When the cymbals come together, whatever was ringing ends. So an open hi-hat rings until the next closed note or the next foot note cuts it off, whichever comes first. On this page the band’s drummer does the same: press “Open, then the foot” and listen to the open note stop dead. Hearing where an open note ends is as important as hearing where it starts.
crumbs: Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths

title: Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths
section: 1. Quarter notes on the closed hi-hat
text:
1. Quarter notes on the closed hi-hat
The plainest rock beat. The closed hi-hat plays all four beats, the bass drum plays on 1 and 3, and the snare plays on 2 and 4. Count “1, 2, 3, 4” out loud and make the hi-hat as even as the clock.



Two things at once, then three. Start with the hi-hat and the snare alone; add the bass drum when the hands are steady. The hi-hat does not slow down when the snare lands.
crumbs: Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths

title: Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths
section: 2. Eighth notes: the basic rock beat
text:
2. Eighth notes: the basic rock beat
Now the hi-hat plays twice as often, eight notes to the bar. Count “1 and 2 and 3 and 4 and”. The notes on the numbers fall with the bass drum and the snare; the notes on the “ands” fall in between. The bass drum is still on 1 and 3 and the snare on 2 and 4.



Keep the right hand moving in one smooth, even stroke, down on the beat and down on the “and”, and let the snare and the bass drum fit themselves around it.
crumbs: Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths

title: Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths
text:
3. Accents
The same eighth notes, but now they are not all the same. Lean on the notes that fall on the beats and play the “ands” lightly. The usual way to get this is to hit the beats with the shoulder of the stick, on the edge of the hi-hat, and the “ands” with the tip, on top of it; the beats come out louder and brighter, the “ands” softer. The groove starts to breathe.
In the notation, an accent mark (>) is written over each note that is meant to be louder than its neighbours. Look for the mark over the beats in the staff below; the “ands” have none.



Listen with Drums alone. Then play it on a practice pad and try making the difference between the two kinds of note smaller and larger.
crumbs: Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths

title: Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths
text:
4. The off-beats alone
Take the hi-hat off the beats and play it only on the “ands”: and of 1, and of 2, and of 3, and of 4. The bass drum plays on every beat, and the snare is still on 2 and 4. The beats are now played by the feet and the left hand, and the right hand plays in the gaps.



Say “1 and 2 and 3 and 4 and” out loud, and tap your foot on the numbers. The hi-hat sits on the words you say between the taps.
crumbs: Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths

title: Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths
text:
5. Opening the hi-hat
Go back to the eighth notes of step 2, and open the hi-hat once: on the and of 4, the last note of the bar. Open it as you hit, let it ring through the end of the bar, and close it on the 1 of the next bar, with the stick and the foot together. Because the cymbals come together, the open note stops right where beat 1 starts.



The open note is written with the small circle. The foot note under the staff, on beat 1 of each bar, is the pedal closing the cymbals. Play it once with the stick alone and once with the foot as well, and listen for the difference.
crumbs: Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths

title: Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths
section: 6. Open on every off-beat: four on the floor
text:
6. Open on every off-beat: four on the floor
The groove of a dance floor. The bass drum plays on every beat, the snare on 2 and 4, and the hi-hat plays closed on the beats and open on every “and”. Each closed note on the next beat shuts the open one before it, so you hear a “tss-tick, tss-tick” pattern. Your foot has to lift the pedal for each “and” and press it down again for each beat.



This is the same groove as “Four on the floor” in the Drums menu of the Backing Track, with the clap taken off so that you can hear the hi-hat by itself.
crumbs: Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths

title: Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths
text:
7. Sixteenth notes with one hand
At a slow tempo the hi-hat can play four notes to every beat: sixteenths. Count “1 e and a 2 e and a 3 e and a 4 e and a”. One hand plays them all, sixteen to the bar. Play the beats a little stronger than the rest. The bass drum is on 1 and 3, the snare on 2 and 4.



Start very slowly. A slow tempo is the whole point of this step: you are learning to keep sixteen even notes going while the other hand and both feet do something else. Speed up by a few beats a minute at a time.
crumbs: Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths

title: Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths
text:
8. Sixteenth notes with two hands
Now use both hands on the hi-hat, right, left, right, left on the four notes of a beat. Both hands play on the hi-hat. On beats 2 and 4 the right hand has a different job: it comes off the hi-hat to play the snare. So the hi-hat is silent on those two notes, and you play fourteen hi-hat notes to the bar instead of sixteen.



The gap in the hi-hat on 2 and 4 is where the snare sits. Listen for it: the left hand keeps the sixteenths going without a break, and the snare lands in the space the right hand leaves.
crumbs: Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths

title: Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths
text:
9. The foot alone
Now the hi-hat’s foot, which keeps time in a different way. First the jazz setting: time is played on the ride cymbal, and the hi-hat foot closes the cymbals on 2 and 4. The foot is the “chick” that goes with the ride pattern.



Next, a rock beat played on the ride cymbal, with eighth notes on the ride, the bass drum on 1 and 3 and the snare on 2 and 4, and the foot closing the hi-hat on all four beats. The right hand is on the ride cymbal, so the hi-hat is played by the foot alone. Count “1, 2, 3, 4” with your foot first, then add the rest.
crumbs: Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths

title: Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths
text:
10. The swing hi-hat
The ride pattern of swing time, played on the hi-hat itself. The pattern is the same as on the ride: a note on each beat, with a skip note after beats 2 and 4. The cymbals are open on 1 and 3, so they ring, and closed on 2 and 4, where the foot closes them with the stick. The skip notes after 2 and 4 are closed. The eighths are swung: the first is long and the second short.



The foot notes on 2 and 4 under the staff are what stop the open notes, and so make the “tss-chick” of swing time. Listen with Drums alone, and notice where the open notes end.
crumbs: Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths

title: Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths
text:
Where to go next

Play step 2 or 3 with the drums left out and keep the form of the vamp for ten choruses.
For the beat that goes with the 12-bar blues, the ride pattern and the shuffle, go to Blues for Drums.
Tools → Backing Track has every groove on this page in its Drums menu, under the names that start “Hi-hat”. The Cymbal menu has “Closed hi-hat”, which puts the hi-hat in place of the ride in the other grooves.

title: Tuning 3: Tuners and Their Limits
text: A tuner is the right tool for a loud stage, a noisy room, or a quick check. It is the wrong tool for learning to play in tune, because it only answers one question (is this one note at this pitch?) and music asks many. This lesson is about what a tuner does well, where it misleads, and how to keep your ear in charge. Before this: Tuning 1 and Tuning 2.

title: Tuning 3: Tuners and Their Limits
text:
1. Kinds of tuner









Kind
How it hears
Strengths
Weaknesses




App, microphone
the air
free, always with you
hears the room too; low strings and noise confuse it


Clip-on
vibration of the headstock
works on a loud stage
a cheap one reads ±3 cents or worse; can be fooled by sympathetic strings


Pedal / cable
the pickup signal

Strobe

The site’s own strobe is in the top bar, and explained in How a strobe tuner works. Try it on a string here, or listen to the page’s own made-up string with demo:

title: Tuning 3: Tuners and Their Limits
text:
2. Why the reading jumps
When you pick a string hard, it goes sharp for a moment: it’s stretched further than usual, and the attack is noisy. Then it settles, and slowly goes a little flat as it dies. So: pick at your normal strength, ignore the first half second, read the settled note. Many beginners chase the attack and end up flat.

title: Tuning 3: Tuners and Their Limits
section: 3. In tune on the tuner, out of tune in the chord
text:
3. In tune on the tuner, out of tune in the chord
The tuner measured the open strings. You play fretted notes, and they can be off for reasons no tuner on an open string can see:

Finger pressure. Pressing hard stretches the string sharp, by 5–10 cents on a high fret. Fret just behind the fret wire, with only as much pressure as makes the note clean.
Intonation. If the bridge saddles are set wrong, fretted notes up the neck go sharp or flat. The Setup Check measures it: the 12th-fret harmonic against the 12th-fret note.
Old strings play sharp up the neck. Change them.
High action or a high nut stretches every fretted note sharp, most near the nut.
Equal temperament itself. A G chord’s major third (B) is 14 cents wider than a pure one. The tuner calls that in tune; your ear may hear it as a little bright. This is why a guitar tuned perfectly by a tuner can still sound “off” in one chord and fine in another.

title: Tuning 3: Tuners and Their Limits
text:
4. Using a tuner well

Ear first. Tune by ear, then look. In the tuning tool, tick Ear first: the reading stays blurred until you say flat, in tune or sharp. Keep score.
Listen, then stop listening. Turn the microphone off, play a chord, decide; turn it on to check.
End with a chord. If the chords you’re about to play sound wrong, trust that over the needle.
Check between songs. By ear: play the open strings against a chord, fix the one that’s moved.

The tuner is a ruler; your ear is the judge.

title: Tuning 1: Your Ear Is the Tuner
text:
You can buy a tuner for the price of a sandwich, so why learn to tune by ear? Because playing in tune is something you hear, not something you see. A string drifts during a song, a singer goes a little flat, the band’s keyboard is tuned slightly high: a screen can’t fix any of that for you, and your ear can. Tuning is the best ear training a guitarist gets, and you do it every time you pick the guitar up. This lesson and the next two compare the ways of tuning, and what each is good and bad at. Practise them in the tuning tool.
Words. Strings are numbered 6 (thickest) to 1 (thinnest). Flat means too low, sharp too high. A cent is a hundredth of a half step (one fret): most people can’t hear 5 cents on one note alone, but they can hear it easily as beating between two notes.
crumbs: Tuning 1: Your Ear Is the Tuner

title: Tuning 1: Your Ear Is the Tuner
text:
1. Matching a reference
The simplest method: something plays the right note (a piano, a tuning fork, an app, the tuning tool’s Play reference), and you make the string match.

Listen to the reference. Hum it.
Pick the open string. Is it higher or lower than what you hummed? Say it out loud.
Turn the peg while the string rings, a little at a time.








Strengths
Weaknesses




Needs nothing but a reference; works in any tuning
A note heard one after another is hard to judge closer than about 10–20 cents


Trains the most important skill: is it higher or lower?
Low strings are harder to hear than high ones


Works with any reference, including a bandmate’s note
You need a reference that is itself in tune
crumbs: Tuning 1: Your Ear Is the Tuner

title: Tuning 1: Your Ear Is the Tuner
section: 2. Beats: the wobble you tune by
text:
2. Beats: the wobble you tune by
Play two notes that are nearly the same and you hear a slow wah-wah-wah. That’s beating: the two waves slide in and out of step. The beat rate is the difference between the two frequencies: notes at 110 and 111 Hz beat once a second, 110 and 113 three times. So the beats tell you how far off you are, and they slow down as you get closer. In tune, they stop. This is far more precise than comparing notes one after another, and it’s what every method in these lessons relies on.
Hear it: the widget below plays two notes. Pick P8 (an octave) or P5, and switch between just (whole-number ratios, no beating) and equal (the guitar’s frets, a slow beat).



Tune up to the note. If you’re sharp, go below and come back up. The gear in the tuning peg then holds against the string’s pull, and the string stays put.
crumbs: Tuning 1: Your Ear Is the Tuner

title: Tuning 1: Your Ear Is the Tuner
text:
3. Tuning to a drone
A drone is a note that keeps sounding. Tune a string against it and you hear the beating the whole time, so you can turn the peg and listen at once. The drone on this site (the Drone button in the top bar, or the one below) holds a note and its fifth; the tuning tool puts one on each string’s note.






Strengths
Weaknesses




The ear hears beats continuously: very precise
A drone on E and B tunes those strings best; the others want their own drone note


Trains hearing in tune against something, the way you play with a band
A pure fifth in the drone isn’t quite the guitar’s fifth (2 cents): see Tuning 2


No microphone, works in a noisy room with headphones
Needs a device



Listening and not listening. Practise both: tune to the drone, then turn the drone off and play a chord. Does it still sound right? Then turn it back on and check. The tool’s Listening switch does the same with the microphone: tune with it off, and only then turn it on to see how close your ear got.
crumbs: Tuning 1: Your Ear Is the Tuner

title: Tuning 1: Your Ear Is the Tuner
text:
4. A practice plan

Every day, tune by ear first, then check with the microphone in the tool, with Ear first ticked: guess flat, in tune or sharp before the reading shows. Watch your score improve.
Detune one string on purpose (a quarter turn) and find it by strumming a chord.
Sing each open string’s note before you play it.

Next: Tuning 2: fifth-fret, harmonics and octaves.

title: Harmonics on Guitar: Natural, Tapped and Pinch
text:
A harmonic is the bell-like note you get when you touch a string lightly at the right spot instead of pressing it to the fret. The finger does not shorten the string: it stops the string from moving at that one point, so only the vibrations that already have a still point there can carry on. What is left is one of the string’s overtones, on its own. This lesson starts with the natural harmonics on open strings, explains where they are and what pitch each one gives, and then moves on to tapped, harp and pinch harmonics. Click a section’s heading to fold it; the “On this page” bar at the right jumps to any section.
How to use the page. Strings are numbered 1 (high E) to 6 (low E); tab has one line a string, high E on top. Start the volume low: the playable string in section 2 makes pure, ringing tones.
crumbs: Harmonics on Guitar: Natural, Tapped and Pinch

title: Harmonics on Guitar: Natural, Tapped and Pinch
text:
1. What a harmonic is
A plucked string does not only swing as one long arc. At the same time it vibrates in 2 halves, in 3 thirds, in 4 quarters, and so on. Each of these patterns sounds a pitch: the whole string gives the note you hear (the fundamental), halves give twice its frequency, thirds three times, quarters four times. Together they are the harmonic series, and their mix is what makes a guitar sound like a guitar.
Each pattern has nodes, points that stay still, and between them antinodes, where the string swings most. Halves have a node in the middle. Thirds have nodes at one third and two thirds of the way along. When you touch the string lightly at one third of its length, every pattern that needs that point to move is choked off; the patterns that have a node there (thirds, sixths, ninths …) keep ringing. You hear the lowest of them: the 3rd harmonic.
Here is the series on the low E string (E2). Click a note to hear it; the numbers under the notes say how many parts the string is divided into, the numbers above how many cents each is from the nearest piano note.



The 2nd, 3rd, 4th and 6th harmonics are octaves and fifths of the open string, and nearly match the piano. The 5th harmonic is a major third, about 14 cents flat of the tempered G♯. That matters when you use harmonics to tune (section 8).
crumbs: Harmonics on Guitar: Natural, Tapped and Pinch

title: Harmonics on Guitar: Natural, Tapped and Pinch
text:
2. Where the natural harmonics are
The nut and the saddle are the string’s two ends, so the 12th fret, halfway, is the node for halves. Frets get closer together as they go up because each one shortens the string by the same ratio, so the other simple fractions land on or near particular frets:

A few things follow from the fractions:

One pitch, several places. Every node of a pattern gives the same note. The 7th and 19th frets give the same B; the 4th, 9th and 16th give the same G♯. The 7th fret harmonic and the 12th fret harmonic are not the same octave: thirds are higher than halves.
The higher the harmonic, the narrower the spot. The 12th is easy; the 5th-of-the-string spots near the 4th and 9th frets need you to be within a millimetre or two, a little toward the nut, and they ring quieter.
The spot is over the fret wire, not between frets where you would fret a note, because that is where the fractions land: at the 12th, 7th and 5th the node is right above the metal.

Click a node to hear the harmonic it leaves ringing; the line shows the pattern of the string for that harmonic, with its still points.

title: Harmonics on Guitar: Natural, Tapped and Pinch
text:
3. Playing natural harmonics

Touch, don’t press. Lay the fleshy pad of a fretting finger on the string directly above the fret wire (12th to begin with). Just touching: the string should not reach the fret. Pressing is the most common reason a harmonic comes out as a dead thud.
Pick near the bridge. A firm pick stroke two or three fingers’ width from the saddle brings out the high patterns more than picking over the soundhole or neck pickup does.
Lift. Take the touching finger off the string straight after the pick stroke. The harmonic then rings on its own for as long as an open string would. Leave it on and the harmonic stays thin and dies.
Go in order. Get the 12th clean on all six strings, then the 7th, then the 5th, then the spots just behind the 4th and 9th, then just past the 3rd.

Several strings at once. Lay one finger flat across all six strings above the 12th fret and strum, then lift: a chord of harmonics, the open-string chord an octave up. The same across the 5th and 7th frets gives the bell chords in many intros.

On electric guitar, the bridge pickup and a little gain make harmonics jump out. On acoustic, pick harder than you think, near the bridge.
crumbs: Harmonics on Guitar: Natural, Tapped and Pinch

title: Harmonics on Guitar: Natural, Tapped and Pinch
text:
4. Tapped and artificial harmonics
Natural harmonics only give the open strings’ overtones. To get harmonics of any note, fret the note, and the halfway point moves: it is now 12 frets above the fretted note. Fret the 3rd fret, and the node is over the 15th.

Tapped harmonic (T.H.): fret the note with the left hand, then strike the string sharply with a right-hand finger on the fret wire 12 frets higher and bounce straight off. The tap both starts the string and stops it at the node. Also works 5 and 7 frets above the fretted note (the 4th and 3rd harmonics), and over a whole chord shape: hold a chord at the 2nd fret, tap across the 14th.
Artificial harmonic (A.H.), picked: fret the note, touch the node (12 frets up) lightly with the right-hand index finger, and pluck the string with the thumb or a pick held between thumb and middle finger, behind the touching finger toward the bridge. Lift the index just after.
Harp harmonics: the same artificial harmonic, alternated with ordinary plucked notes from the ring finger, on neighbouring strings, so harmonics and normal notes overlap like a harp. Fret a chord, then: thumb plucks string 4 while the index touches 12 frets up, ring finger plucks string 3 normally, then the same on strings 3 and 2 … Go slowly; the hand shape takes weeks.
crumbs: Harmonics on Guitar: Natural, Tapped and Pinch

title: Harmonics on Guitar: Natural, Tapped and Pinch
text:
5. Pinch harmonics
The squeal in rock and metal solos is a pinch harmonic (P.H., also “squealie”). It is an artificial harmonic made with the pick hand alone: the pick starts the string, and the edge of the thumb grazes it a split second later and stops it at a node.
The grip. Hold the pick so that only a little of the tip sticks out past the thumb, a couple of millimetres. Pick downward, and roll the thumb’s edge onto the string straight after the pick, as if the stroke ends with the thumb brushing it. Graze, don’t damp: touch and let go. Push the stroke through the string, like an ordinary downstroke, a little harder than usual.
Finding the spot. The harmonic only comes out where the thumb lands on a node, so slide the picking hand slowly from the neck pickup toward the bridge, picking all the way, and listen. You will hear different harmonics pop out in different places; the loud ones are usually between the pickups and just in front of the bridge pickup.
Why the spot moves. The node is a fraction of the length of the string that is vibrating, which runs from the fretted note to the saddle. Fret higher up and that length is shorter, so every node moves toward the bridge with it. On the 5th fret of the G string, the node one quarter of the way from the bridge is somewhere other than on the 12th fret. So for each note you play, the sweet spot is in a slightly different place: practise by playing one note and walking the hand, then a note five frets higher and finding the spot again.
Sound. Pinch harmonics are easiest with the bridge pickup and gain (overdrive or distortion), which bring up the quiet high overtone. On a clean amp or acoustic they still work, quietly. Add vibrato straight after the squeal, or pick the note and bend it up (see String Bends on Guitar): the harmonic bends with it, a whole step on the fretted note being a whole step on the harmonic.

title: Harmonics on Guitar: Natural, Tapped and Pinch
text:
7. Common faults and fixes







Fault
Fix




A dull thud, no ring
You are pressing. Touch so lightly the string could slide under the finger.


The normal note sounds, not the harmonic
You are between frets. Move the finger to sit right above the fret wire.


It rings for a moment, then dies
Lift the touching finger straight after picking.


The 4th/9th/3rd fret ones won’t come
They are narrow and just off the fret (see the table in section 2); creep the finger toward the nut a millimetre at a time, and pick nearer the bridge.


Neighbouring strings ring too
Mute them with the touching finger’s underside and the picking palm.


Pinch harmonics: just a normal note
Less pick showing; make the thumb actually touch the string; move the hand, the spot is small.


Pinch harmonics: a choked click
The thumb stays on the string. Graze and let go.


Pinch harmonics work on one note but not the next
The spot moved with the fretted note (section 5): walk the hand again.


Tapped harmonics buzz
Tap on the fret wire, not behind it, and bounce off at once.
crumbs: Harmonics on Guitar: Natural, Tapped and Pinch

title: Harmonics on Guitar: Natural, Tapped and Pinch
text:
8. Harmonics for tuning
Because the 5th fret harmonic of one string and the 7th fret harmonic of the next one up are (on most string pairs) the same pitch, sounding them together lets you hear beats, a slow wah-wah, when they disagree, and tune until it stops. Two cautions: the 7th fret harmonic is a pure fifth, 2 cents wider than the tempered one, so tuning a whole guitar this way stacks small errors; and the G-to-B pair is a third and doesn’t work this way. Guitar tuning methods goes through this and other methods, and the Guitar tuning tool has a strobe to check each string.
crumbs: Harmonics on Guitar: Natural, Tapped and Pinch

title: Harmonics on Guitar: Natural, Tapped and Pinch
text:
9. Practice, step by step
Five to ten minutes a day, in this order. Move on when the step rings clean nine times in ten.

12th fret, each string. Touch, pick near the bridge, lift. Six strings, three times each.
12th, 7th, 5th on one string. Play them in turn and hear that the 7th is higher than the 12th and the 5th higher again. Check against section 2.
The narrow ones. Behind the 4th, behind the 9th, past the 3rd, on the low E. Compare the 4th and 9th: same note.
Chords of harmonics. One finger flat across the 12th, then the 7th, then the 5th, strum and lift. Then a little tune: 12th on strings 3, 2, 1, then 7th on strings 3, 2, 1, then 5th.
Tapped harmonics. Fret an E major shape at the open strings and tap the 12th fret wire across all strings; then a barre at the 3rd fret, tapping the 15th.
Artificial harmonics. One note at a time: fret, touch 12 frets up with the index, pluck with the thumb. Then a slow C major scale on one string this way.
Pinch harmonic hunt. Bridge pickup, some gain. Fret string 3 at the 7th fret; walk the pick hand from neck to bridge until it squeals. Then fret the 9th and find the new spot.
Pinch with vibrato and a bend. Squeal on string 3 fret 7, add vibrato; then squeal and bend a whole step to the pitch of fret 9.
In a phrase. Play a lick you know and end it on a pinch harmonic with vibrato.

Where to go next: String Bends on Guitar for the bends under a pinch harmonic, Tuning systems for why the 5th harmonic is flat of the piano, and Guitar tuning methods.

title: String Bends on Guitar: Bending in Tune
text:
A bend pushes or pulls a fretted string sideways across the fret so that its pitch rises smoothly, with no second pick stroke. It is the guitar’s version of a singer sliding up to a note, and it is the main way a guitarist reaches the notes between the piano’s keys. This lesson builds the technique first, then the habit of bending to a target pitch, then the variants, and then where bends go in a blues in A. Click a section’s heading to fold it; the “On this page” bar at the right jumps to any section and opens it.
How to use the page. Fingers are numbered 1 (index) to 4 (little finger). Strings are numbered 1 (high E) to 6 (low E). Tablature has one line a string, the high E on top, and a number for the fret. The Drone button in the top bar is the same drone as the one in section 2: keep it sounding on A while you practise, because a bend is only right or wrong against something that stays still. Start the volume low.
crumbs: String Bends on Guitar: Bending in Tune

title: String Bends on Guitar: Bending in Tune
text:
1. The mechanics
Support fingers. One finger alone cannot move a string a whole step. Bend with the ring finger (3) and put the middle (2) and, if you can, the index (1) on the same string, one fret behind it, so that three fingers push together. The fingers behind are not decoration: they share the load and keep the string from sliding off the fret. For a small bend (a half step) with the middle finger, the index finger backs it. When the bend is on the note you are fretting with the little finger, the ring finger backs it.
Push or pull? The string goes across the neck, so it has to go one way or the other.

On the thin strings (1 to 3, the high E, B and G) the usual way is to push the string up toward the ceiling, away from the palm.
On the thick strings (4 to 6) the usual way is to pull it down toward the floor, so that the string does not run off the edge of the fretboard and the pull is not blocked by the neighbouring string. Many players use this for the G string too, and a few bend the B string down. Either direction gives the same note: use whichever your hand finds steadier.

It is the wrist. The bend comes from rotating the forearm and wrist, as if turning a doorknob, and not from squeezing the fingers sideways. The fingers keep their shape and the hand turns about the line of the forearm. Beginners squeeze and the bend stalls at a half step, and the hand tires.
Thumb. Two usual ways, and both are right:

Thumb over the top of the neck, anchored on the low E string. The thumb damps that string and gives the hand a pivot to turn about. This suits push bends.
Thumb behind the neck, as in classical position. It gives more leverage for a pull bend.

Mute the other strings. A bend gets sloppy from strings that were not meant to ring. The fingertip that frets the bend mutes the string below it, the underside of the same finger mutes the one above, and the picking hand’s palm rests lightly at the bridge. The strings you do not bend ring only if you let them.
String gauge and place on the neck. Lighter strings (for example a set of .009 to .042) bend more easily than heavier ones (.011 and up), and are easier on beginners’ fingertips. Heavier strings give a fatter sound and more tension to play against. A longer scale length makes strings tighter, and so does a lower tuning, so a given set bends differently on different guitars. Within one guitar: the frets near the 5th to 12th are friendliest for most players. Near the nut a bend stretches more string and takes more push, and above the 12th the string is short and stiff, so the same push moves it less and the last bit of the bend is hard to hold. Thick strings take the most effort. This is why a first bend is usually on the G or B string at the 7th or 8th fret.
Practice: no pitch goals yet. Fret the G string at the 7th fret (D) with the ring finger, and put the middle and index fingers on frets 6 and 5 of the same string. Rotate the wrist slowly until the pitch has gone up as far as it will, then let it down slowly. Do ten. The bent note should be clean, with no buzzing from the string touching the next fret or ringing neighbours.
crumbs: String Bends on Guitar: Bending in Tune

title: String Bends on Guitar: Bending in Tune
text:
2. Bending in tune
A bend is a slide with no frets in it, so nothing tells you when you have arrived. The fix is to hear the target first. Before you bend, fret the target note (the note a half step, whole step or more above where you start), play it, then go back, play the lower note and bend until it matches. After a few days your ear carries the target and you can skip the check.

The bendboard below shows a bend three ways at once, and lets you try it. On the left is the neck as you see it in tab (the high E on top, the frets running to the right), with box 1 in grey. The filled dot is your finger and the string curves away from it toward the next string by as much as you bend. The dashed dot is the fret that sounds the target pitch, and the arrow between them carries the tab mark: ¼, ½, full, 1½, PB (pre-bend) or R (release). The gauge beside it counts the bend in cents, with ticks at 100, 200 and 300 and the blue-note zones shaded (around 316 to 350 cents above the root for the blue third, and around 583 for the blue fifth). The trace underneath is the pitch against time, with the target shape in dark grey.

Drag the dot toward the next string (or use the Bend slider, or the arrow keys on the dot): a tone glides with it, and the readout says how many cents you are off the target.
Start and Target play the two notes, and Play the shape bends the note for you along the dark line (pick bend, bend and release, pre-bend and release, or vibrato on a bend).
Listen and compare opens the microphone (only when you press it) and draws the pitch of your own guitar over the target: play the first note when the line begins. It needs the guitar in standard tuning and one note at a time.
MIDI wheel lets the pitch wheel or the mod wheel of a MIDI keyboard do the bending.

Choose a bend from box 1 (each one is a note from section 5, with its string and fret). Target, then bend is the practice routine in sound. A bend that is a few cents off beats against the target and against the drone.

The drone, tuned to A and with the E above it:



On the gauge and the trace, a bend that lands inside a blue zone is the blue note: it is neither the piano’s minor third nor its major third. Compare the solid orange line (you) with the dark line (the target): where they drift apart, the sound beats against the target.
Check against something that does not move. The drone is one. Another is the same note on another string: to bend the G string’s 7th fret (D) up a whole step to E, fret the E on the B string (5th fret), pick it, then bend and compare. Hearing two strings settle into one pitch is the most reliable test you have.
Hold the bend with a strobe. A bend that is nearly right looks right on a needle. A strobe shows each partial of the string, and a bend you hold still at the target makes its stripes stand still. Set it to the target note (here E, the pitch of the 9th fret on the G string), press Start, bend, and hold: stripes drifting right mean you are sharp, left flat, and the speed is how far. Use it for long held bends and for the end of a bend with vibrato. Wait a moment after the pick strikes: the attack is ignored.

Tune the guitar first. A bend can’t be in tune with a guitar that isn’t.
crumbs: String Bends on Guitar: Bending in Tune

title: String Bends on Guitar: Bending in Tune
text:
3. Variants
All of these start with the same push. What changes is when the bend happens.

Bend and release. Pick the lower note, bend up to the target, then let the string back down to the start while the note is still sounding. Written 7b9r7.
Pre-bend, and pre-bend and release. Bend the string silently, before the pick strikes it, to the target pitch. Strike it, and then (if it is a pre-bend and release) let it back down. The ear never hears the lower note first. Written PB and PB R. This is harder than it sounds because there is no sliding to correct with: the bend is right or wrong before you hear it. Check against the target note as in section 2.
Unison bend. Two strings play the same pitch: fret the lower string (for example the G string at the 7th fret, D) and, on the next string up, the note a whole step higher (the B string at the 5th fret, E), pick both, and bend the lower one up to meet the one that stays still. You hear one note thicken, then split and merge. A slightly out-of-tune unison beats, which is the sound of a bend that is not quite there.
Double-stop bend. Two strings sound at once, and one or both are bent. With a double stop on strings 2 and 3, bend them together a whole step, or bend one and keep the other still. Listen for it in rock-and-roll and blues lead playing.
Oblique bend. One string is held still (often an open string, or a high fretted note) while another is bent against it. The distance between the two changes while one note does not.
Vibrato on a bend. Reach the target, then wobble the pitch a little below and up to it (and not above it) with small quick rotations of the wrist. A bend with vibrato is how most guitarists end a held note. Keep the target as the top of the wobble.
Quarter-tone bends, the “curl”. A tiny bend, about half a fret. It is not meant to arrive anywhere on the piano. See section 5.

title: String Bends on Guitar: Bending in Tune
text:
5. Bends in the blues
The minor pentatonic scale on the 5th fret (“box 1”) in A is the first place most guitarists use bends. The scale below is written on a staff in A (with the notes’ names); press ▶ Play to hear it, and use the table beneath for the strings and frets.



Box 1 in A, with the string and fret where each note is (string 1 is the high E). Every string has two notes in the box, at the 5th fret and at the 7th or 8th:

1 (root)

♭3

4

♭7
