Bends that blues players reach for early (strings and frets as in the table; the target of each bend is a pitch you can also fret one or two frets up):

4 to 5, a whole step. D to E. On string 3 (G), fret 7 (D), bend to E (the pitch of fret 9). This is a favourite because the 5 is the strongest note against the I chord, and the 4 is the weakest, so the bend is a movement from tension to rest. In tab: G|--7b9--.
♭7 to root, a whole step. G to A. On string 2 (B), fret 8 (G), bend a whole step to A (the pitch of fret 10). The ♭7 pulls towards the root the way it does in the dominant chord. In tab: B|--8b10--.
♭3 up toward the major 3. C toward C♯. On string 1 (high E), fret 8 (or string 3, fret 5), bend a little, about a quarter-tone. The note is not C and not C♯. This is the blue third, between the minor third of the scale and the major third of the A7 chord sounding under it. In tab: a 1/4 over the arrow, not a number of frets.
5 up a step and a half. E up to G, the ♭7. On string 2 (B), fret 5, bend three frets’ worth, to the pitch of fret 8. This is the 1½-step bend of section 2, and takes all three fingers. In tab: B|--5b8--.
♭5 bends. The blues scale adds ♭5 (E♭ in A). On string 3, fret 8 (E♭), bend a half step to E, from the ♭5 to the 5. In tab: G|--8b9--. Likewise a half-step bend from 4 (D, fret 7) to ♭5 (E♭, fret 8): G|--7b8--.

Practise each of them against the A drone from section 2: the whole-step bends of D and G should land on notes (E and A) that are in the drone, so that you hear them lock.

Between the piano’s notes
A piano or a fretted guitar plays the third as either the minor third (300 cents above the root) or the major third (400). The blues third is neither. It sits in the middle, near 350 cents, which is the region of a neutral third. Measurements of recorded blues singing and playing show this. Cutting (2019, Empirical Musicology Review) found clusters of blue-note pitches near 319, 583 and 1038 cents above the tonic, in between the equal-tempered notes at 300 and 400, 500 and 600, and 1000 and 1100. A guitar with frets can’t play those notes on a fretted string. A bend can. This is why the bends in the box are not “mistakes to be corrected”: they are the way the guitar reaches notes the frets leave out.
Hear it in the tool below, with the A drone sounding if you like. Each button plays A (220 Hz) with a second note above it: the minor third, a note 319 cents up (the first of Cutting’s clusters), the neutral third at 350, and the major third. The last button slides from the minor third to the major third; listen for where it stops sounding like either. None of the notes between the minor and major third has a fret.

  Minor third, neutral third, major third
  
    Minor third, 300 cents (C)
    Blue third, 319 cents
    Neutral third, 350 cents
    Major third, 400 cents (C♯)
    Slide from 300 to 400
  
  A220 plus the interval above it, on a sine tone.

Listen to. Pick one phrase from each of these players’ recordings and try to copy its bend.

B.B. King, “The Thrill Is Gone” (1969): the vibrato that ends his phrases, and bends that sing like a voice.
Albert King, “Born Under a Bad Sign” (1967): long, wide bends on the high strings.
Freddie King, “Hide Away” (instrumental, early 1960s): bends inside a driving shuffle.
Stevie Ray Vaughan, “Pride and Joy” and “Texas Flood” (both from the early 1980s): big bends and a heavy touch.

These are pointers for your ears. Check the recordings before repeating any detail about them.

title: String Bends on Guitar: Bending in Tune
text:
6. Practice, step by step
Spend a few minutes on each step, slowly. Do not move on until the previous step is clean three times in a row. Keep the A drone going.

No pitch. Section 1’s practice: ten slow bends with three fingers, then ten releases.
Half step. Fret the target (G string fret 8, E♭), then the start (fret 7, D). Bend until they match. Repeat 10 times; switch to the B string, fret 8 to 9.
Whole step. String 3 fret 7 to the pitch of fret 9. Fret fret 9 first, play it, play fret 7, bend. Aim for the drone’s E.
Whole step, no check. Hear the target in your head, bend, then check with the fretted note afterwards.
Whole step with release. Bend, hold for four slow beats, release to the start without letting the note go sharp or flat on the way down.
Pre-bend and release. Bend silently, pick, release. Check the pitch of the pre-bend against the fretted target before you pick.
Step and a half. String 2: fret 5 to the pitch of fret 8. Use all three fingers.
Vibrato on the bend. Bend to the target, hold it, and add a small wobble that does not drop below the start.
The curl. On string 1 fret 8, bend a little, to between C and C♯, listening for the point where it sounds neither minor nor major. Compare with the neutral third button.
In a phrase. Play four bars over a 12-bar blues in A (the band in Blues for Guitar can play the chords in A) using only the bends 4 to 5 and ♭7 to the root, resting between them.

Where to go next: Hammer-ons and pull-offs for the other ways of changing pitch without picking, Blues for Guitar for the chords under the solo, and Tuning systems for why a pure interval and a piano’s interval are not the same.

title: Gear 5: Setting Up, Packing Down and Your Ears
text: Good habits that make rehearsals start on time, keep the gear working, and keep your hearing for life.

title: Gear 5: Setting Up, Packing Down and Your Ears
text:
Before you arrive

A stage plot: a simple drawing of where everyone stands, what they need (DI, mic, power, monitor).
An input list: channel 1 kick, 2 snare, … vocals. The sound person will love you.
Pack: instrument, cables, spares (Gear 2), tuner, capo or reeds or rosin, power supply, music, water, earplugs.
crumbs: Gear 5: Setting Up, Packing Down and Your Ears

title: Gear 5: Setting Up, Packing Down and Your Ears
text:
Setting up

Big things first: drums and amps in position, then keyboards and stands, then cables.
Power to each position; run cables along the edges, taped down across walkways.
Connect, then switch on in order: sources first, amps and speakers last (Gear 1).
Tune (the strobe tuner) before the sound check, then again before you start.
Sound check (Gear 3).
crumbs: Gear 5: Setting Up, Packing Down and Your Ears

title: Gear 5: Setting Up, Packing Down and Your Ears
text:
Rehearsal etiquette

Don’t noodle while someone else is talking or sound checking.
Ask before touching someone else’s gear or settings.
Keep stage volume down; turn the amp toward yourself.
Mute or turn down before unplugging.
crumbs: Gear 5: Setting Up, Packing Down and Your Ears

title: Gear 5: Setting Up, Packing Down and Your Ears
text:
Packing down

Amps and speakers off first, then everything else.
Unplug by the plug; coil over-under, tie, put in the cable bag.
Instruments into cases first, so they don’t get knocked over.
Stands down, knobs tightened so parts don’t fall off.
A last walk round: adaptors, pedals, phone chargers and music left behind are the commonest losses.
Report anything broken. Tape “BAD” on it.
crumbs: Gear 5: Setting Up, Packing Down and Your Ears

title: Gear 5: Setting Up, Packing Down and Your Ears
text:
Lifting and carrying
Bend your knees, keep heavy things close to your body, ask for help with amps and cases over about 20 kg. Two people for a PA speaker on a stand.
crumbs: Gear 5: Setting Up, Packing Down and Your Ears

title: Gear 5: Setting Up, Packing Down and Your Ears
text:
Protect your hearing
Hearing damage is permanent and painless, and it adds up. Tinnitus (ringing after a loud night) is a warning.

Safe-ish limits get short fast: about 85 dB for 8 hours, 94 dB for 1 hour, 100 dB for 15 minutes. A loud band rehearsal is often 100–110 dB.
Wear earplugs at rehearsals and gigs. Musician’s earplugs (flat response, about 15–25 dB) sound like the band, just quieter; foam plugs work but sound muffled.
Drummers and the players beside the drums need them most. Cymbals are very loud.
In-ears and headphones: keep the level as low as you can, take breaks.
Give your ears quiet time after loud exposure.

title: Gear 1: Power and Safety
text: Every piece of electric music gear starts at the wall socket. Most problems (hum, crackles, gear that won’t turn on, blown speakers) and the only really dangerous ones come from how it’s powered.

title: Gear 1: Power and Safety
section: The order: on last, off first
text:
The order: on last, off first
Speakers and amplifiers make a loud thump when anything before them is switched on or off, and big thumps damage speakers and ears.

Switching on: sources first (keyboards, pedals, mixer, computer, interface), amplifiers and powered speakers last, volume down.
Switching off: the reverse. Amps and speakers off first, then everything else.
Turn the volume down before plugging or unplugging any cable into a live amp.

Easy way to remember: amps are last on, first off.

title: Gear 1: Power and Safety
section: Sockets, power strips and extension leads
text:
Sockets, power strips and extension leads

One wall socket can supply a limited current. In India mains is 230 V, 50 Hz: the small 3-pin socket is 6 A (~1400 W) and the big one 16 A (in the US 15 A at 120 V; UK/EU 13–16 A at 230 V). Add up the watts printed on each piece of gear; a band’s backline plus a PA can get close.
Daisy-chaining power strips into power strips overloads the first one and its cable. One strip per socket.
Unroll extension reels fully: a coiled reel under load heats up and can melt.
Use strips with a surge protector for computers and digital gear; a cheap strip with no breaker is a fire risk.
Voltage swings, power cuts and the inverter/generator switching over send spikes. Where the supply is unsteady, run keyboards, mixers and computers through a stabiliser or UPS, and switch amps off (or down) before power returns after a cut. Many sockets in India have their own switch: turn it off before plugging in.
Plug adaptors (a 2-pin or UK plug in an Indian socket) often fit loosely and lose the earth: use a proper Indian-plug cable or a strip with an earth.
Keep drinks off amps and mixers, cables out of puddles, and water bottles on the floor, not on the keyboard.

title: Gear 1: Power and Safety
text:
Earth (ground) and hum
The third pin is the earth (ground). It’s there so that if something fails inside, the metal case can’t become live.

Never break, tape over or remove the earth pin, or use a “ground lift” plug on the power cable, to stop hum. That’s how musicians have been electrocuted.
Hum (a steady 50 or 60 Hz buzz and its harmonics) usually comes from a ground loop: two pieces of gear earthed at different sockets and also joined by an audio cable. Fixes, safest first:

Power everything that’s connected together from the same socket or strip.
Use balanced cables and DI boxes; press the DI’s ground lift switch (that lifts the audio shield, which is safe; the power earth stays connected).
Keep audio cables away from power cables, or cross them at right angles.
Laptops on chargers hum through their audio out: try running on battery.

Buzz that changes when you touch the strings on a guitar is shielding or grounding in the guitar or its cable, not the wall.

title: Gear 1: Power and Safety
text:
Power supplies

Wall warts (adaptors) must match the gear: voltage, polarity (centre positive or negative, shown by a little diagram), and at least the current (mA) it needs. Wrong voltage or polarity can kill a pedal or keyboard instantly. Label every adaptor with what it belongs to.
Pedalboards: an isolated-output power supply is quieter than a daisy-chain cable.
Travelling: 120 V gear (bought in the US) on India’s 230 V burns out unless it says “100–240 V”. Check the label before using a plug adaptor.
Batteries: take them out of pedals and wireless packs when stored; leaking batteries ruin the contacts. Unplug the input jack of a battery pedal to switch it off.

title: Gear 1: Power and Safety
text:
Phantom power and wireless

+48 V phantom power for condenser mics: switch it on with the channel muted and turn it off before unplugging (Recording 2).
Wireless mics and in-ears: fresh or fully charged batteries before every show, not “it still had a bar”.

title: Gear 1: Power and Safety
text:
Stay safe

A tingle from a microphone or guitar strings is a fault: stop, unplug, and tell someone in charge.
Outdoors, and in the monsoon, power must go through an RCD / RCCB / GFCI (a breaker that trips on a leak to earth).
Don’t open amps, especially valve (tube) amps: they hold lethal voltages after being unplugged.
Tape cables down or use cable ramps across walkways; trips are the most common injury at gigs.

title: Gear 6: Guitar and Bass Care
text: Guitars and basses (acoustic and electric) need little care, but they do need some: clean strings, a stable climate, and a check of the setup now and then.

title: Gear 6: Guitar and Bass Care
text:
Every time you play

Wash your hands first. Sweat and oil kill strings and grime the fingerboard.
Wipe the strings, underneath too, and the back of the neck, with a dry cloth when you finish.
Put it in its case or gig bag or on a stand. Never leaning on an amp or a wall; that’s how necks break.
Use a strap lock or check the strap ends; dropped guitars crack at the headstock.

title: Gear 6: Guitar and Bass Care
text:
Tuning

Tune up to the note (if it’s sharp, go below and come back up), so the string holds.
Standard tuning E A D G B E (bass E A D G); tune often with a tuner.
If it won’t stay in tune: new strings still stretching, worn strings, temperature change, or the string slipping at the tuner.

title: Gear 6: Guitar and Bass Care
text:
Strings

Change them when they sound dull, won’t stay in tune, feel rough, or are discoloured. Every month or two for regular players; basses less often.
Steel strings on acoustics and electrics; nylon strings only on classical guitars. Never put steel strings on a classical guitar: the tension can pull the bridge off.
Change one or a few at a time on guitars with a floating tremolo, so the bridge stays put.
Stretch new strings: pull each gently up from the fingerboard and retune, a few times.
Cut the ends; they’re sharp. Wear eye protection the first time you cut strings.

title: Gear 6: Guitar and Bass Care
text:
Climate

Wood moves with humidity: in dry air (winter heating) the frets can stick out at the edges and acoustic tops can crack; in damp air the action rises.
Keep it at room temperature; never in a hot car. Let it warm up in its case after coming in from the cold.
An acoustic in a dry winter: a soundhole or case humidifier. In the monsoon or a humid city: silica gel or a two-way humidity pack in the case, and wipe strings after playing, since they rust fast in damp air.

title: Gear 6: Guitar and Bass Care
text:
The setup
The setup is how the guitar is adjusted: neck relief (the truss rod), string height (action), intonation, and the nut. A good setup makes a cheap guitar easy to play. Signs you need one:

Strings are high and hard to press down, or buzz against the frets.
Notes up the neck are out of tune even when the open string is in tune (intonation).
After changing to a different string gauge, or with the seasons.

The truss rod adjustment should be done by a teacher or tech the first few times: a little goes a long way, and forcing it can break it.

title: Gear 6: Guitar and Bass Care
text:
Electrics

Crackling when you turn a knob: dust in the pot; a squirt of contact cleaner (by a tech) or work the knob.
Crackle when you move the cable: the jack socket or the cable (Gear 2).
Unplug the cable from active basses and acoustic pickups when not playing; it switches the battery off.

title: Gear 2: Cables and Connectors
text: Most “the sound isn’t working” moments are cables: the wrong one, the wrong socket, or one that’s broken. Learn the connectors, the two kinds of signal level, and how to coil a cable so it lasts.

title: Gear 2: Cables and Connectors
text:
The connectors

1/4” (6.35 mm) jack, two kinds that look almost the same:

TS (tip, sleeve: one black ring): unbalanced. Guitar and instrument cables. Also speaker cables for some amps, which are a different, thicker cable: never use a guitar cable between an amp head and a cabinet.
TRS (tip, ring, sleeve: two rings): balanced mono (keyboards to a mixer, studio monitors) or stereo (headphones, insert cables).

XLR: three pins, locks in place. Microphones, balanced line outputs, DI to mixer. Male end points toward the mixer (the signal flows out of the pins).
3.5 mm mini jack: phones, laptops, small headphones.
RCA (phono): home audio, DJ gear, older keyboards.
speakON: locking speaker connector for PA speakers and amp cabs; can’t be confused with a signal cable.
MIDI (5-pin DIN) and USB (A, B, C, Micro): control data, not audio (except USB audio interfaces).
IEC / kettle lead: the detachable power cable on most gear.


The two you will plug most, opened up:

title: Gear 2: Cables and Connectors
text:
Balanced and unbalanced
An unbalanced cable has a signal wire and a shield. It picks up hum and noise, and longer than about 5–6 m (guitar cables) it also loses treble.
A balanced cable carries the signal twice, once upside down. Any noise picked up along the way is the same on both, and the input flips one and adds them, so the noise cancels. Balanced lines can run 50 m or more.
Both ends must be balanced to get the benefit: TRS to TRS, XLR to XLR, or TRS to XLR.

title: Gear 2: Cables and Connectors
text:
Levels: mic, instrument, line, speaker








Level
Example
Goes into




Mic
microphones (very quiet)
mic input (XLR), with preamp gain


Instrument (Hi-Z)
electric guitar, bass pickups
instrument input, “Hi-Z” or “Inst” switch, or a DI


Line
keyboards, phones, mixers, interfaces
line input


Speaker
amplifier output to a passive speaker
only a speaker. Never into anything else



A DI box turns an instrument or line signal into a balanced mic-level signal for a long run to the mixer. Use one for bass, acoustic guitar with a pickup, and keyboards on stage.

title: Gear 2: Cables and Connectors
text:
Signal flow
Follow the signal from the source to your ears: instrument → cable → (pedals) → amp or DI → mixer → amplifier → speakers. When there’s no sound, check each step in order: is it on, is the volume up, is the cable in the right socket, does a different cable fix it, is the channel muted. Most problems are found in the first three.

title: Gear 2: Cables and Connectors
text:
Coil it right: over-under
Wrapping a cable round your elbow twists it; twisted cables kink and break inside. Use over-under: one loop coiled normally, the next with a twist the other way. The cable lies flat, and thrown out it uncoils with no knots. Close it with a velcro tie.

title: Gear 2: Cables and Connectors
text:
Care and spares

Pull by the plug, never the cable.
Don’t walk on, roll over, or bend cables sharply at the plug.
Mark broken cables (tape: “BAD”) and take them out of the box; don’t coil them back in.
Gig bag spares: two instrument cables, two XLRs, a patch cable, a 3.5 mm-to-two-1/4” lead, a DI, and spare batteries.

title: Lesson: Four-Chord Loops
text:
A great many songs are one loop of four chords, played round and round while the melody, the words and the arrangement change on top. The loops are not very different from each other: they are the same handful of chords (I, ii, IV, V, vi, and a few borrowed from the minor) in a different order, or with one of them swapped. This lesson goes through the loops one at a time. Each has the chords, the same four bars on a grand staff (block chords in the treble, the bass note below) and the site’s backing band, which plays it round and round so that you hear it as a loop.
How to use the page. Press ▶ on any chart and the band plays four times round after a one-bar count-in. The bar that is sounding lights up, on the chart and on the staff. Under every chord is its Roman numeral, which stays the same in every key: C G Am F in the key of C is the same loop as D A Bm G in the key of D. The strip at the bottom of the window sets the key, the feel, the tempo and the chord instrument, and you can change them while the band plays. The shaded bars are the ones that differ from the first loop.

title: Lesson: Four-Chord Loops
section: 1. The axis loop: I V vi IV
text:
1. The axis loop: I V vi IV
C, G, Am, F. The loop that is under Let It Be, No Woman, No Cry and the verse of Don’t Stop Believin’, among a great many others. The bass drops from C to G, rises a step to A and falls a third to F. Three major chords and one minor: the minor chord keeps it from sounding simply happy.



Play it until you can hum the bass note of each bar. Every other loop is compared with this one.

title: Lesson: Four-Chord Loops
section: 2. The same chords, started later: vi IV I V
text:
2. The same chords, started later: vi IV I V
Am, F, C, G. The four chords are the same; the loop starts on the minor chord, so that it sounds like a minor song, and the major chord C arrives in the middle. Zombie by the Cranberries is this loop (in E minor), and so is the chorus of Despacito.



Compare the two charts: there is no new chord. Where a loop starts is what the ear takes for home. The other two starting points are IV I V vi (F, C, G, Am) and V vi IV I (G, Am, F, C).

title: Lesson: Four-Chord Loops
section: 3. The fifties loop: I vi IV V
text:
3. The fifties loop: I vi IV V
C, Am, F, G. The doo-wop loop. It has the chords of the axis loop, but with the minor chord second, so the bass steps down by thirds: C, A, F, and then the G climbs to C again. Stand by Me is built on it. Listen to bar 4: the V chord is the last bar and it leads straight back to C.

title: Lesson: Four-Chord Loops
section: 4. The turnaround: I vi ii V
text:
4. The turnaround: I vi ii V
C, Am, Dm, G. Replace the IV with its relative minor, ii. The bass now moves round the circle of fifths: C, A, D, G, and back to C. This is the turnaround of jazz, and the A section of Gershwin’s I Got Rhythm (the “rhythm changes”) begins this way. Put a seventh on each chord and it is the sound of a standard.



Bar 3 is the only difference from the fifties loop. The ii chord and the IV chord share two of their three notes (F and A), so one can stand in for the other.

title: Lesson: Four-Chord Loops
section: 5. Out and back: I IV V IV
text:
5. Out and back: I IV V IV
C, F, G, F. The loop of Louie Louie and Wild Thing. There is no minor chord and no change of direction; the loop goes up to the dominant and back down by the same step. Because the bar-4 chord is IV, not I, it does not feel finished, and the loop goes round again and again.

title: Lesson: Four-Chord Loops
section: 6. Borrowing a chord: I ♭VII IV I
text:
6. Borrowing a chord: I ♭VII IV I
C, B♭, F, C. B♭ is not in the key of C. It is the chord on the flat seventh, borrowed from the mixolydian mode (a major scale with a flat seventh) and the note that the blues calls the flat seven. Sweet Home Alabama goes I, ♭VII, IV this way. In C the bass goes down a step, then down a fourth, then down a fourth again.

title: Lesson: Four-Chord Loops
text:
7. The minor loops
Two loops in the minor, written here in C minor (three flats in the signature).

i ♭VII ♭VI V: Cm, B♭, A♭, G. The Andalusian loop. The bass falls by step, C, B♭, A♭, G, and the last chord is a major V, with the leading tone B, so that it pulls hard back to Cm. Hit the Road Jack is this loop.
i ♭VI ♭III ♭VII: Cm, A♭, E♭, B♭. The four chords of the axis loop in E♭ major, started on the vi chord: loop 2 in its minor key. It is the sound of much current pop.







Play the two minor loops and then loop 2. The notes are different, but the shape, down by steps then up by a third, is the same.

title: Lesson: Four-Chord Loops
text:
Build your own loop
Choose a chord for each bar, or start from one of the loops above, and the chart and the staff rewrite themselves. Change a menu while the band is playing and the new chords come in at the next bar. The numeral next to each chord is its place in the key of C.

title: Lesson: Four-Chord Loops
text:
Test your ear
The band plays one of the loops. Pick the one you heard. If you are not sure, listen for the bass first: does it fall, climb or leap?

title: Lesson: Four-Chord Loops
text:
Where to go next

Play along. Set the strip at the bottom to Loop, pick a key and play or sing a melody over each loop in turn. Start with just the chord roots.
Take a loop you built to Tools → Backing Track (use Copy as ABC above and paste it into Edit the changes (ABC) there) to choose the bass line, comping rhythm and drum groove.
Try the moves of the lesson on C, Am, F, G (extensions, passing chords, secondary dominants, two-fives) on any of these loops.

title: Elements 10: Texture
text:
Texture is how many layers of sound there are and how they relate to each other. Thin or thick is part of it, but the names below describe the relationship between the parts.
Almost every example on this page uses the same tune (Twinkle, Twinkle), so you hear only the texture change.

title: Elements 10: Texture
text:
1. Monophonic
One line, and nothing else. Any number of people can play or sing it, as long as they all play the same part. No chords.

title: Elements 10: Texture
text:
2. Octaves
Two or more parts playing the same tune an octave apart: the same note names at a different pitch. Still one line, but heavier.

title: Elements 10: Texture
text:
3. Homophonic
All the parts move together, in the same rhythm, making chords, like a hymn. (Homo-phonic = “same sound”.)

title: Elements 10: Texture
text:
4. Melody and accompaniment
A tune with chords or a pattern underneath that supports it. The most common texture in pop music and Classical-period music. An Alberti bass is a Classical piano accompaniment: each chord broken into four equal notes, usually lowest, highest, middle, highest.

title: Elements 10: Texture
text:
5. Polyphonic
Two or more independent lines at once, each a tune in its own right (poly-phonic = “many sounds”). Also called counterpoint. When the lines copy each other it is imitation; a round (Frère Jacques) and a canon are strict imitation.



A countermelody is a second tune that fits with the main one, as in a descant over a hymn.

title: Elements 10: Texture
text:
6. Call and response, antiphonal
Call and response: one performer (or group) plays or sings a phrase, and another answers. Common in African music, blues, gospel, work songs and pop.
Antiphonal: two groups answering each other from different places, such as two choirs on either side of a church.

title: Elements 10: Texture
text:
7. Pedal and drone
A pedal is a long or repeated note, usually in the bass, held while the harmony changes above it. A drone is long or repeated notes, usually two a 5th apart, as on bagpipes.

title: Elements 10: Texture
text:
8. Basso continuo
In the Baroque period, the basso continuo played the bass line and filled in the chords under the melody. The bass was played by a cello, bass viol or bassoon; the chords by a harpsichord, organ or lute, read from a figured bass (numbers under the bass notes showing the chords).

title: Elements 10: Texture
text:
9. Describing texture

Name it, then describe it: thin or thick, sparse or dense, how many parts.
Say what changes: “It starts monophonic (a solo flute), becomes homophonic when the choir comes in, and the middle section is polyphonic, with the voices entering one after another in imitation.”
Which instruments have the melody and which accompany: see Instruments and Voices.

title: Elements 9: Style and Genre
text: A style or genre is recognised by its features: the instruments, the harmony, the rhythm, the textures it likes. Naming the style is only half the answer. Say which features told you.

title: Elements 9: Style and Genre
text:
1. Western classical music










Baroque (about 1600–1750)
Classical (about 1750–1820)
Romantic (about 1800–1910)




Composers
Bach, Vivaldi, Handel
Haydn, Mozart, early Beethoven
Schubert, Chopin, Wagner, late Beethoven


Instruments
harpsichord, small orchestra (mostly strings), basso continuo
the piano replaces the harpsichord; the orchestra grows (clarinets, horns)
a large orchestra, more brass and percussion; piano music for virtuosos


Dynamics
terraced (sudden loud/quiet)
a wider range, crescendos
a huge range, constant change


Melody
long, decorated with ornaments
balanced, regular phrases (4 + 4 measures); elegant
long, expressive; the leitmotif


Harmony
major and minor keys settled in
simple, clear chords; Alberti bass
chromatic chords, unusual key changes


Texture
often polyphonic (counterpoint)
mostly melody and accompaniment
rich and full


Tempo
steady
steady
rubato (pushing and pulling the tempo)



The periods overlap. Beethoven is the usual bridge between Classical and Romantic.











More: Ornaments by Period, Score Reading: History.

title: Elements 9: Style and Genre
text:
2. Jazz and blues

Swung rhythm: pairs of eighth notes played long-short (Reading Swing).
Blue notes: the 3rd, 5th and 7th of the scale bent down, by anything from a quarter tone to a half step.
The 12-bar blues chord pattern (Blues Changes).
Extended chords: 7ths, 9ths and more.
Improvisation: players make up their parts as they perform.
A rhythm section (drums, double bass, piano or guitar) and a front line (saxophones, trumpets, trombones).
Walking bass: a steady line of quarter notes walking up and down through the chords.

title: Elements 9: Style and Genre
text:
3. Musical theatre
A story told through music, singing, acting and dance.







Word
Meaning




Overture
the music before the show begins, usually built from its main tunes


Solo / duet / chorus number
a song for one character, two characters, or the whole company


Recitative
speech-like singing that moves the story on, in shows that are all sung


Kinds of show
book musicals (songs between spoken scenes), sung-through (no speaking), jukebox (built from existing hit songs), film-to-stage



Composers: Leonard Bernstein (West Side Story), Stephen Sondheim, Andrew Lloyd Webber, Lin-Manuel Miranda.

title: Elements 9: Style and Genre
text:
4. Film music
Film music supports what is on screen. Ask how each feature fits the scene:







Scene
Features you might hear




Car chase
fast tempo, loud, driving ostinato, sudden changes


War film
military snare drum, brass fanfares; a lone instrument (monophonic) for isolation


Horror
dissonant chords, a repeated pattern building tension, sudden loud stabs


Romance
strings, legato melody, rich harmony, rubato



A leitmotif is a short idea tied to a character or thing that returns whenever it appears. Composers: John Williams, Hans Zimmer, Howard Shore, Jerry Goldsmith.

title: Elements 9: Style and Genre
text:
5. Pop and rock
Pop is commercial music written to appeal to lots of people. Rock is usually harder and louder, built on guitars and drums, though it includes rock ballads. Both are mostly in verse–chorus form, often with a riff, a repeated pattern that makes a song memorable.



Section
What it does




Intro
sets the mood, often instruments only


Verse
tells the story: same tune, new words each time


Chorus
the main message: same tune and words each time


Bridge / middle 8
a contrasting section, often 8 measures


Outro
finishes the song






More: Your First Rock Song, Four-Chord Loops.

title: Elements 9: Style and Genre
text:
6. Minimalism
From the 1960s, mostly in the USA. Composers: Steve Reich, Philip Glass, Terry Riley, John Adams.

Built on repetition of short patterns.
The patterns change gradually, one note or one beat at a time.
Slow-changing harmony, often one chord for a long time.
Layers that drift in and out of line with each other (phasing).

title: Elements 8: Structure and Form
text: Structure (or form) is how a piece is built from sections. Sections are named with letters: the first idea is A, a different one B, the next new one C. When A comes back it keeps its letter.

title: Elements 8: Structure and Form
text:
1. Phrases and sections
A phrase is a musical sentence, usually 2, 4 or 8 measures, ending in a cadence. Phrases join into sections. To find the sections, listen for where the music changes: a new tune, a new key, new instruments, a new texture or a different mood.

title: Elements 8: Structure and Form
text:
2. Binary form: A B
Two sections. B contrasts with A in some way (a new key, a new tune), and usually both are repeated: A A B B. Common in Baroque dances.

title: Elements 8: Structure and Form
text:
3. Ternary form: A B A
Three sections: A, a contrasting B, then A again. The return can be exact or slightly changed (A B A′).

title: Elements 8: Structure and Form
section: 4. Rondo form: A B A C A
text:
4. Rondo form: A B A C A
The opening section, the refrain, keeps coming back, with contrasting sections called episodes in between.

title: Elements 8: Structure and Form
text:
5. Strophic form: A A A
The same music for every verse (every strophe), with new words each time. Hymns, folk songs, ballads and many children’s songs.
When the music never repeats and keeps changing to follow the words or the story, the opposite of strophic, it is through-composed.

title: Elements 8: Structure and Form
text:
6. Minuet and trio
A minuet is a dance in 3/4 at a moderate tempo, from 17th- and 18th-century Europe. In the Classical period it was paired with a second, contrasting minuet called the trio (once played by just three instruments). Each is in binary form; then the minuet comes back without its repeats. Overall it is ternary:








Minuet
Trio
Minuet




A (repeated) B (repeated)
C (repeated) D (repeated)
A B (no repeats)


tonic key
a related key, lighter or thinner scoring
tonic key

title: Elements 8: Structure and Form
text:
7. Popular song forms



Form
Sections




Verse–chorus
intro, verse, chorus, verse, chorus, bridge, chorus, outro


AABA (32-bar song)
A A B A, each 8 measures; B is the bridge or middle eight


12-bar blues
the same 12-measure chord pattern, repeated (Blues Changes)


Theme and variations
a tune, then changed versions of it (new rhythm, harmony, key, instruments)



Naming the parts of a song and marking them in a recording: Section Labels.

title: Elements 7: Rhythm and Tempo
text: Rhythm is the pattern of long and short sounds and silences. Tempo is the speed of the beat.

title: Elements 7: Rhythm and Tempo
text:
1. Note lengths
Counted in quarter-note beats:



Beats
Note
Rest




4
whole note
whole rest


2
half note
half rest


1
quarter note
quarter rest


½
eighth note
eighth rest


¼
sixteenth note
sixteenth rest



Each note, then its rest, from the longest to the shortest:



The American names count fractions of a whole note. The British names are older: semibreve (whole), minim (half), crotchet (quarter), quaver (eighth), semiquaver (sixteenth). Tick British note names at the top to read this page with them.

title: Elements 7: Rhythm and Tempo
text:
2. Dots, ties and triplets
A dot after a note adds half its value again.



Note
Value
With a dot




half note
2
2 + 1 = 3


quarter note
1
1 + ½ = 1½


eighth note
½
½ + ¼ = ¾



A tie joins two notes of the same pitch into one longer note (often across a measure line).
A triplet is three notes played evenly in the time of two, marked with a 3.

title: Elements 7: Rhythm and Tempo
text:
3. Syncopation
Syncopation puts the accent off the beat: on the “and”, or on a weak beat, often with a note tied over the strong beat. It is the push in a lot of pop, funk, Latin music and jazz.








For swing rhythm, where pairs of eighth notes are played long-short: Reading Swing.

title: Elements 7: Rhythm and Tempo
text:
4. The fermata
A fermata over a note means hold it longer than written; the pulse stops until the performer (or conductor) moves on.

title: Elements 7: Rhythm and Tempo
text:
5. Tempo
Tempo is the speed of the pulse, measured in beats per minute (BPM). 60 BPM is one beat a second; 120 BPM is two. A metronome marking such as ♩ = 120 means 120 quarter-note beats per minute.
To work out a tempo by ear: tap the pulse quietly (your toes, not your whole foot) and ask how fast you are tapping. The Tap Along tool counts it for you.








Marking
Meaning
Roughly




Lento / Adagio
slow
under 70 BPM


Andante
at a walking pace
75–100


Moderato
moderate
100–120


Allegretto
fairly fast (not as fast as allegro)
110–120


Allegro
fast, lively
120–160


Vivace / Presto
very fast
160 and up


Accelerando (accel.)
gradually getting faster



Ritardando (rit.) / Rallentando (rall.)
gradually getting slower



A tempo
back to the original speed



Rubato
stretching and pushing the tempo for expression




The BPM figures are a guide only: composers and periods used these words differently.

title: Elements 11: Mixed Review

title: Elements 11: Mixed Review

2. Writing about a piece
When a question asks you to describe a piece you have just heard:

Go through the elements one at a time. A checklist helps: Articulation, Dynamics, Harmony and tonality, Instruments, Melody, Metre, Rhythm and tempo, Structure, Style, Texture.
Describe changes, in order. “It starts quiet, then…” beats one word for the whole piece.
Use the right word, then say where. “A sequence in the violins at the start of the second section.”
Back up a style with features. Not just “Baroque”, but “Baroque: a harpsichord, terraced dynamics, a busy polyphonic texture”.

The lessons: Articulation · Dynamics · Harmony and Tonality · Instruments and Voices · Melody · Metre · Rhythm and Tempo · Structure · Style and Genre · Texture

title: Metre on One Page
text:
The sheet



Time signatures

Top: how many beats in a measure. Bottom: which note gets the beat (4 = quarter note, 2 = half note, 8 = eighth note). C = 4/4, common time. C with a line = 2/2, cut time.



2/4 simple duple

ONE two. Marches, polkas.






3/4 simple triple

ONE two three. Waltzes, minuets.






4/4 simple quadruple

ONE two three four. Most pop, rock and jazz.






6/8 compound duple

Two dotted-quarter-note beats, each split in three. A lilting, jig feel.






9/8 compound triple

Three beats, each in three.






12/8 compound quadruple

Four beats, each in three. Blues and soul ballads.






Irregular

Can’t divide into equal twos or threes: 5/4 is 3 + 2, 7/8 is 2 + 2 + 3.






Hearing it


Tap the pulse.


Find the strongest beat (where the bass or chord changes) and count from it.


Listen between beats: split in two is simple, in three is compound.




Check yourself

title: Metre on One Page
text:
Describing metre

Give the time signature and its name: “3/4, simple triple, like a waltz”.
In compound time, divide the top number by three to get the beats.

title: Melody on One Page
text:
The sheet



Conjunct

Moving by step, to the next note up or down. A narrow range.






Disjunct

Moving by leap, jumping over notes. A wide range.






Sequence

The same idea again, starting higher or lower. (Repetition: again, unchanged.)






Imitation

One part copies an idea another part has just played, often at a different pitch.






Ostinato

A short idea repeated over and over. In the bass: a ground bass or a riff.






Scalic

Runs up and down the scale.






Triadic

Uses the notes of the chords (broken chords).






Chromatic

Notes outside the key, often moving by half step. (Pentatonic: only five notes.)






Intervals

Count the letter names, both ends included: C to E is C-D-E, a 3rd. Here: 2nd, 3rd, 4th, 5th.






Scale degrees

1 tonic · 2 supertonic · 3 mediant · 4 subdominant · 5 dominant · 6 submediant · 7 leading note. The tonic is home; the leading note pulls up to it.



Check yourself

title: Melody on One Page
text:
Describing a melody

Shape (rising, falling, an arch), movement (conjunct or disjunct), range (narrow or wide), then what it is made of (scalic, triadic, chromatic) and how ideas come back (repetition, sequence, imitation).
Ornaments (trills, mordents, turns): Grace Notes and Ornaments.

title: Instruments on One Page
text:
The sheet



How many

1 solo · 2 duet · 3 trio · 4 quartet · 5 quintet. A string quartet: two violins, viola, cello. A piano trio: piano, violin, cello.



Voices

High to low: soprano, alto, tenor, baritone, bass. Treble: a boy’s high voice. Countertenor: a man in the alto range. An SATB choir: soprano, alto, tenor, bass.



Woodwind

Piccolo, flute, oboe, clarinet, bassoon. Air across a hole (flute) or through a reed. Top of the score.






Brass

Trumpet, French horn, trombone, tuba. Lips buzzing into a mouthpiece.






Percussion

Timpani, snare drum, cymbals, xylophone, glockenspiel… Struck, shaken or scraped.






Strings

Violin, viola, cello, double bass. Bowed or plucked. Bottom of the score.






The low end

Each family has its bass: bassoon, tuba, timpani, cello and double bass.






Band line-ups


Rock / pop: vocals, guitars, bass guitar, drums, keys


Folk: voice, acoustic guitar, fiddle, banjo


Jazz combo: rhythm section (piano, bass, drums) + front line (sax, trumpet)


Big band: sax, trumpet, trombone sections + rhythm section




What each one does


Melody: the tune


Accompaniment: chords, rhythm


Countermelody: a second tune


Bass line: the lowest part


Solo: one instrument featured




Check yourself

title: Instruments on One Page
text:
Describing instruments

Name the instrument and say what it is doing: “the melody is on the violins, the cellos play a slow bass line, the horns hold chords”.
More instruments to hear: Instruments passes one tune round the whole orchestra.

title: Harmony on One Page
text: The whole of Harmony on one sheet. Every ▶ plays the example; the cadences play with chords. Press Full screen to put the sheet on the whole screen for revision or for the class board.

title: Harmony on One Page
text:
The sheet



Key signatures

The sharps or flats at the start of each line. Each major key shares one with its relative minor, three half steps lower.



none: C / A minor


1♯: G / E minor


2♯: D / B minor


1♭: F / D minor


2♭: B♭ / G minor




Major

Often sounds bright. Look at the last note and chord: usually the tonic.






Minor

Often darker. The same signature as its relative major, plus the raised 7th (here G♯).






Modal, pentatonic, atonal


Modal: built on an older scale (Dorian, Mixolydian…)


Pentatonic: five notes, C D E G A (heard here)


Atonal: no key, no home note







Modulation

A change of key mid-piece: often to the dominant or the relative minor; in pop, the last chorus up a step.






Triads

Three notes a 3rd apart: root, 3rd, 5th. Numbered I–vii°: capitals major, small letters minor. In C: I C, ii Dm, IV F, V G, vi Am.






Sevenths and beyond

Another 3rd on top makes a seventh (G7 = G B D F); more make extended chords (9ths, 11ths), common in jazz.






Authentic cadence

V → I. Finished: a full stop.






Plagal cadence

IV → I. Finished, softer: the “Amen” of hymns.






Half cadence

Anything → V. Unfinished: a comma, or a question.






Deceptive cadence

V → vi (usually). A surprise: you expect I and get a minor chord.






Picardy third

A minor-key piece that ends on a major tonic chord.






Check yourself

title: Harmony on One Page
text:
Describing harmony

Say the tonality first (major, minor, modal…), then anything that changes: a modulation, a Picardy third at the end.
The cadence names follow the British note names switch: perfect, imperfect and interrupted are the British authentic, half and deceptive.
The longer lesson, with fuller examples: Elements 3: Harmony and Tonality.

title: Dynamics on One Page
text:
The sheet



From pp to ff

pp very quiet · p quiet · mp moderately quiet · mf moderately loud · f loud · ff very loud.






Crescendo

cresc. or an opening hairpin <: getting gradually louder. Say where it starts and where it ends up.






Diminuendo

dim. or decresc., or a closing hairpin >: getting gradually quieter.






Sforzando

sfz or sf: one note hit hard, then straight back to the dynamic before.






Terraced

Sudden steps between loud and quiet, often by more or fewer players. Baroque.






Gradual

The same notes with one long crescendo. Classical and Romantic.






Where they go


One instrument: under the staff


Piano: between the two staves


Voices: above the staff, clear of the words




Through history


Baroque (about 1600–1750): few marks, p and f, terraced


Classical (about 1750–1820): crescendos and diminuendos, for contrast


Romantic (about 1800–1910): ppp to fff, always changing




Describing dynamics

Describe the changes in order: “starts p, a gradual crescendo to f, a sudden drop to pp, ends ff”. Useful words: sudden, gradual, wide range, contrast, terraced, fades out.



Check yourself

title: Dynamics on One Page
text:
Describing dynamics

One word for a whole piece is only enough if it never changes.
Piano is the Italian for quiet; pianoforte, the instrument’s full name, means “quiet-loud”.

title: Articulation on One Page
text:
The sheet



Staccato

Short and detached: a gap after each note. A dot over or under the notehead.







Legato

Smooth, no gaps. A slur (a curve over different notes) asks for it.







Slur or tie?

A curve over different pitches is a slur: play them smoothly. A curve joining two of the same pitch is a tie: one note, held for both.






Accent

>: a strong start to the note. Marks combine: a dot and an accent is short and strong.






Tenuto and marcato

Tenuto (a short line): hold the full length, with a little weight. Marcato (^): stronger than an accent.






Glissando

A slide from one note to another. Violin, trombone, voice: through every pitch. Piano, harp: a sweep across keys or strings.







Arco

Strings, played with the bow (the normal way). Written arco after a pizzicato passage.






Pizzicato

pizz.: strings plucked with a finger instead of bowed.






Other techniques


Double stopping: two strings at once


Con sordino: with a mute (senza sord. takes it off)


Tremolo: one note repeated very fast


Vibrato: the pitch wavers a little, for warmth


Falsetto: a light, high voice above the normal range




How players slur


Strings: many notes in one bow stroke


Wind, brass: tongue only the first note


Voice: one breath, the vowel kept going


Piano: hold each key until the next is down




Check yourself

title: Articulation on One Page
text:
Describing articulation

Name the mark and say what it does to the sound: “the strings play pizzicato, so the notes are short and light”.
Articulation is how a note is played, not how loud it is: that is dynamics.

title: Playing Brushes
text: Brushes are fans of thin wire (or nylon) fixed in a handle. On a snare drum they make two kinds of sound: a tap (a short, soft hit, like a quiet stick) and a sweep (the wires dragged across the head, a steady “shhh”). Brush playing is mostly about the sweeps, which no stick can make. They’re standard in jazz ballads, quiet swing, country, folk, and any acoustic gig where sticks are too loud.

title: Playing Brushes
text:
The brush and the drum

Wire brushes on a coated snare head (the white, slightly rough kind). A clear smooth head gives almost no sweep sound. A coated head is the one thing brushes really need.
Retractable brushes pull back into the handle to protect the wires; pull them out until they fan to about the width of your palm. Wider is softer and darker.
Nylon brushes are louder and brighter, and closer to sticks, popular in pop and on cajón.
Turn the snares on for a buzzy sweep, off for a smooth one.

title: Playing Brushes
text:
Holding them
Hold a brush like a stick, in matched or traditional grip (see Stick Grips), but lighter, with the wires lying nearly flat on the head. The movement comes from the forearm and wrist, not the fingers. Keep the wires on the head for sweeps; lift them only for taps and accents.

title: Playing Brushes
text:
The basic swing pattern
The classic pattern for a right-handed player:

Left hand: sweeping. In a medium swing, the left hand sweeps back and forth across the head, left to right on beat 1, right to left on beat 2, and so on: one sweep per beat. In a ballad it can draw a full circle (clockwise as seen from above) over two beats, or one a beat.
Right hand: the ride pattern. The right hand taps the swing ride rhythm (“ding, ding-a ding”) on the right side of the head, as it would on a ride cymbal.
Accent 2 and 4. Finish the left-hand sweep with a little push, or tap it, on 2 and 4: the backbeat that a hi-hat would play. The hi-hat foot often plays 2 and 4 as well.
Feathering the bass drum: very soft quarter notes, felt more than heard.

Start slowly: first the left hand alone for a minute without a break, then the right hand alone, then both together. The sweep should sound continuous; any gaps sound like hiccups.

title: Playing Brushes
text:
Other patterns








Pattern
What it does
Used for




Circle
Left hand makes a continuous circle, one or two beats a turn
Ballads


Half-moon
An arc and back each beat, pushing on 2 and 4
Medium swing


Both hands sweep
Two circles going in opposite directions
Very slow ballads


Taps with a sweep
Short sweeps on each eighth, accented taps
Bossa nova, Latin


Stick-like
Taps only, a straight backbeat
Train beat (country), quiet rock and folk



The patterns are a starting point. Drummers such as Philly Joe Jones, Ed Thigpen and Clayton Cameron made brush playing a language of its own, and listening to them teaches more than any page.

title: Playing Brushes
text:
When to use brushes

When a stick is too loud for the room, the singer, or an acoustic band.
A ballad, or the soft opening of a tune that gets louder (switch to sticks at the change).
Play the ride cymbal with brushes too: a soft, washy sound. Don’t push the wires hard against a cymbal edge; they bend.

title: Playing Brushes
text:
Looking after them
Keep retractable brushes closed when not in use. Bent wires can be straightened gently with fingers. A brush spread by the case too much won’t come back: replace it.

title: Playing Brushes
text:
Practice

Left-hand sweeps for two minutes with a metronome at 80, one sweep a beat, without a gap.
Add the right-hand ride rhythm; count “1 2 3 4” aloud.
Add the hi-hat foot on 2 and 4.
Play the same groove at 60 as circles, then at 140 as half-moons.

title: DJ 5: Scratching Basics
text: Scratching is playing the record as an instrument: moving it back and forth under the needle while the other hand opens and closes the sound with a fader. Grand Wizzard Theodore is credited with discovering it in the Bronx in the late 1970s; Grandmaster Flash, DJ Jazzy Jeff, Qbert and the turntablist crews made it an art.

title: DJ 5: Scratching Basics
text:
Set up

A short sound at the start of a cue: “Ahh” or a horn stab. Put a cue point (or a sticker on the record) right at its start.
Record hand on the label; it pushes the record forward and pulls it back.
Fader hand on the crossfader or channel fader, with a sharp curve, so a tiny movement opens or closes the sound.
One revolution of the record at 33⅓ RPM is 1.8 seconds of sound. Short scratches move the record a quarter turn or less.

Below: one deck with the scratch sample, and a mixer with its fader. Click CUE (stopped) at the start of the “Ahh” to mark it. The platter’s label is the record: drag it forwards and backwards. Use your other hand (or a second finger on a touch screen) on the channel fader.

title: DJ 5: Scratching Basics
text:
The scratches
Learn each slowly, then in time with a beat (play a loop on your phone or the next widget’s deck at 90 BPM).

Baby scratch: record hand only, fader open. Push forward a quarter turn, pull back, in steady eighth notes. Forward is the sound played; back is it reversed. Even, smooth movements; the sound should be the same each time.
Forward scratch: push forward with the fader open, close the fader, pull back silently, open it again. Only the forward sound is heard. (The opposite, sound only on the pull, is a backward scratch.)
Chirp: push forward and close the fader during the push; open it as you pull back and close it again during the pull. Each movement gets cut off, making a short “chirp”. Record and fader hands move together.
Transformer: let the record move slowly (a slow push of a long “Ahh”), and tap the fader open and closed in rhythm, so the long sound is chopped into pulses (sixteenths, triplets). Named after the sound effects of the Transformers cartoon.

title: DJ 5: Scratching Basics
text:
Back on the beat
Scratches sit on a beat played by the other deck. Here deck A plays a boom-bap loop at 90 BPM; deck B has the “Ahh”. With the crossfader curve sharp, cut B in and out from the crossfader while scratching it.

title: DJ 5: Scratching Basics
text:
Hamster switch, tips

Many scratch DJs reverse the crossfader direction (hamster style) so the fader hand pushes towards the deck being scratched.
Keep the needle (here, the platter) steady: small, precise movements sound better than big ones.
Practise slowly with a metronome; speed comes later.

title: DJ 6: Harmonic Mixing
text: Two beatmatched tracks in clashing keys sound sour in a long blend, especially with chords or vocals. Harmonic mixing chooses the next track by key, so blends sound like one piece of music.

title: DJ 6: Harmonic Mixing
text:
The Camelot wheel
The Camelot system (by Mark Davis; popularised by Mixed In Key) numbers the keys around a clock, 1 to 12, A for minor and B for major. It is the circle of fifths with easy names: one step round is a fifth up.

















1A A♭m
2A E♭m
3A B♭m
4A Fm
5A Cm
6A Gm
7A Dm
8A Am
9A Em
10A Bm
11A F♯m
12A C♯m




1B B
2B F♯
3B D♭
4B A♭
5B E♭
6B B♭
7B F
8B C
9B G
10B D
11B A
12B E



From a track in 8A (A minor), the safest moves are:

8A (the same key),
7A or 9A (one step: D minor or E minor, keys a fifth apart, sharing six of seven notes),
8B (the relative major, C major: the same notes).

Moving +2 (an “energy boost”, 8A → 10A) or across diagonally works sometimes, and is a choice, not a rule.

title: DJ 6: Harmonic Mixing
section: The pitch fader moves the key
text:
The pitch fader moves the key
Without key lock, speeding a track up raises its key: about 6 % is one semitone. +3 % is a quarter-tone sharp, enough to clash with a track in the “same” key. The decks show it: the key readout adds the shift in semitones. Key lock (Master Tempo) keeps the key while the tempo changes, by time-stretching. Some DJs use the shift on purpose: a track pitched up 6 % moves one semitone, so 8A becomes 3A.

title: DJ 6: Harmonic Mixing
text:
Practise



The loops are in different keys: Warehouse Am (8A), Neon Floor Em (9A), Late Bus Cm (5A), Concrete Fm (4A), Mirrorball G (9B).

A: Warehouse (8A). B: Neon Floor (9A), matched to 124. Blend with both full. One step on the wheel: it works.
Load Late Bus (5A) on B instead (match it to 124: +3.3 %). Three steps away: hear the chords rub.
Load Hey Now (acapella) (8A) on B over Warehouse (8A): same key. Then over Neon Floor on A (9A). Then over Mirrorball (9B, the relative major of 9A): which works best?
Watch the key readout as you push a pitch fader to +8 %: how far has the key moved?

title: DJ 6: Harmonic Mixing
text:
Notes

Software detects keys; it is right most of the time, not always. Trust your ears in the headphones.
Drum-only intros and outros have no key: mix in there and keys don’t matter.
The Camelot code is a nickname for the key: the Circle of Fifths tool shows the circle behind it.

title: DJ 4: EQ Mixing and Transitions
text: Two full tracks at full volume together are loud and muddy: two kicks, two basslines, two sets of hi-hats. EQ mixing gives each track its own space during a blend. The golden rule: only one bassline at a time.

title: DJ 4: EQ Mixing and Transitions
text:
The bass swap

Beatmatched and phrased, bring the incoming track in with its Lo cut right down. You hear its hats and mids over the outgoing track’s full sound.
On the first beat of a phrase, swap: incoming Lo up, outgoing Lo down, at the same moment (one hand on each knob).
Over the next 8 or 16 bars take the outgoing track’s Mid and Hi down, then its fader.

title: DJ 4: EQ Mixing and Transitions
text:
Other transitions

Long blend: both tracks play together for 32 bars or more, EQs moving slowly. House and techno.
Filter mix: sweep the outgoing track’s filter to a high-pass (it thins out to nothing but hats) while the incoming one comes in, or bring the new track in through a low-pass that opens up.
Cut: on the first beat of a phrase, flick the crossfader across. Hip-hop and open-format DJs cut; it’s quick and clean if the phrase is right.
Echo out: an echo or delay effect on the last beat of the outgoing track, then cut it; the echo trails off under the new one.
Gain first: before any of these, set both channels’ gain so the tracks are equally loud. A transition that jumps in volume sounds like a mistake.

title: DJ 4: EQ Mixing and Transitions
text:
Practise




Beatmatch B to A (B: about −1.6 %). With B’s Lo at the bottom (−26 dB, a near kill), start B on a phrase and bring its fader up.
On the next phrase, swap the Lo knobs. Then fade A out over 8 bars, Hi first.
Do it again with the Filter instead: B in at full EQ but low fader; sweep A’s filter to the right (high-pass) over 8 bars while B’s fader rises.
Try a cut: both decks matched, faders up, crossfader full A. On the 1 of a phrase, throw the crossfader to B. Set the Curve towards “cut” and try again: in the middle both channels are now at full, and the change happens only at the very ends.

title: DAW 1: The Timeline and the Transport
text: A DAW (digital audio workstation) is a tape recorder, a mixing desk and a box of instruments in one program. BandLab, Ableton Live, Logic Pro, GarageBand, FL Studio, Reaper and Pro Tools all look different, but they are built from the same handful of parts. These lessons teach those parts on a DAW small enough to see all at once, played by the Backing Track band’s instruments. Each lesson ends with where the same thing is in BandLab, Ableton Live and Logic Pro, so you can do it there next.
crumbs: DAW 1: The Timeline and the Transport

title: DAW 1: The Timeline and the Transport
text:
Time runs left to right
Every DAW draws the song as a timeline: time runs left to right, one row (a track) per instrument. The numbers along the top are the ruler, counted in bars. The red line is the playhead: where playback starts and where you are.
The counter by the buttons reads bar . beat . sixteenth: 3.2.1 is bar 3, beat 2, on the beat. This is how every DAW counts, and it’s why a DAW wants to know your tempo (BPM, beats a minute) before you start: bars only make sense at a tempo.
crumbs: DAW 1: The Timeline and the Transport

title: DAW 1: The Timeline and the Transport
text:
Try it

Press ▶ Play (or Space). Watch the playhead and the counter. Space again stops.
Click the ruler at bar 5: the playhead jumps there. Enter (or ⏮) goes back to the top.
Change the Tempo to 130 and play again. Everything is faster, nothing else changed: the notes are stored in bars and beats, not in seconds.
Switch on ♩ Click, the metronome: a high click on beat 1, a lower one on 2, 3 and 4.
Loop (also called cycle): the yellow bracket under the ruler. Drag along the ruler from bar 3 to bar 4. With ⟲ Loop on, playback goes round those two bars until you stop it. Practising one hard spot, or writing a part over a four-bar loop, is most of what people use a DAW for.
crumbs: DAW 1: The Timeline and the Transport

title: DAW 1: The Timeline and the Transport
text:
Why bars, not seconds
A DAW that knows the tempo can put a note on beat 3 rather than at 4.37 seconds. That is what lets you change the tempo later, line notes up to the grid, copy a bar and have it fit, and hear a click in time. Audio you record is stored in seconds but placed on the same bar grid. Set the tempo before you record, and record to the click, or the grid won’t line up with what you played.

title: DAW 8: Your First Session in a Real DAW
text:
Everything in the small DAW is in BandLab, Ableton Live and Logic Pro, under other names and in other places. This lesson is a checklist for your first session in one of them, then a small project: bring in the song you made here, and add the things the small DAW can’t do.
Each step links to the page in that program’s own manual (BandLab Help Center, the Ableton Live 12 Reference Manual, the Logic Pro 12.3 User Guide). Menus move between versions: if a step doesn’t match what you see, the linked page is the one to trust.
crumbs: DAW 8: Your First Session in a Real DAW

title: DAW 8: Your First Session in a Real DAW
text:
Before you start

Headphones, wired. Bluetooth headphones add a delay you can hear: BandLab’s help puts wired at about 5–10 ms and Bluetooth anywhere from 34 to 300 ms (BandLab: what is latency?).
Your files from DAW 7: mini-daw.mid (the notes) and, if you like, mini-daw.wav (the mix, to compare with).
A name for the project, and a folder to keep it in.
crumbs: DAW 8: Your First Session in a Real DAW

title: DAW 8: Your First Session in a Real DAW
text:
The checklist

BandLabAbleton LiveLogic Pro


BandLab runs in the browser (and as a phone app). Projects are saved to your BandLab account, so there is no folder to choose. Keyboard shortcuts work only in the web Studio (shortcuts).

Open the Studio and start a new project (Getting started with the Studio).
Tempo and metronome. Open the arrow next to the metronome in the transport bar: tempo, click sound, click volume and a count-in for recording. M turns the click on and off (Using the metronome).
Bring in your MIDI file. The web Studio imports MIDI files as well as audio (WAV, MP3 and others) (supported formats). Then pick an instrument for each track; give the drum track a drum kit.
Edit like DAW 3 and 4. Double-click a MIDI region to edit its notes; select notes and quantize (right-click → Quantize, or Q) (Editing MIDI regions). Slice a region at the playhead with S, duplicate with Alt/Option-drag (Slicing and merging, Duplicating and extending).
Record audio. Add a Voice/Audio track, put your headphones on, and press R to record (R again stops). Hearing yourself (monitoring) is offered on Voice/Audio, Guitar and Bass tracks (Studio FAQ).
Fix the latency if your take lands late: BandLab has an automatic latency test; on iPhone and iPad it corrects itself (Fixing latency).
One effect, one automation move. Add an effect to the voice track (an EQ, a limiter), then switch on automation in the timeline and draw points so the voice comes up in the chorus (BandLab blog: the Mix Editor).
Download the mix. Project → Download → Mixdown As, then choose the format; single tracks can be downloaded as audio or MIDI (Downloading tracks, Exporting MIDI).



Live has two views: Arrangement (the timeline, as in these lessons) and Session (a grid of clips to launch). Tab switches. Work in Arrangement for this project. All shortcuts: Live keyboard shortcuts.

Set up audio. Live → Settings (Mac) or Options → Settings (Windows), Cmd/Ctrl+, → Audio: choose the driver and the input and output device (Audio settings; on Windows an ASIO driver is recommended; setting up an audio interface). The same page shows the buffer size and the overall latency.
Save the Set straight away (File → Save Live Set As). Live makes a Project folder for it; when you finish, File → Collect All and Save copies every sound the Set uses into that folder (saving Sets, collecting files).
Tempo and metronome: the tempo box and the metronome switch in the Control Bar (O); the count-in is in the menu next to the metronome (metronome settings, count-in).
Bring in your MIDI file: drag it from Live’s browser into the Arrangement, or Create → Import MIDI File (MIDI files). Each track arrives as a MIDI clip with no sound: drop an instrument on each, and a Drum Rack kit on the drum track.
Edit like DAW 3 and 4. Draw mode B; quantize Cmd/Ctrl+U; split Cmd/Ctrl+E; duplicate Cmd/Ctrl+D; loop the selection Cmd/Ctrl+L (splitting clips, the Arrangement loop).
Record audio. Insert an audio track (Create → Insert Audio Track), choose its input, arm it, and press the Arrangement Record button (F9) (choosing an input, arming tracks). An armed track is monitored by default (Auto); with speakers, set its monitor to Off (monitoring).
Fix the latency if your take lands late: Driver Error Compensation in Settings → Audio. It only applies to tracks with the monitor set to Off (Driver Error Compensation FAQ).
One effect, one automation move. Drag an audio effect onto the voice track. Press A to show automation, pick the track’s volume, and draw (or click) points so the voice comes up in the chorus (drawing and editing automation).
Export. File → Export Audio/Video (Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+R) for the mix; File → Export MIDI Clip for the notes of one clip (exporting audio, exporting MIDI).



Mac only. The user guide is for Logic Pro 12.3 (the version menu on each page goes back to older ones).

Set up audio. Logic Pro → Settings → Audio → Devices: the input and output device, and the I/O Buffer Size. Small for recording (less delay), large for mixing (more plug-ins); clicks and crackles mean it’s too small (Audio Devices settings, managing monitoring latency).
New project. File → New from Template (Cmd+N), New Project; open Details to set the tempo, key, time signature and the input and output device (Create projects). Every Cmd+S keeps a backup; File → Revert to goes back to one (alternatives and backups).
Metronome: K; count-in Shift+K; Control-click the metronome button to choose when it clicks (Use the metronome). Cycle: C (the cycle area).
Bring in your MIDI file: File → Import → MIDI File (it lands at the playhead), or drag it from the Finder into the Tracks area (Standard MIDI files). Choose a patch for each track.
Edit like DAW 3 and 4. Double-click a region for the Piano Roll; quantize with the Time Quantize menu and its Strength slider (it can always be undone) (quantize note timing). Edit → Split → Regions at Playhead (split regions), Edit → Repeat (repeat regions). Mixer: X. The band’s role is played by Session Players (Drummer, Bass Player, Keyboard Player) (Session Players); drum steps by the Step Sequencer (overview).
Record audio. Add Tracks (Option+Cmd+N) → Audio → Mic or Line, choose the Audio Input (Create tracks). Select the track, headphones on, R records, Space stops (record from a microphone). The guide itself says to use headphones when the metronome is on, so the click isn’t recorded.
Monitoring: the I button on the track header; it always adds some delay (input monitoring). Record → Low Latency Mode keeps it small (managing monitoring latency).
One effect, one automation move. Add a plug-in in an Audio FX slot (plug-ins). Press A to show automation, choose Volume, and click to add points (show automation, add points).
Bounce. File → Bounce → Project or Section; move the End a little past the last region so reverb tails aren’t cut off (bounce a project). Notes out: File → Export → Selection as MIDI File.

title: DAW 8: Your First Session in a Real DAW
text:
The project
Rebuild your small-DAW song, then do three things it couldn’t:

Same song, new sounds. Import mini-daw.mid, choose instruments, match the tempo. Play both mixes: what changed?
Record one real part with a microphone, in headphones, to the click (DAW 6). Record it three times and keep the best. Real DAWs keep every pass (takes) and let you build one from the best bits (comping): Logic, Ableton.
Add one effect and one automation move. Reverb on the voice, the chorus louder than the verse.
Bounce it, listen on earbuds and on a phone speaker, and fix the loudest problem (Recording 7: Mixing).
crumbs: DAW 8: Your First Session in a Real DAW

title: DAW 8: Your First Session in a Real DAW
section: What you’ll meet that wasn’t here
text:
What you’ll meet that wasn’t here

A loop and sound library: BandLab’s Sounds, Live’s browser, Logic’s Apple Loops. Fast to start with; remember everyone else has them too.
Plug-ins: EQ, compressors, reverb, delay, amp models, synths. The sound-design lessons taught what they do; now it’s only finding them.
Automation: any knob can move by itself through the song.
Generated parts: Logic’s Session Players and BandLab’s SongStarter do what the band does in DAW 4.
Clip launching: Live’s Session View and Logic’s Live Loops, for trying ideas live before arranging them.

title: DAW 5: The Mixer
text: Each track ends in a channel strip in the mixer: a fader for its level, a pan control for where it sits left to right, mute and solo, and a meter. All the strips add up in the master strip, which is what you hear and what is saved when you bounce. The mixer is the same in every DAW; only the colours change.

title: DAW 5: The Mixer
text:
The controls

Fader, in decibels (dB). 0 dB leaves the track as it is; −6 dB is about half its voltage, and to the ear a little under half as loud takes about −10 dB. Faders move in dB because the ear hears in ratios.
Pan: C is the middle, L100 / R100 hard left / right. Kick, snare, bass and the lead stay in the middle; spread the rest.
Mute (M) silences a track; Solo (S) silences every other track. Solo is for finding a problem; judge balance with everything playing.
Meter: how loud the track is, with a white peak mark. Green is fine, yellow is getting loud, red is close to 0 dBFS, the most a digital file can hold. Past it the waveform is cut off: clipping, a harsh crackle. The CLIP light stays lit once it happens (click it to reset).

title: DAW 5: The Mixer
text:
Fix a bad mix
This mix is wrong on purpose: the keys and guitar are too loud, the bass is nearly gone, the drums are buried, and everything is in the middle.

Play it. Is the master’s CLIP light coming on? Pull the Master down until it stops, then leave it there.
Start with the drums and bass: bring them up until the groove is solid.
Bring the keys and guitar down until they sit around the groove, not on top of it. Turning things down is most of mixing.
Pan the guitar to L40 and the keys to R40. Listen to how they stop fighting.
Solo the bass to hear what it’s doing, then un-solo. Mute the guitar: is the song better without it?
Double-click any fader or pan to put it back to 0 / centre.




The rest of mixing (EQ, compression, reverb on sends, references) is in Recording 7: Mixing; level and headroom before the mix in Recording 1: Gain Staging.

title: DAW 2: Programming a Beat
text: Most beats in pop, hip-hop and dance music are not played: they are programmed, one hit at a time, in a step sequencer. A bar of 4/4 is cut into 16 steps (sixteenth notes). Each row is one drum; each square is a step. Light a square and that drum hits there.

title: DAW 2: Programming a Beat
section: The parts of a drum row
text:
The parts of a drum row
Count a bar of sixteenths as 1 e & a 2 e & a 3 e & a 4 e & a. The thick lines are beats, the thin ones sixteenths.

Kick (bass drum): the low thump, usually on 1 and somewhere around 3.
Snare: the crack on 2 and 4, the backbeat. Move it and it stops sounding like pop music.
Hi-hat: the ticking that keeps time, in eighths (every other step) or sixteenths.

title: DAW 2: Programming a Beat
text:
Try it
The beat below is one bar, looping. The clip is selected, so its steps show under the tracks.

Press Play. Click squares on and off while it plays: a DAW lets you edit as it goes round.
Fill the closed hi-hat on every step, then only every other step. Which is busier?
Add a kick on the a of 2 (step 8). Then one on the & of 3 (step 11). This is the difference between a stiff beat and one that moves.
Velocity is how hard a hit is (0 to 127 in MIDI). Shift+click a hi-hat to make it an accent, Alt+click for a quiet ghost note. Accent every hi-hat on the beat, ghost a snare just before beat 4. Brightness shows velocity.
Try the Grid menu: at 1/8 there are 8 squares a bar; at 1/8 triplet 12, for a shuffle.
When you like it, make it longer: select the clip and press Duplicate (Ctrl/Cmd+D) three times. Now there are four bars; change the last one into a fill (snare and toms on the last few steps).
Switch on ⌨ Keys and play the kit from your computer keyboard: A kick, S snare, D closed hat, F open hat, G H toms, J crash, K ride.
