title: How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao
text:
This is a first lesson for someone who has never played congas. You will learn five ways to strike the drum, how they are written, and the most common conga part there is, the tumbao. You need one drum. If you have no drum yet you can still follow the notation and listen to the band play each step.
How to use the page. Every step has two bars of the part written large, a chord chart, and the whole chorus written on a conga staff. The note that is sounding lights up in the notation as the band plays. Press ▶ and the band plays it; the bar that is sounding lights up on the chart. Tick Congas alone to hear the congas without the bass and piano, and Leave out the congas to play them yourself. Each step starts in its own style and tempo; the strip at the bottom changes both.
About the sounds. The sounds on this page are General MIDI stand-ins. The computer has only an open tone, a muted tone and a low drum, so the heel, toe, slap and bass tones you hear here are approximations. Listen to a real player for the sound.
crumbs: How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao

title: How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao
text:
The drums
The conga is the higher drum of a pair, and the one this lesson uses. The tumba is the lower drum. A conga player often has both, and step 6 uses the tumba for a moment; everything else on this page is played on one drum.
crumbs: How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao

title: How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao
text:
Sitting and hands
This is ordinary advice, not a method. Sit upright, near the front of the chair, with the drum between your knees. Tilt it slightly away from you, or put it on a stand, so the bottom is open and the sound can come out. Keep your wrists and hands loose: a tight hand makes a dead sound and tires quickly. Take rings off. If anything hurts, stop and rest; a drum head is hard, and a beginner’s hands need time.
crumbs: How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao

title: How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao
text:
The five strokes
The names and the first description of each stroke are from the teacher’s handout. Each button plays the stroke.
Bass tone ▶ Hear it Strike the center of the head with the palm of the hand. It is the lowest sound the drum makes.
Open tone ▶ Hear it Strike near the edge of the head with the base of your fingers. Use the first four fingers at the edge and let them bounce off, so that the drum rings.
Muted tone ▶ Hear it Strike the center of the head with the palm of the hand, creating a deep tone. Teachers differ on this name. Some say “muffled”, and some mean a tone where the fingers stay on the head after the strike. The handout’s description is the one used on this page.
Slap tone ▶ Hear it Strike the edge of the head with flat fingertips to create a high, pinging sound. The slap is the hardest stroke to learn and takes time. Do not expect it to ring on the first day.
Heel-toe ▶ Hear it Strike the center of the head with the heel of the palm, then rock forward to slap with the fingers. It is a rocking motion of the hand: first the heel, then the fingertips. It is a quiet stroke, used as filler between the louder ones. On this page the two halves are written as two notes, heel and toe.
crumbs: How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao

title: How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao
text:
Reading a conga part
Click a note head to hear that stroke. The conga is written on the top space of the staff. The head says how it is struck: a plain head for the open tone and the bass tone, an ✕ for the slap, a triangle for the heel and the toe, and a diamond for the muted tone. The open tone and the bass tone look the same, so read the letter.



In a part, two lines of words sit under the notes. The first line is the stroke: H heel, T toe, S slap, O open, M muted, B bass. The second line is the hand: L left and R right. A left-handed player can reverse the hands. A low drum, when there is one, is written on a lower space.
crumbs: How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao

title: How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao
text:
1. The two notes everyone hears
The tumbao is built up from the end of the bar. Start with the two open tones, on 4 and the and of 4. Count “1 and 2 and 3 and 4 and” and play only on the last two. Use the right hand for both, one after the other.



These are the two notes a listener notices. When they come in the right place, the rest of the part has somewhere to go.
crumbs: How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao

title: How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao
text:
2. The right hand
Now add the slap on 2. The right hand plays all of it: the slap on 2, then the two open tones on 4 and the and of 4. Between them the right hand rests, and you keep counting.



If the slap will not come, play it as an open tone for now and come back to it. Take it slowly.
crumbs: How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao

title: How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao
text:
3. The left hand
Put the right hand away and play the other half. The left hand plays heel on 1, toe on the and of 1, toe on the and of 2, heel on 3 and toe on the and of 3. It is the rocking heel-toe stroke, quiet. The gaps left in the bar are where the right hand will go.
crumbs: How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao

title: How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao
text:
4. Both hands, slowly
Put the two hands together. The strokes in order are Heel Toe Slap Toe Heel Toe Open Open, and the hands are L L R L L L R R. The left hand plays every quiet heel and toe; the right hand plays the slap and the two open tones. This is the tumbao, as the handout writes it: a pattern of heel-toe-slap-toe figures and a pair of open tones. The sticking is the one given for the tumbao by Rebeca Mauleón in Salsa Guidebook, as quoted in the Wikipedia article on the tumbao.



This step is slow, and the band has no drummer, so the congas are easy to hear. Loop it and play along until your hands do not argue.
crumbs: How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao

title: How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao
text:
5. With a band
The same part in the Cha-cha, at a moderate tempo, with the drummer in. The tumbao is the most common pattern on congas and bongos, and it fits cha-cha, son and boogaloo. The Feel menu at the bottom plays it in the other two.



Listen for the clave in the other instruments: a rhythm of five notes over two bars, three in one bar and two in the other, that the whole band is built around. You do not need to play it to play the tumbao, but it explains the next step.
crumbs: How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao

title: How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao
text:
6. Two drums
Players who have two drums use the second one in the tumbao. Here, in Son montuno, every second bar the right hand plays two open tones on the low drum, on the and of 2 and on 3, in place of the toe and the heel. It is the bar with three clave notes (the second bar of a 2-3 clave, as Mauleón’s book has it, again via the Wikipedia article). Look at the two bars written large: the second has the notes on a lower space.



Stay on one drum until step 5 is easy. The two-drum bar is an extra, not a part of the basic tumbao.
crumbs: How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao

title: How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao
text:
Where to go next

Play step 5 with Leave out the congas ticked for ten choruses without losing the beat.
Take the tumbao to a tune: Watermelon Man for Congas plays it in a 16-bar blues.
Tools → Backing Track has a Congas menu that works in any style: put a tumbao under a tune you know.
Listen to a real conga player and copy what you hear. A page cannot give you the sound of the hands.
crumbs: How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao

title: Composing 5: Arranging for Orchestra
text:
Arranging means taking music that already exists, a melody with its chords, and deciding who plays what. The band version of this question is in Arranging 1. This lesson asks it for orchestral instruments, starting with the smallest orchestral group that can do everything: the string quartet (two violins, viola, cello).
How to use the page. ▶ plays each example on the piano (the site has no string samples), so listen for the parts: which line moves, which holds, which is on top. Then find a recording of a real quartet and listen for the same things.

title: Composing 5: Arranging for Orchestra
text:
1. Four jobs
Almost every arrangement gives out the same four jobs:








Job
What it does
Usually given to




Melody
the tune: what the listener follows
the highest part, or the instrument with the strongest sound in that register


Bass
the lowest note of each chord, which tells the ear what the harmony is
cello, double bass, bassoon, tuba


Harmony
the rest of the chord, filling the middle
inner parts: second violin, viola, horns, clarinets


Countermelody
a second tune that moves when the melody holds still
a contrasting instrument in a different register



Not every job is needed all the time. Taking one away (no bass, or melody alone) is one of the strongest effects an arranger has.

title: Composing 5: Arranging for Orchestra
text:
2. The same melody, two ways
The melody is the period from Composing 1. First as a chorale: the melody on top, the other three parts holding the chords. The texture is called homophonic: one tune, with chords moving in the same rhythm or slower.



Now with a countermelody in the second violin (it moves when the melody holds a long note, in bars 2, 4 and 6) and a bass that walks in quarter notes. The viola rests. Three lines that each have their own shape make a busier, more polyphonic texture.



Neither is better. The first is calm and warm; the second has more going on, and the melody has to work harder to be heard. Choosing between them depends on what you want the listener to feel. Write that reason down: it is your artistic choice, and explaining it is half of MYP Criterion B (see Process 2).

title: Composing 5: Arranging for Orchestra
text:
3. Techniques
Doubling. Two instruments play the same line, at the same pitch (unison) or an octave apart. Unison makes a new blended colour (flute and violin together sound like neither). Octaves make a line stronger and easier to hear. Doubling the melody is the simplest way to bring it out.
Spacing. Leave wide gaps between the low notes and put the close intervals at the top, the way the harmonic series does (see Sound 1). Close chords low down sound muddy. In the first quartet, the cello sits an octave or more below the viola.
Passing the tune around. Give the melody to a different instrument when it repeats: violin first, then cello an octave lower, then the clarinet. The listener hears the same tune in a new colour, and the players get a turn each.
Balance. A melody in the middle of the texture is easily covered. Make the accompaniment quieter (mark it p when the melody is mf), thinner (fewer notes), or further away in register.
Rests. Wind and brass players have to breathe, and every player needs to rest their lip, arm or hands. A part that plays every bar is tiring to play and to hear. Silence also makes an instrument’s return noticeable.
Write for the instrument. Check every part against the ranges in Composing 4, and write transposing parts in the player’s key. The transposer there does both.

title: Composing 5: Arranging for Orchestra
text:
4. Arrange a melody
Take a melody you know or have written: eight or sixteen bars with chords. Arrange it for the instruments your class has.

List your players, their instruments and their ranges.
Decide the four jobs for each section of the melody. Change something when the melody repeats.
Write it in the Notation page or a notation program. Check the ranges, transpose the parts.
Have the players play it, or play it back. Record it. Write down what didn’t work (a covered melody, a part too high, a muddy chord) and what you changed.
Keep the first version and the last version. The differences, and your reasons for them, are what your process journal shows.

title: Composing 5: Arranging for Orchestra
text:

title: Composing 1: Writing a Melody
text:
A melody is a line of notes that a listener can follow and remember. Most melodies that work have a few things in common. This lesson takes them one at a time, with a short example of each you can play. At the end you write eight bars of your own.
How to use the page. Press ▶ under any staff to hear it on the piano. The note that is sounding turns red.

title: Composing 1: Writing a Melody
text:
1. Shape: where the line goes
Draw a melody as a line on paper, going up and down with the pitch, and you get its contour. A good melody usually has one clear shape: an arch (up, then down), a wave, or a long fall. Most of it moves by step (to the next note of the scale), with a few leaps. After a big leap, the line usually turns and steps back the other way: that fills the gap the leap left.








The first has a climax: one highest note (the high C), reached once, on a strong beat, by a leap, and left by steps going down. The second leaps up and down at random. It is hard to sing back and hard to remember.

Rule of thumb. One high point, reached once. Mostly steps. Leap to a strong note, then step back. Keep it inside about an octave unless you have a reason not to.

title: Composing 1: Writing a Melody
text:
2. Rhythm that comes back
A listener remembers rhythm before pitch. If the opening rhythm comes back, the melody holds together even when the notes change. Here the same rhythm (two eighths and a quarter, twice) is used in three bars out of four, with new notes each time:



Try it the other way too: keep the notes and change the rhythm. Both are ways of developing an idea, which is the subject of Composing 2.

title: Composing 1: Writing a Melody
text:
3. Phrases: question and answer
Melodies come in phrases, usually four bars long, ending with a cadence: a resting point, like a comma or a full stop (see Cadences). Two phrases often pair up as a question and an answer.

The period
A period is eight bars: two four-bar phrases that start the same way. The first, the antecedent, ends with a weak cadence, often on the dominant (a half cadence). The second, the consequent, starts like the first and ends with a strong cadence on the tonic. It sounds like a question and its answer.



Bars 5–6 copy bars 1–2. Bar 4 stops on D over G: it wants to go on. Bar 8 lands on C over C: it is finished.


The sentence
A sentence is also eight bars, but it is built differently. A short basic idea (two bars) is stated and repeated (bars 1–4, the presentation). Then the continuation speeds up: the idea breaks into smaller pieces, and it drives to a cadence (bars 5–8).



Bars 3–4 repeat bars 1–2 a step higher. In bars 5–6 the two-bar idea is cut down to two-beat pieces, which makes the music speed up.

Which plan? A period sounds balanced and song-like: it suits a tune people will sing back. A sentence sounds like it is going somewhere: it suits a theme that has to build. Both are eight bars; both end on the tonic.

title: Composing 1: Writing a Melody
text:
4. Fitting the chords
If the melody has chords under it, the notes on strong beats (beats 1 and 3 in 4/4) usually belong to the chord. Notes between them can be anything that steps: they pass through or turn round and come back. In the period above, every note on beat 1 is in the chord written over it. Guide tones and reharmonizing go further.

title: Composing 1: Writing a Melody
text:
5. Write eight bars
Open the Notation page and write a period or a sentence, in any key you can play. A checklist to read before you start and again when you finish:

Does it have one high point? Where is it?
Is it mostly steps? Does each big leap turn back?
Does a rhythm come back?
Does bar 4 end open (not on the tonic), and bar 8 closed (on the tonic, on a strong beat)?
Can you sing it back without looking?

Keep every version you write, not only the last one, and note what you changed and why. That is the evidence that shows how you developed the piece: see Process 1: Keeping a Process Journal.
Next: Composing 2: Developing a Motif.

title: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz
text:
This lesson is for a pianist who plays pop and rock chords and hasn’t yet met jazz voicings. Its thirteen steps each change one thing from the step before: how many notes, which chord tones, or where they sit. Piano voicings by hand has the same chords in the order the hands find them easy.
How to read the diagrams. Each keyboard shows one voicing. The dots carry the chord tones, counted up from the root: R, 3, 5, ♭7, 9 and so on. The root is a filled square. The staff underneath puts the right hand on the treble clef and the left hand on the bass clef. Press ▶ to hear a voicing.
Fingers are numbered 1 (thumb) to 5 (little finger), listed from the lowest note up. Middle C is C4.
Each step has an ID, such as P-A3, that other lessons use to point back here. The chords stay the same throughout: C, Am, F and G for pop, and Dm7, G7, Cmaj7 for the ii–V–I. That way a step here can be played with the same notes as its partner in the physical order.
crumbs: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz

title: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz
section: P-A1 Root-position triads over a bass root
text:
P-A1 Root-position triads over a bass root
A triad is root, 3rd and 5th. The 3rd decides major or minor, and the 5th gives weight. The left hand names the chord with its root, and the right hand fills it in. This is the sound of most pop piano, and every later step rearranges these notes or adds to them.



Fingering: LH 5 on the root. RH 1-3-5.
Practice: play the four chords on a steady beat. Notice that the right hand jumps every time. The next step gets rid of the jumps.
Unlocks: Piano ballad with Long notes or Quarter-note chords.
crumbs: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz

title: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz
section: P-A2 Inversions and smooth voice leading
text:
P-A2 Inversions and smooth voice leading
Inverting a triad moves its lowest note to the top, so the hand can stay in one place. Here the note C stays put through the first three chords: it is the root of C, the 3rd of Am and the 5th of F. The other notes move by a step at most. This is voice leading: each note travels as little as it can, and the chords sound connected. The bass root still names the chord.



Fingering: RH root position 1-3-5, first inversion (3rd at the bottom) 1-2-5, second inversion (5th at the bottom) 1-3-5.
Practice: loop the four chords with your eyes closed after the first time round. The hand moves no more than a finger’s width. Then play the loop in F and in G.
Unlocks: Ballad: rocking, Ballad: half-broken, Arpeggio up and down.
crumbs: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz

title: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz
text:
P-A3 Sus and add9
Sus2 and sus4 replace the 3rd with the 2nd or the 4th. The chord is then neither major nor minor, and it wants to settle. Add9 keeps the 3rd and adds the 9th, the 2nd an octave up, for the shimmering open sound of pop ballads. Put the 9th above the 3rd, not right next to the root, or it rubs.



Fingering: sus2 1-2-5; sus4 1-4-5; Cadd9 (3–5–9) 1-2-5.
Practice: play Gsus4 and then G. One finger moves, as C falls to B. Then go from C to Cadd9.
Unlocks: Piano ballad, Arpeggio low and high; the Cadd9 bars of pop changes for piano.
crumbs: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz

title: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz
section: P-A4 Slash chords: a moving bass under still triads
text:
P-A4 Slash chords: a moving bass under still triads
The two hands now do separate jobs. The left hand walks the bass line C, B, A, G, F, F♯, G, and the right hand holds triads that barely move. A triad over a bass note other than its root makes a new chord with a new name. F over G, the last chord here, is the first jazz-flavoured sound in the sequence: G with ♭7, 9 and 11. P-A13 comes back to the idea.



Practice: play only the bass line, then only the right hand, then both together, slowly. Keep the right hand soft and let the bass line sing.
Unlocks: the passing chords in pop changes; Motown / soul.
crumbs: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz

title: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz
section: P-A5 Seventh chords in close position
text:
P-A5 Seventh chords in close position
A seventh chord stacks one more 3rd on the triad, and the kind of 7th sets the colour. A major 7th (B in Cmaj7) is bright and floating. A ♭7 (B♭ in C7) is bluesy and restless. In a minor chord the ♭7 is soft. A dominant 7th has a tritone between its 3rd and its 7th (B and F in G7), which wants to resolve.



Fingering: RH 1-2-3-5.
Practice: play C, Cmaj7, C7 and Cm7, changing one finger at a time, and put each colour into words.
Unlocks: Medium swing with Quarter-note chords; the 7th chords in blues for piano.
crumbs: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz

title: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz
text:
P-A6 Inverted 7ths: the ii–V–I
Choose each inversion so that the hand barely moves. From Dm7 to G7, F and D stay, A falls to G and C falls to B. From G7 to Cmaj7, F falls to E, D falls to C, and G and B stay. Each time, the 7th of one chord falls a step to the 3rd of the next: C to B, then F to E. That falling 7th is the engine of jazz harmony.



Fingering: RH 1-2-3-5 for each.
Practice: loop the three chords in time and sing the top line, D–D–C. Then move to F (Gm7, C7, Fmaj7) and B♭.
Unlocks: Medium swing, Charleston, and ii–V–I turnarounds.
crumbs: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz

title: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz
text:
P-A7 Guide tones: 3rd and 7th
The 3rd and the 7th are the only tones that tell major from minor and dominant from major 7th, so two notes can stand for the whole chord. The root belongs to the bass, and the 5th adds little. Follow the lines: C falls to B while F holds, then F falls to E while B holds. Guide tones goes further.



Fingering: RH 1-3 for a 4th; 1-4 for the tritone.
Practice: play the ii–V–I in guide tones, then sing each line. Add a top note of your own, any chord tone.
Unlocks: Charleston and Reverse Charleston without clutter; blues for piano.
crumbs: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz

title: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz
text:
P-A8 Shells: 1–3–7 and 1–7–3
A shell is root, 3rd and 7th in the left hand alone, which leaves the right hand free for a melody. In 1–3–7 order the shape spans a 7th and sits comfortably under one hand. In 1–7–3 order the 3rd is on top, a 10th above the root. That sounds more open, and it is the classic jazz left hand, but most hands need the right thumb to take the 3rd. The root is in the shell because, with no bass player, someone has to play it.



Fingering: LH 5-3-1 for 1–3–7. For 1–7–3, LH 5-1 on root and 7th, and RH 1 on the 3rd.
Practice: play the ii–V–I in the left hand only, then add a melody in the right. Alternate 1–3–7 and 1–7–3 (Dm7 1–3–7, G7 1–7–3, Cmaj7 1–3–7) so the hand hardly moves.
Unlocks: solo piano and comping without a bass; blues for piano.
crumbs: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz

title: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz
section: P-A9 Rootless voicings, A and B
text:
P-A9 Rootless voicings, A and B
With a bass player covering the root, the left hand plays the 3rd, the 7th and two colour tones: the 9th, plus the 13th on a dominant. Form A has the 3rd at the bottom and form B has the 7th at the bottom. Alternate them and each chord is only a step from the last. This has been the left-hand sound of jazz piano since the 1950s, and the site’s jazz styles use it. The Chord Library calls these Rootless A/B.



Fingering: LH 5-3-2-1 for A forms; 5-3-2-1 or 5-4-2-1 for B forms.
Practice: play the first chain (A–B–A) on a metronome, with the bass line D, G, C in the right hand. Then learn the chain that starts on B.
Unlocks: Jazz ballad, Medium swing with Charleston, Bossa nova, and Boogaloo.
crumbs: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz

title: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz
text:
P-A10 Drop 2
Take a four-note chord in close position and drop its second-highest note an octave. Dm7 in close position is D–F–A–C. The second note from the top is A, which drops to A3. The chord now spreads over an octave and a half, with the root back in the middle, and it sounds fuller and more orchestral. Put a melody note on top of a close chord, drop the second voice, and you have harmonised the melody.



Fingering: LH 2-1, RH 1-4 or 1-5.
Practice: take the first phrase of a melody you know. Play each melody note as the top of a close chord, then drop the second voice. Drop 3, where the third voice from the top drops, is the same idea one voice lower.
Unlocks: block-chord melody (George Shearing, Bill Evans), and Long notes under a singer.
crumbs: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz

title: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz
section: P-A11 Spread voicings: low 5th, upper triad
text:
P-A11 Spread voicings: low 5th, upper triad
An open 5th low in the left hand is the cleanest bass a piano has, because it stays out of the muddy middle register. Above it, the right hand plays a triad built from the 3rd, 7th and 9th. For Cmaj9 that is E–B–D, a little like an Em triad over C, which is why a rich chord can feel simple to play. The site has no voicing style for spread voicings yet.



Fingering: LH 5-1, RH 1-3-5 (or 1-4-5 where the lower gap is wide).
Practice: hold the low 5th with the pedal, then place the right hand above it. Learn the low 5th as one shape.
Unlocks: Arpeggio low and high, Ballad: syncopated, Jazz ballad, and gospel and singer-songwriter ballads.
crumbs: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz

title: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz
text:
P-A12 Quartal voicings
Stacking 4ths leaves no 3rd in the chord, so it is neither major nor minor. It sounds open, modern and modal. The best-known example is the “So What” voicing from Miles Davis’s Kind of Blue (1959): three 4ths and a major 3rd on top. Every interval in a stack of 4ths is the same, so the shape can slide up and down and keep its sound. The site has no quartal voicing style yet.



Fingering: LH 5-2-1 with RH 1-3 for the So What chord; RH 1-3-5 for a three-note stack.
Practice: play the So What chord, then the same shape a half step higher, and back. Then slide a three-note stack up the white keys from D.
Unlocks: modal jazz and Bossa nova.
crumbs: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz

title: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz
text:
P-A13 Upper-structure triads
The left hand plays a shell that fixes the chord’s name and type. The right hand plays a plain major triad built from the extensions above it. D major over a C shell gives Cmaj7 with a 9th, a ♯11 and a 13th. A major over a G7 shell is the same colour on a dominant. This is P-A4’s idea again: a triad over a different bass note. The site has no voicing style for upper structures yet.



Fingering: LH 5-3-1, RH 1-3-5.
Practice: play G7 as a shell, then place the A triad on top. Then try the D♭ triad and hear how strongly it pulls to C.
Unlocks: ballad endings, tags and turnarounds; reharmonising.
crumbs: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz

title: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz
text:
Where to go next

Piano voicings by hand has the same chords in physical order.
Guitar chord shapes has the same ideas on the guitar.
The Chord Library, set to Keyboard, has every close, shell, rootless and drop voicing of every chord.

title: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz
text:
This lesson is for a guitarist who knows open chords and strumming but hasn’t played jazz. Its thirteen steps go in order of how simple the voicing is. First come more chord types in familiar shapes, then fewer strings, then fewer chord tones, then more colour. Guitar chord shapes by hand has the same chords in the order the hand finds them easy.
How to read the diagrams. The neck stands upright, with string 6 (low E) on the left and the nut at the top. Each dot shows its chord tone: R is the root, and 3, 5, ♭7, 9 and so on are counted up from it. The fret numbers under each diagram run from low E to high E, and x is a string you don’t play. Press ▶ to hear a shape. The staff writes the chords an octave above where they sound, which is how guitar music is written.
Each step has an ID, such as G-A3, that other lessons use to point back here.
crumbs: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz

title: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz
text:
G-A1 Open triads
A triad is root, 3rd and 5th. A guitar has six strings, so some of those three tones are doubled: C x32010 is C–E–G–C–E, with the 3rd on two strings. The doubled tones and ringing open strings give the bright sound of folk and pop. The 3rd decides major or minor, and it is the only difference between E and Em.



Practice: loop C, Am, F, G (four-chord loops, loop 1) until the changes land in time with no gap. Play F as the small shape xx3211 until you reach the barre (G-A3).
Unlocks: the strummed styles of the Backing Track: Acoustic strum, Straight-eighth rock, Boom-chick.
crumbs: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz

title: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz
text:
G-A2 Fifths (power chords)
Root and 5th, sometimes with the octave on top. There is no 3rd, so the chord is neither major nor minor. Fifths stay clear under distortion, where the 3rds of two chords would clash, and they fit whatever 3rd the bass or the singer supplies. This is also the first time a chord leaves a tone out, which every later step does too. The shape is the same with the root on string 6 or on string 5, so one fingering moves anywhere.



Practice: play a 12-bar blues in fifths. Then rock between the 5th and the 6th on the middle string (E5 to E6 to E5), the classic rock-and-roll rhythm figure.
Unlocks: palm-muted eighth notes in rock and pop-punk.
crumbs: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz

title: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz
section: G-A3 Barre chords: the E and A shapes
text:
G-A3 Barre chords: the E and A shapes
Any open shape can move up the neck if your index finger replaces the nut. The root is under the barre: on string 6 for the E shape and on string 5 for the A shape. Those two shapes give all twelve major and minor chords, and this is the point where the neck becomes a map rather than a list of chords. The physical side is in G-B8 and G-B9.



Practice: play one four-chord loop in three keys, naming each root as you land on it.
Unlocks: the same strums in every key; Motown / soul.
crumbs: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz

title: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz
text:
G-A4 Sus and add9
A sus chord replaces the 3rd with the 2nd (sus2) or the 4th (sus4). With no 3rd it is neither major nor minor, and it leans toward resolving: Dsus4 falls to D as G moves down to F♯. Add9 keeps the 3rd and adds the 9th, the 2nd an octave up. It is sweet rather than tense. These are the colours of pop and 80s rock guitar, and the first chords in this sequence that go beyond a triad.



Practice: D, Dsus4, D, Dsus2, one bar each. Then alternate C and Cadd9.
Unlocks: sixteenth-note strums with hammer-ons, and fingerpicking (Travis pattern).
crumbs: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz

title: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz
text:
G-A5 Dominant 7th
A dominant 7th is root, major 3rd, 5th and flat 7th. The 3rd and the ♭7 are a tritone apart, and a tritone wants to resolve. Going from G7 to C, the 3rd (B) rises a half step to C and the ♭7 (F) falls a half step to E. That pull is what makes a chord dominant, and it drives the blues and every jazz tune.



Practice: play G7 to C slowly and find the two notes that move by one fret. Then see blues for guitar.
Unlocks: Blues shuffle, and a 12-bar blues on I7, IV7 and V7.
crumbs: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz

title: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz
text:
G-A6 Minor 7th and major 7th
A minor 7th is a minor triad plus a ♭7. It sounds soft and open rather than dark. A major 7th is a major triad plus the 7th one fret below the root, and it sounds dreamy. Pop already uses both: Am7 and Cmaj7 turn up all over pop changes for guitar. In jazz these two types, together with the dominant 7th, make up most of the harmony.



Practice: Cmaj7, Am7, Dm7, G7 (I–vi–ii–V) in open shapes. Then play it in F with barre shapes.
Unlocks: Bossa nova, and slow Charleston comping.
crumbs: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz

title: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz
text:
G-A7 Half-diminished and diminished 7th
Half-diminished (m7♭5) is a minor 7th with a flat 5th. It is chord vii in a major key (Bm7♭5 in C) and the ii chord in a minor key (see minor changes). A diminished 7th is a stack of minor 3rds, so the shape repeats every three frets with the same four notes. The F♯dim passing chord in pop changes is this chord.



Practice: slide a dim7 shape up three frets at a time. You’ll hear the same chord four times, with four different names.
Unlocks: the passing chords in turnarounds, and the minor-key ii–V–i.
crumbs: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz

title: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz
text:
G-A8 Shell voicings (root, 3rd, 7th)
The 3rd and the 7th are the guide tones: they say what kind of chord it is. The 5th adds the least, because the bass and the key already imply it, so a shell leaves it out. Root, 3rd and 7th make a chord thin enough to sit under a singer or a solo, which is how a rhythm guitarist plays in a jazz band. Shells come with the root on string 6 (strings 6, 4 and 3) or on string 5 (strings 5, 4 and 2). The Chord Library calls these Shell (R-3-7).



Practice: play C7, F7 and G7 as shells and watch the 3rd and the 7th: each moves a fret or two when the chord changes.
Unlocks: Four to the bar, Charleston, Reverse Charleston, and the Shell voicing in the Backing Track’s guitar menu.
crumbs: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz

title: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz
section: G-A9 Triads on the top strings
text:
G-A9 Triads on the top strings
Three strings and three notes, with nothing doubled. This is the cleanest chord on the guitar, and it sounds best in a band with a keyboard or a second guitar because it takes only a thin slice of the range. A triad has three positions, and each one moves the lowest note to the top. The shapes are small, so you can chain them with almost no movement. The Backing Track calls this Voice-led triads.



Practice: play C, F and G, choosing each time the shape nearest to the last.
Unlocks: funk sixteenths and reggae or ska off-beats on the top three strings.
crumbs: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz

title: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz
text:
G-A10 Drop 2 voicings
Start with a seventh chord in close position, its four tones packed inside an octave. Take the second note from the top and drop it an octave. The chord opens up enough to fit the fingers, and it still has all four tones. On strings 4, 3, 2 and 1, a ii–V–I in C moves every voice by a fret or two. That smooth movement between chords, the voice leading, is what jazz chord shapes are for.



Practice: play that ii–V–I, then move the same three shapes up five frets to F.
Unlocks: the Drop 2 guitar voicing in the Backing Track, with Bossa nova and Charleston comping.
crumbs: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz

title: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz
text:
G-A11 Drop 3 voicings
Drop the third voice from the top instead of the second, and the bass note moves down a string, leaving a string skipped in the middle. From the bottom up the tones are root, 7th, 3rd, 5th. Drop 3 sounds bigger than a shell and still has four notes. Guitarists use drop 3 when the chord needs a low root and weight, and drop 2 when it should sit higher and lighter.



Practice: play the ii–V–I in drop 3 (Dm7 x5x565, G7 3x343x, Cmaj7 x3x453), then in drop 2, and listen to how close the voice leading is.
Unlocks: the Drop 3 guitar voicing in the Backing Track, and slow ballad comping.
crumbs: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz

title: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz
text:
G-A12 Extensions: 9th and 13th
The 9th is the 2nd an octave up, the 11th is the 4th and the 13th is the 6th. An extension adds colour without changing what the chord does. C9 still pulls to F, only richer, and C13 is the dominant chord of a blues band’s horn section. Here’s a shortcut: an Em7 shape over a C bass note is Cmaj9, because E–G–B–D are the 3rd, 5th, 7th and 9th of C.



Practice: swap each dominant 7th of a 12-bar blues for a 9th or a 13th.
Unlocks: funk, Boogaloo stabs, and the jazz blues.
crumbs: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz

title: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz
text:
G-A13 Altered dominants
An altered dominant raises or lowers the 5th or the 9th to add tension just before the chord resolves. The ♭9 and ♯9 pull down toward the chord that follows, and the ♯5 pulls up toward its 3rd. Altered chords are short and high-energy, and they usually come at the end of a phrase. The 7♭9 shape, without its root, is a diminished 7th, which is why a dim7 shape can stand in for a 7♭9.



Practice: in a ii–V–I in C, play G7♯9 instead of G7 and listen to the tension release into Cmaj7.
Unlocks: endings, turnarounds and the last bar of a chorus in jazz comping.
crumbs: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz

title: How to Play Cajón
text: A cajón (“big box” in Spanish) is a wooden box you sit on and play with your hands. It came from Afro-Peruvian music in the 1800s; in the 1970s Paco de Lucía’s band took it into flamenco, and today it’s the drum of choice for acoustic pop and coffee-shop gigs. Most modern cajóns have snare wires or guitar strings inside behind the front face, which make the high notes buzz like a snare drum.

title: How to Play Cajón
text:
Parts of the cajón

The front plate (tapa): the thin face you strike, facing forward between your legs.
The sound hole: at the back. The low note comes out here, so keep it a little away from a wall, or put a microphone there.
Snares or strings: inside, against the top of the front plate. Many have a knob or key to tighten them or turn them off.

title: How to Play Cajón
text:
Sitting
Sit on top of the cajón, near the back edge, feet flat on the floor and apart. Tilt the box back a little on its back edge so the front plate is free and you can reach it; grip it with your calves. Play with the hands loose and the fingers together. Take off rings and watches. Keep your back straight: don’t hunch forward over the box.

title: How to Play Cajón
text:
The two main sounds









Sound
Where
How
Like a kit’s




Bass (B)
Middle of the plate, about a hand’s width below the top
Flat palm and fingers, let the hand bounce off
Bass drum


Slap (S)
Top corner, the top 5 cm or so
Fingers only, relaxed, the fingertips snap against the edge
Snare drum



Add a ghost note (g): a very soft finger tap near the top, felt more than heard, to fill gaps. A tone (T) between them, struck with the fingers in the middle, gives a round sound in between.
Practise the bass and the slap separately until each sounds clean: the bass low and boomy, without a buzz; the slap bright and cracking, without a thud.

text:

Counting in eighths, “1 & 2 & 3 & 4 &”:

Bass on 1 and 3 (and the “&” of 3), slap on 2 and 4: the backbeat. When it’s steady, add ghost notes on the empty eighths with the other hand, softly, to keep the hands moving: R L R L throughout.

title: How to Play Cajón
text:
More grooves

Sixteenths: keep the hands alternating R L R L in sixteenths with ghost notes; bring out the bass on 1 and 3 and the slap on 2 and 4. A busy pop and funk feel.
6/8 ballad: count “1 2 3 4 5 6”: bass on 1, slap on 4, ghost notes between.
Rumba flamenca: bass on 1, slap on 2 and 4, with quick ghost-note “rolls” of the fingers between.
Landó (Afro-Peruvian, in 12/8 or 6/8): the cajón’s own tradition. Listen to Peruvian groups such as Perú Negro before trying it; the accents sit between the beats in a way that’s hard to write down.

title: How to Play Cajón
text:
Extras

Brushes on the front plate, or a cajón brush on the side, give soft sweeps and a snare-like backbeat (see Playing Brushes).
A foot shaker or a jingle on the heel adds a constant eighth pulse.
A cajón pedal lets a drummer play the box with a kit bass-drum pedal.

title: How to Play Cajón
text:
Practice

Bass and slap alternately for a minute at 70 bpm: B S B S, right hand bass, left hand slap.
The first beat at 80, then at 100.
Play the first beat along with a song you know. Leave out the ghost notes until it’s steady.
Try the 6/8 groove against a slow song in 6/8 or 12/8.

title: Trumpet and Tuba Fingering Charts
text: Trumpet and tuba are brass instruments: the sound starts with your lips buzzing in a cup-shaped mouthpiece, and the tube of the instrument decides which pitches come out. The charts on this page are redrawn from two printed fingering charts (see the Works Cited). Use the controls above each chart to show or hide the staff and the letter names, so you can practise reading notes, hearing notes, or matching a fingering to a name.

title: Trumpet and Tuba Fingering Charts
text:
How the valves work

A brass instrument is a long tube. With no valves pressed the player can buzz only the notes of that tube’s harmonic series (the partials): for a trumpet written C4, G4, C5, E5, G5 and so on. Tighter lips and faster air go to a higher partial.
Each valve opens a short extra loop of tubing. A longer tube means a lower pitch.
The usual pattern on a three-valve instrument: valve 2 lowers the note by a half step, valve 1 by a whole step, and valve 3 by a step and a half. Combinations add up (1 + 2 = a step and a half; 1 + 2 + 3 = three whole steps). Those sizes are the standard ones, but they are not printed on these charts (see “What is unverified”).
That is why one fingering plays many notes: a note is a fingering (which valves) plus a partial (how your lips and air are set). The charts print the partials in rows: the row number is the partial and the column is the fingering.
A tuba often has a fourth valve. On the tuba chart, valve 4 is printed as an alternate for the notes of 1 + 3, and 2 + 4 as an alternate for 1 + 2 + 3.

title: Trumpet and Tuba Fingering Charts
text:
Explore the chart
Pick an instrument, then a note. The card shows the staff, the valves (dark = pressed down), any alternate fingering, and the other notes the same fingering plays. Hear it plays a synthesized brass-like buzz.

Trumpet is a transposing instrument: the chart is for a B♭ trumpet. The staff and names show written pitch (what the player reads); choose Concert pitch to see what you hear: a whole step lower.
Tuba is read in the bass clef. This chart does not say which tuba it is for; the page shows it as B♭ tuba at concert pitch.

title: Trumpet and Tuba Fingering Charts
text:
Press valves: which notes?
Press valves and the page lists every note on the chart that fingering can play (low to high). In the quiz you are given a note and press its valves. On the trumpet quiz the note is a written note.

title: Trumpet and Tuba Fingering Charts
section: The printed chart, as a table
text:
The printed chart, as a table
Each column is a valve combination. Each row is one of the chart’s partials. This is the same information as the printed charts. Click a note to hear it.

title: Trumpet and Tuba Fingering Charts
text:
What is unverified
These are the things this page is not sure of. Check them with your teacher.

The tuba chart does not say whether it is for a B♭, C, E♭ or F tuba. The notes it prints fit a B♭ tuba (open notes B♭, F, B♭, D, F), so that is how the page shows it. Other tubas use the same valve patterns for different note names.
The charts number the partials from “1st” at the lowest row they print. Acoustically those are not the 1st partial of the tube (the pedal tone is below them), so the numbers are the chart’s own.
The sizes of what each valve does (half step, whole step, step and a half, perfect fourth for the tuba’s 4th valve) and the trumpet’s B♭ transposition are standard textbook facts, listed in the Works Cited, but not printed on the two charts.
The footnote “move the 3rd valve slide out for low D and C♯” is on the trumpet chart; the page shows the star but not how far to move the slide.
Valve-4 fingerings are shown for the tuba notes F, C (with 4) and E, B (with 2 + 4) only, as the chart prints them.
The sounds are a synthesized buzz, not a recording of a real trumpet or tuba.

title: Blues for Piano: From Roots to Rootless Voicings
text:
This is how a pianist plays chords on a 12-bar blues, built up from one finger. You need to be able to find notes on the keyboard by name. For what the chords are and how the form gets varied, see Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues.
How to use the page. Every step has a keyboard diagram, a chord chart and a ▶ button that starts the band. Above the keys there is one coloured lane for each chord, with a square over every key that chord uses, so you can compare chords by looking straight up and down. Middle C is marked in green. Click a chord’s name at the left of its lane to hear it. Under the keyboard the same notes are written on a grand staff. In every line of notation the note that is sounding lights up, whether the notation is playing by itself or the band is playing. While the band plays, its pianist plays exactly the notes shown, and the bar on the chart and the chord being played both light up. Tick Leave out the piano to take the part yourself. The strip at the bottom sets the key, the tempo and whether the squares show chord tones or note names.
crumbs: Blues for Piano: From Roots to Rootless Voicings

title: Blues for Piano: From Roots to Rootless Voicings
text:
1. The roots
The root is the note a chord is named after: the root of C7 is C. A blues has three chords and so three roots. Play them with the left hand, low on the keyboard, one long note per bar.



Count the form as you play: four bars of I, two of IV, two of I, then V, IV, I, I.
crumbs: Blues for Piano: From Roots to Rootless Voicings

title: Blues for Piano: From Roots to Rootless Voicings
text:
2. What the 3rd and 7th do
A seventh chord has four notes. Starting on the root, take every other note of the scale: the root, the 3rd, the 5th and the 7th. They do different jobs.

The root names the chord. In a band the bass player plays it.
The 5th adds weight and not much else.
The 3rd says whether the chord is major or minor.
The 7th says what kind of seventh chord it is. Every chord in a basic blues has a major 3rd and a flat 7th (♭7), which makes it a dominant seventh chord.

So the 3rd and 7th carry the chord’s character. They are called the guide tones. Here are all four notes of each chord in the right hand, root at the bottom. The 5th is dashed because it is the first note to leave out. Click a chord name to hear the notes climb.




Where the flat 7 comes from
Why is the 7th of these chords called flat? The answer is in the major scale. Press ▶ to hear each line of notation. The explanation follows the key chosen in the strip at the bottom.
crumbs: Blues for Piano: From Roots to Rootless Voicings

title: Blues for Piano: From Roots to Rootless Voicings
text:
3. Guide tones over a root
Now play only the 3rd and 7th in the right hand, with the root in the left. Look down the lanes: the right hand’s two notes hardly move. Going from I7 to IV7, each note drops a half step, and they swap jobs: the 3rd becomes the ♭7th and the ♭7th becomes the 3rd. For V7 both notes sit a half step above the I chord’s.
To keep the hand still, the two notes are not always in the same order. Sometimes the 3rd is on the bottom and sometimes the 7th. Switch the labels to chord tones to see which.



The band’s pianist plays a short chord on beat 1 and another just before beat 3. Try that rhythm once the changes are comfortable.
crumbs: Blues for Piano: From Roots to Rootless Voicings

title: Blues for Piano: From Roots to Rootless Voicings
text:
4. Shells in the left hand
Put root, 3rd and 7th in the left hand alone and the right hand is free for a melody. A three-note chord with the 5th left out is a shell voicing. To keep the hand in one place the notes are rearranged from chord to chord, so the root is not always on the bottom.



Play a chorus of shells with the left hand only. Then add one note of your own in the right hand per bar. Any chord tone will do.
crumbs: Blues for Piano: From Roots to Rootless Voicings

title: Blues for Piano: From Roots to Rootless Voicings
text:
5. Rootless voicings
When there is a bass player, the root is taken care of, and the left hand can spend its fingers on colour instead. A rootless voicing is the two guide tones plus two notes from higher up the chord: the 9th (a whole step above the root) and the 13th (the same note as the 6th). There are two forms, one with the 3rd on the bottom and one with the 7th on the bottom, and they alternate so the hand barely moves. This is the standard left-hand sound of jazz piano since the late 1950s.



The dashed square is the root, shown only so you can see where the voicing sits in relation to it. Leave it to the bass.
crumbs: Blues for Piano: From Roots to Rootless Voicings

title: Blues for Piano: From Roots to Rootless Voicings
text:
6. The jazz blues
The last line of a jazz blues is a two-five: ii7, V7, then home to I, with VI7 in bar 8 to lead into it (the reasons are in section 3 of the changes lesson). The ii chord is a minor seventh chord: its 3rd is a half step lower than a dominant chord’s. Through ii7, V7 and I7 the guide tones take turns to fall by a step: the 7th of each chord drops to become the 3rd of the next.



The same chorus with rootless voicings in the left hand:
crumbs: Blues for Piano: From Roots to Rootless Voicings

title: Blues for Piano: From Roots to Rootless Voicings
section: 7. A tune: Blues in the Closet
text:
7. A tune: Blues in the Closet
Oscar Pettiford’s riff blues. Its changes are the three-chord blues with a two-five in bars 9 and 10 and a V chord in bar 12. The melody is one two-bar riff played three times. Here it is over guide tones and a root.



The riff’s second note is the 3rd of the home chord. In bars 5 and 6 it drops a half step to become the ♭7th of IV, the same move your right hand makes. Once the guide tones are secure, play the riff in the right hand and rootless voicings in the left:
crumbs: Blues for Piano: From Roots to Rootless Voicings

title: Improvising on a Blues: Blues in the Closet
text:
This lesson is about making up your own melody over a twelve-bar blues, using Oscar Pettiford’s Blues in the Closet as the model. It is for any instrument. You should already be able to play the tune (it is taught in Blues for Violin and Saxophone, section 7) and know what the chords are (Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues).
Choose your instrument first. The Instrument menu in the strip at the bottom sets up the page for you.
Where this page says “concert”, it means the note as the piano hears it.
How to use the page. Every line of notation has a ▶ Play button, and the note that is sounding lights up. The chord charts have ▶ Play with the band; the piano plays the written line unless you tick Leave out the melody. Under each note is its place in the chord (R = root) or its number in the scale.
crumbs: Improvising on a Blues: Blues in the Closet

title: Improvising on a Blues: Blues in the Closet
text:
1. Start from the melody
The best first solo on any tune is the tune. It already fits the chords, it already has a rhythm, and the listener already knows it.



Three things about this melody are worth stealing.

It is a riff. One two-bar idea, played three times. A solo built from one idea that is repeated and changed a little sounds like it means something. A solo of new ideas in every bar does not.
It uses four notes: the root, the 3rd, the 4th and the 5th below. You do not need many.
It leaves space. Each line ends on a long note. Half of each phrase is silence or holding.

Exercise. Play the tune. Then play it again and change one thing: leave a note out, repeat a note, or play the rhythm of the riff on a single pitch. Keep the long notes where they are. Do that for several choruses before you go on.
crumbs: Improvising on a Blues: Blues in the Closet

title: Improvising on a Blues: Blues in the Closet
text:
2. Hitting the change
The most important moment in a blues is bar 5, where the home chord gives way to IV. In this tune the melody marks it with one note. In bars 1 to 4 the riff’s second note is the 3rd of the home chord (concert A when the tune is in F). In bars 5 and 6 that note drops a half step (concert A♭), and it is now the ♭7th of the IV chord. In bar 7 it goes back up.
A soloist who plays the higher note in bar 5 sounds lost: it is a half step away from a note the chord needs. A soloist who plays the lower one sounds like they know the tune. That is what players mean by hitting the change (or making the change).
Here is that move alone: one note per bar, the 3rd or 7th of each chord, taking the nearest one at every change.



Exercise. With Leave out the melody ticked, improvise using only the rhythm of the riff and the notes of this line: the upper note in bars 1 to 4, the lower one in bars 5 and 6, the upper again in bar 7. It is very little to play with. Hit the change every time, exactly on bar 5, before you add anything else.
crumbs: Improvising on a Blues: Blues in the Closet

title: Improvising on a Blues: Blues in the Closet
text:
3. The minor blues scale
Six notes, and it can be played over the whole twelve bars without changing anything. That is why it is the first scale most improvisers learn.



Counted from the key note it is R, ♭3, 4, ♯4, 5, ♭7. Two of those are blue notes:

The ♭3 is the same pitch as the note that hit the change in section 2 (concert A♭ in F). Over the IV chord it is a chord tone. Over the home chord it rubs against the chord’s major 3rd, and that rub is the sound of the blues.
The ♯4 is a passing note between 4 and 5. Slide through it; do not sit on it.

What this scale does not have is the major 3rd of the home chord. Played for a whole chorus it sounds dark and tough, and it never quite says which chord you are on.
crumbs: Improvising on a Blues: Blues in the Closet

title: Improvising on a Blues: Blues in the Closet
text:
4. The major blues scale
The brighter one. Counted from the key note: R, 2, ♭3, 3, 5, 6.



It has both thirds: the ♭3 and the major 3rd, side by side. That is the same pair of notes the melody uses to hit the change. Sliding from the ♭3 up to the 3 is one of the most recognisable sounds in the music. This scale fits the home chord perfectly, because its 3, 5 and 6 belong to it.
It fits the IV chord less well. Its major 3rd is the note that section 2 told you to leave in bar 5.
Putting the two together. Use each scale where it is strongest:








Bars
Chord
Scale to favour




1 to 4
I7
major blues: lean on the 3


5 and 6
IV7
minor blues: lean on the ♭3

major blues again


9 to 12
ii7, V7, I7, V7
either; the minor blues scale covers all four



That table is the melody’s own plan. Blues in the Closet uses the major 3rd on the home chord and the lowered one on IV.
crumbs: Improvising on a Blues: Blues in the Closet

title: Improvising on a Blues: Blues in the Closet
text:
5. The pentatonic scales
Take the ♯4 out of the minor blues scale and five notes are left: the minor pentatonic.



Take the ♭3 out of the major blues scale and you have the major pentatonic.



Why bother with scales that have fewer notes?

Nothing in them clashes. Neither scale has a half step in it, so no two of its notes rub against each other, and any of them can be held. They are the safest notes there are.
They fall under the hand. On guitar and bass the minor pentatonic is the first position most players learn, two notes on every string. On a wind or string instrument it is five notes with no awkward corners.
The minor pentatonic covers the whole chorus, exactly as the minor blues scale does. Use it when you want to think about rhythm and phrasing and not about notes.
A major pentatonic built on a chord’s own root always fits that chord. It is the chord’s root, 3rd and 5th plus its 2nd and 6th: no 4th and no 7th, the two notes that cause trouble. So one more way through the form is three pentatonics: the home chord’s in bars 1 to 4, the IV chord’s in bars 5 and 6, and so on.
Two for the price of one. The major pentatonic of the key has the same five notes as the minor pentatonic that starts a minor 3rd below it. Compare the scale below with the major pentatonic above. If you know one shape, you know the other.




The blues scales are these two pentatonics with one extra note each: the ♯4 added to the minor, the ♭3 added to the major. Those added notes are the blue notes.
crumbs: Improvising on a Blues: Blues in the Closet

title: Improvising on a Blues: Blues in the Closet
section: 6. A scale for each chord: Mixolydian
text:
6. A scale for each chord: Mixolydian
The blues scales treat the whole chorus as one sound. The other way to improvise is to give each chord its own scale. A dominant seventh chord takes the Mixolydian scale: a major scale with the 7th lowered. Its 1, 3, 5 and ♭7 are the chord, and the notes between join them up. (Where that lowered 7th comes from is explained in the “flat 7” panel of the instrument lessons.)
For the home chord:



For the IV chord:



Compare them note by note. They share every pitch but one. The home chord’s scale has its major 3rd; the IV chord’s scale has that note a half step lower, as its ♭7. It is the same half step as in section 2, the one the melody plays. Hitting the change and changing scale are the same act.
For the V chord:
crumbs: Improvising on a Blues: Blues in the Closet

title: Improvising on a Blues: Blues in the Closet
text:
7. The two-five: Dorian
Bars 9 and 10 are ii7 then V7. A minor seventh chord takes the Dorian scale: a major scale with the 3rd and the 7th lowered.



Now look back at the V chord’s Mixolydian scale above. It is the same seven notes, started from a different place. The ii chord and the V chord of a two-five share one scale, so bars 9 and 10 need only one set of notes, and the melody shows it: the riff passes over both chords unchanged.
That scale is also the plain major scale of the key. So the whole chorus comes down to three sets of notes, each one note different from the last:

Bars 9, 10 and 12 (ii7 and V7): the major scale of the key.
Bars 1 to 4, 7, 8 and 11 (I7): lower its 7th. That is the home chord’s Mixolydian.
Bars 5 and 6 (IV7): lower the 3rd as well. That is the IV chord’s Mixolydian.

To hear the notes that tell these scales apart, this line plays the ♭7, 6, 5 and 3 of every chord, one bar each:
crumbs: Improvising on a Blues: Blues in the Closet

title: Improvising on a Blues: Blues in the Closet
text:
8. Your chorus
Nothing is written here. The band plays the changes and the chorus is yours. Tick Loop in the strip at the bottom to keep it going.



A plan for practice, one item per session:

The melody, varied a little more each chorus (section 1).
Only the two notes of the change, in the riff’s rhythm (section 2).
Only the minor blues scale, in two-bar phrases with two bars of rest after each.
Major blues scale on the home chord, minor blues on IV, following the table.
Three major pentatonics: the root’s own, for whichever chord is sounding.
Chord scales: one chorus where every phrase ends on the 3rd or ♭7 of the chord of the moment.
Trade fours with the band: you play four bars, rest four, play four.

In every one of them, hit the change in bar 5.
To hear what the chords are doing under your solo, see guide tones and the changes lesson.

title: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle
text:
This is the 12-bar blues from the drum chair, starting with nothing but the beat. You need to be able to hit the ride cymbal (or hi-hat), the snare and the bass drum, and to work the hi-hat pedal. For what the chords are and how the form gets varied, see Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues.
How to use the page. Every step has two bars of the beat written large, a chord chart, and the whole chorus written on a drum staff. The note that is sounding lights up in the notation as the band plays. Press ▶ and the band plays it; the bar that is sounding lights up on the chart. Tick Drums alone to hear the drummer without the bass and piano, and Leave out the drums to take over. Each step starts in its own feel and tempo; the strip at the bottom changes both.
crumbs: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle

title: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle
text:
Reading a drum part
Each line or space of the staff is one part of the kit. Cymbals and anything struck on the rim are written with an ✕. What the hands play has stems up; what the feet play has stems down. Click a piece to hear it: the picture shows where each one is written, and the line under it has the same notes in the same places, so you can click those too. Hover over any drum note on this page and it tells you which piece it is.
crumbs: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle

title: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle
text:
1. The beat and the form
A drummer has two jobs on a blues: keep the time, and know where in the twelve bars the band is. Start with the plainest time there is. The ride cymbal (or the closed hi-hat) plays all four beats. The left foot closes the hi-hat on 2 and 4. Nothing else.



Count the bars out loud while you play: four bars, then four more, then the last four. The chords change at bar 5, bar 7 and bar 9. Listen for the bass moving and learn to hear those moments coming.
crumbs: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle

title: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle
text:
2. The ride pattern
Swing time on the ride cymbal is the four beats plus a skip note just before beats 3 and 1: ding, ding-a, ding, ding-a. It is written as two eighth notes, but the first is long and the second short, as if the beat were divided in three and you played the first and last parts. Keep the hi-hat foot on 2 and 4.



Listen with Drums alone to hear how late the skip note sits. Slow the tempo down and it gets later still.
crumbs: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle

title: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle
text:
3. Swing time
Now the other two limbs. In swing the bass drum is played very quietly on all four beats, felt more than heard (feathering), and it is not written. The snare does not keep time: it answers the band with a note here and there, often on the last part of a beat. The band’s drummer improvises this, so the notation changes every chorus.



Start with the ride pattern and the hi-hat foot. Add one snare note per bar, on the “a” of beat 4, and leave it at that until it is comfortable.
crumbs: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle

title: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle
text:
4. Showing the form
A fill tells the band where it is. On a blues the places to mark are the ends of the three four-bar phrases: bar 4, which leads to the IV chord; bar 8, which leads to the last line; and bar 12, which leads back to the top. The small ones need only a beat or two. The one in bar 12 can be bigger, and the crash on beat 1 of the next chorus is its landing.



Keep the time going right up to the fill and come out of it on beat 1. A fill that loses the beat is worse than no fill.
crumbs: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle

title: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle
text:
5. The shuffle
The beat of Chicago blues. The cymbal plays the swung eighths all the way through, long, short, long, short, with the bass drum on 1 and 3 and a full snare on 2 and 4. This is the first beat on this page with a backbeat.
crumbs: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle

title: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle
text:
6. The slow blues in 12/8
At a slow tempo every beat divides in three, and the cymbal plays all three parts. Kick on 1 and 3, snare on 2 and 4. It is written here in 4/4 with triplets; the same beat is often written in 12/8.
crumbs: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle

title: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle
text:
7. Straight eighths
Not every blues swings. In a boogaloo or a rock blues the eighth notes are even. The cymbal plays eight to the bar, the bass drum is on 1 and 3, and the left hand plays a cross-stick on 2 and 4.
crumbs: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle

title: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle
text:
8. Grabbing the crash
A crash cymbal rings for a long time. Sometimes you want the accent without the ring: hit the crash, then catch its edge with the other hand straight away, so that it stops. Drummers call this a choke. It is written as a short crash with choke over it.
Here the band plays the straight-eighths beat from step 7 with a small fill at the end of bars 4 and 8, and the crash is grabbed on beat 1 of bar 5 and bar 9, the first bar of the second and third lines. Hit the crash together with the bass drum, and have the hand on the cymbal before beat 2. Then go straight back to the time. When the band stops at the end, the last crash is grabbed too.



Try it with the loop on and listen to the gap the choke leaves. A grabbed crash says “here” louder than a ringing one, because of the silence after it.
crumbs: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle

title: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle
section: 9. A tune: Blues in the Closet
text:
9. A tune: Blues in the Closet
Oscar Pettiford’s riff blues, at a medium swing. The melody is one two-bar riff played three times, and each time it ends on a long note, in bars 4, 8 and 12. Those are the same three places step 4 marked with fills. The tune leaves the space; the drummer fills it and sets up the next phrase.



Play time through the riff and stay out of its way: no snare on top of the melody’s accents. Read the melody while you play. A drummer who knows the tune plays the form without counting.
crumbs: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle

title: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle
text:
Where to go next

Loop each step with the drums left out and play it for ten choruses without losing the form.
Play the fills step with your own fills in bars 4, 8 and 12.
Take a chorus from the changes lesson: the busier the chords, the more the band needs the form marked clearly.

title: Blues for Bass: From Roots to a Walking Line
text:
This is the 12-bar blues from the bass player’s chair, starting from one note per chord. You need to know how to fret a note and pluck it. Everything else is built here, one step at a time. For what the chords are and how the form gets varied, see Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues.
How to use the page. Every step has fretboard diagrams, a chord chart and a ▶ button that starts the band. The diagrams read like a bass standing upright in front of you: the low E string is on the left, the nut is at the top, and the numbers down the side are frets. Click a chord’s name above a diagram to hear its notes. Under the diagrams the same notes are written on a staff, and below the chord chart is the bass line the band is playing. In every line of notation the note that is sounding lights up, whether the notation is playing by itself or the band is playing. While the band plays, the bar on the chart and the diagram of the chord being played both light up. Tick Leave out the bass and the band’s bass player stops so that you can take the part. The strip at the bottom sets the key, the tempo and whether the dots show chord tones or note names.
crumbs: Blues for Bass: From Roots to a Walking Line

title: Blues for Bass: From Roots to a Walking Line
text:
1. The roots
The root is the note a chord is named after: the root of G7 is G. A blues has three chords, so it has three roots, and they sit close together. Find the key note on the E string. The root of the IV chord is at the same fret on the next string up. The root of the V chord is two frets higher on that same string. Your hand does not have to move.
In four keys (C, D♭, D and E♭) the key note is a long way up the lowest string, so the diagrams start from the next string instead. Then the root of V is at the same fret on the lowest string and the root of IV is two frets below that.
Start with two notes in each bar, on beats 1 and 3.



Count the bars as you play: four of I, two of IV, two of I, then V, IV, I, I. When that is steady, play the root on every beat. Press Superimposed to see all three roots on one fretboard.
crumbs: Blues for Bass: From Roots to a Walking Line

title: Blues for Bass: From Roots to a Walking Line
text:
2. Root, fifth and octave
The fifth of a chord is one string up and two frets up from its root. The octave (the root again, higher) is two strings up and two frets up. Index finger on the root, ring or little finger on the other two: the three notes make a box that has the same shape on every chord. Move the box to each root you learned in step 1.



The band’s bass plays root on beat 1 and fifth on beat 3. Play that first, then try root, fifth, octave, fifth, one note to a beat.
crumbs: Blues for Bass: From Roots to a Walking Line

title: Blues for Bass: From Roots to a Walking Line
text:
3. The 3rd and the 7th
The root and fifth say which chord it is but not what kind of chord. Two other notes do that job.

The 3rd says major or minor. In a dominant seventh chord (G7) it is a major 3rd: one string up and one fret back from the root.
The 7th in a blues chord is a flat 7th (written ♭7), a whole step below the octave: two strings up at the same fret as the root.

Together they are called the guide tones, because they are the notes that change the most tellingly from one chord to the next. Root, 3rd, 5th and ♭7th are the four chord tones. Click each chord’s name to hear them climb.




Where the flat 7 comes from
Why is the 7th of these chords called flat? The answer is in the major scale. Press ▶ to hear each line of notation. The explanation follows the key chosen in the strip at the bottom.



The band’s bass plays exactly that: root, 3rd, 5th, ♭7th, one note on every beat, the same shape in every bar. The line is written out below the chord chart. It is not a walking line yet. It is the four chord tones in order, so that your hand learns each shape and your ear learns what each note sounds like against its chord.
Work up to it in three stages, each for a few choruses:

Root on beat 1, 3rd on beat 3. Two notes to a bar.
Root, 3rd, 5th, and rest on beat 4.
All four notes, as the band plays them.

Then switch to Superimposed and look at I and IV together. The 3rd of the I chord is one fret below the root of IV, and the ♭7th of I is one fret above the 3rd of IV. Those half steps are how the chords connect.
crumbs: Blues for Bass: From Roots to a Walking Line

title: Blues for Bass: From Roots to a Walking Line
text:
4. Walking
In step 3 every bar went the same way: up the chord from the root. A walking line also has one note on every beat, but it chooses its notes so that each bar leads into the next. Three changes turn the step 3 line into a walking line: the notes after the root can come in any order, the octave joins them, and the last note of the bar points at the next root. A recipe that always works:

Beat 1: the root of the chord.
Beats 2 and 3: any two other chord tones (3rd, 5th, ♭7th, or the octave).
Beat 4: an approach note, one fret below or one fret above the root of the next bar’s chord.

When the next bar is the same chord, beat 4 can be any chord tone. The diagram shows the chord tones of all three chords at once. A split dot is a note two chords share.
Between the chord tones you can also step along the scale that goes with the chord. Over the I chord that is the scale from step 3, the major scale with its 7th lowered a half step (called Mixolydian). Here it is in one place on the neck, with the run written in tablature. Beats 2 and 3 can borrow its notes, so a bar can climb step by step instead of jumping.






Listen to the band’s bass player for a chorus, then tick Leave out the bass and walk it yourself. Slow the tempo down as far as you need. A plain line that lands on the root at every chord change is worth more than a busy one that does not.
crumbs: Blues for Bass: From Roots to a Walking Line

title: Blues for Bass: From Roots to a Walking Line
text:
5. The jazz blues
The last line of a jazz blues is a two-five: ii7, V7, then home to I, with VI7 in bar 8 to lead into it (the reasons are in section 3 of the changes lesson). The ii chord is a minor seventh chord. Its 3rd is a minor 3rd, three frets above the root on the same string. Everything else about the shape stays the same.



In bars 11 and 12 the chords change every two beats. Play the root on the beat each chord arrives and one other note after it: root and 3rd, or root and an approach note into the next root.
crumbs: Blues for Bass: From Roots to a Walking Line

title: Blues for Bass: From Roots to a Walking Line
section: 6. A tune: Blues in the Closet
text:
6. A tune: Blues in the Closet
Oscar Pettiford, who wrote this tune, was a bass player. Its changes are the three-chord blues with a two-five in bars 9 and 10 and a V chord in bar 12 to turn it round. The melody is one two-bar riff played three times, so the bass has room to be heard.



Play roots through the form first, two to a bar, and listen to how the riff sits against them. Then walk it. In bars 4 and 8 the melody holds one long note: that is the place for your line to lead clearly into the next chord. In bar 12, aim for the root of the V chord and then back to the top.
crumbs: Blues for Bass: From Roots to a Walking Line

title: Blues for Bass: From Roots to a Walking Line
text:
Where to go next

Change the key in the strip at the bottom and find the same shapes in the new place. Start with F, B♭, A and E.
Loop a chorus with the bass left out and record yourself over the band.
Learn to improvise over the same tune in the improvising lesson.
Take any chorus from the changes lesson and walk through it with the recipe from step 4.
Next on bass: pop changes for bass, roots and the walking line.
