title: Arranging 4: The Organ
text:
The tonewheel organ (the Hammond B-3 and its relatives) is in gospel, soul, blues, jazz and rock. It looks like a piano but behaves very differently: a key has no touch, a note sounds for as long as you hold it, and the sound is built by the player from nine pitches. Then it goes through a chorus, a volume pedal, and a speaker that spins.
The organ on this page is the band’s own: nothing is recorded, every note is built from the same parts as the real instrument. (How it’s built and where the numbers come from: apps/shared/band/ORGAN.md. It’s a model, so some of its levels are informed guesses.) Everything you set here is also what the organ plays in the band at the bottom of the page.

title: Arranging 4: The Organ
text:
1. The organ
Hold a key on the keyboard, or press Hold a chord, then work the controls while it sounds.

title: Arranging 4: The Organ
text:
2. Tonebars (drawbars)
Each of the nine bars adds one pitch to every key you press. Each bar is named by the length of an organ pipe in feet: the 8′ is the note you play, 16′ is an octave below, 4′ an octave above, and so on. The white bars are octaves of the note. The black ones are the 5ths and 3rd above it, which give the sound its colour. The two brown bars are the sub-octave pitches.
Each bar has nine positions, 0 (in, silent) to 8 (all the way out, loudest). Each step is about 3 dB. A registration is written as the nine numbers in three groups: 88 8000 000 means the first three bars all the way out and the rest pushed in.
Try this:

Start from 00 8000 000: the note alone, nearly a pure tone. Pull out the 4′, then the 2′, and watch the pitches stack up on the right.
Pull out the 1⅗′ alone over the 8′. That’s the 3rd, two octaves up. The organ’s 3rd and 5ths are slightly out of tune with a pure harmonic, because they come from tonewheels tuned to the keyboard. That’s part of the sound.
Pick 88 8888 888: the whole organ.

title: Arranging 4: The Organ
text:
3. Chorus and vibrato
A scanner sweeps the sound through a very short delay, 6.9 times a second. On its own that wobbles the pitch: vibrato (V3). Mixed half and half with the plain sound the wobble becomes a shimmer: chorus (C3), the setting most players leave on for jazz, gospel and soul. Switch between Off and C3 chorus on a held chord to hear it.

title: Arranging 4: The Organ
text:
4. The swell pedal
Because a key sounds the same however hard you press it, the organist plays dynamics with the right foot. The swell pedal is a volume pedal that never quite closes: at its quietest the organ is 24 dB down and the bass is kept up so the sound doesn’t go thin. It sits before the amplifier, so opening it also makes the sound grittier.
Organists open the pedal through the end of a phrase into the next one, pull it back sharply after a big hit, and ride it the way a singer leans into a long note.

title: Arranging 4: The Organ
text:
5. The Leslie speaker
The organ’s sound goes into a cabinet where it is split: the high notes go into a horn and the low notes into a drum, and both spin. As each one turns toward you it gets a bit louder and higher; as it turns away it gets softer and lower. That’s the swirl.

Slow (“chorale”): about 48 turns a minute. A gentle movement.
Fast (“tremolo”): about 400 turns a minute. A shimmering, urgent sound.
Stop: the rotors stand still.

The best part is the change. The light horn reaches its new speed in about a second and a half; the heavy drum takes about five. Switch from Slow to Fast on a held chord and listen to it wind up, then switch back and hear it wind down. The picture spins at the model’s speeds.

title: Arranging 4: The Organ
text:
6. The organ in the band
Here the organ comps in three styles. Unless you’ve taken them over above, the band’s organist works the pedal and switch by itself: the pedal follows how hard the band is playing and opens into each new phrase, and the Leslie goes fast at the end of a phrase that leads into a chorus. In swing, the speaker stays slow until the very end. Untick Let the band’s organist… above (or just move the control) to take them over.
Soul jazz, organ comping a boogaloo:



Swing, organ comping a jazz blues:



Ballad, long organ chords under a slow song (try 68 8600 000 and a low pedal):

title: Arranging 4: The Organ
text:
7. Try it

Set 00 8000 000, chorus Off, Leslie Stop. That’s a plain electronic tone. Now put back the chorus, then the Leslie on Slow, then pull out the 16′ and 5⅓′. Each step makes it more like the organ on a record.
In the boogaloo, take over the Leslie and switch it to Fast just before bar 9 each time round.
In the ballad, take the pedal and play the dynamics: low through the first two bars, opening through bar 4 into the top.

title: Arranging 2: Bass and Drums
text: The bass and drums are the foundation. If they agree, a band can lose everyone else and still sound like a band. This page is about how they agree. How the examples work is explained in the first lesson.

title: Arranging 2: Bass and Drums
text:
1. The bass follows the kick
The kick drum and the bass are both low and both short at the start of a note. When they land together they sound like one big instrument. When they land apart, the bottom of the band sounds busy and blurred.
Below, the drums play the same pop backbeat throughout. Try each bass line against it. Look at the bass staff and the kick drum (the lowest notes on the drum staff) and see where they line up.



The dotted line is the one the style was written with: the bass plays exactly where the kick plays. The others still work, but they make a different song: roots on every beat is plainer, eighths push harder, root and fifth sounds like country.

title: Arranging 2: Bass and Drums
text:
2. The drums choose the feel
Now keep the bass line and change the groove. Each one divides the beat differently or puts the backbeat somewhere else.



Half-time moves the snare from 2 and 4 to 3 only: the chords go by just as fast but the song feels half as fast. Arrangers use it for a breakdown or a big final chorus. Four on the floor puts the kick on every beat, which is why the root-eighths bass now sounds like it’s doubling something.

title: Arranging 2: Bass and Drums
section: 3. Swing: the bass walks, the ride keeps time
text:
3. Swing: the bass walks, the ride keeps time
In jazz the roles change. The ride cymbal carries the time, the kick drum mostly keeps out of the way, and the bass plays a note on every beat. That’s a walking line: the root on beat 1, other notes of the chord and scale in between, and a note on beat 4 that leads into the next chord.
Compare it with the lighter two-feel (half notes) that a band often plays on the melody before walking for the solos, and with plain chord tones.

title: Arranging 2: Bass and Drums
text:
4. Latin: the bass anticipates
In son montuno and salsa, the bass plays the tumbao: it doesn’t land on beat 1 at all. The new chord’s root arrives early, on the and of 2 and on 4, and rings over the barline. The clave and congas mark the beat instead.



Switch the congas off, then the drums. With only the bass left, you can hear that it is always a beat ahead of the chord chart.

title: Arranging 2: Bass and Drums
text:
5. Try it

In section 1, play the Root eighths line, then switch the drums to Half-time in section 2. Which bass line would you choose for a half-time chorus?
Next: Guitar and keyboards.

title: Annotated Bibliography 1: What It Is and Why I Chose It (Grades 6–8)
text:
A bibliography is a list of the sources you used. An annotated bibliography adds a few sentences under each source: what it is, whether it’s any good, and how you’ll use it. It shows your teacher that you didn’t just find sources; you read them and thought about them.
This builds on Sources 1, which covers how to find a good source in the first place.
crumbs: Annotated Bibliography 1: What It Is and Why I Chose It (Grades 6–8)

title: Annotated Bibliography 1: What It Is and Why I Chose It (Grades 6–8)
text:
The three-sentence recipe
Under each source, write three sentences:

What is it? Say in your own words what the source is and what it covers.
Why do I trust it? Who made it, and how do they know? Is there anything to be careful about?
How will I use it? What does it help you find out or do?
crumbs: Annotated Bibliography 1: What It Is and Why I Chose It (Grades 6–8)

title: Annotated Bibliography 1: What It Is and Why I Chose It (Grades 6–8)
text:
An example
Say your project is about the jazz album Kind of Blue. Your annotated bibliography might start like this:

Davis, Miles. Kind of Blue. Columbia, 1959.
This is the album itself, played by Miles Davis’s band, with John Coltrane, Cannonball Adderley and Bill Evans. I trust it because it’s the real recording, not someone describing it. I’ll listen to “So What” to find the places where the band changes from one scale to another, and write down the times.


“Modal Jazz.” Wikipedia, Wikimedia Foundation, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz.
This article explains what modal jazz is and names Kind of Blue as an important example. Anyone can edit Wikipedia, so I’ll only use it to start, and check its facts in the sources listed at the bottom of the page. I’ll use it to learn the words I need, like “mode”, and to find better sources.

The second example is honest: it says what the source is good for and what to be careful about. That’s what a good annotation does.
crumbs: Annotated Bibliography 1: What It Is and Why I Chose It (Grades 6–8)

title: Annotated Bibliography 1: What It Is and Why I Chose It (Grades 6–8)
text:
Rules of thumb

Use your own words. Don’t copy sentences from the source. Read it, look away, then write what you remember. Then check that you got it right.
Don’t quote. An annotation is about the source, not a copy of a piece of it.
Put the list in alphabetical order by the first word of each entry (usually the author’s last name).
Call it “Annotated Bibliography” at the top.
Different kinds of sources are better than many of the same kind. A recording, a score and a book are better than three websites.
crumbs: Annotated Bibliography 1: What It Is and Why I Chose It (Grades 6–8)

title: Annotated Bibliography 1: What It Is and Why I Chose It (Grades 6–8)
section: Things that don’t go on the list
text:
Things that don’t go on the list






WarningThe AI summary is not a source, so it can’t go on your list



The answer that Google, Bing or a chatbot writes at the top of your search was made by a computer. No person wrote it, it can be wrong, and it changes every time you ask. It doesn’t belong in your bibliography. If it gave you an idea, find a real page or book that says the same thing, read it, and put that on your list.


Also leave out anything you didn’t actually read, watch or listen to.
crumbs: Annotated Bibliography 1: What It Is and Why I Chose It (Grades 6–8)

title: Annotated Bibliography 1: What It Is and Why I Chose It (Grades 6–8)
text:
Try it
Pick a song or piece you like.

Find three sources: the recording, one page about the song or the artist from a trusted website, and one more (a video interview, a book from the library, or the sheet music).
Write each one down with who made it, what it’s called, where it is, and when it was made.
Under each, write the three sentences: what is it, why do I trust it, how will I use it.
Swap with a partner. Can they tell, from your annotations alone, which source is the most useful?

Next: Annotated Bibliography 2 (grades 9–10).

title: Annotated Bibliography 2: Summarise, Evaluate, Connect (Grades 9–10)
text:
In Annotated Bibliography 1 each annotation had three sentences: what is it, why do I trust it, how will I use it. At this level, the annotation does more work. It summarises the source, evaluates it (often by comparing it with your other sources), and connects it to your project.
It builds on Sources 2: primary and secondary sources, SIFT, and MLA citations.

title: Annotated Bibliography 2: Summarise, Evaluate, Connect (Grades 9–10)
text:
Descriptive and evaluative
A descriptive annotation says what the source is and what it covers, like the abstract at the top of a journal article. An evaluative (or critical) annotation also judges it:

Authority: who is the author, and why should we listen to them?
Evidence: what is the source based on (recordings, interviews, archives, the author’s own experience)?
Audience and purpose: who was it written for? Is it selling something?
Comparison: how does it fit with your other sources? Does it agree, add something, or contradict them?
Use: what exactly will you take from it, and for which part of your project?

Your teacher may ask for one kind or the other. If they don’t say, write evaluative annotations.

title: Annotated Bibliography 2: Summarise, Evaluate, Connect (Grades 9–10)
text:
MLA format
The MLA Style Center’s guidance:

Write each source’s entry exactly as you would in a Works Cited list. Put the annotation after it.
Annotations can be short phrases. If you write full sentences, leave a line after the entry and start the annotation with a paragraph indent.
Annotations describe or evaluate the source. They don’t quote the author, cite evidence, go over minor details, or retell every step of the argument.
Title the list Annotated Bibliography (or Annotated List of Works Cited).
Order the entries alphabetically, unless your teacher asks for another order (by date, or by topic).

About 50–150 words per source is typical. Check your task, though: some ask for exactly two to four sentences.

title: Annotated Bibliography 2: Summarise, Evaluate, Connect (Grades 9–10)
text:
Paraphrase without copying
A paraphrase that follows the source sentence by sentence, with a few words swapped, is still copying. Here’s a way to avoid it, from Kate Turabian’s guide for writers: read the passage, look away, think about it, and write it in your own words while still looking away. Then check: if you can run your finger along your sentence and find the same ideas in the same order in the source, so can your reader. Try again.

title: Annotated Bibliography 2: Summarise, Evaluate, Connect (Grades 9–10)
text:
Two examples

Chaffin, Roger, and Gabriela Imreh. “‘Pulling Teeth and Torture’: Musical Memory and Problem Solving.” Thinking and Reasoning, vol. 3, no. 4, 1997, pp. 315–36.
A case study of a concert pianist learning a Bach piece for performance, built from video recordings of her practice sessions and her own comments on them. The authors found that she started and stopped her practice segments at the boundaries of the music’s form, not at random. It’s one pianist, so it can’t prove what all musicians do, but it’s careful, detailed evidence from inside an expert’s practice. I’ll use it to justify cutting my piece into sections that follow its phrases, and compare it with the larger survey studies on practice.


“Kind of Blue Transcription.” MuseScore, uploaded by a user.
A note-for-note transcription of the album’s first track, uploaded by an anonymous user. There’s no named transcriber and no edition, and I found two wrong notes in bars 9–12 when I checked it against the recording. I’ll use it only as a rough guide, correct it by ear, and cite the recording as my main source.

(The second example is invented, to show the kind of thing to write.) It’s a weak source, honestly evaluated. Including a weak source with a clear-eyed annotation is better than pretending it’s strong. If it’s too weak to use, leave it out.

title: Annotated Bibliography 2: Summarise, Evaluate, Connect (Grades 9–10)
section: AI summaries don’t get an entry
text:
AI summaries don’t get an entry






WarningAI-generated answers are not sources, and they aren’t reliable



An AI summary from Google, Bing or a chatbot has no author and no fixed text, so your reader can’t check it. These summaries often get facts wrong, and AI tools regularly invent sources that don’t exist: book titles, authors, and links that lead nowhere.

Never put an AI summary in your annotated bibliography as a source.
Never copy a reference an AI tool suggested unless you’ve found the real thing and read it yourself.
If an AI answer pointed you somewhere, go to that place. Read the actual source, and annotate that.

title: Annotated Bibliography 2: Summarise, Evaluate, Connect (Grades 9–10)
text:
Try it
Choose a research question about a style you’re studying.

Find four sources: at least one primary (a recording, a score, an interview) and at least one scholarly secondary source (a book from the library, or an article from Grove Music Online or JSTOR).
Run SIFT on each one.
Write an MLA entry and an evaluative annotation of 50–150 words for each, comparing each source with at least one of the others.
Swap with a partner. Underline every phrase in their annotations that could be copied from the source. Rewrite your own underlined phrases using the look-away method.

Next: Annotated Bibliography 3: DP Music (grades 11–12).

title: X32: Drums on One Fader
text:
A miked drum kit takes up eight or nine channels. During a show you want to turn the whole kit up or down with one hand, and mute it with one button. The X32 has two tools for this:
Page numbers below are the PDF pages of the Behringer X32 Preliminary User Manual (links in Works Cited).

title: X32: Drums on One Fader
section: Before you start: a channel plan
text:
Before you start: a channel plan
Plug the drum mics into neighbouring channels and name them. A typical kit:



Ch
Mic
Name on the scribble strip




1
Kick (inside)
KICK IN


2
Kick (outside)
KICK OUT


3
Snare top
SNARE T


4
Snare bottom
SNARE B


5
Hi-hat
HAT


6
Rack tom
TOM 1


7
Floor tom
TOM 2


8
Overhead left
OH L


9
Overhead right
OH R



Your kit may have fewer mics; the steps are the same. Set each drum’s gain, low cut, gate and EQ first (Live Sound lessons 2–5) and get a rough balance between them on their own faders. The DCA then moves that balance up and down as one.

title: X32: Drums on One Fader
text:
DCA or group bus?
A DCA (digitally controlled amplifier) does not mix the drums into a new signal. It just moves every assigned channel’s level at once, so each drum still has its own fader for small fixes (manual p. 32).
A group is a mix bus that the channels feed at unity gain: the drums really are summed into one signal. Use one when you want to process the whole kit together, for example one compressor across all the drums, which “would not be possible with a DCA group” (manual p. 32–33). For one fader to ride the kit during a show, use a DCA. You can use both.

title: X32: Drums on One Fader
text:
Overheads on a noisy stage
The overheads (channels 8 and 9) are the hardest mics on the kit. They hang over the cymbals, a long way from any drum, so they also hear the guitar amps, the bass rig, the wedges and the singer. On a loud stage that bleed can make up more of their signal than the drums do. Push the DRUMS DCA up and the whole band gets louder with it.
Use directional mics. Use cardioid or hypercardioid overheads, not omnis. With hypercardioids, watch for “hot spots” when they point straight down (La Cerra). Omnis only work set low and close over the kit.
Pick a height. La Cerra’s starting point is “approximately six feet high, pointing either straight down to the floor or angled toward the center of the kit.” Higher gives a more even blend of the cymbals. Lower and closer gives more drum and less stage. On a noisy stage, start low, just above the cymbals’ reach, and raise them only as far as the blend needs.
Aim the dead side at the noise. A cardioid hears least from directly behind. Angling the overheads slightly toward the audience “increase[s] rejection of the drum monitors” (La Cerra). Do the same for a guitar amp or a wedge that sits close to the kit: turn the back of the mic toward it.
Keep them in step. Two mics at different distances from the snare cause phase trouble (thin, hollow drums). Measure from the centre of the snare to each overhead and make the two distances equal. Then press the X32’s mono button in the monitor section and listen: if the kit goes thin when both are up, move one mic. The 3:1 rule (mics at least three times as far from each other as from their source) is a rough guide for spaced mics often quoted by engineers (unverified: no source checked yet).
Clean them up on the console.

Low cut high. The kick and toms have their own mics, so the overheads only need cymbals and some snare. Try 150–300 Hz; the X32 goes up to 400 Hz (Maillot p. 26).
No gate. Cymbals ring for a long time and a gate chops them off (Live Sound 4).
Less fader. In a small, loud room the cymbals carry on their own. Bring the overheads up only until the cymbals sit right in the PA. Sometimes the right level is very low, or one overhead, or none.

Turn the stage down. No mic choice fixes everything. Ask the guitarist to point the amp away from the kit or turn it down. Turn down the drummer’s wedge, or fill it with less of everything else. A quieter stage helps every mic, not only the overheads.

title: X32: Drums on One Fader
text:
Make the DCA

On the right-hand fader section, press GROUP DCA 1-8 so the eight faders there are DCAs (p. 16, 32).
Hold the Select button of DCA 1.
While holding it, press Select on every drum channel: 1 through 9. If the channels are on another layer (17–32), switch the left-hand layer while still holding DCA 1’s Select. Inputs, aux channels, FX returns and bus masters can all go in a DCA (p. 32).
Let go. To check, press DCA 1’s Select again: the Select buttons of its channels light up (p. 8, 32).
To take a channel out, hold DCA 1’s Select and press that channel’s Select again (it toggles; not stated in the manual, so check that the light goes off).

Name it. Press SETUP, page right to DCA GROUPS, turn the first encoder to DCA 1 and press it. Pick a colour, an icon and the name DRUMS, then press the sixth encoder to leave (p. 32).
Use it. Leave DCA 1 at 0 dB (unity) while you build the drum balance on the channel faders. In the show, ride DCA 1. Its Mute button mutes the DCA and its Solo solos all its channels (p. 16). Solo on a DCA is PFL unless you choose DCA Group AFL in the monitor’s solo preferences (p. 31).







Monitor mixes. A DCA works by moving channel levels after the fader. Sends to the stage monitors that are set pre-fader should not follow it; post-fader sends (reverb, for example) should. The manual does not spell this out: check it once by watching a monitor bus meter while you move DCA 1.

title: X32: Drums on One Fader
text:
Make the mute group
A mute group has a safety step so you can’t mute channels by accident while you set it up (p. 8):

Press MUTE GRP next to the main screen. The screen shows the mute group view, and the channel Mute buttons stop muting while you assign (p. 32, 59).
Hold Mute Group button 1 (bottom right of the console, beside the Main LR fader).
While holding it, press Select on drum channels 1–9 (any layer, inputs or outputs) (p. 59).
Let go, and press MUTE GRP again. The buttons work normally again (p. 32).
Press Mute Group 1 to mute the whole kit; press it again to bring it back (p. 32).

Good uses: mute the drums between songs or while the drummer is setting up; put the drum reverb return in the same mute group so the reverb tail mutes too.

Mute Group 1 mutes the drums wherever they go. Muting DCA 1 does the same job from the DCA fader. Pick one and tell the other people who run the board, so nobody wonders why the drums won’t come back.

title: X32: Drums on One Fader
text:
Save it
Store a scene once it works (the Scenes buttons, p. 17). The DCA names and assignments live in the console’s setup, and the manual says DCA group settings “are stored with the Scene data” (p. 28). Load the scene at the start of the next rehearsal, and press DCA 1’s Select to check the drums are still in it.

title: X32: Drums on One Fader
text:
If it doesn’t work







Problem
Check




Pressing channel Selects just selects them
You let go of the DCA’s (or mute group’s) button too soon. Hold it the whole time.


The faders on the right are buses, not DCAs
Press GROUP DCA 1-8 (p. 16).


Mute group buttons mute nothing
MUTE GRP is still on (assign mode). Press it again (p. 32).


Drums silent and nothing looks muted
Check DCA 1’s Mute and Mute Group 1. Both can mute the kit.


The drum balance changed
Someone moved a channel fader. The DCA keeps the channels’ balance; it doesn’t store it.

title: X32: Drums on One Fader
section: For the curious: what the console stores
text:
For the curious: what the console stores
In Maillot’s OSC reference, each channel keeps its groups as two numbers: /ch/01/grp/dca (8 bits, one per DCA) and /ch/01/grp/mute (6 bits, one per mute group) (p. 28). Each DCA has its own on, fader, name, icon and color (p. 39). The Config → Mute System preferences include “Hard Mutes” and “DCA groups” (p. 56); the reference names them but doesn’t say what they do, so leave them alone unless you’ve tested them.

title: Yamaha MODX
text: The Yamaha MODX is a synthesizer keyboard. It has pianos, organs, strings, synths and drum kits built in. It can also be a sound card for the computer. Plug in one USB cable, and the computer can record the MODX and play sound back through it. You don’t need a separate audio interface.

title: Yamaha MODX
text:
The parts you’ll use







Part
What it’s for




Touch screen
Choose sounds (a sound is called a Performance), change settings


Super Knob (the big knob)
Changes several settings at once. Turn it while you play to change the sound


Scene buttons
Up to 8 saved versions of the current sound. Press one to switch


CATEGORY SEARCH
Find a sound by type: Piano, Keyboard, Organ, Strings, Synth Lead, Drum…


[EXIT]
Goes back one screen. Press it again and again to get home


Back panel: OUTPUT L/MONO, R
Two 1/4” jacks to the mixer or speakers. Use only L for mono


Back panel: A/D INPUT
Plug in a mic or guitar here to send it through the MODX


Back panel: USB TO HOST
USB cable to the computer, for MIDI and audio


PHONES
Headphones. Turn the master volume down before you put them on

title: Yamaha MODX
text:
Find a sound

Press [CATEGORY SEARCH].
Touch a category (for example Piano), then touch a sound in the list.
Play. Turn the Super Knob to hear how the sound changes.
Press [EXIT] when you’re done.

You don’t need to save to play a sound. Save only if you change one and want to keep it.

title: Yamaha MODX
section: Using the MODX as an audio interface
text:
Using the MODX as an audio interface
This is the easiest way to record a keyboard part. One USB cable carries everything: the notes you play (MIDI), the sound of the MODX (audio into the computer), and the computer’s sound (audio back out of the MODX’s outputs and headphones).

Setup

Connect USB TO HOST on the MODX to the computer with a USB cable (USB-A to USB-B).
Turn the MODX on.
On the computer, open your DAW’s audio settings:

Input device: Yamaha MODX
Output device: Yamaha MODX
Sample rate: 44.1 kHz

Make an audio track. Set its input to the first stereo pair (1–2). Arm it and press record.
Plug headphones into the MODX, or run its outputs to the mixer. You hear the computer and the keyboard together, from one place.

That’s all. No extra boxes, no extra cables, no mic stand.


Why it’s easy

One cable. A normal setup needs a keyboard, an audio interface, two audio cables and a USB cable. The MODX does all of it.
Clean sound. The audio stays digital from the MODX into the computer. Nothing to hum, no gain knob to set too high or too low.
One place to listen. The computer’s playback comes out of the MODX’s headphone jack, so you hear the backing track and your playing together, with no lag.
Mic or guitar too. Plug a mic or guitar into A/D INPUT and it goes to the computer over the same USB cable.



Things to check if it doesn’t work







Problem
Try




The computer doesn’t list “Yamaha MODX”
Use a different USB cable (some only charge). Plug straight into the computer, not a hub


Windows: no MODX audio device
Install the Yamaha Steinberg USB Driver from Yamaha’s website


You hear yourself twice, a little late
Turn off input monitoring on the DAW track. You already hear the MODX directly


No sound from the computer
Check the DAW’s output device is the MODX, and the MODX master volume is up


Recording is silent
Check the track’s input is 1–2 and the track is armed









Note



Unverified: Yamaha community forums disagree on whether a Mac needs the Yamaha driver or works without one, and on the exact number of USB audio channels (often quoted as 10 out to the computer and 4 back, at 44.1 kHz). Check the MODX Owner’s Manual before relying on these.

title: Yamaha MODX
section: Play the site’s band on it
text:
Play the site’s band on it
The MODX band page sends the Backing Track band’s notes to the MODX, so its bass, keys, guitar or drums play on the board instead of in the browser. It compares each sound side by side so you can pick which instruments to send. If the computer’s sound also comes out of the MODX (set the computer’s output to the MODX), both come out of the same speakers, and the timing is easier to line up.

Shared links and your data
Your ticks and choices are saved only in the browser you use. Each page has a share link that holds them, so you can send your plan to your teacher or open it on another device. Nothing is sent anywhere until you share the link yourself.

title: Enrichment
text:
How it works

Everyone does the common core. A few minutes of tonal and rhythm patterns each week, one song by ear each unit, and the unit’s words. This is how everyone grows in audiation, whatever else they choose.
Choose one or two options each unit. Pick from any strand. Set each one to Planning, Working on it or Done, and note what you did or made: that note is evidence you can use.
Enrichment can feed your assessed work. Each option says where it can show up: a technique to explore in Bi, a skill for your Criterion C piece, research for Ai, or a DP component.
Watch your growth. Every option is tagged with the Music Learning Theory level it mostly trains. The ladder at the bottom shows the levels you have reached and suggests what to try next.

title: Enrichment
section: Your growth through the MLT levels
text:
Your growth through the MLT levels
Gordon’s skill learning sequence (Learning Sequences in Music, Table 17, p. 230) runs from learning by ear, through naming and reading, to the inference levels where you teach yourself: working out unfamiliar music, creating, and explaining. You don’t climb it once: a new tonality, meter or instrument starts lower down again. Gordon also lets students bridge across to the inference levels as soon as they are ready, so creating does not have to wait until you can read. The tags on the options are this course’s reading of what each activity mostly asks of you.

Skill learning sequence: partial synthesis (pp. 111–117), the verbal association warning (p. 108), generalization-aural/oral and -verbal (pp. 131–133); same is easier to hear than different (p. 219); tonal and rhythm patterns kept apart (p. 223); rhythm patterns chanted with vocal inflection like speech (p. 101); macrobeats stressed, not accented, and approached with a decrescendo, expression found between macrobeats, anacruses given special attention, weight and flow, displaced energy in rests and long durations (pp. 187–190).; Theory Concepts pages: Keyality versus key signature (p. xiii); tonality “best refers to what is usually called a mode,” the eight tonalities (p. 149); movable-do with la-based minor and the rhythm syllables du de, du da di (p. 105); resting tone and tonic, a tonality in any keyality (p. 150); unitonal and multitonal music (pp. 152, 157); usual duple, triple and combined meter (pp. 175–176); no direct relation between measure signatures and meter, 6/8 as “duple compound” called inaccurate (p. 176); accents and microbeat divisions do not make meter (pp. 176–177); unusual meter, paired and unpaired, intact, macrobeats versus microbeats establishing meter (pp. 179–180); key signatures as do signatures, one signature for many tonalities (pp. 155–156); rhythm syllables by beat function (p. 86); time-value names lead to counting (p. 38); writing tonal patterns from a familiar do signature (p. 125); letter names and time-value names as the alphabet of music (pp. 36–37); interval names learned in context of tonality and keyality (p. 65); the raised seventh of harmonic minor as si (p. 70); mi si ti re as a harmonic minor dominant pattern (p. 100).; Course pages (glossary, enrichment): audiation defined and compared with imitation (Introduction; pp. 3, 9); notation as a window (p. 8); patterns as units of meaning (pp. 99–100); the aural/oral level and the pause (pp. 101–102); discrimination and inference learning, theory delayed (p. 106); levels of the skill learning sequence (from pp. 111, 117, 126, 129, 136, 141); stepwise and bridging movement, Table 17 (pp. 230–231).; Hearing Harmony: four stages of readiness for chord changes (p. 305); harmonic patterns I V7 I, I IV I, I II V7 I, I II7 V7 I (p. 313); I V7 I, then I IV I, then I IV V7 I and I V7 IV I in three sung parts, then harmonic minor (pp. 318–319); easy and moderately difficult harmonic patterns, the supertonic delayed (p. 320).; Bass Lines by Ear: macrobeats in usual duple and triple meter (pp. 175–176); same is easier to hear than different (p. 219).

title: Using a Mic: A Guide for Speakers
text: This guide is for people who speak through a microphone: announcements, assemblies, presentations, readings, introducing a band. You don’t need to know anything about the sound system. A few habits matter much more than the gear.
crumbs: Using a Mic: A Guide for Speakers

title: Using a Mic: A Guide for Speakers
text:
The two most important things
1. Slow down. You will feel like you are speaking far too slowly. You aren’t. A hall full of people echoes: every word you say bounces around the room for a moment after you’ve said it. If the next word comes too fast, it lands on top of that echo and both get smeared. “Clear speech,” the kind people use to be understood, has “a slower speaking rate, more and longer pauses” (Wikipedia, “Intelligibility”). Pause at the end of each sentence. Let the room go quiet before the next one.
2. Say every consonant. Vowels (a, e, o) are long and loud and survive the echo. Consonants (t, k, p, s, d) are short and quiet, and the echo covers them up: reverberation favours “vowels with steady states, while masking stops, glides and vowel transitions” (Wikipedia, “Intelligibility”). But the consonants are what tell “fifteen” from “fifty,” and “can” from “can’t.” Clear speech has “increased consonant intensity compared to adjacent vowels” (same source). Finish the ends of words. Over-pronounce a little: what sounds fussy up close sounds normal at the back of the room.

Try it: read one sentence at your normal speed, then again at about two-thirds the speed, hitting every final t and d. Record both on your phone from across the room and listen back.

Numbers, names and times are the easiest things to lose. Say them slowly, and say the important ones twice: “Room two-oh-four. That’s two, oh, four.”
crumbs: Using a Mic: A Guide for Speakers

title: Using a Mic: A Guide for Speakers
text:
Holding a handheld mic

Close, and the same distance all the time. A few centimetres to about a hand’s width from your mouth. The closer the mic, the more of you and the less of the room it hears (Wikipedia, “Gain before feedback”). The level changes fast with distance: halve the distance and you are about 6 dB louder. Keep the distance steady and the engineer can set you once.
Point it at your mouth, not at your chin or chest. Most mics hear from the end, not the side.
Turn your head with the mic. If you look at someone on your left, take the mic with you.
Very close sounds boomy. Right on your lips the mic adds bass (the proximity effect: Wikipedia, “Proximity effect”). A little is warm; a lot is muddy.
Pops. “P” and “b” push a puff of air into the mic and it thumps. Hold the mic slightly below or to the side of your mouth, so you speak across it, not straight into it.
Hold the handle, not the ball at the top. Covering the grille muffles the sound and can cause feedback.
Don’t tap it or blow into it to check it’s on. Just say “Good morning” at your normal level.
crumbs: Using a Mic: A Guide for Speakers

title: Using a Mic: A Guide for Speakers
section: On a stand or a lectern
text:
On a stand or a lectern
Adjust the stand before you start, not halfway through. Bring the mic to your mouth, not your mouth to the mic. At a lectern, keep the same distance when you look down at your notes: lean with the mic, or lift your notes. If you move away from the lectern, you have left the mic.
crumbs: Using a Mic: A Guide for Speakers

title: Using a Mic: A Guide for Speakers
text:
Clip-on (lavalier) and headset mics

A clip-on mic goes in the middle of your chest, a hand’s width below your chin, on the outside of your clothes. Scarves, jackets and lanyards rubbing on it are very loud.
Turning your head away from it makes you quieter. Talk forward.
Before you go on: ask where the mute switch is. Assume the mic is always on. People in the hall hear backstage conversations.
crumbs: Using a Mic: A Guide for Speakers

title: Using a Mic: A Guide for Speakers
text:
Walking around
Don’t walk in front of the loudspeakers with a live mic. A mic pointed at a speaker hears itself, the sound goes round the loop, and it squeals: feedback (Wikipedia, “Audio feedback”). If it starts squealing, step back behind the speakers or turn the mic away. Don’t cover it with your hand.
crumbs: Using a Mic: A Guide for Speakers

title: Using a Mic: A Guide for Speakers
section: What the sound engineer can and can’t do
text:
What the sound engineer can and can’t do
The engineer has a lot of tools, but they all work on the sound that reaches the mic. They can’t put back what the mic never heard.







The engineer can
The engineer can’t




Set your level so you are clear, if you stay at a steady distance
Make you loud when the mic is far away. Turning up a distant mic turns up the room too, and it squeals before you are loud enough (Wikipedia, “Gain before feedback”)


Take some boominess out of your voice with EQ, and cut low rumble
Make a mumbled word clear, or separate two words you ran together


Smooth out some loud/soft swings with a compressor
Keep up with a sudden shout after a whisper. Shouting into the mic just distorts. Step back instead


Reduce pops a little with a low cut
Remove a pop completely. Speak across the mic


Turn you up for the room, and mute you between speakers
Know you’re about to speak. Tell them your cue, and don’t start until you hear yourself


Fix feedback by turning you down
Turn you back up while you’re standing in front of the speakers


Help you before the event, at a sound check
Fix in the moment what a two-minute sound check would have caught



The engineer can only turn up what’s there. A clear, steady voice can be made bigger. A muddled one only becomes louder and muddled.
crumbs: Using a Mic: A Guide for Speakers

title: Using a Mic: A Guide for Speakers
text:
Before you speak: a checklist

Sound check. Say a sentence or two at the level you’ll really use (not quieter, and not “check one two”).
Ask the engineer: is the mic on now? Who switches it on?
Find your distance and keep it.
Mark slow-down and pause points in your notes.
Practise the names and numbers out loud.
Water nearby. A dry mouth loses consonants first.
crumbs: Using a Mic: A Guide for Speakers

“Gain before feedback.” Wikipedia, Wikimedia Foundation, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gain_before_feedback. Mic distance; halving it gives about 6 dB.
“Intelligibility (communication).” Wikipedia, Wikimedia Foundation, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intelligibility_(communication). Clear speech: slower rate, more pauses, stronger consonants; reverberation masks stops and transitions.

title: Annotated Bibliography 3: DP Music (Grades 11–12)
text:
In DP Music the annotated bibliography is a planning task. It’s where you show, before you write or play anything, that your research rests on sources an examiner would accept. Each component’s task asks for different sources and different annotations; the course book’s task references have the details. This lesson takes each one in turn.
It assumes Sources 3, on what examiners say about research and evidence, and Annotated Bibliography 2, on MLA format and evaluative annotations. Use MLA throughout. Whatever the format, clear attribution and in-text citations are what matter most.

title: Annotated Bibliography 3: DP Music (Grades 11–12)
text:
Exploring Music in Context
Your bibliography must include:

a visual representation of the piece you selected (a score, a lead sheet, a transcription or a graphic score)
a recording of the piece
at least one journal article or book chapter
one other high-quality source

Annotations:

For the visual representation and the recording: briefly explain the resource’s strengths and why you chose it.
For the other two: a summary of the source as it relates to your Exploring report, in two to four sentences each.

Submit three files: the annotated bibliography (PDF), the score or visual representation (PDF), and an audio excerpt of the reference recording, cut to one minute (MP3).
What makes these strong:

The score: say what edition it is, and why it’s authoritative. Is it a published edition, the composer’s own, or a scholarly transcription? A MuseScore upload is not an authentic score (see Sources 3). If it’s all there is, say how you checked it against the recording.
The recording: give full release details. Say why this performance: is it the original, a recording by the tradition’s own performers, a historically informed one? Your one-minute excerpt is the start of your Upload 3, so choose it with your Section 1 timestamps in mind.
The article or chapter: summarise only the part that bears on your report. Name the conventions or context it gives you that you can test against the music.

Model annotation for a recording (its form, not a template to copy):

Davis, Miles. “So What.” Kind of Blue, Columbia, 1959.
The original studio recording, by the sextet that first played the piece. I chose it over later live versions because it is the session that Ashley Kahn’s history of the album studies. Its slow-moving harmony (long stretches on one mode) is clear here, which gives me precise timestamps for Section 1.

title: Annotated Bibliography 3: DP Music (Grades 11–12)
section: Experimenting with Music: as a performer
text:
Experimenting with Music: as a performer
Your bibliography must include, at a minimum:

a recording of someone performing the piece you selected
a recording showing a different interpretation
a recording of a different piece that includes a technique or interpretation you’ll use to transform your stimulus
notation for the piece you selected
written and/or video analysis or instruction about the piece or a technique you’ve chosen to experiment with

Annotations: explain how you’ll use each resource as you carry out Exercise 1. If you have ideas for Exercises 2 and 3, include them. Submit one PDF.
What makes these strong:

The task is about use, so each annotation should name a decision: “I’ll take the shorter phrasing in bars 1–8 from this recording,” not “this is a good recording.”
The two recordings of your piece should differ in a way you can name and point to (tempo, ornamentation, articulation, rubato). If you can’t say how they differ, find a more different second recording.
The “different piece” is where your transformation comes from. Say exactly which technique you’re borrowing, and where in that recording it happens.
This feeds Criterion C (rationale and commentary). An annotation that already explains why you’ll make a choice is the start of a purposeful rationale.

Model annotation for written instruction:

Chaffin, Roger, and Gabriela Imreh. “‘Pulling Teeth and Torture’: Musical Memory and Problem Solving.” Thinking and Reasoning, vol. 3, no. 4, 1997, pp. 315–36.
A case study of a concert pianist preparing a Bach piece. Her practice segments followed the piece’s formal structure. I’ll plan my first experiment the same way, practising and recording it phrase by phrase, and use the study in my commentary to explain why I divided the stimulus where I did.

title: Annotated Bibliography 3: DP Music (Grades 11–12)
text:
Collaborative Musical Project (HL)
This task has two parts.
Part 1: Problem identification. Name two or three problems that now stand between you and finishing your project. Problems are things that need a solution. They show growth, not that something has gone wrong. For each, write one or two sentences: what you already know, and why the problem matters to the project.
Part 2: Annotated bibliography. For each problem, find a high-quality source that will help you solve it. Write a two-to-four-sentence annotation for each. Submit both parts as a single PDF.
What makes these strong:

A specific problem leads to a specific source. “Rehearsals are disorganised” is hard to research. “Our drummer and bassist drift apart in the bridge, and I don’t know how to rehearse a rhythm section” leads somewhere.
The source should come from someone who knows: a rehearsal-technique text, a conductor’s or producer’s interview, a recording-engineering manual, an article on collaborative creativity.
Say what you’ll try. End the annotation with the step you’ll take and how you’ll know whether it worked. That is the beginning of the process evidence CMM rewards.

title: Annotated Bibliography 3: DP Music (Grades 11–12)
section: From annotated bibliography to final submission
text:
From annotated bibliography to final submission

The annotated bibliography is not your final bibliography. The submission needs a plain bibliography, with every score, recording and secondary source, plus in-text references at every point you use a source.
Annotations are a draft of your thinking, not a draft of your text. Don’t paste them into the report. Write fresh, and cite.
Keep it up to date. When you add or drop a source, change the bibliography the same day.

title: Annotated Bibliography 3: DP Music (Grades 11–12)
text:
Paraphrasing
Each task carries the same advice, from Kate Turabian: read the passage, look away, think about it, and paraphrase it while still looking away. Then run your finger along your sentence. If you find the same ideas in the same order in the source, so will your reader. Try again.

title: Annotated Bibliography 3: DP Music (Grades 11–12)
text:
AI summaries are not sources






ImportantNo AI-generated summary belongs in a DP annotated bibliography as a source




A Google AI Overview or a chatbot answer has no author, no stable text, and no way for an examiner to check it. It is not a primary source and it is not musicology. Listing it as a source shows only that the research stopped where it started.
AI tools invent references: plausible authors, titles, journals and DOIs that don’t exist. Every entry in your bibliography must be a source you’ve found and read, watched or listened to yourself.
The IB doesn’t regard work produced, even in part, by an AI tool as yours. If your school allows you to use AI at all, its output must be credited in the text and in the bibliography, like any quotation. Crediting it still doesn’t make it evidence for a claim about the music.
What to do instead: if an AI answer gave you a lead, trace it to a real source (a journal article, a book chapter, Grove Music Online, an interview, a score, a recording). Read it, and annotate that.

title: Annotated Bibliography 3: DP Music (Grades 11–12)
text:
Check before you submit

Every required source type is there, for this component’s task.
Each entry is complete MLA, in alphabetical order, under the heading Annotated Bibliography.
Each annotation says what’s needed: strengths and reasons, a summary as it pertains to your report, how you’ll use it, or how it solves a named problem.
Annotations are in your own words, with no quotation from the source.
No AI summaries, and nothing you haven’t read, heard or watched.
For Exploring: the score PDF and the one-minute MP3 are attached.

title: Arranging 1: Who Plays What in a Band
text:
An arrangement is a set of decisions about who plays what, where, and when they keep quiet. This series takes the site’s backing band apart one player at a time. Each example below is the band itself: press ▶ Play, then use the buttons under Who plays to switch players in and out while it runs. Under the buttons, what the band will play is written out a whole pass ahead, one staff per player, so you can see what is coming before you hear it.
The four lessons:
crumbs: Arranging 1: Who Plays What in a Band

title: Arranging 1: Who Plays What in a Band
text:
1. Four jobs
A rhythm section shares out four jobs:

Time. The drums say where the beat is and how it is divided: straight or swung, busy or calm. Everyone else leans on them.
The bottom. The bass says which chord this is by playing its root, mostly on the strong beats, and it ties the harmony to the drums’ rhythm.
The harmony and the inner rhythm. Guitar and keyboards fill the middle: the rest of the chord, played in a pattern that sits between the drums’ hits.
The melody. A singer or soloist. The rhythm section’s job is to leave room for it.

A band sounds good when those jobs don’t step on each other. Most of arranging is deciding who doesn’t play.
crumbs: Arranging 1: Who Plays What in a Band

title: Arranging 1: Who Plays What in a Band
section: 2. Build it up one player at a time
text:
2. Build it up one player at a time
Start with only the drums, then add the bass, then the guitar. Listen for what each player adds. The drums alone have rhythm but no key. The bass adds the chord changes. The guitar adds the colour of each chord (major or minor) and fills the gaps in the rhythm.



Now take one away at a time. Without the bass, the band suddenly sounds thin and high. Without the drums, the guitar and bass have to keep time themselves and they sound loose. Without the guitar, the bass and drums still hold the song up: that’s why they are called the foundation.
crumbs: Arranging 1: Who Plays What in a Band

title: Arranging 1: Who Plays What in a Band
section: 3. Register: everyone gets a floor of the house
text:
3. Register: everyone gets a floor of the house
Look at the written parts while the band plays. The bass sits low, under the bass clef. The guitar sits in the middle. The drums aren’t pitched, but the kick is low, the snare is in the middle and the cymbals are high.
When two players share a register they blur together. The easiest fix is to move one of them. Here the piano comps in a ballad, then plays the same notes an octave higher, then an octave lower. Hear how the low one gets in the way of the bass and muddies the chords, and how the high one leaves the middle empty for a singer.
crumbs: Arranging 1: Who Plays What in a Band

title: Arranging 1: Who Plays What in a Band
text:
4. Same chords, three bands
A style is a set of these decisions made together. These three play the same four chords. Switch players off in each to hear how the jobs are shared out differently.
Rock: bass on every eighth note, guitar strumming eighths, a backbeat on 2 and 4. Everyone plays the same grid, so it drives.



Reggae: the guitar plays only on the off-beats and the drums leave beat 1 empty. The bass carries the downbeat by itself. Take the bass out and the beat is gone.



Swing: the bass walks a note on every beat, the ride cymbal plays the swung pattern, and the piano plays short chords now and then, mostly off the beat. The piano part changes every time round: in jazz the comping is a conversation, not a fixed pattern.
crumbs: Arranging 1: Who Plays What in a Band

title: Arranging 1: Who Plays What in a Band
text:
5. Try it

In each example, find the one player you could lose with the least damage. That player is the first to drop out when a singer comes in.
Turn on only bass and drums in the reggae example, then only guitar and drums. Which pair still sounds like reggae?
Next: Bass and drums.
crumbs: Arranging 1: Who Plays What in a Band

title: Arranging 3: Guitar and Keyboards
text: The chord instruments fill the middle of the band. They play the notes the bass leaves out, in a rhythm that fits between the drums’ hits. This is called comping (short for accompanying). How the examples work is explained in the first lesson.

title: Arranging 3: Guitar and Keyboards
text:
1. The rhythm is the part
A guitar part is mostly a rhythm. The chords here never change, only the strumming pattern. Each one gives the same song a different energy.



Under a singer, long chords and fingerpicking leave the most room. Down-up eighths fill everything and suit a loud chorus. Many arrangements go from sparse in the verse to full in the chorus with the same chords.

title: Arranging 3: Guitar and Keyboards
text:
2. Voicing: which notes, how high
The same chord can be played with all six strings ringing (an open chord) or as three notes higher up the neck (a triad). Open chords fill the whole range from low to high. A small triad stays out of the bass’s way and out of the singer’s.

title: Arranging 3: Guitar and Keyboards
text:
3. Off the beat: the chop
In reggae and ska the guitar plays only on the off-beats: short and choked. Motown guitarists did something similar on 2 and 4, doubling the snare. A chord instrument that plays very little can still be the part everyone remembers.

title: Arranging 3: Guitar and Keyboards
text:
4. Jazz comping: piano and guitar
In jazz, the piano doesn’t play a pattern. It plays short chords, mostly off the beat, and answers the soloist. It also leaves out the root (the bass has it) and plays rootless voicings: the 3rd, 7th and colour notes.



A swing-era guitarist (Freddie Green in the Count Basie band) did the opposite: a short three-note chord on every beat, felt more than heard. Here are the two together. That’s what the next section is about.

title: Arranging 3: Guitar and Keyboards
text:
5. Two chord players at once
Two chord instruments that both play busy patterns in the same register fight. The fix is to give them different jobs: one plays the rhythm, the other holds long chords, or one plays low and the other high. The band does this by itself when a second chord player is added: switch each one off in turn.
Swing: piano comps, the guitar plays four to the bar.



Rock: the guitar strums, an organ holds long chords behind it. This is the classic “pad” organ of 60s and 70s rock and soul.



The organ is its own world. The next lesson takes it apart.

title: Arranging 3: Guitar and Keyboards
text:
6. Try it

In section 2, pick Open chords and turn the bass off. Then pick Triads. Which one needs the bass more?
In section 5, switch off the drums and bass and listen to only the two chord players. Can you hear which one keeps the rhythm and which one holds the harmony?

title: Bass for Guitarists
text:
You already know the fretboard: the bass’s four strings are tuned E A D G, the same as the guitar’s lowest four, an octave lower. So the notes are where you expect them. What is new is the job, the size of everything, and above all silence: on bass, the notes you stop matter as much as the notes you play. This lesson covers the hands, fingerstyle and pick playing, and every kind of muting bassists use. Click a section’s heading to fold it; the “On this page” bar at the right jumps to any section.
How to read the page. Strings are numbered 1 (G) to 4 (low E). Tab has one line a string, G on top. Fingers: i index, m middle, p thumb (the classical letters).

title: Bass for Guitarists
text:
1. The job changes
On guitar you fill the middle of the sound with chords and lines. On bass you hold up the floor: you lock with the kick drum, play the root of each chord on the beat where it changes, and lead the band from one chord to the next. A guitarist’s first habit to drop is playing more: one well-placed, well-stopped note a beat is often the whole part.

Time first. Where the note starts and where it stops are both part of the groove. A note held into the next beat blurs the kick drum.
Roots, then fifths, then the walk. Root on beat 1, the fifth or the octave on the way, a step or half step into the next root. The Blues Bass and Pop Changes on Bass lessons build these lines.
Fewer chords, never full ones. Low notes close together sound muddy; two-note shapes (root and tenth, root and fifth up high) are about as far as most bass parts go.

title: Bass for Guitarists
text:
2. The fretting hand
The frets on a 34-inch bass are far wider than on a guitar, so the guitar habit of reaching with the fingers strains the hand.

One finger per fret, below the 5th fret, is too wide for most hands. Many players use the 1-2-4 system low on the neck: index, middle and little finger cover three frets, the ring finger helps the little finger push. Higher up, one finger per fret works.
Thumb behind the neck, roughly behind the middle finger, not wrapped over the top as for guitar bends and thumb-over chords.
Press just behind the fret, no harder than needed. Heavier strings need firmer pressure than guitar, but squeezing the neck tires the hand in one song.
Shift, don’t stretch. Move the whole hand along the neck; keep fingers hovering close to the strings.

title: Bass for Guitarists
text:
3. Fingerstyle: two fingers
Most electric bass is played with the fingers, and the motion is not guitar fingerpicking.

Rest the thumb. Lay it on the pickup, or on the E string when you play higher strings (see section 6).
Pull across, into the next string: the rest stroke. The index or middle finger plucks the string with the side of the fingertip, moving toward you, and comes to rest on the next lower string (lower in pitch is toward you: pluck the G, land on the D). The guitar free stroke, curling up into the palm, makes a thinner sound and leaves the string ringing unstopped.
Alternate i and m, like alternate picking. Don’t always start with the same finger; for string changes, the finger nearer the next string usually takes it.
Where you pluck changes the tone: near the neck it is round and deep, near the bridge it is tight and punchy.

   i m i m  i m i m      (alternate, evenly, every note)
G|---------|---------|
D|---------|---------|
A|---------|3-3-3-3--|
E|3-3-3-3--|---------|

Rakes. Moving down to a lower string (toward you), let the same finger play both notes in one movement, the way a guitarist sweeps: pluck the D string with m, let it fall onto the A string and pluck that with m too.
One finger is enough. James Jamerson, the bassist on most of Motown’s 1960s hits, plucked almost everything with his right index finger alone (the finger earned its own nickname, “the Hook”), resting his other fingers on the pickup cover. Two fingers are the usual way, not the only one.
The thumb. Plucking down with the side of the thumb gives a soft, dark sound (many players use it for warm ballad parts). The slap section has the thumb’s percussive cousin.

title: Bass for Guitarists
text:
4. With a pick
A pick is a fine bass sound, not a guitarist’s crutch: punchy and clear, and used on countless rock, punk and studio records. Carol Kaye, who played on hundreds of 1960s sessions, used one.

Use a heavier pick than for guitar and a steady alternate down-up stroke, or all downstrokes for driving eighths (punk and metal).
Pick near the bridge for attack, over the neck for a rounder note.
Palm muting with a pick is a whole sound of its own (section 6).

title: Bass for Guitarists
section: 5. Why bass needs so much muting
text:
5. Why bass needs so much muting
A low string vibrates for a long time and sets the other open strings ringing in sympathy, and the low notes cover each other. On guitar a little leftover ringing becomes part of the chord; on bass it becomes a wash of mud under the band. So a bassist mutes in two ways at once:

Stopping the note you played so it ends exactly where the rhythm says (note length).
Keeping every other string quiet so only one note sounds at a time (unwanted noise).

The left hand mostly does the first; the right hand mostly does the second.

title: Bass for Guitarists
text:
6. Every kind of muting

Left-hand release
To end a note, ease the pressure on the fretted note without lifting the finger off the string. The string leaves the fret and is damped by the finger still resting on it. Lifting off completely lets it ring as an open string.
Open strings need a different finger: lay any free finger (often the ring or little finger, or the side of the index) on the string to stop it.


Left-hand blanket
The fingers not in use rest lightly across the higher strings, and the underside of the fretting finger touches the string below. A fretted note on the A string: the index’s tip leans on the E string, the other fingers rest across D and G. Only the fretted string can ring.


Right-hand: the moveable anchor
The thumb moves with the plucking hand. Playing the E string, rest the thumb on the pickup. Playing the A string, rest the thumb on the E string: it anchors the hand and mutes the E at once. Playing D, the thumb moves to the A string, and now the E is left uncovered: that gap is why the next method exists.


Right-hand: the floating thumb
The thumb lies along the strings below the one you’re playing, its side touching all of them, sliding up and down with the hand. Playing the G string, the thumb covers D, A and E. Players with five- and six-string basses depend on it.


Right-hand: the resting finger
With rest strokes (section 3), the plucking finger ends on the next string down, muting it. Combined with the thumb, every string on both sides of the one you play is touched.


Palm muting
The side of the picking hand (the outer edge of the palm, below the little finger) rests on the strings right at the bridge saddles, and you pick as normal. The note thuds and dies fast: the 1970s pick-and-palm-mute sound. Closer to the saddles is more ring, further onto the strings more thud. With the fingers, the same edge of the palm rests on the strings while the thumb plucks: a short, upright-bass-like tone.


Foam and string mutes
Many old basses had a foam pad under the bridge cover. A piece of foam under the strings near the bridge, or a clip-on string mute, gives the same short, dead note for a whole song.


Ghost notes
A ghost note is a pluck on a string that the left hand is touching but not pressing: a pitchless click that keeps the rhythm moving, written x in tab. Funk lines live on them.
   1 e + a 2 e + a 3 e + a 4 e + a
G|---------------|---------------|
D|------5-x-5----|------5-x-5----|
A|3-x-3-------x--|3-x-3-------x--|
E|---------------|---------------|



Rests that you play
Count rests as carefully as notes. A quarter note followed by a quarter rest is not a half note: stop it on the beat with the left-hand release.

Test: play a line, then stop dead. If anything at all is still sounding, find which hand should have covered it.

title: Bass for Guitarists
text:
7. Slap and pop, briefly
The thumb strikes the E or A string with its bony side near the end of the neck and bounces off (slap, written T); the index or middle finger hooks under the D or G string and snaps it against the frets (pop, written P). Muting holds it together: left-hand fingers make ghosted “hammer” slaps (x) between the notes. Start slowly with octaves: thumb on the E string 3rd fret, pop the D string 5th fret.

title: Bass for Guitarists
section: 8. Bends, hammer-ons, pull-offs and slides on both instruments
text:
8. Bends, hammer-ons, pull-offs and slides on both instruments
The left-hand techniques are the same on both instruments; what changes is the string. A bass string is several times thicker and under more tension, its notes last longer, and they sit an octave lower, where small changes of pitch are harder to hear. So the same motion gives a different result.



Technique
On guitar
On bass




Bend
A half, whole step or more is normal; push or pull across the neck, two or three fingers together. A main sound of lead guitar.
Heavy strings allow about a half step, often less, and it costs effort. Used as a short, bluesy lean into a note, or a quarter-step “curl”, not as a melody move. Pull the E and A strings down toward the floor, so they don’t slide off the neck.


Vibrato
Wrist rotation, as for a bend, quick and wide in rock, narrow in jazz.
Mostly along the string (rolling the fingertip toward and away from the nut) or a small sideways shake. It shows on long notes in ballads and fretless playing; on short groove notes leave it out.


Hammer-on
Light strings, quick decay: hammer firmly and exactly behind the fret or the note is weak.
Easier: the heavy string keeps sounding, so a hammered note is almost as loud as a plucked one. Watch that the first note doesn’t keep ringing over it.


Pull-off
Pull the string slightly sideways as you lift, plucking it with the fretting finger.
The same motion, more force; it is easy to drag the string into the next one, so the other strings must be muted (see the muting section).


Slide
Fast and common: into notes, between chord shapes, the whole hand moves.
One of the bass’s main sounds: a slide into the root from a few frets below, a long slide down the E string at the end of a song. Ease off the pressure slightly or the frets click.


Grace note / glissando
Short slides and hammers ornament a melody.
A short slide or hammer into the root on beat 1 is a common move in soul and R&B lines.


Tapping
Right-hand taps on the fretboard; two-handed lead.
Works well (strings ring long); used for chords and two-handed lines on extended-range basses.


Harmonics
Bright and bell-like; see Harmonics on Guitar.
Very strong and low; used for tuning and as melody notes (the 12th, 7th and 5th fret spots are the same).



Crossing over. Guitarists on bass: bend less, slide more, and keep vibrato for long notes. Bassists on guitar: lighten the touch, because the same force that hammers a bass string bends a guitar string out of tune, and practise bends against a reference note until they land exactly on pitch. The Bends and Hammer-ons and Pull-offs lessons go into each technique.

title: Bass for Guitarists
text:
9. Things guitarists get wrong







Fault
Fix




Notes ring into the next one
Left-hand release on the beat; count the note’s length


Open strings hum while playing up high
Floating thumb, or anchor on the string below


Hand aches after a song
1-2-4 fingering low on the neck; lighter fretting pressure


Guitar-style free stroke, thin tone
Rest stroke, finger lands on the next string


Too many notes
Root on the chord change, then one note a beat


Strumming two-note “power chords” low down
Single notes; save double stops for high on the neck

title: Bass for Guitarists
text:
10. A practice plan

Week 1: one note a beat, roots only, through a song you know, stopping each note exactly on the next beat. Metronome on 2 and 4.
Week 2: alternate i-m on every string, with the moveable anchor. Then the floating thumb.
Week 3: the ghost-note line above at 70 bpm, then 90.
Week 4: a pick line with palm muting; then the same line with the fingers. Record both and listen to how long the notes are.

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues
text:
The twelve-bar blues is three four-bar phrases on three chords. Almost everything players have done to it since is one of a small number of moves: go to a chord sooner, approach a chord with its own dominant, split a dominant into a two-five, or replace a dominant with the one a tritone away. This lesson adds those moves one at a time. The site’s backing band plays every chart on this page, so you can hear each change as it arrives.
How to use the page. Press ▶ on any chart and the band plays two choruses after a one-bar count-in. Section 8 has a tune written in notation, where the note that is sounding lights up. The bar that is sounding lights up. The strip at the bottom of the window sets the key, the feel, the tempo and the chord instrument for the whole page, and you can change them while the band plays. Under every chord is its Roman numeral, which stays the same in every key.
crumbs: Lesson: Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues
text:
1. The three-chord blues
Four bars of I, two of IV and two of I, then V, IV, I, I. Every chord is a dominant seventh, including the home chord. That is the sound of the blues: a tonic that carries a flat seventh and does not need to resolve.



Listen for the two places the form turns. Bar 5 is the first move away from home. Bar 9 is the highest point of tension, and the last four bars walk it back down.
crumbs: Lesson: Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues
section: 2. The quick change and the turnaround
text:
2. The quick change and the turnaround
Two small changes, both very common. In bar 2 the band goes to IV for one bar and comes straight back (the quick change), which breaks up four bars of the same chord. In bar 12 the band plays V instead of resting on I, so the end of the chorus pulls into the top of the next one (a turnaround).



Use Hear it without the changes to compare with the chart before. The shaded bars are the ones that differ.
crumbs: Lesson: Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues
section: 3. The jazz blues: a two-five in the last line
text:
3. The jazz blues: a two-five in the last line
Swing and bebop players turned the last line round. Instead of V then IV, they play ii7 then V7: the bass now moves by fifths (G, C, F in the key of F) all the way home. To set up the ii chord, bar 8 becomes VI7, the dominant of ii. The turnaround in bars 11 and 12 is the same idea at twice the speed: I, VI7, ii7, V7, two beats each.
crumbs: Lesson: Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues
section: 4. Getting to IV, and getting back
text:
4. Getting to IV, and getting back
Three more moves, each of them a way to make an arrival stronger.

Bar 4: a two-five into IV. The I7 chord in bar 4 is already the dominant of IV, so put its ii chord in front of it (v7 I7, two beats each).
Bar 6: the bass climbs a half step from IV to ♯iv°7, and that chord pulls back to I in bar 7. This one is as old as the blues on the piano.
Bar 8: split VI7 into its own two-five, iii7 VI7.
crumbs: Lesson: Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues
text:
5. Tritone substitution
A dominant seventh chord and the dominant seventh a tritone away share the same third and seventh (swapped). So either can stand in for the other, and the substitute’s root arrives by a half step from above instead of by a fifth. Here it is in four places: the end of bar 4 (♯IV7 falling to IV), the end of bar 8 (♭III7 falling to ii), bar 10 (♭II7 falling to I), and a turnaround built entirely of substitutes: I, ♭III7, ♭VI7, ♭II7.



Listen to the bass. Wherever a substitute is used, the line slides down by half step.
crumbs: Lesson: Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues
text:
6. The Bird blues
Charlie Parker’s “Blues for Alice” keeps only three landmarks of the form: I in bar 1, IV in bar 5 and the two-five in bars 9 and 10. Everything between is a chain of two-fives. Bars 2 to 4 descend by step to reach IV. Bars 6 to 9 descend by half step to reach ii. The home chord is a major seventh, not a dominant.



Compare it with the jazz blues of section 3. The shaded bars show how little is left.
crumbs: Lesson: Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues
text:
7. The minor blues
The same twelve bars with minor i and iv chords. The last line is usually ♭VI7 to V7: a dominant a half step above the dominant (the tritone substitute of V’s own dominant). The turnaround uses a half-diminished ii chord. “Mr. P.C.” and “Equinox” are both built this way.
crumbs: Lesson: Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues
section: 8. A tune on these changes: Blues in the Closet
text:
8. A tune on these changes: Blues in the Closet
Oscar Pettiford’s Blues in the Closet is a good first tune because its changes are the three-chord blues with just two of the moves above.

Bars 9 and 10 are a two-five, ii7 then V7, as in the jazz blues of section 3.
Bar 12 is V7, the turnaround of section 2.

Everything else is plain. There is no quick change in bar 2 (four full bars of I), bars 5 and 6 are IV, bars 7 and 8 stay on I with no VI7, and bar 11 is one bar of I. The shaded bars are the ones that differ from the three-chord blues of section 1.



The melody is one two-bar riff played three times, and the note that is sounding lights up as it plays. Listen to bars 5 and 6: one note of the riff is a half step lower there than in bars 1 and 2, because the 3rd of the I chord has become the ♭7th of the IV chord. The changes are in the melody. In bars 9 and 10 the riff does not change at all, even though the chords under it are new: every note of it belongs to both the ii chord and the V chord.
To build this chorus yourself in the next section, choose Stay on I, Stay on I, Stay on IV, Stay on I, Two-five and V in the last bar. Open in the Backing Track puts the tune on that page in a new tab, where the bass line, comping and drums can each be chosen. The instrument lessons each end with this tune, and the improvising lesson is built on it.
crumbs: Lesson: Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues
text:
Build your own chorus
Choose one option for each pair of bars and the chart rewrites itself. Change a menu while the band is playing and the new chords come in at the next bar. All of the options fit together, so there is no wrong combination: try the plainest first line with the busiest turnaround, or the reverse.
crumbs: Lesson: Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues
text:
Test your ear
The band plays a plain blues with one pair of bars changed. The question tells you which bars to listen to; the counter shows where the band is. Pick what you heard.
crumbs: Lesson: Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues
text:
Where to go next

Play along. Set the strip at the bottom to Loop, pick a key and improvise over each version in turn. Bars 4, 8 and 12 are where the new chords ask for new notes.
Take a chorus you built to Tools → Backing Track (use Copy as ABC above and paste it into Edit the changes (ABC) there) to choose the bass line, comping rhythm and drum groove part by part.
Learn each version in the keys you play most: F and B♭ for horns, E, A and G for guitar.
Chord changes beyond the blues: cadences, turnarounds and rhythm changes, guide tones and borrowed chords.
