title: Blues for Guitar: From Roots to Shell Chords
text:
This is how a guitarist plays chords in a band on a 12-bar blues without a single barre chord: two or three well-chosen notes, moved by a fret at a time. You need to know how to fret a note and how the strings are numbered (6 is the low E, 1 is the high E). For what the chords are and how the form gets varied, see Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues.
How to use the page. Every step has fretboard diagrams, a chord chart and a ▶ button that starts the band. The diagrams show the neck standing upright: string 6 is on the left, the nut is at the top, and the numbers down the side are frets. Click a chord’s name above a diagram to hear it. Under the diagrams the same notes are written on a staff. In every line of notation the note that is sounding lights up, whether the notation is playing by itself or the band is playing. While the band plays, its guitarist plays exactly the notes in the diagrams, and the bar on the chart and the chord being played both light up. Tick Leave out the guitar to take the part yourself. The strip at the bottom sets the key, the tempo and whether the dots show chord tones or note names.
crumbs: Blues for Guitar: From Roots to Shell Chords

title: Blues for Guitar: From Roots to Shell Chords
text:
1. The roots
The root is the note a chord is named after: the root of G7 is G. Find the key note on string 6. The root of the IV chord is at the same fret on string 5. The root of the V chord is two frets higher on string 5. Three chords, three notes, and the hand stays where it is.
In four keys (C, D♭, D and E♭) the key note is a long way up the lowest string, so the diagrams start from the next string instead. Then the root of V is at the same fret on the lowest string and the root of IV is two frets below that.



Play one long note per bar with the band and count the form: four bars of I, two of IV, two of I, then V, IV, I, I. Knowing where the roots are is what lets you find every chord shape that follows.
crumbs: Blues for Guitar: From Roots to Shell Chords

title: Blues for Guitar: From Roots to Shell Chords
text:
2. What the 3rd and 7th do
A seventh chord has four notes, counted up the scale from the root: the root, the 3rd, the 5th and the 7th. They do different jobs.

The root names the chord. In a band the bass player plays it.
The 5th adds weight and not much else.
The 3rd says whether the chord is major or minor.
The 7th says what kind of seventh chord it is. Every chord in a basic blues has a major 3rd and a flat 7th (♭7), which makes it a dominant seventh chord.

So the 3rd and 7th carry the chord’s character. They are called the guide tones. Play only those two notes and a listener still hears the chord, especially with a bass player underneath. The diagrams show all four notes of each chord, with the guide tones filled in. Click a chord name to hear the four notes climb.




Where the flat 7 comes from
Why is the 7th of these chords called flat? The answer is in the major scale. Press ▶ to hear each line of notation. The explanation follows the key chosen in the strip at the bottom.



From the root: the 3rd is one string up and one fret back, the 5th is one string up and two frets on, and the ♭7th is two strings up at the same fret as the root.
crumbs: Blues for Guitar: From Roots to Shell Chords

title: Blues for Guitar: From Roots to Shell Chords
text:
3. Guide tones on strings 5 and 4
Now play just the 3rd and 7th, as a two-note chord on strings 5 and 4. Look at the Superimposed view to see what makes this worth learning: the three chords are the same two-finger shape, one fret apart. From the I chord, move both fingers down one fret for IV and up one fret for V.
That works because the 3rd of one chord is a half step from the 7th of the next. Going from I7 to IV7, the 3rd drops a fret and becomes the ♭7th, and the ♭7th drops a fret and becomes the 3rd. Switch the labels to chord tones and watch the two notes swap names.
Up a tritone. The 3rd and ♭7th of a dominant chord are six frets’ worth of pitch apart, an interval called a tritone, and a tritone turned upside down is still a tritone. So the same two-finger shape six frets higher gives the same two notes of the same chord, with the 3rd and ♭7th changing places. Press Up a tritone to move all three chords there. That gives every chord two homes on each pair of strings. In keys where the lower home would run off the end of the neck (F and G♭ here), the diagrams start in the upper one, so the three shapes always stay one fret apart.



The hollow dot is the root. Where one is shown it is in reach on string 6 and you can add it; where none is shown, leave it to the bass player.
crumbs: Blues for Guitar: From Roots to Shell Chords

title: Blues for Guitar: From Roots to Shell Chords
section: 4. Guide tones on strings 4 and 3, and the root
text:
4. Guide tones on strings 4 and 3, and the root
The same pairs one string set higher sit under roots on both low strings, so every chord can have its root added. These three-note chords are shell voicings: root, 3rd and 7th with the 5th left out. A chord with its root on string 6 has the 7th on string 4 and the 3rd on string 3. A chord with its root on string 5 has the 3rd on string 4 and the 7th on string 3. Mute string 5 with the side of your finger when the root is on string 6.
First the two notes alone:



Then with the root. This is the rhythm guitar sound of the swing era. Up a tritone here moves each chord to its other shell: the root changes string and the 3rd and 7th change places above it.



The band’s guitarist plays a short chord on beat 1 and another just before beat 3. Try that rhythm, then try four even strokes to the bar (set the feel and tempo to taste).
crumbs: Blues for Guitar: From Roots to Shell Chords

title: Blues for Guitar: From Roots to Shell Chords
text:
5. The jazz blues
The last line of a jazz blues is a two-five: ii7, V7, then home to I, with VI7 in bar 8 to lead into it (the reasons are in section 3 of the changes lesson). The ii chord is a minor seventh chord: its 3rd is one fret lower than a dominant chord’s. In a shell with the root on string 6, that puts the 7th and the minor 3rd at the same fret, under one finger.



In bars 11 and 12 the chords change every two beats. Press Superimposed to see how little the hand moves through ii7, V7 and I7.
crumbs: Blues for Guitar: From Roots to Shell Chords

title: Blues for Guitar: From Roots to Shell Chords
section: 6. A tune: Blues in the Closet
text:
6. A tune: Blues in the Closet
Oscar Pettiford’s riff blues. Its changes are the three-chord blues with a two-five in bars 9 and 10 and a V chord in bar 12. The melody is one two-bar riff played three times. Here it is with the shells from step 4 underneath.



Comp under the tune with a short chord on beat 1 and another just before beat 3, and leave the riff room. Then look at the guide tones alone. The riff’s second note is the 3rd of the home chord. In bars 5 and 6 it drops a fret to become the ♭7th of IV, which is exactly what your guide-tone shape does at the same moment.
crumbs: Blues for Guitar: From Roots to Shell Chords

title: Blues for Guitar: From Roots to Shell Chords
text:
Where to go next

Change the key in the strip at the bottom and find the same shapes in the new place. Start with F, B♭, A and C.
Loop a chorus with the guitar left out and comp for yourself.
Learn to improvise over the same tune in the improvising lesson.
Take any chorus from the changes lesson and find the guide tones of each new chord from its root.
The Chord Sheet tool (Tools menu) draws these and fuller voicings for any chords you type in, one at a time or superimposed.
Next on guitar: pop changes for guitar, from open chords to passing chords.

title: Blues for Violin and Saxophone: Playing the Changes
text:
This is the 12-bar blues for instruments that play one note at a time: violin, saxophones, and anything else with a single line. It starts with one note per chord and ends with a line that spells out a jazz blues. You need to be able to read notes in your instrument’s range. For what the chords are and how the form gets varied, see Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues.
Choose your instrument first. The Instrument menu in the strip at the bottom transposes the page. Violinists choose Violin, and the scale under Where the flat 7 comes from then also shows the finger for every note. Flutes stay on concert pitch. Alto and tenor players choose their saxophone, and every chart and line of notation is then written in their key, while the band plays in the concert key shown beside it. A B♭ tenor and an E♭ alto reading this page at the same time see different notes and sound the same ones.
How to use the page. Every step is a twelve-bar line. Under each note is the name of its place in the chord at that moment: R for the root, then 3, 5, ♭7. Press ▶ Play beside the notation to hear the line alone, or ▶ Play with the band to hear it over the rhythm section, where the piano plays it. Tick Leave out the melody to play it yourself. The note that is sounding lights up in the notation either way.
Sections 1 to 6 build the skills. Section 7 puts them to work on a tune, Oscar Pettiford’s Blues in the Closet. If you would rather start with the tune, go there first and come back.
crumbs: Blues for Violin and Saxophone: Playing the Changes

title: Blues for Violin and Saxophone: Playing the Changes
text:
1. The roots
The root is the note a chord is named after. A blues has three chords and three roots. Play each one as a long note and count the bars: four of I, two of IV, two of I, then V, IV, I, I.



A bass player would play these notes. Playing them yourself is the quickest way to hear where the form turns.
crumbs: Blues for Violin and Saxophone: Playing the Changes

title: Blues for Violin and Saxophone: Playing the Changes
text:
2. Chord tones, and the 3rd and 7th
A seventh chord has four notes, counted up the scale from the root: the root, the 3rd, the 5th and the 7th. Every chord in a basic blues has a major 3rd and a flat 7th (♭7), which makes it a dominant seventh chord. Here are the four notes of each chord, played up from the root.



The 3rd and the 7th are the guide tones. They are the two notes that tell a listener which chord this is, and they are the notes a good melody leans on.

Where the flat 7 comes from
Why is the 7th of these chords called flat? The answer is in the major scale. Press ▶ to hear each line. The explanation follows the key and instrument chosen in the strip at the bottom.
crumbs: Blues for Violin and Saxophone: Playing the Changes

title: Blues for Violin and Saxophone: Playing the Changes
text:
3. Guide-tone lines
Play only a guide tone of each chord, and at each change move to the nearest guide tone of the new chord. The line barely moves: when I7 goes to IV7 the 3rd falls a half step and becomes the ♭7th of the new chord. One note per bar, and the whole harmony of the blues is in it.
Starting on the 3rd:



Starting on the 7th. Two players can take one line each.
crumbs: Blues for Violin and Saxophone: Playing the Changes

title: Blues for Violin and Saxophone: Playing the Changes
text:
4. Guide tones in rhythm
The same notes become a background figure when they are given a rhythm. This one is the Charleston: a note on beat 1 and another on the “and” of 2. A horn section plays exactly this kind of thing behind a soloist.
crumbs: Blues for Violin and Saxophone: Playing the Changes

title: Blues for Violin and Saxophone: Playing the Changes
text:
5. A riff
A riff is a short figure repeated through the form and adjusted to fit the chords. This one is the 3rd, 5th, 6th and 5th of the home chord. Over the IV chord only its first note changes: it drops a half step, which makes it the ♭7th of IV. Over the V chord the whole figure moves up to that chord.



Look at the names under the notes in bars 5 and 6. The fingers play almost the same thing, and every note has a new job.
crumbs: Blues for Violin and Saxophone: Playing the Changes

title: Blues for Violin and Saxophone: Playing the Changes
text:
6. The jazz blues
The last line of a jazz blues is a two-five: ii7, V7, then home to I, with VI7 in bar 8 to lead into it (the reasons are in section 3 of the changes lesson). The ii chord is a minor seventh chord, with a minor 3rd. Through ii7, V7 and I7 the guide-tone line steps down: the 7th of each chord falls to the 3rd of the next.



The chord tones of the same chorus:
crumbs: Blues for Violin and Saxophone: Playing the Changes

title: Blues for Violin and Saxophone: Playing the Changes
section: 7. The tune: Blues in the Closet
text:
7. The tune: Blues in the Closet
Oscar Pettiford wrote this blues in the early 1950s. It is a riff blues: one two-bar idea, played three times over the twelve bars. Learn the first two bars and you know nearly all of it.




How it is built

Four notes. The whole melody uses the root, the 3rd, the 4th and the 5th below. Look at the names under bars 1 and 2: R, 3, R, 4, 3, R.
Three lines. Bars 1 to 4, 5 to 8 and 9 to 12 are the same riff. Each ends on a long note, which is where the rhythm section answers.
Notes that arrive early. Several notes are tied across the barline. They are played an eighth note before the beat and held into the next bar. Clap the rhythm before you play it. These early notes are what make the riff swing.



The one note that changes
In bars 5 and 6 the riff’s second note is a half step lower than it was in bars 1 and 2. It is the only accidental in the tune. Over the home chord that note was the 3rd. The IV chord has that pitch a half step lower, as its ♭7th, so the melody moves with the chord. In bar 7 the home chord returns and so does the original note. This is the sound of a blues going to IV, and the melody tells you the chord has changed without any help from the band.
Hear that move by itself. This is the guide-tone line from section 3 on the tune’s changes. Play it, then play the tune again and listen for the same half step inside the riff.





The last line
Bars 9 and 10 are a two-five (ii7 then V7) instead of V then IV. The melody does not change at all, but look at the names under it: the same pitches are now the 9th and ♭7th of the ii chord. A riff this simple fits because every one of its notes belongs to the key.
The roots of the tune, to learn where the chords fall:





Practising it

Sing the riff with the band before you play it.
Play bars 1 and 2 alone until the tied notes sit right. Use ▶ Play beside the notation to check yourself.
Play the whole tune with Leave out the melody ticked.
Change the concert key. A riff you can play in three keys is a riff you know.

When the tune is secure, go on to the improvising lesson, which uses this melody as its starting point.
crumbs: Blues for Violin and Saxophone: Playing the Changes

title: Blues for Violin and Saxophone: Playing the Changes
text:
Where to go next

Change the concert key and play every step again. F, B♭, C and G are the keys a blues is most often called in.
Loop a chorus with the melody left out and make up your own line from the chord tones, landing on a guide tone at each change.
Take a chorus from the changes lesson and write its guide-tone line.
Write guide-tone lines over other progressions in the guide tones lesson, or put new chords under a melody in reharmonizing.

title: Lesson: Borrowed Chords
text:
A song in C major is not limited to the chords of C major. It may borrow chords from the parallel minor (C minor) or from the mixolydian mode (a major scale with a flat 7). The borrowed chord has a note that is not in the key, and it sounds like a colour change. This lesson adds those chords one at a time to a plain I, IV, V, I.
How to use the page. Press ▶ on a chart and the band plays it four times after a one-bar count-in. The bar that is sounding lights up, on the chart and on the staff. Under every chord is its Roman numeral, which stays the same in every key. The strip at the bottom of the window sets the key, the feel, the tempo and the chord instrument, and you can change them while the band plays. Shaded bars are the ones that differ from the version named under the chart.

title: Lesson: Borrowed Chords
text:
1. The plain version
C, F, G, C. Every chord is in the key of C major.

title: Lesson: Borrowed Chords
text:
2. The minor iv
C, F, Fm, C. Replace the IV with the iv. F minor has A♭, a note that is not in C major and that falls to G, the 5th of C. It is the sound of a major song turning wistful for one bar.

title: Lesson: Borrowed Chords
text:
3. The ♭VII
C, F, B♭, C. B♭ is the chord of the flat seventh (the 7th of the mixolydian mode). It falls a step to C. It sounds natural after F because the two roots are a whole step apart and the chords share the note F.

title: Lesson: Borrowed Chords
text:
4. The ♭VI and ♭VII together
C, A♭, B♭, C. Two borrowed chords, each a whole step above the last, rising to C. A♭ has A♭, C and E♭ (a minor-key chord), and B♭ has B♭, D and F. It sounds big and triumphant, and is sometimes called the “Mario cadence”.

title: Lesson: Borrowed Chords
text:
5. All three together
C, Fm, A♭ B♭, C. The minor iv in bar 2, then the ♭VI and ♭VII together in bar 3.

title: Lesson: Borrowed Chords
text:
Build your own
Choose a chord for each bar, or start from one of the versions above.

title: Lesson: Borrowed Chords
text:
Test your ear
The band plays a four-bar phrase. Name its borrowed chord (or the lack of one).

title: Lesson: Borrowed Chords
text:
Where to go next

Play each version in a different key with the Key menu. The borrowed chords move with you.
The ♭VII to I ending also appears in the lesson on cadences.
Four-chord loops uses the ♭VII in its sixth loop.

title: Lesson: Cadences, and the One That Is Not
text:
A cadence is how a phrase ends. Every ending has a different feel, and the feel comes from the two chords that make it. This lesson plays the five you will meet most, each as a four-bar phrase, and then asks a harder question about one of them: is it a cadence at all?
How to use the page. Press ▶ on a chart and the band plays it four times after a one-bar count-in. The bar that is sounding lights up, on the chart and on the staff. Under every chord is its Roman numeral, which stays the same in every key. The strip at the bottom of the window sets the key, the feel, the tempo and the chord instrument, and you can change them while the band plays. Shaded bars are the ones that differ from the version named under the chart.
crumbs: Lesson: Cadences, and the One That Is Not

title: Lesson: Cadences, and the One That Is Not
section: 1. The authentic cadence: V7 to I
text:
1. The authentic cadence: V7 to I
C, F, G7, C. The strongest ending there is. G7 contains the leading tone B and the note F, which are a tritone apart. Both are unstable: B wants to rise a half step to C and F wants to fall a half step to E. The tonic chord that follows is where they land. The bass falls a fifth, and everything leans the same way.



Learn this one first. Every other ending on the page is compared with it.
crumbs: Lesson: Cadences, and the One That Is Not

title: Lesson: Cadences, and the One That Is Not
section: 2. The half cadence: ending on V
text:
2. The half cadence: ending on V
C, F, C, G. The phrase stops on the dominant, with the tension still in the air. It is a comma, not a full stop: the ear expects an answer, and the next phrase usually supplies it.
crumbs: Lesson: Cadences, and the One That Is Not

title: Lesson: Cadences, and the One That Is Not
section: 3. The deceptive cadence: V7 to vi
text:
3. The deceptive cadence: V7 to vi
C, F, G7, Am. Everything points at C, and then the last chord is Am, which shares two notes with C (C and E). The leading tone still rises to C, but the chord on top of it is Am. The listener expects a full stop and gets a surprise.
crumbs: Lesson: Cadences, and the One That Is Not

title: Lesson: Cadences, and the One That Is Not
section: 4. The plagal cadence, and why it is the fake one
text:
4. The plagal cadence, and why it is the fake one
C, Am, F, C. IV to I, the “Amen”. Most books call this a cadence. This lesson does not, and here is the argument.

A cadence is made by the dominant. What ends a phrase in tonal music is the leading tone rising to the tonic and the tritone of V7 resolving inward. IV to I has neither. No note in F is pulled toward C, so nothing is resolved.
IV is a neighbour of I. I, IV, I leaves home and comes back, exactly as I, vi, I does. That is a prolongation of the tonic chord, not an arrival.
It comes after the real cadence. The “Amen” at the end of a hymn follows a V to I that has already closed the phrase. The plagal is tacked on afterwards, so it cannot be what made the ending.
Some theorists agree. William Caplin’s Classical Form counts only authentic and half cadences, and does not count IV to I as a cadence.




Here is the “Amen” in its usual place: an authentic cadence first, then the plagal after it. Listen to bars 1 and 2, which end the phrase, and then to bars 3 and 4, which only soften it.



There is a fair reply. In the blues, in gospel and in much rock, IV to I really is how a tune ends, because those styles never relied on a leading tone. So whether “fake” means “not a cadence” or “a different kind of ending” depends on the style. In the classical tradition the first reading is the one with the support.
crumbs: Lesson: Cadences, and the One That Is Not

title: Lesson: Cadences, and the One That Is Not
text:
5. The backdoor: ♭VII to I
C, F, B♭, C. The chord on the flat seventh is B♭, and it falls a whole step to C. There is no leading tone here either. The ending sounds relaxed, a door left open instead of shut. Compare it with the plagal ending: both arrive without a dominant.

title: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings
text:
This lesson orders chord shapes by what the fretting hand finds hard, starting from a first lesson on guitar. Each step adds one physical demand: more fingers, a stretch, a barre, a muted string, a shift along the neck. Each step says what makes the shape easy, what makes it hard, and what usually goes wrong. Guitar chord shapes has the same chords in harmonic order, from pop toward jazz.
How to read the diagrams. The neck stands upright, with string 6 (low E) on the left. Each dot shows its chord tone, R for the root. The numbers under each diagram are the frets from low E to high E, and x is a string you don’t play. Fingers are numbered 1 (index) to 4 (little finger). Press ▶ to hear a shape.
Finger numbers and barres. The button below puts the finger numbers in the dots instead of the chord tones, on every diagram on the page. Where one finger lies across several strings, a shaded bar joins those dots. The bar is drawn only where a barre is new: the small barre in G-B6, the first full barres in G-B8 and G-B9, and the barre with a silent string in G-B13. Tick the box to draw it on every diagram.
Finger numbers on guitar and on piano. The two instruments count differently. On guitar the thumb is not counted: the index finger is 1, then middle 2, ring 3 and little finger 4, and a thumb fretting a bass note over the top of the neck is written T. On piano the thumb is 1 and the little finger 5, and the left hand is numbered the same way as the right, so its little finger plays the lowest note. A “3” is the ring finger to a guitarist and the middle finger to a pianist. Picking-hand fingers on guitar have letters of their own (p, i, m, a), so they are never mixed up with these.
crumbs: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings

title: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings
text:
Hand position
Good position is what makes every shape below easier, so set it up before the first chord and check it again whenever a shape feels hard.

Thumb: behind the neck, roughly opposite finger 2, with the pad (not the flat of the thumb) on the wood. It is a rest to push against, not a clamp. Squeezing harder does not make the note clearer.
Fingertips: arch each finger so that the tip comes down on the string from above, just behind the fret wire (the side towards the tuning pegs). Close to the fret needs the least pressure and buzzes least. The middle of the gap between frets needs more pressure and still buzzes.
Fingers: curved, with the knuckle joints bent. A curved finger lets the strings next to it ring.
Wrist and elbow: the wrist stays fairly straight, not bent sharply down or back, and the elbow hangs relaxed instead of pinned to the ribs or lifted. The palm stays a little away from the neck, so there is a gap you could slide a finger through.
Guitar angle: sit with the guitar body against your right thigh and the neck pointing slightly upward. Looking down at the fretboard should not need you to twist your wrist.
Easy because: with the thumb behind the neck, the fingers fall on the frets and need very little effort.
Hard because: it is not how the hand sits when it rests, so for the first weeks it takes thought.
What goes wrong:

The thumb climbs over the top of the neck. That makes the fingers flat, and they mute the strings next to them. (An occasional thumb over the top for a bass note is fine: that is the T in the diagrams.)
Flat fingers: the pad lies on the string and touches its neighbour.
The tip sits in the middle of the fret space, or on the fret wire, and the note buzzes or dies.
The wrist collapses and the palm presses on the neck, which is tiring and slows changes.
Long nails stop the fingertip landing; trim the fretting hand’s nails short.


Practice: place the fingers of a chord one at a time, checking each tip. Pick the strings one by one. If a string buzzes, move that fingertip closer to the fret before pressing harder.
crumbs: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings

title: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings
text:
G-B1 One or two fingers



Em7 takes finger 2. Em uses 2 and 3, and E5 does too, with the higher strings left silent. E7 uses fingers 2 and 1, and Am7 uses 2 and 1.

Easy because: one or two fingers, no stretch, and everything is within two frets.
Hard because: each finger has to press firmly enough to make a clean note, and the strum has to land on the right strings.
What goes wrong:

Fingertips hurt for the first week or two.
A string buzzes when the finger sits back from the fret instead of just behind it.
A fingertip leans on the next string and mutes it.


Practice: hold Em and pick one string at a time, so you can hear that each one rings. Five minutes a day builds calluses.
Unlocks: two-chord strums; G-A1 and G-A2.
crumbs: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings

title: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings
text:
G-B2 Three fingers, close together



Am and E are the same shape, moved over one string; both are fingered 2-3-1. A is 1-2-3, or a small index-finger barre across three strings. D is 1-3-2, with finger 1 on string 3, finger 3 on string 2 and finger 2 on string 1. Dm is the same three fingers in a different order, 2-3-1. D7 is 2-1-3: it is D with the middle finger moved to the other side, so the three fingers sit close together as in D.

Easy because: the fingers stay together and no finger reaches across another.
Hard because: three fingers have to land at once, and in A they crowd into one fret.
What goes wrong:

In D and D7, finger 3 touches the high E string and mutes it.
In A, the fingers collide.
Changing between E and A is slow.


Practice: move from Am to E. Fingers 2 and 3 move across one string together, and finger 1 stays on its fret, moving from string 2 to string 3. Go as slowly as you need to keep the shape.
Unlocks: four-chord loops that use only these chords; Boom-chick.
crumbs: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings

title: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings
text:
G-B3 Reaching: C and G



C is fingered 3-2-1, from string 5 up to string 2. Cadd9 adds finger 4 on string 2 in place of finger 1. G is 2-1-3, or 3-2-4 with finger 4 on both of the top two strings.

Easy because: everything is within the first three frets.
Hard because: in C the fingers spread diagonally over three frets and three strings. In G the fingers are far apart across the neck, and the strings between them have to ring open.
What goes wrong:

In C, finger 1 leans on the high E string.
The thumb rides high over the neck, which shortens the reach. Keep it low, behind the neck.


A note on the B string in G. In G the B string rings open, and it sits right beside the finger on the high E string. That finger, finger 3 or 4, can lean back and touch the B string, and then the string goes dull or silent. The chord is still G, because the B on string 5 still sounds, but it is thinner and the strum sounds uneven. To avoid it, press with the tip and keep the knuckle arched. Damping the B string can also be a choice: let the finger on string 1 lie lightly against it, and the chord loses one of its two B’s and sounds more open. The X in the second diagram marks the B string damped.



Practice: form C, lift all three fingers together, and put them down again without looking. Repeat ten times.
Unlocks: C, Am, F, G, and the pop changes of G-A1 and G-A4.
crumbs: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings

title: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings
text:
G-B4 Four fingers: open 7ths



C7 is C with finger 4 added on string 3. B7 uses all four fingers in a cluster: 2-1-3-4. Fmaj7 is a small shape on the top four strings.

Easy because: each shape is a small change from one you already know.
Hard because: four fingers are down at once, including the weak little finger, and B7 is a cramped cluster.
What goes wrong:

The little finger lands on the pad instead of the tip and mutes the next string.
The change from C to C7 is slow because finger 4 starts far away.


Practice: hold C and tap finger 4 on and off string 3, fret 3 (C to C7 and back), without lifting the other fingers.
Unlocks: Blues shuffle and the open-position 12-bar blues; G-A5.
crumbs: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings

title: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings
text:
G-B5 Reach: a wide stretch



The reach of a hand is how far apart the fingers can press at once. G7 is G with the little finger’s note moved down: finger 3 on string 6 at fret 3, finger 2 on string 5 at fret 2, and finger 1 on string 1 at fret 1. The fingers sit on the two outer strings and on opposite sides of the neck, so the hand opens as wide as it does in any open chord. Compare it with G above it.

Easy because: only three fingers, and the strings between them ring open.
Hard because: the hand has to open across all six strings and three frets at the same time. Small hands feel it most.
What goes wrong:

The thumb creeps up over the neck, which shortens the reach and makes it worse.
Finger 1 reaches the high E string at an angle and touches the string next to it.
The wrist bends sharply to make up the distance. Keep it fairly straight, with the elbow close to the body.


Practice: form G, then change to G7 by lifting finger 3 and putting down finger 1, with fingers 2 and 3 staying where they are. Do not hurry. If the stretch hurts, stop and rest, and do a little each day. The span grows with patience.
Unlocks: the G7 in blues and country changes; G-A5.
crumbs: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings

title: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings
section: G-B6 Two strings under one finger
text:
G-B6 Two strings under one finger



In Dm7, finger 1 lies flat across strings 2 and 1 at the first fret. In F, fingers 3 and 2 go down beside that small barre.

Easy because: the barre covers only two strings.
Hard because: for the first time, one finger presses two strings, and it has to lie flat rather than on its tip.
What goes wrong:

String 2 is dull because it falls in the crease of the finger. Roll the finger slightly onto its outer edge.
The thumb creeps around the front of the neck.


Practice: put finger 1 alone across strings 2 and 1 and pick each string, until both ring. Then add the other fingers.
Unlocks: the F chord in the pop changes.
crumbs: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings

title: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings
text:
G-B7 Top-string triads



Moveable shapes. A chord shape can slide up and down the neck as long as it has no open string. An open string stays at the same pitch when the hand moves, so the shape would change. If every note is fretted, the whole shape moves together, and the chord’s name changes with the root. Of the shapes above, C xxx010 and Am xxx210 use open strings and stay where they are. C xxx553, C xxx988 and F xxx565 are fully fretted, so they move. The same is true of the barre chords in G-B8 and G-B9.
Three positions of the same triad. A triad has three notes, and any of them can be the lowest. On strings 3, 2 and 1 these are the moveable shapes. The root is on string 3 in root position, on string 1 in first inversion, and on string 2 in second inversion. Find the root and you know the chord.






In root position the root is the lowest note. In first inversion the 3rd is the lowest, and in second inversion the 5th is. The inversions lesson explains the names and how to write them, and pianists can see the same idea in piano inversions. The next step is voice leading: when you change chords, choose the inversion that is nearest, so each note moves a fret or two, or stays put. That is how a few small shapes on the top strings can follow a whole progression, and it is where this lesson leads.

Easy because: only three notes, and at most three fingers.
Hard because: strings 6, 5 and 4 must stay silent. Either pick only the top three strings, or let your fretting fingers rest lightly against the low strings to damp them. Higher up the neck the frets get closer together.
What goes wrong:

The open low strings ring.
The pick catches string 4.
The chord sounds thin. It is meant to: it is one part in a band.


Practice: play the three C shapes in a loop, picking the strings one at a time and then together.
Unlocks: funk and reggae chops; G-A9.
crumbs: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings

title: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings
text:
G-B8 Full barre, E shape



Finger 1 lies across all six strings, and the other fingers make the E shape in front of it: the open E chord, fingered 2-3-4 instead of 1-2-3, moved up so that the barre does the nut’s job. The root is on string 6, under the barre. Here the barre is at fret 5, which makes these A, Am, A7 and Am7.
Start at fret 5, not at F. The usual first barre chord is F, at fret 1, and it is the hardest place to learn it. Near the nut the strings sit highest above the frets and are under the most tension there, so the barre has to press hardest, and the frets are widest, so the hand has to stretch furthest. Around fret 5, closer to the bridge, the strings give more easily and the frets are closer together. Get the shape ringing there, then move it down a fret at a time (A♭, G, G♭) until you reach F. G-B10 does that move on purpose.

Easy because: the shape on top of the barre is E, which you already know.
Hard because: one finger presses six strings, which takes strength, and the hand tires quickly.
What goes wrong:

Strings buzz. Put the barre right behind the fret, and roll the finger so that its firmer outer edge, not the soft pad, meets the strings.
String 2 or 3 falls in a crease of the finger.
The elbow sticks out.

Fm and Fm7 are a little easier, since they need fewer fingers on top of the barre.

Practice: play the barre alone at fret 5, no other fingers, until all six strings ring. Hold for 10 seconds and rest for 20. Or put a capo at fret 5 and play E shapes above it, then do the capo’s job with your finger. When fret 5 is easy, do the same at fret 3, then fret 1.
Unlocks: every major and minor chord; G-A3.
crumbs: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings

title: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings
text:
G-B9 Barre, A shape
The A shape: the open A chord with a barre behind it on string 5, the root under the barre. String 6 is not played. At fret 5 these are D, Dm, Dm7, D7 and Dmaj7; the same shapes at fret 1 are B♭, B♭m and the rest, where the stretch and the pressure are greater for the same reasons as F.




Easy because: the barre covers five strings, not six.
Hard because: three fingers squeeze into one fret space on adjacent strings. Many players flatten finger 3 across strings 4, 3 and 2 instead, which takes practice of its own.
What goes wrong:

When finger 3 lies flat, it mutes string 1.
Finger 1 bends at the knuckle and lets string 1 go dead.


Practice: play Dm at fret 5 with the barre and finger 3 only, then add fingers 4 and 2. Then move it down to Cm (fret 3) and Bm (fret 2).
Unlocks: barre chords anywhere on the neck.
crumbs: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings

title: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings
section: G-B10 Moving a shape along the neck
text:
G-B10 Moving a shape along the neck



The first three are the E shape (root on string 6) at frets 5, 3 and 1: A, G and F. The last three are the A shape (root on string 5) at frets 5, 3 and 2: Dm, Cm and Bm. They are written in that order, from fret 5 down, so that the move takes you from the easy end of the neck toward the hard one. Name the chord by the note under the barre: on string 6 for the E shape, on string 5 for the A shape.

Easy because: the shape doesn’t change, only the fret.
Hard because: you have to find the new fret without looking, and release just enough pressure to slide without the strings squeaking, all without dropping the beat.
What goes wrong:

A gap between chords.
Landing a fret off.
A scrape on the slide. Ease off the pressure, but don’t lift the fingers.


Practice: slide A down to G and back on a steady beat, then G down to F, using the fret markers at 3, 5, 7 and 9 as landmarks.
Unlocks: I–IV–V and the 12-bar blues in barre chords, in any key.
crumbs: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings

title: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings
text:
G-B11 Barre 7ths: finger independence



A7 and Am7 are the E shape at fret 5 with a finger taken away, so the barre itself plays the 7th on string 4; F7 is the same at fret 1. D7, Dmaj7 and Cmaj7 are the A shape, with the root on string 5. Learn them at fret 5 first, as in G-B8.

Easy because: A7 and Am7 are barres you already know, with a finger taken away.
Hard because: the little finger now has to press at the far end of a barre. Cmaj7 x35453 needs fingers 2, 3 and 4 spread across strings 4, 3 and 2.
What goes wrong:

The little finger collapses and mutes a neighbouring string.
It hasn’t the strength yet.


Practice: hold a barre and tap finger 4 on one string, fret by fret.
Unlocks: Bossa nova in barre positions; G-A6.
crumbs: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings

title: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings
text:
G-B12 Skipped strings: shells



In the shapes with the root on string 6, the underside of finger 1 (on the root) also touches string 5 to mute it. In the shapes with the root on string 5, the finger on the root leans against string 4.

Easy because: three notes, three fingers, and the shapes move anywhere.
Hard because: the skipped string must not sound. It is muted by a finger resting on it without pressing, and the strings above the shape are muted too.
What goes wrong:

The skipped string rings, because the muting finger isn’t touching it.
Playing too hard, which brings the muted strings back.


Practice: strum all six strings with the shape held. Only three notes should come out.
Unlocks: Four to the bar, Charleston, and blues for guitar; G-A8.
crumbs: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings

title: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings
section: G-B13 Barre with a skipped string: drop 3
text:
G-B13 Barre with a skipped string: drop 3




Easy because: the shapes are a barre plus at most two notes, and Cm7 is a barre alone.
Hard because: you need barre strength, but string 5 under the barre has to be silent. Lift the barre slightly where it crosses string 5 so it only touches the string.
What goes wrong:

String 5 sounds.
String 1 rings.


Practice: play Cm7 alone, then add finger 3 for C7. Then try fingers 3 and 4 together for Cmaj7.
Unlocks: the Drop 3 guitar voicing; G-A11.
crumbs: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings

title: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings
section: G-B14 Drop 2 and extensions: unusual fingerings
text:
G-B14 Drop 2 and extensions: unusual fingerings



Cmaj7 xx2413 is fingered 2-4-1-3. That’s an order the hand hasn’t used before.

Easy because: only four strings, close together.
Hard because: the fingers come in unusual orders, and some shapes combine a small barre, a skipped string and a stretch of three or four frets.
What goes wrong:

Hand ache from long sessions.
Grabbing the wrong finger.
One note losing pressure in the stretch.


Practice: learn one ii–V–I in drop 2, saying the finger numbers out loud. Then move it up two frets.
Unlocks: the Drop 2 voicing, jazz comping, and the altered chords of G-A13.
crumbs: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings

title: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings
text:
Where the two sequences meet








Harmonic order
By hand





G-A1 Open triads
G-B1, G-B2, G-B3
The same chords, sorted by how many fingers they need and how far they reach.


G-A2 Fifths
G-B1
E5 is one of the first shapes.


G-A3 Barre chords
G-B8, G-B9, G-B10
The barre, then the slide.


G-A4 Sus and add9
G-B2, G-B3
One finger moved.


G-A5 Dominant 7th
G-B4, G-B5, G-B11
Open 7ths, then barre 7ths.


G-A6 m7 and maj7
G-B6, G-B11
Small barre, then full barre.


G-A8 Shells
G-B12
The first skipped strings.


G-A9 Top-string triads
G-B7
Physically easy, but they come later in the harmonic order.


G-A10 Drop 2
G-B14
The hardest fingerings.


G-A11 Drop 3
G-B13
A barre with a skipped string.



The orders differ most in the middle. In the harmonic order a shell (G-A8) is simpler than a full 7th chord. Physically it is harder, because the string between has to be muted. A player who knows G-B4 can try shells with the root on string 6 without learning the barre first.
crumbs: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings

title: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard
text:
This lesson orders piano voicings by what the hands find hard, starting from a first lesson. Each step adds one task: more notes, a wider span, black keys, two hands at once, leaps, and finally hands that move independently. Each step says what makes the voicing easy, what makes it hard, and what usually goes wrong. Piano chord voicings has the same chords in harmonic order, from pop toward jazz.
How to read the diagrams. Each keyboard shows one voicing. The dots carry the chord tones, R for the root. The staff puts the right hand on the treble clef and the left hand on the bass clef. Press Show finger numbers below to put the fingering in the dots instead of the chord tones. The span is the distance from a hand’s lowest note to its highest, counted in half steps: an octave is 12. Press ▶ to hear a voicing.
Finger numbers on piano and on guitar. The two instruments count differently. On piano the thumb is 1 and the fingers go 2, 3, 4 to the little finger, 5, in both hands. Because the hands are mirror images, the right hand plays a chord from the bottom 1-3-5 and the left hand 5-3-1: the left hand’s little finger takes the lowest note. On guitar the thumb is not counted: the index finger is 1 and the little finger is 4 (the thumb, when it frets a bass note over the neck, is written T). So a “3” means the middle finger to a pianist and the ring finger to a guitarist. The fingerings here are the usual ones; a hand of a different size may choose another.
crumbs: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard

title: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard
text:
Hand position
Set this up before the first chord, and check it when a voicing feels clumsy.

Sitting: sit on the front half of the stool, far enough from the keys that your forearms are level, or slope slightly down towards the keys, with your elbows a little in front of your body. A stool too low pushes the wrists up; too high pushes them down.
Fingers: curved, as if holding a ball. The knuckles are arched and the fingertip pad lands on the key. Fingers 2, 3 and 4 are about the same length when curved, so they land together.
Wrist: level with the back of the hand and the forearm, neither drooping below the keys nor lifted above them. The hand can float a little as it moves; it does not rest on the keys.
Thumb: it plays on its side, near the corner of the nail, not flat on its pad. Keep it relaxed and slightly curved, level with the other fingers.
Where on the key: play white keys near the front edge, where they go down most easily. Play a black key in the middle, not on its edge. When a chord mixes the two, the longer fingers (2, 3 and 4) usually take the black keys further back, while the thumb and little finger stay on the white keys at the front.
Easy because: a curved hand has every finger above its key, so the hand needs no tension to hold the position.
Hard because: the fingers tire when starting out, and it is tempting to flatten them to reach.
What goes wrong:

Flat fingers: the pad lies on the key, the hand has less strength, and the fingers play neighbouring keys too.
A dropped wrist, with the knuckles sinking below the hand.
The little finger collapses, and its first joint folds in.
The thumb plays flat on its pad and sticks out, and the hand twists.
Shoulders lifted, with the arms held up from the shoulder instead of hanging.


Practice: put the hand on C, E and G in 1-3-5 with the wrist level. Press each key, and check the wrist and finger tips between presses. Keep the fingers curved when the hand moves to the next chord.
crumbs: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard

title: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard
text:
P-B1 White-key triads, one hand



RH 1-3-5, and LH 5-3-1 an octave lower.

Easy because: each finger has a white key of its own: thumb, middle finger and little finger, with a key left out between each.
Hard because: the three notes have to sound together and evenly. The thumb is strongest, so the bottom note comes out loud and the top note thin.
What goes wrong:

The notes split instead of sounding as one chord.
The top note is lost.


Practice: play a chord, lift the hand, and put it back on the next chord without looking. Keep the wrist level.
Unlocks: P-A1.
crumbs: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard

title: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard
section: P-B2 Bass note plus triad: two hands
text:
P-B2 Bass note plus triad: two hands




Easy because: the left hand plays one note, so it has one job.
Hard because: the two hands have to land together, and the right hand jumps a 4th or more between chords.
What goes wrong:

The stronger hand arrives first and the other drags.
One hand lifts early.
Watching one hand loses the other.


Practice: play C–Am–F–G in half notes, counting out loud. Close your eyes after one time through.
Unlocks: P-A1; Piano ballad with Long notes.
crumbs: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard

title: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard
section: P-B3 Inversions: small moves instead of jumps
text:
P-B3 Inversions: small moves instead of jumps



RH 1-3-5 for root position and second inversion; 1-2-5 for first inversion.

Easy because: the hand moves by a step instead of a jump, and there are only two finger patterns.
Hard because: the span grows to 8 or 9 half steps. The open space in a 1-2-5 shape tempts fingers 3 and 4 to fill it.
What goes wrong:

Squeezing with finger 2, which makes the chord uneven.
Choosing the wrong finger for the new note.


Practice: play C in root position, first and second inversion, up the keyboard and back. Then do the same on F and G.
Unlocks: P-A2.
crumbs: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard

title: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard
text:
P-B4 Black keys in triads



All RH 1-3-5.

Easy because: in D, A and E the black key falls under finger 3, the longest finger, which reaches in easily.
Hard because: in B♭ and E♭ the thumb or finger 5 lands on a black key. Those fingers are short and prefer white keys, so the whole hand has to move further in toward the fallboard.
What goes wrong:

The thumb slips off the black key.
Finger 5 flattens.
Reading the key signature becomes a second task.


Practice: play D, A and E first, and B♭ and E♭ after them. Then do the same with the left hand.
Unlocks: every key in the Key menu of the lesson pages, and four-chord loops in all twelve keys.
crumbs: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard

title: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard
text:
P-B5 Two-note guide-tone shapes



RH 1-3 for the 4ths; 1-4 for the tritone.

Easy because: only two notes, so the hand is always relaxed. The span is 5 or 6.
Hard because: the interval changes from chord to chord (4th, tritone, 4th), so the fingers have to adjust each time.
What goes wrong:

Reaching with the arm instead of letting the fingers open.
Losing track of which note is the 3rd.


Practice: hold one pair, then change to the next while keeping the arm still.
Unlocks: P-A7; Charleston comping and blues guide tones. This step comes before four-note 7ths (P-B6) because two notes are easier on the hand. In the harmonic order it comes after them.
crumbs: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard

title: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard
text:
P-B6 Four-note 7ths in one hand



RH 1-2-3-5. The span is 10 or 11.

Easy because: the notes are a 3rd apart, so the fingers fall on every other key.
Hard because: the hand opens to a 7th, and finger 5 has to reach while fingers 2 and 3 stay curved.
What goes wrong:

The thumb lies flat.
Finger 5’s note is weak.
The chord comes out uneven.


Practice: play each chord, then its closest inversion (as in P-A6), and compare how the hand feels. If the hand aches, leave out the top note.
Unlocks: P-A5 and P-A6; the 7th chords in blues for piano.
crumbs: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard

title: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard
section: P-B7 Shells in the left hand
text:
P-B7 Shells in the left hand



LH 5-3-1 for 1–3–7. For 1–7–3 (span 16), LH 5-1 and the right thumb on the top note.

Easy because: three notes in one hand, about the same span as P-B6.
Hard because: the left hand is usually the weaker one, and mistakes are easy to hear down low. The 1–7–3 order is a 10th wide, too wide for most hands to play alone.
What goes wrong:

The thumb hangs over the edge of the key.
The middle note doesn’t sound.


Practice: play the three shells slowly and listen for every note.
Unlocks: P-A8; solo piano.
crumbs: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard

title: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard
section: P-B8 Rootless voicings: four notes in the left hand
text:
P-B8 Rootless voicings: four notes in the left hand



LH 5-3-2-1 throughout. The span is 9 to 11.

Easy because: the A and B forms alternate, so the hand moves by a step or less. The B forms are the narrowest.
Hard because: four fingers sound at once in the weaker hand, and you need the forms in every key. Black keys fall under different fingers in each key.
What goes wrong:

Forgetting which form comes next.
One note missing.


Practice: learn the chain in F first, which sits well under the left hand, and then the chain in C. Then add a bass line in the right hand.
Unlocks: P-A9; Jazz ballad, Bossa nova, Boogaloo.
crumbs: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard

title: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard
section: P-B9 Leaps: bass note, then chord
text:
P-B9 Leaps: bass note, then chord



The left hand alone, as in stride or boom-chick: a low bass note, then a chord about an octave and a half higher.

Easy because: the shapes are triads you already know.
Hard because: the hand jumps 1½ octaves on the beat. The eyes want to follow the hand, and the rhythm slips.
What goes wrong:

The chord is late or too loud because the hand crashes onto it.
Looking down and losing the place.


Practice: left hand only, bass–chord–bass–chord, with a metronome at 60. Move in an arc and shape the chord in the air before it lands. Close your eyes once the landing is reliable.
Unlocks: stride and boom-chick left hands; country and folk comping.
crumbs: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard

title: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard
section: P-B10 Stacked 4ths: one shape that moves
text:
P-B10 Stacked 4ths: one shape that moves



RH 1-3-5, span 10. For the So What chord, LH 5-2-1 and RH 1-3.

Easy because: every interval is the same, so there is one hand shape.
Hard because: each stack of 4ths lands on a different mix of black and white keys, so the same shape feels different in each place.
What goes wrong:

The hand follows the key colours and loses the shape.


Practice: slide the stack of 4ths up the white keys from D to D, one hand at a time, noticing which positions feel best.
Unlocks: P-A12; modal jazz.
crumbs: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard

title: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard
text:
P-B11 Wide spans: octaves, 9ths and 10ths



LH 5-1 for the octave, the 9th and the 10th. LH 5-2-1, rolled, for C–G–E.

Easy because: most adult hands can play an octave, and a 9th is possible with a firm wrist.
Hard because: a 10th is beyond most hands played as one chord.
What goes wrong:

Forcing the stretch. Roll the chord from the bottom instead, and never play through pain.


Practice: roll C–G–E slowly and listen for the three notes blending into one sound. Then play it with the pedal.
Unlocks: P-A11; Arpeggio low and high, Ballad: syncopated, Piano ballad.
crumbs: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard

title: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard
section: P-B12 Independence: a held shell, a moving right hand
text:
P-B12 Independence: a held shell, a moving right hand



LH 5-3-1, RH 1-3-5.

Easy because: the left hand holds still, and the right hand plays a plain triad.
Hard because: the hands play different rhythms, three notes each, and each hand plays a different chord.
What goes wrong:

Both hands playing on the same beat.
The black keys in the right-hand triad (C♯, F♯) being missed.


Practice: hold the shell on beat 1 and play the right-hand triad on the “and” of 2. Then on the “and” of 4. Tap your foot on the beat.
Unlocks: P-A13; Charleston, Reverse Charleston, Boogaloo stabs and Son montuno.
crumbs: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard

title: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard
text:
Where the two sequences meet

P-B1, P-B2

The same notes: the triad, then both hands.

title: Composing 4: Instruments, Ranges and Transposing
text: When you write for a real player, you need to know three things about their instrument. Which notes it can play (its range), how its part is written (its clef, and whether it transposes), and what is easy or hard on it. This lesson covers the first two for the orchestra, the saxophones and the guitar. The next lesson uses them to arrange.

title: Composing 4: Instruments, Ranges and Transposing
text:
1. The families
The orchestra is described in four families:








Family
Instruments (high to low)
How the sound is made




Woodwinds
piccolo, flute, oboe, English horn, clarinet, bass clarinet, bassoon, contrabassoon
air across an edge (flutes), or a reed (one: clarinet, saxophone; two: oboe, bassoon)


Brass
trumpet, horn, trombone, tuba
the player’s lips buzzing in a cup-shaped mouthpiece


Percussion
timpani, then everything struck, shaken or scraped; harp and piano are often placed nearby
striking


Strings
violin (in two sections, firsts and seconds), viola, cello, double bass
a bow drawn across the string, or plucking (pizzicato)



Saxophones belong with the woodwinds (they have a single reed). They are not regular members of the orchestra, but some scores from the 19th century on use them.

title: Composing 4: Instruments, Ranges and Transposing
text:
2. Ranges
These are the sounding ranges: the notes the audience hears, with middle C as C4. The top notes are approximate: good players go higher, and young players should usually stay well below them.

The middle is where it sounds best. The lowest notes of a flute are quiet and breathy; the highest notes of a trumpet are loud and tiring. If a part has to be heard, put it where the instrument is strong, not where it only just reaches.

title: Composing 4: Instruments, Ranges and Transposing
text:
3. Transposing instruments
On a transposing instrument the written note is not the note that sounds. A clarinet in B♭ that reads C plays a B♭: everything sounds a major second lower than written. So the clarinet’s part has to be written a major second higher than the music should sound.
Why do it? So that one set of fingerings works for every size of the instrument. A player who learns the alto saxophone can pick up a tenor and read the same written notes with the same fingers; the tenor just sounds lower. Instruments that sound an octave away from their written notes (guitar, double bass, piccolo) are written that way to avoid a staff full of ledger lines.
Concert pitch is what the piano plays: the sounding note. A score “in C” shows every part at concert pitch; a transposed score shows each part as its player reads it.








Instrument
A written C sounds
So write the part




Clarinet in B♭, trumpet in B♭
B♭, a major 2nd lower
a major 2nd higher


Horn in F, English horn
F, a perfect 5th lower
a perfect 5th higher


Alto saxophone (E♭)
E♭, a major 6th lower
a major 6th higher


Tenor saxophone (B♭)
B♭, a major 9th lower
a major 9th higher


Guitar, double bass
C, an octave lower
an octave higher


Piccolo
C, an octave higher
an octave lower



The key signature moves too. Music in F for the band is in G for the clarinets and trumpets (one flat becomes one sharp), and in D for the alto saxophones.

title: Composing 4: Instruments, Ranges and Transposing
text:
4. Try it: the transposer
Write the music as it should sound (in ABC, concert pitch), pick an instrument, and read the part its player would get. The check underneath says whether every note is inside that instrument’s range.





Try putting the melody in the bass clef range (add , after the letters to move notes down an octave) and pick the cello, then the trombone, then the alto saxophone. Notice which instruments can’t reach it.

Ask the player. The table gives the limits; a player can tell you what is comfortable at their level, which notes are awkward, and how long they can play before they need a rest. Recording a player trying your part, and writing down what they said, is some of the best evidence of developing a piece you can have (see Process 1).

title: Composing 2: Developing a Motif
text:
A motif is a short musical idea, often only three to six notes, that a piece keeps coming back to. It is recognised by its rhythm and its shape more than by its exact notes, so it can change and still be heard as the same idea. That is what developing a motif means: changing it step by step so the music grows out of one idea instead of jumping from one new idea to the next.
The best-known example is the opening of Beethoven’s Fifth Symphony: three short notes and one long one. The whole first movement is built from that rhythm, on different notes, in different instruments, louder and softer.
How to use the page. Each technique below has a short example: the motif, then the change. The motif is always the same one, C E G E with the rhythm short short short long, so you can hear what each change does to it.

title: Composing 2: Developing a Motif
text:
The techniques

Repetition
Play it again, exactly. It sounds simple, but a listener needs to hear an idea twice before it sticks. Most motifs are repeated straight away.





Sequence
The same shape, starting on a different note: usually a step higher or lower each time. Sequences make the music feel like it is moving somewhere. In a diatonic sequence the notes stay in the key, so the steps between them may change size slightly (a major third becomes a minor one).





Inversion
Turn it upside down. Each step up becomes the same step down. The rhythm stays the same, so it is still recognisable.





Retrograde
Play it backwards: the last note first. Retrograde is harder to hear than the others, so composers often use it as a hidden link rather than an obvious one.





Augmentation and diminution
Make every note twice as long (augmentation) or half as long (diminution). Augmentation sounds broader and more serious: it is a common way to end a piece. Diminution sounds more urgent.





Fragmentation
Use only part of it: the first two or three notes, repeated or sequenced on their own. Breaking an idea into pieces speeds the music up. It is how the continuation of a sentence works (see Composing 1).





Changing one thing at a time
You can also keep the rhythm and change the notes, keep the notes and change the rhythm, change the harmony under it, the instrument, the register, the dynamics, or the articulation. The rule that keeps it recognisable: change one or two things, keep the rest.

title: Composing 2: Developing a Motif
text:
The motif lab
Pick a motif or type your own. Then build a phrase: each button adds a changed copy of the last group. Start with Motif, then try, for example, Repeat, Sequence up, Fragment, Fragment, Land on C. Play it and decide what to keep. Copy ABC gives the phrase in ABC, which the Notation page opens (paste it into its ABC box).






Explore, then choose. Make three different phrases from the same motif before you pick one. Copy each into your process journal with one line on what you changed and how it sounds. That record of trying several ideas and choosing between them is exactly what MYP Criterion B asks you to show: see Process 2.

title: Composing 2: Developing a Motif
text:
Listen for it
Motifs are everywhere once you listen for them. A few to try (find a recording, and count how many times you hear the idea):

Beethoven, Symphony No. 5, first movement: the rhythm short short short long, in every instrument, all the way through.
John Williams, Jaws: two notes a half step apart, alternating, low in the bass. Almost nothing but repetition, and it works.
A song’s chorus hook: in most pop songs the hook is a motif, repeated several times in each chorus.

Next: Composing 3: Words and Music.

title: Composing 3: Words and Music
text:
A song is words and music working together. You can start from either one. Some writers start with a line of lyrics they like and find the melody hidden in how it is spoken. Others start with a chord loop or a riff and sing nonsense syllables over it until words arrive. Whichever comes first, the two have to fit, and this lesson is mostly about how they fit.
How to use the page. Press ▶ under a staff to hear the melody. The chorus example also has chords, so the band plays them with it, and ▶ Chords plays the chords alone.

title: Composing 3: Words and Music
section: 1. Stress: the words already have a rhythm
text:
1. Stress: the words already have a rhythm
Say this line out loud: I can’t stop thinking about you. Some syllables are louder and longer than others: i CAN’T STOP THINK-ing a-BOUT you. Those are the stressed syllables. Matching the words to the music is called prosody. Good prosody puts the stressed syllables on strong beats or on notes that stand out (higher, longer). Then the line is sung the way it is spoken, and it is easy to understand.








In the second one, the long high note is on -ing, and -bout is squeezed onto a weak beat. It sounds like thinkING aBOUT. Singers can force it, but listeners have to work to hear the words.

Test it. Speak your line in time to a beat, clapping on the strong beats. The syllables you clap on are the ones that should land on beats 1 and 3 (in 4/4). If you have to bend the word to make it fit, change the rhythm or change the word.

Prosody is wider than stress. The songwriter Pat Pattison describes it as the music supporting what the words say. A line about falling can fall; a line about being stuck can stay on one note; a question can end up in the air, on a note that is not the tonic.

title: Composing 3: Words and Music
text:
2. Lines and rhyme
Lyrics usually come in groups of lines (a verse, a chorus). How the lines rhyme gives the section its shape. Label each line’s last sound with a letter:








Scheme
What happens
How it feels




AABB
lines 1 and 2 rhyme, then 3 and 4
simple, settled, a bit nursery-rhyme


ABAB
lines 1 and 3, then 2 and 4
flowing, the rhyme always pulls you on to the next line


XAXA
only lines 2 and 4 rhyme
the most common in songs: room to say what you mean in lines 1 and 3


AAAX
three rhymes, then a line that doesn’t
the odd line stands out: put the title or the twist there



A perfect rhyme has the same vowel and the same ending (go / slow). A near rhyme shares only the vowel or only the ending (go / home, time / mine). Most songwriters use both. A near rhyme often sounds less forced than a perfect one.
Line length matters too. Lines with the same number of stressed syllables can be sung to the same melody. If line 3 is much longer, the melody has to change there, which can be good (contrast) or awkward (crowding).

title: Composing 3: Words and Music
text:
3. Song form
Most popular songs are built from a few kinds of section:

Verse: tells the story. The music is usually the same each time; the words change.
Pre-chorus (optional): a short section that builds from the verse into the chorus.
Chorus: the main message, with the same words and music every time. Usually the title is here.
Bridge: a contrasting section, once, usually after the second chorus: new chords, new melody, a new angle on the lyric.

A common plan is verse, chorus, verse, chorus, bridge, chorus. An older one, the AABA or 32-bar form of many jazz standards and show tunes, has four eight-bar sections: a melody (A), the same again (A), a contrasting middle eight (B), and the melody once more (A). Practise naming the sections of songs you know with Section Labels.

title: Composing 3: Words and Music
section: 4. The hook, and making the chorus different
text:
4. The hook, and making the chorus different
A hook is the short idea a listener remembers: often the title, sung on a motif that repeats (see Composing 2). Here is a four-bar chorus over the loop C, G, Am, F. Its two lines use the same rhythm, and the hook hold on, hold on opens both:



The chorus has to sound like arrival. If the verse and chorus sound alike, the listener can’t tell where the chorus starts. Change something, or several things:




Verse
Chorus




Register
lower, closer to speech
higher: the melody’s high point is usually here


Rhythm
more words, shorter notes
fewer words, longer notes


Harmony
can avoid the tonic, or start somewhere else
lands on the tonic, often on its first chord


Arrangement
thinner (see Arranging 1)
fuller: more instruments, drums open up


Lyric
details, story
the main idea, said simply

title: Composing 3: Words and Music
section: 5. Write a verse and a chorus
text:
5. Write a verse and a chorus

Write the chorus lyric first: two or four lines with the title in them. Speak it in time and mark the stresses.
Find a chord loop (see Four-Chord Loops), or use the one above.
Sing the chorus lyric over the loop several times, a different way each time. Record each take on your phone. Pick the best one and write down why it was the best.
Write the verse: lower, more words, and an ending that leads into the chorus.
Put it in the Notation page with its words and chords (it reads ChordPro too), and hear it with the band.

Those recordings are evidence of your process. Keep them, give each a name and a date, and note which one you chose: see Process 1: Keeping a Process Journal.

title: DAW 4: Arranging a Song
text: A loop is not a song. Arranging is laying parts out along the timeline so the song has sections (intro, verse, chorus, bridge, outro) and changes as it goes: instruments come in and drop out, the drums get busier for the chorus, everything stops for a beat. In a DAW you arrange by moving clips (Logic and BandLab call them regions) on the tracks.

title: DAW 4: Arranging a Song
text:
Session players
Instead of writing every part, let the band write a start. Under the tracks, type chords (bars split by |), pick a Style and press Write the parts: the Backing Track band’s drummer, bassist and chord player each write their part into a clip at the playhead. Logic’s Drummer and Session Players, BandLab’s SongStarter and Ableton’s MIDI generators do the same job. The parts are now ordinary MIDI clips: open them in the editor and change any note.

title: DAW 4: Arranging a Song
text:
Build a song

Press Write the parts with C | Am | F | G, Rock, 2 times. That’s 8 bars: call it the verse.
Move the playhead to bar 9 (click the ruler), type F | G | C | Am and write 2 times again: the chorus.
Select a clip and Duplicate (Ctrl/Cmd+D) to repeat a section. Set Song length longer first if you run out of room.
Drop a part out: delete the Chords clip in the first verse, or drag the drum clip later so the drums enter at bar 5. An arrangement is as much about who isn’t playing.
Split a clip at the playhead (put the playhead inside the clip, press Split) and delete the second half for a stop.
Drag a clip by its right edge to change its length; drag the clip to move it (hold Alt to move by beats, not bars), or onto another track.
Try a different Style for the chorus only: the band rewrites the clips under it, the verse stays.

title: DAW 4: Arranging a Song
text:
Common shapes

Build: start with one or two instruments, add one every 4 or 8 bars.
Contrast: verse sparse and low, chorus full and wide; a bridge in other chords.
Fewer is louder: dropping the drums for two bars makes their return hit harder.
Sections are usually 4, 8 or 16 bars. The DAW’s grid makes it easy to keep them that way.

Arranging for a band in more depth: Arranging 1: Who Plays What. Naming sections: Section labels.

text:
What this small DAW leaves out
Real DAWs do much more. In the order you’ll want them:

Audio editing: many takes of one part and the best bits of each (comping), fades, time-stretching (Recording 1: Gain Staging, Recording 2: Microphones).
Effects / plug-ins on each track: EQ, compression, reverb, delay (Sound 11: The Equaliser onwards).
Sends and buses: one reverb shared by many tracks (Recording 7: Mixing).
Automation: a fader or knob that moves by itself as the song plays.
Meter and tempo changes, takes and comping, time-stretching audio, software synths (the sound-design lessons).

title: DAW 3: The Piano Roll and MIDI
text:
A clip on an instrument track holds MIDI notes, not sound. Each note is only: which key, when, how long, and how hard (velocity). The instrument turns them into sound when you play. So you can change any note, the tempo, or the instrument afterwards, and nothing is lost. That is the big difference from audio, a recording of sound, which you can cut and move but not re-voice note by note.
The piano roll shows the notes: pitch up the side (a piano keyboard on its edge), time across, each note a bar whose length is its length.
crumbs: DAW 3: The Piano Roll and MIDI

title: DAW 3: The Piano Roll and MIDI
text:
Writing notes
The Keys track below has the four chords of a C Am F G loop as whole notes, and an empty Bass clip is waiting.

Click the clip on the Keys track. Its notes show in the piano roll. Click a key on the left to hear it.
Draw: click an empty spot to write a note one grid step long. Drag the note up or down to change its pitch, drag its right end to make it longer.
Velocity: the bars under the notes. Drag them down for softer notes. Shift+click several notes to select them, then use the Velocity slider.
Transpose: select notes (or none, for all) and press +12 / −12 for an octave, +1 / −1 for a semitone.
Select the Bass clip and write a bass line: one note a bar, the chord’s root (C, A, F, G), then try root on 1 and 3.
crumbs: DAW 3: The Piano Roll and MIDI

title: DAW 3: The Piano Roll and MIDI
text:
Recording and quantizing
Clicking notes in is precise but slow. Most people record from a keyboard and then fix the timing.

Select a track (click its name). Press ● Rec (or R): one bar of clicks to count you in, then it records. Play with the computer keyboard (A W S E D F T G Y H U J K: the white and black keys from C; Z / X octave down / up) or a MIDI keyboard plugged in (Chrome or Edge). Space stops; the take becomes a new clip.
Your notes will be a little early or late: that’s human. Quantize (Q) moves them onto the grid. Set Grid to the smallest note you played first.
Quantize 50% moves them only half way: tighter, still human. Producers often quantize less than fully for this reason.
Undo (Ctrl/Cmd+Z) whenever an edit goes wrong. Every DAW keeps a long undo history: use it freely.

Quantizing to the wrong grid is the commonest beginner mistake: triplets forced onto a 1/16 grid, or a swung part straightened. Listen after you quantize.

title: DAW 6: Recording Audio: Bleed and Headphones
text:
So far every track has held MIDI notes. An audio track holds sound: what a microphone heard. Recording one is simple (pick the track, press record, play), but the microphone hears everything in the room, including the song you are playing along to. This lesson records twice, once with speakers and once with headphones, and measures the difference.
You need a microphone (the one in a laptop or a headset is fine), Chrome or Edge, and a pair of headphones.
crumbs: DAW 6: Recording Audio: Bleed and Headphones

title: DAW 6: Recording Audio: Bleed and Headphones
text:
The setup
The Voice track below is an audio track; the band has 8 bars of drums, bass and keys to play along with. With the Voice track selected, the ● Rec button records from the microphone: a short sound check first (it tells speakers from headphones and asks for your loudest phrase), then one bar of count-in, then recording. The small meter by the buttons is the microphone’s input level: keep your loudest moments out of the red (Recording 1: Gain Staging).
crumbs: DAW 6: Recording Audio: Bleed and Headphones

title: DAW 6: Recording Audio: Bleed and Headphones
text:
Experiment 1: speakers

Take off your headphones and play the band through your speakers at a normal listening level.
Select the Voice track, press ● Rec and stay silent for the whole 8 bars. Press Space to stop.
Under the tracks, This take gives the take’s average level. Write it down: everything in that take is bleed, the band and the click coming back into the microphone.
Click S on the Voice track to solo it and play. You hear the band, thin and roomy, and the click.
Now record yourself singing or clapping along. Solo it again: you, plus the band, plus the click.

Why it matters: that copy of the band is now part of your vocal for good. Turn the vocal up and the band comes up too. Change a chord in the keys part, and the old chord is still faintly in the vocal. Compress or EQ the vocal and you compress and EQ the band in it. And the click, which nobody is meant to hear, is in the song.
crumbs: DAW 6: Recording Audio: Bleed and Headphones

title: DAW 6: Recording Audio: Bleed and Headphones
text:
Experiment 2: headphones

Plug in headphones, put them on, and record 8 silent bars again.
Compare the average level with the speaker take. Closed headphones at a sensible level are usually 20 to 40 dB quieter in the microphone: almost nothing.
Now turn the headphones up loud, or take one side off, and record silence again. Headphones leak too: open-back ones, loud clicks and a mic close to the ear all bring bleed back.




Take (silent)
Average level




Speakers
______ dBFS


Headphones
______ dBFS


Headphones, loud / one side off
______ dBFS



Every studio records vocals and overdubs in headphones for this reason. More on headphones and the cue mix: Recording 6: Monitoring and Headphones; on bleed between instruments in one room: Recording 3: Distance, Bleed and Phase.
crumbs: DAW 6: Recording Audio: Bleed and Headphones

title: DAW 6: Recording Audio: Bleed and Headphones
text:
Monitoring and latency
🎧 Monitor sends the microphone through the Voice track so you hear yourself in the headphones, as a DAW’s input monitoring does. Two things to notice:

Only with headphones. Monitoring through speakers sends the mic to the speakers, back into the mic, round and round: feedback, a howl.
You hear yourself a little late. Sound takes time to go through the computer and back out: latency, here shown in milliseconds. Over about 10 ms it starts to feel odd; over 30 ms it’s hard to sing with. Audio interfaces have direct monitoring (the mic straight to the headphones, before the computer) to get round it.

Latency also makes recordings land late on the timeline. The DAW moves each take earlier by the measured amount: the Latency fix box in the editor. Set it to 0 on a take and look at the waveform: everything has slid late against the grid.
crumbs: DAW 6: Recording Audio: Bleed and Headphones

title: DAW 6: Recording Audio: Bleed and Headphones
section: Why phone calls don’t sound like this
text:
Why phone calls don’t sound like this
Video-call apps and voice memos run echo cancellation: they subtract what the speakers played from what the mic heard. It’s good for calls and bad for music (it chews up singing and room sound), so this DAW, like every real one, switches it off and records exactly what the microphone hears.
crumbs: DAW 6: Recording Audio: Bleed and Headphones

title: DAW 6: Recording Audio: Bleed and Headphones
text:
Tips for a clean take

Headphones on, closed-back if you have them. The click quieter than you think.
Point the microphone away from the headphones and the speakers; get close to the mic.
Record a few seconds of the room in silence: you will hear what noise is there before it is under your voice.
Watch the input meter: peaks around −10 dBFS, never in the red.
