title: DJ 2: Beatmatching by Ear
text: Beatmatching is making two tracks play at the same tempo with their beats together, so you can blend them without a clatter. DJ software has a SYNC button for this; learn it by ear anyway. Sync needs a correct beatgrid and fails on live drummers, old records and tempo changes, and hearing two beats drift apart is the skill under every other one.

title: DJ 2: Beatmatching by Ear
text:
Two problems, two controls

Tempo (are they going at the same speed?): the pitch fader. A track at 120 BPM against one at 124 needs +3.3 % (124 ÷ 120 = 1.033).
Phase (are the beats on top of each other?): a nudge. Push the side of the platter, or the jog wheel, to speed it a moment (or hold it back) until the kicks line up.

Get the tempo close first; otherwise the beats line up for a moment and drift apart again.

title: DJ 2: Beatmatching by Ear
text:
The routine

Deck A plays out loud. Cue deck B in the headphones (here: CUE on B, then Listen: phones).
Start B on a downbeat of A (the “1” of a bar): on a turntable, hold the record, let it go exactly on A’s kick.
Listen: do the kicks flam (two hits close together, “ka-tunk”)? Which is first?

If B’s kick comes before A’s, B is ahead: hold it back (drag the rim backwards, or the ‹ button) and, if it keeps getting ahead, pull B’s pitch slower.
If after, push it forward and make B faster.

Make small pitch corrections (0.1–0.3 %) and keep listening for a minute. When the beats stay together, the tempo is right.

title: DJ 2: Beatmatching by Ear
text:
Practise
Deck A: Warehouse at 124 BPM. Deck B: Late Bus at 120. The Match line below the decks shows the tempo difference, and once both play, how far apart the beats are. Cover it with your hand (or a sticky note) once you’ve got the idea.




Start A. Press CUE on B and set Listen: phones, with the phones knob in the middle: you hear both.
Set B’s pitch fader to about +3.3 % (the shown number can be typed into: click it). Read B’s BPM: about 124.0.
Start B on one of A’s kicks. Hear the flam? Nudge with ‹ › (hold) until the kicks hit as one.
Now the hard way: reset B’s pitch to 0, start both, and find the tempo by ear: B’s kicks will drift behind A’s, slowly at first. Each time, push the fader a little faster and nudge back into place.
Swap: let B be the one playing out, and match A to it at 120 (pitch about −3.2 %).

title: DJ 2: Beatmatching by Ear
text:
Tips

Listen to the kick and the hats, not the melody. On a fast flam, the hats are easier to hear than the kick.
Count. If they drift apart within one bar, the tempo is far off; within 8 bars, close; staying together over 32 bars, done.
Tap: tap the TAP button on the beat to measure a track’s tempo when you don’t know it (records don’t print it).
A track’s tempo is a number you can read off a deck or software, but on a record you’re often matching by ear: that is the skill.

title: DJ 1: The Gear
text: A DJ plays recorded music for people, one track flowing into the next. The job needs two (or more) sources you can start, stop and speed up independently, and a mixer to blend them, with headphones to hear the next track before anyone else does.

title: DJ 1: The Gear
text:
The decks

Turntables. The Technics SL-1200 (1972 onwards) became the club standard: a direct-drive motor that gets to speed in under a second, a heavy platter, and a pitch fader (±8 %, later ±16 % on some models). A slipmat lets the record slip over the spinning platter, so you can hold the record still while the platter turns, then let go on the beat.
CDJs (Pioneer’s name, now used for all such players) play files from USB sticks. A jog wheel stands in for the record: touch the top to scratch, turn the side to nudge. Tempo range, cue and loop buttons, key lock (Master Tempo) and a waveform display.
DVS (digital vinyl systems): turntables playing records of a timecode signal that software reads, so a laptop file follows the record’s speed and direction. Serato, rekordbox and Traktor all offer it with supported audio interfaces.
Controllers: two jog wheels, a mixer and pads in one box, for DJ software on a laptop. Cheaper and lighter; the same skills.

title: DJ 1: The Gear
text:
The mixer
Each channel has, top to bottom: gain (trim the input so loud and quiet tracks match), EQ (usually three bands: high, mid, low, cutting well below the boost, so a band can be nearly “killed”), often a filter, a cue button (send this channel to the headphones), and the channel fader. Then the crossfader blends the two sides, and the master sets the output level.

Headphones: the cue mix (or “cue/master”) knob blends what you’ve cued with the master. Some DJs use split cue: cue in one ear, master in the other.
Crossfader curve: smooth (both sides at full in the middle, for long blends) or sharp (a cut, for scratching: the sound comes in within a millimetre of the edge).

title: DJ 1: The Gear
text:
Your decks
The widget below is the practice rig for these lessons: two decks and a two-channel mixer. Everything here works with a mouse or a finger.




Press ▶ on deck A. Notice the platter turning, the waveform scrolling past the red line (now), and the time readout.
Stop and start it again: the “motor” takes a moment to reach speed and to stop, as a real turntable does.
Pull the Lo knob on channel A all the way down: the kick and bass vanish. Bring it back.
Move the crossfader from A to B, with deck B playing. Then press CUE on channel B, and click Listen: speakers to switch to what the headphones would hear. A browser has one output, so this is how you hear the cue here; with Split cue ticked and headphones on, cue is in the left ear and the master in the right.
Drag the label of a playing record: you are holding it. Move it back and forth. Then drag the rim (the outer ring) while it plays: the side of the platter, to speed it up or slow it down a touch (a nudge).

title: DJ 3: Phrasing and Counting Bars
text: Beatmatched tracks can still clash: if one reaches its drop while the other is halfway through a breakdown, the mix sounds wrong even with the beats together. Dance music is built in phrases, and a good mix lines phrases up.

title: DJ 3: Phrasing and Counting Bars
text:
Counting

A beat is one kick in four-on-the-floor music. A bar is four beats.
A phrase is usually 8 bars (32 beats). Changes (a new sound, a fill, a breakdown) arrive on the first beat of a phrase, and often bigger changes every 16 or 32 bars.
Many tracks start with a 16- or 32-bar intro of mostly drums (made for DJs to mix in) and end with a matching outro.

Count bars on your fingers: 1 2 3 4, 2 2 3 4, 3 2 3 4, …, 8 2 3 4. A drum fill or a cymbal crash in bar 8 tells you the next phrase is coming.

title: DJ 3: Phrasing and Counting Bars
text:
The rule
Start the incoming track on the first beat of a phrase of the playing track. Then their phrases line up: when the outgoing track changes, so does the incoming one, and the switch sounds planned. A common plan: incoming intro (16 bars) under the outgoing outro (16 bars), then the outgoing track is gone exactly as the incoming one’s main part starts.

title: DJ 3: Phrasing and Counting Bars
text:
Practise
The decks have 8-bar loops, so each loop is one phrase (the long tick on the waveform marks each bar; the overview shows the whole phrase).




Start A. Watch the overview: the playhead goes round once per phrase. Count the bars aloud.
Match B to A (B needs about +1.6 %; use the readout to check).
Set a cue on B at its start: with B stopped at 0:00, press CUE.
Start B exactly when A’s playhead returns to the start of its loop (bar 1 of a phrase). Bring B’s fader up over the next 8 bars.
Now start B on bar 3 of A’s phrase instead. Listen for the chord change in B arriving at a different moment from A’s. That’s what phrasing avoids.

title: DJ 3: Phrasing and Counting Bars
text:
Reading a track’s structure
DJs learn their records. In software you see it: the waveform’s dense parts are full sections, the thin parts are breakdowns. Mark the phrases you’ll mix at with hot cues (the first beat of the intro, the drop, the outro), and colour them so you know at a glance.

title: DJ 7: Building a Set and Reading a Room
text: Skills mix two tracks. A set is an hour or more of them, chosen for these people at this moment. The best technical mix of the wrong record empties a floor; a rough mix of the right one fills it.
crumbs: DJ 7: Building a Set and Reading a Room

title: DJ 7: Building a Set and Reading a Room
text:
The energy curve
A set usually builds: start below the room’s energy, raise it in steps, give it a peak, let it breathe, raise it again. Ways to raise energy: faster tempo (a few BPM at a time), busier drums, a brighter key step (+1 or +2 on the Camelot wheel), a familiar song. Ways to let it breathe: a breakdown, a vocal track, a lower tempo, a classic everyone sings.
Warm-up DJs keep the energy below the headliner’s, playing deeper, slower music. Playing your biggest tracks at 10 pm to an empty room is a classic beginner’s mistake.
crumbs: DJ 7: Building a Set and Reading a Room

title: DJ 7: Building a Set and Reading a Room
text:
Prepare

Crates / playlists by mood and energy, not only genre: “openers”, “builders”, “peak”, “breathers”, “closers”.
Know each track’s BPM, key, where its intro and outro are, and how long it takes to mix in. Set hot cues before the gig.
Plan the first three tracks and a few pairs that mix well. Then be ready to throw the plan away.
Gain: check levels so the meter peaks the same on every track; leave the master below the red (the venue’s sound system adds volume, not you).
crumbs: DJ 7: Building a Set and Reading a Room

title: DJ 7: Building a Set and Reading a Room
text:
Read the room
Watch the floor, not the screen:

Are people dancing? Growing or shrinking? People leaving the floor after a track tells you something.
Who is dancing? Different crowds want different things; a room of friends of the birthday girl wants songs they know.
Energy: heads down and dancing hard, hands up at the drop, or talking at the bar?
Change direction one step at a time. A sudden switch of genre or tempo loses people; a bridge track (the same key, a shared rhythm) keeps them.
The request you get repeatedly tells you what the room wants, even if you don’t play it.
crumbs: DJ 7: Building a Set and Reading a Room

title: DJ 7: Building a Set and Reading a Room
text:
Practise a mini-set
Plan a four-track set from the loops (each listed with BPM and Camelot code), then play it with transitions from the earlier lessons.



One plan: Mirrorball 118 (9B) → Late Bus 120 (5A: a contrast, use a drum intro or a cut) → Warehouse 124 (8A) → Neon Floor 126 (9A) → Concrete 128 (4A, by a filter mix or a cut). Tempo rises 2–4 BPM each time. Where would the acapella go?

Write the order down with each track’s BPM and key before you play.
Mix each pair on a phrase, with an EQ bass swap or a filter.
Record yourself (your phone, or the navbar’s tools) and listen back: are the transitions even in level? Any clash of keys or phrases?
crumbs: DJ 7: Building a Set and Reading a Room

title: DJ 7: Building a Set and Reading a Room
text:
After the gig

Write down what worked and what emptied the floor.
Update your crates: tracks that worked well together become pairs.

title: Stick Grips and Other Ways Drummers Differ
text: Ask ten drummers how to hold a stick and you’ll get several answers, and most of them are right. This lesson shows the common grips, why each exists, and then the other places where good kit players do things differently. Its aim is to tell a choice from a mistake: a choice suits a style or a body; a mistake causes pain or a choked sound in any style.
crumbs: Stick Grips and Other Ways Drummers Differ

title: Stick Grips and Other Ways Drummers Differ
text:
What every grip shares

A fulcrum. The stick pivots at one point, held between the thumb and a finger (the first or middle finger). About a third of the way up from the butt end is a usual starting place; slide it until the stick bounces most freely off a pad.
Rebound. Let the stick come back up by itself. The hand guides it and doesn’t fight it. Gripping hard kills the rebound, dulls the sound and tires the forearm.
Back fingers loose. The other fingers wrap the stick lightly, never squeezing; there should be a little air between the palm and the stick.
crumbs: Stick Grips and Other Ways Drummers Differ

title: Stick Grips and Other Ways Drummers Differ
text:
Matched grip
Both hands hold the stick the same way, palm roughly down. Most kit players today use it. There are three named positions; they differ only in how far the hand is turned.









Grip
Palms
Moves mostly with
Good for




German
Flat, facing the floor; sticks about 90° apart
The wrist (up and down)
Volume, backbeats, big strokes


American
Turned about 45°
Wrist and fingers together
An all-round default, moving around the kit


French
Thumbs on top, palms facing each other
The fingers
Speed and finesse at low volume, cymbal work, jazz



Most players move between them in a single song: closer to German for a loud backbeat, closer to French for fast ride-cymbal patterns. Start with American.
crumbs: Stick Grips and Other Ways Drummers Differ

title: Stick Grips and Other Ways Drummers Differ
text:
Traditional grip
The left hand (for a right-handed player) holds the stick differently: it sits in the web between thumb and first finger, resting on the third finger, palm turned up; the hand turns like turning a doorknob. It comes from marching drums slung at an angle on a strap, where a matched left hand hit the tilted head awkwardly. It’s still common in jazz and drum corps for the light, controlled touch it gives the left hand, and many players simply like how it feels.
Choose traditional grip if you want it, not because a style requires it: plenty of jazz drummers play matched grip. It takes longer to learn, and the snare is usually tilted toward the player to suit it.
crumbs: Stick Grips and Other Ways Drummers Differ

title: Stick Grips and Other Ways Drummers Differ
text:
Stroke types
The grip matters less than the motion. Four strokes cover nearly everything:

Full stroke: start high, strike, let it rebound back to high. Loud notes in a row.
Down stroke: start high, strike, stop the stick low. An accent followed by a quiet note.
Tap: start low, strike, return low. Quiet notes.
Up stroke: start low, strike quietly, lift to high. A quiet note followed by an accent.

Moeller (after Sanford Moeller, a teacher of drum corps drummers) is a whipping motion of the forearm, wrist and stick that gets an accent and a tap or two out of one throw. Many drummers use something like it without the name.
crumbs: Stick Grips and Other Ways Drummers Differ

title: Stick Grips and Other Ways Drummers Differ
text:
Other places drummers differ



Choice
The options
What decides it




Which hand leads
Right-handed kit (hi-hat on the left, right hand crosses over to it), left-handed kit (a mirror image), or open-handed (right-handed kit, left hand plays the hi-hat, no crossing)
Comfort. Open-handed frees the right hand for the snare and toms; Billy Cobham and Simon Phillips play this way.


Leading foot
Bass drum on the right foot or the left
Usually the same side as the strong hand; a left-footed player often plays a left-handed kit.


Bass drum pedal
Heel up (on the ball of the foot, the leg does the work) or heel down (the ankle does it)
Heel up: power, rock. Heel down: control and quiet, jazz. Many players change in a song.


Burying the beater
Leave the beater against the head after a stroke, or let it bounce off
Buried: a short, punchy note. Off the head: a fuller, open note.


Hi-hat foot
Keep it closed, rock the foot heel-toe to keep time, or play it on 2 and 4
Style. Jazz drummers often play the foot on 2 and 4.


Throne height
Thighs level or sloping slightly down to the knee
Higher gives power; lower gives a stable seat. Too low hurts the hips and lower back.


Kit size
Four pieces (kick, snare, one rack tom, floor tom) up to large kits
The music and the room. Four or five pieces is enough for most styles.


Cymbal height and angle
Flat and low, or high and tilted
Reach without stretching; flat for jazz ride playing, angled so the stick hits with the side of the tip, not the edge with the shoulder of the stick (which cracks cymbals).


Sticks
7A (thin, light), 5A (the default), 5B and 2B (thick, heavy); wood or nylon tips
Volume and the hand. Nylon tips make a brighter cymbal sound.


Matched or traditional
See above
Taste.


Reading and counting
Read notation, count aloud, learn by ear
Most professionals do all three; the Drum Set page writes grooves in notation.
crumbs: Stick Grips and Other Ways Drummers Differ

title: Stick Grips and Other Ways Drummers Differ
section: Signs of a mistake, not a choice
text:
Signs of a mistake, not a choice

Pain in the wrist, forearm or lower back. Stop, rest, and look at your grip and throne height.
White knuckles, or the stick buzzing in a tight hand.
Hitting rim and cymbal edges with the shaft of the stick (chipped sticks, cracked cymbals).
Every stroke the same height: no accents and a flat sound.
Reaching or leaning to play anything you play often.
crumbs: Stick Grips and Other Ways Drummers Differ

title: Stick Grips and Other Ways Drummers Differ
text:
Practice

On a practice pad, play 8 full strokes per hand at a slow tempo with a metronome. Watch that each stick comes back to the height it started at.
Play the same 8 strokes in German, then American, then French grip. Listen for the change in sound.
Accents: alternate a down stroke and three taps (R L L L, then L R R R), then put them in a groove.
Try one foot setting you don’t use: heel down if you play heel up, or the reverse.

title: Elements 1: Articulation
text: Articulation is how a note is played: how it starts, how long it lasts and how it joins the next one. It is not how loud it is (that is dynamics). The same eight notes can sound bouncy, smooth or aggressive depending on articulation alone.

title: Elements 1: Articulation
text:
1. Staccato and legato
Staccato means short and detached. You hear a gap after each note. It is written as a dot above or below the notehead (on the opposite side from the stem).
Legato means smooth, with no breaks between the notes. A slur (a curved line over or under notes of different pitches) asks for legato.











Slur or tie? Both are curves. A curve joining two notes of the same pitch is a tie: play one note, held for both lengths. A curve over different pitches is a slur: play them all, smoothly.

How players make a slur








Instrument
Legato / slurred
Detached




Strings (violin, cello…)
all the slurred notes in one bow stroke, no change of direction
a new bow stroke (or a lifted bow) for each note


Woodwind and brass
tongue only the first note; the rest change by fingers (or slide) alone
tongue every note


Voice
one breath, the vowel kept going between notes
a little stop of the breath or a consonant on each note


Piano
hold each key until the next one is down
lift each finger early

title: Elements 1: Articulation
text:
2. Accents and other marks
An accent (>) asks for extra force on the start of the note. Marks can be combined: a staccato dot and an accent means short and strong.











Sign
Name
Meaning




. over/under the notehead
staccato
short, detached


>
accent
strong start


- (a short line)
tenuto
hold for its full length, a slight weight


^
marcato
stronger than an accent


curve over different notes
slur
legato


straight or wavy line between two notes, often marked gliss.
glissando
slide from one to the other

title: Elements 1: Articulation
text:
3. Glissando
A glissando is a slide from one note to another. On a violin, trombone or voice it is a smooth slide through every pitch in between. On a piano or harp it is a sweep across the keys or strings.

title: Elements 1: Articulation
text:
4. Playing techniques
Some articulations change the kind of sound an instrument makes. Each is a word above the staff.








Technique
Who
What it is




Pizzicato (pizz.)
strings
pluck the strings; arco goes back to the bow


Double stopping
strings
two strings at once


Con sordino (con sord.)
strings, brass
play with a mute; senza sord. takes it off


Tremolo
strings (and others)
repeat one note very fast (a trembling sound)


Vibrato
strings, voice, wind, brass
let the pitch waver a little, for warmth


Falsetto
voice
a light, high register above the normal voice, used mostly by men

title: Elements 1: Articulation
text:
5. Writing your own

Choose the articulation for what you want the listener to feel: staccato for light or playful, legato for calm or sad, accents to push the beat or make a rhythm stand out.
Put articulation on the notes; dynamics go under the staff.
Check each mark with a player of that instrument: a slur on a trumpet is easy, a slur across a big leap on a trombone is not.

title: Elements 1: Articulation
text: 6. Check yourself

title: Elements 2: Dynamics
text: Dynamics are the volume of the music: how loud or quiet it is, and how that changes.

title: Elements 2: Dynamics
text:
1. The markings
Dynamics are written as Italian words, shortened to letters.








Marking
Italian
Meaning




pp
pianissimo
very quiet


p
piano
quiet


mp
mezzo piano
moderately quiet


mf
mezzo forte
moderately loud


f
forte
loud


ff
fortissimo
very loud


cresc. or a widening hairpin <
crescendo
getting gradually louder


dim. / decresc. or a closing hairpin >
diminuendo / decrescendo
getting gradually quieter


sfz or sf
sforzando
a sudden strong accent on one note



Piano is the Italian for quiet; the instrument’s full name, pianoforte, means “quiet-loud”, because it could play both.
The same phrase at three levels:

title: Elements 2: Dynamics
text:
2. Crescendo and diminuendo
A hairpin opens as the music gets louder and closes as it gets quieter. Always say where it starts and where it ends up: a crescendo from p to f is a different thing from one from mf to ff.



A sforzando hits one note hard and drops back at once:

title: Elements 2: Dynamics
section: 3. Where they go on the score
text:
3. Where they go on the score

For an instrument on one staff: under the staff.
For piano: between the two staves, so one marking covers both hands.
For voices: above the staff, so the dynamics don’t get mixed up with the words underneath.

title: Elements 2: Dynamics
text:
4. Dynamics through history







Period
Dynamics




Baroque (about 1600–1750)
few markings, mostly p and f; terraced dynamics: sudden steps between loud and quiet sections (often by more or fewer instruments playing), not gradual changes


Classical (about 1750–1820)
more markings, crescendos and diminuendos, used for contrast; the new piano could play both quiet and loud


Romantic (about 1800–1910)
a huge range, from ppp to fff, with constant crescendos and diminuendos for expression



Terraced against gradual:

title: Elements 2: Dynamics
text:
5. Describing what you hear
When you describe dynamics in a listening question, describe the changes in order. One word for the whole piece is not enough unless it really never changes.

The music starts p… then a gradual crescendo to f when the brass come in… a sudden drop to pp for the quiet middle section… then it ends ff.

Useful words: sudden, gradual, a wide range, a narrow range, contrast, terraced, fades out.

title: Elements 2: Dynamics
text:
6. Writing your own

Give every entry a starting dynamic.
A crescendo needs somewhere to go: mark where it ends.
Contrast is what the ear notices. A piece that is mf throughout sounds flat, however good the notes.

title: Elements 3: Harmony and Tonality
text: Harmony is the chords. Tonality is the key: which note feels like home, and whether the music is major, minor, or something else.

title: Elements 3: Harmony and Tonality
text:
1. Key signatures
The sharps or flats at the start of every line show the key. Each major key shares its signature with a relative minor, three half steps below it.



Signature
Major key
Relative minor




none

Major or minor? The signature alone doesn’t tell you. Look at the last note and chord (usually the tonic), and in minor look for the raised 7th: music in A minor uses G♯, a sharp that is not in the key signature.

title: Elements 3: Harmony and Tonality
text:
2. Major, minor, modal, atonal







Tonality
What you hear




Major
in a major key; often sounds bright


Minor
in a minor key; often sounds darker or sadder


Modal
built on a mode, an older scale such as Dorian or Mixolydian; folk songs, medieval music, a lot of rock


Pentatonic
uses only five notes (C D E G A, the black keys of a piano); folk music round the world, blues, pop


Atonal
no key at all, no note that feels like home; some 20th-century classical music, film horror

title: Elements 3: Harmony and Tonality
text:
3. Modulation
A modulation is a change of key in the middle of a piece. The most common moves are to the dominant (the key a 5th up, C to G) and to the relative major or minor (C major to A minor). In pop songs the last chorus often modulates up a half step or whole step for a lift.

title: Elements 3: Harmony and Tonality
text:
4. Chords
A triad is a chord of three notes, each a 3rd apart: root, 3rd and 5th. Built on each note of the scale, triads are numbered with Roman numerals: capitals for major, small letters for minor.














I
ii
iii
IV
V
vi
vii°




In C
C
Dm
Em
F
G
Am
B°


Name
tonic
supertonic
mediant
subdominant
dominant
submediant
leading note



Adding another 3rd on top makes a seventh chord (G7 = G B D F). Adding more makes extended chords (9ths, 11ths, 13ths), common in jazz.



For the rest of this: Inversions, Borrowed Chords.

title: Elements 3: Harmony and Tonality
text:
5. Cadences
A cadence is the last two chords of a phrase, like punctuation. Two sound finished, two don’t.








Cadence
Chords
Sounds




Authentic cadence
V → I
finished, a full stop


Plagal
IV → I
finished, softer: the “Amen” of hymns


Half cadence
anything → V
unfinished, a comma or a question


Deceptive cadence
V → vi (usually)
a surprise: you expect I and get a minor chord



The names in this table follow the British names switch at the top of the page. The US and UK names differ here: the British perfect, imperfect and interrupted are the American authentic, half and deceptive.
















The Picardy third (Tierce de Picardie): a piece in a minor key that ends on a major tonic chord instead of the minor one you expect.



More: Cadences, Write an Ending.

4. Rock, pop and jazz line-ups







Group
Usual instruments

lead vocals, electric guitar(s), bass guitar, drum kit, keyboards

title: Elements 4: Instruments and Voices
text:
5. What is each instrument doing?
Naming the instrument is half the answer. Say what it is doing, too:



Role
Meaning




Melody
the tune


Accompaniment
the parts that support the tune (chords, rhythm)


Countermelody
a second tune that fits with the main one


Bass line

Solo
one instrument featured, often improvising




The melody is on the violins, with cellos playing a slow bass line and the horns holding chords. In the second section the melody passes to the flute, and the strings change to pizzicato.

The techniques that change an instrument’s sound (pizzicato, mutes, tremolo, vibrato, falsetto) are in Articulation.

title: Elements 5: Melody
text: The melody is the tune: the line you would sing back. These are the words for describing one.

title: Elements 5: Melody
text:
1. Direction and movement







Word
Meaning




Rising / ascending
going up


Falling / descending
going down


Conjunct
moving by step, to the next note up or down


Disjunct
moving by leap, jumping over notes


Range
the distance from the lowest note to the highest: narrow or wide

title: Elements 5: Melody
text:
2. Repetition and its relatives







Word
Meaning




Repetition
the same idea again, unchanged


Sequence
the same idea again, starting on a higher or lower note


Imitation
one part copies an idea another part has just played, often at a different pitch


Ostinato
a short idea repeated over and over (in the bass it is a ground bass or a riff)


Contrast
something completely different

title: Elements 5: Melody
section: 3. What the melody is made of
text:
3. What the melody is made of







Word
Meaning




Scalic
runs up and down the scale


Triadic
uses the notes of the chords (broken chords)


Chromatic
uses notes outside the key, often moving by half step


Pentatonic
uses only five notes


Ornamented
decorated with trills, mordents, turns, grace notes

title: Elements 5: Melody
text:
4. Intervals
An interval is the distance between two notes. Count the letter names, including both the first and the last: C up to E is C-D-E, three letters, a 3rd.

title: Elements 6: Metre and Time Signatures
text: Metre is how the steady beat (the pulse) is grouped. The strong beat comes round regularly: every 2, 3 or 4 beats. Each group is a measure.

title: Elements 6: Metre and Time Signatures
text:
1. Time signatures
A time signature is written at the start of the music, and again wherever it changes.

The top number says how many beats in each measure (in simple time).
The bottom number says what kind of note gets the beat: 4 = quarter note, 2 = half note, 8 = eighth note.

C is short for 4/4, called common time. C with a line through it is 2/2, cut time (alla breve).

title: Elements 6: Metre and Time Signatures
text:
2. Simple time
In simple time each beat splits into two equal halves.









Time signature
Beats in a measure
Name
Often heard in




2/4
2 quarter notes
simple duple
marches, polkas


3/4
3 quarter notes
simple triple
waltzes, minuets


4/4
4 quarter notes
simple quadruple
most pop, rock and jazz



Listen for where the strong beat (the accent) falls:

title: Elements 6: Metre and Time Signatures
text:
3. Compound time
In compound time each beat is a dotted note and splits into three. The top number counts the eighth notes, not the beats: divide it by three to get the beats.









Time signature
Eighth notes
Beats (dotted quarter notes)
Name




6/8
6
2
compound duple


9/8
9
3
compound triple


12/8
12
4
compound quadruple



The same tune in 2/4 and in 6/8. Both have two beats in a measure; listen to how each beat divides:








12/8 is the slow, rolling feel of many blues and soul ballads: four beats, each in three.

title: Elements 6: Metre and Time Signatures
text:
4. Hearing the metre

Tap the pulse with your foot.
Listen for the strongest beat, often where the bass note or the chord changes, and count from it: 1 2 3 1 2 3…
Listen between the beats. If the beat naturally splits in two, it is simple time; if it splits in three (a lilting, “jig” feel), it is compound.

A march is usually in two (left, right, left, right). A waltz is a dance in three.

title: Elements 6: Metre and Time Signatures
text:
5. Regular and irregular metres
A regular metre divides into equal groups of two or three beats (2/4, 3/4, 4/4, 6/8, 9/8, 12/8). An irregular metre can’t: 5/4 is counted 3 + 2 (or 2 + 3), 7/8 as 2 + 2 + 3. Some music also changes metre as it goes, which is a good way to make contrast in your own pieces.

title: Elements 6: Metre and Time Signatures
text:

title: Elements 6: Metre and Time Signatures
text:
7. Writing your own
Every measure must add up to the time signature: check each one before you hand it in. Changing metre for one section is a simple way to make contrast.

title: Rhythm on One Page
text: The whole of Rhythm on one sheet. Every ▶ plays the example. Tick British note names for crotchets and quavers. Press Full screen to put the sheet on the whole screen for revision or for the class board.

title: Rhythm on One Page
text:
The sheet



Note lengths

In beats: whole note 4 · half note 2 · quarter note 1 · eighth note ½ · sixteenth note ¼.






Rests

Every note length has a matching rest: a silence of the same length.






Dots

A dot adds half the note’s value again: a dotted half note is 3 beats, a dotted quarter note 1½.






Ties

Joins two notes of the same pitch into one longer note, often across a measure line.






Triplets

Three notes played evenly in the time of two, marked 3.






Syncopation

The accent off the beat, often a note tied over the strong beat. Pop, funk, Latin, jazz.






Fermata

Hold the note longer than written; the pulse waits.






Tempo words

BPM = beats per minute. A rough guide:



Lento, adagio: slow, under 70


Andante: walking pace, 75–100


Moderato: moderate, 100–120


Allegro: fast, 120–160


Vivace, presto: very fast, 160+




Changing tempo

Accelerando: getting faster. Ritardando / rallentando: slower. A tempo: back to speed. Rubato: stretching the tempo for expression.






Check yourself

title: Rhythm on One Page
text:
Describing rhythm and tempo

Name the tempo with a word and a rough BPM, then any changes: “allegro, about 140 BPM, with a ritardando at the end”.
To find a tempo by ear, tap along: the Tap Along tool counts it for you.
The longer lesson, with fuller examples: Elements 7: Rhythm and Tempo.

title: Structure on One Page
text: The whole of Structure on one sheet. Each example is a miniature of the form, its sections labelled with letters. Press Full screen to put the sheet on the whole screen for revision or for the class board.

title: Structure on One Page
text:
The sheet



Phrases and sections

A phrase is a musical sentence, usually 2, 4 or 8 measures, ending in a cadence. Sections change: new tune, key, instruments, texture or mood. The first idea is A, the next new one B.



Binary: A B

Two sections, usually both repeated (A A B B). Baroque dances.






Ternary: A B A

A, a contrasting B, then A again (exact, or changed: A B A′).






Rondo: A B A C A

A refrain keeps coming back, with contrasting episodes between.






Strophic: A A A

The same music for every verse, new words each time: hymns, folk songs. The opposite, music that keeps changing to follow the words, is through-composed.



Minuet and trio

A dance in 3/4. Minuet (A A B B), a contrasting trio (C C D D), then the minuet again without repeats (A B). Ternary overall.



Theme and variations

A tune, then changed versions of it: new rhythm, harmony, key or instruments.






Song forms


Verse–chorus: intro, verse, chorus, verse, chorus, bridge, chorus, outro


AABA (32-bar song): four 8-measure sections; B is the bridge or middle eight


12-bar blues: one 12-measure chord pattern, repeated




Check yourself

title: Structure on One Page
text:
Describing structure

Label the sections with letters as they come, and say what changes at each new letter.
Marking sections in a recording: Section Labels.

title: Style on One Page
text: The whole of Style on one sheet. Every ▶ plays a few measures in that style. Press Full screen to put the sheet on the whole screen for revision or for the class board.

title: Style on One Page
text:
The sheet



Baroque (about 1600–1750)

Bach, Vivaldi, Handel. Harpsichord, basso continuo, mostly strings; terraced dynamics; ornaments; often polyphonic.






Classical (about 1750–1820)

Haydn, Mozart, early Beethoven. Piano; balanced 4 + 4 phrases; simple chords, Alberti bass; melody and accompaniment.






Romantic (about 1800–1910)

Schubert, Chopin, Wagner. Big orchestra; huge dynamic range; chromatic harmony; long expressive melody; rubato; leitmotifs.






Jazz and blues

Swing, blue notes (3rd, 5th, 7th bent down), 12-bar blues, 7th chords, improvisation, walking bass, rhythm section and front line.






Pop and rock

Verse–chorus form, a memorable riff, guitars, bass and drums. Rock is usually louder and harder.






Minimalism

From the 1960s: Reich, Glass, Riley, Adams. Short patterns repeated, changing gradually; slow-changing harmony; phasing.






Musical theatre

A story in songs, acting and dance. Overture; solo, duet and chorus numbers; recitative; book, sung-through and jukebox musicals. Bernstein, Sondheim, Lloyd Webber.



Film music

Fits the scene. A leitmotif returns with its character.



Chase: fast, loud, driving ostinato


Horror: dissonance, building tension, stabs


Romance: strings, legato, rubato




Check yourself

title: Style on One Page
text:
Describing style

Name the style, then give the features that told you: “Baroque: a harpsichord, a busy bass line and lots of ornaments”.
The periods overlap; Beethoven is the usual bridge from Classical to Romantic.

title: Texture on One Page
text: The whole of Texture on one sheet, the way the school handout lays it out. Every ▶ plays the example; most use the same two measures of Twinkle, Twinkle so you hear only the texture change. Press Full screen to put the sheet on the whole screen for revision or for the class board.

title: Texture on One Page
text:
The sheet



Monophonic

One line only. Any number of players, as long as they all play the same part. No chords.






Octaves

The same tune in two parts, an octave apart: same note names, different pitch. Still one line, heavier.






Homophonic

All parts move together in the same rhythm, as chords. Like a hymn. Homo-phonic: “same sound”.






Melody and accompaniment

A tune, with chords or a pattern underneath supporting it. The most common texture in pop.






Polyphonic

Two or more independent lines, each a tune (counterpoint). Copying each other is imitation; a round is strict imitation.






Who does what


Melody: the tune


Accompaniment: the parts supporting it


Countermelody: a second tune that fits with the main one


Bass line: the lowest part







Call and response

One performer or group plays a phrase; another answers. Blues, gospel, work songs, African music, pop.






Antiphonal

Two groups answering each other from different places, such as two choirs on opposite sides of a church.






Pedal

A long or repeated note, usually in the bass, held while the chords change above it.






Drone

Long or repeated notes, usually two a 5th apart, as on bagpipes.






Alberti bass

A Classical piano accompaniment: each chord broken into four equal notes, lowest, highest, middle, highest.






Basso continuo

Baroque: a bass instrument (cello, bass viol, bassoon) plays the bass line while a harpsichord, organ or lute fills in chords, read from figured bass.






Check yourself

text:
Describing texture

Name it, then describe it: thin or thick, sparse or dense, how many parts.
Say what changes, in order: “It starts monophonic (a solo flute), becomes homophonic when the choir comes in, and the middle is polyphonic, the voices entering one by one in imitation.”

title: First Rock Song: One Loop, a Part for Everyone
text:
This whole song is four chords, played over and over: G, D, Em, C. Many hit songs are built on this loop. Everyone in the class plays the same song at the same time. Each player picks a level.
How to use the page. Press ▶ Play and the band plays the loop. Under Who plays, switch your own instrument off and play its part yourself. The buttons under each example pick the level. The band plays exactly the part you choose, and it is written out underneath. Use the tempo control at the bottom of the window to slow it down.
Count it. Every chord lasts one bar: four beats. Count “1, 2, 3, 4” out loud. The chord changes on every “1”.
crumbs: First Rock Song: One Loop, a Part for Everyone

title: First Rock Song: One Loop, a Part for Everyone
text:
Drums
You play with both feet and both hands. The bass drum (right foot) and the snare drum are the two most important sounds. The bass drum is low and goes on 1 and 3. The snare is sharp and goes on 2 and 4. Together they make the backbeat, the beat under nearly all rock.

Level 1: Bass drum and snare. Bass drum on 1 and 3, snare on 2 and 4. Just “boom, crack, boom, crack”. (The band’s drummer also taps the hi-hat pedal on 2 and 4. Skip that at first.)
Level 2: Add the hi-hat in quarter notes. Your right hand plays the closed hi-hat on every beat. Your left hand plays the snare on 2 and 4. On 2 and 4, both hands hit at once.
Level 3: Hi-hat in eighth notes. Count “1 and 2 and 3 and 4 and”. The hi-hat plays on every number and every “and”.
Level 4: The rock beat. The bass drum moves around a little, and you play a fill at the end of each time through the loop. Next: Hi-hat Grooves.
crumbs: First Rock Song: One Loop, a Part for Everyone

title: First Rock Song: One Loop, a Part for Everyone
text:
Bass
The bass plays the lowest note of each chord. That note is the root, the letter name of the chord: G, D, E, C. On a bass in standard tuning (E A D G, lowest string first):



Chord

Level 1: One note a bar. Play the root on “1” and let it ring for four beats.
Level 2: Two notes a bar. The root on 1 and on 3.
Level 3: Four notes a bar. The root on every beat.
Level 4: Eighth notes. The root eight times a bar: “1 and 2 and 3 and 4 and”. This is the classic rock bass part. Lock in with the drummer’s bass drum.
crumbs: First Rock Song: One Loop, a Part for Everyone

title: First Rock Song: One Loop, a Part for Everyone
text:
Guitar
There are two things to learn: the chord shapes (left hand) and the strum (right hand). Pick a level of each. They do not have to match.
Chord shapes. Pick one row. The dots show where your fingers go; the number in each dot is the note’s place in the chord (1 = the root, 3, 5). An x above a string means don’t play it. Every shape opens in the Chord Library, with the other ways to play it.
Easy shapes (one or two fingers). The D is a D5: it has no F♯, but it fits the song.



Full open chords. More on these in Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand.



Power chords (for a louder, harder rock sound). Two fingers, the same shape every time; only E5 uses an open string.



Strum.

Level 1: One strum a bar. Strum down on “1” and let it ring. This gives you three beats to get to the next chord.
Level 2: Down on every beat. Four downstrokes a bar.
Level 3: Down, up. Eight strums a bar: down on the numbers, up on the “and”s. Keep your arm moving even when you miss a string.
Level 4: D, D-U, D, D-U. The folk-rock strum. Count “1, 2 and, 3, 4 and”.
crumbs: First Rock Song: One Loop, a Part for Everyone

title: First Rock Song: One Loop, a Part for Everyone
text:
Keyboard
The notes below stay close together, so your right hand barely moves.
Level 1 plays only the root, the note marked 1 (G, D, E, C). Level 2 and up play all three notes.




Level 1: One note a bar. Play the root with your right thumb on “1” and hold it.
Level 2: The chord, once a bar. Three notes together on “1”, held for four beats.
Level 3: The chord on every beat, with your left hand playing the root on “1”.
Level 4: Driving eighths. The chord eight times a bar, left hand on the root. Keep it light so that it does not cover the guitar.
crumbs: First Rock Song: One Loop, a Part for Everyone

title: First Rock Song: One Loop, a Part for Everyone
section: Voice, and instruments that play one note at a time
text:
Voice, and instruments that play one note at a time
This is for singers, saxophone, violin, flute, trumpet and any other instrument that plays one note at a time. (Saxophone and trumpet players: these are concert pitches. Ask which notes to read on your instrument.)

Level 1: The roots. Sing or play G, D, E, C, one long note a bar. This is the bass part sung higher.
Level 2: A smooth line. B, A, B, C. Every note is in its chord, and each one is a step from the last. Sing it on “oo”, then make up words.
Level 3: Make up a riff. Use only the notes G A B D E (the G major pentatonic scale). They fit all four chords. Make a short rhythm, two beats long, and repeat it every bar.
Level 4: Make up a melody. Use the same five notes. Play a short idea, then answer it with a different one, like a question and an answer. See also Pop Singing.

Switch on all the players below and play along.
crumbs: First Rock Song: One Loop, a Part for Everyone

title: First Rock Song: One Loop, a Part for Everyone
text:
The whole band
Everyone together. Turn off the players your class is covering. The buttons set every player in the band to the same level, so you can hear what level 1 and level 4 sound like as a band. They don’t have to match: a level 1 bass under a level 4 drummer sounds fine.
crumbs: First Rock Song: One Loop, a Part for Everyone

title: First Rock Song: One Loop, a Part for Everyone
text:
Make it a song
A loop becomes a song when the parts change between sections.

Verse: quieter. Drums at level 1 or 2, guitars at level 1.
Chorus: everybody up a level. Louder.
Ending: play the G one last time on “1” and let it ring.

Try verse, chorus, verse, chorus, ending. Somebody counts it in: “1, 2, 3, 4”.
crumbs: First Rock Song: One Loop, a Part for Everyone

title: First Rock Song: One Loop, a Part for Everyone
text:
For the teacher

Grouping. A band of four to six covers drums, bass, one or two guitars, keys and a voice or melody player. Students who don’t play yet can start on drums level 1, bass level 1 or the voice level 1 line.
Tempo. 92 is a starting point. Slow the band to 70 for level 1 players. Speed it up for the final performance.
Checking progress. For each student, note the level they can play four times through without stopping, in time with the band. Four times through at a level is the goal before moving up.
Other loops. The same parts work over C, G, Am, F and the other loops in Four-Chord Loops. Change the chord names and the bass notes.

title: Gear 3: Amps, Speakers and the PA
text: An amplifier makes a small signal big enough to move a speaker. Instrument amps are part of the instrument’s sound; a PA (public address) should just make everything louder, faithfully.
crumbs: Gear 3: Amps, Speakers and the PA

title: Gear 3: Amps, Speakers and the PA
text:
Instrument amps

Combo (amp and speaker in one box) or head and cabinet.
The usual controls: Gain (or Drive) sets how hard the preamp is pushed: low is clean, high distorts. Volume / Master sets how loud. Bass, Mid, Treble shape it; Presence adds upper bite.
Guitar amps colour the sound heavily and are meant to. Bass amps need much more power for the same loudness (low notes take more energy), and are built to stay clean and reach low. Keyboard amps are flatter, more like a small PA. (More below: Guitar amps and bass amps.)
Start everything at noon (12 o’clock), gain low, then adjust. Small changes.
Valve (tube) amps need a minute to warm up and should go into standby for breaks. Never run one without a speaker connected: it can destroy the output transformer.
Impedance (ohms) of the cabinet must match what the head expects (printed by the speaker jack).


Gain (or Volume) and Master: two volume knobs
An amp is two amplifiers in a row. The preamp takes the tiny signal from the guitar and shapes it; the power amp makes it strong enough to drive the speaker. Each knob sits in front of one of them:

Gain, Drive, or on many amps a knob just called Volume (sometimes per channel), sets how hard the signal hits the preamp. That decides the sound: low is clean, higher breaks up, highest is full distortion. It changes loudness too, but only until the preamp is clipping; after that more gain means more distortion, not more level.
Master sits between the preamp and the power amp and decides how loud all of that is in the room. It doesn’t change the character, so you can have a fully distorted sound quietly at home, or a clean one loud.

Set them in that order: Master low, Gain for the sound you want, then Master up to the level the room needs. It’s the same idea as gain staging on a mixer: the first knob sets the sound, the last one the loudness.
An old-style amp with only one Volume (many vintage Fenders and Voxes) has no master: the one knob does both, so it is clean when quiet and only starts to break up when it is loud. That’s why those amps are “too loud” to get their overdrive at home. On a valve amp, turning the Master far up drives the power valves too, which adds a second, looser kind of distortion that a low-master setting can’t give you.


Treble and Presence
Both turn up the high end, and on a lot of amps they sit side by side, so they look like the same knob twice. They aren’t. Presence is a treble control, but not a second Treble knob. It works on a higher band (roughly 2–6 kHz: pick attack, string edge, the “cut” that lets a guitar be heard through a band), and it sits in a different place:

Treble is in the preamp’s tone stack, before or in the middle of the distortion. Turning it up also changes what gets distorted, and so how the distortion sounds.
Presence is in the power amp, after the distortion. On a valve amp it reduces the power amp’s negative feedback at high frequencies (the circuit that keeps the power amp flat), so those frequencies come through stronger. On a solid-state or modelling amp it’s a high-frequency boost placed at the same point. It adds clarity without changing how the drive feels.

Too little and the amp sounds woolly and lost in the mix, even when it’s loud. Too much sounds harsh and fizzy (the “ice pick”, worst with high gain and in small rooms). Start it at noon, set Treble first, then use Presence to make the guitar cut through the band. Some amps have a matching low control, Resonance or Depth, which does the same thing for the low end. On a bass amp the equivalent (sometimes Bright) helps slap and fingernoise speak.









Treble
Presence




Where

To hear it, set High gain, quiet, then turn Treble from 3 to 8: the distortion itself changes, getting buzzier and tighter. Back to 5, and turn Presence from 3 to 8 instead: the same distortion, just brighter on top.


Middle and the Mid frequency
The Middle knob boosts or cuts one band, and where that band sits matters as much as how much. On most guitar amps it is fixed, somewhere around 500 Hz to 800 Hz. Many bass amps and some guitar amps (and almost every mixer channel, see the mixer) let you move it with a second knob, Mid frequency (a “sweepable” or semi-parametric mid):

200–400 Hz: body and boom. Cut here when the guitar is muddy or fights the bass; boost on a thin bass.
500 Hz–1 kHz: the honk and growl. A guitar’s mids live here; so does the “growl” of a bass that cuts through.
1.5–3 kHz: bite, pick and finger attack. Boost for a bass that has to be heard on small speakers.

To find a frequency: boost the Middle a lot (8 or 9), sweep the Mid frequency until it sounds worst (or best), then set the Middle back to the amount you want. The scooped sound (Middle at 2 or 3, bass and treble up) is big and exciting alone, and disappears as soon as the band plays, because the middle is where a guitar is heard.


Guitar amps and bass amps
A bass’s low E is 41 Hz; a guitar’s is 82 Hz. Most of the differences follow from that octave:

Power. Moving the air for low notes takes far more energy: a bass amp needs several times the watts of a guitar amp to keep up with it (300–500 W against a 30–50 W guitar valve amp in a band).
Clean on purpose. A guitar amp is designed to distort when pushed. A bass amp is designed to stay clean (more headroom, in the simulation: the same Gain distorts later); bass drive is something added on purpose, gently, usually keeping the clean lows underneath (Bass, growl).
The EQ sits lower. Bass at about 40–60 Hz instead of 100 Hz, a mid that is often sweepable, treble at 4–5 kHz and up for string and slap noise. Many bass amps add a graphic EQ.
The cabinet goes deeper and is closed, often with a horn tweeter for the top (see Cabinets below).
A DI out. Bass amps nearly always have an XLR DI output, so the PA gets the bass directly while the amp is only for the stage.

Playing bass through a guitar amp works quietly, but the amp throws away the bottom octave (the low-cut at the input and the cabinet’s roll-off), and loud low notes can tear a guitar speaker, which isn’t built to move that far. Try Bass through a guitar amp, then Bass amp. A guitar through a bass amp is safe, just clean and polite.


Cabinets
The speaker cabinet is the last, and largest, tone control. The amp’s raw output is harsh and fizzy (pick No cabinet to hear it); the speakers roll off almost everything above 5 kHz, and that roll-off is a large part of what “guitar tone” is. This is also why recording a guitar amp means a mic on a speaker (Recording 4), or a cabinet simulation (an IR, impulse response) when there is no speaker. What decides a cabinet’s sound:

Speaker size. A smaller cone moves faster and reaches higher but goes less deep: 10″ speakers sound quick, bright and punchy; 12″ is the usual guitar speaker, fuller, rolling off around 5 kHz; 15″ goes deep and round and has almost no top (old-school bass).
How many. More speakers move more air: louder, and fuller at the bottom, at the same amp power. They also interfere with each other a little (a dip in the upper mids, which changes where you stand) and spread the sound more narrowly. A 4×10 and a 2×12 have roughly the same cone area but sound different: the 4×10 tighter and brighter, the 2×12 warmer.
Open or closed back. An open-back combo also radiates from the back, and the back wave cancels the front’s lowest notes: airy, spread out, less bass, fills a room. A closed-back cabinet (most 4×12s and nearly all bass cabinets) traps that air: tight, punchy low end with a thump around 100 Hz, and more directional (beamy).
A horn tweeter (bass cabinets): a small extra speaker that adds back the top end that big cones can’t make, with a level knob or switch on the back. Turn it down for an old-school sound.
Impedance and power handling must match the amp (printed on the back, see above).

In the simulation, the cabinet changes the low end, the upper mids and the roll-off; switch between 2×12 open back and 4×10 open back on the same setting, or 4×12 closed back with high gain. It can’t model the real differences in loudness, spread and how a cab interacts with the room, but you can hear the colour.


Try it
Start with Clean, then Crunch: the Gain moved (and the cabinet is a 2×12). High gain, quiet is a full distortion at a low Master; Clean, loud is the opposite. Vintage, cranked greys out the Master: the one Volume knob makes it dirty and loud together. Then sweep Presence from 0 to 10 with the Treble left alone. Play your own notes from the keys at the foot of the page, or plug in a guitar (Source: Microphone, through an audio interface; headphones on). The guitar and bass riffs are the band’s own recorded samples, unamplified, as if the instrument were plugged straight into a desk. Bass amp, Bass, growl and Bass through a guitar amp switch the source to the bass riff. View switches the controls between sliders and knobs; click any number to type a value.









WarningModelling amps: the knobs may be lying



Many small practice amps are modelling amps: a computer that imitates many amps and stores presets. The Fender Mustang series, Boss Katana, Line 6 Spider, Positive Grid Spark and Yamaha THR are all like this. When you choose a preset (or switch the amp on, which loads one), the amp uses the preset’s stored Gain, Volume and EQ, not what the physical knobs point at. A Volume knob sitting at 2 can be playing a preset saved at 10. Turn a knob and the setting jumps to where the knob is.
So:

Before switching on and before changing presets, turn Master to 1 (on amps where Master is the one real, unstored knob, as on the Mustangs, it is the one control you can trust).
Choose the preset, play, and bring the Master up slowly to the level you want.
Then touch the other knobs one at a time to take control of them, and save if you want to keep the result.
crumbs: Gear 3: Amps, Speakers and the PA

title: Gear 3: Amps, Speakers and the PA
text:
Powered and passive speakers

Powered (active): the amplifier is inside. Plug in power and a line-level signal. Most small PAs and studio monitors.
Passive: needs a separate power amp and speaker cable. Never plug a passive speaker into a line output, or a speaker output into a line input.
crumbs: Gear 3: Amps, Speakers and the PA

title: Gear 3: Amps, Speakers and the PA
text:
A small PA
A typical small rig: mics and instruments → mixer → two powered speakers on stands (the mains), plus monitor wedges for the players.
On each mixer channel, top to bottom:

Gain / Trim: set this first. Play or sing at full performance level and turn up until the peak light only just flickers, or the meter sits around 0 to −6. (Recording 1)
High-pass (low cut) on for vocals and anything without real bass.
EQ: small cuts, not big boosts.
Aux sends: the monitor mixes (pre-fader) and effects (post-fader).
Pan, Mute, and the fader, near 0 for the main sound.


Try it: one channel
Press Start here, then work down the strip in the lesson’s order. Bring the Gain up while the singer sings until the After-gain meter sits near the dashed line and PEAK only flickers, switch the High-pass on, then the Fader to about 0. Too hot shows what the fader can’t fix. Feedback turns the monitor up with the wedge in front of the mic (keep your volume low); the two Fixed presets show the two cures: the mic’s dead side toward the wedge, or a narrow cut at the frequency that rings.
crumbs: Gear 3: Amps, Speakers and the PA

title: Gear 3: Amps, Speakers and the PA
text:
Sound check

Everything on in the right order (Gear 1), master down.
One channel at a time: gain, then fader.
Monitors: ask each player what they need more of. Their voice/instrument first.
The whole band: balance from the audience, not from behind the mixer if you can help it.
Leave headroom. A crowd absorbs sound, and everyone plays louder at the gig.
crumbs: Gear 3: Amps, Speakers and the PA

title: Gear 3: Amps, Speakers and the PA
text:
Feedback
The howl or squeal when a mic hears a speaker that’s playing that mic.

Keep the mains in front of the mics, never behind.
Point the mic’s dead side at the monitor (the back of a cardioid; the sides at ~120° for a supercardioid).
Sing close to the mic: then the gain can stay lower.
Don’t cup the mic’s grille: it changes the pattern to omni and feeds back.
If it rings, pull the monitor or that channel down first, then find the ringing frequency with EQ.
crumbs: Gear 3: Amps, Speakers and the PA

title: Gear 3: Amps, Speakers and the PA
text:
Loudness and stage volume
The quietest stage that still works sounds best out front. Turn amps toward the players (tilt them back, or put them on a stand) rather than turning them up. See also Recording 9: Mono and Stereo for live speaker placement and subwoofers.

title: Gear 9: Drum Kit Setup and Care
text: A drum kit that’s set up to fit the player is easier to play and easier on the body. Tuned and looked after, it sounds much better than an expensive kit that isn’t.
crumbs: Gear 9: Drum Kit Setup and Care

title: Gear 9: Drum Kit Setup and Care
text:
Setting up

Throne (stool) first: thighs level or sloping slightly down from the hips.
Snare between your knees, a few cm above them, flat or tilted slightly toward you.
Bass drum where your right foot (left, if left-footed) lands naturally on the pedal; spurs out so it doesn’t creep. A rug under the kit.
Hi-hat to the other side of the snare, its pedal where the other foot falls.
Toms close and angled toward you so the sticks hit the middle without reaching.
Cymbals: ride and crashes within reach, not so high you lift your shoulders.
Tighten every wing nut and memory lock. Felts and a plastic sleeve on every cymbal stand: metal touching the cymbal’s hole cracks it.
crumbs: Gear 9: Drum Kit Setup and Care

title: Gear 9: Drum Kit Setup and Care
text:
Tuning

Tighten the lugs in a star pattern, a quarter turn at a time, finger tight first, then with the key, so the head is even all round.
Tap 2–3 cm in from each lug: they should sound the same pitch.
The snare is tighter and higher; the snare wires under it are adjusted by the strainer knob until they respond crisply without choking the sound.
Toms get lower as they get bigger. Bass drum: a little above wrinkle-free, with a pillow or muffling inside if it booms too long.
crumbs: Gear 9: Drum Kit Setup and Care

title: Gear 9: Drum Kit Setup and Care
text:
Care

Heads wear: replace when dented, dead-sounding or won’t tune. Snare and batter heads go first.
Cymbals: hold by the edges, not the face. Clean (or not) with cymbal cleaner only; never polish a cymbal with household cleaner. Never fully tighten the stand’s wing nut on a cymbal: it needs to move, or it cracks.
Sticks: turn them as you play; replace splintered ones (splinters fly).
Hardware: a drop of oil on the pedals’ moving parts a few times a year; keep the springs adjusted equally.
Moving: cases or bags for every drum and a cymbal bag. Cymbals never in with the hardware.
Keep drums away from heaters and out of hot cars; the wood and the heads both suffer.
crumbs: Gear 9: Drum Kit Setup and Care

title: Gear 9: Drum Kit Setup and Care
text:
Electronic kits

Same setup heights. Pad cables unplugged by the plug; don’t hit the rims of mesh pads hard without a rim zone.
Volume down before putting on headphones; drums are the most hearing-damaging instrument (Gear 5).
crumbs: Gear 9: Drum Kit Setup and Care

title: Gear 9: Drum Kit Setup and Care
text:
Hand drums
Hover any part of a drawing for its name.
Congas come in three sizes of the same barrel-shaped drum. Tuning bolts (lugs) pull the hoop down onto the head; tune with the drum standing, a quarter turn at a time round the drum, as on a kit.



Bongos are a joined pair played with the fingers, held between the knees or on a stand. They are tuned high and tight; loosen them after playing so the heads aren’t under tension all week.



Djembe is carved from one piece of wood with a goatskin head, tuned by its ropes. Tightening is a job for someone who has done it: a skin pulled too far splits.



Tabla is a pair from North India: the wooden dayan (right hand) is tuned to the key of the music by tapping the gatta and the rim with a small hammer; the metal bayan (left hand) gives the bass. The black syahi on each head is what makes them ring with a clear pitch. Keep them covered and never put them down on their heads.



Natural skins (all of these, often) go slack when it’s damp and tight when it’s dry: let a drum get used to the room before tuning, and keep them out of sun and away from heaters.

title: Gear 4: Keyboards
text: Digital pianos, stage pianos, synths and MIDI controllers look alike and are set up alike. Here’s what the connections do, and how to look after them.

title: Gear 4: Keyboards
text:
Kinds of keyboard

Digital piano: weighted keys, built-in speakers, mostly piano sounds. Good for practice.
Stage piano / workstation: weighted or semi-weighted keys, many sounds, no speakers (needs an amp or PA).
Synthesizer: sound design controls (filter, envelopes; the Sound lessons), usually light synth-action keys.
MIDI controller: no sounds of its own. It sends MIDI to a computer or another instrument.
Arranger keyboard: auto-accompaniment styles and built-in speakers.

Key count: 88 is a full piano; 61 and 76 are common on stage; 25–49 for controllers.

title: Gear 4: Keyboards
text:
Connections

Outputs: usually L/Mono and R (1/4”). Mono gig? Use only L/Mono; the keyboard then sums both sides. Stereo: both, into two channels panned left and right, or a stereo DI.
Headphones: often mutes the speakers. Turn the volume down before putting them on.
Sustain pedal: plug it in before switching on; many keyboards read the pedal’s polarity at power-up, and if it was plugged in later the sustain works backwards (on when lifted). Fix: switch off, plug in, switch on with the foot off. Or use the polarity switch on the pedal.
Expression pedal: volume or other control, a separate TRS jack.
MIDI: USB to a computer (the site’s Notation page can take a MIDI keyboard in Chrome), or 5-pin MIDI Out → In to another instrument.
Power: many keyboards use a specific adaptor: wrong voltage or polarity can kill them (Gear 1).

title: Gear 4: Keyboards
text:
Settings worth knowing

Local Off: the keys stop playing the keyboard’s own sounds and only send MIDI. Use it when the computer plays the sound back, or you’ll hear two of everything.
Transpose: shifts all keys. Easy to leave on by accident: if you sound in the wrong key, check it first.
Split / Layer: two sounds on two halves, or two at once.
Touch / velocity curve: lighter or heavier response.
Volume slider: keep it fairly high (around ¾) and do the balance on the mixer, for less noise.

title: Gear 4: Keyboards
text:
Setup and care

Stand: an X stand at a height where your forearms are level with the keys (elbows slightly above). Tighten every knob; check it doesn’t wobble.
Dust cover when not in use; no drinks on top.
Cleaning: unplugged, a soft cloth very slightly damp with water (a drop of mild soap). Never spray onto the keys. Liquid between keys breaks contacts.
Moving: a padded bag or case, keys facing your body. Don’t stand it on its end without a case.
Cold: a keyboard brought in from a cold car should warm up before switching on, so condensation doesn’t form.
Sticking or dead key: note which one and report it; don’t prise keys up.

title: Gear 8: Saxophone Care for Beginners
text: Saxophones are tough metal tubes, but their pads, springs and keys are delicate, and they get wet every time you play. Clean and dry it after every practice and it will stay airtight, which is what makes it play easily.

title: Gear 8: Saxophone Care for Beginners
text:
Assembling

Reed in your mouth first to wet it while you set up (or soak it a minute in water).
Neck strap on, hooked to the ring on the sax’s back.
Remove the end plug. Fit the neck: hold it by its socket, twist gently, and tighten the screw. Don’t grab the octave key on the neck; it bends.
Mouthpiece on the neck cork, about halfway (it sets the tuning: further on = sharper). Grease the cork if it’s stiff.
Reed flat against the table of the mouthpiece, its tip lined up with the tip of the mouthpiece, a hair’s width of black showing. Ligature over it, screws snug, not crushing.
Always lift the sax by the body and bell, never by the keys or rods.

title: Gear 8: Saxophone Care for Beginners
text:
Reeds

Reeds come in strengths (1.5, 2, 2.5, 3 …). Most beginners start at 2 or 2.5.
Rotate three or four, numbered, so none wears out too fast. Keep them in a ventilated reed case, flat.
Break in new reeds: play each only a few minutes a day for the first few days.
After playing, rinse the reed in clean water, wipe it from heel to tip, and let it dry before closing the case.
Don’t share reeds, and don’t chew or bite them.
Mould on a reed (black, green or fuzzy spots) means throw it away. In humid weather, store reeds with a humidity pack rather than shut in a damp box, and swap reeds every few weeks even if they still play.
A chipped, cracked or warped reed squeaks and buzzes: throw it away.
Never leave the reed on the mouthpiece in the case; it warps.

title: Gear 8: Saxophone Care for Beginners
text:
After every practice

Take off the reed, wipe it, put it in its case.
Take off the mouthpiece; run water through it (cool, not hot) or swab it, and dry.
Swab the body: drop the weighted end of the pull-through into the bell, turn the sax so it falls out of the top, pull it through gently. Two or three times.
Swab the neck with a neck swab.
Wipe the pads that stick (often the G♯ and octave pads) with pad paper if they’re tacky.
Wipe fingerprints off with a soft cloth.
Put the end plug in and everything in its place in the case, latches closed.

Don’t leave a swab inside the sax: it holds the moisture against the pads.

title: Gear 8: Saxophone Care for Beginners
text:
Mould
A wet sax shut in its case grows mould: in the mouthpiece, the neck, the swab, the case lining, and on the pads. It smells musty, can make you ill, and rots pads. It’s worst in humid weather (the monsoon, coastal cities).

Swab and dry after every practice; let the swab dry outside the case, and wash it every week or two.
Wash the mouthpiece weekly in lukewarm water with a little mild soap and a mouthpiece brush; rinse and dry. (Not hot water: it can discolour or warp hard rubber.)
Leave the case open for a while after practice in a dry room, so it airs out; keep silica gel in the case.
If the case smells musty or you see spots: clean the mouthpiece and neck, air and sun the empty case, and have the pads checked. Throw away any mouldy reeds.

title: Gear 8: Saxophone Care for Beginners
text:
What not to do

No polish on lacquer; no metal polish. Just a soft cloth.
Don’t eat sweets or drink sugary drinks before playing: sugar sticks the pads. Rinse your mouth first.
Don’t stand it on its bell, or lay it on a chair. A sax stand or the case.
Don’t oil or adjust the keys and screws yourself.
Don’t put music or a lyre in the case where it presses on the keys.

title: Gear 8: Saxophone Care for Beginners
text:
Signs it needs a repair

Notes that won’t sound, low notes that gurgle, or it got hard to play: a leak (a pad not sealing). Often after a knock.
A key that sticks, sits crooked, or is slow to return: a bent rod or a loose spring.
A buzz or rattle from the body. Missing felts or corks.
Take it to a repair technician every year or so for a check (a “play condition” service).

title: Gear 7: Violin Care for Beginners
text: A violin is made of thin wood held under a lot of string tension. Looked after, it lasts centuries; a few minutes a week of care keeps yours sounding and playing well. (The same goes for viola, and mostly for cello and bass.)

title: Gear 7: Violin Care for Beginners
section: Opening the case and holding it
text:
Opening the case and holding it

Lay the case flat, latches up, before opening. Close every latch and zip when you put it away; many violins are broken by falling out of a half-closed case.
Pick the violin up by the neck or the edges, not the bridge or strings.
Never leave it on a chair or the floor. In the case, or in your hands.

title: Gear 7: Violin Care for Beginners
text:
The bow

Tighten the hair before playing by turning the screw at the frog: until there’s a gap about the width of a pencil between the hair and the stick at the middle. The stick should still curve toward the hair.
Loosen it completely every time you put it away. A bow left tight warps.
Rosin: a few strokes along the hair when the bow slides without gripping. New hair needs a lot; usually a few swipes per practice is plenty. Too much makes a scratchy sound and white dust.
Don’t touch the hair: skin oil stops the rosin working.
Hair breaks now and then: snip it close to the ends, don’t pull it out. When a lot is gone, it needs a rehair.

title: Gear 7: Violin Care for Beginners
text:
Wiping down
After every practice, with a soft dry cloth:

Wipe the rosin dust off the strings, the top under the strings, and the stick of the bow. Built-up rosin eats into the varnish.
Wipe the strings and fingerboard.
Never use furniture polish, alcohol or water on the varnish. Ask a luthier for proper cleaner.

title: Gear 7: Violin Care for Beginners
text:
Tuning

Use the fine tuners (small screws on the tailpiece) for small changes. Tighten = higher.
Pegs are for larger changes: push in slightly while turning, so they hold. If pegs slip or stick, a teacher or luthier can treat them (peg compound).
Tune A first, to A = 440 (the strobe tuner), then D, G and E.
When fine tuners are screwed all the way in, back them out and bring the string up with the peg instead.

title: Gear 7: Violin Care for Beginners
text:
The bridge
The bridge isn’t glued; the strings hold it on. Tightening strings pulls its top toward the fingerboard.

Check it every week or two from the side: it should stand straight, at a right angle to the top (the back face, toward the tailpiece, perpendicular).
If it leans, a teacher can show you how to ease it back, holding it with both hands while the strings stay at pitch. If it falls, loosen all the strings and take it to your teacher: don’t play without it.
The sound post inside is wedged, not glued. If it falls (a rattle and a weak sound), loosen the strings and see a luthier.

title: Gear 7: Violin Care for Beginners
text:
Strings

Change a full set about every 6–12 months for regular players, sooner if they sound dull or won’t stay in tune, or one is fraying.
Change one at a time, so the bridge and sound post stay in place.
New strings stretch for a day or two: retune often.

title: Gear 7: Violin Care for Beginners
text:
Temperature and humidity

Wood swells and shrinks with humidity. Dry air (winter heating) cracks violins and opens seams; very damp air makes pegs stick.
Keep it at room temperature: never in a car, in the sun, or by a radiator.
Aim for 40–60% humidity. In dry winters (north India), a case humidifier (such as a Dampit) helps.
In the monsoon and humid coastal cities the danger is the other way: swollen wood, sticking pegs, rising action, softened glue and mould in the case. Use silica gel or a two-way humidity pack in the case, open the case to air in a dry room now and then, and don’t keep it in a damp almirah or next to a wall.
Air conditioners dry the air fast: don’t leave the violin in the blast of an AC.
Coming in from the cold: leave it in the closed case 15–30 minutes before opening.

title: Gear 7: Violin Care for Beginners
text:
When to see a luthier
Open seams (a buzz, a gap at the edge), cracks, a warped bridge, a fallen sound post, slipping pegs, a bow that won’t tighten, or rehairs. Don’t glue anything yourself.

title: Lesson: Guide Tones
text:
In a seventh chord the 3rd and the 7th say what the chord is. A line made of those notes, one for each chord, is called a guide-tone line, and it moves by step or by nothing at all. This lesson writes that line over four-chord loops, on a staff, so that you can hear what the chords are doing inside.
How to use the page. Press ▶ on a chart and the band plays it four times after a one-bar count-in. The bar that is sounding lights up, on the chart and on the staff. Under every chord is its Roman numeral, which stays the same in every key. The strip at the bottom of the window sets the key, the feel, the tempo and the chord instrument, and you can change them while the band plays. Shaded bars are the ones that differ from the version named under the chart. Under each chart is a one-voice staff with the line, and the band’s piano plays the line over the chords.

title: Lesson: Guide Tones
text:
1. Just the 3rds
C, G, Am, F as plain triads, with the 3rd of each chord on the staff. The 3rd is the note that makes a chord major or minor. Listen to the line E, B, C, A: it is the loop with the chords taken away.

title: Lesson: Guide Tones
text:
2. Sevenths, and the 3rds again
Cmaj7, G7, Am7, Fmaj7. The same loop with a 7th on every chord. The 3rds are the same notes. The 7ths are new, and they are what the next step uses.

title: Lesson: Guide Tones
text:
3. Just the 7ths
The 7ths of those chords: B, F, G and E. The 7th of one chord is often the 3rd of the next, or a step from it: the B of Cmaj7 is the 3rd of G7, and the G of Am7 rises a step to the A that is the 3rd of Fmaj7.

title: Lesson: Guide Tones
text:
4. The guide-tone line
For each chord, take whichever of its 3rd and 7th is nearer the last note you played. The line now moves by a step or a skip, and it holds a note where it can.

title: Lesson: Guide Tones
text:
5. Over a two-five-one
Dm7, G7, Cmaj7. The most important use of the line. The F is the 3rd of Dm7 and the 7th of G7: it does not move at all. It then falls a half step to E, the 3rd of Cmaj7, which is the note that tells you the chord has changed to major.

title: Lesson: Guide Tones
text:
6. Over the turnaround
Cmaj7, Am7, Dm7, G7. Four chords, and the line moves by half steps and whole steps through all of them. A bass player and a pianist who both play the guide tones will be in tune with each other without having said a word.

title: Lesson: Guide Tones
text:
Build your own
Choose a progression and what the staff shows: the chords, the 3rds, the 7ths or the guide-tone line. The band plays the line when the staff shows one.

title: Lesson: Guide Tones
text:
Where to go next

Play each line on your instrument over the band, then try singing it.
The guitar and piano lessons on the blues use the same 3rd and 7th as their shell chords.
In turnarounds the line is the same, with a tritone substitution in the V.
