title: Guitar for Bassists
text:
The guitar’s four lowest strings are your bass’s E A D G, an octave higher, so the bottom half of the neck is already yours. What is new is two more strings, chords, a right hand that plays several strings at once, and a different kind of muting: on bass you mute so one note sounds; on guitar you mute so the right notes of a chord sound, and to make rhythm out of strings that don’t. Click a section’s heading to fold it; the “On this page” bar at the right jumps to any section.
How to read the page. Strings are numbered 1 (high E) to 6 (low E); tab has one line a string, high E on top. Right-hand fingers: p thumb, i index, m middle, a ring.

title: Guitar for Bassists
text:
1. The job changes
You are no longer the floor; you are the middle. The guitar fills in the harmony and the rhythm between the bass and the voice. A bassist’s habits help here: you already listen to the kick drum and stop notes on time. What to drop is the instinct to always play the root on the bottom: in a band the bass has it, so a guitar part is often clearer without the low strings.

title: Guitar for Bassists
section: 2. The fretboard: two more strings and one odd one
text:
2. The fretboard: two more strings and one odd one

The 2nd and 1st strings (B and high E) sit above your G. Every pair of neighbouring strings is a fourth apart, like on bass, except G to B, a major third. Any shape that crosses from the G string to the B string moves up one fret on the B and above. That is why the chord shapes look irregular.
The frets are narrower, so one finger per fret works everywhere. Light gauge strings need much less pressure than bass strings: if your fingertips go white, you are squeezing too hard.
The thumb often comes over the top of the neck in open chords and to fret or mute the low E. Bassists keep it behind; on guitar both are right, depending on the shape.

The chord shapes lesson covers the open chords; start with E minor, A minor, E, A, D, G and C.

title: Guitar for Bassists
text:
3. Strumming

Down-up all the time. The hand moves down on the beats and up on the “and”s whether it hits the strings or not; rhythm comes from which strokes touch the strings. That steady arm is a bassist’s metronome sense, moved to the wrist.
Loose wrist, light pick (thinner than a bass pick), held with only a few millimetres showing.
Aim. Down-strokes on low strings, up-strokes on the top three or four. You don’t have to hit all six.

   1   +   2   +   3   +   4   +
   D       D   U       U   D   U      (the "folk strum")

title: Guitar for Bassists
text:
4. Fingerpicking
This is the biggest change. On bass you pluck one string at a time with alternating i and m, usually rest strokes, pulling across the string. Guitar fingerpicking gives each finger its own string.

The hand

p (thumb) plays the three bass strings, 6, 5 and 4. It moves down through the string, toward the floor, with the side of the thumb, and stays to the left of the fingers (toward the neck).
i, m, a play strings 3, 2 and 1, one finger a string. They pluck up toward the palm, from the knuckle, not the fingertip joint.
The wrist is still and slightly arched; the hand does not bounce. Fingers move; the hand stays put.
The little finger does nothing, or rests lightly on the top of the guitar to steady the hand (classical players don’t; many folk players do).



Free stroke and rest stroke

Free stroke (tirando): the finger plucks and curls up into the air above the next string, missing it. This is the normal guitar stroke, because the next string is usually part of the chord and must ring.
Rest stroke (apoyando): the finger plucks and lands on the next string, as on bass. Louder and fuller; used for melody notes, scales, and to bring out a tune over an accompaniment. The thumb has its own rest stroke, landing on the next higher string.

Your bass rest stroke is a strength, but on guitar it mutes the string it lands on. In an arpeggio that is the note you wanted to ring.


Nails or flesh
Nails, shaped slightly and kept smooth, give a bright, clear sound (classical and much fingerstyle); the flesh of the fingertip gives a soft, round one (the sound most bassists already have). Both are right; try plucking with the side where nail and flesh meet.


Patterns to start
Hold a C chord. Thumb on the root, then the fingers.
   p   i   m   a   m   i        (arpeggio up and back)
e|-----------0-----------|
B|-------1-------1-------|
G|---0---------------0---|
D|-----------------------|
A|-3---------------------|
E|-----------------------|



p-i-m-a, a-m-i arpeggio (above).
Pinch: thumb and a finger pluck at the same time, a bass note and a melody note together.
Block chord: p, i, m and a all together, like a piano chord.

Practise each slowly with a metronome until the thumb never drifts onto the fingers’ strings.
Thumb only. Wes Montgomery played single lines, octaves and chords with the side of his thumb, no pick and no fingers: a warm, round sound a bassist’s thumb already knows.


Travis picking
The thumb alternates between two bass strings on every beat, like a bassist playing root-fifth, while the fingers play off the beat on the top strings. This is where your bass playing pays off: the thumb is a bass line. The Travis picking lesson teaches it step by step.


Hybrid picking
Hold the pick between thumb and index, and pluck higher strings with m and a at the same time as the pick plays a bass note. Country and rock players use it for double stops and chicken-picking. The Picking lesson covers it, along with alternate, economy and sweep picking.

title: Guitar for Bassists
text:
5. Every kind of muting

Palm muting
The edge of the picking hand rests on the strings right at the bridge saddles while you pick. Low strings thud with a short, chunky pitch: the sound of rock and metal rhythm guitar. Exactly as on bass, nearer the saddles rings more, further in thuds more. Written P.M. with a dashed line over the notes. Keep the palm there between notes; lifting it for an accent is a sound of its own.
P.M.- - - - - - -|         P.M.- - -|
e|-----------------|-----------------|
B|-----------------|-----------------|
G|-----------------|-----------------|
D|-----------------|-----------------|
A|-----------------|-----------------|
E|0-0-0-0-0-0-3-3--|0-0-0-0-5---3----|



Fret-hand muting: releasing
Exactly as on bass: ease the pressure on a fretted note or chord and it stops, the fingers still touching. Strum a barre chord, release, strum, release: a staccato rhythm part (reggae and funk “skank”).


Fret-hand muting: unplayed strings
A full strum hits all six strings, so chords that use fewer must mute the rest with the fretting hand:

Fingertip lean: in a D chord (strings 4 to 1), the thumb comes over the neck to touch the low E, and the tip of the finger nearest the A string leans back to touch it.
Underside of a finger: the flat part of a finger lies across a string it isn’t fretting. In a power chord on the 5th string, the fretting finger’s tip touches the low E, and the underside of the fingers lies across the higher strings, so you can strum hard and only two notes sound.
Thumb over the top mutes or frets the low E.



Chucks and scratches
Lay the fretting fingers lightly across all the strings without pressing, and strum: a pitchless “chk”, written x. In a strum pattern it lands on the backbeat or fills the gaps:
   1   +   2   +   3   +   4   +
   D   U   D   U   D   U   D   U
   C   C   x   C   C   C   x   C       (C = chord, x = muted chuck)

Funk rhythm guitar is sixteenth notes of this: the hand never stops, the left hand presses for chords and relaxes for scratches.


Right-hand chuck (slap strum)
On acoustic, the side of the strumming hand comes down on the strings on the backbeat, muting them with a percussive slap, in place of a down-stroke. Many solo singers use it to stand in for a snare drum.


Muting while picking single notes
The right-hand tricks you know from bass all transfer: the picking hand’s palm rests on the lower strings, the fretting hand’s free fingers cover the higher ones. With gain, this matters even more than on bass, because every open string feeds back.


Fingerstyle damping
In fingerpicking, a plucking finger or the thumb placed back on a string stops it: the thumb returns to the bass string to cut a note short, the fingers replant on the top strings at the end of a phrase. Rest strokes damp the next string automatically, which you can use on purpose.

Test: strum hard with the chord shape held and listen for any string you did not want. Then the same with a chuck: there should be no pitch at all.

title: Guitar for Bassists
section: 6. Bends, hammer-ons, pull-offs and slides on both instruments
text:
6. Bends, hammer-ons, pull-offs and slides on both instruments
The left-hand techniques are the same on both instruments; what changes is the string. A bass string is several times thicker and under more tension, its notes last longer, and they sit an octave lower, where small changes of pitch are harder to hear. So the same motion gives a different result.



Technique
On guitar
On bass




Bend
A half, whole step or more is normal; push or pull across the neck, two or three fingers together. A main sound of lead guitar.
Heavy strings allow about a half step, often less, and it costs effort. Used as a short, bluesy lean into a note, or a quarter-step “curl”, not as a melody move. Pull the E and A strings down toward the floor, so they don’t slide off the neck.


Vibrato
Wrist rotation, as for a bend, quick and wide in rock, narrow in jazz.
Mostly along the string (rolling the fingertip toward and away from the nut) or a small sideways shake. It shows on long notes in ballads and fretless playing; on short groove notes leave it out.


Hammer-on
Light strings, quick decay: hammer firmly and exactly behind the fret or the note is weak.
Easier: the heavy string keeps sounding, so a hammered note is almost as loud as a plucked one. Watch that the first note doesn’t keep ringing over it.


Pull-off
Pull the string slightly sideways as you lift, plucking it with the fretting finger.
The same motion, more force; it is easy to drag the string into the next one, so the other strings must be muted (see the muting section).


Slide
Fast and common: into notes, between chord shapes, the whole hand moves.
One of the bass’s main sounds: a slide into the root from a few frets below, a long slide down the E string at the end of a song. Ease off the pressure slightly or the frets click.


Grace note / glissando
Short slides and hammers ornament a melody.
A short slide or hammer into the root on beat 1 is a common move in soul and R&B lines.


Tapping
Right-hand taps on the fretboard; two-handed lead.
Works well (strings ring long); used for chords and two-handed lines on extended-range basses.


Harmonics
Bright and bell-like; see Harmonics on Guitar.
Very strong and low; used for tuning and as melody notes (the 12th, 7th and 5th fret spots are the same).



Crossing over. Guitarists on bass: bend less, slide more, and keep vibrato for long notes. Bassists on guitar: lighten the touch, because the same force that hammers a bass string bends a guitar string out of tune, and practise bends against a reference note until they land exactly on pitch. The Bends and Hammer-ons and Pull-offs lessons go into each technique.

title: Guitar for Bassists
text:
7. Things bassists get wrong







Fault
Fix




Rest strokes in arpeggios kill notes
Free stroke: curl the finger up past the next string


Thumb and fingers on the same strings
p on 6-5-4, i-m-a on 3-2-1, one finger a string


Fretting too hard, sharp chords
Light pressure, just behind the fret


Every chord has a low root
In a band, leave the low strings to the bass


Strumming arm stops on rests
Keep it moving down-up; miss the strings instead


Unwanted strings in a strum
Fingertip lean, underside of a finger, thumb over

title: Guitar for Bassists
text:
8. A practice plan

Week 1: E minor, A minor, D, G, C. Change on beat 1, folk strum.
Week 2: the same chords with chucks on 2 and 4; then palm-muted eighths on the low E.
Week 3: p-i-m-a arpeggios over each chord, free strokes, metronome at 60.
Week 4: the thumb alternating bass notes under a held chord, then start the Travis picking lesson.

title: Picking: Alternate, Economy, Sweep and Hybrid
text:
How the pick moves from one note to the next decides how fast and how even a line can be. There are four main ways: alternate, economy, sweep and hybrid picking. The first three are about the direction of each stroke; the fourth adds the fingers. (You may hear “sweet picking”: it’s a mishearing of sweep picking, not a separate technique.) Click a section’s heading to fold it; the “On this page” bar at the right jumps to any section.
How to read the page. Tab has one line a string, high E on top. ⊓ = down-stroke, V = up-stroke; m and a = middle and ring finger.
crumbs: Picking: Alternate, Economy, Sweep and Hybrid

title: Picking: Alternate, Economy, Sweep and Hybrid
text:
1. Alternate picking
Down, up, down, up, every note, whatever string comes next. The hand moves like strumming: down on the beat, up on the off-beat. Its strength is time: the strokes line up with the rhythm, so fast lines stay even.
   ⊓ V ⊓ V ⊓ V ⊓ V
e|-----------------|
B|-----------------|
G|-----------2-4-5-|
D|-----2-4-5-------|
A|-3-5-------------|
E|-----------------|

The hard part is string crossing. Going from an up-stroke on one string to a down-stroke on the next higher string (toward the floor) means hopping over the string: “outside” picking. The reverse is “inside” picking, the pick trapped between the two strings. Practise both slowly.
crumbs: Picking: Alternate, Economy, Sweep and Hybrid

title: Picking: Alternate, Economy, Sweep and Hybrid
text:
2. Economy picking
Alternate picking, except that when you change string, the pick keeps going the same way it was already moving. Down-stroke on the A string, next note on the D string: another down-stroke, one movement through both. Fewer and shorter movements, which is why it is called economy picking. The same three-notes-a-string scale as above:
   ⊓ V ⊓ ⊓ V ⊓ ⊓ V ⊓
G|-------------4-5-7-|
D|-------3-5-7-------|
A|-3-5-7-------------|

That shape, three notes a string, gives down-up-down then down again on the next string. Economy picking is a halfway step to sweeping: the string change is a small sweep. Frank Gambale’s book Speed Picking is the standard text on it.
crumbs: Picking: Alternate, Economy, Sweep and Hybrid

title: Picking: Alternate, Economy, Sweep and Hybrid
text:
3. Sweep picking
One note a string, one stroke for several strings. The pick drags across the strings in a single slow push, down for higher strings, up for lower, and the fretting hand plays one note on each, letting each go before the next sounds. The result is an arpeggio fast enough to sound like a harp glissando. It became the trademark of 1980s shred players.
A three-string A minor shape, then a five-string one (A minor at the 12th fret: A, E, A, C, E):
   ⊓ ⊓ ⊓ V V               ⊓  ⊓  ⊓  ⊓  ⊓  V  V  V  V
e|-------5-8p5----|     |-------------12-15p12----------|
B|-----5-----5----|     |----------13----------13-------|
G|---5---------5--|     |-------14----------------14----|
D|----------------|     |----14----------------------14-|
A|----------------|     |-12----------------------------|

The pull-off (p) at the top turns the stroke around without an extra pick.
What makes it clean is not the pick but the fretting hand:

One note at a time. Each finger presses only while its note sounds, then lifts (keeping contact) as the next string is picked. Held down together, the notes ring as a strummed chord.
Rolling. When two neighbouring strings are on the same fret, one finger plays both by rolling: the tip presses the first string, then the finger flattens to press the next while the tip lifts off the first.
Palm muting. The picking hand’s palm rests lightly on the strings already played, so they stop as the pick moves on.
A push, not a strum. The pick moves at the speed of the notes and rests briefly against each next string before going through it: a rest stroke with a pick.


Start so slowly that every note is a separate event. If two notes overlap, the fretting hand is late letting go.
crumbs: Picking: Alternate, Economy, Sweep and Hybrid

title: Picking: Alternate, Economy, Sweep and Hybrid
text:
4. Hybrid picking
Hold the pick between thumb and index as usual and pluck higher strings with the middle and ring fingers (sometimes the little finger too). The pick takes the low strings, the fingers the high ones, so you can play notes on non-neighbouring strings at the same time or skip strings without a jump.

Double stops and chords. Pick on the D string, m on the B string at the same time: a sixth, the country-and-soul sound.
Banjo-style rolls: pick, m, a across three strings, over and over.
Chicken picking: the finger snaps the string up so it slaps the fretboard, and the pick plays muted notes between them; the cluck of country lead guitar.
String skipping: the pick plays the low note, a finger the high one, instead of the pick jumping across.

   pick m  pick m  pick a  pick m
e|-------------------5---------|
B|-----5-------6-----------5---|
G|-----------------------------|
D|-5-------7-------5-------5---|
A|-----------------------------|

Hybrid picking is how pick players get the fingerstyle sound of the Guitar for Bassists lesson without putting the pick down. Fingerstyle players without a pick, Wes Montgomery most famously, plucked everything with the side of the thumb: there is more than one right answer.
crumbs: Picking: Alternate, Economy, Sweep and Hybrid

text:

title: Picking: Alternate, Economy, Sweep and Hybrid
text:
6. A practice plan

Alternate: a scale at 60 bpm, eighths, strict down-up; raise 4 bpm a day.
Economy: the same scale with three notes a string; listen for even spacing at the string changes.
Sweep: the three-string shape at 50 bpm, one note a click. Only add the five-string shape when the three-string one is clean.
Hybrid: the double-stop example, until the pick and finger sound as one.

title: Tuning 2: Fifth-Fret, Harmonics and Octaves
text: With no reference at all, you can still tune the guitar to itself: get one string right (or just leave it where it is), and tune the others from it. The pitch may not match a piano, but the guitar will agree with itself, which matters more when you play alone. Each method compares two notes that should be the same, so you listen for the beating of Tuning 1 to stop. Every method is in the tuning tool, drawn on a fretboard.

title: Tuning 2: Fifth-Fret, Harmonics and Octaves
text:
1. The fifth-fret method
Press string 6 at the 5th fret: that’s A, the note of open string 5. Tune string 5 to it. Then string 5 fret 5 gives string 4, and string 4 fret 5 gives string 3. String 3 (G) to string 2 (B) is a smaller gap: use the 4th fret. Then string 2 fret 5 gives string 1. (On a bass, the 5th fret every time.)







Strengths
Weaknesses




Needs nothing; easy to remember
Errors add up: a 3-cent mistake on each step leaves string 1 up to 15 cents off string 6


Gives equal temperament, the tuning the frets are made for
A fretted note is only as good as the guitar’s intonation and your finger: press hard and it goes sharp


Teaches where the notes are on the neck
The first note dies away while you tune the second

title: Tuning 2: Fifth-Fret, Harmonics and Octaves
text:
2. The harmonics method
Touch a string lightly over the 5th fret wire (don’t press), pick and lift: a bell-like harmonic, two octaves above the open string. The harmonic over the 7th fret of the next string is the same note, and harmonics ring for a long time, so you can play both and tune while they beat. (How to play harmonics: Guitar harmonics.)
The catch: harmonics are notes from the harmonic series, which is pure, while frets are equal-tempered. The 5th-fret harmonic is the string’s 4th harmonic, the 7th-fret one its 3rd, so matching them makes the two strings a pure fourth (ratio 4:3, 498 cents) instead of the frets’ 500 cents: 2 cents narrow. Hear the difference:



Tune strings 6 → 5 → 4 → 3 that way and string 3 ends about 6 cents flat of where the frets want it. Two cents on one string is nothing; six starts to show in chords.
The G-to-B trap. An old instruction says: harmonic at the 4th fret of string 3 against open string 2. The 4th-fret harmonic is the string’s 5th harmonic, a pure major third, which is 14 cents flatter than the frets’ major third. Tuned that way, the B string is 14 cents flat: clearly sour in a G or E chord. Use instead the 7th-fret harmonic of string 6 (a B) against open string 2, and the 5th-fret harmonic of string 6 (an E) against open string 1: unisons, off by only 2 cents and 0. The tuning tool does this.







Strengths
Weaknesses




Harmonics ring on while you turn the peg: both hands free
Pure intervals: 2 cents a step, adding up


No fretting, so finger pressure and fret errors don’t enter
Wrong pairs (the G–B 4th-fret one) are badly out


Clear beats, easy to hear
Hard to play harmonics on day one; weak on some guitars

title: Tuning 2: Fifth-Fret, Harmonics and Octaves
text:
3. Octaves and unisons
Some shapes give the octave of an open string: string 4 fret 2 is the E an octave above string 6. String 3 fret 2 is the A above string 5, string 2 fret 3 the D above string 4, string 1 fret 3 the G above string 3. Strings 6 and 1 are two octaves apart. An octave in tune sounds like one fat note; out of tune it shimmers. Octaves don’t add up errors the way a chain does: each one compares against a string further away, so they catch the drift of the other two methods.

title: Tuning 2: Fifth-Fret, Harmonics and Octaves
text:
4. The last check: a chord
Every method ends at your ear. Strum chords that use all six strings (E, A minor, G, C, D) and listen. If one sounds sour, play its strings two at a time to find the culprit. A small adjustment that makes the chords you play sound right is the right adjustment, even if the tuner disagrees by a cent or two. (Guitarists sometimes shade the B string a little flat for this reason.)



Method
Accuracy
Best for




Reference by ear
~10–20 cents note-by-note, much better with beats
Matching a band, any tuning


Drone
very fine
Practice; training the ear


Fifth-fret
adds up, 5–15 cents worst
No device at all


Harmonics
2 cents a step, ~6 worst; 14 with the wrong pair
Fast, hands free


Octaves
fine, doesn’t add up
Checking the others


Tuner
~1 cent, if used well
Stage, loud rooms: see Tuning 3



Next: Tuning 3: tuners and their limits.

title: Hammer-ons and Pull-offs on Guitar
text:
A hammer-on and a pull-off make a second note without a second pick stroke. The fretting hand does the work. This lesson builds both from one finger on one string up to licks, scale runs and chord embellishments. Each step says what makes it easy, what makes it hard, and what usually goes wrong, then gives something to practice. The same technique is the left-hand half of Travis picking with hammer-ons and pull-offs.
How to read the examples. Each exercise is written on a staff and in tablature. Tablature has one line a string, the high E on top, and a number for the fret. A slur between two notes is a hammer-on (the second note is higher, marked H) or a pull-off (the second note is lower, marked P), and both notes lie on one string. The staff is written an octave above where a guitar sounds, as guitarists read it. Press ▶ to hear it. The player picks every note, so on the recording the hammer-ons and pull-offs are separate soft attacks. Listen for the pitches and the rhythm and make the legato yourself. Fingers are numbered 1 (index) to 4 (little finger).

title: Hammer-ons and Pull-offs on Guitar
text:
1. One finger on one string
Pick the open G string once. Then bring finger 2 down on the 2nd fret from above, quickly, with the tip, just behind the fret wire. The string rings the higher note with no pick. That is a hammer-on.




Easy because: one finger, one string and one pick stroke.
Hard because: the finger has to land hard enough to sound a note with nothing but its own speed. A soft landing gives a faint or no note.
What goes wrong:

The finger lands flat or too far back from the fret, and the note is dull or buzzes.
The hand lifts the finger a long way before it falls. A short, quick drop is enough, and it keeps the hand relaxed.
The other fingers fly up in sympathy. Let them hang near the strings.


Practice: ten hammer-ons in a row, each one picked once, with a rest between. Listen for the hammered note being as loud as the picked one. That takes some weeks to get.

title: Hammer-ons and Pull-offs on Guitar
section: 2. From an open string: each finger
text:
2. From an open string: each finger
An open string is the easiest start, because no finger is holding the lower note. On the high E string, hammer each finger in turn: finger 1 at fret 1, finger 2 at fret 2, finger 3 at fret 3, finger 4 at fret 4.




Easy because: the open string is a fixed, ringing starting point.
Hard because: fingers 3 and 4 are weaker than 1 and 2, and they land softly at first.
What goes wrong: the weak fingers give the faintest notes. A finger landing next to the fret rather than behind it, a thumb riding over the neck, and the wrist drooping all make it worse.

Practice: the same drill on every string. Spend most of the time on fingers 3 and 4.

title: Hammer-ons and Pull-offs on Guitar
text:
3. Fretted to fretted
Now the lower note is fretted too. Press finger 1 down on the 2nd fret of the A string and pick. Finger 1 stays down while finger 2 hammers onto fret 3. When the higher finger lands it shortens the string, and the higher note sounds. Then try fret 4 with finger 3, then move up one fret and do it again.




Easy because: you already know both halves. The picked note is a plain fretted note, and the hammer is the move from section 2.
Hard because: two fingers have to be placed at once, one to keep the lower note ringing and one to hammer.
What goes wrong: the lower finger relaxes when the upper one lands and the first note dies. The hammer lands on a different string from the one picked. The hammered note is quieter than the picked one.

Practice: hold finger 1 down and hammer with finger 2, then 3, then 4, up and down the neck on one string.

title: Hammer-ons and Pull-offs on Guitar
text:
4. Pull-offs
A pull-off is the mirror image. Put two fingers down on the same string, the upper one at the higher fret and the lower one at the lower fret. Pick, then pull the upper finger off, and as it leaves, pull it a little sideways, toward the floor, so that it plucks the string. The lower finger or the open string rings.



Then with the lower note fretted:




Easy because: a pull-off is a hammer-on backwards. Section 3’s two-finger shape is the same.
Hard because: the lower finger must already be in place before the pull. A pull-off that only lifts the finger sounds weak. It has to flick.
What goes wrong:

The upper finger lifts straight up and the lower note is barely heard.
The finger drags across the next string and mutes it or sounds it.
The lower finger is not down yet when the upper one leaves.


Practice: put both fingers down, pick, and pull off. Play the picked note and the pulled note at an even loudness. Do the open-string version on every string, then the fretted one.

title: Hammer-ons and Pull-offs on Guitar
text:
5. Trills and hammer-pull loops
Put the two together. Pick once, hammer on, pull off, hammer on, and keep going, and the picked note turns into a trill. This is how guitarists get a long, fluttering note out of one pick stroke, and it is a fine test of both techniques at once.



Make it faster by halving the note values. Then end with a picked note, so the trill has a landing.




Easy because: nothing new: a hammer-on, a pull-off and a repeat.
Hard because: the notes have to stay even and loud while the hand tires.
What goes wrong: the notes fade away as the hand tires. The rhythm rushes. The lower finger gets pushed off when the upper finger hammers.

Practice: one measure at a slow tempo, with a metronome, and then speed up 4 beats a minute at a time. Stop when the notes begin to fade. Try it with fingers 1-2, 1-3, 2-3 and 3-4.

title: Hammer-ons and Pull-offs on Guitar
text:
6. In licks and scale runs
A lick is a short phrase. Written below are three, all in the key of A minor, in the first of the pentatonic positions, with the index finger on the 5th fret. Each slur is on one string. The first goes up with hammer-ons and the second comes down with pull-offs:



The third is in the open position and mixes both. The hammer-on from the open D string, and the pull-off back to the open G string, are the sound of a lot of blues and country playing:




Easy because: a pentatonic run is only two notes a string, and each pair is a hammer-on or a pull-off you know.
Hard because: the picks and the slurs alternate, and the hand has to change strings after each pair.
What goes wrong: the picked note at the start of each pair is rushed, and then the slurred notes sound like they are in a hurry. Playing it fast without the pick on the first note of each pair is the quickest way to lose the beat.

Practice: play the first two bars with a metronome at 70, and say the rhythm out loud, “one-and two-and”. When the slurred notes are as loud as the picked ones, speed up.

title: Hammer-ons and Pull-offs on Guitar
section: 7. Inside chord shapes: the Sus embellishment
text:
7. Inside chord shapes: the Sus embellishment
Hammer-ons and pull-offs also decorate a chord. The best known is the Sus embellishment: strum an open chord, then hammer one finger onto a note next to a chord tone, so that the chord briefly becomes a sus chord, and pull it off to come home again. Jimi Hendrix used the idea all through Little Wing and Castles Made of Sand, and rock, folk and country guitarists use it all the time. On D, A and C the moving finger is the little finger or the ring finger on the top strings, and the rest of the chord stays put.
D. Strum D. The finger on the high E string (fret 2) stays down. Hammer the little finger onto fret 3 of the same string: the 3rd of the chord (F♯) becomes the 4th (G), and D becomes Dsus4. Pull off to come back.






A. Strum A. Hammer the little finger onto fret 3 of the B string, over the finger that holds fret 2: A becomes Asus4.






C. Strum C. The high E string is open. Hammer the little finger onto fret 3 of that string, then pull off. The top note moves from E to G and back.







Easy because: the chord is already under your hand. Only one finger moves, and only one fret.
Hard because: the hammering finger is the little finger, and it has to land without touching the next string or lifting a finger that is holding the chord.
What goes wrong:

The chord gets thinner because a finger of the shape lifted when the pinky came down.
The pinky lands on the pad instead of the tip, and mutes the string next to it.
It is played so fast and so loud that it stops sounding like a chord with a flourish.


Practice: strum the chord once, then hammer and pull off with a steady pulse, one decoration to a chord. Play along with the band: the chart is D, A, C, D, one bar each. Do the embellishment on each chord in time.



Unlocks: Travis picking with hammer-ons and pull-offs; the open-chord decorations of pop changes for guitar; guitar chord shapes by hand.

title: Lessons
text:
The site's backing band plays every example in these lessons. Choose an instrument, a topic, or both. They run roughly from simpler to more involved.

Improvising on a Blues: Blues in the Closet

Starting from the melody: hitting the change in bar 5, the blues and pentatonic scales, and a scale for each chord. Scales are shown as tablature, keyboard fingerings or a violin fingerboard, whichever you play.



Blues for Violin and Saxophone: Playing the Changes

For any instrument that plays one note at a time. Roots, chord tones, guide-tone lines, a riff, and the melody of Blues in the Closet, written in your own key.



Lesson: Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues

What the chords of a blues are and how players vary them, from three chords to a jazz blues, with a chorus you can build yourself and an ear test.



Blues for Bass: From Roots to a Walking Line

Roots, then root and fifth, then the chord tones as a written line, then walking. Fretboard diagrams, bass-clef notation and the band's own bass line written out.



Blues for Guitar: From Roots to Shell Chords

Two- and three-note chords built from the 3rd and 7th, on strings 5 and 4 and on strings 4 and 3, with the same shapes a tritone higher. No barre chords.



Blues for Piano: From Roots to Rootless Voicings

Left-hand roots, guide tones in the right hand, three-note shells and rootless left-hand voicings, each on a keyboard diagram and a grand staff.



Two Left Hands: Stride and Boogie-Woogie

The two great left hands of early jazz piano, played on the band one at a time, side by side on a blues, and swapped: stride leaps between bass and chord, boogie-woogie walks in eighths.



Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle

How to read a drum part, then the beat, the ride pattern, swing time, fills that mark the form, the shuffle, the slow 12/8 and straight eighths.



Reading Swing from a Lead Sheet

Why swing eighths are written as plain eighths, how far the long-short can stretch with tempo and style, and the range of good readings, with Blues in the Closet swung and Watermelon Man straight for contrast. Every example plays, with a swing slider.



Is Watermelon Man a Blues?

Whether Herbie Hancock's Watermelon Man is a blues: its 16-bar form, its dominant-seventh chords, and what the site's "(Blues)" label means.



Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths

For a drummer who can already play a basic beat. The three sounds of the hi-hat, then quarter notes, eighths, accents, off-beats, an open note, open off-beats, sixteenths with one hand and with two, the foot alone and the swing hi-hat.



How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao

The drums, how to sit, the five strokes (bass, open, muted, slap, heel-toe) and how they are written, then the tumbao built in six steps with the band: open tones, right hand, left hand, both hands, a cha-cha band and two drums.



Watermelon Man for Congas

The tumbao over a 16-bar blues: the form, the break on bar 14, the melody, and the same part in Mongo Santamaría's cha-cha and in a boogaloo.



Stick Grips and Other Ways Drummers Differ

Matched grip (German, American, French) and traditional grip, fulcrum, rebound and the Moeller whip; then the other places kit players part ways: kit layout, left-handed and open-handed playing, throne height, pedal heel up or down, stick choice, and counting.



Playing Brushes

What brushes are, how to hold them, sweeps against taps, the circle and the half-moon patterns for ballads and swing, the ride on a brush, and when to use them.



How to Play Cajón

The Peruvian box drum: how to sit, the bass and slap tones, ghost notes, a basic rock and pop beat, a 6/8 feel, the Afro-Peruvian landó, and using brushes and extras.



The Saxophone

Everything a beginning saxophonist needs: where the sax came from, the family, the parts, putting it together, holding it, your embouchure and first note, an interactive fingering chart and trill chart, fixing tone problems, tuning, vibrato, care, and players to listen to.



Trumpet and Tuba Fingering Charts

How valves change the pitch of a brass instrument, and interactive trumpet and tuba fingering charts: pick a note, press valves to see which notes they play, quiz yourself, and switch the staff and note names on and off.



What Is a Polyrhythm?

Two rhythms at once: 3 against 2, 4 against 3 and 5 against 4, the grid that holds them, how to clap them, and how a polyrhythm differs from polymeter and hemiola.



West African Bell Patterns and Cross-Rhythm

The 12-pulse bell pattern, 3 against 2 (and 4 against 3) as the ground of much sub-Saharan African drumming, layered parts in an Ewe-style ensemble, and how to hear the beat.



Clave and 6/8 in Afro-Cuban Music

Tresillo, son clave and rumba clave over a steady pulse, the 6/8 bell against four, and how 3 against 2 lives inside Cuban rhythm.



Polyrhythm in Jazz

Swing's built-in 3 against 2, dotted-quarter figures that cross the bar, 3 against 4 in comping and drum solos, and how to practise playing across the time without losing it.



Polymeter and Polyrhythm in Math Rock

Odd-length riffs over steady drums, 5 and 7 against 4, guitars in different cycles, and the difference between a polyrhythm and a riff that drifts until it lines up again.



First Rock Song: One Loop, a Part for Everyone

G, D, Em, C for a whole class at once. Drums, bass, guitar, keyboard and voice each have four levels, from a first day on the instrument to a rock beat, root eighths and a folk-rock strum. The band plays the level you pick.



Lesson: Changing the Changes in C, Am, F, G

The four chords under most pop songs, made richer one move at a time: extensions, passing chords, secondary dominants and ii-V-Is. With a chorus you can build yourself and an ear test.



Pop Changes for Guitar: From Open Chords to Passing Chords

The C, Am, F, G changes as fretboard diagrams: open shapes, extensions, passing chords and secondary dominants.



Pop Changes for Piano: From Triads to Passing Chords

The C, Am, F, G changes with a left-hand root and a right-hand chord, on a keyboard diagram and a grand staff.



Pop Changes for Bass: Roots and the Walking Line

The root of each chord, then the stepwise walking line through the passing chords, in bass clef and on a fretboard.



Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz

Thirteen steps from open triads and power chords through barre chords, 7ths, shells and top-string triads to drop 2, drop 3 and altered dominants, each with diagrams, a staff and sound.



Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings

The same chords ordered by what the fretting hand finds hard, from one-finger shapes to barres, muted strings and stretches, with what goes wrong at each step.



Hammer-ons and Pull-offs on Guitar

From one finger on one string to trills, licks and the Sus embellishment on open D, A and C, each written in notation and tablature that plays.



Tuning 1: Your Ear Is the Tuner

Why a beginner tunes by ear from day one: matching a reference pitch, hearing beats (the wobble two nearly-equal notes make), tuning up to the note, and tuning against a drone. Strengths and weaknesses of each.



Tuning 2: Fifth-Fret, Harmonics and Octaves

Tuning the guitar to itself: the fifth-fret method, the harmonics method (and why its pure fourths are 2 cents off, and the G-to-B harmonic is 14 cents off), octave checks, and the final chord check. What each gets right and wrong.



Tuning 3: Tuners and Their Limits

Needle, clip-on and strobe tuners: how they hear a note, why the reading jumps at the attack, why a guitar in tune on a tuner can still sound out (intonation, finger pressure, old strings), and how to use a tuner without letting it replace your ear.



String Bends on Guitar: Bending in Tune

Half-step, whole-step and 1½-step bends, curls, pre-bends, unison and double-stop bends, how they're written in tab, and the blue notes they reach in the A minor pentatonic box, with a drone to bend against.



Harmonics on Guitar: Natural, Tapped and Pinch

Natural harmonics at the 12th, 7th, 5th, 4th/9th and 3rd frets and why they are there, how to touch and lift, tapped and harp harmonics, pinch harmonics with gain, bends and vibrato, how harmonics are written, faults and fixes, and a practice plan.



Travis Picking on Guitar

The thumb alone, pinches, fingers between the thumb notes, then C, G, Am and D, chord changes, hammer-ons and pull-offs, and the band. Ends with a note on chicken pickin'.



Picking: Alternate, Economy, Sweep and Hybrid

The four ways to move a pick across the strings: strict alternate picking, economy picking, sweep picking (arpeggios in one stroke, with the rolls and muting that keep it clean) and hybrid picking (pick plus fingers), with tab, faults and a practice plan.



Guitar for Bassists

What changes when a bassist picks up the guitar: two more strings and the B-string shift, chords and strumming, fingerpicking (free and rest strokes, p-i-m-a, patterns, Travis picking, hybrid picking), and every kind of muting (palm mute, fret-hand mute, thumb over the top, chucks, string skipping), plus a practice plan.



Bass for Guitarists

What changes when a guitarist picks up the bass: the job in the band, the one-finger-per-fret hand, fingerstyle with two fingers and the thumb, playing with a pick, and every kind of muting (left-hand, floating thumb, moveable anchor, palm mute, ghost notes), plus a practice plan.



Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz

Thirteen steps from triads and inversions through slash chords, 7ths, guide tones and shells to rootless, drop 2, spread, quartal and upper-structure voicings.



Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard

The same voicings ordered by what the hands find hard: span, black keys, two hands together, leaps, stretches and independence.



Inversions: Root Position, First and Second Inversion

Major and minor triads with the root, 3rd or 5th in the bass, their figured-bass names (<span class="fb one"><span>6</span></span> and <span class="fb"><span>6</span><span>4</span></span>) and slash-chord names (C/E, C/G), on piano and guitar.



Pop Singing: Speech, Mix, Runs and the Mic

Breath, onsets, speech-level singing and the mix, words, safe belting, pentatonic runs, cry and flips, phrasing with a mic, and singing a third above. Exercises move into your range.



Jazz Singing: Swing, Scat and the Changes

Conversational tone, swing eighths and ghost notes, scat syllables, the blues scale, arpeggios and guide tones through a ii-V-I, back-phrasing a ballad, and trading fours.



Classical Singing: Breath, Pure Vowels and Legato

Appoggio breathing, onset and legato, the five Italian vowels, resonance, registers and the passaggio, the nine-note scale, messa di voce, vibrato, diction and solfège.



Formants: What Makes a Vowel

What makes one vowel sound different from another: F1 and F2, the third formant, the singer's formant and formant tuning, heard on a synthesised voice.



Lesson: Four-Chord Loops

The loops under a great many songs (I V vi IV, vi IV I V, the fifties loop, the turnaround, a borrowed chord, two minor loops) one at a time, each on a chart and a staff, with a loop builder and an ear test.



Lesson: Cadences, and the One That Is Not

Authentic, half, deceptive, plagal and backdoor endings, each as a four-bar phrase on a staff, with the argument for why the plagal "Amen" is not a cadence, a phrase builder and two ear tests.



Lesson: Write an Ending

The tune library's Unfinished Songs stop two bars short over V and I. Write the melody that ends them, in the Notation page, and hear it with the chords.



Lesson: Guide Tones

The 3rd and 7th of each chord written as a single line over four-chord loops, a two-five-one and the turnaround. The band plays the line.



Lesson: Changes in a Minor Key

From natural-minor i, iv, v to the harmonic-minor V7, the Picardy third, a walking bass and the ii°-V-i, in A minor.



Lesson: Borrowed Chords

The minor iv, the ♭VII and the ♭VI borrowed into a major key, one at a time, with a chord-by-chord builder and an ear test.



Lesson: Turnarounds and Rhythm Changes

I-vi-ii-V made richer: sevenths, a dominant on the vi, starting on the iii, tritone substitutions and the first four bars of I Got Rhythm.



Lesson: Reharmonizing a Melody

One tune, Ode to Joy, with four sets of chords under it, played with the melody. Mix the settings two bars at a time.



Arranging 1: Who Plays What in a Band

The four jobs in a rhythm section, built up one player at a time. Switch players in and out while the band plays and see each part written out.



Arranging 2: Bass and Drums

Why the bass follows the kick, how the groove sets the feel, walking in swing and the tumbao in Latin music.



Arranging 3: Guitar and Keyboards

Comping: strum patterns, voicing and register, the off-beat chop, jazz comping, and two chord players without a fight.



Arranging 4: The Organ

A playable tonewheel organ: pull the nine tonebars, switch the chorus, work the swell pedal and spin the Leslie, then hear it in the band.



Accompaniment Patterns

A lesson for every bass line, comping rhythm, drum groove and conga part the band plays, each built up from simpler ones, played on the band and written out.



Composing 1: Writing a Melody

Shape, steps and leaps, a climax, rhythm that repeats, and two classic eight-bar plans (the period and the sentence), each heard on the staff, then a melody of your own in the Notation page.



Composing 2: Developing a Motif

A motif is a short idea that a piece keeps coming back to. Repetition, sequence, inversion, retrograde, augmentation, diminution and fragmentation, each heard, and a motif lab that builds a phrase from your own idea, one change at a time.



Composing 3: Words and Music

Writing a song: putting stressed syllables on strong beats (prosody), rhyme and line length, verse, pre-chorus, chorus and bridge, the hook, and making the chorus sound different from the verse.



Composing 4: Instruments, Ranges and Transposing

The orchestra's families, each instrument's lowest and highest notes, clefs, and transposing instruments (clarinet, trumpet, horn, saxophones), with a transposer that writes the part a player reads and checks it fits the instrument.



Composing 5: Arranging for Orchestra

Melody, bass, harmony and countermelody: the four jobs in any arrangement, given to string quartet two ways, with doubling, spacing, passing the tune around, balance and rests, and a checklist for your own arrangement.



Process 1: Keeping a Process Journal

Documenting how a piece was made: what to capture (ideas, versions, tests, feedback, decisions and reasons), recordings named so they can be found, annotated screenshots and scores, a weak entry next to a strong one, and an entry builder.



Process 2: MYP Criterion B, Developing (Grades 6–10)

What MYP Arts Criterion B asks of a music student: practical exploration of ideas, and a clear artistic intention linked to the statement of inquiry, with choices stated, described, explained or justified. Ways to explore in sound, a sorting exercise, and an intention builder.



Writing Music Down: Choosing the Right Notation

One melody as staff notation, jianpu, Hindustani and Carnatic sargam, a DAW piano roll and arrangement, a waveform and a spectrogram: what each shows, what it hides, and when to use it. With MYP and DP notes.



Elements 1: Articulation

How each note is started, held and let go: staccato, accent, legato and slurs, tenuto and glissando, with how string, wind and brass players make them, and the techniques that change an instrument's sound (pizzicato, mutes, tremolo, vibrato).

Every articulation term on one revision sheet: staccato, legato, slurs and ties, accents, tenuto and marcato, glissando, pizzicato and arco, and the other playing techniques, each with a short example to play. Opens full screen.



Elements 2: Dynamics

How loud or quiet the music is: the markings from pp to ff, crescendo and diminuendo, sforzando, where dynamics are written for instruments, piano and voices, how each period used them, and how to describe what you hear.



Dynamics on One Page

Every dynamics term on one revision sheet: pp to ff, crescendo, diminuendo, sforzando, where the markings go, terraced and gradual dynamics, and how each period used them, each with a short example to play. Opens full screen.



Elements 3: Harmony and Tonality

Harmony on One Page

Every harmony and tonality term on one revision sheet: key signatures, major and minor, modal, pentatonic and atonal, modulation, triads and seventh chords, the four cadences and the Picardy third, each with a short example to play. Opens full screen.



Elements 4: Instruments and Voices

Every instrumentation term on one revision sheet: ensemble sizes, voices, the four orchestral families with an instrument from each to play, rock, pop and jazz line-ups, and the roles instruments take. Opens full screen.



Elements 5: Melody

Every melody term on one revision sheet: conjunct and disjunct, range, repetition, sequence, imitation, ostinato, triadic, scalic and chromatic melody, intervals and scale degrees, each with a short example to play. Opens full screen.



Elements 6: Metre and Time Signatures

How the beats are grouped into measures: time signatures, simple and compound time, duple, triple and quadruple, common and cut time, and how to tell them apart by ear.



Metre on One Page

Every metre term on one revision sheet: time signatures, common and cut time, simple duple, triple and quadruple, compound 6/8, 9/8 and 12/8, irregular metres, and how to hear them, each with a short example to play. Opens full screen.



Elements 7: Rhythm and Tempo

Elements 8: Structure and Form

title: Inversions: Root Position, First and Second Inversion
text: A triad has three notes: the root, the 3rd and the 5th. You can stack them in any order. The note you put lowest decides which inversion you are playing. The chord keeps its name, because the three notes are the same. Only the arrangement changes, and with it the sound and the way the hand moves. This lesson covers major and minor triads: how to build the three positions, what they are called, and how to write them. Press ▶ to hear a shape.

title: Inversions: Root Position, First and Second Inversion
section: Root position, first inversion, second inversion
text:
Root position, first inversion, second inversion
In root position the root is the lowest note. In first inversion the 3rd is lowest. In second inversion the 5th is lowest. To invert a chord, take the lowest note and move it to the top, an octave higher. Do it once for first inversion and twice for second inversion. Do it a third time and you are back in root position, an octave up.
Finger numbers. Press Show finger numbers to see the fingering in the dots instead of the chord tones. On piano the thumb is 1 and the little finger 5, in both hands, so the right hand plays a root-position triad 1-3-5 and the left hand 5-3-1. On guitar the index finger is 1 and the little finger 4. Notice that on piano the inversions change the fingering (first inversion in the right hand is 1-2-5), because the wide gap moves.






Look at the dots. In the first chord the root is on the bottom. In the second the 3rd is on the bottom and the root has moved to the top. In the third the 5th is on the bottom. The same three letters, C, E and G, are in all of them.
Telling them apart on the page. Look at the lowest note and ask what it is for the chord. If it is the root, the chord is in root position. A 3rd means first inversion, and a 5th means second inversion. The way the notes sit also gives a clue. In root position the notes are stacked in 3rds (C to E to G). In first inversion the top two notes are a 4th apart (G to C). In second inversion the bottom two notes are a 4th apart (G to C).
Practice: play C in root position, then first inversion, then second inversion, then root position an octave higher. Say the name of the lowest note each time. Repeat on F and G.

title: Inversions: Root Position, First and Second Inversion
text:
Minor triads
Minor triads invert in the same way. The only difference is that the 3rd is a half step lower.



The intervals inside the chord are the thing that changes. A major triad is a major 3rd with a minor 3rd on top; a minor triad is the reverse. So root-position Am (A C E) has a minor 3rd (A to C) and then a major 3rd (C to E). First inversion (C E A) has a major 3rd and then a 4th. Second inversion (E A C) has a 4th and then a minor 3rd. Whatever the quality, a 4th sits at the top of first inversion and at the bottom of second inversion, and that 4th is how you spot an inversion by eye.
Practice: play Am in the three positions, then C and Am one after the other in first inversion. Notice that the two chords share two notes, and only one finger moves.
crumbs: Inversions: Root Position, First and Second Inversion

title: Inversions: Root Position, First and Second Inversion
text:
Names: figured bass
Classical musicians have a shorthand for the inversions that goes back to the 1600s. It is called figured bass, and it labels the chord by the intervals above the lowest note. You will still see it in theory books and in Roman-numeral analysis.










Position
Lowest note
Intervals above the bass
Figure
Say it




Root position
root
3rd and 5th
5/3 (usually left out)
“five-three”


First inversion
3rd
3rd and 6th
6
“six”


Second inversion
5th
4th and 6th
64
“six-four”



The 6 stands for the interval of a 6th above the bass note. In first inversion of C, the bass is E and the other notes are G (a 3rd up) and C (a 6th up). In second inversion, the bass is G, with C above it (a 4th up) and E (a 6th up). The figure for first inversion is simply 6, because the 3rd is understood and left unwritten. The second inversion needs both numbers, 64.
With Roman numerals the figures go beside the numeral: I is a tonic triad in root position, I6 is in first inversion, and I64 is in second inversion. In C major, I6 is C/E and I64 is C/G.
To see what each number points to on the staff, for triads and seventh chords in any key, try the inversion explorer on Figured Bass: Practice for Chapter 16.
crumbs: Inversions: Root Position, First and Second Inversion

title: Inversions: Root Position, First and Second Inversion
text:
Names: slash chords
Pop, rock and jazz players use a simpler system. They write the chord, a slash, and then the bass note. C/E means a C chord with E in the bass: first inversion. C/G means a C chord with G in the bass: second inversion. A plain C means the root is in the bass, although the player decides which notes go above.



Position
Written as
In C
In Am




Root position
C
C
Am


First inversion
C/E
C/E
Am/C


Second inversion
C/G
C/G

Say it as “C over E”. The note after the slash is always the bass. A slash chord can also have a bass note that isn’t in the chord at all, such as C/D. That is not an inversion, and we leave it for another lesson. Chart writers use the slash form because it tells the bassist what to play, and the chord symbol alone does not.
crumbs: Inversions: Root Position, First and Second Inversion

title: Inversions: Root Position, First and Second Inversion
text:
Inversions on the guitar
On the guitar an inversion is a different set of strings and frets, and the shape moves anywhere on the neck if it has no open string. These are on strings 3, 2 and 1. The root is on string 3 in root position, on string 1 in first inversion, and on string 2 in second inversion. Compare the F shapes with the C shapes on the piano above.






The numbers under each diagram are the frets from the low E string to the high E string, and x is a string you don’t play. Move any of these along the neck and the root moves with it. The F shapes become G shapes two frets higher. More about moveable shapes is in Guitar chord shapes by hand.
Practice: play the three F shapes in order, then slide each up two frets and name the new chord.
crumbs: Inversions: Root Position, First and Second Inversion

title: Inversions: Root Position, First and Second Inversion
text:
Why use them: voice leading
Without inversions, every chord change makes the hand jump. With them you can choose the position of each chord so that the notes move as little as possible, and some notes stay where they are. This is voice leading. It makes a progression sound smooth and connected, and it is much easier on the hand. For example, going from C to Am to F, the top note C stays put in all three chords, as the root, the 3rd and the 5th, while the other notes move a step at most. That example is worked out in piano chord voicings, and Piano voicings by hand shows how it feels under the fingers.
Practice: play C, then F in second inversion (F/C), then C again. The C stays where it is, and the other two notes each move a step. Then play C, F in root position, C and feel how much farther the hand travels.

title: Live Sound 3: Low Cut and EQ
text: EQ on a live desk is mostly about removing things: rumble the mic picks up from the stage, the boom of a mic held too close, a harsh ring that hurts. Cut first; boost only a little, and only if you must.
crumbs: Live Sound 3: Low Cut and EQ

title: Live Sound 3: Low Cut and EQ
text:
Low cut first
The Low Cut on the X32 sits in the Config/Preamp section, before the gate and the EQ. It removes everything below its frequency (20–400 Hz), at 12, 18 or 24 dB per octave. Almost every channel that isn’t a kick drum, bass or floor tom wants it on: vocals around 80–150 Hz, guitars around 80–120 Hz. It takes away stage rumble, footsteps, handling thumps and wind, and gives the amplifiers less useless work.
crumbs: Live Sound 3: Low Cut and EQ

title: Live Sound 3: Low Cut and EQ
text:
The X32’s four bands
Each channel’s EQ has four bands. Choose a band (Low, Lo Mid, Hi Mid, High), then:

Type: LCut (low cut), LShv (low shelf), PEQ (a bell), VEQ (a vintage-style bell), HShv (high shelf), HCut (high cut).
Freq: where (20 Hz – 20 kHz).
Gain: how much, ±15 dB.
Q: how wide (0.3 is very wide, 10 is very narrow).

title: Live Sound 3: Low Cut and EQ
text:
Finding the bad frequency: sweep
When you can hear something wrong but not where it is:

Choose a PEQ band, set Gain +10 dB and a narrow Q (around 4–6).
Turn Freq slowly. When the problem jumps out and sounds awful, that’s it.
Now turn the Gain down to a cut, −4 to −10 dB, and widen the Q a little.

Keep the speakers low while you sweep a boost.

title: Live Sound 3: Low Cut and EQ
text:
Try it: a boomy vocal
A singer with the mic right on their lips (the proximity effect boosts the bass), on a stage with rumble, and two thumps where they knock the stand.



Switch on LOW CUT first and set it around 100 Hz: the rumble and thumps go. Then sweep the Lo Mid band for the boom (the graph helps) and cut it. Press Check my channel.

Try it: a harsh guitar
An electric guitar with a piercing peak and a fizzy top.



Sweep the Hi Mid band with a narrow boost until it hurts, then cut. Use the High band (HShv) or an HCut for the fizz.

title: Live Sound 2: Gain vs. Volume
text: Gain and volume both make a channel louder, so they are easy to confuse. On the X32 they are at opposite ends of the strip, and for a good reason.

title: Live Sound 2: Gain vs. Volume
text:
Why gain comes first
The X32’s preamps have a 72 dB gain range and clip at +23 dBu. Past that, the converter writes the biggest number it can and cuts the top off the wave. That is clipping, and nothing later in the strip can undo it, the fader included: a clipped signal turned down is just a quieter clipped signal.
Too little gain is a problem too. The fader only goes to +10 dB. If the gain is far too low you run out of fader, and the gate and compressor, whose thresholds are set in dB, never see the level they expect.

Rule of thumb: set the gain so the loudest part of the song peaks around −12 to −6 on the channel meter, never in the red. Then bring the fader up to around 0 dB. If the fader ends up near the top or the bottom to get a good balance, go back and fix the gain.

title: Live Sound 2: Gain vs. Volume
text:
Try it: the quiet talker
A speaker at a podium, quietly, a little far from the mic. The Gain starts much too low.




Press ▶. The fader is already at +10, the top, and it’s still quiet; the meter barely moves.
Pull the fader back to 0 dB and raise the Gain until the peaks sit between −12 and −6. Press Check my channel.
Try Way too hot, fader down: the output meter looks safe, but the CLIP light has latched and it sounds broken. Turning down the fader didn’t help.

Notice the hiss: with the gain very high (around +60), the preamp’s own noise comes up with it.

title: Live Sound 2: Gain vs. Volume
text:
Gain moves everything after it
Change the gain after setting a gate or a compressor and they stop working properly, because their thresholds stay where they were while the signal moves. On this kick drum the gate is set well.



With the gain 10 dB lower, quieter kicks fall below the threshold and get lost; 10 dB higher and the snare bleed starts opening the gate. That is why the order is always: gain first, then everything else.

title: Live Sound 2: Gain vs. Volume
text:
On the X32

The gain knob is at the top left of the channel strip. Its LED collar shows the setting; the screen (View) shows the number.
The meter next to it, and the meter on the fader strip, are the input level. The screen meter goes up to clip.
Mute a channel before switching 48 V on or off (the manual’s advice), and don’t touch the gain right after: it can pop.
Gain on the X32 is for the local inputs and stage boxes. If a channel comes from USB or a card, its trim is digital (±18 dB).

title: Live Sound 7: Soundcheck
text: Everything so far, in the order you’d do it on the X32 before a show.

title: Live Sound 7: Soundcheck
text:
The order on the X32
The X32 manual’s own steps for a microphone on a channel:

Plug in; mute the channel and switch 48 V on if it’s a condenser.
Gain, using the input meter (loudest part around −12 to −6).
Low Cut, to remove rumble or wind.
EQ.
Gate and Compressor.
Stereo Bus on, and Pan.
The channel fader to around 0 dB, then slowly bring up the Main LR fader.

Then the monitor sends (Live Sound 6), one channel at a time, and finally the whole band together, listened to from where the audience will be.

When it’s right, save a scene (Scenes, View, Save). Next week you can recall it and start from there instead of from zero.

title: Live Sound 7: Soundcheck
text:
Mystery channel
Each problem is one of these channels with one thing wrong. Listen, look at the meters, and say what it needs first. Then fix it and press Check my channel.

title: Live Sound 7: Soundcheck
text:
Practice on the real X32
Every channel in these lessons can be played through the real desk. On a channel above, choose a source and press ⤓ WAV: 32 seconds of that sound, raw, with the problem still in it.

How to get them into a channel with the full strip:

From a laptop or phone: its headphone output into a DI box, and the DI into any input 1–32. The DI turns it into a mic-level signal, so you set the Gain just like a mic.
Over USB (if the desk has the X-USB card): play the file from the computer and patch the card’s returns to input channels on the Routing screen.
The X32’s USB stick player comes back on the Aux 7/8 channels. Aux In channels have EQ but no gate or compressor, so it’s fine for the EQ files and not for the gate and compressor ones.

title: Lesson: Changes in a Minor Key
text:
The first lesson on this page’s loops stayed in major. Minor is different in one important way: the scale you play on is not the scale the chords come from. Natural minor has no leading tone, so the V chord is changed to get one. This lesson writes everything in A minor.
How to use the page. Press ▶ on a chart and the band plays it four times after a one-bar count-in. The bar that is sounding lights up, on the chart and on the staff. Under every chord is its Roman numeral, which stays the same in every key. The strip at the bottom of the window sets the key, the feel, the tempo and the chord instrument, and you can change them while the band plays. Shaded bars are the ones that differ from the version named under the chart.
crumbs: Lesson: Changes in a Minor Key

title: Lesson: Changes in a Minor Key
text:
1. The basic minor changes
Am, Dm, Em, Am: i, iv, v, i, all from the natural minor scale. The v chord, Em, is minor. It is pleasant and it is also weak: it has G, not G♯, so there is no leading tone to pull to A.
crumbs: Lesson: Changes in a Minor Key

title: Lesson: Changes in a Minor Key
text:
2. The harmonic-minor V7
Am, Dm, E7, Am. One note changes, G to G♯, and the chord becomes the dominant. The G♯ is the leading tone and it rises to A. This is the chord that makes minor feel like a key and not a mode.
crumbs: Lesson: Changes in a Minor Key

title: Lesson: Changes in a Minor Key
text:
3. The Picardy third
Am, Dm, E7, A. Finish on a major chord. The C of the A minor chord is raised to C♯. It is an old trick, for a hymn or a baroque piece: the music goes dark and the last chord turns the lights on.
crumbs: Lesson: Changes in a Minor Key

title: Lesson: Changes in a Minor Key
text:
4. A walking bass
Am Am/G | Dm/F Dm | E7 | Am. The bass steps down A, G, F, then falls a third to D, and E7 and Am follow. The slash chord Am/G is an A minor chord over a G in the bass.
crumbs: Lesson: Changes in a Minor Key

title: Lesson: Changes in a Minor Key
text:
5. ii° to V to i
Am, Dm, Bm7♭5 E7, Am. Put the half-diminished ii chord in front of the dominant. It is the minor version of the two-five: B, D, F, A, then E7. The bass falls a fifth from B to E, and again from E to A, the same circle-of-fifths motion as in the major two-five-one.
crumbs: Lesson: Changes in a Minor Key

title: Lesson: Changes in a Minor Key
text:
Build your own
Choose each chord. The shaded bars differ from the basic minor changes.
crumbs: Lesson: Changes in a Minor Key

title: Lesson: Changes in a Minor Key
text:
Test your ear
The band plays one of the endings. Pick the version you heard.

title: Bass line: All Blues: 6/8 vamp
text:
This is a lesson on one bass line the Backing Track band plays: All Blues: 6/8 vamp. It is built up from 2 simpler patterns, one step at a time, and every step is played by the band and written out as it plays. How the examples work: press ▶ Play, switch players in and out with the buttons beside it, and read what the band will play on the staff underneath: the whole pass is written out when Play starts, before it sounds. The tempo slider at the bottom of the page slows everything down.
All the accompaniment patterns · Bass lines

title: Bass line: All Blues: 6/8 vamp
text:
The pattern
A two-bar figure in 6/8. Each bar is a long note and two short ones: root, fifth, sixth, then seventh, sixth, fifth.
It belongs in Swing. Here it is in the swing style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Bass line: All Blues: 6/8 vamp
text:
Step 1: Held roots (the bass voice)
Start with something simpler. The root of every chord, held until the next chord: the bass part of a four-part hymn.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Bass line: All Blues: 6/8 vamp
text:
Step 2: 12/8 ballad
Long notes on beats 1 and 3, root then fifth, each set up by a short note on the last eighth of the beat before.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Bass line: All Blues: 6/8 vamp
text:
Step 3: All Blues: 6/8 vamp, slowly
Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.
How to play it. 6/8: two beats of three eighths. Each bar is a long note and two short ones: root, fifth, sixth, then seventh, sixth, fifth. Rock gently on the long notes.

section: Step 4: Up to tempo, with the band

title: Bass line: Chord tones (learning to walk)
text:
The pattern
The chord spelled out, one note on every beat: root, 3rd, 5th, 7th, the same in every bar. When a bar has two chords, each gets its root and one more note. A step between playing roots and walking.
It belongs in Swing, Jazz ballad, Boogaloo and Boogie-woogie. Here it is in the swing style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Bass line: Chord tones (learning to walk)
text:
Step 1: Roots on 1 and 3
Start with something simpler. The root on beats 1 and 3, held; one note a bar in 3/4. A chord that changes in between gets its root when it arrives.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Bass line: Chord tones (learning to walk)
text:
Step 2: Roots on every beat
The root of the chord on every beat and nothing else. The plainest line there is, under driving eighths or a strummed song.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Bass line: Chord tones (learning to walk)
section: Step 3: Chord tones (learning to walk), slowly
text:
Step 3: Chord tones (learning to walk), slowly
Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.
How to play it. Root, 3rd, 5th, 7th, one to a beat, the same shape every bar. On a minor seventh chord the 3rd is three frets above the root; on a dominant or major chord, four. Say the chord tones as you play them.

The pattern
Eight swung eighth notes a bar walking up the chord and back down: root, 3rd, 5th, 6th, flat 7th, 6th, 5th, 3rd, the same every bar. It is the boogie-woogie pianist’s left hand, played on the bass. A chord that arrives on beat 3 starts the walk again from its root.
It belongs in Boogie-woogie and Jump blues. Here it is in the boogie-woogie style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Bass line: Boogie-woogie
text:
Step 1: Roots on every beat
Start with something simpler. The root of the chord on every beat and nothing else. The plainest line there is, under driving eighths or a strummed song.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Bass line: Boogie-woogie
text:
Step 2: Chord tones (learning to walk)
The chord spelled out, one note on every beat: root, 3rd, 5th, 7th, the same in every bar. When a bar has two chords, each gets its root and one more note. A step between playing roots and walking.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Bass line: Boogie-woogie
text:
Step 3: Boogie-woogie, slowly
Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.
How to play it. Eight swung eighths a bar, up the chord and back down: root, 3rd, 5th, 6th, flat 7th, 6th, 5th, 3rd. Learn the shape on one chord until the hand knows it, then move it up a fourth for the IV chord and a fifth for the V. The shape stays the same; only the root changes. Lean on beats 1 and 3.

title: Comping rhythm: Son montuno
text:
The pattern
A two-bar pattern of short chords. First bar (shown): 1, 2, the and of 2, the and of 3, the and of 4. Second bar: every off-beat. Here it is played as block chords, not the pianist’s broken octaves.
It belongs in Son montuno. Here it is in the son montuno style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Comping rhythm: Son montuno
text:
Step 1: Quarter-note chords
Start with something simpler. The chord on every beat, held. On the piano the left hand adds the root underneath as each chord arrives: Let It Be, Imagine, Someone Like You.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Comping rhythm: Son montuno
text:
Step 2: Every off-beat
A short chord on the and of every beat and never on the beat: the ska and calypso afterbeat.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Comping rhythm: Son montuno
text:
Step 3: Son montuno, slowly
Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.
How to play it. Two bars of short chords: 1, 2, the and of 2, the and of 3, the and of 4; then every off-beat. Keep it dry and even. The second bar is the off-beat chop you learned in the step before.
The band plays it on piano here; the step after next has it on guitar.

title: Comping rhythm: Son montuno
section: Step 4: Up to tempo, with the band

text:

The same rhythm on the guitar. On guitar each chord is a strum or a pluck of a chord shape; a short chord is choked by easing the fretting hand off the strings.

text:
The pattern
Thumb and fingers, after John Prine. The thumb plays every beat on the low strings: the root, an inner string, the alternate bass, the inner string again. The fingers pinch a treble string with the thumb on 2 and 4 and add the string below it on the and after. In 3/4 the pinches are on 2 and 3.

text:
The pattern
The stride pianist’s left hand: a low bass note on beats 1 and 3 (the root in octaves where a chord starts, its fifth on beat 3) and the chord in the middle of the keyboard on beats 2 and 4. In 3/4 the bass on 1 and the chord on 2 and 3. On the guitar it is plain boom-chick.
It belongs in Stride piano and Ragtime. Here it is in the stride piano style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.
How to play it. The left hand alone first: a low octave on the root on beat 1, a chord about two octaves higher on beat 2, the fifth down low on beat 3, the chord again on 4. Look at where the hand lands, not where it has been: the leap down is the hard one. Keep the bass notes short and the chords lighter. When it is steady, let the band’s bass and drums join.

text:
The pattern
Palm-muted eighth-note downstrokes in the verse, then open down-up eighths in the Chorus bars. On guitar the chords become power chords on the low strings. With no Chorus bars set, the second half of the form is the open part.
It belongs in Emo / pop-punk and Straight-eighth rock. Here it is in the emo / pop-punk style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Comping rhythm: Fingerpicking: Travis pattern
text:
The pattern
The same thumb on every beat: root, inner string, alternate bass, inner string. The fingers pinch with it on beat 1, then play between the thumb’s notes: the and of 2, the and of 3, the and of 4.
It belongs in John Prine Fingerpicking, Boom-chick, Acoustic strum, Folk carol and Country train beat. Here it is in the john prine fingerpicking style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

Step 1: Fingerpicking: thumb, pinch-and
Start with something simpler. Thumb and fingers, after John Prine. The thumb plays every beat on the low strings: the root, an inner string, the alternate bass, the inner string again. The fingers pinch a treble string with the thumb on 2 and 4 and add the string below it on the and after. In 3/4 the pinches are on 2 and 3.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Drum groove: Ballad
text:
The pattern
Quiet eighths on the cymbal, a cross-stick on 2 and 4 and a soft kick on 1, the and of 2 and 3. In a chorus bar the cross-stick becomes the snare.
It belongs in Piano ballad and Acoustic strum. Here it is in the piano ballad style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Drum groove: Ballad
text:
Step 1: Hi-hat: eighth notes
Start with something simpler. Closed hi-hat on every eighth note, all of one weight, kick on 1 and 3, snare on 2 and 4. The basic rock beat. In 3/4: six eighths, kick on 1, snare on 3.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums play alone first; switch the bass and chords on when it is steady.

title: Drum groove: Ballad
text:
Step 2: Pop backbeat
A lighter backbeat for a strummed song: kick on 1, the and of 2 and 3, with the Dotted bass line. Fills are a snare note or two.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums play alone first; switch the bass and chords on when it is steady.

title: Drum groove: Ballad
text:
Step 3: Ballad, slowly
Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.
How to play it. Quiet eighths on the cymbal, cross-stick on 2 and 4 (the stick laid across the snare, tapping the rim), soft kick on 1, the and of 2 and 3. Play with half the force of a rock beat.

title: Drum groove: Ballad
section: Step 4: Up to tempo, with the band
text:

The whole band, at 72 beats a minute. Play along, then switch the band’s drum kit off and take the part yourself.

title: Drum groove: Brushes, ballad
text:
The pattern
One long sweep of the brush across the snare on 1 and another on 3, a tap on 2 and 4, a soft kick on 1 and the hi-hat foot on 2 and 4. In 3/4 one sweep to the bar and a tap on 2 and 3. No fills.
It belongs in Jazz ballad, Swing, Piano ballad, Boom-chick, Folk carol and Hymn (four parts). Here it is in the jazz ballad style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Drum groove: Brushes, ballad
text:
Step 1: Quarter notes (learning swing, 1)
Start with something simpler. Only the beat: the cymbal on 1, 2, 3 and 4 and the hi-hat foot on 2 and 4. No kick, no snare, no fills. The first thing to play on a blues.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums play alone first; switch the bass and chords on when it is steady.

How to play it. One slow circle across the snare head to the bar, a long sweep landing on 1 and again on 3, a light tap on 2 and 4. Let the sound hang; do not press the wires.

title: Drum groove: Jump blues
text:
The pattern
The blues shuffle pushed harder: swung eighths on the cymbal, the kick feathered on all four beats, and a loud backbeat on the snare on 2 and 4. In 3/4 the snare on 2 and 3.
It belongs in Jump blues and Boogie-woogie. Here it is in the jump blues style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Drum groove: Jump blues
text:

Start with something simpler. Swung eighths all the way through on the cymbal, kick on 1 and 3 and a full snare on 2 and 4. The Chicago blues beat.

text:

Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.
How to play it. The blues shuffle, harder: swung eighths on the cymbal, the snare hit hard on 2 and 4, and the kick played softly on all four beats (feathered: felt more than heard). Get the shuffle steady, then add the kick on 2 and 4 under the snare, quietly.
