title: What Is a Polyrhythm?
text: A polyrhythm is two or more rhythms played at the same time that divide the same span of time into different numbers of even parts. In 3 against 2, one part plays three even notes while another plays two, and both start together. Each player on this page draws the cycle as a circle (the hand goes round once per cycle) and as a grid (time runs left to right). Click a layer’s name to mute it.

title: What Is a Polyrhythm?
text:
3 against 2



The two layers meet only on the first beat. In between, the notes fall at different places: the “two” lands exactly between the second and third “three”. A common way to say it is “nice cup of tea”:
Count six even pulses. The three falls on pulses 1, 3 and 5; the two on 1 and 4. Together they sound on pulses 1, 3, 4 and 5, one syllable each: nice (both), cup (three), of (two), tea (three).
Try it. Tap the three with your right hand on your knee and the two with your left. Mute one layer and play it yourself; then mute the other.

title: What Is a Polyrhythm?
section: The grid underneath: least common multiple
text:
The grid underneath: least common multiple
To write two even layers on one grid, you need a pulse that both fit into. That pulse count is the least common multiple of the two numbers.

title: What Is a Polyrhythm?
text:
4 against 3



A common saying for 4 against 3 is “pass the golden butter”, said evenly over twelve pulses. Hear the three as the beat first (it is the lower sound), then switch: mute the three, feel the four as the beat, and the three becomes the cross-rhythm.

title: What Is a Polyrhythm?
text:
5 against 4 and beyond



With bigger numbers no one counts the grid. Players hear the outer layer as a steady line that slides against the beat and meets it again at the start of the cycle.

title: What Is a Polyrhythm?
text:
Polyrhythm, polymeter and hemiola
These three words are often mixed up:

Polyrhythm: different even divisions of the same span (3 notes and 2 notes in one bar).
Polymeter: patterns of different lengths on the same pulse (a 5-step riff over 4-step bars). They drift apart and meet again after a while. The math rock lesson is about this.
Hemiola: three groups of two heard against two groups of three, as in 6/8 heard as 3/4. It is 3 against 2 at the level of beats.




This one is polymeter: every step is the same length. Watch the 5-step pattern start in a different place each bar until it lines up after 20 steps.

title: What Is a Polyrhythm?
text:
Make your own
The Polyrhythm tool lets you type layers, choose sounds and switch between polyrhythm and polymeter.

title: Polymeter and Polyrhythm in Math Rock
text: Math rock is a style of rock from the late 1980s and 1990s on, built on odd meters, changing meters, and riffs that run against the beat. Much of what sounds like “polyrhythm” in it is polymeter: riffs of different lengths on the same pulse.
crumbs: Polymeter and Polyrhythm in Math Rock

title: Polymeter and Polyrhythm in Math Rock
section: A riff in five over four
text:
A riff in five over four
The guitar repeats a five-step riff while the drums keep a four-step bar. Every step is the same length, so the riff starts one step earlier in each new bar, and the two meet again after 20 steps.



Try it. Mute the guitar and play the riff on your instrument (any five-note figure works) while the drums play. Count “1 2 3 4 5” for the riff and feel the drums’ “1 2 3 4” at the same time.
crumbs: Polymeter and Polyrhythm in Math Rock

title: Polymeter and Polyrhythm in Math Rock
text:
Seven over four



Seven and four meet after 28 steps. Long cycles like this sound unpredictable but are fully fixed.
crumbs: Polymeter and Polyrhythm in Math Rock

title: Polymeter and Polyrhythm in Math Rock
text:
Two guitars in two cycles
A trick heard in math rock and in progressive rock before it: two guitars play riffs of different lengths at the same time. Here one guitar is in 5 and the other in 6, over drums in 4.



All three line up after 60 steps. Mute layers to hear each pair.
crumbs: Polymeter and Polyrhythm in Math Rock

title: Polymeter and Polyrhythm in Math Rock
text:
True polyrhythm: 3 and 5 against 4
Math rock also uses even polyrhythms, for example a guitar playing five even notes over a drummer’s four beats, both starting together each bar.



The difference from the riffs above: here every layer starts again on each bar. In polymeter, the layers drift and meet only after many bars.
crumbs: Polymeter and Polyrhythm in Math Rock

title: Polymeter and Polyrhythm in Math Rock
text:
Bands to hear
From memory, as a listening list rather than checked claims about particular songs: Don Caballero, Hella, Battles, Tera Melos, toe and Covet. King Crimson’s early-1980s albums (Discipline) are often cited for two guitars in different cycles, and Meshuggah, a metal band, for long riffs over a steady 4/4 hi-hat.
crumbs: Polymeter and Polyrhythm in Math Rock

title: Polymeter and Polyrhythm in Math Rock
text:
Write your own
In the Polyrhythm tool, tick Polymeter, keep a 4-step drum layer, and type a riff of 3, 5, 7 or 9 steps. Then add a second riff of another length. The line under the grid tells you when they all line up again: that is the length of your section.
Back to the start: What Is a Polyrhythm?

title: Pop Changes for Bass: Roots and the Walking Line
text:
This lesson is for a bass player. The bass is the instrument that plays the lowest note of every chord, so on the changes of C, Am, F, G it is the part that decides which passing chords are heard. Each step has the line in bass clef, a fretboard for it and the chart.
How to use the page. Press ▶ on a chart and the band plays it four times after a one-bar count-in. The bar that is sounding lights up, on the chart and on the staff. Under every chord is its Roman numeral, which stays the same in every key. The strip at the bottom of the window sets the key, the feel, the tempo and the chord instrument, and you can change them while the band plays. Shaded bars are the ones that differ from the version named under the chart.
crumbs: Pop Changes for Bass: Roots and the Walking Line

title: Pop Changes for Bass: Roots and the Walking Line
text:
1. The roots
C, Am, F, G. One note for each chord, the root. The bass-clef staff shows the line and the fretboard shows where to play it, on a four-string bass in the lowest position that has the note.
crumbs: Pop Changes for Bass: Roots and the Walking Line

title: Pop Changes for Bass: Roots and the Walking Line
text:
2. Extensions
Cadd9, Am7, Fadd9, Gsus2. The roots are the same. The extensions are for the chord instruments, so the bass line does not change.
crumbs: Pop Changes for Bass: Roots and the Walking Line

title: Pop Changes for Bass: Roots and the Walking Line
text:
3. The walking line
C, G/B | Am, C/G | F, F♯dim | G. Now the bass is the part that carries the passing chords: C, B, A, G, F, F♯, G. Every note is one step from the last. This is the line to learn.
crumbs: Pop Changes for Bass: Roots and the Walking Line

title: Pop Changes for Bass: Roots and the Walking Line
text:
4. Leading into the next chord
C, E7 | Am, C7 | F, D7 | G7. The bass plays the root of the dominant, which is a fifth above the note that follows. E, then A. C, then F. D, then G.
crumbs: Pop Changes for Bass: Roots and the Walking Line

title: Pop Changes for Bass: Roots and the Walking Line
text:
5. The two-five-one
Dm7, G7, Cmaj7. Roots first: D, G, C. Each is a fifth below the one before, so the bass falls to the home note by the strongest move there is.
crumbs: Pop Changes for Bass: Roots and the Walking Line

title: Pop Changes for Bass: Roots and the Walking Line
text:
6. A line through the two-five-one
Dm7, G7, Cmaj7, written as D C | B G | C B | C G. The C is the 7th of Dm7 and it falls a half step to the B, the 3rd of G7: the guide tones of the guide-tones lesson, now in the bass. The line steps down to the root of Cmaj7, touches its 7th, and ends on the 5th. The staff keeps every bass note between E2 and E♭3, so the line stays in one hand position.
crumbs: Pop Changes for Bass: Roots and the Walking Line

title: Pop Changes for Bass: Roots and the Walking Line
text:
7. In minor
Dm7♭5, G7, Cm7, the same line: D C | B G | C B♭ | C G. The B in bar 2 is still the 3rd of G7. The new note is the B♭, the 7th of Cm7, and it is what makes the end sound minor.
crumbs: Pop Changes for Bass: Roots and the Walking Line

title: Pop Changes for Bass: Roots and the Walking Line
text:
Build your own
Pick a chord for each bar; the bass note and the staff follow. Play the root of each, then try the 3rd.
crumbs: Pop Changes for Bass: Roots and the Walking Line

title: Pop Changes for Bass: Roots and the Walking Line
text:
Test your ear
The band plays four bars with one of five kinds of change in them. Say which. The chart appears when you answer.
crumbs: Pop Changes for Bass: Roots and the Walking Line

title: Pop Changes for Bass: Roots and the Walking Line
text:

Take the line to the key menu and play it in G, D and A.
The blues bass lesson goes further with the walk.

title: Pop Changes for Piano: From Triads to Passing Chords
text:
This lesson is for a pianist who can play triads. It puts the chords of the lesson on C, Am, F, G on the keyboard: a left-hand root and a close-position chord in the right hand. Each step has a keyboard diagram, the chart and a grand staff, and the band plays along.
How to use the page. Press ▶ on a chart and the band plays it four times after a one-bar count-in. The bar that is sounding lights up, on the chart and on the staff. Under every chord is its Roman numeral, which stays the same in every key. The strip at the bottom of the window sets the key, the feel, the tempo and the chord instrument, and you can change them while the band plays. Shaded bars are the ones that differ from the version named under the chart.
crumbs: Pop Changes for Piano: From Triads to Passing Chords

title: Pop Changes for Piano: From Triads to Passing Chords
text:
1. The basic chords
C, Am, F, G. The keyboard diagram shows one lane for each chord: the left-hand root (square) and a right-hand chord above it. The staff under the chart shows the same notes: treble clef for the right hand, bass clef for the left.
crumbs: Pop Changes for Piano: From Triads to Passing Chords

title: Pop Changes for Piano: From Triads to Passing Chords
text:
2. Extensions
Cadd9, Am7, Fadd9, Gsus2. The right hand keeps its shape and adds one note. Look for the 9 or the 7 in the diagram.
crumbs: Pop Changes for Piano: From Triads to Passing Chords

title: Pop Changes for Piano: From Triads to Passing Chords
text:
3. Passing chords
C, G/B | Am, C/G | F, F♯dim | G. The left hand walks: C, B, A, G, F, F♯, G. Each right-hand chord changes only where it has to.
crumbs: Pop Changes for Piano: From Triads to Passing Chords

title: Pop Changes for Piano: From Triads to Passing Chords
text:
4. Secondary dominants
C, E7 | Am, C7 | F, D7 | G7. The chord with the outside note leads by half step into the next bar.
crumbs: Pop Changes for Piano: From Triads to Passing Chords

title: Pop Changes for Piano: From Triads to Passing Chords
text:
5. The two-five-one
Dm7, G7, Cmaj7. The most common move in jazz and in many pop bridges: the chord before the dominant, the dominant, home. The left-hand roots fall a fifth each time (D, G, C). In the right hand, look for the note that stays and the one that moves by a half step: the F of Dm7 is the 7th of G7, and it falls to the E, the 3rd of Cmaj7.
crumbs: Pop Changes for Piano: From Triads to Passing Chords

title: Pop Changes for Piano: From Triads to Passing Chords
text:
6. The two-five-one in minor
Dm7♭5, G7, Cm7. The same fall in C minor. The first chord is half-diminished: a minor triad with a flat 5th and a 7th (D, F, A♭, C). Compare it with Dm7 above: one note has moved down a half step.
crumbs: Pop Changes for Piano: From Triads to Passing Chords

title: Pop Changes for Piano: From Triads to Passing Chords
text:

Pick a chord for each bar. The keyboard diagram and the staff follow your choices. Try Dm7 and G7 in bars 3 and 4.

title: Process 2: MYP Criterion B, Developing (Grades 6–10)
text:
MYP Arts is assessed on four criteria, each out of 8: A Investigating, B Developing, C Creating/Performing and D Evaluating. This lesson is about B: how you get from an idea to the piece you will make or perform. It is shown almost entirely through your process journal.
The wording below is from the IB’s Arts guide for use from September 2022, Year 5 (the last year of the MYP). Years 1 and 3 have their own, simpler wording. Ask your teacher for the version for your year.

title: Process 2: MYP Criterion B, Developing (Grades 6–10)
text:
1. What Criterion B asks
At the end of Year 5, students should be able to:


practically explore ideas to inform development of a final artwork or performance
present a clear artistic intention for the final artwork or performance in line with the statement of inquiry.


That is two things: exploring in practice, and saying what you intend and why.

title: Process 2: MYP Criterion B, Developing (Grades 6–10)
text:
2. Strand i: practical exploration
Practical means in sound, with your instrument, voice, software or players, not only thinking about it. Explore means trying more than one possibility before choosing. The levels go from limited, through sufficient and substantial, to extensive and varied practical exploration.
Extensive means a lot of it. Varied means different kinds. Ten versions of the same melody with one note changed is a lot, but it isn’t varied. Ways to explore in music:



Explore
For example




Material
three different motifs for the opening; three chord progressions under the same melody


Development
the motif in sequence, inversion, augmentation (try them in the motif lab)


Form
verse–chorus or AABA; where the climax goes; how it ends


Sound
which instrument plays the tune; doubling; register; a synth patch or an effect


Performance
tempo, dynamics, articulation, phrasing: record it three ways and compare


Testing
a player tries your part; a friend hears two versions without being told which is which



Each one counts as exploration in your journal only with evidence (the recordings, scores or screenshots of each version) and a line on what you found out.

Explore before you settle. If your first idea is in the final piece unchanged, there is little exploration to show, however good the idea is. Try alternatives even when you like the first one. Keeping it after a fair comparison is a decision you can explain.

title: Process 2: MYP Criterion B, Developing (Grades 6–10)
text:
3. Strand ii: the artistic intention
An artistic intention says what you are going to make or perform and what you want it to do, and it connects to your unit’s statement of inquiry (the big idea your teacher gives the unit). In the Year 5 descriptors, every level asks for a clear artistic intention in line with the statement of inquiry. What changes from level to level is what you do with your artistic choices:



Level
The student presents a clear artistic intention … and




1–2
states artistic choices


3–4
describes artistic choices


5–6
explains artistic choices


7–8
justifies artistic choices



These are command terms, and the IB defines each one:

State: give a specific name, value or other brief answer without explanation or calculation.
Describe: give a detailed account or picture of a situation, event, pattern or process.
Explain: give a detailed account including reasons or causes.
Justify: give valid reasons or evidence to support an answer or conclusion.

In practice: state names the choice. Describe adds the musical detail. Explain adds the reason. Justify backs the reason with evidence: a piece you studied, a test you recorded, feedback you got.

Try it: which is which?
Four sentences about the same choice. Match each to its command term.

title: Process 2: MYP Criterion B, Developing (Grades 6–10)
text:
4. Build your intention
Fill in the boxes. The intention is written as you type, and kept in this browser. Under it is a rough guide to how far your choices go, from state to justify. It only counts words, though: it can’t judge whether your reasons are good. Your teacher can.

title: Process 2: MYP Criterion B, Developing (Grades 6–10)
text:
5. A worked example
A Year 5 unit with the statement of inquiry “Composers use repetition and contrast to shape a listener’s experience over time.”

Intention. I intend to make a 24-bar piano piece in ABA form for the class recital, so that the listener feels settled, then unsettled, then settled again but changed. Choices. The A section uses a four-note motif in a period, in C major, mostly steps, mp, because steps and repeated rhythm sound settled. I tested this: in A_v1 the melody leapt a lot and two classmates called it “restless”; in A_v3, mostly steps, they called it “calm”. The B section develops the same motif by inversion and sequence, in A minor, f, because I want the contrast to come from the same idea. In Beethoven’s Fifth (first movement) the opening motif returns throughout in changed forms, and I wanted that unity. The return of A is in augmentation so it sounds familiar but slower and further on.

This intention is clear, connected to the statement of inquiry, and its choices come with reasons and evidence (tests and a piece studied). That evidence is in the journal: A_v1 and A_v3, the classmates’ comments, the score of B with the inversions labelled.

title: Process 2: MYP Criterion B, Developing (Grades 6–10)
text:
6. For teachers

These strands, descriptors and command terms are from the Year 5 criteria of the Arts guide (for use from September 2022/January 2023), read from a school’s published copy. Years 1 and 3 differ in wording.
The earlier Arts guide, which this one replaced, has a Criterion B called Developing skills, about acquiring and applying skills and techniques; its Criterion C, Thinking creatively, held the artistic intention and the exploration of ideas. Students’ older exemplars and school documents may still use that wording.
The composing lessons give B-friendly tasks: the motif lab (explore by development), the takes in Composing 3 (explore by performance), and the two quartet textures in Composing 5 (a choice to explain).

title: Reading Swing from a Lead Sheet
text:
A lead sheet writes swing eighths as plain eighth notes, and that is not an error. The way they are written is shorthand, the way a chord symbol is. It tells you which notes come where, and the style tells you how to play them. This lesson covers what the shorthand means, how much room it leaves you, and how to know when it does not mean swing. The two examples are Oscar Pettiford’s Blues in the Closet, which swings, and Herbie Hancock’s Watermelon Man, which does not.
How to use the page. Every example is written out and can be played. Press ▶ Play to hear it. Examples that have a Swing slider let you set how long the first eighth of each pair is held, from even (50%) up to a dotted-eighth-and-sixteenth (75%). The Tempo box sets the speed. Play each example at more than one setting before you read on.
crumbs: Reading Swing from a Lead Sheet

title: Reading Swing from a Lead Sheet
section: 1. What the page says, and what it means
text:
1. What the page says, and what it means
Here is the first bar of Blues in the Closet exactly as a lead sheet writes it.


Played as written, the eighths are even: each beat is split exactly in half. No jazz player reads it that way. In a swing tune each pair of eighths is played long-short: the note on the beat is held longer and the note on the “and” comes late. The usual way to explain it is with a triplet: the beat is split into three, the first note gets two thirds and the second gets one.


Arrangers almost never write that, because it is hard to read and because, as the rest of this lesson shows, it is not quite right either. Instead they write plain eighths and put a word or a sign at the top of the chart:

Swing, Med. swing, Shuffle, Bluesy, or just a tempo and a style name.
The sign ♫ = ♩ ♪³: “a pair of eighths equals a quarter and an eighth under a triplet”.
Nothing at all. On a jazz lead sheet, swing is the default, and you are expected to know it.

The one way not to read swing eighths is as a dotted eighth and a sixteenth. That is a ratio of 3 to 1, and at most tempos it sounds stiff and jerky, like a march. Compare it with the triplet version above.
crumbs: Reading Swing from a Lead Sheet

title: Reading Swing from a Lead Sheet
section: 2. Swing is a range, not a ratio
text:
2. Swing is a range, not a ratio
The triplet is a useful first picture and a poor final answer. Measurements of recordings find that players swing anywhere from nearly even to a little past the triplet, and that the same player changes ratio with the tempo. The rough rule:




Tempo


Typical long:short


Slider


What it sounds like






Ballad, slow blues (under 80)


about 2:1, sometimes more


65–70%


Lazy, heavy triplet feel, often a 12/8 shuffle




Medium (100–160)


between 3:2 and 2:1


62–68%


The “standard” swing of a blues like Blues in the Closet




Up-tempo (over 220)


close to even


55–60%


Eighths almost straight; the swing is in the accents




The band on this site follows the same rule: its swing is 68% at 100 beats a minute or slower, 66% at 120, 64% at 160, 60% at 220 and 55% at 300 (the Swing menu’s Auto). Try it here. Set the slider to 66% and raise the tempo to 240: it becomes hard to play and starts to sound like a shuffle. Then lower the slider to 55% at the same tempo.



Everything else the shorthand leaves to you
The ratio is only one of the choices a plain line of eighths leaves open. Others matter at least as much, and the lead sheet says nothing about any of them.
Each choice below shows the line as written, two ways to play it that are both swing, and one way that is not. The played versions are written out more exactly than any chart would be: accent marks (>), staccato dots, and “ghost” over a note that is barely played.
With a MIDI keyboard plugged in (Chrome or Edge), Play it on a keyboard under any example counts you in for a bar, records you against a click, and says how you did: your swing ratio for the tempo, which notes you leaned on, ghosts, note lengths and ties, how far ahead of or behind the click you sat, and any notes you moved by an eighth.

Accents on the off-beats
Swing players lean on the “and”, not the beat. A line of eighths is usually played doo-BAH doo-BAH, with the beat note soft and the off-beat note pushed. This is why fast swing still swings at nearly even eighths.










Ghosted notes
A note in the middle of a run may be barely played at all, more felt than heard.










Length
A written quarter note is often played short (dit), especially on beats 2 and 4 and at the end of a phrase. A written eighth tied over the bar line is played long.










Where in the beat
Some players sit right on the beat, others play a fraction behind it (“laid back”) against a drummer who is on top of it. Neither is written; both are swing. Laid back is far smaller than any written note value; the sixteenth rest below is an exaggeration so it can be seen.








Small changes to the rhythm
Players anticipate a note by an eighth, delay one, or add a pickup. On a lead sheet, that is interpretation, not a wrong note.








What is not up to you: where the bar lines are, where the notes fall in the beat (on it or on the “and”), and the form. A swing eighth on the “and” of 2 is late, but it is still the “and” of 2.
crumbs: Reading Swing from a Lead Sheet

title: Reading Swing from a Lead Sheet
text:
3. Blues in the Closet
Blues in the Closet is a medium-tempo jazz blues, usually played somewhere between 120 and 180 beats a minute. Here is the whole melody, in F, as it is written in the tune library.


There is no “Swing” marking on it, and none is needed: it is a bebop-era blues, every recording of it swings, and the eighth-note pairs are written the way every jazz player expects. Play it at 50% and then at 64% to hear what the marking would have told you.

The places that change when it swings

The pickup and the ties. The tune starts on the “and” of 4 and ties it into the bar. In swing, that pickup is late (it is the short note of a pair), so the first note of the tune arrives just before the bar line and pulls the band into it. The same figure ends bars 4 and 8. These anticipations are the strongest swing feature in the tune: give them a little accent.
The figure A F. In every bar the melody drops from the 3rd to the root in a pair of eighths. Swung, it is long-short, and the short F is the one to lean on.
The tied F in bar 2. A/F/- F/ C is four eighths, with the second tied to the third. Swung, the tied F lands on the late “and” of 2 and sustains through beat 3. Played even, the syncopation is weaker and the bar sounds square.
The long notes. The C in bars 4 and 8 is a dotted quarter tied to a quarter. It can be held full length or cut off early; both are common. The rest that follows is where the rhythm section, or another player, answers.



A range of good readings
Three players reading the same lead sheet would not play the same thing, and all three would be right. Try these settings and decide which one you like:




Setting


Tempo


Slider


Feel






Relaxed


120


66–68%


Close to the triplet, heavy, bluesy




Medium


150


62–66%


The usual jam-session reading




Up


220+


55–60%


Nearly even; put the swing in accents on the off-beats




What no setting allows is 50% at a medium tempo with every note accented equally. That is the one clear misreading.
crumbs: Reading Swing from a Lead Sheet

title: Reading Swing from a Lead Sheet
section: 4. Watermelon Man: eighths that do not swing
text:
4. Watermelon Man: eighths that do not swing
Watermelon Man (from Takin’ Off, 1962) is also a blues, with 16 bars instead of 12, and it is written in exactly the same way: plain eighth notes, no triplets, no dots. Here are its first eight bars and the four-bar riff that follows.


On the page it looks like Blues in the Closet: eighth notes, ties over the bar line, anticipations. The difference is the style. This is a straight-eighth tune: the eighths are even, and they stay even when the tempo drops. It is often marked “Funky”, “Latin”, “Even 8ths” or “Straight 8ths”, but on many lead sheets it is not marked at all, and you are expected to know it from the record, the same as with a swing tune.
Now move the slider to 66% and play it again. Bars 9 to 12 suffer most: z2 cc g2 a2 starts on an off-beat pair, and swinging it turns a crisp, funky riff into something closer to a nursery rhyme. The off-beat F in bars 2 and 6, which should snap against the beat, goes soft.

“Somewhere between”
Even this tune is not perfectly even. Hancock said that Billy Higgins played it “somewhere between straight eighth notes and the swinging triplets of jazz”. That is a slider setting of perhaps 53 to 56%, which is not enough to sound like swing but is enough to keep the line from sounding mechanical. Mongo Santamaría’s hit version a year later is a cha-cha, and its eighths are straight. Both are good readings of the same lead sheet; a 66% swing is not.
So the range of acceptable readings exists for straight tunes too. It is just centred in a different place.
crumbs: Reading Swing from a Lead Sheet

title: Reading Swing from a Lead Sheet
text:
5. The contrast, side by side






Blues in the Closet


Watermelon Man






Written as


Plain eighths


Plain eighths




Played as


Swing, long-short


Even, or very nearly




Slider


55–68%, by tempo


50–56%




Where the energy is


Accents on the off-beats, late pickups


Crisp, equal subdivisions locked to a backbeat or a Latin pattern




How you know


Jazz blues, bebop era, every recording


The record, the style (“funk”, “Latin”, “even 8ths”)




The point is that the notation is identical. Everything that separates these two tunes in performance comes from outside the notes: the style, the era, the recording and the band.
crumbs: Reading Swing from a Lead Sheet

title: Reading Swing from a Lead Sheet
text:
6. Reading a new lead sheet
When you open a chart you have not played before, before you play a note:

Look at the top of the page for a style or feel word, a ♫ = ♩ ♪³ sign, or “even 8ths”.
Look at the tempo. The faster it is, the straighter the swing.
Know where the tune comes from. A jazz standard or a bebop blues swings unless told otherwise. A funk, Latin, rock, soul or bossa nova tune does not.
Listen to a recording. It is the only thing that settles the question, and it tells you about the accents and the note lengths too, which no lead sheet shows.
Listen to the band. If the drummer plays the swing ride pattern, match its ratio; if the drummer plays straight eighths on the hi-hat, play straight. The ratio is shared, not chosen alone.

Then practise both tunes in this lesson at three tempos each, and play the slider settings from the tables until you can hear the difference without looking.

title: Recording 4: Miking a Guitar Amp
text: A guitar amp’s sound is mostly its speaker: little above 5–6 kHz comes out of one at all, and what does changes a lot across its face. So the first decision is not which mic, but where to put it.

title: Recording 4: Miking a Guitar Amp
text:
Which mic

Dynamic (the SM57 type): the usual first choice. Takes any level, sounds right close up, its lift around 4–6 kHz helps a guitar cut through. Cheap enough to own two.
Ribbon: darker and smoother; takes the fizz off a distorted amp. A figure-8, so its back hears the room (or the ceiling) as much as its front hears the speaker. Some ribbons can’t take a loud amp close up; check the manual, and never send them phantom power from a miswired cable (Recording 2).
Condenser (large diaphragm): detailed and open, best a little back from the amp, or as a room mic.
Two at once: a dynamic and a ribbon side by side on the same speaker, blended, is a classic.

title: Recording 4: Miking a Guitar Amp
text:
Where on the speaker
Shine a torch through the grille cloth to find the speaker and its dust cap. In a cabinet with several speakers, listen to each with your ear close (at low volume) and pick the best-sounding one; they are rarely identical.




On the dust cap: brightest, most bite, can be harsh or fizzy.
At the cap’s edge: bright and full. Start here.
On the cone: warmer and rounder.
Near the edge: dark and woolly, rarely what you want.

A centimetre matters. Have someone move the mic while you listen in closed headphones in another room.

title: Recording 4: Miking a Guitar Amp
text:
Distance and angle

Close (1–5 cm from the grille cloth): the speaker’s own sound, little room, and the most proximity bass. Most rock and pop guitar is recorded like this.
Further back (20–60 cm): the speaker’s sound “comes together”; the room starts to join in.
Angled 30–45°: a little darker, less fizz, without moving across the speaker. Try it before reaching for the EQ.

Drag the mic across the speaker, then change the distance, angle, mic and room:

title: Recording 4: Miking a Guitar Amp
section: A room mic, and two mics
text:
A room mic, and two mics
A second mic 1–2 m back (a condenser, or a ribbon) records the amp in the room. Blend a little under the close mic for size. Two mics on one amp are two distances, so check their phase: flip the polarity of one and keep whichever sounds fuller, and keep two close mics the same distance from the speaker (Recording 3: Phase). An open-back combo can be miked from behind as well; the back mic faces the other way, so flip its polarity.

title: Recording 4: Miking a Guitar Amp
text:
Volume
The amp doesn’t need to be loud to sound good on a mic. Many amps sound best with their power section working, but a small amp turned up often records better than a big one turned down. Loud amps go in another room, or facing a wall with a blanket over them and the mic, so they don’t bleed into everything else (Recording 3: Bleed).

title: Recording 4: Miking a Guitar Amp
text:
DI and re-amping
Record a DI of the guitar (straight from the guitar through a DI box or the interface’s instrument input) at the same time as the mic. Later the clean DI can be sent back out to an amp (re-amping, through a re-amp box) or into an amp simulator, if the sound you chose doesn’t fit the mix. Bass is usually recorded with a DI and a mic on the cab, blended.

title: Recording 2: Microphones and Phantom Power
text: Every microphone turns air pressure into voltage, but the three main types do it differently, and that changes how they sound, how loud a source they can take and how fragile they are.

title: Recording 2: Microphones and Phantom Power
text:
Dynamic
A thin diaphragm glued to a coil of wire, sitting in a magnet. Sound moves the coil, the magnet makes a current. The Shure SM57 and SM58 are the classic examples.

Tough: dropped, rained on, shouted into, they keep working.
Handles very loud sources: snare, kick, guitar amps, brass close up.
Less detail in the highs and less sensitive, so it picks up less of the room and less bleed. That is why it is the default for live sound and for recording in an untreated bedroom.
Needs a lot of preamp gain (often 50–60 dB on a quiet voice). Some very low-output ones (the Shure SM7B) are used with an inline booster.
No phantom power needed.

title: Recording 2: Microphones and Phantom Power
text:
Condenser
A very thin, electrically charged diaphragm close to a metal back plate: a capacitor whose value changes as the diaphragm moves. It needs power to hold the charge and to run its small internal amplifier.

Detailed and sensitive: the air on a voice, the pick on an acoustic guitar, cymbals, overheads, a piano, a choir or a room.
Large-diaphragm (an inch or so; the studio vocal mic) sounds warm and flattering; small-diaphragm (“pencil” mics) is more accurate and even off-axis, good for acoustic instruments and stereo pairs.
Picks up everything: the fridge, the computer fan, the reflections off the walls. In a bare room a condenser can sound worse than a dynamic.
More fragile. Keep it out of the damp and away from kick drums unless it is built for it.
Needs phantom power (or its own power supply, for valve/tube condensers).

title: Recording 2: Microphones and Phantom Power
text:
Ribbon
A strip of very thin corrugated aluminium hung in a magnetic field.

Smooth, dark, natural highs; loved on guitar amps, brass, strings and drum rooms.
Almost always figure-8 (picks up front and back equally).
Fragile: a blast of air (a kick drum, a puff into it, being carried quickly) can stretch the ribbon. Keep it covered when not in use.
Classic passive ribbons do not want phantom power, and old ones can be damaged by a faulty cable with it on. Active ribbons (they say so) need it.

title: Recording 2: Microphones and Phantom Power
text:
Phantom power (+48 V)
Phantom power sends 48 volts DC down the same balanced XLR cable that brings the signal back. It is “phantom” because a dynamic mic, wired the usual way, doesn’t see it at all.

Turn it on for condensers (and active ribbons, and some DI boxes).
Plug in first, then switch on. Switch off and wait a few seconds before unplugging. Plugging in with 48 V live makes a loud pop through the speakers and can, rarely, harm gear.
Monitors down when switching it on or off.
On many cheap interfaces one 48 V button powers two or all inputs at once. Fine for dynamics; check before plugging an old ribbon into any of them.
If a condenser makes no sound: is 48 V on? Is it an XLR cable (not a jack)?


Never patch an XLR in or out with phantom power on, and keep vintage ribbon mics on a channel with 48 V off.

Try the order yourself. Press Monitors on (speakers low), choose a mic, then plug in and switch +48 V in the right and the wrong order:

title: Recording 2: Microphones and Phantom Power
text:
Polar patterns
The polar pattern is how sensitive a mic is from each direction.

Cardioid (heart-shaped): picks up the front, rejects the back. The default for almost everything. Point the back at what you don’t want (the drums, the monitor, the window).
Supercardioid / hypercardioid: narrower in front, with a small lobe at the back. Common on live vocal mics. Point the side (not the back) at the monitor.
Omni: everything equally. Natural, no proximity effect (see placement), but hears the whole room.
Figure-8: front and back, nothing from the sides. Ribbons; two singers facing each other; the side mic of a mid/side pair (Sound 23: Stereo).

Many large-diaphragm condensers have a switch for several of these.



Drag the singer and the drums, turn the mic, and compare patterns and mic types. Watch the voice against the drum bleed in dB:




Off axis
A pattern drawing is for the middle frequencies. Off to the side, a mic doesn’t just get quieter: the treble drops first, because a diaphragm stops hearing high sounds that arrive from the side. So a singer who wanders off the mic sounds further away and duller.



Walk the singer round the mic and listen:





Don’t cup the mic
A cardioid is directional because of the rear ports, slots behind the capsule: sound reaching them from behind arrives at the back of the diaphragm too, and cancels. Wrap a hand round the grille and the ports are covered. The mic becomes almost omni, hears the wedge monitor it was meant to ignore, and feeds back. The hollow of the hand also makes a little chamber: the voice goes boxy and honky, and the sound engineer can’t EQ it back. Hold the handle.



Press Cup the grille to hear (and see) it:

title: Recording 2: Microphones and Phantom Power
text:
Which mic for what
No mic is flat on purpose. A handheld vocal dynamic trims the bass (you’ll be close, and proximity effect puts it back) and lifts 4–6 kHz, where words are clear; a studio condenser stays near flat.

title: Recording 6: Monitoring and Headphones
text: Monitoring is what you listen on: while recording, while performing, while mixing. The rule of thumb is simple: headphones while a microphone is open, speakers while mixing. But each has its reasons and its traps.

title: Recording 6: Monitoring and Headphones
text:
When to use headphones

Any time a mic is recording in the same room as the playback. Speakers playing the backing track, the click or the other parts will get into the mic (bleed). With the click, it can’t be removed.
Overdubbing: singing or playing to tracks already recorded.
Feedback: a mic, turned up, pointed near speakers playing that mic, howls. Headphones stop it.
Placing the mic: listen in headphones while the mic is moved.
Checking detail: clicks, edits, noise, breaths, distortion are easier to hear.
Late at night or in shared spaces.

title: Recording 6: Monitoring and Headphones
text:
Closed or open

Closed-back headphones seal round the ear. Little sound gets in or out. Use them for recording: a loud click in open-backs leaks into a sensitive condenser.
Open-back headphones are vented; they sound more natural and are more comfortable for hours, but leak both ways. Use them for mixing and listening, not next to an open mic.
In-ear monitors (IEMs): very good isolation; used live and by drummers.

title: Recording 6: Monitoring and Headphones
text:
When to use speakers

Mixing and mastering. In headphones, each ear hears only one side; on speakers, both ears hear both speakers, and the room, the way listeners will. Panning, reverb and bass sound very different. Headphone mixes often end up with too little reverb and wrong bass.
Tracking a band live in one room where everyone wants to hear each other and bleed is accepted.
Recording with no microphones: DI guitar, keyboards, drum machines, synths.
Set monitors in an equilateral triangle with your head, tweeters at ear height, away from the walls. Listen at a moderate level (around 75–85 dB SPL): ears hear less bass and treble when quiet, and tire when loud.

Do the mix on speakers, then check on headphones, earbuds, a phone and a car. Most people will hear it on one of those.

title: Recording 6: Monitoring and Headphones
text:
Latency and direct monitoring
Sound going into the computer and out again takes time: the buffer. At 256 samples and 48 kHz, each way is about 5 ms plus the converters; with a big buffer it can be 20–40 ms. A singer hearing their own voice that late sounds as if they’re singing in a tunnel, and timing suffers.

Direct monitoring (a knob or switch on the interface) sends the input straight to the headphones, with no delay, before the computer. Mute the track’s input monitoring in the DAW, or you hear yourself twice, slightly apart (a flanger, see Sound 18).
Or use a small buffer (64–128 samples) while recording, and a big one while mixing.
Under about 10 ms most players won’t notice. Drummers and singers notice soonest.


Try it: hear the delay
Press ▶ (headphones on), clap or speak along with the click, and try the buffer sizes. Then choose “Both on” to hear the flanging double.

title: Recording 6: Monitoring and Headphones
text:
The headphone mix
A performer plays better when the headphones sound good.

Hear yourself enough. Singers who can’t hear themselves sing sharp and push; too much and they sing flat.
Pulling one side off the ear helps some singers pitch; it also leaks the click into the mic: turn it down if they do.
A little reverb in the headphones (not recorded) helps singers.
Click: as quiet as still usable. A cowbell or rim click, not a high beep. Turn it off for the quiet ending, or it’ll be there in the mic.
Careful with level. Long sessions at high volume damage hearing for ever. If you need it very loud to hear yourself, turn the backing down instead.


Try it: build a cue mix
Set each fader, add the reverb, then switch to speakers to see how much click and backing would end up in the recording. Switch “Listen to” to the recorded track to hear it.

title: Recording 9: Mono and Stereo
text: A mono signal is one channel: one microphone, one cable, one speaker or many speakers all playing the same thing. A stereo signal is two channels, left and right, that differ a little, and the differences are what put sounds somewhere between the speakers (Sound 23: Stereo). Most music is recorded largely in mono, mixed into stereo, and then heard, quite often, back in mono. Each step has its traps.

title: Recording 9: Mono and Stereo
text:
Recording: mostly mono

One source, one mic is a mono track: vocal, bass DI, kick, snare, guitar amp. That isn’t a weakness: the mix places each mono track in the stereo picture with the pan knob. A “stereo” vocal is almost never wanted.
Two mics on one source is not automatically stereo. Two mics at different distances on a guitar amp hear the same sound at slightly different times; mixed together they comb-filter (cancel some frequencies, boost others). Check the polarity button and nudge the far track in time until the low end is fullest. The 3:1 rule helps: the second mic at least three times as far from the first as the first is from its source.
Stereo pairs record space on purpose (Recording 2: Microphones):

XY: two cardioids, capsules touching at 90–135°. Only level differences, no time differences, so it sums to mono cleanly. Narrower image.
ORTF / spaced pair (AB): capsules apart. Time differences give a wide, airy image, but in mono the delays comb-filter: the more spaced, the more it can go hollow.
Mid/side: a forward mic (mid) and a sideways figure-8 (side), decoded to L = M + S, R = M − S. In mono the side cancels exactly and you get the mid mic, perfectly. Width is adjustable after the fact.

Stereo sources: keyboards, synths and drum machines often come out stereo (L/R outputs). Record both if the patch is really stereo (a chorus, a Leslie, a stereo piano sample); record one if the two sides are identical.
Room and overhead mics are where stereo recording matters most: the drum kit, the choir, the piano, the hall.

title: Recording 9: Mono and Stereo
text:
Mixing: building the stereo picture
The mixing rules all serve two listeners at once, the one on stereo speakers and the one in mono:

Centre the things that carry the song: kick, snare, bass, lead vocal. A centred (mono) sound is equal in both channels, so it survives every playback system, and its bass energy is shared by both speakers.
Pan the rest. Pan is a level difference; it sums to mono without cancelling.
Pan law: a sound panned centre plays in both speakers; to sound as loud as when it’s hard to one side, the centre is turned down 3 dB (or 4.5 or 6, the DAW decides). When the mix folds to mono, centre sounds come up relative to hard-panned ones, so a balance can shift a little.
Wideners (Haas delays, phase tricks, stereo chorus, some “stereo enhancer” plug-ins) make width out of time and phase differences, and those are exactly what cancel in mono.
Double-tracking (playing the part twice, panned left and right) is the safe way to wide: the two takes differ naturally, so in mono they just sound like two players, not a comb filter.

title: Recording 9: Mono and Stereo
section: One earbud: what happens when stereo is summed to mono
text:
One earbud: what happens when stereo is summed to mono
Take one earbud out and the other still plays one channel only: you’d hear the left side of the mix, missing whatever was panned hard right (the second guitar, half the drum kit, a backing vocal). That’s why phones and operating systems have a Mono Audio setting (iOS: Accessibility → Audio & Visual; Android, macOS and Windows have one too), and many earbuds switch to mono by themselves when only one is in. A single Bluetooth speaker, a phone’s speaker, a smart speaker, a shop’s ceiling speakers and many club and church PAs do the same thing: they play L + R (usually scaled by ½, or −3 dB, to keep it from clipping).
What summing does to a mix:

Anything equal in both channels (the centred vocal, kick, bass) adds up and comes through solid. In fact it gets louder relative to the sides (up to 6 dB on a plain L + R, 3 dB with a pan-law sum), so a mono mix sounds more vocal-and-bass heavy.
Hard-panned parts stay, at their own level. Nothing is lost, but they drop back relative to the centre.
Anything that’s different in the two channels only by timing or phase cancels partly or completely:

A Haas widener (the same part a few ms late on one side) becomes a comb filter: hollow, thin, phasey.
Out-of-polarity content (one side inverted, often from a miswired mic, a cable, or an overenthusiastic widener) disappears entirely. Instruments or reverb vanish.
Spaced-pair overheads and room mics go hollow; the cymbals can swish.
Stereo reverb loses much of its tail (a reverb’s two sides are deliberately decorrelated), so a mono mix sounds drier than you meant.
Very wide synths and pads (detuned unison spread across the field, stereo chorus) shrink, thin out, and sometimes almost vanish behind the vocal.
The side of a mid/side signal is gone: at 200% width you were only turning up what mono throws away.

Bass is the worst place for any of this: a bass note slightly out of phase between the sides loses its weight in mono, and a mono subwoofer (see below) gets exactly that cancelled version.

How to check it: press the DAW’s Mono button (or put a utility plug-in on the master set to mono) several times while mixing, and watch a correlation meter or vectorscope. +1 is mono, 0 is wide and unrelated, anything heading toward −1 is trouble. Try it on the widget in Sound 23: Haas delay at 1, 3, 5, 10 ms with Mono on. If a part disappears in mono, fix the source: narrow the widener, use a real double, flip a polarity, or keep the low end (below about 120–150 Hz) mono with a mid/side EQ or a “mono bass” utility.

title: Recording 9: Mono and Stereo
text:
Live sound
Most of a live audience doesn’t hear stereo. Stereo needs you to sit between the speakers, roughly as far from each, and on a festival field or in a bar almost everyone is much nearer one stack than the other: they hear that side, plus a late copy of the other. So:

Many live mixes are mono, or nearly: both sides of the PA play the same mix, and nothing important is panned. If a hard-left guitar plays only from the left stack, the people on the right don’t get the guitar.
Stereo is used lightly: reverbs and delays, a little spread on keyboards and overheads, panning a few degrees.
Front fills, delay towers and side fills cover the parts of the room the main speakers miss. Delay speakers are delayed to arrive just after the main PA (Haas again, 5–20 ms) so the sound still seems to come from the stage.
Monitors (wedges and in-ears) are separate mixes for each player (Recording 6). In-ears are often stereo, for comfort and a sense of the band; wedges are mono.
Feedback: a mic in front of a speaker playing it howls. Keep mics behind the main PA, wedges in the mic’s dead zone (behind a cardioid, at the sides of a supercardioid).

title: Recording 9: Mono and Stereo
text:
Studio listening and speaker placement
In the studio you’re the one listener in the right seat, so stereo works fully, if the room and speakers allow it:

Equilateral triangle: the two speakers and your head at its three corners, 1–2 m on a side, tweeters at ear height, speakers angled to point at (or just behind) your head. The phantom centre (a centred vocal floating between them) is the test: if it’s blurred or pulled to one side, the triangle is off.
Symmetry: the same distance from each side wall, so both sides reflect alike. Put the desk along the short wall, firing down the room’s long dimension.
Off the walls: a speaker near the wall behind it gets extra bass (and a dip where its reflection cancels). Either keep it a metre or more out, or push it nearly flush and use the speaker’s “boundary” EQ switch. Avoid the room’s exact centre (between front and back walls): bass standing waves are worst there.
Decouple: stands or isolation pads, not a resonant desk; the desk surface also reflects into your ears.
First reflections: absorbers on the side walls (where a mirror would show you the speaker) and above.
Level: moderate, ~75–85 dB SPL, then checked quiet.

title: Recording 9: Mono and Stereo
text:
Laptops, phones and small speakers

Laptop speakers are tiny and a few centimetres apart: almost no stereo width (some laptops fake it with processing), and almost nothing below 150–200 Hz. Phones are often one speaker, or two that sum to near-mono.
Your bass line has to be heard through its harmonics: a bass with some upper-mid character (pick attack, a little saturation, 700 Hz–1.5 kHz) stays audible; a pure sub-bass sine disappears.
Check mixes on the laptop and a phone, in mono. If the vocal is clear, the bass line can be followed and nothing has vanished, the mix translates.
Laptop headphone outputs are usually fine; built-in microphones are mono, noisy, and processed (noise suppression, echo cancellation): not for recording music if anything else is available.

title: Recording 9: Mono and Stereo
text:
Subwoofers, and why two
A subwoofer plays only the deep bass (below a crossover, often 80 Hz). Low frequencies are hard to locate by ear, so one subwoofer is usually fed a mono sum of L + R. That’s another mono fold: any bass that cancels in mono cancels in the sub.

Why two? Not mainly for stereo bass (below about 80 Hz you can hardly tell where it comes from). The reason is the room. Bass wavelengths (4 m at 80 Hz, 17 m at 20 Hz) are the size of the room, so the room sets up standing waves: at some seats a note booms, at others it nearly vanishes. Two subs in different places excite those modes differently and fill in each other’s holes, so the bass is even across more seats (and each sub works less hard, with more headroom).
Placement: studies (Todd Welti and Allan Devantier at Harman) found two subs at the midpoints of opposite walls, or four at the midpoints of all four, smooth the bass best across a listening area. A corner gives the most level and the most uneven bass.
Phase and time: two subs must arrive together at the listener. Use each sub’s phase (0/180° or a dial) and delay so the bass gets louder at the crossover, not thinner; a sub out of phase with the mains causes the same cancellation as an out-of-phase stereo pair.
Live, subs are often in a cardioid arrangement (one turned backward and delayed) to keep bass off the stage, or spread across the front in an end-fire or arc. Two stacks far apart, left and right, with the same signal, make a bass power alley down the middle and dead spots in between: the same comb filter as a Haas delay, but a room-sized one.
Studio: the sub level is set so it continues the mains smoothly, not as an effect. A mix made with a loud sub will be bass-light everywhere else.

title: Recording 9: Mono and Stereo
text:
Checklist

Kick, bass, snare, lead vocal centred; low end (below ~120 Hz) mono.
Mono button pressed often; correlation meter mostly positive.
No part disappears in mono; wideners and polarity checked.
Checked on speakers, headphones, one earbud, a laptop and a phone.
Speakers in a symmetrical triangle; sub(s) in phase with the mains.

title: Lesson: Reharmonizing a Melody
text:
One melody can sit on many sets of chords. A chord is right for a melody note if the note is in it (a chord tone) or if it passes quickly (a passing note). This lesson takes one tune, Ode to Joy, and puts four sets of chords under it.
How to use the page. Press ▶ on a chart and the band plays it twice after a one-bar count-in. The bar that is sounding lights up, on the chart and on the staff. Under every chord is its Roman numeral, which stays the same in every key. The strip at the bottom of the window sets the key, the feel, the tempo and the chord instrument, and you can change them while the band plays. Shaded bars are the ones that differ from the version named under the chart. The tune is written above the chart and its notes light up as they sound. ▶ Play with the band plays the melody on the piano with the chords under it.

title: Lesson: Reharmonizing a Melody
text:
1. A plain setting
C and G, mostly. Two chords. Every note of the tune is a chord tone or a passing note on one of them. This is how the tune is usually harmonised in a school songbook.

title: Lesson: Reharmonizing a Melody
text:
2. Sevenths on the dominants
G7 for G. The tune does not change. The chord under it does: G7 adds an F, and the F is a note the tune already passes through in bar 2. Now it is a chord tone.

title: Lesson: Reharmonizing a Melody
text:
3. Secondary dominants
Am in bar 3, E7 in bar 4, and Am then D7 in bar 7. The notes of the tune are the same. Under bar 4, E7 has the tune’s E as its root and its D as the 7th. In bar 7, D7 holds the tune’s D, and the E after it is the 9th.

title: Lesson: Reharmonizing a Melody
section: 4. A chord for every pair of notes
text:
4. A chord for every pair of notes
C F | C/E Dm7 | Am7 | Dm7 G7 | C F | C/E Dm7 | Am7 | Dm7 C. Now the chords change every two beats and the bass moves by step: C, F, E, D. It is the tune as a jazz pianist might play it, and it sounds quite different even though the tune has not changed a note.

title: Lesson: Reharmonizing a Melody
text:
Build your own
Choose one of the four settings for each pair of bars, and mix them. The tune is above the chart. All of the settings fit the tune, so there is no wrong combination.

title: Lesson: Reharmonizing a Melody
text:
Where to go next

Pick your own tune and try three sets of chords on it. Play the melody note by note against each chord.
The question to ask of every chord is: is this melody note a chord tone, or is it passing?

title: Sampling 2: Chopping and Slicing
text: Chopping is cutting a sample into pieces so each can be played on its own. On an Akai MPC the pieces go onto the 16 pads; on a Roland SP-404 each pad holds a sample with its own start and end; in a DAW the pieces become slices of a clip or notes of a sampler.

title: Sampling 2: Chopping and Slicing
text:
Three ways to cut

Equal slices: cut the loop into 16 equal parts. For a one-bar loop in 4/4 each slice is a sixteenth note; for two bars, an eighth. Quick, and it keeps the timing grid, but a slice can start just before or after a hit.
One a beat: cut at every beat (from the loop’s tempo). Good for chord samples, where each beat is a chord.
At the transients: cut where the sound suddenly gets louder (a transient: the attack of a drum or a plucked note). Each slice starts exactly on a hit, so it sounds clean; the slices are of different lengths.

title: Sampling 2: Chopping and Slicing
text:
Try it




With 16 equal slices, play pads 1–16. Some slices start with a click or a bit of the hit before. Listen for it.
Switch to At the hits. Now pads start on kicks, snares and hats. Play pads 1–4: each is a clean one-shot.
Move a chop: drag one of the marker lines on the waveform left or right. The pad plays as you let go. Put a marker exactly at the start of a snare: the slice before it now ends cleanly too.
Load Old Soul Record (chords) from the menu and choose One a beat: each pad is now a chord. Play a new progression with them.

title: Sampling 2: Chopping and Slicing
text:
The art of the chop

Short chops (a single hit or a word) become an instrument: you play a new rhythm with them.
Long chops (a bar, a phrase) keep the feel of the original: you rearrange them like building blocks, as J Dilla and Pete Rock did with soul records.
Leave out the obvious bit. The famous hook of a record is the hardest to clear and the most recognised; a tiny chord stab from the middle of side B is yours to transform.
Fades: a slice that starts or ends in the middle of a sound clicks. This sampler fades each slice in and out over 1.5 ms; a DAW or MPC has fade or “attack/release” settings for the same reason.

title: Sampling 2: Chopping and Slicing
section: The DJ’s version: loops and cue points
text:
The DJ’s version: loops and cue points
A DJ chops live. A cue point is a marked spot in a track to jump to; a loop repeats a stretch (a bar, four bars) until it is released. With hot cues on the four snare hits of a break, a DJ can “finger drum” a new pattern over the next record: a chop made in the moment. On the deck below, press CUE while stopped to set a cue point where you are, then ▶; press CUE while it plays and it jumps back and stops.

title: Sampling 6: Clearing Samples and the Law
text: This lesson explains how sampling law has worked, mainly in the United States, so you know which questions to ask. It is not legal advice: for a release that matters, ask a music lawyer or a sample-clearance service.
crumbs: Sampling 6: Clearing Samples and the Law

title: Sampling 6: Clearing Samples and the Law
text:
Two copyrights in every recording
A commercial recording usually carries two separate copyrights:

The musical work (the composition: melody, harmony, words), owned by the songwriters and their publisher.
The sound recording (the “master”: that particular performance, captured), usually owned by the record label.

Sampling a recording uses both. Clearing a sample means getting permission (a licence) from the publisher and the master owner. If you replay (interpolate) the part yourself instead of sampling the record, you use only the composition, so you need only the publisher’s permission. That is why many producers re-record samples.
crumbs: Sampling 6: Clearing Samples and the Law

title: Sampling 6: Clearing Samples and the Law
text:
What the courts have said

Grand Upright Music v. Warner Bros. Records (1991). Biz Markie’s “Alone Again” used a piece of Gilbert O’Sullivan’s “Alone Again (Naturally)” without permission. The judge found infringement and referred the case for criminal prosecution. After it, labels started clearing samples routinely.
Campbell v. Acuff-Rose Music (1994). The US Supreme Court held that 2 Live Crew’s parody of “Oh, Pretty Woman” could be fair use: a new work that comments on the old one weighs strongly in its favour. Fair use is decided case by case; it is not a rule like “under two seconds is fine” (there is no such rule).
Newton v. Diamond (2004). The Beastie Boys licensed the recording of a flute passage from James Newton but not the composition. The court held the three-note composition use was too small to matter (de minimis).
Bridgeport Music v. Dimension Films (2005). A two-second guitar chord, pitched down and looped, from a Funkadelic recording. The Sixth Circuit court said that for sound recordings there is no “too small to matter”: “Get a license or do not sample.”
VMG Salsoul v. Ciccone (2016). A 0.23-second horn hit in Madonna’s “Vogue”. The Ninth Circuit disagreed with Bridgeport: a use too small for the public to recognise is de minimis. So US courts are split by region.
crumbs: Sampling 6: Clearing Samples and the Law

title: Sampling 6: Clearing Samples and the Law
text:
How clearing works

Find out who owns the composition (the performing-rights databases, ASCAP / BMI / SOCAN / PRS, list publishers) and who owns the master (the label on the release, or its current owner).
Ask both, saying how much you used, how, and how the song will be released.
Expect an up-front fee, a share of the new song’s publishing, a royalty on sales, or a mix. A famous hook costs far more than an obscure bar, and an owner can simply say no.
Get it in writing before release. Clearing after a song is out is harder and dearer.
crumbs: Sampling 6: Clearing Samples and the Law

title: Sampling 6: Clearing Samples and the Law
text:
The safe routes

Royalty-free sample packs and loops sold for production: read the licence (most allow use in your music, not resale of the samples).
Public domain: compositions whose copyright has expired. Note that a recording of an old composition can still be protected.
Creative Commons recordings, under the terms of their licence (CC BY: credit the creator).
Your own recordings: sample yourself, your band, the street. Every loop in these lessons was made on this site, so you may use them.
Replay the part (an interpolation) and clear only the composition.
crumbs: Sampling 6: Clearing Samples and the Law

title: Sampling 6: Clearing Samples and the Law
text:
Where DJs stand

Playing records in public is a public performance of the songs. Venues (clubs, bars) normally hold blanket licences from the performing-rights organisations that cover the DJ playing commercially released music there.
Mixes posted online are copies and performances of every track in them. Streaming sites that host DJ mixes either hold licences for that (some have agreements with labels and rights organisations) or remove mixes when rights holders object.
Edits, bootlegs and mashups use others’ recordings in a new one: legally, they are unlicensed derivative works unless cleared. Many are played and tolerated in clubs; releasing or selling them is where the trouble starts.

title: Sampling 1: What a Sample Is
text: A sample is a piece of a recording reused in a new piece of music. It can be one drum hit, a bar of a drum break, a chord from an old soul record, a word from a film, or a whole chorus. Hip-hop was built on samples; so were house, jungle, much of pop since the 1990s, and every DJ set ever played.

title: Sampling 1: What a Sample Is
text:
Three sizes of sample

One-shot: a single sound (a kick, a snare, a horn stab, “Ahh”). You play it from a pad or key; it lasts as long as it lasts.
Loop: one, two or four bars that repeat seamlessly. A loop has a tempo (BPM) and usually a key.
Phrase: a longer piece (a sung line, a riff, a speech) placed once, not looped.

A break is a special loop: the moment in a funk or soul record when everything drops out but the drums. DJ Kool Herc played two copies of the same record in the Bronx in the 1970s and switched between them to stretch the break out for dancers: the “merry-go-round” that started hip-hop. The most sampled break is probably the Winstons’ “Amen, Brother” (1969), the basis of jungle and drum and bass.

title: Sampling 1: What a Sample Is
section: Two ways to use a sample
text:
Two ways to use a sample









The producer
The DJ




Where the sample lives
Inside a new track (a DAW, an MPC, an SP-404)
On a record, a USB stick or a laptop, played live


What changes it
Chopping, re-pitching, re-sequencing, effects
Mixing, EQ, loops, cue points, scratching


The result
A new recording
A performance (a set, a mix)


Typical material
Breaks, one-shots, chords, vocal phrases
Whole songs, acapellas (vocals only), instrumentals, edits



The two overlap more every year: DJ software can loop, slice and separate a song into stems live, and producers make “DJ tools” (intros, edits, loops) for other DJs to play.

title: Sampling 1: What a Sample Is
section: Hear a loop, then pieces of it
text:
Hear a loop, then pieces of it
The sampler below has a two-bar drum break loaded (made on this site, so it is free to use). Press ▶ Whole loop to hear it, then click the pads: each plays one of 16 equal slices. The waveform shows where each slice starts.




Find the pads that hold a kick, a snare and a hi-hat. Those are one-shots cut out of a loop.
Play the pads in order, 1 to 16, steadily. You have rebuilt the loop by hand.
Now play 1, 1, 5, 1, 1, 1, 5, 7. The same sounds, a new rhythm: that is sampling in one sentence.

title: Sampling 1: What a Sample Is
text:
A loop on a deck
A DJ hears the same material as a whole. Press ▶ on the deck, then pull the pitch fader: the loop speeds up and its pitch rises, like a record on a faster turntable. Drag the label on the platter to move the record by hand.

title: Sampling 1: What a Sample Is
text:
What makes a good sample

Space: a few bars where one instrument plays alone, or the drums play alone, are easier to reuse than a full mix.
A clean start: a hit right on the beat makes a loop that lines up.
Character: tape hiss, room sound and a drummer’s swing are part of why producers sample old records rather than programming drums.

Every sample of someone else’s recording also raises a question of permission: Sampling 6 is about that.

title: Score Reading 1: Alto and Tenor Clefs
text: Open an orchestral score and the viola line looks wrong: a strange bracket-shaped clef, and notes that make no sense if you read them as treble or bass. That is the alto clef. A few staves lower, the cello and bassoon may switch to the tenor clef for their high passages. Both are the same sign, the C clef, placed on a different line. This lesson teaches you to read both.
crumbs: Score Reading 1: Alto and Tenor Clefs

title: Score Reading 1: Alto and Tenor Clefs
section: 1. One sign, movable: the C clef
text:
1. One sign, movable: the C clef
Every clef is a letter that names one line. The treble clef is a G, and its curl wraps the line that is G above middle C. The bass clef is an F, and its two dots sit either side of the line that is F below middle C. The C clef points, with the middle of its bracket, at the line that is middle C.
The C clef can sit on any line. Two of those positions survive in everyday use:








Clef
Middle C is on
Used by




Alto
the middle (3rd) line
viola; alto trombone; older music for alto voice


Tenor
the 4th line from the bottom
cello, bassoon and tenor trombone in their high range; sometimes double bass and euphonium



Older music also has soprano clef (C on the bottom line), mezzo-soprano (2nd line) and baritone clef. You meet them in early editions and in score-reading exams, rarely anywhere else.
Here is middle C in four clefs. Same sound, four different places on the staff:
crumbs: Score Reading 1: Alto and Tenor Clefs

title: Score Reading 1: Alto and Tenor Clefs
text:
2. Why bother with another clef?
The answer is ledger lines. A viola’s range runs from the C below middle C up through the middle of the treble staff. In treble clef its lowest notes need three or four ledger lines below; in bass clef its upper notes climb above the staff. The alto clef centres the staff on middle C, which is roughly the middle of the viola, so almost everything it plays sits on the five lines.
The tenor clef does the same for the cello and bassoon’s upper register: the passage that would hover above the bass staff sits inside the tenor staff instead. Here is the same cello line in bass clef and in tenor clef:
crumbs: Score Reading 1: Alto and Tenor Clefs

title: Score Reading 1: Alto and Tenor Clefs
text:
3. Reading alto clef
The anchor. The middle line is middle C. Learn the notes next to it: the space above is D, the space below is B, the line above is E, the line below is A.
The shortcut. Read the note as if it were treble clef, then go one letter up and an octave down. A note on the middle line would be B in treble clef; in alto clef it is C (the one below).
Landmarks. Bottom line F (below middle C), top line G (above middle C). Bottom space G, top space F.
Here is a familiar tune in alto clef, at viola pitch. Name the first four notes before you press ▶:
crumbs: Score Reading 1: Alto and Tenor Clefs

title: Score Reading 1: Alto and Tenor Clefs
text:
4. Reading tenor clef
The anchor. The fourth line (one below the top) is middle C.
Shortcut one. Read it as bass clef, then go up a fifth. The middle line in bass clef is D; in tenor clef it is A, a fifth higher.
Shortcut two. Read it as treble clef, then one letter down and an octave lower. The middle line is B in treble; in tenor clef it is the A below middle C.
Landmarks. Bottom line D (an octave and a step below middle C), top line E (above middle C).







Do not read clefs by converting. The shortcuts get you started. Real fluency comes from knowing each clef’s landmarks directly, the way you know treble clef. Ten minutes a day of the drills below, for two weeks, does it.
crumbs: Score Reading 1: Alto and Tenor Clefs

title: Score Reading 1: Alto and Tenor Clefs
text:
5. All four clefs, mixed
Score reading means switching clef every staff. This drill shows treble, bass, alto or tenor at random.



Next: Score Reading 2, instruments that change clef mid-part. For the complete drill set, see Score Reading 6: Practice.

title: Score Reading 2: Instruments with Several Clefs
text: Most instruments live in one clef. A few move between two, three or even four, choosing whichever keeps the notes on the staff. When you read a score you have to follow the switches, and for a handful of instruments you also have to know an old convention that changes the octave.
crumbs: Score Reading 2: Instruments with Several Clefs

title: Score Reading 2: Instruments with Several Clefs
text:

title: Score Reading 2: Instruments with Several Clefs
text:
2. Following a cello part
A clef change in the middle of a line is drawn small, just before the note it affects. It lasts until the next change. This cello line climbs from bass clef through tenor into treble:



Notice that each switch happens where the old clef would have needed ledger lines. A good part changes clef as rarely as it can: one long passage in tenor clef is easier than switching every bar.
crumbs: Score Reading 2: Instruments with Several Clefs

title: Score Reading 2: Instruments with Several Clefs
text:
3. The octave traps
Three conventions change the octave, and editions disagree about them. When in doubt, check the edition’s preface or compare with another part playing the same line.
Old-style cello treble clef. In some 18th- and 19th-century editions, when a cello part moved into treble clef straight from bass clef, the treble-clef notes were meant an octave lower than written. Modern editions write treble clef at its real pitch. If a cello treble passage looks implausibly high, this may be why.
Horn in bass clef, “old notation”. Horn parts in bass clef come in two kinds. In new notation the horn in F sounds a fifth lower than written, in bass clef just as in treble. In old notation the bass-clef notes are written an octave lower, so they sound a fourth higher than written. Composers disagreed for a long time; many modern parts say “new notation” in a footnote because both are still met.
Bass clarinet, French and German. The bass clarinet in B♭ is now usually written in treble clef and sounds a major ninth lower (the “French” way), so it reads exactly like a B♭ clarinet. Older German scores (Wagner, Strauss, Mahler) often use bass clef, sounding only a major second lower, and may mix the two in one part.
crumbs: Score Reading 2: Instruments with Several Clefs

title: Score Reading 2: Instruments with Several Clefs
section: 4. Double bass, guitar and tenor voice
text:
4. Double bass, guitar and tenor voice
These read in their normal clefs but sound an octave lower. That is not a clef switch, it is an octave transposition, and it is so standard that a concert-pitch score keeps it. The guitar’s and tenor’s clef is often drawn with a small 8 under the treble clef to say so. More in lesson 3.
crumbs: Score Reading 2: Instruments with Several Clefs

title: Score Reading 2: Instruments with Several Clefs
section: 5. Choir scores and the tenor’s clef
text:
5. Choir scores and the tenor’s clef
A choir score has four parts, soprano, alto, tenor and bass (SATB), laid out in one of two ways.
Open score: one staff per voice. Soprano and alto read treble clef, bass reads bass clef, and the tenor reads the octave treble clef: a treble clef with a small 8 underneath. The 8 means “sounds an octave lower than written”. A tenor’s written G on the second line sings the G below middle C, and the middle C a tenor sings is written in the third space. Without the clef the tenor line would sit in the bass staff’s top ledger lines or hover across middle C; with it, the line sits in the middle of a staff. Because the old C tenor clef has dropped out of choral music, singers often call this octave treble clef “the tenor clef” too. Ask which one is meant.



Closed score: two staves, as in a hymnal. Soprano and alto share the treble staff (soprano stems up, alto stems down); tenor and bass share the bass staff (tenor up, bass down). Here the tenor is written at sounding pitch in bass clef, so the same tenor notes look an octave lower on the page than in open score, and sit in the bass staff’s upper half. Same music, same sound:



Reading tenor parts.

The notes read like treble clef, an octave down. A tenor reads the names exactly as in treble clef; only the sound moves. Nothing changes in the key signature.
Not every edition draws the 8. Many choral editions print a plain treble clef on the tenor staff and expect you to know. A treble staff labelled Tenor (or T., or Men in a men’s part) is sung an octave lower, 8 or no 8. Some older editions use a double treble clef (two treble clefs side by side) for the same meaning.
Older scores use the C clef. Choral music printed before the 20th century often put the tenor in the tenor clef (the C clef on the fourth line, lesson 1), and the alto and soprano in their own C clefs too. Modern editions replaced them with treble and octave treble.
Switching between scores. A tenor who sings from a hymnal (bass clef, closed score) and from an octave-edition (octave treble, open score) sees the same notes in two places. Find middle C in each: third space in octave treble, first ledger line above the bass staff in bass clef.
Accompanists and conductors reading open score at the piano play the tenor line an octave below what the treble clef shows; played as written, the tenors’ notes would sound above the altos’.
crumbs: Score Reading 2: Instruments with Several Clefs

title: Score Reading 2: Instruments with Several Clefs
text:
6. Check yourself
Clefs shuffle at random. Aim for 20 in a row without a mistake before moving on.

4. Read a chord from a transposed score
Four instruments each hold one note. Work out what each one sounds, then name the chord. Open the answer when you have it.









TipAnswer





Clarinet written D5 sounds C5 (a 2nd lower). Alto sax written E5 sounds G4 (a 6th lower). Horn written B4 sounds E4 (a 5th lower). Viola reads at pitch: middle C. The chord is C major: C4, E4, G4, C5.

title: Score Reading 6: Practice
text:
5. Unison or not?
A flute, a B♭ clarinet and a horn in F play this bar from a transposed score. Do they play the same notes?









TipAnswer





Yes. Concert key G major: the clarinet part is in A major (a 2nd up) and the horn in D major (a 5th up). All three sound G4, A4, B4, C5: a unison.
