title: Section Labels: Naming the Parts of a Song
text: When you map a recording in the Timestamp Notes, S stamps a section and gives it a label from a menu. This lesson covers what each label means, when to use letters instead of words, and how the page counts the choruses each player takes.
crumbs: Section Labels: Naming the Parts of a Song

title: Section Labels: Naming the Parts of a Song
text:
Two kinds of stamp

S marks a section: the place where a new part of the form starts. It gets a label from the menu, and the bar map, the chord grid, the phrases and Send on all use it.
C marks a note: anything else worth finding again (“drum fill”, “key change”, “wrong note at 1:12”). A note is just text, and it doesn’t split the song into sections.

Both kinds of stamp go in the same Timestamps list, in time order. Section stamps are tinted blue and have the menu.
crumbs: Section Labels: Naming the Parts of a Song

title: Section Labels: Naming the Parts of a Song
text:
The words








Label
What it is
Where you hear it




Intro
Music before the first real section, often a vamp or the last bars of the tune
Pop, rock, jazz


Head
The tune itself, played straight through, before and after the solos
Jazz


Verse
Words that change each time over the same music
Songs


Pre-chorus
A short build that lifts the verse into the chorus
Pop


Chorus
The part that comes back with the same words: the hook
Songs


Bridge
Contrasting music, usually heard once or twice
Songs, jazz (the B of AABA)


Interlude
An instrumental passage between sung sections
Songs


Solo
One player improvising over the form. Choose the instrument (Sax solo, Piano solo…)
Jazz, rock


Shout
A written ensemble chorus, the whole band loud together, often after the solos
Big band, small group arrangements


Outro
Whatever comes after the last real section: a tag, a vamp, a fade
Everywhere



The same word in pop and in jazz can mean different things. In a song a chorus is a section with the hook. In jazz a chorus is one time through the whole form: “he took three choruses” means the soloist went through the form three times.
crumbs: Section Labels: Naming the Parts of a Song

title: Section Labels: Naming the Parts of a Song
text:
The letters
Jazz standards and older songs are usually described by form letters: each new piece of music gets the next letter, and a piece that comes back gets its old letter.

AABA (32 bars, 8 each): I Got Rhythm, Satin Doll. The B is the bridge.
ABAC: All of Me. The second A returns, but the end goes somewhere new.
A A′: the A comes back with a different ending. A′ (“A prime”) means nearly A.

The menu starts by offering A. Once you’ve used A, it also offers A′ (A changed) and B (something new). Each letter you use adds the next one: B brings B′ and C, A′ brings A″. You never have to type a prime mark.
Letters aren’t numbered. An AABA tune should have three A’s, so they all stay “A”.
crumbs: Section Labels: Naming the Parts of a Song

title: Section Labels: Naming the Parts of a Song
text:
Numbering is automatic
Pick the same word twice and both are numbered: two Heads become Head 1 and Head 2 everywhere they appear (the bar map, the chord grid, the Notation page). Delete one and the other goes back to plain Head. Move a stamp earlier and the numbers follow time order, not the order you stamped them.
Need a label that isn’t on the menu? Choose Other… at the bottom and type it (“Vamp”, “Drum break”, “Trading 4s”). A typed label is kept exactly as you wrote it. The ▾ next to it takes you back to the menu.
crumbs: Section Labels: Naming the Parts of a Song

title: Section Labels: Naming the Parts of a Song
text:
Choruses: who soloed how long
Once the bars are tapped (B), the page measures each section and divides it by the length of one chorus:

One chorus is the length of the first Head stamp. If you stamped letters, it’s the A A B A (or whatever pattern repeats). If the guess is wrong, type the bar count into a chorus is __ bars.
Back-to-back stamps with the same label are one solo. It doesn’t matter whether you stamp the sax solo once or at the top of every chorus: three stamps of Sax solo, 32 bars each, make Sax 3 choruses.
Untapped bars are worked out from the tempo, so you can tap one chorus, stamp the rest with S and still get a count. The last section runs to the end of the recording.
A count of 1.5 means the solo stopped halfway through the form. That happens, but check that your stamp is in the right place.

In a song (no Head and no letters), sections can each be a different length, so a solo is counted in bars instead, along with the section it matches in length: “Guitar 8 bars (as long as the Verse)”. A last chorus tapped twice as long as the first plays its chords through twice rather than holding each one twice as long. If one section is a bar over a multiple of four and the next is a bar under (9 then 7), the Sections panel marks both with ⚠: one stamp is probably a bar off.
Fill from the tempo (in the Bar map panel) goes further: tap the head, stamp where each solo starts, and it puts in every bar after the taps. Between two stamps the bars are spread evenly, so a band that speeds up or slows down lands back on each stamp. A head or solo that comes out within about a tenth of a chorus of a whole number becomes that many choruses. The guessed bars are grey in the Bars table. Tap B on any downbeat where they drift: your tap is kept and the bars around it are worked out again. Clear guesses takes them all out.
Each count appears next to the solo’s first stamp, and the full list is under the Timestamps.
crumbs: Section Labels: Naming the Parts of a Song

Head 1 is 32 bars, so a chorus is 32 bars. The two sax stamps together are 64 bars, so the list shows Sax 2 choruses.
You can also stamp each half: A at 0:01, A′ at 0:26. The page then finds that A A′ repeats and uses its 32 bars as one chorus.

title: Sound 24: The Signal Chain
text:
Real rigs use several effects one after another: a guitarist’s pedalboard, the plug-ins on a channel in a DAW. The order matters, often a lot. And the level going from one to the next matters too: that’s gain staging.
How to use the page. Choose an effect for each of the three slots, or press a preset. The bars show the peak level after each stage. The dashed line is 0 dB, the ceiling.

title: Sound 24: The Signal Chain
text:
Order



Compare each pair of presets on the Synth riff and the Drum loop:

Distortion → Delay: clean echoes of a distorted note. The usual order. Delay → Distortion: the echoes are distorted together with the new notes, so they pile into each other and turn to mush.
Distortion → Reverb: a distorted guitar in a room. Reverb → Distortion: a distorted room, a roaring wash.
Compressor → Wah: the compressor evens out the playing, then the wah sweeps it. Wah → Compressor: the compressor flattens the wah’s sweep back out.

A rough rule for a guitarist’s board: things that shape the note first (wah, compressor, overdrive, distortion), then things that change the sound (chorus, phaser, tremolo), then things that put it in a space (delay, reverb). Break the rule on purpose, not by accident.

title: Sound 24: The Signal Chain
text:
Gain staging
In the computer, signals can get as loud as they like. Real equipment can’t: every pedal, preamp and converter has a ceiling, and above it the wave is chopped flat (hard clipping). The switch Clip above 0 dB at every stage makes this page behave like real gear.
Press Too hot: a big bass boost, then a compressor, then a delay, with the input turned up. Watch for a stage going red: everything after it carries that damage, and no amount of turning down later removes it. Now lower the Input gain until no bar goes red. The rule is simple: at every stage, loud enough to be well above the noise, never over the ceiling. Engineers aim for peaks around −18 to −6 dB at each stage, which leaves room for surprises.

title: Sound 24: The Signal Chain
text:
Your own rig
Choose Microphone (headphones on) and build a chain for your voice or instrument. Try the order you’d expect, then the opposite, and decide which you prefer.

title: Sound 18: Chorus and Flanger
text:
When a choir or a string section plays a note, no two players are exactly in tune or exactly in time. The tiny differences make the sound wide and shimmering instead of one thin line. A chorus effect fakes that with a single sound: it adds copies of the sound, each delayed by a few milliseconds, and an LFO keeps changing those delays.
How to use the page. The source starts as chords. Use headphones if you can: the copies are spread left and right. The strip under the controls draws each copy’s delay time over the last four seconds.

title: Sound 18: Chorus and Flanger
text: The effect

title: Sound 18: Chorus and Flanger
section: Why a moving delay changes the pitch
text:
Why a moving delay changes the pitch
A delay on its own only makes a sound later. But when the delay is getting longer, the sound coming out is slowed down a little, so it’s a little flat. When the delay is getting shorter, the sound is sped up, so it’s a little sharp. It’s the Doppler effect of a passing siren. So an LFO on the delay time is a gentle vibrato on the copy. Mixed with the original, the slightly detuned copy beats against it, and that beating is the shimmer.
Press Vibrato: the mix is 100% wet, so you hear only the moving copy. Its pitch wobbles. Now press Chorus and the same wobble mixed with the dry sound becomes a shimmer.

title: Sound 18: Chorus and Flanger
text:
The controls

Delay: the average delay. About 15 to 30 ms for chorus. Below 10 ms the copy no longer sounds like a separate player; above 35 ms it starts to sound like a slap-back echo (try Doubler: a single slowly moving copy at 35 ms sounds like the part was recorded twice).
Depth: how far the delay swings, and so how far the pitch wobbles.
Rate: how fast. Slow (0.3 to 1 Hz) is lush; fast is seasick.
Voices: more copies, each with its own swing, spread across the stereo field.
Feedback: feeds the delayed copy back into the delay.

title: Sound 18: Chorus and Flanger
text:
The flanger
Press Flanger. The delay is now very short (1 to 5 ms), and the feedback is high. At delays this short the copy doesn’t sound like a second player. Instead it cancels some frequencies and reinforces others in an evenly spaced pattern, a comb filter. As the delay changes, the teeth of the comb sweep up and down: the jet-plane “whoosh”. It was first done with two tape machines running together, an engineer pressing a thumb on the flange of one reel to slow it. Try it on the drum loop and on the noise source, where the moving comb is easiest to see on the spectrum.

title: Sound 17: Delay
text:
Shout at a cliff and your voice comes back a moment later: an echo. A delay effect records the sound and plays it back a set time later, mixed in with the original. Feed some of that copy back into the delay and it repeats again, and again, each time quieter. It’s the simplest effect there is, and the building block of chorus and flanger and of most of reverb.
How to use the page. The source starts as single hits, so each echo is easy to hear. The strip under the controls shows one hit and every echo that follows it, as tall as it is loud.

title: Sound 17: Delay
text:
The echo




Delay time: how long until the copy comes back. Under about 30 ms you don’t hear an echo at all, just a thicker sound (that’s where chorus and flanger live). From about 60 to 150 ms you hear a slapback. Longer, and you hear separate repeats.
Feedback: how much of each echo is sent round again. 0% is a single echo; 50% means each repeat is half as loud as the last. Push it past 100% and every repeat is louder: the echoes pile up into a roar (this delay squashes them so they can’t blow up; real tape echoes do the same).
Tone of the repeats: a low-pass inside the loop, so every trip round loses more top end. The echoes get darker as they fade, which is what tape and old analog delays did and why they sit so well behind the music.
Wow and flutter: tape never runs at quite a steady speed. A slow wobble (wow) and a fast one (flutter) bend the pitch of the repeats.
Ping-pong: two delays feeding each other, one on the left and one on the right, so the echoes bounce between your ears. Headphones on.

title: Sound 17: Delay
text:
The presets







Preset
Where you’ve heard it




Slapback
1950s rock ‘n’ roll: Elvis’s voice and Scotty Moore’s guitar at Sun Records, one quick echo from a second tape machine


Echo
a voice in a big space, a few repeats


Dotted eighth
the Edge (U2): the echo lands between the notes, so a plain run of eighth notes becomes a sixteenth-note pattern. Try it on the Synth riff


Ping-pong
a stereo bounce, timed to the beat


Tape echo
a Roland Space Echo or an Echoplex: dark, wobbly repeats


Dub
King Tubby and Lee “Scratch” Perry: long, dark repeats that hang on after the band drops out


Runaway
feedback over 100%. While it plays, drag the Delay time: the repeats slide in pitch, the way a tape echo does when you turn its speed knob



Timing to the beat. At a tempo of B beats per minute, one beat lasts 60000 ÷ B milliseconds. The riff here is at 112 bpm, so a quarter note is 536 ms, an eighth note 268 ms, and a dotted eighth (three sixteenths) 402 ms. Most delays have a tap button or tempo sync to do this for you.

title: Sound 17: Delay
text:
Glitch: stutter and beat repeat
Electronic producers break the music on purpose. One of the commonest tricks is the stutter (or beat repeat): grab a tiny slice of the music and loop it, rat-a-tat-tat, for a beat or two.
It’s a delay used in a strange way. The delay time is set to the length of one slice. When a glitch fires, the input is cut and the feedback goes to exactly 100%, so the last slice goes round and round, never fading. When the glitch ends, the music comes back.




Slice: how long the looped bit is. Short slices (1/32, 1/64) loop so fast they buzz with a pitch of their own.
Chance: how likely a glitch is on each half beat. Press Glitch now to fire one yourself.
Pitch drift: the delay time shrinks (or grows) while the slice loops, so the repeats get faster and rise (a riser) or slow down and fall (a tape stop).
Crush the repeats and backwards slices add the other two classic glitch sounds: a bit crusher and a slice played in reverse.

Glitch effects are everywhere in electronic dance music, in Aphex Twin and Squarepusher, in trap hi-hat rolls, and in vocal chops in pop. Plug-ins like Ableton’s Beat Repeat and iZotope’s Stutter Edit are built on this idea. Used for a beat at the end of a phrase, it’s a fill; used everywhere, it’s annoying. Try your Microphone and say a sentence while it plays.

title: Sound 5: Envelopes
text:
Play a piano note and hold it: it starts with a hard knock and then fades, even while you hold the key. Bow a violin note: it swells in gently and stays as long as the bow moves. Same pitch, same harmonics perhaps, but they don’t sound like the same instrument. The difference is the envelope: how the loudness of a note changes from the moment it starts to the moment it is gone.
How to use the page. Press ▶ Demo, or play the computer keys (a w s e d f t g y h u j k), the on-screen keyboard or a MIDI keyboard. Hold some notes down and let go of others quickly: the envelope only makes sense when you hear the difference between pressing and letting go.

title: Sound 5: Envelopes
text:
The four stages: ADSR



A synth describes an envelope with four numbers, A D S R:

Attack: how long the note takes to reach full volume after you press the key. Short for a drum or a pluck; long for strings swelling in.
Decay: how long it then takes to fall to the sustain level.
Sustain: a level, not a time: how loud the note stays while you hold the key. 100% means no decay at all (an organ); 0% means the note dies away even if you hold it (a piano, a guitar).
Release: how long the note takes to fade to silence after you let go.

The strip draws the shape: rising for the attack, falling for the decay, flat while you hold, falling after you let go. The part that is flat lasts as long as your finger is down; the other three are times.

Click shows why attack and release are never quite zero: switching a wave on or off instantly makes a click, because a sudden jump has every frequency in it (look at the spectrum as a note starts).
Now play fast notes with the Pad preset: the notes never get loud before you let go. A long attack and fast playing don’t mix. That’s why string sections can’t play very fast passages loudly.

title: Sound 5: Envelopes
section: The VCA, and envelopes on other things
text:
The VCA, and envelopes on other things
In a synth the envelope drives an amplifier (on analog synths a VCA, voltage-controlled amplifier). But an envelope is just a shape that rises and falls with each note, so it can move anything. In subtractive synthesis a second envelope opens and closes the filter, so a note can start bright and turn dull, which is how most synth basses and brass work. On a drum synth an envelope bends the pitch: the “boom” of a kick drum is a sine wave whose pitch drops fast.

title: Sound 4: Filters
text:
A filter turns some frequencies down and lets others through. It is the most-used control on a synthesizer and on a mixing desk: the treble and bass knobs on a stereo, the “wah” in a wah-wah pedal and the “wow” in a synth bass are all filters.
How to use the page. Press ▶. The Source menu picks what goes into the filter: noise shows the filter’s shape most clearly; the riff and chords show what it does to music; Your keyboard plays the keys or MIDI; Microphone filters your own voice (wear headphones). The red line on the spectrum is the filter’s response: above the middle line it boosts, below it cuts. Bypass switches the filter out so you can compare.

title: Sound 4: Filters
text:
Low-pass and high-pass



A low-pass filter lets the lows through and cuts the highs. The frequency where it starts cutting is the cutoff. Drag Cutoff down slowly with noise playing: the hiss becomes a rush and then a rumble. Switch the source to the synth riff and do the same: the sound goes from bright to muffled, as if behind a wall.
A high-pass does the opposite: it removes the lows. That’s how a sound is made thin, like a telephone or a small radio, and how mixing engineers clear rumble out of everything except the bass and kick drum.
The slope is how fast the filter cuts beyond the cutoff: 12 dB per octave is gentle, 24 dB per octave is the steep, classic “Moog” low-pass.

Why low-pass sounds “darker”. From the harmonic series lesson: brightness is the strength of the high harmonics. A low-pass removes those harmonics, starting from the top. On a sawtooth (all harmonics) you can hear them go one by one as the cutoff passes them.

title: Sound 4: Filters
text:
Resonance
Resonance (or Q) boosts a narrow band right at the cutoff. With the riff playing and the cutoff around 800 Hz, turn Resonance up to 10 or more. A whistling peak appears on the red line and you can hear it ring. Now press Sweep: the cutoff moves up and down by itself, and the resonant peak sweeps through the harmonics. That’s the classic synth “wow”, and with a guitar it’s a wah pedal.
At very high resonance the filter rings at the cutoff frequency on its own, almost like a sine wave. Some synths let the filter self-oscillate and play it as an extra oscillator.

title: Sound 4: Filters
text:
Band-pass, notch and EQ




Band-pass keeps a band around the cutoff and cuts both sides. Higher Q, narrower band. It’s the sound of a telephone or a megaphone, and it’s how a vocoder splits a voice into bands (Sound 22).
Notch is the opposite: it removes a narrow band and leaves everything else. Engineers use it to remove a hum. A phaser is several moving notches.
Peak (bell), low shelf and high shelf are the filters of an equaliser (EQ). They boost or cut (the Boost/cut slider) instead of removing. A shelf lifts or lowers everything above or below the cutoff, like the treble and bass knobs. A bell lifts or lowers a band in the middle.

title: Sound 4: Filters
text:
Filters on your voice
Choose Microphone as the source (with headphones on), choose Band-pass and sweep the cutoff while you talk. The vowels in speech are themselves made by filters: your mouth and throat are resonant tubes, and moving your tongue and lips moves their resonances (the formants). Say “ee-ah-oo” slowly and watch the bumps in the spectrum move.

title: Sound 15: Gates and Transients
text: A compressor turns loud sounds down. A gate does the opposite: it turns quiet sounds down, all the way to silence. Below its threshold it’s shut; when the sound gets loud enough, it opens. A transient shaper changes the start of each note without touching the rest. Both work on the shape in time of a sound, the envelope, after it has been recorded.

title: Sound 15: Gates and Transients
text:
The noise gate



The source is drum hits with hiss and hum mixed in, like a noisy recording or a guitar amp buzzing between notes. The strip shows the level, the threshold (dashed) and where the gate is open (shaded).

Threshold: the gate opens when the level goes above it. Set it just above the noise and just below the quietest note you want to keep.
Attack: how fast it opens. Too slow and the start of each hit is cut off.
Hold: how long it stays open after the level falls, so it doesn’t flutter.
Release: how fast it closes. Too fast cuts off the tail of each note; too slow lets the noise back in.
Range: how far it closes. −80 dB is silence; −12 dB just tucks the noise down, which sounds more natural.

Try Clean up hiss, then raise the threshold too far and listen to the hits getting chopped.

title: Sound 15: Gates and Transients
text:
The 80s gated snare
Choose 80s gated snare: there is now a big reverb before the gate, and the gate is keyed by the dry drums. Every hit gets a huge, explosive burst of reverb that stops dead a fraction of a second later instead of fading. Phil Collins’ “In the Air Tonight” made it famous in 1981 (the engineer Hugh Padgham found it by accident on a talkback mic), and it’s on half the pop records of the decade. Change Hold to change the length of the burst.

title: Sound 15: Gates and Transients
text:
The transient shaper
The transient is the first few milliseconds of a sound: the stick hitting the drum, the pick on the string. The rest is the sustain (the drum ringing, the room).




Attack up: every hit gets punchier and closer. Down: softer and further away.
Sustain up: the ring and the room come forward. Down: the drums get tight and dry, as if the room were dead.

It does this with two envelope followers, one fast and one slow. Where the fast one is above the slow one, a hit is starting: that gets the attack amount. Where it’s below, the sound is ringing on: that gets the sustain amount. Unlike a compressor, it doesn’t care how loud the sound is, only whether it’s starting or fading. Try it on the Synth riff and on your microphone (clap).

title: Sound 1: The Harmonic Series and Fourier
text:
A note played on a real instrument is never one frequency. It is a stack of frequencies, all at whole-number multiples of the lowest one. That stack is the harmonic series, and it explains why a violin and a flute playing the same A sound different, why the octave and the fifth sound “pure”, and how every synthesizer on the following pages works.
How to use the page. Every widget has a ▶ button, a picture of the wave’s shape (an oscilloscope) and a picture of its spectrum (how loud each frequency is, low on the left, high on the right). The bar at the bottom of the window sets the volume. You can play the widgets from the computer keyboard (a w s e d f t g y h u j k is one octave, z and x move it), from the on-screen keyboard, or from a MIDI keyboard. Notes go to the widget you clicked last. Click a heading to fold a section away. Start with the volume low.
crumbs: Sound 1: The Harmonic Series and Fourier

title: Sound 1: The Harmonic Series and Fourier
text:
A string vibrates in pieces
Pluck a string and it swings as a whole, but it also swings in halves, thirds, quarters and so on, all at once. Half the length vibrates twice as fast, a third of it three times as fast. If the whole string gives 100 Hz, the halves give 200 Hz, the thirds 300 Hz, and so on. The same happens in the air column of a trumpet or a clarinet, and in your voice.
Each of those frequencies is a harmonic. The first harmonic, the whole string, is the fundamental, and it’s the pitch you name. The others are overtones. You don’t hear them as separate notes. You hear them as the colour (the timbre) of the one note.
crumbs: Sound 1: The Harmonic Series and Fourier

title: Sound 1: The Harmonic Series and Fourier
text:
The series, written out
Here are the first sixteen harmonics written as notes. The number under each note is the harmonic’s number: harmonic n vibrates n times as fast as the fundamental. The number above is how far the real harmonic is from the piano’s version of that note, in cents (100 cents = one half step). Choose a different fundamental and the whole series is transposed. The pattern of steps never changes.



Things to notice:

The octaves are 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16. Doubling the frequency always gives an octave.
The gaps shrink as you go up. Octave, then a fifth (2 to 3), a fourth (3 to 4), a major third (4 to 5), a minor third (5 to 6), and then steps smaller than a minor third. The higher harmonics are close enough to make scales.
Harmonics 4, 5 and 6 are a major triad (C, E, G over a C fundamental). The major chord is built into every pitched sound.
Harmonic 7 is about a third of a half step flat of the piano’s B♭, harmonic 11 sits almost exactly between F and F♯, and harmonic 13 is well sharp of A♭. Press Harmonic, then tempered and listen at those three. Piano tuning (equal temperament) moves every note slightly so that all keys work. The pure intervals are the harmonics.
The 5th harmonic is 14 cents flat of the piano’s major third. Barbershop singers and string quartets lean their major thirds that way, toward the harmonic.

Press Build the tone to hear the harmonics enter one at a time, each a little quieter than the one before (harmonic n at strength 1/n). With all sixteen it no longer sounds like a chord. It sounds like one buzzy note: a sawtooth wave.
crumbs: Sound 1: The Harmonic Series and Fourier

title: Sound 1: The Harmonic Series and Fourier
section: Fourier: every wave is a stack of sine waves
text:
Fourier: every wave is a stack of sine waves
The sine wave is the simplest sound there is: one frequency and nothing else. It sounds pure and a little dull, like a tuning fork or a whistle.
In 1807 Joseph Fourier showed that any repeating wave, whatever its shape, can be built by adding sine waves at whole-number multiples of its frequency. Each sine wave has its own strength (and it can be upside down). The recipe of strengths is the wave’s spectrum. Going from a wave to its recipe is the Fourier transform; going from the recipe back to the wave is Fourier synthesis.
You don’t need the maths to use the idea:

The shape of a wave (the oscilloscope) and its recipe (the spectrum) are two views of the same sound. Change one and the other changes.
Sharp corners and sudden jumps need lots of high harmonics. Smooth, rounded shapes need few. Bright sounds have strong high harmonics; dark, mellow sounds don’t.
The ear mostly hears the recipe, not the shape. Flip a harmonic upside down and the shape changes a lot while the sound hardly changes.

The spectrum display under every widget on these pages is a Fourier transform done about sixty times a second, by the browser.

title: Sound 1: The Harmonic Series and Fourier
text:
Build waves from harmonics
Each slider is one harmonic. Up is louder; below the middle line it is upside down. The numbers under the sliders play that harmonic alone. The drawing shows the harmonics faintly and their sum in bold. Press ▶ and move the sliders while it plays.



Try this:

Press Sine. One harmonic, one frequency. The spectrum shows a single spike.
Press Sawtooth: every harmonic, harmonic n at strength 1/n. Now turn Harmonics used down to 1 and slowly back up. Each added harmonic sharpens the ramp. With few harmonics the edge wobbles; the wobble (the Gibbs effect) gets narrower but never quite goes away.
Drag the slider for harmonic 2 to zero. The note now sounds hollow, a little like a clarinet.
Press Organ. Organ stops add harmonics 1, 2, 3, 4, 8 and so on (see the organ lesson): the tonebars are an additive synthesizer.

title: Sound 3: Noise
text:
A pitched note has its energy at a few frequencies (the harmonics). Noise has its energy spread over all of them at once, with no pattern and no repeating shape. It’s the hiss of a cymbal, the breath in a flute, the “s” and “f” in speech, wind and rain. Synthesizers include a noise source for exactly these sounds.
How to use the page. Press ▶ to hear the colour you chose, or press one of the Made from noise buttons. Noise is loud for its size: start with the volume low.

title: Sound 3: Noise
text:
The colours of noise




White noise has equal energy at every frequency. Because each octave up holds twice as many frequencies as the one below, it sounds very bright: a hiss.
Pink noise has equal energy in every octave, so it falls away toward the highs. It sounds more even to the ear, like steady rain or a waterfall, and sound engineers use it to test speakers.
Brown noise (named after Brownian motion, not the colour) falls away faster still: a deep rumble, like surf heard from inside a house.

Watch the spectrum as you switch. White is flat, pink tilts down gently, brown tilts down steeply. The oscilloscope never settles into a shape, because noise never repeats.

title: Sound 3: Noise
text:
Sounds made from noise
Noise on its own is not very musical. Its use comes from shaping it: a filter picks out a band of frequencies, an envelope makes it short or long, and an LFO makes it move.







Button
Recipe




Wind
pink noise through a narrow band-pass filter whose centre drifts slowly


Surf
pink noise through a low-pass, both the volume and the brightness swelling every eight seconds


Hi-hat
white noise, only the highs, cut off within 50 ms (longer for the open hat)


Snare
a burst of noise for the wires with a short low tone for the drum head


Steam
white noise with the lows removed


Rain
soft pink noise for the background, plus thousands of tiny filtered clicks for drops



Every drum sound in the site’s backing band except the kick is made from noise in roughly this way.

title: Sound 21: Pitch Effects
text: Some effects change the pitch of a sound while it plays: an octave below to fatten a bass, a harmony above a voice, or a nudge to put a singer exactly in tune. All of them start from the same trick.

title: Sound 21: Pitch Effects
section: How to change pitch without changing speed
text:
How to change pitch without changing speed
Play a tape faster and it gets higher, but it also gets shorter. A pitch shifter wants the pitch without the speed. It reads the sound through a short delay whose time keeps changing: a delay that keeps getting shorter plays the sound back faster (higher), one that keeps getting longer plays it slower (lower). That’s the Doppler effect again. Of course a delay can’t keep shrinking forever, so every few hundredths of a second it jumps back and starts again, and a second delay line, half a step behind, crossfades over the jump. Listen closely to big shifts and you can hear a faint flutter from the jumps: that’s the price.

title: Sound 21: Pitch Effects
text:
The octaver



The octaver adds the same notes an octave (or two) below, or above. Bass players use the octave down to sound like a synth bass; guitarists use the octave up to sound like a twelve-string.
Octave up made by: there’s an old analog trick. Fold the bottom half of the wave up so it’s all positive (a rectifier), and the wave now repeats twice as often: an octave up. It’s rough and buzzy, and it only works cleanly on one note at a time: Octave fuzz is the Jimi Hendrix “Purple Haze” solo sound. Switch between the two kinds and compare. Play the Chords through each: the digital shifter copes; the analog trick turns chords to mush.

title: Sound 21: Pitch Effects
text:
The harmonizer



A harmonizer adds one or two more voices at set intervals, so one singer becomes a trio.

Fixed intervals: always the same distance, say a major third and a fifth. Sing a scale and listen: some of the harmonies are out of the key, because the thirds in a major key are not all the same size.
In the key of C major: the harmonizer works out which note you’re singing and picks the third or fifth in the key, sometimes major, sometimes minor. This is how the “intelligent” harmonizers (Eventide, TC-Helicon, the ones built into vocal pedals) work. Try your Microphone and sing a C major scale slowly.

title: Sound 21: Pitch Effects
text:
Pitch correction (auto-tune)



The source is an out-of-tune singer: every note lands 20 to 50 cents sharp or flat. The graph shows the pitch as sung (grey) and after correction (pink), against the notes of the scale.

Key and Scale: which notes are “right”. Every sung note is pulled to the nearest one.
Retune speed: how quickly. At around 100 ms the correction is gentle: the slides and the vibrato survive, and you mostly can’t tell. This is what happens, invisibly, on most pop vocals today.
At 1 ms the pitch jumps instantly from note to note, with no slide at all. It sounds robotic, and that became a style of its own: Cher’s “Believe” (1998), T-Pain, Kanye West’s 808s & Heartbreak, much of trap and Afrobeats.
Wrong key: correct to the wrong scale and the singer is snapped confidently onto wrong notes.

Antares Auto-Tune came out in 1997, invented by an engineer who had used the same mathematics to look for oil underground. Try your own voice, on Hard and Natural.

title: Sound 14: Sidechain
text:
A compressor turns a sound down when that sound gets loud. A sidechain lets a different sound decide. The music is turned down when the kick drum hits, or when the DJ talks. The sound that decides is called the key.
How to use the page. The source (what gets turned down) starts as chords. The key is a kick drum playing four to the floor. The strip draws the chords’ volume.

title: Sound 14: Sidechain
text:
Ducking under the kick



Start with Depth at 0 and raise it. Each kick pushes the chords down, and they swell back up between kicks.

Depth: how far the music is pushed down.
Attack: how fast it goes down when the kick hits. Fast, so the kick’s start is clear.
Release: how fast the music comes back. This sets the rhythm of the effect.

Turn Hear the key off: the kick is gone but you can still hear where it was, because the chords breathe in its rhythm. Producers often key the sidechain from a kick nobody hears.

title: Sound 14: Sidechain
text:
Glue or pump?

Glue: a little ducking, quick release. You barely hear it, but the kick cuts through and the mix sounds tighter. Almost every mix with a bass line and a kick does this: the bass ducks for a moment under each kick so the two don’t fight over the low end.
Pumping: deep ducking and a release that lasts most of a beat. The chords swell up after every kick: whoom, whoom, whoom. This is the sound of French house (Daft Punk’s “One More Time”, Eric Prydz’s “Call on Me”) and most EDM since. Try it at different tempos: the release has to fit the gap between kicks.

title: Sound 14: Sidechain
text:
Ducking a voice
Choose Radio voice-over: the key is now a voice. Whenever it talks, the music dips under it, and comes back slowly when it stops. Radio stations, podcasts, sat-navs talking over the car stereo and announcements at a station all do this automatically.

title: Sound 7: Subtractive Synthesis
text:
Subtractive synthesis starts with a wave full of harmonics and takes some away with a filter. It was the design of the Moog, the ARP, the Prophet-5 and the Minimoog that defined synth bass and synth lead, and most software synths still start from it. It is three parts in a row, each with a helper:
Oscillators (the raw tone) → filter (the brightness) → amplifier (the loudness). Envelopes shape the filter and the amplifier over the length of each note, and an LFO adds movement.
How to use the page. Press ▶ Demo to hear the synth play, or play it from the computer keys (a w s e d…), the on-screen keyboard or a MIDI keyboard. It plays chords. Start with the presets, then change one control at a time.

title: Sound 7: Subtractive Synthesis
text: The synth

title: Sound 7: Subtractive Synthesis
text:
1. Oscillators
Two oscillators, each with a shape from Sound 2. A sawtooth is the usual starting point because it has every harmonic for the filter to work on. A square or narrow pulse is hollower. Osc 2 detune sets the second oscillator a few cents off the first: the two drift in and out of phase and the sound becomes thick and moving. 5 to 15 cents is the classic “fat” sound; 0 is thin and still. Set Osc 2 octave to −1 for weight under a bass, or +1 for brightness. Noise adds breath, from Sound 3.

title: Sound 7: Subtractive Synthesis
text:
2. Filter
The low-pass filter is where the character comes from. Cutoff sets how bright the note is, resonance adds the peak at the cutoff. The filter here is the steep 24 dB-per-octave kind.

title: Sound 7: Subtractive Synthesis
text:
3. Envelopes: ADSR
An envelope is a shape that runs once each time you play a note. It has four stages:

Attack: how long it takes to rise from nothing to full when the key goes down.
Decay: how long it takes to fall from full to the sustain level.
Sustain: the level it holds while the key stays down (a level, not a time).
Release: how long it takes to fade to nothing after the key comes up.

The amp envelope shapes the loudness: a piano has fast attack, long decay, no sustain; an organ has instant attack, full sustain, instant release; a string pad has slow attack and slow release.
The filter envelope moves the cutoff, by up to Envelope amount octaves. This is the secret of most good synth sounds: real instruments are brightest at the start of a note. A fast filter attack and short decay give the “pew” of a synth bass; a slow attack gives a brass “swell”. The drawing under the controls shows both envelopes.

title: Sound 7: Subtractive Synthesis
text:
4. LFO
The LFO (Sound 6) adds vibrato (→ Pitch) or a slow filter sweep (→ Cutoff).

title: Sound 7: Subtractive Synthesis
text:
Recipes to try

Bass. Press Bass. Turn Envelope amount to 0: the note goes dull and loses its “pluck”. Put it back and change Decay in the filter envelope: short is a click, long is a wow.
From brass to strings. Press Brass, then raise the amp Attack to 0.3 s and set the filter Envelope amount to 0. The swell becomes a bowed string pad.
Pluck. Press Pluck and play fast. Everything happens in the filter envelope: sustain at 0, so every note closes down by itself.
No oscillator at all. Press Wind (noise): noise through a resonant band-pass, with the LFO moving the band. Play different keys: nothing changes, because noise has no pitch.

title: Sound 22: The Vocoder
text:
A vocoder makes an instrument talk. It takes two sounds: a modulator (usually a voice) and a carrier (usually a synth playing chords). It measures how loud each band of frequencies is in the voice, moment by moment, and sets the loudness of the same bands in the synth to match. The synth keeps its pitch and chords; the voice supplies the words. It’s the robot voice of Kraftwerk, Herbie Hancock, Daft Punk and Laurie Anderson. It was invented at Bell Labs in the 1930s to squeeze speech down telephone lines.
How to use the page. Put on headphones: the microphone hears the speakers otherwise. Choose Microphone as the modulator (or the built-in Robot voice if there’s no mic), press ▶, then talk or sing while you play chords on the computer keys, the on-screen keyboard or a MIDI keyboard. Until you play, a chord is held for you.

title: Sound 22: The Vocoder
text: The vocoder

title: Sound 22: The Vocoder
text:
How it works
The vocoder is built from parts you have already met:

Split the voice into bands. A row of band-pass filters, each a different frequency from low to high, splits the voice into 16 or so bands.
Measure each band. An envelope follower on each band turns the wobbling band into a smooth level: how loud that band is right now. The bars under the controls show those levels.
Split the synth the same way. A second row of band-pass filters, at the same frequencies, splits the carrier.
Let the voice turn the synth up and down. Each band of the synth is turned up and down by the level of the matching band of the voice, and the bands are added back together.

A vowel is a pattern of loud bands (the formants, from the filter lesson), so the synth takes on the vowel. The pitch comes from the synth, which is why you can speak in a monotone and have it sing in chords.

title: Sound 22: The Vocoder
text:
Things to try

Bands. With 4 bands the words are barely understandable; with 16 they’re clear; with 32 it sounds almost like a voice through a synth-shaped filter. Old hardware vocoders had 8 to 20.
Band sharpness. Higher Q makes each band narrower: more ringing and more “robot”.
Envelope speed. Slow (5 Hz) blurs the words into a smooth pad; fast (60 Hz) keeps every consonant but gets gritty.
Let “s” sounds through. A synth has little energy in the very top, so “s”, “t” and “f” disappear. Real vocoders pass the voice’s top end straight through to keep the words clear.
Carrier. A sawtooth is best, because it has energy in every band for the voice to shape. A square works less well (it is missing every other harmonic). Noise as the carrier gives a whisper with no pitch at all.
Listen to the modulator or the carrier alone to hear what goes in.
Drum loop as the modulator makes the chord pulse in the rhythm of the drums, a trick used in dance music.

title: Sound 9: Wavetable Synthesis
text:
A wavetable is a list of different single-cycle wave shapes, one after another. The oscillator plays one shape, and a position control chooses which. Move the position while a note is playing and the sound morphs smoothly from one shape to the next. Wolfgang Palm’s PPG Wave (1981) made the idea famous; today it’s the heart of software synths like Serum and Vital.
How to use the page. Press ▶ Demo or play the keys or MIDI. Drag Position in the table while a note plays. The drawing shows every shape in the table, front to back, with the current one in red.

title: Sound 9: Wavetable Synthesis
text:
The synth



This table has eight shapes: sine, triangle, sawtooth, square, a narrow pulse, a vowel (“ah”), a hollow wave and a sparse glassy one. Between two shapes the oscillator mixes them: halfway between sawtooth and square is half of each. Look at the spectrum as you drag: each shape is a different recipe of harmonics (see Sound 1), and the morph moves smoothly from one recipe to the next.

title: Sound 9: Wavetable Synthesis
text:
Scanning the table
A wavetable is most interesting when the position moves by itself. Raise Scan LFO depth and the LFO sweeps the position back and forth through the table. A slow scan (0.1 Hz) gives a pad that slowly changes colour. A fast scan (4 Hz or more) gives a talking, rhythmic wobble.
In a full wavetable synth an envelope can also move the position, so that every note starts on one shape and ends on another. That’s the same idea as the filter envelope in subtractive synthesis, but the movement can be through any timbres at all, not just from bright to dark.

title: Sound 9: Wavetable Synthesis
text:
How it is built here
A full wavetable synth stores each shape as hundreds or thousands of samples and plays them back very fast. For a lesson that is more than we need. The browser can build an oscillator from a list of harmonic strengths (as in the additive widget in Sound 1), so each shape in this table is stored as 48 harmonic strengths, and the position mixes neighbouring lists about thirty times a second. Mixing harmonic recipes and mixing wave shapes give exactly the same result, so it sounds and looks the same as the real thing, just with a smaller table.

title: Sources 3: Research for DP Music (Grades 11–12)
text:
In DP Music, research is assessed. In Exploring Music in Context it’s Criterion B1 (Conducting Musical Research), and the rest of the portfolio is built on it. If what you find in Section 1 is weak, your implications (B2) and both practical exercises (C1, C2) have nothing to stand on. This lesson collects what the IB’s guidance and the subject reports from November 2022 to May 2025 say about sources and evidence, as summarised in the DP Music course book.
It assumes Sources 2: primary and secondary sources, SIFT, and MLA citations.

title: Sources 3: Research for DP Music (Grades 11–12)
text:
The IB’s definitions
Examiners read your work with these definitions, from the IB’s glossary:

Primary sources: the music itself and the people directly involved in creating or performing it: scores, live performances, recordings, composer interviews.
Secondary sources: materials about the music by researchers not directly connected to it: critiques, documentaries, journal articles, editions.
Musical findings: what you find by looking at the music itself.
Extra-musical findings: what you find from sources outside the music (articles, interviews, documentaries), used to put your musical findings in context.
Conventions: “accepted norms of creating music according to the chosen style, which are determined by historical research and authentic examples.”

That last definition has two halves. A convention needs research (secondary sources) and authentic examples (more than one piece).

title: Sources 3: Research for DP Music (Grades 11–12)
text:
What examiners keep finding

“The first website found”
The guidance is blunt. Research limited to the first website you find is not likely to be purposeful. It should draw on primary sources (scores, recordings, interviews with performers or composers) and credible secondary sources (musicological texts, journal articles).


One piece is not a convention
A feature you find in your one stimulus may belong to that piece, not to the style. Check each convention against your secondary sources. If it doesn’t appear in any general account of the style, it’s probably a feature of your piece, not a convention of the tradition. Listen to more authentic examples too.


Put a piece in an area of inquiry by research, not assumption
One example examiners gave: Piazzolla’s tango works placed in AOI 3 because “tango is dance music.” Widely available scholarship shows that Piazzolla’s nuevo tango was written for concert listening, not for dancing. Piazzolla himself insisted on the difference. A quick check of a secondary source would have caught it.


Extra-musical findings must do work
Background from an article or documentary is purposeful when it explains a musical finding: its history, its cultural meaning, the composer’s intention. It is not purposeful when it’s general background with no bearing on your analysis. A paragraph of biography that never meets the music earns nothing.


Ask “so what?”
For every finding, ask “so what?” If the answer is “nothing much, it’s just a fact about the piece” (it’s in 4/4, it’s allegro, it’s forte), the finding isn’t purposeful. If the answer is “this is what makes the style distinctive, and it’s why I can use it in my creating exercise,” it is.

title: Sources 3: Research for DP Music (Grades 11–12)
text:
Evidence the examiner can check

In-text references are not optional
Every claim that depends on a source (a recording, a score, a journal article, an interview) needs an in-text reference at the point where you use it. A bibliography at the end doesn’t replace in-text references. Without them, a claim is unsubstantiated, however well it’s written. The bibliography still has to list every score, recording and secondary source. In-text citations and the bibliography don’t count toward the 2,400-word limit.


Timestamps point to Upload 3, not YouTube
Every musical observation needs a bar number or a timestamp. Timestamps must point to your submitted audio reference material (Upload 3 in Exploring). They must not point to YouTube, Spotify or the original commercial track: the examiner can’t verify those. Be precise. “Here you will find contrasting dynamics,” attached to a 40-second clip, makes the examiner do your analysis for you.


Score excerpts must be annotated and in the body
Put score excerpts in the body of the work, not only in an appendix. Label them with bar numbers, instruments, clef and key, and annotate them so they show your point. An unannotated excerpt, a score’s front page or a picture of the composer is decoration, not evidence.


No hyperlinks
Examiners can’t click links in a submission. Anything that exists only behind a URL can’t be assessed. Cite web sources in the bibliography, and put the evidence itself (the excerpt, the clip) in the submission.


MuseScore is not an authentic score
MuseScore is a library of user-submitted transcriptions, with no guarantee that they’re accurate. You can use it to find material, but check it against an authoritative source (a published edition, or the recording) before you treat it as a primary score.

title: Sources 3: Research for DP Music (Grades 11–12)
text:
AI summaries are never evidence






ImportantGoogle’s AI Overviews and chatbot answers cannot be cited as sources, and they are unreliable




They aren’t sources. No author stands behind the claim, there’s no stable text, and the examiner can’t retrieve what you saw. In-text references exist so that the examiner can verify every claim. A generated summary can’t be verified.
They’re unreliable. Google’s AI Overviews have told users to put glue on pizza, from a joke Reddit post. They have also turned an academic chapter’s question into a false statement of fact. In a 2025 Columbia Journalism Review / Tow Center test, eight AI search tools misidentified the source of real news quotes more than 60% of the time, and often made up links.
They’re not your work. The IB doesn’t regard work produced, even in part, by AI tools as the student’s own. Any AI-generated text, image or graph you include must be credited in the body of the text and in the bibliography, like any other quoted material. Your school’s policy may be stricter. A mostly-quoted essay earns little, and so does a mostly-generated one.
Crediting it doesn’t make it evidence. Even correctly credited, “according to ChatGPT” or “according to Google’s AI” supports nothing about the music. It’s not a primary source and it’s not musicology.



What to do instead:

If an AI answer gives you a lead, trace it to a real source: a musicological text, a journal article, an interview, a score or a recording. Read that source. Often it says something different.
Cite the source you read, with an in-text reference, and list it in the bibliography.
Never cite a reference that an AI tool listed unless you’ve found and read it yourself. AI tools invent plausible titles, authors and links.
Keep a research log (what you searched, what you read, what you used) so that you can show your process if asked.

title: Sources 3: Research for DP Music (Grades 11–12)
text:
Where DP research comes from

Grove Music Online (Oxford Music Online): signed articles by specialists, each with a bibliography to follow.
RILM Abstracts of Music Literature and JSTOR: journal articles. Ask your school or local library for access.
Academic books: the Cambridge Companion series, university-press monographs, and ethnomusicology studies of the tradition you’re exploring.
Primary material: published scores (with IMSLP for public-domain editions), recordings with full release details, liner notes, interviews with the musicians, archive and museum collections.
People: an interview you conduct with a performer of the tradition is a primary source. Record the date, and cite it.

title: Sources 3: Research for DP Music (Grades 11–12)
text:
A research routine for Exploring

Choose the music, then find at least two authentic examples of the style and one or two scholarly accounts of it.
Find the conventions in the music (bar numbers, timestamps). Confirm them in the secondary sources.
Contextualise with extra-musical findings that explain your musical ones.
Log every source as you go, with its full citation.
Write with an in-text reference at every claim, timestamps to Upload 3, and annotated excerpts in the body.
Check before you submit: no hyperlinks needed to follow the argument, no AI summaries cited as evidence, every timestamp matches Upload 3, and every source is in the bibliography.

title: Sources 3: Research for DP Music (Grades 11–12)
text:
Try it
Take a draft paragraph from your Exploring Section 1, or a classmate’s (with permission).

Highlight every claim. Mark which have an in-text reference, and which need one.
For each musical claim, check that it gives a bar number or an Upload 3 timestamp.
Run the “so what?” test on each finding.
For each convention, name the secondary source that confirms it. If there isn’t one, find one, or call it a feature of the piece.
Search one of your claims and read the AI summary. Is it right? Can you trace it to a source you could cite?

title: Two Left Hands: Stride and Boogie-Woogie
text:
Stride and boogie-woogie are the two great left hands of early jazz piano. Both are solo piano music for dancing, both swing, and both make the pianist’s left hand do the work of a bass player and a rhythm guitarist at once. They do it in opposite ways: stride leaps, boogie-woogie walks. This page plays them on the band one at a time, then side by side, then swaps their parts.
How the examples work: press ▶ Play, switch players in and out with the buttons beside it, and read what the band will play on the staff underneath: the whole pass is written out when Play starts, before it sounds. The tempo slider at the bottom of the page slows everything down. For the history of each, see the Style Notes on Stride piano and Boogie-woogie.
crumbs: Two Left Hands: Stride and Boogie-Woogie

title: Two Left Hands: Stride and Boogie-Woogie
text:
1. Where they meet

Rent parties. In the 1920s, tenants in Harlem and on Chicago’s South Side paid the rent by throwing a party with food, drink and a pianist. Harlem’s pianists played stride; Chicago’s played boogie-woogie. One piano had to be the whole band.
The left hand keeps time. In both, the left hand never stops and never changes its pattern much. The right hand is free to play the tune, riffs and runs on top.
Swing eighths. Both are swung: the eighth notes go long-short.
The same players. Count Basie began as a stride pianist taught by Fats Waller, and his band recorded Boogie Woogie in 1936. Fats Waller played boogie-woogie too, and the boogie-woogie pianists knew stride.
Where they went. Stride turned into swing piano (Teddy Wilson, Art Tatum, Basie); boogie-woogie into jump blues and rock and roll.
crumbs: Two Left Hands: Stride and Boogie-Woogie

title: Two Left Hands: Stride and Boogie-Woogie
text:
2. Stride: bass, chord, bass, chord
The stride left hand plays a low bass note on beats 1 and 3 and a chord in the middle of the keyboard on 2 and 4. Here the band’s pianist plays only that left hand. Compare it with plain boom-chick, where the bass note is left to the bass player.



What to look for. On the staff the left hand jumps about two octaves on every beat. Stride pianists practise the jump with their eyes on the landing note: the low one. Start with the root on 1 and 3, then play the fifth on 3. Full lesson: Stride.
crumbs: Two Left Hands: Stride and Boogie-Woogie

title: Two Left Hands: Stride and Boogie-Woogie
text:
3. Boogie-woogie: eight to the bar
The boogie-woogie left hand walks up the chord and back down in swung eighth notes: root, 3rd, 5th, 6th, flat 7th, 6th, 5th, 3rd. The band gives it to the bass player. Compare it with the simpler lines it is built from.



What to look for. The shape is the same on every chord; only the root moves. On the piano the hand stays in one position, fingers 5 1 on the root and 6th. Full lesson: Boogie-woogie.
crumbs: Two Left Hands: Stride and Boogie-Woogie

title: Two Left Hands: Stride and Boogie-Woogie
section: 4. Side by side on a blues
text:
4. Side by side on a blues
The same 12-bar blues in C, once in each style, with the whole band. Listen to the bottom of the band: stride bounces between low and middle on the beats; boogie-woogie rolls along underneath in eighths.
Stride



Boogie-woogie



The charts differ too. A stride player on a blues borrows the songs’ turnarounds (A7, D7, G7 leading home); a boogie-woogie player keeps to three chords, because the left hand is the interest.
crumbs: Two Left Hands: Stride and Boogie-Woogie

title: Two Left Hands: Stride and Boogie-Woogie
text:
5. Swap the parts
Both styles’ parts can be played in the other’s band. Below is the boogie-woogie band; swap its bass and piano for stride’s and back. The drums keep the shuffle.



The last one is busy: two left hands at once, one leaping, one walking. Real players choose one.
crumbs: Two Left Hands: Stride and Boogie-Woogie

title: Two Left Hands: Stride and Boogie-Woogie
section: 6. Before and after: ragtime and jump blues
text:
6. Before and after: ragtime and jump blues
Stride came from ragtime: the same left hand in straight eighths, under a written, syncopated melody. Boogie-woogie went into jump blues: the same bass in a small band, with a hard backbeat on the drums. Switch between each pair and listen for what changes and what stays.






See the Style Notes on Ragtime and Jump blues.
crumbs: Two Left Hands: Stride and Boogie-Woogie

title: Two Left Hands: Stride and Boogie-Woogie
text:
7. Try it

Pianists: switch the band’s piano off in section 2 and play the stride left hand yourself, slowly. Then switch the bass off in section 3 and play the boogie line with your left hand.
Bass players: the boogie-woogie line is a classic bass part in its own right. Play it on a 12-bar blues in section 4.
Listen to Fats Waller’s Handful of Keys and Albert Ammons’s Boogie Woogie Stomp back to back.

title: Mapping a Recording with the Timestamp Notes
text:
The Timestamp Notes turns a recording into a map: where each section starts, where every bar falls, and how fast the band is really playing. With the map you can jump straight to the bridge, loop a verse until you have it, and see whether the drummer speeds up in the last chorus.
Keep the player open in a second tab and work through the steps with a song you know.
crumbs: Mapping a Recording with the Timestamp Notes

title: Mapping a Recording with the Timestamp Notes
text:
1. Load a recording
Open the player. There are three ways in:

A file. Drop a video or audio file (MP3, M4A, WAV, MP4…) on the box that says Drop a video or audio file here, or press Choose file. A file is the best choice: it plays on this page, the timing is exact, and nothing can block it.
A YouTube link. Paste it into the box and press Load (or Return).
A link in the address. timestamp-player.html?v= followed by a YouTube link or id loads it straight away, which is handy for a link on a class page.

The big clock shows where the recording is. Space or Return plays and pauses from anywhere on the page; the arrows (or h / l) go 5 seconds back or on.
If YouTube says the video won’t play here, skip to When YouTube won’t play it.
crumbs: Mapping a Recording with the Timestamp Notes

title: Mapping a Recording with the Timestamp Notes
section: 2. Stamp the sections and the moments
text:
2. Stamp the sections and the moments
Listen through once. There are two keys, and both put a row in the Timestamps column, in time order:

S where a section starts (the next step).
C whenever anything else happens: a key change, a fill you want to learn, a wrong note in your own recording.

For a C note:

Press C. A row appears with the time.
The cursor jumps into the row’s note field. Type what happened (“Chorus”, “sax fill”, “key change”).
Leave the note with Esc, or type jk quickly. The letters are taken back out.
Keep listening and stamping.

Click any time in the list to jump there. Untick Jump to the note field after a stamp if you’d rather stamp everything first and write the notes afterwards.
Everything is saved in the browser as you go, so a reload doesn’t lose it. Copy all gives you a plain list (01:23  Chorus) and Paste… reads one back. Saving the whole song is covered in step 7.
crumbs: Mapping a Recording with the Timestamp Notes

title: Mapping a Recording with the Timestamp Notes
text:
3. Name the sections
Press S where a section starts. The row is tinted blue and has a menu: Intro, Head, Verse, Pre-chorus, Chorus, Bridge, Interlude, a solo for each instrument, Shout, Outro, and the form letters (A, then A′ and B, and so on). Other… at the bottom lets you type a label of your own. A new stamp starts with the label of the one before it, so chorus after chorus is just S, S, S.

A label used more than once is numbered for you: two Heads become Head 1 and Head 2 everywhere.
Under the Timestamps, the page counts how many choruses each soloist takes (in a pop song, how many bars).
If you’ve pasted the words (step 6), S stamps their next section instead.

What each label means, and how the counting works: Section Labels.
A C note that names a section also counts as one (older song files work this way):







Write
For example




A section word first
Intro, Verse 1, Pre-chorus, Chorus 2, Bridge, Solo, Instrumental, Interlude, Break, Outro, Coda, Tag, Vamp, Head, Ending, Turnaround


A letter, with or without a number
A, B, A2


Anything after §
§ horns come in, § modulation



Any other note (“sax fill”, “check this bar”) stays a plain stamp.
Stamp each section on its first downbeat. You don’t have to be exact; the next step fixes that.
crumbs: Mapping a Recording with the Timestamp Notes

title: Mapping a Recording with the Timestamp Notes
text:
4. Tap the bars
Now give the recording its bars.

Set Beats a bar: 4 for most pop and rock, 3 for a waltz, 6 for a slow 6/8 counted in six.
Go back to the start (click the first stamp, or drag the video’s own slider).
Press Return to play, and press B on beat 1 of every bar. Count “1 2 3 4” under your breath and press on each “1”.
Watch the line above the panels. It shows Bar 7 · Chorus and flashes on every tap.

Fixing mistakes:

Backspace takes back the last tap.
Tapping near a bar you already tapped (within about a sixth of a second) replaces it. So to fix one spot, go back a few bars before it and tap through it again.
Open the Bars panel. Any bar much longer or shorter than the others is highlighted yellow: that is almost always a missed or doubled tap. Click its time to jump there and tap it again.
Fill from the tempo: tap a stretch (the head), stamp where each later section starts (S), and it puts in the rest of the bars, each solo a whole number of choruses when it’s close. Tap B where a guessed bar drifts. See Section Labels.
Fill gaps puts in the bars of a stretch you missed. Halve bars / Double bars fix taps made every half bar or every other bar (Undo puts them back).
A bar really in another meter (a bar of 2 before a chorus)? Change its Beats in the Bars panel.
In the Sections panel, ⚠ beside two sections next to each other (9 bars then 7, say) means the stamp between them is probably a bar off.

Once the bars are in, every section moves onto the nearest tapped bar, so a stamp a little early or late lands on the right downbeat. The Sections panel now says Verse 1 · bars 9–16.
The summary line tells you the tempo: 64 bars · about 118 bpm (114–122). A narrow range means a steady band (or a click track); a range that climbs through the song means it speeds up.
Tip: listen to the first bars a couple of times before tapping. Tapping goes much better when you already know where “1” is. In a song with a pickup, start tapping at the first full bar.
crumbs: Mapping a Recording with the Timestamp Notes

title: Mapping a Recording with the Timestamp Notes
text:
5. Use the map

Jump. Click a section’s time, or a bar’s time in the Bars panel.
Loop. Press Loop beside a section, or Shift+L while the playhead is in it. The recording goes back to the start of the section every time it reaches the next one. Press Shift+L again (or the button, now saying Looping) to stop.
Phrases. The Phrases panel cuts each section into 2-, 4- or 8-bar phrases, each looped from its lead-in. P loops the phrase under the playhead, , and . step to the one before or after, and T sends it to the Notation page to write down.
Without the audio. Once the timings are in, clicking a section (in the chord grid, the menu in Now playing, or the Sections panel) moves to it even with nothing loaded, so you can check and fix the map anywhere.
crumbs: Mapping a Recording with the Timestamp Notes

title: Mapping a Recording with the Timestamp Notes
section: 6. Words, chords and the chord grid
text:
6. Words, chords and the chord grid

Words and chords. Paste a song from Ultimate Guitar (chords above the words, [Verse 1] headings) and press Convert: it becomes ChordPro. No words yet? Sections from stamps puts your section labels in instead, so the chord grid shows each section’s bars anyway.
Chord timing. Press N as each chord starts (Shift+N takes the last one back); which chord it is comes from the words. Or play it all in from a MIDI keyboard: connect it in the box at the top of the right sidebar. The left hand plays a note on every barline (two together where a section starts), the right hand the chords.
The chord grid follows the section under the playhead. When a section’s chords are in the right places, press Timing is right to show them all.
Send on. Notation page (melody) sends the sections and chords for writing down the tune; Backing Track (style) sends the chart to play along with, at the tapped tempo.
crumbs: Mapping a Recording with the Timestamp Notes

title: Mapping a Recording with the Timestamp Notes
text:
7. Save and start again

Save song file saves everything in one .json: the stamps, the bars, the words and chords, the chord timing, the phrases and the link. Open file reads one back (older .txt stamp lists and bar-map .json files open too).
The browser keeps one song at a time. Before you start on another, save the song file, then press Clear all data. It asks first (press it again within a few seconds), then empties everything kept for the song: stamps, bars, words and chords, chord timing, grids and phrases. The page reloads with nothing loaded. Your page settings (column widths, folded parts, the MIDI keyboard) stay.
crumbs: Mapping a Recording with the Timestamp Notes

title: Mapping a Recording with the Timestamp Notes
text:
When YouTube won’t play it
Some videos show Video unavailable with a message like “…blocked it from display on this website or application”. The player shows the reason and YouTube’s error number in its own words:







Error
Means




101 or 150
The owner, or a rights holder such as a music publisher, blocks it from playing here


100
Removed, or private


2
Not a valid video link


153
YouTube couldn’t tell which page asked for it



First, try another browser window. These blocks depend on the browser as well as the website. The same video can play in one browser and be refused in another. Try a private window with extensions off, or another browser. If it plays there, use that.
If it still won’t play, follow along in a YouTube tab. The video plays on YouTube itself, and the player keeps its own clock in step with it.

Press Follow in a tab (next to Load, or on the error message). YouTube opens in a new tab.
Put the two windows side by side, so you can see YouTube and press keys on the player.
In YouTube, pause the video at a time you can read, for example 0:00 or 1:05.
On the player, type that time into Clock to and press Return. The big clock shows it.
Start the video in YouTube, click back onto the player straight away, and press Return as close to the same moment as you can. Or start the clock on a sound you can hear: pause at the start of a bar, set the clock to that time, then press Return here on the first note.
Check it after a few seconds. If the clock is ahead, press [** to pull it back 0.1 s; if it’s behind, press **].
If you slow YouTube down (its settings gear, Playback speed), choose the same Speed on the player.

Now C, B, section names and the bar map work as before.
What can’t work: the player can’t see or steer YouTube’s tab. YouTube’s tab cuts itself off from the page that opened it, so the player can’t pause it, move it, or close it.

Jumping (clicking a stamp, section or bar) opens a new YouTube tab at that time, and the clock stops there. Pause the old tab first, or you’ll hear two copies, then close it yourself. Press Return when the new tab starts playing.
Looping isn’t available. Loop in YouTube instead (right-click the video and choose Loop) or drag its slider back.
The clock drifts a little. Expect to nudge by a tenth of a second or two, and check it again when you jump.

The best fix is a file. If you have the recording (bought, from the band, from your own phone), drop it on the player instead. Everything works, exactly.
crumbs: Mapping a Recording with the Timestamp Notes

title: Mapping a Recording with the Timestamp Notes
section: Exercise: map a song in 15 minutes
text:
Exercise: map a song in 15 minutes
Choose a song you’re learning and do this in one sitting.

Load it (5 min). Play it through once, stamping and naming every section.
Bars (5 min). Set the beats, go back to the start, tap every bar. Fix the yellow bars.
Check (3 min). Click through the sections. Does each one start on a downbeat? Write down the tempo and whether it changes.
Practise (2 min, then as long as you like). Loop the hardest section and play or sing along.
Save the song file.

Questions to answer about your song:

How many bars is each section? Are the verses and choruses the same length every time?
Is the tempo steady? Where does it change?
Is there a bar of 2 or a bar of 6 anywhere? (A bar in the Bars panel whose length is half or one and a half times the others, that you tapped correctly, is one.)
