title: Travis Picking on Guitar
text:
Travis picking is a fingerpicking pattern in which the thumb plays a steady bass on every beat and the fingers play the melody or the chord notes on the strings above it, between the thumb notes. It is named for Merle Travis, from Muhlenberg County, Kentucky, and was spread by Chet Atkins and, later, by folk and country guitarists everywhere. The thumb is a bass player, and the fingers are a rhythm section that plays off it. This lesson builds it a step at a time, from the thumb alone to the band, with hammer-ons and pull-offs added at the end.
The Backing Track band plays the pattern as the comping rhythm Fingerpicking: Travis pattern. There is a lesson on that pattern in the band’s own terms, Comping rhythm: Travis pattern, and one on the simpler pattern before it, John Prine fingerpicking. This lesson is the hands.
How to read the examples. Each exercise is written on a staff and in tablature. Tablature has one line a string, with the high E on top and a number for the fret. The staff is written an octave above where a guitar sounds, as guitarists read it. Press ▶ to hear it, and ↻ Loop to repeat it. The strings are numbered 6 (low E) to 1 (high E). The right hand uses p for the thumb, and i, m and a for the index, middle and ring fingers.
Here is what you are working toward, played by the band. Switch the other players off to hear the guitar alone, and slow the tempo with the slider at the bottom of the page.

title: Travis Picking on Guitar
text:
1. The thumb alone
Start with the thumb, and only the thumb. On a chord, the thumb plays four bass notes in a bar, one on every beat: the root, an inner string, the alternate bass, and the inner string again. For C the root is the 5th string, the alternate bass is the 6th string (fret 3, which is a G), and the inner string is the 4th string, fret 2 (an E). Hold the C shape and play 5, 4, 6, 4.






The alternate bass is the string on the other side of the root, so the thumb swings between a low note and a higher one. That is where the oom-pah comes from, and this pattern is the same as the band’s bass line in its folk and country styles.

Easy because: one finger plays one note on every beat, and your fretting hand holds a chord you already know.
Hard because: the thumb has to find three strings without looking, and keep going in time.
What goes wrong:

The thumb plays the wrong string, usually the next one over.
The beat is uneven because the 5-to-6 jump takes longer than 5-to-4.
The strings ring into each other. Rest the side of the right hand lightly on the bridge to damp the bass, and the notes come out shorter and cleaner.


Practice: play it with a metronome at 60, with your eyes closed, for a minute. Then do the same on G, Am and D (section 4 has the strings).

title: Travis Picking on Guitar
text:
2. Pinches on beat 1
Now add a note on beat 1 only. Pick a treble string with a finger at the same moment as the thumb plays the root: that is a pinch. For C, use the B string (fret 1) with the middle finger. The other beats stay the same, thumb alone.




Easy because: the thumb pattern is unchanged, and only one other note arrives, always on the same beat.
Hard because: the thumb and the finger have to start the note at the same instant. If they drift apart it sounds like a clumsy strum, not a pinch.
What goes wrong: the finger plays first or late. The pinch is louder than the thumb notes that follow.

Practice: play only the pinches, with the thumb and finger leaving the strings together, then add the other three beats.

title: Travis Picking on Guitar
text:
3. Fingers between the thumb notes
Now give the fingers their place. On each beat the thumb plays its note on the beat, and a finger plays a note on the “and” after beats 2, 3 and 4. Beat 1 stays a pinch, so there is nothing on its “and”. Count it “1 2-and 3-and 4-and”. The fingers play the treble strings: the middle finger on the B string and the ring finger on the high E string work, or the index finger on the G string. Use whichever fingers you prefer, and keep them the same from bar to bar.



This is the Travis pattern. The thumb and the fingers alternate, so each one has a note, then a gap, then a note, and your hand feels like two people taking turns. Listen to the band play it in the demo above, and look at the staff to see how it matches.

Easy because: the thumb part is the same one from section 2, and the fingers play only three notes in a bar.
Hard because: the thumb and the fingers have to be independent. The thumb keeps its beat while the fingers play off it, and the thumb wants to follow the fingers.
What goes wrong:

The thumb stops or stumbles when the fingers come in.
The finger notes land on the beat instead of after it.
The treble notes are as loud as the bass notes. Play the thumb a little louder and the fingers more lightly.


Practice: count out loud, “one, two-and, three-and, four-and”. Slow it down until it is steady, then bring it up in small steps. Spend a week on this step before the next.

title: Travis Picking on Guitar
section: 4. On C, G, Am and D
text:
4. On C, G, Am and D
The same pattern needs a root, an inner string and an alternate bass for each chord. The thumb always plays the root of the chord on beat 1.




C: root on string 5, inner string 4 (fret 2), alternate bass on string 6 (fret 3). Treble: strings 2 and 1.
G: root on string 6 (fret 3), inner string 4 (open), alternate bass on string 5 (fret 2). Treble: strings 2 and 1.
Am: root on string 5 (open), inner string 4 (fret 2), alternate bass on string 6 (open). Treble: strings 2 and 1.
D: root on string 4 (open), inner string 3 (fret 2), alternate bass on string 5 (open). The strings below the root, 6, stay silent. Treble: strings 2 and 1.





Easy because: the pattern is the same each time, and the four chords are open shapes you know.
Hard because: the thumb has to learn a new set of strings for each chord. D, with only four strings in use, is the one that trips people up.
What goes wrong: the thumb plays a string that is not in the chord, and the bass sounds wrong. The alternate bass on D should be the open 5th string, not the low E.

Practice: one chord for four bars, until the thumb finds the strings by feel. Then the next chord. For the chord shapes and the fretting hand see guitar chord shapes by hand.

title: Travis Picking on Guitar
text:
5. Changing chords
Now move from one chord to the next without breaking the thumb’s beat. The thumb keeps going while the fretting hand moves. The change lands on beat 1 of the next bar, on the root. The thumb notes on beats 3 and 4 are the time you have to move: let go of the old shape on beat 4 and have the new one down for beat 1.




Easy because: you can think of a bar at a time, and a bar of a chord you have already played is a bar you know.
Hard because: the picking hand cannot slow down while the fretting hand moves, and the roots of the chords move around on strings 4 to 6.
What goes wrong:

The pattern stops dead at the change, because the picking hand waits for the fretting hand.
The thumb plays the old chord’s root on the new chord.
The last beat of a bar is rushed.


Practice: play C and G, two bars each, with a metronome. Do not stop. If the change is late, drop one beat of the picking (rest the fingers) and keep the thumb going. Then play it with the band.

title: Travis Picking on Guitar
section: 6. Travis picking with hammer-ons and pull-offs
text:
6. Travis picking with hammer-ons and pull-offs
Hammer-ons and pull-offs make the pattern sound like Chet Atkins instead of a practice exercise. The hand technique is in Hammer-ons and Pull-offs on Guitar; you should be comfortable with sections 1 to 4 of that lesson first.
Hammer onto the 3rd of the chord, on beat 1. The 3rd of a major chord is the note that makes it major, and in an open chord the string next to the root is often an open string a hammer-on away from it. On G, the thumb picks the open 5th string (A) and hammers to fret 2 (B, the 3rd). On C, it picks the open 4th string (D) and hammers to fret 2 (E, the 3rd). The hammered note takes the place of the pinch on beat 1, and then the pattern goes on.



Pull-offs in the treble, between the thumb notes. The “and” after beat 2 can be two quick notes instead of one: pick the higher note, then pull off to the lower. On C the high E string is picked at fret 3 and pulled off to the open string. On Am the B string is picked at fret 1 and pulled off to the open B string.




Easy because: the thumb never changes. The hammer-ons and pull-offs are all in the fingers, and each one fits in one place in the pattern.
Hard because: the fretting hand has to do something while it is also holding the chord, and the picking hand has to stay steady while it waits for the hammer or the pull.
What goes wrong: the decorated beat gets rushed, or the thumb loses its place. The hammer-on is too soft to hear. A pull-off is not loud enough to match the picked notes.

Practice: put one decoration in a four-bar phrase, in the same place each time, until you do not have to think about it. Then try a second one.

title: Travis Picking on Guitar
text:
7. With the band
Now play the part with the band. The chart is G, C, D, G. The band’s guitarist plays the pattern in section 3, and its bass plays the root and alternate bass with the thumb. Take the guitar off (the Chords button) and play the part yourself. Start at 70 beats a minute and speed up when it is steady.



The second button is the simpler pattern the band calls thumb, pinch-and. Use it to rehearse the thumb with fewer finger notes, and then play the Travis pattern.

title: Travis Picking on Guitar
text:
8. A neighbour: chicken pickin’
Chicken pickin’ is a cousin of Travis picking that sounds very different. It is a country guitar technique played with a flat pick and the middle and ring fingers (hybrid picking). The pick plays a bass or chord note, and the fingers snap the treble strings, pulling each one up and letting it slap against the frets. Notes are also muted by the picking hand, and the short, dry, clucking sound that results gives it the name. It began in the Telecaster-based country playing of the 1950s and 1960s, and you can hear it in the work of James Burton, Albert Lee and, more recently, Brad Paisley. This lesson does not teach it. If you can play the Travis pattern, you already have the independence of thumb and fingers that it takes.
Unlocks: the band’s other fingerpicking pattern, Prine; Hammer-ons and Pull-offs.

title: Lesson: Turnarounds and Rhythm Changes
text:
The turnaround is a short chord pattern that sends a tune back to its beginning: I, vi, ii, V. Jazz players have been changing it for a century. This lesson starts with the plain one and adds the standard changes one at a time, and ends with the first four bars of I Got Rhythm.
How to use the page. Press ▶ on a chart and the band plays it four times after a one-bar count-in. The bar that is sounding lights up, on the chart and on the staff. Under every chord is its Roman numeral, which stays the same in every key. The strip at the bottom of the window sets the key, the feel, the tempo and the chord instrument, and you can change them while the band plays. Shaded bars are the ones that differ from the version named under the chart.

title: Lesson: Turnarounds and Rhythm Changes
text:
1. The plain turnaround
C, Am, Dm, G: I, vi, ii, V. The bass follows the circle of fifths: C, then A, D, G, and back to C.

title: Lesson: Turnarounds and Rhythm Changes
text:
2. Sevenths
Cmaj7, Am7, Dm7, G7. Every chord gets its 7th. The 7th of one chord is often a step from the 3rd of the next, which is what makes the guide-tone line smooth (see the lesson on guide tones).

title: Lesson: Turnarounds and Rhythm Changes
text:
3. A dominant on the vi
Cmaj7, A7, Dm7, G7. Make the vi a dominant. A7 is the V of Dm7, and its C♯ pulls up to D.

title: Lesson: Turnarounds and Rhythm Changes
text:
4. Start on the iii
Em7, A7, Dm7, G7. iii, VI, ii, V: the turnaround begun a step earlier. Em7 is a good stand-in for Cmaj7 (it has E, G and B, three of its four notes), and it makes a chain of fifths that is a link longer.

title: Lesson: Turnarounds and Rhythm Changes
text:
5. Tritone substitution
Cmaj7, E♭7, Dm7, D♭7. Replace each dominant with the one a tritone away. A7 becomes E♭7 and G7 becomes D♭7. The bass line now falls by half step wherever a substitute is used: E♭ to D, D♭ to C.

title: Lesson: Turnarounds and Rhythm Changes
text:
6. Rhythm changes
C A7 | Dm7 G7 | Em7 A7 | Dm7 G7. The first four bars of Gershwin’s I Got Rhythm (in B♭ in the original, here in C). Two chords in every bar. Jazz players have written hundreds of tunes on these changes.

title: Lesson: Turnarounds and Rhythm Changes
text:
Build your own
Choose a version of each bar. The shaded bars differ from the plain turnaround.

title: Lesson: Turnarounds and Rhythm Changes
text:
Test your ear
The band plays one of the versions. Pick the one you heard.

title: Lesson: Turnarounds and Rhythm Changes
text:
Where to go next

Play the guide-tone line over each version, from the guide tones lesson.
Learn the rhythm changes in two or three keys.

title: Jazz Singing: Swing, Scat and the Changes
text:
A jazz singer is part of the band. The tone is conversational, the rhythm swings, and the melody is something to reshape rather than repeat. This lesson moves from tone and swing to scat, blue notes, singing the chords, and the back-phrasing of a ballad.
How to use the page. Each exercise has a staff and a ▶ button. Choose Your voice once and every exercise moves into your range; men read treble-clef notes an octave lower. The playback is straight, but swing the eighth notes when you sing (see the next section). Click a heading to fold a section away.
crumbs: Jazz Singing: Swing, Scat and the Changes

title: Jazz Singing: Swing, Scat and the Changes
text:
Tone: talk the tune
Jazz singers from Billie Holiday to Shirley Horn sound like they are telling you something. Keep the tone close to your speaking voice, with clear words.
Vibrato is a natural, regular wobble in a held note’s pitch. Use it as a colour, not a constant. A common habit is to start a long note straight and let the vibrato bloom near the end.
Sing the note below, straight for two beats and then letting it relax into vibrato.
crumbs: Jazz Singing: Swing, Scat and the Changes

title: Jazz Singing: Swing, Scat and the Changes
text:
Swing eighths
In swing, a pair of eighth notes is played long–short, roughly like the first and last notes of a triplet: “doo-ba doo-ba”. Accent the off-beats (the “and”s) a little, and let some notes almost disappear. Those are ghost notes, shown in parentheses in the syllables under the staff.
The playback here is straight; sing it swung. For a swung band to sing with, try Reading swing or the Backing Track on a swing style.




Tap your foot on beats 2 and 4, not 1 and 3. That is where the drummer’s hi-hat closes in a swing feel, and it puts your body in the groove.
crumbs: Jazz Singing: Swing, Scat and the Changes

title: Jazz Singing: Swing, Scat and the Changes
text:
Scat syllables
Scat is improvising with syllables instead of words. The syllables work like articulation on a horn:

“doo” for a smooth, legato note.
“ba” and “da” for a note with an attack.
“dat” and “dot” for a short note at the end of a phrase.
“bee”, “bop”, “doo-dle” for quick runs.

Start by copying a horn line. Sing this phrase with the syllables written under it. Then make up your own syllables on the same notes.
crumbs: Jazz Singing: Swing, Scat and the Changes

title: Jazz Singing: Swing, Scat and the Changes
section: Blue notes and the blues scale
text:
Blue notes and the blues scale
The blues scale adds the “blue notes” to a minor pentatonic: in C, that’s C, E♭, F, F♯ (the ♭5), G and B♭. The ♭3 and ♭7 sung over major chords give blues and jazz their bite. Slide into them, and bend them slightly sharp.



Practice: sing the scale over a 12-bar blues in C with the Backing Track, then improvise a two-bar phrase using only C, E♭, F and G.
crumbs: Jazz Singing: Swing, Scat and the Changes

title: Jazz Singing: Swing, Scat and the Changes
text:
Singing the changes: arpeggios
Improvisers outline the chords as they go by. Sing each chord’s tones from the root up: 1, 3, 5, 7. Here is a ii–V–I in C, the most common progression in jazz.



Then sing them going down, from the 7th of each chord, and you’ll see how the notes join up.
crumbs: Jazz Singing: Swing, Scat and the Changes

title: Jazz Singing: Swing, Scat and the Changes
section: Guide tones: the line inside the changes
text:
Guide tones: the line inside the changes
The 3rd and 7th of each chord are its guide tones. Sung in a row they make a smooth line that moves by a half step or not at all, and it outlines the harmony with only two notes per chord. Guide tones covers the idea in depth.



Practice: sing the guide tones while the Backing Track plays a ii–V–I. Then add one passing note between each pair.
crumbs: Jazz Singing: Swing, Scat and the Changes

title: Jazz Singing: Swing, Scat and the Changes
text:
Back-phrasing a ballad
On a ballad, jazz singers float the words over the beat. They start a phrase late and then catch up, stretch one word, and rush the next. This is back-phrasing. The band keeps strict time; the singer’s line is free on top of it.
Here is a phrase written plainly, then back-phrased, with each entry a beat or more late and some notes pulled together.






(The words are a stand-in to sing on, not a real tune.)
Practice: sing a ballad you know with a slow backing track. Say the words in rhythm first, as speech, then sing them with the same freedom.
crumbs: Jazz Singing: Swing, Scat and the Changes

title: Jazz Singing: Swing, Scat and the Changes
text:
Trading fours
In a jam the soloists trade fours: each takes four bars in turn, often answering what the last one played. Practise call and response: play the call, then sing a four-bar answer that starts with the same rhythm and ends somewhere new.
crumbs: Jazz Singing: Swing, Scat and the Changes

title: Jazz Singing: Swing, Scat and the Changes
text:
Where to go next

Pop singing: mix, belt and runs.
Classical singing: breath, pure vowels and legato.
Improvising on a blues: the same ideas for any instrument.

title: Formants: What Makes a Vowel
text:
Sing ee and then ah on the same note. The pitch stays the same, yet anyone can hear which vowel is which. Your vocal folds make the same buzz both times; what changes is the shape of the tube above them, and that tube boosts some frequencies and damps others. The boosted regions are the formants, numbered from the bottom: F1, F2, F3 and so on. Two of them, F1 and F2, are enough to tell most vowels apart, and they line up closely with the vowel chart singers already use. This lesson takes you through them with a synthesised voice. Click a section’s heading to fold it; the “On this page” bar at the right jumps to any section and opens it.
How to use the page. Each widget has a ▶ button that starts a sustained voice and ■ to stop it (only one plays at a time; start with your volume low). The pictures are spectra: frequency runs left to right up to 4 kHz, each vertical line is one harmonic of the voice, and the curve is the filter the vocal tract puts on top. The same synthesiser drives the vowel chart on the IPA chart, where you can drag through the vowel space.

title: Formants: What Makes a Vowel
text:
1. Source and filter
The voice is two things in a row. The source is the vocal folds: they open and shut at the pitch you sing, so they make a buzz at that pitch plus every whole-number multiple of it (the harmonic series), each one a little quieter than the one below. The filter is the throat, mouth and lips: a tube about 17 cm long in an adult, and like any tube it resonates at certain frequencies. Where it resonates, the harmonics come through strongly; between resonances they are damped.
The pitch belongs to the source and the vowel belongs to the filter, which is why you can sing any vowel on any note. Play the buzz on its own, then put a vowel’s filter on it.



The buzz is rich but has no vowel. With the filter on, the harmonics near each peak of the curve stand out, and that pattern of peaks is what your ear reads as a vowel. Change the pitch: the harmonic lines get closer or further apart, but the curve, and the vowel, stays where it is.

title: Formants: What Makes a Vowel
text:
2. F1: tongue height and jaw
The first formant, F1, is the lowest peak, between about 250 Hz and 850 Hz. It follows how open the vocal tract is: a close vowel like [i] or [u] has a low F1, an open vowel like [a] a high one. Dropping the jaw and lowering the tongue raises F1.



Slide F1 up with F2 high and you go from [i] through [e] and [ɛ] towards [a]. With F2 low you go from [u] through [o] towards [ɔ] and [ɑ]. On the vowel chart, F1 is the vertical axis: close at the top, open at the bottom.

title: Formants: What Makes a Vowel
text:
3. F2: front and back
The second formant, F2, runs from about 700 Hz to 2400 Hz. It follows where the tongue is bunched: forward in the mouth gives a high F2 ([i], [e]), back gives a low F2 ([u], [o]). Rounding the lips lengthens the tube and pulls F2 (and F3) down, so a rounded front vowel like [y] sits between [i] and [u].



On the vowel chart, F2 is the horizontal axis, with high F2 (front) on the left. Try holding F1 low and sweeping F2: [i] to [y] to [ɨ] to [u] is the whole top row of the chart.

title: Formants: What Makes a Vowel
section: 4. The F1–F2 plane is the vowel chart
text:
4. The F1–F2 plane is the vowel chart
Put F1 down the page and F2 across it, high on the left, and the vowels fall into a shape that is close to the IPA trapezoid. The phonetics chart started as a map of the tongue; formant measurements in the twentieth century showed that it is just as much a map of sound. Drag anywhere in the plane.



The trapezoid shape comes from acoustics: front vowels can spread across a wide range of F2, while back vowels are squeezed into a narrow one, so the chart is wider at the top than at the bottom. The values here are averages for an adult male voice; a higher, shorter vocal tract (women, children) moves everything up by roughly 15–20 %, but the shape stays the same, which is how we hear the same vowel from different speakers.

title: Formants: What Makes a Vowel
text:
5. F3, r-colouring and lip rounding
The third formant, F3 (around 2200–3000 Hz), changes less from vowel to vowel, but it carries two things. Lip rounding lowers it along with F2. And an r-coloured vowel, like the General American nurse [ɝ] or butter [ɚ], has a strikingly low F3, down near 1600 Hz, sitting just above F2. Drag F3 down on [ə] and listen to it turn into an American er.



F4 and above vary even less and mostly reflect the size of the singer’s head and throat: they are part of what makes a voice sound like that person.

title: Formants: What Makes a Vowel
text:
6. The singer’s formant
Trained classical singers, especially men, make a strong peak around 2.5–3.2 kHz by clustering F3, F4 and F5 together, mostly by lowering the larynx and narrowing the tube just above the vocal folds. This singer’s formant is the “ring” or squillo that lets an unamplified voice carry over an orchestra: the orchestra is loudest below 1 kHz, and the ear is most sensitive near 3 kHz. Turn it on and off on the same vowel.



The vowel does not change, because F1 and F2 do not move. What changes is the brightness and the carrying power. Pop and musical theatre singers use the same region with a more speech-like vowel; a microphone means they need less of it.

title: Formants: What Makes a Vowel
section: 7. High notes: when the pitch outruns the formants
text:
7. High notes: when the pitch outruns the formants
The harmonics sample the filter curve only at multiples of the pitch. At a speaking pitch they are close together and trace the curve well. A soprano at 880 Hz has harmonics only at 880, 1760, 2640 Hz and so on, so F1 for [i] (about 300 Hz) is below the lowest note she can produce. No harmonic falls near it, and the vowel can’t be heard as [i] any more.



Raise the pitch on [i] and listen to the vowels blur together above about 600 Hz. Then turn on Tune F1 to the pitch: this raises F1 to just above the fundamental, which is what sopranos do by opening the jaw on high notes. It is called formant tuning, and it is the acoustic reason for vowel modification: a high [i] is sung towards [ɪ] or [e], and a high [u] towards [ʊ] or [o], so that F1 stays with the fundamental and the note keeps its power. The cost is that the vowel is less clear, and on the very highest notes listeners cannot tell vowels apart at all.

For singers: if a high note feels thin or hard on a closed vowel, open the jaw and let the vowel drift towards its open neighbour ([i]→[ɪ]→[e], [u]→[ʊ]→[o]). In the words, keep the consonants clear; they carry more of the meaning than the vowels do up there.

title: Formants: What Makes a Vowel
text:
Things to try

In section 4, find your own vowels: say a word, hold the vowel, and hunt for it in the plane. Vowels in your accent may sit between the symbols.
In section 1, play [a] and drag the pitch slowly: the vowel stays put while the harmonics slide under the curve.
On the IPA chart, switch on Hold and click from [i] to [y] to [u]: one formant moves at a time.
In section 7, find the pitch where [i] and [e] stop sounding different without formant tuning.

title: Formants: What Makes a Vowel
text:

The harmonic series: where the vertical lines in these pictures come from.
Filters: the same idea of a resonant filter, on a synthesiser.
The vocoder: a machine that copies one sound’s formants onto another.

title: Is Watermelon Man a Blues?
text: Short answer: yes, by its chords and its form. Herbie Hancock’s Watermelon Man (Takin’ Off, Blue Note, 1962) is a 16-bar blues in F: the first eight bars are an ordinary blues, then the V–IV pair (C7–B♭7) is played three times before two bars of F7. Every chord is a dominant seventh on I, IV or V, which is exactly what this site’s F Major (Blues) label means. By genre, though, critics file the record as hard bop, soul jazz or (in 1973) funk, and Hancock himself describes a street cry, not “a blues”. This page sets out the evidence and how sure we can be.

title: Is Watermelon Man a Blues?
text:
The form, bar by bar

Set it beside the standard 12-bar blues (I for four bars, IV for two, I for two, then V, IV, I, I): bars 1–8 are identical, and the V–IV pair that ends a 12-bar blues is stated three times instead of once. 8 + 3 × 2 + 2 = 16. The analyst Ethan Hein puts it the same way: “essentially a twelve-bar blues in F, but with bars nine and ten repeated three times.” The original liner notes call it a “modified blues” and “a strongly gospel-infused 16-bar theme.”
There are two ways to read a 16-bar form like this:

A 12-bar blues with its ending stretched. This fits Watermelon Man closely, because the first eight bars are unchanged.
An 8 + 8 form, a verse and a refrain. Scholars who read 16-bar blues this way (for example Carter, Music Theory Online, 2025) still count them as blues: the blues is “inherently hybrid”, and blues that met the popular mainstream “did not cease to be blues”.

Either way it is a blues by form.

title: Is Watermelon Man a Blues?
text:
What makes something “a blues”?
“Blues” means at least three different things, and they give different answers:

A form and a set of chords. The textbook prototype is 12 bars, I–IV–V, every chord a dominant seventh, often with an AAB lyric. Watermelon Man: yes, with a stretched ending.
A genre or marketing category. The record industry of the 1920s named “blues” as a kind of record. Takin’ Off is filed as hard bop or soul jazz, and the 1973 Head Hunters version as jazz-funk. Watermelon Man: no.
An idiom or feeling. Albert Murray separated the blues as a mood from blues music; reviewers call this track “bluesy”. Watermelon Man: arguably.

Historians also warn that the 12-bar prototype is a later standardization: early blues used 8-bar, 16-bar and irregular forms (for example “Sitting on Top of the World”, nine bars), so counting only 12 bars as “a blues” would be arbitrary. 8-bar blues (“Key to the Highway”, “Trouble in Mind”) and 16-bar blues are treated as blues forms in the reference books and teaching sites we could reach.

title: Is Watermelon Man a Blues?
text:
What the published sources say
Every source that names the form calls it a blues of some kind:

AllSolos: “Blues – 16 bars”, “built on an extended blues structure”.
Standard Repertoire: an “Altered blues”, 16 bars.
Learn Jazz Standards: “This 16 bar blues is played in a straight eight groove.”
JazzFuel: “essentially a sixteen-bar blues: the first 8 bars mimic a classic blues exactly.”
FretDojo: “a 16 bar blues, rather than a 12 bar blues.”
Wikipedia: “written in a sixteen-bar blues form” (no source given).

No source we found says it is not a blues. These are mostly teaching and reference websites, and several probably repeat one another, so they are weaker evidence than they look. Critics and encyclopedias mostly use genre words instead: hard bop, soul jazz, R&B, funk, boogaloo, “bluesy”.

title: Is Watermelon Man a Blues?
text:
What Hancock says
Hancock tells the story of the tune, not its form. In the 1962 liner notes he recalls “the cry of the watermelon man making his rounds through the back streets and alleys” of his Chicago childhood, and in his memoir Possibilities (2014) the “clackety-clack” of the horse-drawn wagon. He has said it “took 15 minutes to write” and that he wanted it to be “real”, not just commercial; he also says that growing up in Chicago he “heard the real blues, Muddy Waters and Howlin’ Wolf”. In no source we found does he call Watermelon Man itself a blues. The groove is straight eighths over a gospel-style piano vamp, closer to soul jazz than to a shuffle.

title: Is Watermelon Man a Blues?
text:
The other famous versions

Mongo Santamaría (1963). A Latin version that reached No. 10 on the Billboard Hot 100 and entered the Grammy Hall of Fame in 1998. It keeps the 16-bar form (with two extra groove bars on the second time through) over a slower guajira-based groove. Its chords match as far as we can tell, but we found no published chart.
Head Hunters (1973). A slow (about 75 beats per minute) funk re-composition with the hindewhu (whistle-and-voice) introduction, no solos, and a new section that leaves the I–IV–V frame. Sources disagree about the new chord (G♭7 or A♭7). This version should not be labelled “(Blues)” automatically.

title: Is Watermelon Man a Blues?
section: So what does the site say?
text:
So what does the site say?
The tune is labelled F Major (Blues). On this site “(Blues)” describes the harmony: the chords on I and IV are dominant sevenths. Watermelon Man meets that test exactly. It is not a claim about genre, and it does not mean a shuffle feel.
We considered “(16-bar blues)” and decided against it: that puts a fact about the form into a label about the key, and would make a category with one tune in it. The 16-bar form is described in the lessons instead (see Watermelon Man for Congas, which uses the same form as the Backing Track’s “Watermelon Man (16 bars)” preset).

title: Is Watermelon Man a Blues?
section: How sure are we, and what would change it?
text:
How sure are we, and what would change it?

Not checked: the printed lead sheets (The Real Book, Sher’s New Real Book), Ted Gioia’s entry in The Jazz Standards (2012, p. 446), Grove Music Online, the Penguin Guide, Steven Pond’s book on Head Hunters, and Hancock’s memoir in his own words (quoted here second-hand). The bar-by-bar chart above comes from a teaching site and an independent analysis, not a published lead sheet.
Not analysed: the melody. Whether it uses blue notes or the blues scale was not checked; a transcription would settle it.
What would change the answer: only a printed chart in which the I or IV chord is not a dominant seventh, or a respected source arguing it is not a blues. A published chart with the same F7 / B♭7 / C7 changes would simply confirm it. A melody with no blues-scale notes would deserve a footnote, not a different label, because the label is about the chords.

title: MLT Lesson Planner
text:
How it works


A plan follows Mullen’s Whole-Part-Whole: a first whole (the unit’s song), the part (the LSA: Pre-LSA, then a three-minute Go Mode), then second-whole activities that put the LSA’s content back into music, a bridge to an inference skill when the unit has one, and a short close.
Lesson numbers walk through the unit: lesson 2 takes the unit’s next LSA (rhythm after tonal, as Mullen alternates) and a different set of activities.
The class screen opens in a new window: drag it to the TV (an extended display). It shows only the students’ side of the current item and the timer, and follows this window as you go. Both windows must be in the same browser.

title: Hear, Compare, Translate
text:
Six levels of the skill learning sequence. The first three are by ear only and come before reading; Read it and the series section add notation, and the last asks for patterns of your own. Use headphones or speakers, sing and chant out loud, and take a breath before you answer.
The order follows Andy Mullen’s: familiar patterns first, then unfamiliar ones. Where Edwin Gordon disagrees, the note under each section says so.

title: Hear, Compare, Translate
section: Partial synthesis: name the tonality or meter
text:
Partial synthesis: name the tonality or meter
You hear two series of familiar patterns with no tonality or meter set up first. Name the tonality (or meter) of each. This is still discrimination learning, so the page teaches: after you answer, or when you press Tell me, it explains what to audiate.




Sources. Gordon: at partial synthesis the teacher does not establish tonality or meter, sings the series on a neutral syllable, and gives the answers; to leave them out would wrongly bridge to generalization-verbal (Learning Sequences in Music, pp. 113, 116; Reference Handbook, Tonal Unit 6, pp. 48–49). Both series share one keyality, so only the resting tone changes. Mullen’s objective: “aurally name tonality of a series of familiar patterns with teacher guidance” (MLT Any Music Teacher Can Du…De, p. 74). The meter explanation names the microbeats you audiate (DU DE or DU DA DI), as Mullen does (p. 85).

title: Hear, Compare, Translate
text:
Same or different (generalization-aural/oral)
The tonality or meter is set up, then you hear two patterns, once each, and say whether they were the same. Start with familiar patterns; add unfamiliar ones when that is easy.




Sources. Gordon: the teacher establishes tonality on a neutral syllable and performs two patterns or sets; at an inference level the pattern is heard only once, and a student who can’t do it goes back to aural/oral (Learning Sequences in Music, pp. 131–132). Gordon uses familiar and unfamiliar patterns here; Mullen starts with familiar ones, “Ss can identify if patterns are the same or different” right after the aural/oral objectives (MLT Any Music Teacher Can Du…De, pp. 66, 74). Students find same easier to hear than different (Gordon, p. 219).

title: Hear, Compare, Translate
text:
Translate to solfège (generalization-verbal)
You hear the tonality or meter set up, then one pattern on a neutral syllable. Sing or chant it back in syllables, then check. It opens only when the verbal association objective for the same content is done.




Sources. Gordon warns against this at the verbal association level (“it is not appropriate at this level…”); it belongs to generalization-verbal, where students repeat the teacher’s neutral-syllable pattern “using tonal syllables or rhythm syllables instead” (Learning Sequences in Music, pp. 108, 132; Reference Handbook, Tonal Unit 9, Criteria 2–3, pp. 52–54). If students can’t, instruction goes back to verbal association; the teacher guides but does not give the answer first (p. 132). Gordon uses familiar and unfamiliar patterns; Mullen practises the skill with familiar patterns first (“students need practice with that skill using familiar patterns before they try it with unfamiliar patterns”, p. 66) and calls it translation (The Literate Musician, Rhythm Lessons 8, 9.3, 10.3; Harmony Lesson 9). This page follows Mullen and offers Gordon’s unfamiliar patterns as the next step.
Not checked by the page: your syllables. You judge them against the answer. Rhythm syllables are the Gordon/Froseth system: duple DU DE (divisions DU TA DE TA), triple DU DA DI (divisions DU TA DA TA DI TA).

title: Hear, Compare, Translate
text:
Read it (symbolic association and generalization-symbolic)
A pattern appears in notation, drawn the way the pattern sets write it: no stems, no rhythm, no syllables. Read it in syllables, out loud, then hear it and check. Start with familiar patterns in a new order; move to unfamiliar ones once you can read the familiar ones yourself. The name it choices mix two tonalities or meters and set neither up first, so you name it from the page.




Sources. Reading comes after aural/oral, verbal association and partial synthesis, and students first read patterns they already audiate; tonal patterns are shown on the staff without syllables or rhythm, with DO found from the DO signature (Gordon, Learning Sequences in Music, pp. 117–123). Generalization-symbolic is reading “one unfamiliar pattern of a mix of familiar and unfamiliar” patterns without the teacher’s help and naming the tonality or meter; if students can’t, go back to symbolic association or composite synthesis (pp. 133–134). Mullen: “read unfamiliar patterns (on the basis of familiar patterns)” (MLT Any Music Teacher Can Du…De, p. 39), and reading familiar patterns in unfamiliar order in a new DO signature (The Literate Musician, Reading Lesson 3.1, pp. 122–123).

title: Hear, Compare, Translate
section: Read and write a series (composite synthesis)
text:
Read and write a series (composite synthesis)
Now several familiar patterns at once, and you name the tonality or meter while you read or write them. Read: a series appears; with a name it choice nothing is set up, so you name it from the page, then sing or chant it straight through. Write from dictation: hear the series, name it, then write it by choosing each pattern’s notation in order. Write from memory: the series shows for three seconds a pattern, then you write it.




Sources. Composite synthesis joins partial synthesis and symbolic association: students “audiate tonality or meter of one or more series of familiar tonal patterns or rhythm patterns in familiar or unfamiliar order as they read and write patterns”, and “read with contextual comprehension”; patterns are still read as tonal or rhythm patterns, never combined into melodic patterns (Gordon, Learning Sequences in Music, pp. 126–127). It comes before generalization-symbolic, and students who struggle there go back to it (pp. 129, 133). Mullen lists the “can do” objectives used here: read a series of familiar patterns in familiar or unfamiliar order; write a series from dictation; write a series from memory after seeing it; give the tonality or meter to a series in notation and from dictation (How to Teach the Language of Music, p. 36). Not the same as real writing: the page has you choose each pattern’s notation from the set rather than draw it on the staff, so it checks recognition of the notation, not handwriting.

title: Hear, Compare, Translate
text:
Answer with your own pattern (creativity/improvisation)
You hear a pattern; answer it out loud with one of your own. Create asks only for something different in the same tonality or meter. Improvise adds a rule: the same function, the other function, or (in rhythm) a division. There is no single right answer: the page can play or list answers from the set that fit, and you judge your own.




Sources. Creativity sets few restrictions; improvisation adds more, such as function (Gordon, Learning Sequences in Music, p. 136; Mullen, MLT Any Music Teacher Can Du…De, pp. 40–41, from exploration through creativity and improvisation to composition). A tonal answer has as many patterns as the teacher’s; a rhythm answer need not (Gordon, pp. 138–139). Answering on a neutral syllable is creativity/improvisation-aural/oral, which Mullen bridges to straight after aural/oral; answering in syllables comes after verbal association (Mullen, pp. 66–67, 74). Gordon’s Reference Handbook places no restriction on a creative response beyond being tonal, sets function rules for improvisation, and asks the teacher to be lenient, because bridging to an inference level reinforces the discrimination level it came from (Tonal Unit 3, pp. 43–45).

title: Hear, Compare, Translate
text:
About the patterns and sound

Tonal, familiar: Mullen’s familiar patterns in a familiar order (FPIFO), major and minor tonic and dominant, 15 each (The Literate Musician, pp. 57, 59). They are also on Tonal Patterns as mullen-fpifo-major and mullen-fpifo-minor, with solfège, for verbal association practice.
Tonal, unfamiliar: the site’s Register-style sets (322a, 322b, 322b-major), tonic and dominant only.
Dorian and Mixolydian: the site’s tonic/subtonic sets (323a, 324a).
Rhythm: the site’s duple (2/4) and triple (6/8) macro/microbeat and division sets, chanted on one pitch.
Tonality is set with the tonal sequence 5 6 5 4 3 2 7 1 at double speed (Gordon, Reference Handbook, p. 33; Mullen, p. 79). Meter is set with two bars of microbeats and two of macrobeats; that chant is this site’s own.
Every pitch in a tonal pattern has the same length and every rhythm pattern uses one pitch, as in learning sequence activities (Gordon, p. 223). Resting tones stay between D and G above middle C, in the singing range Gordon gives (Reference Handbook, p. 32).
The instruments stand in for the neutral syllables “bum” and “bah”.

title: Blues Changes by Ear
text:
Choose major or minor blues, a level, and press Start. You hear three choruses of the blues, A, B and C, each in its own band style. Two use the same changes; the third makes one different choice somewhere in the twelve bars. Which is different? Space plays all three again, A / B / C answer, N shows or hides notation, Enter goes on.



Bars sets how much of the chorus you hear:

Four: the phrase with the change (the default): bars 1–4, 5–8 or 9–12, whichever holds the difference. At levels 1–2 that is usually bars 1–4 (the quick change) or 9–12 (bar 10, the turnaround); at level 4 it is bars 1–4 or 5–8 (the passing chords); at levels 5–7 it is nearly always bars 9–12 (the turnaround). When a change runs across phrases (Bird changes at level 8), you hear the phrase where it starts.
Any four bars: four bars in a row starting anywhere (bars 3–6, 8–11…), always including a bar that changes. The start is not a phrase start, so finding your place is part of the task.
All 12: the whole chorus.
Bars I choose: type the first and last bar (1–12). Questions are then made only from changes inside those bars; if no change at the level falls inside them (bars 1–4 at level 5, say), you are told so.

Busyness (under The band) calms the band down when a style gets too busy to hear the chords through: Less busy drops the drum fills, has the bass play a two-feel (swing styles) or roots on beats 1 and 3, and the chords played steadily on the beat; Calm holds each bass note and chord for its whole length over light brushes.

title: Blues Changes by Ear
text:
What can change
A version of the blues is a set of choices on top of the basic twelve bars (in F: F7 for I7, Bb7 for IV7, C7 for V7):







Where
The choices




Bar 2
stay on I7, or the quick change to IV7


Bar 4
I7, or v7 I7, a ii–V into IV


Bar 6
IV7, or #iv°7, a passing diminished chord leading back to I


Bar 8
I7, or VI7, the V of ii


Bars 9–10
V7 IV7 (the blues way down), V7 V7, the jazz ii7 V7, or the backdoor: ii7, then iv7 bVII7


Bars 11–12
no turnaround, V7 in bar 12, I VI7 | ii V, or I bIII7 | bVI7 bII7 (the Tadd Dameron turnaround)


Tritone substitutes
bII7 for the last V7, bVI7 for the turnaround’s VI7: the bass moves by semitone instead of by fifth


Bird blues
bars 1–10 as in Charlie Parker’s “Blues for Alice”: Imaj7, then ii–V’s stepping down to IV, then down again to ii


Minor blues
i7 and iv7; bars 9–10 bVI7 V7 or iiø7 V7; turnaround V7 or i bVI7 | iiø7 V7; bII7 for the last V7



Unverified: these are the common jazz-blues reharmonisations as they are usually taught, written here from memory, and the Bird changes are from memory of “Blues for Alice” (Parker, 1951). Neither is yet checked against a source.

Minor blues has three levels: bar 2 and the turnaround; bars 9–10; substitutes.
Levels 1–2 use blues and rock styles (jump blues, boogie-woogie, rock, swing, doo-wop, Motown), with plain 7th chords. From level 4 the styles are jazz: swing, jazz ballad, bossa nova, boogaloo, stride. The band → Styles overrides this.

title: Blues Changes by Ear
text:
Listening tips

Count the bars. Most changes are in bars 2, 4–6, 8, or 9–12; mark where the chorus turns around.
A tritone substitute keeps the same sound but slides: the bass goes down by semitone into I instead of by a fifth.
A tune on top plays the same melody over all three choruses, so only the chords underneath change.
Notation (block voicings with a bass line, and the tune when it is on) can be shown at any time; chord symbols appear after you answer, or always if you set Notation → Chord symbols to Always.

Related: Odd Progression Out, Hearing Harmony, Bass Lines by Ear.

title: Chord Grid by Ear
text:
Learn a tune’s chords (and melody) from a recording. Each box is one bar: click it to play from there, Shift+click a second bar to loop the bars between, Space plays and pauses. Type what you hear in each bar: a chord name (C, G7, Am) or a Roman numeral (I, V7, vi); two chords in a bar go in with a space between. Check colours each bar: green right, orange the right root but another chord, red wrong. Checking needs the recording to be linked to a tune with chords (see the Recordings Catalogue); chords are compared by function, so a recording in D is checked against notation in C. Set Key to the key the recording is in when you type chord names. Underneath, the tune’s notation (in the recording’s key) checks the melody.
The bars come from the recording’s timing map when it has one (made in Timestamp Notes). Without one, set where the first bar starts (play to the first downbeat and press = now), tap the tempo, and the grid is drawn at that steady tempo. Your guesses are kept in this browser, for each recording.

title: Sax Patterns by Ear
text:
How it works

Written notes. Everything on this page is in written pitch, the notes on your part. The page plays them at the pitch your saxophone really sounds (alto a major 6th lower, tenor a 9th, bari an octave and a 6th), and the microphone turns what it hears back into written notes. So pick your saxophone above.
Range. Each set is moved to the written key you pick and placed between written D4 and C6, where no low pinky keys or palm keys are needed, when it fits.
Fingerings. The usual fingering from the fingering chart. Your teacher may prefer an alternate (for example the bis key for B♭).
What counts. The notes in order; rhythm isn’t checked. Each new note must hold steady for about a tenth of a second. To play the same note twice, stop the sound briefly between them (tongue it). With Any octave counts on, the whole pattern may be an octave away. Stopping for more than four seconds starts the try again.
The microphone ignores everything while the page is playing. Headphones still help: a loud room can confuse it.
No sax handy? A MIDI keyboard or wind controller, or the computer keys, count as written notes.

title: Jazz ballad
text: Open the Jazz ballad style in the Backing Track

title: Jazz ballad
text:
What it is
A slow standard played by a jazz rhythm section: the bass on beats 1 and 3 (a two-feel), held chords on the piano, and brushes stirring the snare or a soft ride. The band leaves room for the melody.

title: Jazz ballad
text:
A little history
The two-feel is older than walking bass. New Orleans and 1920s dance bands put the tuba or string bass on 1 and 3, and when the bass began walking in the 1930s (see Swing), the two-feel stayed on as the lighter gear: bands play the head of a tune in two and start walking for the solos. On ballads it never has to leave. Brushes, used on drums since the 1920s, became the ballad sound through drummers such as Jo Jones and later Philly Joe Jones and Ed Thigpen. Pianists filled the long chords with the rich voicings that came from Ellington, Billy Strayhorn and later Bill Evans.

title: Jazz ballad
text:
The band’s version

Bass: Two-feel: root on 1, fifth on 3, now and then a pickup into the next bar.
Comping: long held chords (pad).
Drums: quiet time. Voicings: rootless, with unmarked extensions.

title: Boogie-Woogie
text: Open the Boogie-woogie style in the Backing Track

title: Boogie-Woogie
text:
What it is
Blues piano with a left hand that never stops: eight notes to the bar, swung, repeating one figure up and down the chord while the right hand plays riffs, tremolos and blue notes against it. It is almost always a 12-bar blues.
Boogie-woogie and stride are close relations: both are piano music for dancing at parties, both put a band into the left hand, and the same pianists often played both. Stride’s left hand leaps between bass and chord on the beats; boogie-woogie’s walks along the bass in eighth notes. The lesson Two Left Hands plays them side by side.

title: Boogie-Woogie
text:
A little history
The style began in the lumber, turpentine and railroad camps of Texas and Louisiana in the first years of the 1900s, played on “barrelhouse” pianos in the camps’ bars, and travelled north with the migration. In Chicago in the 1920s it was the music of rent parties, as stride was in Harlem. Pinetop Smith’s Pine Top’s Boogie Woogie (1928) gave the style its name; Jimmy Yancey, Meade Lux Lewis and Albert Ammons played it in Chicago.
In December 1938 the producer John Hammond put Ammons, Lewis and Pete Johnson on stage at Carnegie Hall in the From Spirituals to Swing concert, and boogie-woogie became a national craze. Big bands arranged it (Count Basie’s Boogie Woogie, Tommy Dorsey’s version of Pinetop’s piece), and the Andrews Sisters sang it. Its eight-to-the-bar bass went into jump blues, rhythm and blues and early rock and roll: Chuck Berry’s guitar plays a boogie left hand.

title: Boogie-Woogie
text:
The band’s version

Bass: Boogie-woogie: swung eighths walking up the chord and back down, root 3rd 5th 6th flat-7th 6th 5th 3rd, every bar. The pianist’s left hand, on the bass.
Comping: Boogie-woogie right hand: a two-bar riff of short swung chords against the bass.
Drums: Blues shuffle: swung eighths on the cymbal, kick on 1 and 3, snare on 2 and 4.
Voicings: plain triads and seventh chords, all their notes.

Boogie-woogie pianists have dozens of left-hand patterns (rolling octaves, the Yancey bass, broken sixths) and their right hands play the lead. The band’s bassist has one pattern and its pianist one riff, so a melody or a solo on top is your part.

title: Calypso
text: Open the Calypso style in the Backing Track

title: Calypso
text:
What it is
The topical song of Trinidad: a singer (the calypsonian) with a witty, often political lyric over a bouncing 2/4, with a strummed guitar or cuatro, a bass on root and fifth, and chords on the off-beats.

title: Calypso
text:
A little history
Calypso (earlier kaiso) grew out of the songs of Trinidad’s Carnival in the 1800s: the chantwell leading call-and-response songs in French Creole, stick-fighting songs, and the music of the Spanish Venezuelan string bands. By the 1910s-20s it was sung in English and recorded in New York. Calypso tents competed each Carnival season, and singers took grand names: Atilla the Hun, Roaring Lion, Lord Invader, Lord Kitchener, the Mighty Sparrow. Lord Invader’s Rum and Coca-Cola (sung at the 1943 Carnival) became an American hit for the Andrews Sisters in 1945, and Invader later won a lawsuit over its royalties; and Harry Belafonte’s album Calypso (1956) was the first LP to sell a million copies. Jamaica’s mento is a cousin, and in the 1970s Lord Shorty mixed calypso with Indian rhythms into soca, now Carnival’s main music.

title: Calypso
text:

title: Cha-cha
text:
What it is
A medium-tempo Cuban dance rhythm, steadier and simpler than mambo, with a cowbell on every beat and the three quick steps (cha-cha-chá) on beat 3, the and of 3, and beat 4.

title: Cha-cha
text:
A little history
Violinist Enrique Jorrín, of the charanga orchestra Orquesta América, wrote La engañadora (1951, recorded 1953). The orchestra’s dancers found its rhythm easier than the danzón-mambo, and the steps’ scuffing sound named the dance. Charangas played it on flute, violins, piano, bass, timbales, güiro and conga; Orquesta Aragón made it famous across Latin America. By the late 1950s it was a ballroom dance in the US and Europe, and American pop recorded “cha-cha” versions of everything.

text:

Bass: the cha-cha bass line. Comping: chords on the cha-cha figure.

title: 12/8 doo-wop
text:
What it is
The slow 1950s ballad: piano chords repeated in triplets, three to every beat, over a slow backbeat, usually on the I-vi-IV-V chords, behind a lead singer and vocal group.

title: 12/8 doo-wop
text:
A little history
Doo-wop came from African American vocal groups on street corners in New York, Philadelphia, Baltimore and Chicago in the late 1940s and ’50s, following the Ink Spots and the Mills Brothers. The backing singers sang nonsense syllables (doo-wop, sh-boom) in place of instruments. On record, small bands added a pianist hammering triplets, an idea from New Orleans rhythm and blues (Fats Domino) and the slow blues. The same 12/8 feel carries soul ballads into the 1960s, from Etta James’s At Last onward.

title: Boom-chick
text: Open the Boom-chick style in the Backing Track

title: Boom-chick
text:
What it is
The oldest accompaniment in popular music: a bass note on the strong beats and a chord on the weak ones. In 2/4 or 4/4 it is boom-chick; in 3/4 it is oom-pah-pah.

title: Boom-chick
text:
A little history
Brass bands and dance orchestras of the 1800s split the beat between the tuba (or bass) and the horns or second violins: marches, polkas and waltzes all run on it, and so does the stride and ragtime piano left hand (bass note, chord, bass note, chord). Guitarists in American old-time and country music used the same idea, a thumbed bass on the beat and a strum after it: Maybelle Carter’s guitar with the Carter Family from 1927, and later the folk revival. Sing-along songs from campfire to music hall still use it.

title: Boom-chick
text:

Bass: Root and fifth. Comping: oompah. Drums: boom-chick.

title: Hymn (four parts)
text:
What it is
Congregational hymn accompaniment: soprano, alto, tenor and bass moving together, one chord per melody note or two, each held until the next, no drums. The organ is the obvious instrument.

title: Hymn (four parts)
text:
A little history
Martin Luther’s chorales (from the 1520s) gave Protestant congregations hymns to sing; J. S. Bach’s four-part harmonisations of them in his cantatas and passions (1720s-40s) became the model of how to write harmony, and still are in theory classes. In England, Isaac Watts and Charles Wesley in the 1700s wrote the texts; the collection Hymns Ancient and Modern (1861) and The English Hymnal (1906, music edited by Ralph Vaughan Williams) set the four-part style of the Anglican hymnal. American hymnals, gospel song and shape-note singing grew from the same roots.

Bass: Held roots. Comping: hymn: three voices over the root. Drums: none.

title: Jump Blues
text: Open the Jump blues style in the Backing Track

title: Jump Blues
text:
What it is
Up-tempo blues for dancing, played by small bands of the 1940s: a rhythm section, two or three horns riffing together, and a singer. The bass plays the boogie-woogie left hand, the drums play a shuffle with a hard backbeat on 2 and 4, and the horns and piano play short riffs. It is the bridge from swing and boogie-woogie to rhythm and blues and rock and roll.

title: Jump Blues
text:
A little history
When the big bands became too costly during the Second World War, many of their players formed small groups that kept the swing bands’ riffs and the boogie-woogie bass but played them louder, on the backbeat, for dancers and jukeboxes. Louis Jordan and his Tympany Five were the most popular: Caldonia (1945) and Choo Choo Ch’Boogie (1946) topped the race-record charts, which Billboard renamed rhythm and blues in 1949. Big Joe Turner, Wynonie Harris, Roy Brown and Amos Milburn sang it; Lionel Hampton’s Flying Home gave it a honking tenor sax. By the early 1950s the same music, with an electric guitar in front, was being called rock and roll.

title: Jump Blues
text:
The band’s version

Bass: Boogie-woogie: swung eighths, root 3rd 5th 6th flat-7th 6th 5th 3rd.
Comping: Boogie-woogie right hand: a two-bar riff of short swung chords.
Drums: Jump blues: the shuffle on the cymbal, the kick feathered on every beat, a loud snare on 2 and 4.
Voicings: plain triads and seventh chords, all their notes.

The horns are what most people remember of a jump band, and the band has none. Play the riffs yourself, or sing.

title: Motown / soul
text:
What it is
The 1960s Detroit sound of Motown Records: a snare (often with a tambourine) hitting every beat, a busy electric bass, guitars chopping chords, and a song built for radio and dancing.

title: Motown / soul
text:
A little history
Berry Gordy started Motown in Detroit in 1959. Its records were cut by a house band later known as the Funk Brothers: drummer Benny Benjamin, bassist James Jamerson, pianist Earl Van Dyke, and others, playing in Studio A (“the Snakepit”). The songwriting team Holland-Dozier-Holland wrote the mid-’60s run of hits for the Supremes and the Four Tops, many on a stomping four-beat snare. Jamerson’s bass lines, played with one finger on a Fender Precision, moved far more than any pattern can show. The band played uncredited until the film Standing in the Shadows of Motown (2002).

title: Motown / soul
text:
The band’s version

Bass: Motown: root, fifth, octave, a stand-in for Jamerson’s lines.
Comping: the two-bar rhythm of You Can’t Hurry Love. Drums: snare on every beat.

title: John Prine Fingerpicking
text: Open the John Prine Fingerpicking style in the Backing Track

title: John Prine Fingerpicking
text:
What it is
A steel-string guitar played with the thumb and fingers at once: the thumb alternates between two bass strings on every beat while the fingers pluck the chord on the off-beats or pinch with the thumb. No drums, an upright bass doubling the thumb.

title: John Prine Fingerpicking
text:
A little history
Alternating-thumb picking runs back to Black guitarists in the South of the 1920s: Mississippi John Hurt recorded for OKeh in 1928, and Elizabeth Cotten played Freight Train left-handed. In Kentucky, Arnold Shultz, Ike Everly and Mose Rager handed it to Merle Travis, after whom “Travis picking” is named, and Chet Atkins spread it through country guitar. The 1960s folk revival brought it to singer-songwriters. John Prine (1946-2020), the Chicago postman whose first album (John Prine, 1971) contains Paradise, Hello in There and Angel from Montgomery, played a plain thumb-and-fingers style under plain-spoken songs.

title: John Prine Fingerpicking
text:

Comping: the prine and travis patterns. Bass: root and fifth with the thumb. Drums: none.

title: Ska / reggae
text: Open the Ska / reggae style in the Backing Track

title: Ska / reggae
text:
What it is
Jamaican popular music since about 1960: guitar and keyboard chords on the off-beats (the skank), a bass that carries the melody of the groove, and, in reggae, a one-drop drum beat with nothing on beat 1 and the kick and snare (or rim) together on beat 3.

title: Ska / reggae
text:
A little history
Ska (c. 1960-66) came from Jamaican musicians playing American R&B for sound systems and stressing the off-beat; studio bands such as the Skatalites played it fast with horns. Around 1966 the tempo slowed into rocksteady, with the bass more prominent (Alton Ellis, the Paragons). By 1968 the beat had changed again into reggae: Toots and the Maytals’ Do the Reggay (1968) is one of the first records to use the word. Drummer Carlton Barrett of Bob Marley’s Wailers made the one-drop the standard reggae beat, and Island Records’ Catch a Fire (1973) took the Wailers worldwide. Later strands include dub, roots, lovers rock, dancehall (see Reggaeton) and Britain’s 2 Tone ska revival (c. 1979).

Bass: Roots on every beat, plainer than a real reggae bass line, which moves and leaves gaps.

title: Straight-eighth rock
text: Open the Straight-eighth rock style in the Backing Track

title: Straight-eighth rock
text:
What it is
The basic rock band: drums with a snare backbeat on 2 and 4 and even eighth notes on the hi-hat, an electric bass on the root in eighths, and guitar strumming every eighth note.

title: Straight-eighth rock
text:
A little history
Rhythm and blues of the late 1940s and early ’50s was mostly shuffled (swung) eighths. Through the 1950s, records by Little Richard, Chuck Berry and Ray Charles mixed straight eighths in, and by the early 1960s even eighths were the norm in rock and soul; Alexander Stewart traces the shift through New Orleans drummers such as Earl Palmer. The backbeat came from gospel handclaps and R&B. The British Invasion, then punk’s down-stroke eighths (the Ramones, 1976) and new wave, kept the plain driving eighths at the centre of the style.

title: Straight-eighth rock
text:
The band’s version

Bass: Root eighths. Comping: down-up eighths on the guitar. Drums: a backbeat whose kick varies from bar to bar. Chords are pushed (they arrive an eighth early) the way rock bands do.

title: Acoustic strum
text:
A little history
The steel-string guitar became a popular accompanying instrument through country and blues players in the 1920s-30s and the folk revival of the 1950s-60s (Woody Guthrie, then Bob Dylan, Joan Baez). From the late 1960s singer-songwriters (James Taylor, Joni Mitchell, Cat Stevens) put a band around the strummed guitar. The 1990s Britpop and “unplugged” years (Oasis’s Wonderwall) and the 2000s-2010s folk-pop of Jason Mraz, Mumford & Sons and Ed Sheeran kept it among the most common sounds in pop.

text:
What it is
The dance music of Buenos Aires and Montevideo, in 2/4 or 4/4, played here on its oldest rhythm: the habanera (dotted eighth, sixteenth, two eighths), which also underlies the 3+3+2 of a lot of later pop.

title: Tango
text:
A little history
The habanera was a Cuban song and dance of the mid-1800s that spread through Spain, Mexico and the Río de la Plata ports (Bizet borrowed one for Carmen, 1875). In the poor neighbourhoods of Buenos Aires in the 1880s and ’90s it mixed with the milonga, Spanish and Italian song, and African Argentine candombe into the tango. Early groups were flute, violin and guitar; the bandoneón (a German button accordion) arrived around 1900 and became the tango’s voice. Carlos Gardel’s Mi noche triste (1917) began the sung tango. The 1940s orquestas típicas (Juan D’Arienzo, Aníbal Troilo, Osvaldo Pugliese) moved to a driving marcato in four; from the 1950s Astor Piazzolla’s nuevo tango added jazz and classical counterpoint.
The band plays the habanera rhythm, the older and more widely useful of tango’s rhythms; the four-beat marcato of the dance orchestras is not modelled.

title: Waltz (in one)
text:
What it is
A fast 3/4 in which the listener feels one beat a bar, not three: the bass on 1, light chords on 2 and 3, brushes, bars grouped in fours.

title: Waltz (in one)
text:
A little history
The waltz rose from Austrian and South German country dances in the late 1700s and took over the ballrooms of Vienna in the early 1800s with Joseph Lanner and the Strauss family (Johann Strauss II’s The Blue Danube, 1867). Played fast, the pulse is one per bar, and phrases come in fours and eights. The waltz then spread everywhere: music-hall and parlour songs, country waltzes (Tennessee Waltz), jazz waltzes, and many carols and folk songs that are sung in a quick 3/4.

title: Waltz (in one)

The band’s version

title: Beethoven: “Moonlight” Sonata, I
text:
The whole first movement (Adagio sostenuto). Triplets run under a slow melody throughout. The harmony changes slowly, usually once or twice a bar, so this is a good piece for following an analysis by ear. How to read the labels and use the score: Analysed Scores.
Things to find:
Above the score, the key strip shows every key the analysts name, in order: c♯, E, e, b, f♯ and home. Click a key to light its bars and hear them.
Analysis: Tsung-Ping Chen and Li Su (BPS dataset), proof-read by Mark Gotham.

title: Beethoven: “Moonlight” Sonata, I
text:
The form, part by part
The outline below summarises a published guide to the movement (a page headed “The Opus 27 Set”, p. 161). Press ▶ on a row to light those bars in the score above and hear them. “Upbeat to” means the part starts on the last beat of the bar before. The outline skips the first theme’s return at bar 42, where the recapitulation begins.








Bars
What happens




Exposition



1–4
Introduction: the right hand’s triplet figure is set going.


Upbeat to 5–14
The first theme, heard twice: first from c♯ minor to E major, then from e minor to b minor.


Upbeat to 16–23
The second theme, also twice, each time starting on a B major chord that sounds like a dominant of e minor that never resolves. The second statement is stretched to end the exposition with a cadence in f♯ minor.


Development



Upbeat to 24–27
The opening theme, now starting in f♯ minor, extended.


28–31
A three-note fragment, perhaps taken from the shape of the second theme.


32–42
Broken chords unfold: diminished seventh and tonic.


37–42
Retransition: a melodic fragment in the rhythm of the second theme. Some details here are disputed (the stemming in bar 37, and the uneven phrase lengths in bars 37–39).


Recapitulation



Upbeat to 52–60
The second theme, now starting on C♯ major. It sounds like an unresolved dominant of f♯ minor, but the section ends in the home key.


Upbeat to 61–69
Coda: the first theme in the left hand, and a quiet close.

title: Beethoven: “Moonlight” Sonata, I
text:
The modulations, one by one
The movement uses most of the kinds of modulation in Chapter 22. Click the bars to hear each one in the score. The Modulation page explains each kind with short examples. The readings are Chen and Su’s; where another analyst in When in Rome, Dmitri Tymoczko, hears it differently, the row says so.



Bars
From → to
How
Kind (Ch. 22)




▶ 5–9
c♯ → E
In bar 7 the F♯ minor chord, iv in c♯, is labelled ii in E: pre-dominant in the new key. E is confirmed by I⁶₄–V⁷–I (bars 8–9).
Diatonic pivot chord


▶ 9–10
E → e
Same tonic, and the G♯ becomes G♮. There is no pivot: the music simply turns minor.
Direct (a change of mode)


▶ 11–14
e → b
Bar 11 is V⁴₃/VI in e. The analysis turns to b in bar 12 on a G major chord, VI in b (it is also III in e), and b is confirmed by vii°⁷–V⁶₅–i and i⁶₄–V. Tymoczko hears V⁷/V in e become V⁷ in b instead.
Diatonic pivot chord; for Tymoczko, a secondary common chord


▶ 15–19
B major: b or e?
The B major chord of the second theme, taking turns with N6: V/iv in b, a tonicization of e. Nothing cadences in e, which is why the guide calls it a dominant that never resolves. Tymoczko calls it V in e, a modulation.
Tonicization or modulation?


▶ 19–23
→ f♯
f♯ is reached through its own vii°⁶₅ and V⁶₅ and confirmed by i⁶₄–V–i: an authentic cadence ends the exposition.
Direct (by the new key’s dominant)


▶ 23–27
f♯ → c♯
After V⁶₅ in f♯ (bar 24), the analysis is back in c♯ at bar 25. Tymoczko reads the f♯ minor chord in bar 25 as i in f♯ and iv in c♯, a pivot.
Direct; for Tymoczko, a diatonic pivot


▶ 42–51
c♯ → E → c♯
The recapitulation passes through E only briefly (bars 44–46) before the music returns home.
Compare with bars 5–9


▶ 52–60
C♯ major: f♯ or c♯?
The second theme returns a fourth higher, on C♯ major: V/iv, still in c♯. Tymoczko: V in f♯, back and forth.
Tonicization or modulation?

title: Harmony by the Numbers
text:
Chromatic chords in each repertoire
How many of every 100 chords are each kind of chromatic chord from the theory chapters (click a heading for its chapter). Darker means more, compared with the other repertoires in the same column.

Things to notice: applied dominants are the most common chromatic chord everywhere, and Romantic piano music uses them most. The Neapolitan and the augmented sixths are rare in every repertoire, about one chord in a hundred at most. Mixture hardly appears in Bach’s chorales but grows through the 19th century.

title: Harmony by the Numbers
text:
How this was counted

Labels, not time. A chord held for four bars counts the same as one lasting an eighth note.
Analysts differ. Most of the Bach chorales were analysed by one person (Dmitri Tymoczko), who marks a new key at most phrases; that is why the chorales show 38 key changes per 100 bars and Mozart under 4. Some of the difference between repertoires is the analysts’ and not the composers’.
Applied chords are V or vii° of another degree (V/V, vii°⁷/ii). Chords inside a tonicized key written that way (I/V, ii/V) are not counted as applied.
Mixture counts only in major keys: iv, i, v, ♭III, ♭VI, ♭VII, ii° / iiø⁷ and a fully diminished vii°⁷.
The cadential six-four is a label written Cad64, or I⁶₄ followed by V.
About 250 of the 186,000 labels could not be read and are left out.
Made by scripts/when-in-rome/stats.mjs. The numbers are counts of the analysts’ labels; the analyses have not been checked here.

title: Kodály: Dances of Galánta
text:
Zoltán Kodály (1882–1967) spent seven childhood years in Galánta, a small market town between Vienna and Budapest (now in Slovakia), where his father was stationmaster. There he first heard a Roma (Gypsy) band, “the first ‘orchestral’ sonority that came to the ears of the child”, as he later wrote. He returned there in 1905 on his first trip collecting folk songs. Dances of Galánta was written for the 80th anniversary of the Budapest Philharmonic Society and first played on 23 October 1933, conducted by Ernő Dohnányi.
With the score scrolling. Bar numbers on this page follow the corrected count: see the note on bar numbers.

title: Kodály: Dances of Galánta
text:
Verbunkos: slow, then fast
The piece is written in the style of verbunkos, a Hungarian dance first danced at army recruiting events in the 18th century to make life in the cavalry look glamorous. It has two halves:

Lassú (slow): rubato, dotted rhythms, an improvised feel. The senior officers danced first, slowly and with dignity.
Friss (fresh, fast): virtuoso and getting ever faster, as the youngest soldiers joined in with leaps and spur-clicking.

Verbunkos was not “Gypsy music”, but it was mostly Roma professional bands who played it, and their style (rubato, ornament, fiery violin playing) shaped how 19th-century composers wrote in the style hongrois: think of Liszt’s Hungarian Rhapsodies or Brahms’s Hungarian Dances. The csárdás, which grew out of verbunkos, has the same slow–fast plan.
Two accompaniment patterns to listen for:

Düvő: a note repeated in pairs, the second slightly longer, as a string player bows down-up (bar 285, lower strings).
Esztam: an off-beat “oom-pah”, the low instrument on the beat and a higher one off it (bars 94, 119, 147, 250).




Esztam in the score




Esztam




The clarinet cadenzas (bars 34 and 45, and again at the end) may imitate the tárogató, a Hungarian single-reed folk instrument.

title: Kodály: Dances of Galánta
text:
Where the tunes come from
Kodály didn’t use folk songs he had collected. The main themes come from books of Hungarian dances printed in Vienna around 1800, one of them “after several Gypsies from Galánta”, which he chose to keep that tradition alive. The guide labels the ten tunes he used A to J. He rarely quotes a whole tune at once: he splits them into parts, introduces the first part, and brings in the rest later.



The ten Viennese tunes, A–J

title: Kodály: Dances of Galánta
text:
The form
The form is famously hard to pin down. The published score calls it a slow rondo (bars 1–412) followed by a fast movement. Others call it a rondo with a very long finale. The guide this page comes from questions the score’s version: the music is already fast at bar 238 (♩ = 140), and most of the fast tunes are new Viennese tunes, not variants of the slow ones. Its reading is a verbunkos–rondo hybrid: a slow rondo whose refrain is Theme B, then a fast chain of new dances.

title: Kodály: Dances of Galánta
text:
Things to discuss

Listen to the opening and to bar 238. Which features of lassú and friss can you hear in each?
Choose one of the excerpts above. What did Kodály change in the old tune, and why might he have changed it?
Is the piece a rondo? Argue for or against the form table above.
Compare the clarinet cadenzas with a recording of a tárogató. What is Kodály imitating?

title: Kodály: Dances of Galánta
text:
Bar numbers
The Universal Edition score (UE 34121) misnumbers some bars: there are six bars between its printed 90 and 95, and between 130 and 135. To get the bar numbers used on this page, add 1 to printed numbers from 95 to 134, and 2 from 135 on (printed 140 is bar 142).

title: Modulation Finder
text:
Pick the mode of the starting key, the mode of the key it ends in, and how far apart the two tonics are, counted in half steps up from the first tonic (7 half steps: C major to G major, or A minor to E minor). The bars show how many examples there are at each distance; click one to list them. Each result shows the whole path of keys the analysis names, and plays like the scores on the book pages. How to read the labels: Analysed Scores.
There are two kinds of example. The textbook ones are written to show a modulation, a few chords long. The real pieces are short passages, two bars before a key change to three after, from Bach’s four-part chorales and from 19th-century songs; their headings give the bars, and the link opens the full analysis.

  
    Starts in major or minora major keya minor key
    Ends in major or minora major keya minor key
    From 
    Clear
  
  Distance from the first tonic up to the last, in half steps
  
  
  











NoteFor teachers






Which keys count: the start is the example’s first key and the end its last, as the book’s title names them where it does (Reger, Rimsky-Korsakov, Tchaikovsky and the textbooks’ own progressions); otherwise the analysis’s first and last keys. An example that goes out and comes back (Kostka 19-4, C → E♭ → G♭ → C) counts as 0 half steps; its path shows where it went.
Distance is counted up from the first tonic, so 7 is a 5th up or a 4th down. Enharmonic keys count the same (C to D♭ and C to C♯ are both 1).
Data: the textbook examples are written by scripts/when-in-rome/build.mjs with the book pages, so they always match them (Reger’s example 41 has no notes in the corpus and is left out). The passages from real pieces are written by scripts/when-in-rome/corpus.mjs to apps/shared/data/modulation-corpus.json, loaded after the page shows.
Which key changes become passages: the old key lasted at least 2 bars and the new one lasts at least 2, so a chord or two tonicizing a key is not counted; at most 2 a piece. A passage is kept only if the analysis fits its notes: at three quarters or more of the numerals, at least two of the chord’s notes are sounding. That threw out the passages whose bar numbers did not line up.
Analysts differ: the chorales are Dmitri Tymoczko’s analyses, which name a new key at most cadences; the songs are by contributors to the Working in Harmony app, proof-read by Mark Gotham. Some keys they name, a teacher might call a tonicization.
Left out of the songs: the words, and grace notes.

title: Chord Analysis, Step by Step
text:
This page teaches one method for working out the chords in a short passage of music, and gives you passages to practise on. The method is the same for every kind of music. What changes is how hard the notes are to find: a chord written as three stacked notes is easy to read, but a guitar chord, a four-part chorale or a melody with extra notes takes more work.
The exercises follow the chapters of Robert Hutchinson’s Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom. Chord symbols come first (Chapter 6), then Roman numerals (Chapter 7), then seventh chords (Chapter 8). The same exercises also appear on those chapter pages, under Analysis practice.

title: Chord Analysis, Step by Step
text:
The method
For each chord:

Collect the notes. Take every note that sounds from the chord’s number to the next number, on every staff.
Leave out the non-chord tones. These are short notes that step between chord tones, or step away from one and come back. They first appear in Stage 5.
Keep one of each. Cross out repeated letters, in any octave. A chord often doubles a note, and the doubling doesn’t change the chord.
Rearrange into close root position. Put the notes in the order where each one is a third above the one below: two letters apart, skipping one letter (C–E–G–B, D–F–A–C). The bottom note of that stack is the root.
Find the quality. Measure the 3rd, 5th (and 7th) above the root: major, minor, diminished or augmented; for sevenths, major 7th, dominant 7th, minor 7th, half-diminished or fully diminished.
Find the bass. The lowest note in the passage (not in your stack) tells you the inversion: root, 3rd, 5th or 7th in the bass.
Name it. A chord symbol (C, Am/C, G7), or a Roman numeral in the key (I, vi6, V7).

Every exercise below has a Steps button on each chord. It walks through these steps for that chord, one at a time.

title: Chord Analysis, Step by Step
section: Step 4: rearranging into close root position
text:
Step 4: rearranging into close root position
Step 4 is the one this page practises most. Rearranging a chord is just like solving a word puzzle: you know the letters, and you need the order where they all fit. Two quick ways to find that order:

Rotate. Write the notes from the lowest up. If they aren’t all thirds apart, move the bottom note to the top and look again. A triad needs at most two moves; a seventh chord, at most three.
Skip a letter. Start on any note and go up by skipping one letter each time (C, E, G, B, D, F, A, C …). The notes of the chord come up together, one after another; the first one of the run is the root.

Accidentals don’t change the order: E♭–G–B♭ stacks exactly as E–G–B does.
Ways to enter a stack. Choose one in each exercise’s Settings (Enter the stack by). All four give the same answer:

Stage 1: a piano right hand
