title: Chord Analysis, Step by Step
text:
Stage 2: guitar voicings
Guitar chords spread over five or six strings, so they double notes (the open-position E chord, E B E G♯ B E, has three Es) and reach below the staff on ledger lines. Guitar music is written an octave higher than it sounds (the treble clef with a small 8 under it means the same). The TAB under the staff gives the same notes as frets: one line a string, the high E string on top, 0 an open string, x a string not played. Read whichever is easier; they say the same thing.

title: Chord Analysis, Step by Step
text:
Stage 3: an SATB chorale
Four voices on two staves. In a chorale, soprano and alto share the top staff (stems up for the soprano, down for the alto) and tenor and bass share the bottom one. In keyboard style the tenor moves up into the treble staff with the soprano and alto, and the bass is alone. Choose either under SATB: the tenor. The bass is the bass voice; one note (usually the root) is doubled.

title: Chord Analysis, Step by Step
text:
Stage 4: broken chords
The right hand plays the chord one note at a time, over a bass note held in the left hand. Gather every note from the chord’s number to the next number. The bass note is still the lowest one.

title: Chord Analysis, Step by Step
section: Stage 5: a melody with non-chord tones
text:
Stage 5: a melody with non-chord tones
Now a melody sits over the chords: an Alberti bass (bottom, top, middle, top) or held chords. Most melody notes belong to the chord, but some short ones on the second half of a beat don’t. A passing tone steps between two chord tones (G–A–B over a G chord); a neighbor tone steps away and comes back (E–F–E). Leave them out before you stack. Chapter 10 of Hutchinson names the other kinds; the exercises here use only these two.

title: Chord Analysis, Step by Step
text:
Reports for your teacher
Every exercise on this page, the Analysis practice on the chapter pages, and every Theory Drill keep a record of what you do: each stack and name you check, right or wrong, the Steps you looked at, and whether you pressed Show the answers. My report shows it (today’s work, or everything), with each passage’s score. Type your name, then Print or save as PDF, or Copy the report to paste it into an assignment. Nothing is sent anywhere.
A copied report ends with a report code. Your teacher pastes it on the My Report page to see the same report with every answer, and to check that it wasn’t changed.

title: Chord Analysis, Step by Step
text:
What comes next
These steps are planned but not built yet. The checker already reads applied chords (V7/V) and the Neapolitan (N6), so most of the work is new progressions and new Steps text.

Chapter 9, function. After naming each chord, choose T, TP, PD or D (the book’s flowcharts, as in the Harmonic function drill), and name the cadence at the end.
Chapter 10, non-chord tones by name. Mark each non-chord tone and name it (passing, neighbor, suspension, appoggiatura, escape tone, anticipation), with accented ones on the beat. Stage 5 would add suspensions, which change what “the chord’s beats” means.
Chapter 16, figures. Answers in figures only (I6, V65), and the cadential 6/4 (I64 before V, Cad64 accepted).
Chapters 17–18, applied chords. A note outside the key: look at the next chord. A major chord or dominant 7th a 5th above it is V(7)/x; a diminished chord a half step below it is vii°(7)/x.
Chapter 19, mixture. ♭3, ♭6 or ♭7 in a major key: a chord borrowed from the parallel minor (iv, ♭VI, ♭VII, ii°, iiø7).
Chapters 20–21, the Neapolitan and augmented sixths. ♭2 in a major triad: N6. ♭6 in the bass with ♯4 above it: an augmented sixth, which doesn’t stack in thirds at all, so Step 4 changes to “find the augmented 6th”.







NoteFor teachers






Links: each exercise’s Copy a link to this passage gives a link to this page with that level, stage and passage (seed=). Everyone who opens it gets the same passage. Add &lock=1 to hide the settings.
Settings in a link: level (ch6a ch6b ch7a ch7b ch8a ch8b), texture (rh guitar satb broken melody mixed), task (both stack name), entry (tap staff rotate type), answer (auto sym rn), tenor (bass treble), mode, most (0–5), key (show find), rhythm (auto bar half).
What counts as right: a name is right when it means the same spelled notes over the same bass: I6 = I/3rd, V65 = V7/3rd, a = Am. Spelling counts (A♭ is not G♯). Root-position levels don’t ask for the bass, so a slash or a figure there isn’t needed.
The passages are made by the site from short progressions (the ones in the book’s chapters and common pop ones), in a random key. The voicings follow the stage, not the rules of part-writing: the SATB stage spaces the voices sensibly but isn’t checked for parallel fifths. Guitar shapes are found by a search for playable shapes in open position or a four-fret span (at most four fingers, no skipped strings); they’re common shapes but not always the most usual fingering. The answers and every drawn note are checked by a script for each level and stage (node tests/analysis/chord-analysis.test.js).
The text on this page is written for the site, not copied from the book (the book is under the GNU Free Documentation License).

title: Figured Bass: Practice for Chapter 16
text:
This page goes with Chapter 16, Figured Bass of Robert Hutchinson’s open textbook Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom. Read each section there first; the book is the reference for the terms used here. It builds on the Roman numerals of Chapter 7 and the seventh chords of Chapter 8, where inversions were written /3rd, /5th and /7th. From this chapter on, the book writes them with figures instead.
Every drill has Settings, and is also on the Theory Drills page. Click a section’s heading to fold it; the list on the right jumps to a section.
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Figured Bass: Practice for Chapter 16
text:
16.1 Historical context
In the Baroque era (roughly 1600–1750) a keyboard or lute player often read only a bass line with numbers under it, and filled in the chords. That shorthand is figured bass (also called thoroughbass). The numbers are intervals above the bass note, counted in the key signature. They say which notes to play, not how to space them, so players chose their own voicings, the way a pianist reading lead-sheet symbols does today. Modern editions often “realize” the figures: they write the chords out. Today theory classes use figured bass mostly as a shorthand for inversions, written after a Roman numeral. Read 16.1



Handel, Recorder Sonata in A minor, HWV 362, I. Larghetto (the book’s Figure 16.1.3)





Counting an interval: count letter names from the bass up to the note, counting both ends. From G up to E is G A B C D E, six letters: a 6th. Octaves don’t matter (a 13th still counts as a 6), and neither does which voice has the note.
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Figured Bass: Practice for Chapter 16

Pick a chord and a bass note. Each bracket on the staff runs from the bass to one of the notes above it, with the interval it makes. The figures under the bass are in the colour of the chord member they land on: root, 3rd, 5th, 7th. Faint figures in brackets are understood but not written. The short forms keep just the numbers that tell one position from another. Four rules from 16.2:

The figures go after the Roman numeral (I64, V65), not under the bass as in Baroque scores.
Compare the slash labels of earlier chapters: I/3rd = I6, I/5th = I64, V7/3rd = V65, V7/5th = V43, V7/7th = V42.
Since 6/5, 4/3 and 4/2 only ever mean seventh chords, an inverted seventh chord drops the 7: V65, not V7 65.
The quality signs stay: IM43 (a major seventh chord), viiø65, vii°42.

Given the numeral, write the notes, lowest first:



Without Roman numerals: count up from the lowest note and choose the figure.




What the numbers mean, the other way round
A Baroque player sees a bass note and figures and works out the notes: count each interval up from the bass, using the key signature’s sharps and flats. In C major, 6/4 over D is D, then a 4th up (G), then a 6th up (B): the G chord with its 5th in the bass. Type every note, bass first:

title: Figured Bass: Practice for Chapter 16
text:
16.3 The cadential six-four chord
The I64 that so often comes just before V at a cadence is called the cadential six-four. The bass stays on scale degree 5 for both chords, and the 6th and 4th above it fall to a 5th and a 3rd: really V with two notes delayed. So the book counts it as dominant function, like the V after it. Earlier chapters called it I/5th. Read 16.3



Mozart, Piano Sonata K. 331, I (the book’s Figure 16.3.1)






Key and Smith, “The Star-Spangled Banner” (the book’s Figure 16.3.2)





In the explorer, choose I, then 5th 6/4, then V, root 5/3: the bass doesn’t move; the C and E above it step down to B and D.
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Figured Bass: Practice for Chapter 16
text:
16.4 Other six-four chords
A six-four chord (the 5th in the bass) turns up in only four situations in classical music:

Cadential: I64 before V over the same bass note (16.3).
Passing: the bass moves by step through three notes, and the middle chord is a six-four (I – V64 – I6, the bass going 1–2–3).
Pedal: the bass repeats one note three times, and the middle chord is a six-four (I – IV64 – I over a held tonic).
Melodic bass: the bass has the tune, and when the tune lands on the chord’s 5th the chord is a six-four.

Read 16.4
Four chords, the second a six-four. Which kind? Watch (or hear) the bass:



By ear, and in minor keys too:
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Figured Bass: Practice for Chapter 16
text:
16.5 Additional information
In Baroque scores you’ll sometimes see every interval written out (6/5/3 for 6/5, 6/4/3 for 4/3). The short symbols are abbreviations of those; the table in 16.2 gives both. Figures in real music can also carry accidentals for notes outside the key signature, such as the raised leading tone in a minor key. An accidental with no number beside it means the 3rd above the bass. Roman-numeral analysis leaves these accidentals out. To see one, set the explorer to a minor key and choose V. Read 16.5
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Figured Bass: Practice for Chapter 16
text:
16.6 Practice exercises
Set Questions to 20 for a score. Practice exercises with answers (16.6)
The book’s exercise 1: triads, named with Roman numerals and figures (I64, vii°6, ii64). Type o for °.



Exercises 2 and 3: seventh chords (iii65, V42, IM43, IVM7). Type M for a major 7th, h for ø.



Exercise 4: write the chord from its numeral and figures.



Exercise 5 is an analysis of a Bach chorale, best done from the book’s score:



J. S. Bach, Chorale 175, “Jesus, meine Zuversicht” (the book’s Figure 16.6.1)











NoteFor teachers






Links with your settings: open a drill’s Settings, then Copy a link with these settings. Add &lock=1 for a test, &count=20 for a score. The explorer takes data-key, data-mode, data-chord (0 = tonic), data-seventh="1" and data-inv (0–3) to open on a given chord.
Answers accepted: the figures (I64, V65, IM43, viiø42) and the older slash labels (I/5th, V7/3rd) both count. An inverted seventh chord written with the 7 (V765) is not accepted, following 16.2.
Chords drilled: in minor, the book’s common set (i ii° III iv V VI VII vii°, and i7 iiø7 IIIM7 iv7 V7 VIM7 vii°7).
Realizing figures uses the key signature only, as 16.1 describes; the minor-key V comes out minor there, and the explorer shows the accidental a Baroque figure would add (a lone accidental for the 3rd).
The six-four drill’s voicings are this site’s own: IV – I64 – V – I (cadential), I – V64 – I6 – IV (passing, with a voice exchange between bass and alto), I – IV64 – I – V (pedal). The melodic-bass six-four is not drilled.
Checked: node tests/lessons/figured-drill.test.js generates about nine thousand questions and checks each by its own arithmetic: the figure is read from the sounding notes, realized notes count up the right number of letters in the key signature, each six-four type has the book’s bass shape (NEG=1 breaks the engine on purpose and must fail).
Not from the book (unverified against a source here): two common-practice statements are the site’s own: that a lone accidental in a figure means the 3rd above the bass (16.5 only shows that figures can carry accidentals), and that the cadential six-four’s 6th and 4th fall to a 5th and 3rd over the same bass (16.3 says only that it has dominant function).
Videos: the book’s YouTube links with its start and end times, each checked against YouTube.

title: Intervals from the Patterns You Sing
text:
This page goes with Chapter 5, Intervals of Robert Hutchinson’s open textbook Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom.
You already know this. Every tonal pattern you sing is made of intervals: do–mi, mi–so, so–do. An interval is the distance between two of those pitches. This chapter gives each distance a name.
A caution from Gordon. He argues that intervals should be learned in a tonality and keyality, not as bare distances: patterns of three to five pitches carry meaning, while an interval is only two, and C up to F sounds different in F than in C (Gordon 65). So on this page every interval starts as a pair of syllables inside a pattern you know.
Press ▶ to hear an example, or ▶ Sing to hear it sung on syllables. Click any heading to fold its section.
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Intervals from the Patterns You Sing
text:
5.1 Number: count the letters
Read 5.1
The number of an interval counts letters, including both ends: C to E is C D E, a 3rd. In syllables, count the same way: do re mi is a 3rd. The number doesn’t care about sharps or flats: C to E♭ and C to E♯ are both 3rds.
Melodic intervals are one note after the other (as you sing them); harmonic intervals sound together.
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Intervals from the Patterns You Sing
text:
5.2 Quality: major, minor, perfect
Read 5.2
The book’s method measures from the lower note, as if it were do of a major scale:

If the top note is in that major scale, the interval is major (2nds, 3rds, 6ths, 7ths) or perfect (unisons, 4ths, 5ths, octaves).
If the top note is a half step lower than that, a major interval becomes minor.

You already have this: think the lower note as do, sing up to the top note, and ask whether you passed through the major scale’s notes. Up from do, every interval is major or perfect:



The minor intervals come from inside your patterns. These are the ones you sing most:



Counting half steps also works and is a good check: m2 = 1, M2 = 2, m3 = 3, M3 = 4, P4 = 5, A4/d5 = 6, P5 = 7, m6 = 8, M6 = 9, m7 = 10, M7 = 11, P8 = 12.

Practise: name the interval
Start with the intervals up from do, then add the minor ones under Settings. Set Show to Sound only for ear training.
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Intervals from the Patterns You Sing
text:
5.3 Writing intervals
Read 5.3
To write “a M6 above F”: make F do, sing up to la (do re mi fa so la), and write the letter: F G A B♭ C D. For a minor interval, write the major one and lower the top note a half step: a m6 above F is D♭.
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Intervals from the Patterns You Sing
text:
5.4 Inversion
Read 5.4
Flip an interval by moving the bottom note up an octave. You already sing both halves: do up to mi is a M3, and mi up to do is a m6. The rules:

The numbers add to 9: a 3rd inverts to a 6th, a 2nd to a 7th, a 4th to a 5th.
Major ↔︎ minor, perfect stays perfect, augmented ↔︎ diminished.
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Intervals from the Patterns You Sing
text:
5.5 Augmented and diminished
Read 5.5
Make a major or perfect interval a half step larger and it is augmented. Make a minor or perfect interval a half step smaller and it is diminished. The one you already sing every day is between fa and ti: fa up to ti is an augmented 4th (three whole steps, the tritone), and ti up to fa is a diminished 5th. Both are 6 half steps. You hear it in the dominant seventh, so–ti–re–fa.
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Intervals from the Patterns You Sing
section: Bridging: from syllable pairs to names
text:
Bridging: from syllable pairs to names

Hear it in a pattern. Find the two pitches inside a tonal pattern you know.
Name the syllables. “Re up to fa.”
Count the letters for the number: re mi fa = 3rd.
Check the quality against do: from re, the major 3rd would be fa♯ (re is do of D major: D E F♯). Fa is a half step lower: minor 3rd.
Check by half steps if you’re unsure.
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Intervals from the Patterns You Sing
text:
Check yourself

Name the interval do up to la.
Name the interval la up to do.
Mi up to ti: number and quality?
Invert a M2. What do you get?
Write a m3 above G.







TipAnswers






Major 6th.
Minor 3rd (it’s the inversion of do–la).

title: Major Scales and Key Signatures: From Do to the Names
text:
This page goes with Chapter 2, Major Scales and Key Signatures of Robert Hutchinson’s open textbook Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom.
You already know this. You can sing in major tonality on movable do, find do on the staff, and read and write tonal patterns. This chapter adds no new sounds. It gives names to things you already hear and write. Each section below starts from what you know, then gives the textbook’s word for it.
Press ▶ to hear an example, or ▶ Sing to hear it sung on syllables. Click any heading to fold its section.
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Major Scales and Key Signatures: From Do to the Names

title: Major Scales and Key Signatures: From Do to the Names
text:
2.1 Half steps and whole steps
Sing the major scale up on syllables and listen to the size of each step. Two of them are smaller: mi–fa and ti–do. The book calls a small step a half step (on a keyboard, the very next key) and a big one a whole step (two half steps). Read 2.1



So the pattern of steps in every major scale is W W H W W W H. That isn’t a new rule to learn: it’s the shape of the scale you already sing, written down.
On the staff. In C, the half steps fall on E–F and B–C, where there is no black key between. That’s why C major needs no sharps or flats. Start the same pattern on another note and some letters have to change to keep the half steps on mi–fa and ti–do. That is all a key signature is.
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Major Scales and Key Signatures: From Do to the Names
text:
2.2 Scale degrees and their names
The book numbers the notes of the scale from do: 1̂ to 7̂. Each also has a name. Read 2.2

(The degree names are standard; Hutchinson’s own list is in 3.3 Scale Degree Names.)
You already sing tonic and dominant patterns: do–mi–so is a tonic pattern, so–ti–re a dominant pattern. Those words come from these degree names: the patterns are built on do (the tonic) and so (the dominant).
Do and the tonic. Usually the same note in major, but not always the same idea. Do is a syllable and moves with the keyality. Tonic is the resting tone of whatever key you are in. In minor you rest on la, and the book will call la the tonic of the minor key (Chapter 3).
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Major Scales and Key Signatures: From Do to the Names
text:
2.3 Key signatures are do signatures
You already find do from the key signature. Gordon calls a key signature a do signature: it shows where do is on the staff, and nothing more. The same signature can be major, minor, Dorian and so on, depending on which note the music rests on (Gordon 155–156). Read 2.3
The book reads a signature as the name of a major key, which is the same as asking “where is do?”:

Sharps: the last sharp is ti. Do is the next note up. Last sharp F♯ → do is G → G major.
Flats: the last flat is fa. Do is four notes down (or five up). With two or more flats, the second-to-last flat is do: B♭ E♭ → do is B♭ → B♭ major. One flat (B♭) → do is F.

Here is the same tune with three different do signatures. Your syllables stay the same, only the letters change:









Where the book and MLT disagree. Hutchinson reads three flats as “E♭ major or C minor”. Gordon reads it as do on E♭, and the music decides the rest: E♭ major if it rests on do, C minor if it rests on la, F Dorian if on re (Gordon 155–156). Both are right; the book names the two keys you’ll meet most often.

Practise: name the major key
Name the major key from the signature (that is, find do). Start with up to three sharps and flats in treble clef, then open Settings and add more.
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Major Scales and Key Signatures: From Do to the Names
text:
Bridging: from syllables to letters
The book expects you to write scales and key signatures from letter names. You can already write tonal patterns from a familiar do signature (Gordon 125). To get from there to the book’s tasks:

Name do. Look at the signature and say the letter of do aloud (“do is D”).
Sing, then spell. Sing do re mi fa so la ti do, and say each letter as you go: D E F♯ G A B C♯ D. If a letter sounds wrong for the syllable, it needs an accidental.
Check the half steps. mi–fa and ti–do should be the only neighbours with no key between them.
Go the other way. Given “write A♭ major”, put do on A♭, sing up, and write each letter. Then collect the accidentals: that’s the key signature.
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Time Signatures: Two Ways to Sort Them
text:
There are two common ways to sort meters. Classical theory reads the time signature and sorts by two questions: how many beats in a bar and how is each beat divided. Music Learning Theory (MLT) sorts by what you hear and move to: how the big beats are divided, and whether the big beats are all the same length. The two systems often give different names to the same music.
Click any heading to fold its section.
crumbs: Time Signatures: Two Ways to Sort Them

title: Time Signatures: Two Ways to Sort Them
text:
The classical grid: simple/compound × duple/triple/quadruple
Two questions, two words (Hutchinson, “Meter”):

How is the beat divided? Into two parts: simple. Into three parts: compound.
How many beats in a bar? Two: duple. Three: triple. Four: quadruple.





Duple (2 beats)
Triple (3 beats)
Quadruple (4 beats)




Simple (beat ÷ 2)
2/4, 2/2, 2/8
3/4, 3/8, 3/2
4/4, 4/2


Compound (beat ÷ 3)
6/8, 6/4, 6/16
9/8, 9/4
12/8, 12/4



The quick rule: if the top number is 6, 9 or 12, the meter is compound, and the beat is a dotted note. Divide the top number by 3 to get the number of beats: 6/8 has two dotted-quarter beats, so it is compound duple. Otherwise the top number is the number of beats: 3/4 is simple triple.
Meters that don’t fit the grid. Signatures such as 5/8 and 7/8 have beats of unequal length (5/8 is usually felt as 2+3 or 3+2 eighths; 7/8 as 2+2+3 or another order). Textbooks call these asymmetrical, irregular or complex meters, and the names vary from book to book (these names are from general use and not yet checked against a source).
The classical question: What does the time signature say? You can answer it by looking, without hearing the music.
crumbs: Time Signatures: Two Ways to Sort Them

title: Time Signatures: Two Ways to Sort Them
section: The MLT way: usual and unusual meter
text:
The MLT way: usual and unusual meter
Gordon builds meter from two layers you feel in your body: macrobeats (big beats; tap them with your heels) and microbeats (the smaller beats that divide them; tap them with your hands) (Gordon 175).

Usual meter: big beats all the same length
When the macrobeats are equal and come in pairs, the meter is usual. Then the question is how is each macrobeat divided? (Gordon 175–176):

Usual duple: each macrobeat divides into 2 microbeats. Chant: du de du de.
Usual triple: each macrobeat divides into 3 microbeats. Chant: du da di du da di.
Usual combined: some macrobeats divide into 2 and some into 3, while the macrobeats stay the same length.

(Rhythm syllables: Gordon 105.)


Unusual meter: big beats of different lengths
When the macrobeats are not all the same length, the meter is unusual. Now the question is how are the macrobeats grouped? (Gordon 179–180):

Unusual paired: two macrobeats in a group, one longer than the other. Five microbeats as 2+3 or 3+2, often written 5/8.
Unusual unpaired: three macrobeats in a group, of unequal lengths, such as 2+2+3, often written 7/8. Two of them form a pair and one is left over; the listener decides which.
Intact: in unusual paired intact and unusual unpaired intact meters, the macrobeats are felt without being divided into microbeats.

Gordon sums up the difference: “In usual meter, microbeats establish meter, and macrobeats establish tempo. In unusual meter, macrobeats establish meter, and microbeats establish tempo” (Gordon 180).


The meter is heard, not read
Gordon says “there is no direct relation between notation, particularly measure signatures and meter.” He calls the textbook label of 6/8 as “duple compound meter” “inaccurate”: in 6/8 you hear two macrobeats, each divided into three, which is usual triple (Gordon 176). Three more things that, for Gordon, do not change the meter (Gordon 176–177):

Tempo: fast or slow macrobeats are still the same meter.
Accents: a waltz is usual triple whichever beats a dancer or band accents.
Smaller divisions: sixteenth-note triplets in 2/4 don’t make it triple; sixteenths in 6/8 don’t make it duple.

The MLT question: Move to it. Are the big beats equal? Then how many small beats fit in each? You answer it by listening and moving, before you have seen any notation.
crumbs: Time Signatures: Two Ways to Sort Them

title: Time Signatures: Two Ways to Sort Them
section: The two systems side by side
text:
The two systems side by side
The same signatures, sorted both ways. The MLT column is what you would usually hear; for Gordon the music, not the signature, decides.

The key difference:

In classical names, duple / triple / quadruple counts beats in a bar, and simple / compound names how each beat divides.
In MLT names, duple / triple names how each macrobeat divides (that is, what classical theory calls simple and compound), and paired / unpaired counts macrobeats in a group, which only matters when they are unequal.

So the classical word triple and the MLT word triple answer different questions. “Simple triple” (3/4) and “compound duple” (6/8) are different meters in classical theory, but both are usual triple in MLT.

title: Mode Mixture: Practice for Chapter 19
text:
This page goes with Chapter 19, Mode Mixture of Robert Hutchinson’s open textbook Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom. Read each section there first; the book is the reference for the terms used here. It follows Chapter 18, Secondary Diminished Chords, and uses the Roman numerals of Chapter 7 and the seventh chords of Chapter 8.
Every drill has Settings, and is also on the Theory Drills page.
Typing a borrowed chord: case and the sign after the numeral give the quality, as always: iv, ii°, iiø7, vii°7, ♭VI, ♭VII7. Type b for ♭ (bVI), o for °, h for ø. Inversions take the figures 6 and 64 for triads, 65, 43 and 42 for seventh chords: iv6, ♭VI64, iiø65, vii°42.

title: Mode Mixture: Practice for Chapter 19
text:
19.1 Mode mixture
Mode mixture means using, in a major key, chords that belong to the parallel minor (the minor key on the same tonic). The book also calls them borrowed chords. You spot them by their lowered notes: most often ♭6̂ (A♭ in C major), sometimes ♭3̂ (E♭) and ♭7̂ (B♭). Listen for the sudden darkening when a minor-key chord appears in a major-key passage. Read 19.1






NoteListen: the book’s examples








Lennon–McCartney, “Blackbird”

Richard Strauss, Also sprach Zarathustra: a second borrowed chord

Hoyt Axton, “Joy to the World”: the same bass line

Radiohead, “Creep”: IV, then the borrowed iv

title: Mode Mixture: Practice for Chapter 19
text:
19.3 Analysing and writing borrowed chords
Analysing a borrowed chord is easier than analysing a secondary chord: there is no slash. You give its root, quality and inversion, as for any chord. The book’s example: in G major, the notes C–E♭–G–A stack in thirds as A–C–E♭–G. The root is A (2̂), the thirds are m3–m3–M3, so it is half-diminished, and C (the 3rd) is in the bass: iiø65.
To write one, read the numeral’s quality carefully. The ♭ in ♭VI means the root is a half step below the major key’s 6̂; it does not mean “write a flat”. In A major, 6̂ is F♯, so ♭VI is built on F♮: F–A–C. Read 19.3
Name the chord on the staff:



With inversions. Stack it in thirds to find the root, then read the bass for the figure:



Write it, lowest note first:

title: Mode Mixture: Practice for Chapter 19
text:
19.4 The deceptive cadence with ♭VI
The usual deceptive cadence goes V–vi. Going instead to the major chord on ♭6̂, V–♭VI, is a stronger surprise. The book’s examples are endings of “The Star-Spangled Banner” as sung at Super Bowls and inaugurations, where ♭VI then moves to ♭VII and I. Read 19.4






NoteListen: the book’s examples








“The Star-Spangled Banner”, Whitney Houston, Super Bowl 1991






“The Star-Spangled Banner”, Beyoncé, Presidential Inauguration 2013






“The Star-Spangled Banner”, Lady Gaga, Super Bowl 2016








By ear: the phrase is I, then IV or ii, then V, then either vi or ♭VI. Which one? (The staff appears after you answer.)

title: Mode Mixture: Practice for Chapter 19
text:
19.5 The Picardy third
Borrowing the other way, from major into minor, is rare. The one common case is the last chord of a minor-key piece: a major I instead of i. Its raised 3rd is the Picardy third. The book notes it was most common in the Baroque, and is still used now and then. Read 19.5



J. S. Bach, French Suite No. 1 in D minor, BWV 812, Sarabande





A minor-key phrase, i, then iv or VI, then V, then the tonic. Does it end minor or major?
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

19.6 Everything together
All borrowed chords, all positions. Set Questions to 20 for a score. Practice exercises with answers (19.6)

The book’s exercise 2, writing:

Links with your settings: open a drill’s Settings, then Copy a link with these settings. Add &lock=1 for a test, &count=20 for a score.
Chords drilled: the book’s Figures 19.2.1 and 19.2.2: i, ii°, iiø7, ♭III, iv, v, ♭VI, ♭VII, ♭VII7 and vii°7, in major keys, plus iv7, which is not in those figures. Pick any of them under Settings → Chords. Every one has at least one note outside the key signature, and no two of them, nor any diatonic chord of the major key, have the same spelled notes, so each question has one answer. Keys that would need a double flat for a chord are skipped for that chord.

Ear drills: four chords, one a bar, root in the bass and a close triad above. The deceptive cadence drill is I, IV or ii, V, then vi or ♭VI; the Picardy drill is i, iv or VI, V, then i or I.

title: Modulation: Practice for Chapter 22
text:
This page goes with Chapter 22, Modulation of Robert Hutchinson’s open textbook Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom. Read each section there first; the book is the reference for the terms used here. Everything on this page plays: the examples are written out in four parts with the Roman numerals under the bass, and a pivot chord shows both of its numerals, the old key’s above the new one’s (the book draws a bracket). Each section folds from its ▾; the list on the right jumps to any of them.
The examples use the numerals of Chapter 7, the functions of Chapter 9 (T tonic, TP tonic prolongation, PD pre-dominant, D dominant), and the chromatic chords of Chapters 17, 19 and 20. Analysed Scores has a whole movement full of modulations to listen to: see the last section.
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Modulation: Practice for Chapter 22
text:
22.1–22.2 Tonicization or modulation?
A modulation moves the music to a new key and stays there long enough to make it the key: in the book’s words, it needs an eventual cadence that confirms the new key, often the full pre-dominant – I⁶₄ – V – I formula. A tonicization only borrows a chord’s dominant for a moment (V/V – V, from Chapter 17) and the home key never goes away.
Telling them apart is not always easy. A short passage ending with an authentic cadence in a new key could be either, and analysts disagree. The book’s method: find the cadence in the new key, then work backwards to the point where the new key’s chords begin; that is where to look for the pivot.
Hear the difference. Both start in C. The first touches G (V/V – V) and comes home; the second goes to G and confirms it with a cadence.






In the Moonlight: the B major chord at the start of the second theme (bars 15–19) is read both ways by two analysts in When in Rome: Chen and Su (on Analysed Scores) call it V/iv in B minor, a tonicization; Dmitri Tymoczko calls it V in E minor, a modulation. Nothing ever cadences in E minor. See and hear it.
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Modulation: Practice for Chapter 22
text:
22.3 Key relationships
Closely related keys have key signatures that differ by at most one sharp or flat. Every key has five: its relative major or minor, and the keys one sharp and one flat away, with their relatives. Any other key is foreign (distantly related). Classical composers most often go from a major key to its dominant and from a minor key to its relative major.
Pick a home key, then click any of its relatives to hear a modulation there (the page finds a pivot chord for it; see 22.4).
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Modulation: Practice for Chapter 22
text:
22.4 Modulations with diatonic pivot chords
A pivot (common) chord belongs to both keys: the same root, spelled the same, and the same quality. It is heard first in the old key and then reheard in the new one. Find candidates by listing the diatonic triads of both keys and matching them.
The book’s advice on choosing one:

a pivot that is pre-dominant in the new key (ii, IV, ii°, iv) makes the smoothest move;
one that is dominant in the new key is usually avoided: the change sounds abrupt;
in the old key the pivot is often tonic or tonic prolongation (I, vi, iii).

Choose two keys. Shared chords are highlighted, with each one’s function in both keys; Pivot ▶ writes out and plays a modulation through that chord, confirmed by a cadence in the new key. Try C to G, C to a minor, c♯ minor to E major (the Moonlight’s first move), and C to F♯ (no common chords).






In the Moonlight: bar 7. The F♯ minor chord is iv in c♯ minor and ii in E major, pre-dominant in the new key, followed by I⁶₄ – V⁷ – I in E. See and hear it. In Tymoczko’s reading, the f♯ minor chord in bar 25, i in f♯, becomes iv in c♯ on the way home.
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Modulation: Practice for Chapter 22
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Modulation: Practice for Chapter 22
text:
22.6 Modulations with chromatic pivot chords
A pivot can be chromatic in one or both keys, which lets the music reach keys that share few or no diatonic chords.
Secondary common chord: a secondary chord in both keys.



Borrowed common chord: a chord borrowed from the parallel mode (Chapter 19) in one key, ordinary in the other. The book’s example is from Beethoven’s Op. 110: a borrowed i⁶ in D♭ major, respelled as C♯ minor, becomes vi⁶ in E major.



Neapolitan common chord: the Neapolitan can link distantly related keys.



Augmented sixth common chord: an augmented sixth chord reheard as a dominant seventh (or the other way round) is an enharmonic modulation, the subject of the book’s next chapter.
In the Moonlight: bars 11–14. Tymoczko hears V⁷/V in E minor become V⁷ in B minor, a secondary common chord. (Chen and Su, on Analysed Scores, turn to B minor on a G major chord, III in E minor and VI in B minor.) See and hear it.
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Modulation: Practice for Chapter 22
text:
22.7 Modulations without pivot chords
Direct modulation (also called phrase modulation): a phrase ends in one key and the next simply starts in another, with no pivot. The book’s example is Schubert’s “Kriegers Ahnung”: a half cadence in C minor, then straight into A♭ major.



Common-tone modulation: two chords from different keys are joined by a single shared note, held while the rest moves. It often links chromatic mediants: chords whose roots are a third apart, of the same quality (both major or both minor), that share just one note. C major and E major share only E.



Sequential modulation: a passage and its harmony are repeated at a new pitch, and the repetition settles in (or leads to) a new key. The book cites Mozart’s Oboe Concerto, K. 314, III, which moves up by step from C major to D major to E minor.



In the Moonlight: bars 9–10. E major turns into E minor with no pivot: a direct change of mode. See and hear it.
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Modulation: Practice for Chapter 22
text:
Which kind is it?
An example in a random key, without its numerals. Listen, look at where the key signature changes and what is happening just before it, and choose. The numerals appear once you answer.
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Modulation: Practice for Chapter 22
text:
In the Moonlight Sonata
The first movement of Beethoven’s Op. 27 No. 2 travels from c♯ minor to E major, E minor, B minor and F♯ minor before coming home, and it uses almost every kind of modulation on this page. Analysed Scores has the whole movement with Chen and Su’s Roman numerals, a strip of the keys they hear, the form part by part, and a table of every modulation with links that play each one.



Bars
Move
Kind




5–9
c♯ → E
Diatonic pivot: iv = ii


9–10
E → e
Direct, a change of mode


11–14
e → b
Diatonic pivot: III = VI (Chen and Su); secondary common chord (Tymoczko)


15–19

NoteFor teachers






The examples are this site’s, not the book’s (the book’s are recordings and score images), each written in four parts: the bass, and three upper voices that move as little as possible from chord to chord. They are not checked for every part-writing rule. The quiz transposes them to any key that needs no double sharps or flats and no more than six sharps or flats.
Common chords are the diatonic triads only. Minor keys list i ii° III iv v V VI VII vii° (both forms of the dominant and of the 7th degree), so a chord made from the natural minor counts. A pivot is chosen automatically for the closely related key buttons: pre-dominant in the new key if possible, never dominant there.
Functions follow Chapter 9: I and i are T; vi, VI, iii and III are TP; IV, iv, ii and ii° are PD; V, v, vii° and VII are D. The book treats VII in minor and iii in major more carefully than this table does.
The Moonlight links open Analysed Scores with the bars lit; press ▶ there (or the bar links in its modulation table) to hear them.

Tymoczko, Dmitri, analyst. Roman-numeral analyses of the Bach chorales and of Beethoven, Piano Sonata Op. 27 No. 2, in When in Rome. github.com/MarkGotham/When-in-Rome/tree/master/Corpus. The chorale’s analysis; his readings of the Moonlight are quoted where they differ from Chen and Su’s.

title: Non-Chord Tones: Practice for Chapter 10
text:
This page goes with Chapter 10, Non-Chord Tones of Robert Hutchinson’s open textbook Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom. Read each section there first; the book is the reference for the terms used here. It builds on Chapter 6, Triads and Chapter 9, Harmonic Progression.
How the drills work: each one shows two bars of melody over chords (the chords are also in the bass clef) and plays them. One note of the melody is marked *: it is not in the chord under it. Name it with the buttons or a key (shown under each drill). After you answer, the drill says whether it was accented and how it was approached and left. Each section adds the new type to the ones before. Every drill has Settings (keys, minor, hiding the chord symbols), and is also on the Theory Drills page.
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Non-Chord Tones: Practice for Chapter 10
text:
10.1 What a non-chord tone is
A non-chord tone (also called an embellishing or non-harmonic tone) is a note that is not part of the chord sounding with it. The book names nine kinds, told apart by how the note is approached and how it is left: by the same note, by a step, or by a leap.








Non-chord tone
Approached by
Left by




Passing tone
step
step in the same direction


Neighbor tone
step
step in the opposite direction (back to the first note)


Appoggiatura
leap
step


Escape tone
step
leap in the opposite direction


Double neighbor
step
two non-chord tones, one each side of a chord tone, then back to it


Anticipation
step
the same note (it arrives early, before its chord)


Pedal point
the same note
the same note (held while the chords change)


Suspension
the same note
step down


Retardation
the same note
step up



Words that can go in front of any of them: accented (on the beat) or unaccented (off the beat); chromatic (outside the key); and metrical, sub-metrical or super-metrical (as long as a beat, shorter, longer). Read 10.1 · Open Music Theory: Embellishing Tones
Learn the table first. This is the book’s exercise 1, as a drill:



To find one in music: name the chord, then go through the melody note by note asking “is this in the chord?” For each note that is not, look at the note before and the note after.
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Non-Chord Tones: Practice for Chapter 10
text:
10.2 Passing tones
A passing tone fills the gap between two chord tones a third apart, moving by step in one direction. Two passing tones in a row can fill a fourth (from the root down to the fifth, say). Most are unaccented; an accented one lands on the beat and moves on to the chord tone. Read 10.2






Jason Derulo, “Want to Want Me”: an unaccented passing tone, then an appoggiatura, then an accented passing tone






Herman Hupfeld, “As Time Goes By”: two passing tones in a row






Thelonious Monk, “Blue Monk”: chromatic passing tones
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Non-Chord Tones: Practice for Chapter 10
text:
10.3 Neighbor tones
A neighbor tone steps away from a chord tone and steps straight back to it: an upper neighbor above, a lower neighbor below. Read 10.3






Beethoven, Minuet in G, WoO 10 No. 2
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Non-Chord Tones: Practice for Chapter 10
text:
10.4 Appoggiatura
An appoggiatura is reached by a leap and left by a step. It is usually on the beat, which is what makes it so expressive: the dissonance is the strong note and the resolution the weak one. The leap and the step can go either way; the drills use the most common shape, the step going back against the leap. Read 10.4






Horner and Jennings, “My Heart Will Go On” (Céline Dion): an appoggiatura, and an anticipation






Bruce Springsteen, “Born to Run”






Mozart, Symphony No. 40, K. 550, II: two appoggiaturas that resolve up
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Non-Chord Tones: Practice for Chapter 10
text:
10.5 Escape tone
An escape tone is the appoggiatura turned around: a step away from a chord tone, then a leap the other way. It is usually unaccented. The word “of” in “home of the brave”, at the end of “The Star-Spangled Banner”, is one. Read 10.5






“The Star-Spangled Banner”: listen for “of”






Haydn, Piano Sonata in C, Hob. XVI:35, III: escape tones in a sequence






Paul and Linda McCartney, “Silly Love Songs” (Wings)
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Non-Chord Tones: Practice for Chapter 10
text:
10.6 Double neighbor
A double neighbor (or neighbor group) visits both neighbors, upper and lower in either order, before returning to the chord tone. Two non-chord tones in a row, so it is easy to mistake for an escape tone followed by an appoggiatura: keep track of which notes are in the chord. (The drills mark both notes.) Read 10.6






Kuhlau, Sonatina in C, Op. 55 No. 1, I






Mozart, Piano Sonata K. 333, I. The book’s question: how would you analyse the harmony and the non-chord tones on beat 4 of the first bar? Look at its Figure 10.6.3 while you listen.
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Non-Chord Tones: Practice for Chapter 10
text:
10.7 Anticipation
An anticipation sounds a note of the next chord just before that chord arrives, so it is heard twice: early (a non-chord tone) and on time (a chord tone). It is common at cadences, and syncopated pop melodies are full of them. Read 10.7






Handel, Rinaldo, “Lascia ch’io pianga”: an anticipation at the cadence






Harry and Moroder, “Call Me” (Blondie): syncopated anticipations at the ends of bars 1, 2 and 3
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Non-Chord Tones: Practice for Chapter 10
text:
10.8 Pedal point
A pedal point is a note held (or repeated) while the chords change around it. It starts as a chord tone, becomes a non-chord tone when the harmony moves away, and usually ends as a chord tone again. Pedals are most often in the bass (the name comes from the organ’s foot pedals), where they make the chord’s inversion not worth naming; they can also be in an upper voice, as in the drills, or two at once (a double pedal, often a fifth apart). Read 10.8






Bach, Well-Tempered Clavier I, Prelude in C, BWV 846: the bass holds one note while the chords change






Clara Schumann, “Sie liebten sich beide”, Op. 13 No. 2: a pedal point, and a 3-2 suspension
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Non-Chord Tones: Practice for Chapter 10
text:
10.9 Suspension
A suspension holds a note over from one chord into the next, where it no longer fits, then resolves down by step. It has three parts: the preparation (a chord tone), the suspension (the same note, now dissonant, on the beat) and the resolution. The preparation is often tied to the suspension.
Suspensions are named by two intervals above the bass: the suspended note, then its resolution, with compound intervals reduced: 4-3, 7-6, 9-8 (kept as 9, not 2), 6-5, and 2-3, the bass suspension, measured from the bass up to an upper voice. With an inverted chord you will meet other numbers (5-4, 3-2). The drill’s feedback names the figure. Read 10.9 · Open Music Theory: Embellishing Tones






Samuel Barber, Adagio for Strings: a 4-3 suspension






Handel, Water Music Suite No. 2 in D, HWV 349, Alla Hornpipe: 7-6 and 9-8 suspensions






Bach, “Liebster Jesu, wir sind hier”, BWV 373: a 2-3 (bass) suspension






Bach, French Suite No. 1 in D minor, BWV 812, Sarabande: decorated suspensions (other notes before the resolution), and a retardation
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Non-Chord Tones: Practice for Chapter 10
text:
10.10 Retardation
A retardation is a suspension that resolves up by step. Like a suspension it is held over and usually on the beat. Classical composers liked both at cadences in slow movements. Read 10.10






Mozart, Piano Sonata in C, K. 545, II
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Non-Chord Tones: Practice for Chapter 10
text:
10.11 Incomplete neighbor
Real music does not always fit the table. A note may have two good explanations, or none. The book’s catch-all is the incomplete neighbor: a neighbor tone with one side missing. Keep an open mind, and say what you hear. (It is not in the drills, because the book leaves it loosely defined.) Read 10.11



Puccini, Gianni Schicchi, “O mio babbino caro”
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Non-Chord Tones: Practice for Chapter 10

10.12 Everything together
All nine kinds, major and minor. Set Questions to 20 for a score. Practice exercises with answers (10.12)

What the drills write: two bars of 4/4, a melody over three chords (two in the first bar, one in the second) taken from short diatonic progressions (I–V–I, ii–V–I, I–vi–V, i–iv–i, …), with the chords as close triads in the bass clef. Every melody note is a chord tone except the marked one (two for a double neighbor). Unaccented tones are eighth notes off the beat; accented ones fall on beat 1 or 3 (a double neighbor is two quarter notes, beats 2 and 3). Pedal points are a held tonic in the melody over I–IV–V–I (or I–vi–V–I, i–iv–V–i).
Not drilled: chromatic non-chord tones (the melodies stay in the key; in minor, the leading tone is raised only over V), appoggiaturas whose step goes the same way as the leap, incomplete neighbors, and bass pedals and bass (2-3) suspensions. The text covers them.

title: Form in Popular Music: Practice for Chapter 12
text:
This page goes with Chapter 12, Form in Popular Music of Robert Hutchinson’s open textbook Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom. Read each section there first. The book draws on John Covach’s essay “Form in Rock Music” and analyses real songs with timings. Here, the site’s backing band plays each form on made-up chord progressions, so you can hear how it is built without a melody or lyrics.
How the demos work: press ▶ Play. The strip at the bottom of the page shows the bar and the section the band is in (“Bar 9 · A2”). Each demo shows its chord grid with the sections labelled, the whole form at once (or one section at a time: pick it above the grid). The bar being played lights up. The buttons change the form; the band starts the new one from bar 1. As soon as the band starts, what it will play the whole way through is written out under the grid, section by section, so you can read ahead. Most forms here are 32 bars, about a minute at this tempo. Listen through at least once.
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Form in Popular Music: Practice for Chapter 12
text:
12.1 Verse–chorus form
The most common form in popular music today. The chorus has the hook, the part everyone remembers. The verses have different words each time and usually a less memorable tune. Songs often add an introduction, a pre-chorus (leading into the chorus), a post-chorus, and a bridge (something new, usually once, late in the song). The book also notes that people disagree about what to call some sections, and that is normal. Read 12.1
The book separates simple verse–chorus form (the verse and chorus use the same chord progression, so only the melody and words tell them apart) from contrasting verse–chorus form (the chorus has its own progression). Here are both, as verse, chorus, verse, chorus:



In the simple form, nothing in the chords tells you where the chorus starts. The singer’s melody and the words would do that, and a band usually plays the chorus fuller and louder. In the contrasting form you can hear the change of progression at bar 9.
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Form in Popular Music: Practice for Chapter 12
text:
12.2 AABA form
The form of Broadway and the Great American Songbook from the 1930s to the 1950s, and of many 1960s songs (the book names “Yesterday” and “Hey Jude”). There are four sections of eight bars. The A section is the main tune and comes three times. B, the bridge or “middle eight”, is the contrast. The whole 32 bars is sometimes called the refrain or chorus, and some songs put a verse in front of it. Read 12.2



Notice where the bridge goes: it leaves C, moves through other keys (E7 to Am, D7 to G), and ends on G7, the V chord. That makes the return of A sound like coming home.
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Form in Popular Music: Practice for Chapter 12
text:
12.3 ABAC form
Also 32 bars of four eight-bar sections, but the A section comes back only once, halfway through. The book’s examples are “White Christmas”, “Someday My Prince Will Come”, “When I Fall in Love” and “Star Dust”. It also notes ABAB′, where the last section starts like B and ends differently. Read 12.3



The first A ends on G7, so it is open and leads on. Only C, the last section, really ends.
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Form in Popular Music: Practice for Chapter 12
text:
12.4 The 12-bar blues
Twelve bars in three lines of four: I I I I | IV IV I I | V IV I I. It started in the blues in the early 1900s and was carried into swing (“In the Mood”) and early rock and roll (“Johnny B. Goode”, “Hound Dog”, “Rock Around the Clock”). The book’s table is “Johnny B. Goode”. Read 12.4 · The site’s blues lessons go further: the quick change, turnarounds and the jazz blues.
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Form in Popular Music: Practice for Chapter 12
text:
12.5 Harmonically closed and open sections
A section is closed when it ends on the tonic chord (I) and open when it ends somewhere else, usually V and sometimes IV. Open sections lead on to the next section; closed sections can end the song. Read 12.5
Typical places, from the book:



Form

Usually open




AABA

B (the bridge), ending on V


Verse–chorus

verse, pre-chorus, bridge



The same eight bars, closed and then open. Only the last two bars change:

title: Form in Popular Music: Practice for Chapter 12
text:
Quizzes
Open or closed? The band plays one eight-bar section, in different keys, again and again. Does it end on I or not?



Which form? The band plays a whole form, chords only. Listen for what comes back and when, then choose. The section names appear in the strip at the bottom once you have answered.
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Form in Popular Music: Practice for Chapter 12
text:
12.6 Practice: real songs
The book’s exercise asks for a timeline of two songs: when each section starts, what it is, and how many bars it lasts. Its answers are in 12.6. Do the same with any song you know well:

Start a timer with the song. Write the time each time something new starts.
Count bars: count the beats in fours, and add a mark for every 1.
Name each section. Which one has the hook? Which one comes back with the same words? Which comes once?
Mark each section open or closed. Does it end on the home chord?

The site’s Timestamp Notes tool keeps timed notes against a recording, if you want to save your timeline.






NoteFor teachers






The band: every demo and quiz runs on the site’s Backing Track band. The progressions are made up for this page, not taken from songs. AABA and ABAC share their bridge so that the only difference is the order of the sections.
The quizzes: Open or closed plays one of five eight-bar sections for each answer, in C, G, F, D or A. Which form plays one chart for each form, in C. So once students know the charts, they can recognize them rather than the form. Use it for listening practice, not as a test.
Section names: the strip at the bottom shows the section while the band plays (in a quiz, only after the answer).
Not here: intros, pre-choruses, post-choruses and codas, and the book’s song timelines (the songs are under copyright). The book’s chapter has no video clips.
Not checked by ear: the demos were checked by a test that plays each one and checks the notes are written out. Whether they sound convincing has not been checked by listening.

title: Rhythm Notation from Du De: Note Values and Time Signatures
text:
This page goes with Chapter 4, Basics of Rhythm of Robert Hutchinson’s open textbook Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom.
You already know this. You move to macrobeats and microbeats, chant rhythm patterns on du de (usual duple) and du da di (usual triple) (Gordon 86, 105), and read and write those patterns. This chapter gives the textbook’s names for the symbols you already read. Gordon’s warning applies: a player who only knows the time-value names “resort[s] to counting”, and the tempo and meter suffer (Gordon 38). So keep chanting: the names are for talking about the notation, not for performing from it.
Press ▶ to hear an example. Click any heading to fold its section.
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Rhythm Notation from Du De: Note Values and Time Signatures
section: What you know → what the book calls it
text:
What you know → what the book calls it

title: Rhythm Notation from Du De: Note Values and Time Signatures
text:
4.1 and 4.4 Time signatures and meter
The book reads the time signature as two numbers: how many beats in a bar, and what kind of note gets the beat. Read 4.1 · Read 4.4
The two systems sort meters differently, and this is the one place in the chapter where they disagree. The full comparison is on Meter: Two Ways to Sort Time Signatures. The short version:

Simple meter (2/4, 3/4, 4/4): each beat divides in 2. You chant it du de: usual duple.
Compound meter (6/8, 9/8, 12/8): each beat divides in 3. You chant it du da di: usual triple.
The book’s duple / triple / quadruple counts beats in a bar. Your duple / triple names how each beat divides. So 6/8 is “compound duple” in the book and “usual triple” to you (Gordon 176).
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Rhythm Notation from Du De: Note Values and Time Signatures
section: 4.2 Note values: naming what you chant
text:
4.2 Note values: naming what you chant
Here is one bar of usual duple in 2/4 and one of usual triple in 6/8, with your syllables under the notes. Read 4.2






In 2/4 you chant
The book’s name

In 6/8 you chant
The book’s name

The thing to notice: in 2/4 the macrobeat is a quarter note; in 6/8 it is a dotted quarter. That is why compound meters need dots: a plain note can’t be split evenly into three.
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Rhythm Notation from Du De: Note Values and Time Signatures
section: 4.3 Dots and ties: names for elongations
text:
4.3 Dots and ties: names for elongations
A note longer than a microbeat is an elongation. You already read them. The book has two ways to write them. Read 4.3

A dot adds half the note’s value. In 2/4, a dotted quarter + eighth is the pattern you chant du — de, held through the first microbeat of the next beat.
A tie joins two notes into one sound. Use it when the sound crosses a barline, or a beat the reader needs to see.
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Rhythm Notation from Du De: Note Values and Time Signatures
text:
4.5 Tuplets: usual combined
When a duple beat is split into three, you chant du da di inside usual duple: Gordon calls the mix usual combined (Gordon 175–176). The book writes it as a triplet, with a 3 over the notes. Read 4.5
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Rhythm Notation from Du De: Note Values and Time Signatures
section: 4.6 Writing rhythms the reader can audiate
text:
4.6 Writing rhythms the reader can audiate
The book’s list of common errors is mostly one rule: show the beat. Beam notes so each macrobeat’s microbeats are grouped together, and tie across the middle of the bar rather than hiding it inside one long note. If you can see where each du falls, you can chant it at sight. Read 4.6
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Rhythm Notation from Du De: Note Values and Time Signatures
text:
Bridging: from syllables to names

Chant first. Chant the pattern on du de or du da di, moving to the macrobeats.
Find du. Every du is a macrobeat. Say which note value it is: quarter in 2/4, 3/4 and 4/4; dotted quarter in 6/8.
Name the rest from du. A de is half of it, a ta a quarter of it. A note held through a du is an elongation: name it as a longer note, a dot or a tie.
Go the other way. Given “write four eighths and a half note in 2/4”, chant it first (du de du de | du), then write it.
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Rhythm Notation from Du De: Note Values and Time Signatures
text:
Check yourself

In 3/4, what note value is du?
In 6/8, you chant du da di. What are the three notes called?
In 2/4, you chant du ta de ta. Name the notes.
What does the book call usual combined meter’s triple division inside a duple beat?
Why does 6/8 need a dotted quarter for its beat?







TipAnswers






A quarter note.
Eighth notes.
Four sixteenth notes.
A triplet (a kind of tuplet).
Its beat divides in three eighths; only a dotted quarter lasts three eighths.




Practise reading and chanting with Rhythm Patterns. Related: Major Scales and Key Signatures.

title: Secondary Diminished Chords: Practice for Chapter 18
text:
This page goes with Chapter 18, Secondary Diminished Chords of Robert Hutchinson’s open textbook Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom. Read each section there first; the book is the reference for the terms used here. It follows Chapter 17, Secondary Dominants, and uses the seventh-chord qualities of Chapter 8.
Every drill has Settings, and is also on the Theory Drills page. ▶ Hear it plays the chord and then the chord it resolves to.
Typing a secondary diminished chord: vii°/V, vii°7/ii, viiø7/IV. Type o (or dim) for °, and h (or Ø) for ø. After the slash comes the chord being tonicized, and its case is its quality: ii is minor, IV is major. Inversions take the figures the book uses: vii°6/V and vii°64/V for triads, viiø65/V, vii°43/iv and vii°42/vi for seventh chords. vii°6/5/V and vii°7 of iv work too.
crumbs: Hutchinson, Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom

title: Secondary Diminished Chords: Practice for Chapter 18
text:
18.1 Secondary diminished chords
In Chapter 9, vii° is a dominant-function chord, like V: it leads to the tonic. So a leading-tone chord can be borrowed for any major or minor chord of the key, just as V was in Chapter 17. It sits a half step below the chord it tonicizes, and it can be a diminished triad, a half-diminished seventh (ø7) or a fully-diminished seventh (°7). It is written vii°/x, viiø7/x or vii°7/x. Its chromatic note is part of the chord, not a passing decoration. Read 18.1






NoteListen: the book’s examples








J. S. Bach, Cantata BWV 147, “Jesu, Joy of Man’s Desiring”






Tchaikovsky, The Nutcracker, “Trepak”

title: Secondary Diminished Chords: Practice for Chapter 18
text:

Which seventh chord? The book’s rule: a minor chord is tonicized by a fully-diminished seventh (vii°7/ii in C is C♯–E–G–B♭), and a major chord is usually tonicized by a half-diminished seventh (viiø7/V in C is F♯–A–C–E), though °7 is also found before major chords. That matches the key each target would be the tonic of: vii°7 belongs to harmonic minor, viiø7 to major. Read 18.2

title: Secondary Diminished Chords: Practice for Chapter 18
text:
18.3 Analysing secondary diminished chords
The book’s two steps for a chord with a chromatic note:

Stack it in thirds to find the root and the quality. If it isn’t a diminished triad, a half-diminished seventh or a fully-diminished seventh, it isn’t a secondary diminished chord.
Go up a minor 2nd from the root. If that note is the root of a major or minor chord in the key, the chord is vii of that chord.

The book’s example: in D major, a G♯ half-diminished seventh with B in the bass (first inversion). A minor 2nd above G♯ is A, the root of V, so the chord is viiø65/V. Read 18.3
The chord on the staff is followed by the chord it tonicizes. Name the first one:

title: Secondary Diminished Chords: Practice for Chapter 18
text:
18.4 Writing secondary diminished chords
The book’s procedure, worked here for vii°43/ii in E♭ major (the book’s own example is a different chord):

Find the root of the chord after the slash: ii in E♭ is F (F minor).
Go down a minor 2nd: E (E natural, not E♭).
Build the chord there. F minor is minor, so fully diminished: E–G–B♭–D♭.
Put it in the inversion asked for. 43 means the 5th is in the bass: B♭–D♭–E–G.

6.3 Inverted triads and slash chords
The root is the bottom note when the chord is stacked in thirds; the bass is whatever note is actually lowest. When the third is in the bass the triad is in first inversion, when the fifth is, second inversion. A lead-sheet symbol shows an inversion with a slash: the chord, then the bass note. C/E is a C major triad with E at the bottom. Read 6.3 · musictheory.net: Triad Inversion · Open Music Theory: Inversion

text:
6.4 Naming a chord spread over the staff
In real music a triad is spread out, with notes doubled, across both staves. To name it: find the root (stack the notes in thirds), then the quality (measure the two thirds), then the bass (is the lowest note the root?). Then write the symbol, with a slash if it is inverted. 6.5 Sus chords
In a sus4 chord a perfect 4th takes the place of the third; in a sus2 chord a major 2nd does. Both keep the perfect 5th. Without a third, a sus chord is neither major nor minor. The book does not invert sus chords, and neither does the drill. Read 6.5 · Open Music Theory: Chord Symbols, “sus”

title: Style Arranger
text: An arranger keyboard turns one chord in your left hand into a band. Each style has eight channels (two rhythm, bass, two chord, pad, two phrase), and each channel’s pattern is written once, over a C major seventh chord. When you hold a different chord, the keyboard moves every note of every pattern to fit it, using a rule set per channel. Press Start (or turn on Sync Start and play a chord), then change chords and sections as you go.

title: Style Arranger

title: Style Arranger
text:
Channels
Each channel can be switched off, given another sound, or have its rules changed. The rules are what decide where the notes go when the chord changes; open one to try them, and watch the score below change.

text:
Score
Each channel of the section, drawn from the stored pattern. As written is what the style’s author recorded over CM7; As it sounds is the same pattern moved to the chord you hold.

title: Style Arranger
section: How a style follows your chord
text:
How a style follows your chord
Written over CM7. Yamaha’s style recording rules ask for every Main and Fill In pattern to be recorded over CM7: the bass and phrase channels using only the notes of its scale (C D E G A B), the chord and pad channels only its chord tones (C E G B). Every pattern on this page follows that rule, and a test checks it.
Root: NTR. Root Trans moves the whole pattern by the distance between the roots, so a line keeps its shape: C3 E3 G3 over F becomes F3 A3 C4. High Key stops it climbing forever: roots above it move down instead of up. Root Fixed keeps notes near where they were written, so chords don’t jump around: C3 E3 G3 over F becomes C3 F3 A3.
Chord type: NTT. Melody moves each scale note to the matching note of the new chord’s scale (over a minor seventh, E becomes E♭ and B becomes B♭). Chord moves each chord tone to the matching tone of the new chord. Bypass changes nothing but the root; with Root Fixed it changes nothing at all, which is what the rhythm channels use. The minor tables (Melodic, Harmonic, Natural Minor, Dorian) only switch between major and minor, lowering the 3rd and some of the 6th and 7th.
Fingering. Fingered reads the chord from all its notes. Single Finger builds it from one to three keys: one key for major, the nearest black key to its left added for minor, the nearest white key for a seventh, both for a minor seventh. Multi Finger takes either. Fingered On Bass uses your lowest key as the bass note, so C/E is possible.
Sections. The Intro plays first and leads into a Main. A Main repeats until you press another section; with Auto Fill on, changing Main plays that Main’s Fill In to the end of the bar first. Break is a one-bar gap; Ending plays out and stops.
Unverified. The manuals give the rules but not the exact tables, so the scale chosen for each chord type (Dorian over minor sevenths, for instance), how Root Fixed picks its octave, the High Key default (F), and the exact moment fills and endings start are this site’s reading. The styles are this site’s own patterns, not Yamaha’s.

text:
Themes from the classical repertoire, one or two phrases each: the openings of symphonies, sonatas, operas,

title: Guitar and Bass Setup Check
text:
A guitar that's hard to play, buzzes, or won't play in tune up the neck usually needs an adjustment, not a new guitar. Work through the
checks below with the instrument in tune (tune it here) and in your playing position. Each answer
goes into the list at the bottom: what's wrong, what to change, and who should change it: you, your teacher, or a repair tech.
Answers are kept in this browser.

Before anyone turns anything: the truss rod is a steel rod inside the neck. A quarter turn at a time, never forced,
and wait for the neck to settle before judging. Bridge screws are safe to turn and easy to undo; nut slots and acoustic saddles are not
(material taken off doesn't come back). When in doubt, it's a tech's job: a setup costs about as much as a few sets of strings.


  The instrument
  What is it? 
  Clear answers
  



  1. Neck relief: is the neck bowed?
  A neck should bow very slightly forward under string tension, so the vibrating string clears the frets. Put a capo at the 1st fret.
  With your right hand (or arm), press the lowest string down at the fret where the neck meets the body (around fret 14–17). The string is now a
  straight edge. Look at the gap between the string and the top of the 7th or 8th fret, and tap the string there: a tiny click means a small gap.
  The gap
  
    not checked
    none: the string touches, no click
    barely: a faint click
    a sheet of paper's thickness, a clear click
    a business card fits
    more than a business card
  
  or feeler gauge, mm 
  



  2. Where does it buzz?
  Play every string at every fret in each zone, at the strength you normally play (not harder: everything buzzes if you dig in). Listen
  acoustically, not through an amp: tick each place where a note buzzes or dies early. This is your ear's job, and the most telling test on the page.
  
  Only at one fret, on several strings?
  



  3. String height (action)
  Measure from the top of the 12th fret to the bottom of the string, with a steel ruler that reads half millimetres (no capo, nothing pressed).
  Lowest string, mm 
  Highest string, mm 
  



  4. The nut
  Press a string at the 3rd fret, and look at (and tap) the string over the 1st fret. Then play an open chord, then the same notes fretted near
  the nut: if the fretted ones sound sharp to your ear, the nut is likely high.
  Gap at the 1st fret
  not checkednone: string touches the 1st fret
  tiny: you can just see it, a clickclearly visible, and first-fret notes sound sharp



  5. Intonation: does it play in tune up the neck?
  On each string, play the harmonic at the 12th fret (touch lightly right over the fret wire, pick, lift), then press the 12th
  fret and pick. They are the same note when the string length is right. Listen first: is the fretted note the same, higher, or lower? Then let the
  microphone measure it (🎤 buttons; let each note ring for two seconds). Retune the open string before each one.
  
  With old strings this test lies: they play sharp up the neck however the saddles are set. Fit new strings first if they're
  more than a few months old.



  6. Anything else?
  
     It won't stay in tune
     Fret ends feel sharp at the edge of the neck
     Dents worn into the frets under the strings
     The bridge is lifting at the back (acoustic)
     A crack anywhere
     The truss rod won't turn, or is already very tight
     Crackles or cuts out (electric)
  



  What to do

title: Tools
text:
Pick the group closest to what you're doing; each tool has a line on what it's for. Not sure where to start? The home page starts from the task.




  Play with a band
  
    Backing Track — type or paste chords, pick a style, and a full band plays them.
    Style Notes — what each groove does, swing to reggaeton, before you choose one.
    Accompaniment Styles — named comping rhythms, from the Charleston on, each described and played.
    Drumset — build a drum groove piece by piece and play it.
    Sequencers & Arpeggiators — every kind of step sequencer and arpeggiator on one clock.
    Style Arranger — an arranger keyboard: hold a chord and an eight-part band follows it through intro, four mains, fills, break and ending.
    Polyrhythm — two to four rhythms at once, as polyrhythm or polymeter, on a circle and a grid.
  



  Chords and harmony
  
    Chord Library — every shape, with the lessons that teach it.
    Chord Sheet — type chords and get diagrams for your instruments, with notation and playback.
    Chord Entry — play chords on a MIDI keyboard and get a chart for the band.
    Chords and Solfège — play notes and see the chord, its Roman numeral, and each note in solfège, degrees or Sargam.
    Circle of Fifths — keys, signatures and related chords on one wheel.
  



  Scales and reading
  
    Scales — any scale in any key, drawn and played.
    Scale Patterns — scale exercises written out for any key, style and instrument, Hanon included.
    Part Reader — what a transposing part's key and notes are in concert pitch.
    Classical Themes — 2,067 themes from the repertoire to read and hear.
  



  Write music down
  
    Notation — play or type a melody; add chords and words, then hear it.
    Notation Rules — how the entry pages decide what to write from the keys you play.
  



  Learn from a recording
  
    Timestamp Notes — stamp the sections, tap the bars, loop phrase by phrase.
    Tap Along — the same mapping on a phone while the song plays.
    Tap Latency — how late your taps land, so Tap Along can allow for it.
    Chunk Practice — break a fast passage into chunks and build it up to speed.
  



  Voice
  
    Vocal Warm-up — a routine built for your voice and your time.
    IPA Chart for Singers — the sounds of sung vowels and consonants.
  



  Guitar and bass
  
    Guitar Tuning — tune by ear six ways, any tuning, with the mic as a check.
    Setup Check — buzz, action, relief, intonation: what to adjust, and who should.
    Guitar Input Check — play a note or chord and the page says whether it heard what it asked for.

title: Polyrhythm
text: Player

title: Polyrhythm
text:
How to use it

Layers. Each layer is a number (that many even hits per cycle) or a pattern: x a hit, X an accent, . a rest. x.x.xx.x.x.x is the 12-pulse bell pattern; x..x..x...x.x... is son clave.
Beat. The tempo counts the hits of the layer marked beat. For a pattern it counts the pattern’s main beats (12 pulses are four beats of three; 16 pulses four beats of four).
Polymeter. Ticked, every step of every layer is the same length, so a 5-step riff against a 4-step bar drifts and lines up again only after 20 steps. Unticked, each layer is stretched over one cycle: a polyrhythm.
Mute. Click a layer’s name to mute it, then clap or play that layer yourself.

The lessons that use this player are in the Polyrhythm part of the Lessons sidebar, starting with What Is a Polyrhythm?.
